According to the mall, one of the screening rooms of the Kinoman cinema and the Zviropolis petting zoo were damaged. Shop windows of Duna, Tommy Hilfiger, Roshen and others were also damaged. The CAO cafe in Block B was almost completely destroyed and will have to be fully rebuilt. The Fifty Ice ice rink and the Ultramarket hypermarket were not hit.
Ultramarket (formerly MegaMarket) is a hypermarket chain owned by businessman Oleh Vyshniakov and currently has four hypermarkets.

Parliament's Security Information, Risk and Advisory Service handled 216 requests for assistance between Sept. 28 and Oct. 18, including 81 operational deployments, according to Radio New Zealand.
Parliamentary Service Chief Executive Rafael Gonzalez-Montero said the unit supported lawmakers attending public events, traveling and responding to protests and threatening behavior.
He said the service has expanded ahead of the election amid growing security concerns.
Brownlee said threats have increased sharply over the past three years, prompting what he called the "strongest protocol we've ever had with the New Zealand Police."
He attributed the rising hostility to economic pressures, public frustration and global instability, warning that social media amplified abusive behavior.
The warning followed an attack on Australian independent lawmaker Helen Haines, who was critically injured and lost a leg after being struck by a vehicle in Victoria.
Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese condemned the attack.
Brownlee warned that continued intimidation could isolate elected representatives from their communities.
"Democracy is a relatively fragile thing," he said.
New Zealand authorities have withheld details of specific threats for security reasons.

Luxury homeowner fined HK$255,800 after eighth prosecution over illegal renovations
Hong Kong’s Buildings Department says owner of house in Tuen Mun was prosecuted eight times for failing to comply with removal order over illegal structures
A luxury house owner in Hong Kong has been fined HK$255,800 (US$32,600) for persistently failing to comply with a statutory removal order even after being prosecuted seven times for illegal site works and unauthorised structures found at his property.
The Buildings Department said on Tuesday that the owner of a Beaulieu Peninsula detached house on Yu Chui Street in Tuen Mun was convicted and fined at Tuen Mun Court last Friday. It was the eighth time the owner faced prosecution for ignoring the removal order.
“Failing to comply with the removal order, the owner had been prosecuted by the Buildings Department seven times and was fined and sentenced to four months’ imprisonment, suspended for two years, upon convictions by the court,” a department spokesman said.
“As the owner persisted in not complying with the removal order, the owner was prosecuted for the eighth time.”

Rubio's Samarkand visit gives fresh momentum to U.S.-Central Asia ties
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
06:36:38 UTC
15:36:38 KST

Rubio's Samarkand visit gives fresh momentum to U.S.-Central Asia ties
U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio's visit to Samarkand produced a new C5+1 statement on regional cooperation, advancing priorities closely aligned with Kazakhstan's economic and diplomatic interests, Qazinform News Agency correspondent reports.
Rubio arrived in Samarkand on October 18, accompanied by a delegation representing more than 200 American businesses. His program included a C5+1 ministerial meeting with the foreign ministers of Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan and Uzbekistan, alongside separate bilateral talks. The visit followed the November 2025 summit hosted by President Donald Trump at the White House, where Kazakh President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev and his Central Asian counterparts discussed expanding economic and strategic cooperation with Washington. Speaking in Samarkand, Rubio said the United States and Central Asian countries had secured more than $25 billion in commercial arrangements since that summit, with plans to pursue over $100 billion in additional trade and investment.
Jeanette and I stood at the heart of Samarkand’s Registan Square, where the richness of Uzbekistan’s history, culture, and architecture is undeniable. At this historic crossroads where diplomacy, trade, and culture of the ancient Silk Road took place, it is fitting that the U.S. and Central Asia continue securing economic opportunities and strengthening diplomatic ties to transform the future.
— Secretary Marco Rubio (@SecRubio) October 19, 2026
Few places on Earth have historically played such an important role in global trade and commerce as Samarkand. It’s an honor to be here today — not just to remember the history, but the opportunities for the future. https://t.co/SymeQhOUag
— Secretary Marco Rubio (@SecRubio) October 19, 2026
A decade of regional diplomacy
Samarkand holds historical significance for the C5+1 format. The first ministerial meeting took place there on November 1, 2015, bringing together then-U.S. Secretary of State John Kerry and the five Central Asian foreign ministers. Kazakhstan played an early role in establishing the mechanism, with the proposal for regular dialogue between Washington and the five republics put forward in 2013 by Kazakhstan's then-ambassador to the United States, Kairat Umarov. Astana subsequently hosted a C5+1 ministerial meeting in 2023, reaffirming its commitment to the format. More than a decade after its establishment, the platform has evolved into an important channel for regional diplomacy, particularly as Central Asian governments seek to strengthen economic cooperation and diversify their international partnerships.
Washington's renewed engagement reflects growing recognition of Central Asia's strategic location and economic potential. Critical minerals, energy security, transport connectivity and technological cooperation have emerged as priorities for both sides. For the United States, the region offers opportunities to diversify supply chains and expand access to strategic resources, while Central Asian governments are seeking foreign investment, advanced technologies and access to international markets. Rubio also emphasized that Washington was not asking regional countries to abandon their existing partnerships with Russia, China or other powers. This approach is consistent with the multi-vector foreign policy pursued by Kazakhstan under President Tokayev, which emphasizes balanced international relations while advancing national economic interests.
Regional cooperation and economic opportunities
The principal multilateral outcome of the Samarkand meeting was the adoption of the joint statement "C5+1: Historic Partnership, Prosperous Future." The document outlines cooperation in transport, trade, investment, energy, critical minerals, security and cultural exchange. Particular attention is given to strengthening intraregional economic integration through expanded trade, harmonized customs procedures and industrial cooperation. The statement also supports greater opportunities for Central Asian businesses to operate in the United States. Although it does not establish specific financial commitments or implementation schedules, it provides a framework for expanding cooperation in areas where the region has substantial economic potential.
Among the priorities is the further development of the Trans-Caspian Trade Route, commonly known as the Middle Corridor, which connects Central Asia with European markets through the Caspian Sea, the South Caucasus and Türkiye. The corridor has attracted increasing international attention since 2022 as businesses seek alternative transportation routes between Asia and Europe. Kazakhstan occupies a central position along this network, with its railway infrastructure and Caspian ports at Aktau and Kuryk providing essential connections for east-west cargo flows. Greater American involvement in regional transport projects could support infrastructure modernization, increase transit capacity and strengthen Kazakhstan's role as a Eurasian logistics hub, an objective repeatedly emphasized by Tokayev.
Critical minerals represent another area where regional and national interests converge. The joint statement supports cooperation in geological data management, resource development, processing and higher value-added production. For Kazakhstan, the world's largest uranium producer and a country with substantial reserves of strategically important minerals, these priorities offer opportunities to expand industrial cooperation beyond raw material exports. Astana has increasingly emphasized attracting foreign technologies and developing domestic processing capacity, making the C5+1 agenda relevant to its broader economic diversification strategy. The ministers also reaffirmed cooperation on counterterrorism, organized crime, cybersecurity, nuclear security and the peaceful use of nuclear energy, reflecting the continued importance of security alongside economic diplomacy.
Kazakhstan builds on Washington agreements
For Kazakhstan, the Samarkand meeting provided an opportunity to advance the results of Tokayev's November 2025 visit to Washington. Foreign Minister Mukhtar Tileuberdi held bilateral talks with Rubio focused on implementing agreements reached by the two presidents and expanding cooperation in investment, energy, critical minerals, digitalization and transport. The Washington visit produced 29 commercial agreements worth approximately $17 billion, including projects involving John Deere, Wabtec and the development of tungsten deposits. These arrangements cover sectors important to Kazakhstan's industrial modernization and demonstrate how high-level diplomatic engagement has helped open opportunities for long-term economic cooperation.
Great meeting with each of the C5 foreign ministers. Together, we are creating commercial opportunities, strengthening economies, and increasing regional security. https://t.co/VDLTgP4WYp
— Secretary Marco Rubio (@SecRubio) October 19, 2026
The U.S. State Department also reaffirmed Washington's interest in cooperation with Kazakhstan on information and communications technology infrastructure, energy security and natural resources. Rubio thanked Astana for its support of President Trump's peace initiatives and welcomed Kazakhstan's accession to the Abraham Accords, while underscoring the importance of bilateral security cooperation and the C5+1 platform for regional stability. The talks highlighted a partnership extending beyond commercial interests to encompass regional diplomacy and international security. Kazakhstan's ability to maintain constructive relations with major powers while advancing its own economic priorities has been a defining feature of Tokayev's foreign policy, and the latest engagement with Washington offers another opportunity to build on that approach.
Importantly, Kazakhstan's bilateral achievements complement its participation in broader regional initiatives. The country's transport infrastructure, industrial capacity and experience in attracting foreign investment give it a substantial interest in the success of the C5+1 agenda. Expanded trade and industrial activity elsewhere in Central Asia could also increase demand for Kazakh logistics services and transport routes. Uzbekistan, for instance, announced more than 50 commercial agreements with American partners worth approximately $12 billion during Rubio's visit, covering technology, energy, transportation and industrial modernization. While these were bilateral arrangements, their implementation could contribute to wider regional economic activity, particularly where manufacturing and trade rely on shared transport corridors and cross-border supply chains.
I met with Uzbekistan President Mirziyoyev to express my sincere thanks to the government of Uzbekistan for hosting the C5+1 in beautiful and historic Samarkand. We discussed working together to promote economic opportunities and creating jobs in both our countries, and strengthening security cooperation, as well as working together through the C5+1 diplomatic platform. I was also deeply honored to be awarded the Order of Outstanding Merit by President Mirziyoyev.
— Secretary Marco Rubio (@SecRubio) October 19, 2026
The road ahead
Despite the diplomatic progress, several challenges remain. The Cold War-era Jackson-Vanik amendment continues to affect U.S. trade relations with countries including Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan, which have yet to obtain permanent normal trade relations status. Rubio has expressed support for repealing the restrictions, and bipartisan legislation has been introduced in Congress, although its adoption remains pending. Implementation of commercial agreements will be another important measure of progress. The figures announced in Washington and Samarkand represent contracts and planned transactions rather than investments already completed, while the C5+1 statement establishes shared objectives without binding financial commitments. For projects involving the Middle Corridor and mineral processing, progress will depend on financing, infrastructure development and sustained coordination among participating countries.
The next opportunity for high-level engagement will come at the G20 summit in Miami on December 14-15, which Tokayev is expected to attend as a guest of the U.S. presidency. According to Kazakhstan's Foreign Ministry, Rubio also expressed interest in making a full-fledged visit to Kazakhstan soon after the summit, although no date has been announced. Such a visit would allow both sides to assess progress on existing agreements and explore additional projects under their Enhanced Strategic Partnership. More broadly, the Samarkand meeting demonstrates Central Asia's growing importance in Washington's economic and diplomatic agenda. For Kazakhstan, which has consistently promoted regional cooperation while pursuing a multi-vector foreign policy, the renewed engagement creates additional opportunities to turn established diplomatic relationships into investment, industrial development and stronger international connectivity.
Earlier, Qazinform reported that Donald Trump invited President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev to join the G20 Summit in Miami.

Separatist leaders vow to fight on, warning the province’s governing party could split over the issue.
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney has welcomed Alberta’s decisive rejection of a move towards independence, saying the province had chosen national unity at a time of mounting pressure from Washington.
"On October 19, Albertans made a clear choice. They chose unity, to build together, and to take care of each other. Above all, Albertans chose Canada," Carney said in a statement on Tuesday.
With more than one million votes counted, 77 per cent backed remaining in Canada, according to unofficial results from Elections Alberta.
Monday’s vote was not a direct ballot on independence. A win for the separatists would instead have set the western province on a path towards a binding referendum on leaving Canada.
The result is a boost for Carney, who grew up in Alberta and had urged a decisive outcome as US President Donald Trump wages a trade war against Canada and threatens to make it the 51st US state.
Alberta, a conservative stronghold with the world’s fourth-largest proven oil reserves, has long resented the federal government in Ottawa, largely over the management of its oil industry. Premier Danielle Smith has accused Carney’s predecessor, Justin Trudeau, of trying to curb oil production to advance his climate agenda.
Separatist parties once won only 1 or 2 per cent of the vote, but anger over COVID-19 restrictions helped energise the movement.
Smith opposes independence but called the referendum under pressure from separatists within her United Conservative Party.
"Albertans have voted for a stronger Alberta in a united Canada," she posted on social media.
The separatist campaign drew interest from Trump’s allies. US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent described Alberta as a natural partner for the United States, and billionaire Elon Musk posted on X that the province should separate. Separatist leaders also met officials at the US State Department.
Thomas Lukaszuk, a former deputy premier who led the Forever Canadian campaign against separation, told supporters: "We are a solid country that’s united from coast to coast to coast."
Separatists insist their cause is not finished. Jeffrey Rath, a leader of the Alberta Prosperity Project, said the push for independence would continue.
"We’ve learned a lot of lessons from this fight," he said.

South Korea to deploy military satellites using homegrown Nuri rocket
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
06:36:27 UTC
15:36:27 KST

South Korea to deploy military satellites using homegrown Nuri rocket
KASA Administrator Oh Tae-seok announced the plan during a Cabinet meeting following the successful fifth launch of the Nuri rocket earlier this month. The mission placed five Earth observation microsatellites into orbit.
Under the agency’s plan, South Korea intends to conduct at least one Nuri launch annually through 2032.
The rocket’s 11th launch, scheduled for 2031, will carry four electro-optical (EO) reconnaissance microsatellites. South Korea has previously relied on foreign launch vehicles to deploy its military satellites.
The 12th Nuri launch, planned for 2032, will carry three companion satellites designed to operate alongside the Arirang 8 multipurpose satellite. Arirang 8 will be equipped with synthetic aperture radar (SAR), enabling it to capture images regardless of weather conditions or daylight.
KASA also outlined plans to expand the country’s Earth observation capabilities in the coming years. The agency aims to launch five additional Earth observation microsatellites in the second half of 2027, followed by the fifth next-generation medium-sized satellite in 2028.

“Leave, or end up behind bars”: The FSB has revived the Soviet practice of forcing dissidents abroad
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
06:35:22 UTC
15:35:22 KST

The Russian authorities have increasingly begun using repressive tactics to force dissidents out of the country. Security officers may say so outright during detentions, or it may be inferred from the conduct of investigators who, after opening a criminal case, do not immediately arrest a suspect, leaving them an opportunity to flee. Numerous examples suggest that pressuring people to leave is a deliberate policy. Rita Flores, a former member of Pussy Riot who collaborated with the FSB for three years, said she had acted at the security service's behest when working to persuaded other artists to leave Russia. Forcing “enemies of the regime” abroad is nothing new — the FSB has essentially revived a favorite practice of the Soviet-era KGB.
In August 2026, former Pussy Riot member Rita Flores revealed that in 2023 she had been pressured into working as an undercover informant for the FSB. Flores said she gathered information on artists and activists — including their individual plans, connections, habits, and activities. Those she was assigned to target included street artist Philippenzo and performance artist Pavel Krisevich.
Both later left Russia under pressure from the security services, and Flores admitted that she had helped push them out at the FSB’s request. Her handler viewed emigration as one of two ways to resolve the “problem”: either they leave the country or they would go to prison. The demand to leave can be made explicitly or conveyed through hints, as can be observed in the cases of sociologist Boris Kagarlitsky and of politician Boris Nadezhdin.
“You and your loved ones will be the ones crying”: The final warning to Pavel Krisevich
Artist Pavel Krisevich was released from a penal colony in January 2025 after serving three and a half years for a protest performance in Red Square. According to Rita Flores, when Krisevich resumed staging performances, her FSB handler made it clear that he would have to stop or face prison again. She began pressuring Krisevich to leave Russia.
During this period, he was placed under administrative arrest several times, and his home was searched. Then in late 2025, during his last arrest, Krisevich was taken from his cell to a dark room where two FSB officers were waiting. They made him face the wall and threatened him: “We warned you; you and your loved ones will be the ones crying. Pack your things and leave, or we’ll lock you up.”
The performance that had led to his latest arrest was provocative: dressed as a cowboy, Krisevich climbed onto a monument to a Soviet S-75 surface-to-air missile in Istra, outside Moscow, recreating a scene from Stanley Kubrick’s Dr. Strangelove in which Major Kong rides an atomic bomb toward its target.
Krisevich later explained that the performance was about the fact of society growing accustomed to war, weapons, and talk of the possible use of nuclear weapons. He had originally intended to keep the photo shoot under wraps and publish the pictures only after leaving Russia or in a free Russia. He understood that another public performance could expose him to criminal prosecution. However, he was detained almost as soon as filming began.
Krisevich had shared his plans for the performance with Rita Flores, but it remains unclear whether the FSB learned about it from her or from another source. “At some point, my handler Ivan said that either he stops, or we arrest him during the performance,” Flores said in an interview.
At some point, my handler Ivan said, “Either he stops, or we nab him at the next performance”
After two consecutive administrative arrests and a direct ultimatum from FSB officers, Krisevich decided to leave Russia. Released in late December, he discussed the situation with his wife and soon left the country.
Later, commenting on Rita Flores’s interview, Krisevich stressed that he had left not because of her attempts to influence him, but because of a direct warning from FSB officers: “It was the FSB officers who persuaded me to leave. They came to see me at the special detention center and told me outright: either I leave or they put me in prison.”
“We’ll put him in prison, or you get him out”: How Philippenzo was forced out of Russia
On June 12, 2023, a huge graffiti mural appeared beneath the Elektrozavodsky Bridge in Moscow bearing the word “Izrossilovanie” — a portmantaeau word combinging "Russia" and "rape" — along with Russia’s coat of arms. It was an anti-war work by artist Philippenzo, whose real name is Filipp Kozlov. At the time, he wrote that “there is no other word” to describe what was happening in the country.
Philippenzo had already come under scrutiny from the security services several times. In 2022, he was fined three times under the law on “discrediting” the army, including over his “Zinc Is Ours” graffiti depicting coffins — this one a play on the 2014 slogan "Crimea is ours" and the material that Russian military coffins are made of.
After the graffiti appeared, police came to Philippenzo’s home, and he temporarily left Russia. Then on July 29, Philippenzo returned from Georgia and was detained at Domodedovo Airport. He was initially sentenced to 15 days in detention for disobeying police orders. Shortly before his term expired, he was given another 15 days on the same charge before being released on August 26.
A few days later, Philippenzo noticed he was being followed. He later recounted that Rita Flores had hinted that he was under surveillance. “A criminal case had already been opened against me, so they tailed me for four days before coming to search my home,” the artist said.
On August 31, police searched Kozlov’s home and studio. It also emerged that he was facing a criminal case on charges of vandalism motivated by political hatred over the “Izrossilovanie” graffiti.
Only three years later did it emerge that the FSB had explicitly considered forcing Philippenzo to leave Russia as an alternative to imprisoning him. “We’ll put him in prison for this [the ‘Izrossilovanie’ piece] — lock him up good and proper. Or, if you can, get him out of the country as soon as possible,” Flores recalled her handler saying.
She said she then began pressuring the artist to leave, even deliberately picking a fight with him. Philippenzo later confirmed to the independent outlet Agentstvo that Flores had warned him he was under surveillance and, after the searches, urged him to leave Russia immediately.
By October of 2023, it had become publicly known that Philippenzo was in Lithuania. That same month, Russia’s Interior Ministry put him on its wanted list.
“I was simply forced out of the country”: Surveillance and arrests as a means of forcing people to leave
In August of 2023, St. Petersburg street artist BFMTH was sentenced to 15 days of administrative detention. Three hours before his release, an unidentified man in plain clothes and a medical mask approached him at the detention center.
“Listen, buddy, if you don’t leave after you get out, you’re f**ked,” the artist recalled being told. He suspected the man was an officer from Center E, the FSB's anti-extremism unit.
Listen, buddy, if you don’t leave after you get out, you’re f**ked.
By then, BFMTH was already known for his political street art — including a portrait of Vladimir Putin behind bars, a poster reading “The country is big, there’s enough z-land for everyone,” and other anti-war and anti-government works. In the summer of 2023, he embarked on a tour of Russian cities, planning to create new works in Moscow, St. Petersburg, the Moscow region, Samara, and Rostov-on-Don. In St. Petersburg, his performance was titled “The Thousand-Year Russian World,” while in Moscow it was called “Your Adults Are F**king Monsters.”
In Moscow, BFMTH was detained two days after arriving and was sentenced to 15 days in detention, ostensibly for disobeying police orders. He believed the arrest was targeted: police were waiting for him outside the house where he was staying. One officer later hinted that he knew about the artist’s latest work in Moscow.
After his release, BFMTH initially had no plans to leave Russia. He went to the town Murom, hoping to lie low there for a while, but the very next day a car appeared outside his rented apartment, and several people began conspicuously following him around. They “weren’t exactly trying to hide,” he said. The same car followed him to the bus station, and one of the people tailing him later turned up at the railway station as well.
The pressure continued. Before his train to Kazan, police officers approached BFMTH and said they needed to search him for drugs. The search was conducted in the presence of witnesses, but no drugs were found, and he was released. When the artist arrived in the Tatarstan capital, police were already waiting for him on the platform. One officer told him, “I hope you leave the city very soon.” He then ordered BFMTH to buy tickets by 9 a.m., warning, “Otherwise, we’ll have a different kind of conversation.”
The artist bought a ticket to Yerevan, but even during a transfer in Sochi, he was detained again and questioned about why his name appeared in police databases.
Until then, BFMTH had been determined not to emigrate, intending to continue making street art in Russia. However, after several days of threats, surveillance, and detentions, he changed his mind. “Now it’s simply dangerous for me to visit any Russian city — I’ll be detained as soon as I arrive. I was simply forced out of the country,” he said from Yerevan.
It’s simply dangerous for me to visit any Russian city – I’ll be detained as soon as I arrive. I was simply forced out of the country
In all three cases, the security services were less interested in imprisoning the artists than in putting a stop to their activities inside Russia. Krisevich’s performance, Philippenzo’s graffiti, and BFMTH’s posters attract attention precisely because they appear in Moscow, St. Petersburg, or other places where the authorities seek to control both public spaces and political expression. In exile, an artist can continue working, but stripped of the original context, their work no longer has the same political impact.
It is also clear why the FSB prefers to let artists go abroad rather than locking them up at home: imprisoning an artist can draw even greater attention to their work inside Russia and trigger an international campaign on their behalf.
Signals to politicians and public figures
The same approach has been applied to politicians and prominent intellectuals.
In the summer of 2026, Boris Nadezhdin, who rose to prominence after attempting to run in the 2024 presidential election, was preparing to take part in the State Duma election campaign. In July, he was designated a “foreign agent,” subjected to administrative penalties, barred from leaving the country, and then summoned to the Investigative Committee.
Nadezhdin himself linked the pressure to his plans to participate in the Duma campaign. Yet on July 21, the day he received the summons, the travel ban unexpectedly disappeared from the Gosuslugi government services portal. The very next day, he was able to fly to Astana.
For the authorities, this was a far more convenient outcome. Nadezhdin had campaign experience and name recognition from the presidential race, making him a potential asset to independent candidates running for the State Duma even if he withdrew his own candidacy. At the same time, imprisoning someone who had recently sought the presidency would inevitably have generated unwanted political fallout.
Another telling example is the case of sociologist Boris Kagarlitsky. In July 2023, he was arrested on charges of “justifying terrorism.” But on Dec. 12 of that year, the court unexpectedly imposed only a 600,000-ruble ($7,250) fine and ordered his release from custody.
The prosecution appealed the verdict, demanding a prison sentence. Kagarlitsky had two months to leave the country but chose to remain in Russia. On Feb. 13, 2024, the fine was replaced with a five-year prison sentence.
This sequence of events communicated the FSB's clear message: leave, or go to prison. The authorities evidently preferred Kagarlitsky to emigrate; otherwise, they would not have released him and left him two months to flee the country.
In fact, Kagarlitsky's imprisonment brought precisely the consequences the authorities wanted to avoid. An international solidarity campaign formed around the prominent left-wing figure, with British socialist politician Jeremy Corbyn, French presidential candidate Jean-Luc Mélenchon, Greek left-wing party leader Yanis Varoufakis, Amnesty International, and dozens of other politicians and intellectuals from countries as far-flug as Brazil calling for his release.
How dissidents were forced out of the USSR
Forcing prominent opponents of the regime to leave the country is nothing new. For years, the KGB used similar tactics against dissidents and “anti-Soviet” writers. In the most prominent cases, the choice between exile and imprisonment was even discussed at the level of the Politburo.
By early 1974, Alexander Solzhenitsyn was already one of the best-known Soviet writers in the West. He had received the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1970 but had not traveled to Stockholm for the award ceremony, fearing the authorities would refuse to let him return to the USSR. By January 1974, his magnum opus The Gulag Archipelago was being published abroad. The Soviet leadership regarded the book as a direct political challenge.
On Jan. 7, 1974, Solzhenitsyn’s fate was discussed at a Politburo meeting. General Secretary Leonid Brezhnev took a pragmatic approach from the outset: Soviet law allowed Solzhenitsyn to be imprisoned, he said, but the leadership needed to consider “whether it would be to our advantage” and how “Western propaganda” might exploit a trial. KGB Chairman Yuri Andropov proposed an alternative: “I believe Solzhenitsyn should be expelled from the country against his will.”
Nikolai Podgorny, chairman of the Presidium of the Supreme Soviet, framed the choice bluntly: “Let’s see what would be more advantageous for us, a trial or expulsion.” Podgorny favored a trial, fearing that Solzhenitsyn would continue to damage the USSR from abroad. Foreign Minister Andrei Gromyko, meanwhile, warned that forced expulsion could also provoke an international campaign against Moscow. KGB head Andropov argued that delaying a decision would be even worse and therefore proposed preparing for Solzhenitsyn’s expulsion while simultaneously opening a criminal case (though Andropov, too, considered expulsion preferable to imprisonment).
Andropov proposed preparing for Solzhenitsyn’s expulsion while simultaneously opening a criminal case, but considered expulsion the preferable option
The Politburo formally opted for criminal prosecution that January, but Andropov continued to press for Solzhenitsyn’s expulsion. Then, on Feb. 7, the KGB submitted a separate proposal to Brezhnev to send the writer to West Germany.
The plan was carried out just days later. Solzhenitsyn was arrested on Feb. 12, stripped of his Soviet citizenship the following day, and forcibly deported to West Germany. He returned to Russia only in 1994.
In 1972, the authorities used a similar tactic to force poet Joseph Brodsky out of the USSR. By then, he had already endured a show trial over his “social parasitism,” along with forced psychiatric treatment and internal exile in the Arkhangelsk region. After returning to Leningrad, he continued to face persecution and restrictions on publishing his work.
On May 10, 1972, Brodsky was summoned to the Office of Visas and Registration (OVIR). Until then, he had had no intention of leaving the country. At OVIR, an official whom Brodsky described as “a colonel, at least” told him:
“All right, Brodsky. We want you to submit all your [emigration] papers within three days. If you submit them by Friday, we’ll give you an answer quickly. After that, we’ll be entering a busy period. Vacations and so on.”
Brodsky accepted the offer but described his departure as involuntary, interpreting the reference to a “busy period” — later recalled as “hot days” — as a direct threat.
Solzhenitsyn and Brodsky were not exceptions. In the 1970s and 1980s, dozens of dissidents, writers, and artists were forced out of the USSR in a similar way.
In 1980, for example, writer and dissident Lev Kopelev obtained permission to travel to West Germany for research after being expelled from the Writers’ Union, barred from working in his profession, and summoned to the Lubyanka. Two months after his departure, Kopelev and his wife were stripped of their Soviet citizenship, effectively preventing them from returning. Kopelev later said, “I am not an emigrant. I did not want to leave.”
The Russian authorities have evidently revived this tactic, seeking to remove prominent figures from the country’s public and political life in ways that carry the least political cost. Imprisoning a well-known artist, intellectual, or politician can trigger public outcry, a solidarity campaign, and an international backlash. Once they leave Russia, however, they are likely to lose their influence inside the country.
The same approach does not apply to people unknown to the wider public. In their cases, the security services impose prison sentences without hesitation, knowing such repressive acts are unlikely to provoke significant public backlash.

The referendum asked voters: "Should Alberta remain a province of Canada, or should the Government of Alberta commence the legal process required under the Canadian Constitution to hold a binding provincial referendum on whether or not Alberta should separate from Canada?"

Gatherings have also been prohibited in several other parts of the city. Partial curfews—which restrict the gathering of young people in various ways—have been declared in several cities, including Marseille, Bordeaux, Nice, and Lyon.
French Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez acknowledged that, in some cities, the police lost control of the situation. He has faced sharp criticism from opposition politicians for a lack of preparedness regarding the unrest; however, French President Emmanuel Macron rejected his offer to resign.
The protests began in September, when students demanded improvements to conditions in educational institutions; since then, however, the movement has intensified and now encompasses a much broader range of issues. Various trade unions and other protest groups have also joined several of the demonstrations. Officials have reported that more than 2,500 people have been arrested. One protester lost an arm after police used a crowd-control grenade. Approximately 1,000 police officers have been injured.
Following a crisis management meeting on the 19th of October, French Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu stated that 
local government leaders have been authorized to impose curfews if necessary.
 He did not rule out the possibility of declaring a state of emergency nationwide, adding that the government would allocate funds to address the damage—costs that would subsequently be recovered from those who instigated the violence. Lecornu indicated that legislation would be employed to ensure that those responsible for the destruction are held financially liable. The Prime Minister also announced financial assistance for individuals currently unable to continue working due to the unrest.
Meanwhile, Nuñez reported that 200 investigators are reviewing surveillance camera footage in an effort to identify the ringleaders of the unrest. On the 18th of October, the Minister of the Interior sought to resign, but Macron refused to accept the resignation, emphasizing the need for continued leadership within the authorities. 
Alain Di Crescenzo, head of the French Chamber of Commerce and Industry, stated that the unrest has directly affected more than 2,000 shops and other businesses, with the damage estimated in the hundreds of millions of euros. Two French government ministers indicated that stolen goods have been found on various online marketplaces. A representative for the platform Vinted stated that the sale of stolen items is strictly prohibited; since the weekend, the platform’s staff have been working to identify and remove listings for items linked to the looting of businesses.

She was harassed for crude remarks about Modi at a Cockroach protest. Now she can’t leave home
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
06:30:18 UTC
15:30:18 KST

Before 24 July, a person I will call R was preoccupied with the ordinary routines of teenage life: experimenting with makeup, grumbling over mathematics homework and hanging out with friends at a tea stall.
That month, as the fever of student protests spread across the country, the 15-year-old watched on her phone as young people poured into Jantar Mantar, the designated protest site in Delhi, demanding education reform. She went too. But an 11-second video clip from the protest site, in which she made crude and profane remarks about the prime minister, Narendra Modi, upended her life.
“I feel like a criminal, as if I murdered someone,” R said in her first interview about life since the backlash. “I didn’t get a chance to make amends. In my own country, I am being treated like an enemy.”
It’s been 86 days since that protest, but R doesn’t leave home over safety concerns, trapped in the reality the ordeal created.
The summer agitation had for weeks demanded the ousting of the then-education minister, Dharmendra Pradhan, over repeated examination paper leaks. But after a violent police crackdown on a student march the anger spilled over to the Modi government.
I went to Jantar Mantar every night that week as people from all walks of life streamed in. Protest signs once directed largely against Pradhan now increasingly targeted Modi and his powerful deputy, Amit Shah, whose ministry controls Delhi Police.
The language was often profane and sexualised, and was quickly seized on by government supporters to condemn the protesters. Pro-government media channels ran heated debates about the disrespectful language and questioned the motives of those gathered. Women were singled out; BJP supporters identified them from social media clips and doxed them.
R found herself at the centre of this storm. A police case was filed against her for insult intended to provoke a breach of the peace, and statements that could lead to public mischief and defamation. The complainant told Scroll, an independent news organisation, that she had called R and asked her to publicly apologise.
After Pradhan resigned, Modi posted on Instagram about the use of vulgar abuses against him by “some mischievous children”, saying: “It is a cultural shock. How can our daughters speak like this?” Modi added that the children must be forgiven, instead of being punished.
Meanwhile, R issued an apology to Modi. In a grainy video filmed in low light, R stands against a dull white wall wearing a striped T-shirt, her hands folded in a namaste. “I am so ashamed of saying those things that I am not even able to raise my eyes. I apologise to the whole nation for it. This is my first and last mistake,” she said. (Local media reported that the complainant withdrew the police case after R’s video was posted.)
“I cried after making that video,” she told me. “I was feeling so helpless.”
But her apology did little to stem the abuse. She received rape and death threats, abusive phone calls, incessant warnings on text, knocks on doors and cars outside her apartment building in a Delhi suburb.
“I couldn’t understand what was happening,” R said, her eyes misting up as she recalled the initial days after the incident. “People older than my mother were calling me randi (prostitute), aatankwadi (terrorist), deshdrohi (enemy of the state). Others were offering Rs11,000 to find me and Rs21,000 to beat me.”
With her phone and address leaked, R and her mother were compelled to leave their home. They struggled to find landlords willing to rent them a place to stay. They found one apartment, then another and then another. Her mother, a single parent, lost the income she earned from tutoring. To pay for the repeated moves, she sold her gold jewellery. That money is keeping them afloat. She estimates it will probably last another four months. As the clock runs out, her mother is desperately searching for work.
During this time, R has not been to school and can no longer imagine returning. Some friends have cut off contact, leaving her increasingly isolated.
Despite her apology video, pro-government media continued to hound her, she said. In late August, frustrated and angry at yet another media crew showing up, she uploaded a video to social media laying bare what she was going through.
“Modiji, my life has become hell,” R said addressing the prime minister. “Now I can’t go anywhere, neither do I have any freedom. I can’t live anywhere. I have to live hiding my face,” she said.
R told me she wants people to understand how traumatising her experience has been. “To make someone homeless overnight is a big deal,” she said.
Now, stuck indoors, she is watching another wave of protests unfold. This time it’s over the controversial electoral rolls revision that has removed 130 million voters from the register. (If you missed it, read last week’s newsletter about this issue.)
R feels solidarity with the students getting brutalised and detained. There have been moments she has felt tempted to join them. But the thought of her mother and their uncertain housing situation have held her back.
“I am not scared any more. I have gone through the worst already,” she said. But she doesn’t want to put her mother through more pain.
Days before the protest, R had been planning her 15th birthday. She wanted to cut her birthday cake inside an autorickshaw, to remake a trend she had seen on social media.
It’s been a couple of months since she turned 15. I asked her what she wants or hopes for now. She paused and then said: “My past is not in my hands. I can’t change that. Now, I just want to look ahead and do well in my board exams.”
What else we’re reading about
Culture | Two Indian films won awards at the Busan international film festival. Birds in the Dark by Shashank Walia was awarded the Songwon Vision audience prize and Sailesh Rathnakumar’s Selvi won the HyLife Vision as well as the Taipei Film Commission award.
Politics | The US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, will land in Mumbai on 20 October for his second visit to India this year. Rubio will meet foreign minister S Jaishankar and then travel to Jamnagar, home to Reliance Industries’ massive refinery.
Imran Khan | Days after the Bollywood actor Imran Khan appeared at a Mumbai protest against the chief election commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar, authorities asked him to leave the country by 28 October over what they described as a violation of the Foreigners Act. The action followed a complaint by BJP leader Kirit Somaiya against Khan, who is a US citizen.
Guest shelf
A recommendation from someone with great taste
With the chief justice of India criticising citizen journalist covering the recent protests, veteran television reporter Ravish Kumar, who now hosts a YouTube show, recommends a relevant book.
“I had just finished reading Vineet Kumar’s book Media Ka Loktantra (Democracy of Media) when the chief justice’s statement came out, saying that if every citizen becomes a journalist, it will create problems for all of us. Published in 2024, Vineet’s book discusses the idea of do-it-yourself journalism. He shows how, when mainstream journalism began silencing the voices of ordinary people, they picked up cameras themselves and started practising journalism. They are becoming journalists to also assert their citizenship and rights guaranteed to them by the constitution. The mainstream media has a problem with journalism emerging on social media platforms because stories that it refuses to report – such as those concerning the electoral rolls – are being covered by others. The conflict between the media and DIY journalism has only now reached the courts. But it began a long time ago.”
Count it
A number worth knowing
84
Close to 45% of thermal power plants in India – as many as 84 out of 191 – were critically low on coal stocks (£) as of early October. At the same time, the country’s demand for power grew by 10% this year, the highest year-on-year increase in the past 10 years.
Vibe check
Artist Sagarika Sundaram has spent a decade working with wool, transforming it into felt for expansive sculptural pieces that feel almost otherworldly. Her latest exhibition, Reservoir recently opened at the Henry Moore Institute, in Leeds, and runs until 10 January.
“There’s a clearer commitment to sculpture in this body of work, even though I’m still working with felt. I’m thinking spatially and making large volumes that explore what cloth can do: bend, collapse, gather, turn inward and support or surrender to its own weight,” she said of her latest works. Among them is Blue Mountain, which stretches almost seven metres long, creating a cave-like space that viewers can move through. That’s what I find compelling in the way her works are presented: they are not static objects offering a single perspective.
The New York-based artist finds it exciting to give up a degree of agency during the making process, allowing the material to determine, in part, how the final form will unfurl. “Wool is a wonderfully responsive material. It can be soft and pliable but also dense, strong and structural. Wool takes dye exceptionally well and I can be quite expressive with colour and mark-making,” she said.

Euro-area inflation climbed to 3.8% in September, up from 3.2% in August, according to Eurostat’s flash estimate. Energy prices rose 18.8% year on year, with Lithuania (6.1%), Bulgaria (5.6%) and Spain (5%) recording the highest rates.

But the EU does not set prices, rents or tuition fees. National governments largely control those levers, and pressure to deliver keeps rising. Can the EU help citizens deal with inflation?

If Tedesco aims up, it could leave Walters with a major selection call to make at the pointy end of the tournament.
"Those big moments; he hadn't played in six, seven weeks but he turned up in big moments and nailed them," Tedesco, the oldest member of the squad at 33, said of Walsh.

"Walshy does things on the field so it's about knowing my game and being an experienced leader.
"Walshy, he was soaking up anything I had to say last week and I enjoy that role."

Dozens of Chabad students detained at Ben Gurion Airport as suspected draft dodgers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
06:27:58 UTC
15:27:58 KST

More than 40 ultra-Orthodox Chabad students were detained at Ben Gurion Airport on Tuesday morning after returning to Israel from a year of religious studies in the United States, when authorities identified them as suspected military draft dodgers. Some had their passports confiscated and were informed that they were suspected of failing to report for mandatory military service.
The students had spent the past year studying at the Chabad-Lubavitch movement's international headquarters, known as 770, in Brooklyn, New York. Upon landing in Israel, they were stopped by authorities over their military service status. Initially, they believed they would be released because military police lacked the capacity to arrest such a large number of suspected draft evaders simultaneously. However, they were eventually told they would be detained for disciplinary proceedings.
The incident came as Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu publicly criticized the arrest of ultra-Orthodox draft evaders. In an interview Tuesday with the Haredi Kol Barama radio station, Netanyahu described the arrests as "unacceptable," arguing that they were undermining efforts to reach an agreement on military conscription within the ultra-Orthodox community.
"We must preserve the world of Torah study because it has preserved us," Netanyahu said. "These arrests are a deliberate attempt to undermine the process of recruiting Haredim without coercion." He nevertheless stressed that not every ultra-Orthodox man should be exempt from military service. "I have great respect for the world of Torah study, but anyone who isn't studying should enlist," he said.
Netanyahu also did not rule out a demand by ultra-Orthodox parties to pass legislation exempting yeshiva students from military service before the next government is sworn in. "I wish we could do that," he said. "Can we do it before the government is formed? Who knows? It depends on goodwill, understanding and cooperation. I know that many in the Haredi community understand that there needs to be a new sharing of the burden."
Addressing the sharp criticism directed at him by senior ultra-Orthodox rabbis over the failure to pass a conscription law, Netanyahu acknowledged their frustration. "I understand there has been a lot of frustration and pain," he said. "We were on the verge of passing a real conscription law, and we were missing just one vote." He argued that such legislation could be passed during the next parliamentary term and establish a lasting arrangement between ultra-Orthodox and secular Israelis, preserving Torah study while introducing a new distribution of military service obligations.
Asked whether he believed Torah study protected the Jewish people and the State of Israel, Netanyahu replied: "What do you mean? It preserved the Jewish people. What preserved us in exile and throughout all those generations? Torah study. We cannot throw away our heritage."
Former Prime Minister Naftali Bennett, chairman of the Beyahad party, sharply criticized Netanyahu's remarks, accusing him of preparing to grant sweeping military service exemptions to ultra-Orthodox men in exchange for political support.
"The Bibi-Deri deal has been exposed, and now it's official: draft evasion in exchange for power," Bennett said, referring to Netanyahu and Shas chairman Aryeh Deri. He claimed Netanyahu had promised to pass a draft exemption law before the formation of the next government, although the prime minister had stopped short of making an explicit commitment.
"Netanyahu is dismantling the IDF and the future of those who serve and the reservists," Bennett said. He accused the prime minister of seeking to give official approval to mass draft evasion by what he described as 120,000 healthy young ultra-Orthodox men.
The confrontation comes one week before Israel's October 27 election, with the future of military service exemptions for ultra-Orthodox men remaining a major point of contention between Netanyahu, his potential coalition partners and opposition leaders.

Unemployment climbs again as Finland's economic recovery fails to affect jobs market
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
09:25:40 EEST
15:25:40 KST

The recent signs that Finland's economy is making tentative steps towards recovery are yet to have any impact on the jobs market.
The latest Labour Force Survey, compiled on a monthly basis by Statistics Finland, makes for grim reading — with some 39,000 more people out of work last month compared to the same period last year.
Finland's unemployment rate in September was 10.5 percent, up from 10.1 percent in August, with nearly 300,000 people aged 15 to 74 looking for work.
In its report, Statistics Finland noted that the situation for unemployed men is particularly bleak, with about 59,000 fewer men in employment last month compared to September 2025. This means the unemployment rate for men stood at 10.9 percent, some 1.4 percentage points higher than one year ago.
Figures from the KEHA Centre, a state agency specialising in employment support, revealed that long-term unemployment is also on the increase. At the end of September, according to KEHA's data, there were about 143,000 people who had been continuously registered as unemployed job seekers for at least a year, a 9 percent increase from last year.
Although the Finnish economy is in the early stages of recovery, economists predict that it could take up to a year before any knock-on effect positively impacts the jobs market.
Uncertainty holding employers back, organisation says
According to Petri Malinen, Chief Economist of the Finnish Federation of Entrepreneurs (known in Finnish as Suomen Yrittäjät), ongoing geopolitical uncertainties are clouding Finnish firms' outlooks and leading them to postpone recruitment.
He further noted that companies as well as consumers have cautious confidence in the future prospects of the Finnish economy because the recovery is not yet visible in everyday lives.
"As long as economic growth doesn't seem to materialise concretely, consumers will remain cautious and consumption will recover slowly. In this situation, growth in demand for companies is modest, and they have no need to recruit," Malinen said.
Yle News reporter Hannah Anderson attended the recent Talent Boost Summit in Helsinki to hear what participants think about Finland's need to attract international talent against the backdrop of a tough jobs market.

Introduction: UK unemployment rate falls in pre-budget boost
Good morning, and welcome to our rolling coverage of business, the financial markets and the world economy.
The UK unemployment rate has fallen, in a pre-budget boost to chancellor John Healey, but the number of vacancies available for workers continues to shrink.
The latest data on the UK labour market, just released, shows that the UK unemployment rate fell to 4.7% in June to August, down from 4.9% a month ago.
That’s better than expected – City economists had forecast a rise to 5%.
In its final snapshot of Britain’s jobs market ahead of the budget in two week’s time, the Office for National Statistics reports that employment rose, by 102,000 jobs, to 34.577m in the last quarter.
The number of people unemployed fell by 47,000 in the quarter to 1.712m, and there was a small (16,000) drop in the number of people ‘economically inactive’, to 9.091m.
But worryingly, the number of vacancies has seen its largest fall since the start of the year, falling by 21,000 in the last quarter.
That pulled the number of vacancies down to 691,000 in July to September, down from over 1.2m in early 2022. This is the first time the total has been below 700,000 since February to April 2021.
The ONS says:
This is mainly from smaller firms, who continue to suggest that they may not be recruiting because of increased labour costs.
That’s a reference to the higher employer National Insurance Contributions (NICs) brought in by Healey’s predecessor, Rachel Reeves, and the rise in the minimum wage, which have made it costlier to hire staff.

Pay continued to rise faster in the public sector than in the private sector, today’s labour market report shows.

Lithuania seeks NATO talks on shooting down drones without visual confirmation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
06:25:00 UTC
15:25:00 KST

Lithuania is seeking consultations with NATO on changing procedures to allow military aircraft to shoot down objects violating the country’s airspace even when pilots cannot identify them visually, Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevičius said Monday.
“I requested that we start consultations with NATO. [...] That will probably be implemented within a month, so that we can review that algorithm,” Sinkevičius told LRT.
The prime minister said fighter pilots can detect objects on radar but may be unable to see them because of cloud cover or poor weather. Under current procedures, pilots cannot use force to shoot down an object if they cannot visually confirm its identity.
Sinkevičius said the rules could be revised to give countries greater discretion in responding to potential airspace violations, allowing Lithuania to decide to shoot down an object detected by radar even without visual confirmation.
The proposal follows an incident Sunday in which a drone entered Lithuanian airspace from Poland. NATO fighter jets were scrambled, but the pilots did not see the object and could not confirm that it was a drone, so they did not shoot it down.
Debris from an explosion was later found in the village of Juodžioniai, in the Pasvalys district of northern Lithuania.
Lithuanian officials said the drone was Ukrainian and carried explosives. Ukraine apologised for the incident, saying the drone may have been diverted by Russia.

====================================================================================================

The more that big companies axe staff, the closer we get to a recession
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
06:24:37 UTC
15:24:37 KST

analysis
Some of Australia's biggest companies are axing thousands of staff. It may come back to bite them
You won't find NAB employees exiting their offices in Sydney and Melbourne carrying cardboard boxes with small ferns sticking out the top.
There's been no major financial or economic shock, notwithstanding ongoing oil market turmoil.
Instead, NAB's cold and brutal axing of 2,500 staff, announced this week, is a calculated move to make one of Australia's biggest companies nimbler.
"Our ambition and strategy remain unchanged," NAB Group Chief Executive Andrew Irvine said.
"We will improve productivity, risk outcomes and execution to be a simpler and more efficient bank."
It's not alone.
Late last year ANZ flagged a reduction in "duplication and internal complexity" as part of its own organisational restructure and, as NAB said on Tuesday, that there would be limited impact on frontline, customer-facing roles.
If the Commonwealth Bank and Westpac follow suit, along with other large non-bank corporations letting staff go, we might have a major problem.
Economic head winds
Australia's big four banks are operating in a challenging economic environment and, they insist, need to adapt.
The root of their problems comes from Australia's astounding inability to generate reasonable levels of productivity growth.
Productivity (as measured by the ABS as GDP per hour worked) was -0.2 per cent in the 12 months to June.
This means the national economy can only grow so fast before generating inflation, because businesses struggle to absorb the costs of production and so need to pass those costs onto customers when they demand goods and services.
Add to this an oil price shock, and the Reserve Bank has been forced to hike interest rates four times this year to tame inflation.
The Commonwealth Bank's chief economist Luke Yeaman says, in a worst-case scenario, the RBA may need to hike interest rates on Melbourne Cup Day, and again early next year.
"If you look at these structural factors, we've got a historic AI boom coming through the system, driving up inflation, driving up costs," Mr Yeaman said.
"You've got still strong government spending; you've got low productivity, and rising neutral interest rates around the world.
"So you put all that together and actually inflation might be much more persistent and the RBA may have to continue hiking rates through this year and even into early next year."
Cost crunch
It means the big four banks are being financially squeezed.
Money is seeping out of the housing market, for example.
The total number of new loan commitments for dwellings, according to the ABS's June quarter lending indicators report, fell 5.4 per cent.
The number of new investor loan commitments for dwellings fell 8.6 per cent in the quarter.
The bank's net interest margins or, very loosely speaking, the margin between the interest rate they pay depositors and the rates they charge borrowers, is also coming under pressure as interest rates rise.
Meanwhile, their combined profit after tax was $15.2 billion, down by 2.1 per cent compared to the first half.
Enter the lure of outsourcing roles offshore and rolling out artificial intelligence (AI), and you have several vehicles at management's disposal to cut costs in the face of weakening revenue.
There were no specific references to any of this in the NAB's public statements today, though.
"We are particularly focused on reducing the size of corporate functions," Andrew Irvine said.
"There will be no material impact to customer-facing banking roles.
"We have also deliberately made deeper changes to senior management positions which will broaden leadership responsibilities across the bank," he said.
Nimbler? Yes. How will this be achieved? That's harder to say.
Loading
Biting the hand that feeds you
Section 181 of the Corporations Act 2001 requires directors to "exercise their powers and discharge their duties: in good faith in the best interests of the corporation; and for a proper purpose".
The final report of the Royal Commission into Misconduct in the Banking, Superannuation and Financial Services Industry was submitted by Commissioner Kenneth Hayne who noted, "self-interest will almost always trump duty".
This was a reference to chasing profits for a company ahead of the best interests of the client.
For banks, at the very top levels, it's a painfully simple maths problem: grow revenue and cut costs.
It boosts the banks' bottom lines, which grows shareholder value and, in turn, lines the pocket of executives.
But is that too short sighted?
Those who have been let go from ANZ Bank and those about to be let go from NAB are facing a deteriorating jobs market, and rising interest rates.
If CBA and Westpac follow suit, it could be a real problem for the economy.
Because it's not just the banks letting go of workers.
Mining giant BHP last week confirmed job cuts at its iron ore operations in Western Australia.
And Microsoft announced it would cut 4,800 jobs, or about 2.1 per cent of its global workforce, in July.
The Reserve Bank wants to reduce "aggregate demand" in the economy to help lower inflation.
Governor Michele Bullock said it might take an unemployment rate of 5 per cent to achieve that.
You can see now, though, why Bullock could "possibly" see a recession in sight, given how many companies may choose to become "more agile" as times get tougher.
The negative feedback loop in the economy is plain to see: more job losses feed more job losses.
What is less clear is how much further interest rates can rise before that feedback loop is turbo-charged — though some in finance have a view on it.
ABC business editor Michael Janda asked panellists at the Citi Investment Conference in Sydney today how much further the RBA could raise interest rates before bigger cracks appeared in the mortgage market, with rising arrears and forced sales.
"I don't think it's a lot more," said James Boyle, the chief executive of major non-bank lender Liberty Financial Group.
"There's an increase in hardship … borrowers are doing it tough with rates at the current levels."
He added: "The stress is there if you go looking for it."
David Bailey, chief executive of large mortgage broking group AFG, agreed, saying inflation and falling real wages had eroded many borrowers' financial buffers.
"The cost of living has increased at the same time … that causes real cracks to start to appear," he warned.
"An extra 25 [basis points] is really starting to push the envelope."
Former NAB chief economist Alan Oster said, all else being equal, Australia would hit an unemployment rate of 4.8 per cent by early next year.
If the RBA hikes interest rates again, he said, it will move higher to 5 per cent. He characterised that as a recession.
With gross federal government debt of roughly $1 trillion, business confidence in the doldrums and weak productivity, the economy is in a particular vulnerable position to handle a corporate Australia race to the bottom in cutting costs.

“She’s useless,” the outspoken CEO said of the Commission chief. “Ursula von der Leyen hides in the Berlaymont, doing nothing but giving speeches.” He also criticised European countries – notably Belgium and France – for high aviation taxes, saying European people will end up paying the price. Watch.
French fallout: As France continues to recover from a weekend of unprecedented violence that has shaken the country to its core, questions are now being raised about where the political responsibility lies – and how the episode could play into the consequential presidential elections happening in just six months’ time.
Macron isolated: My colleague Maïa de la Baume writes in this must-read analysis that the mounting social unrest could ultimately shape French President Emmanuel Macron’s legacy, as he prepares to step down in the spring.

US-Ukraine relations sour as Trump, Zelenskyy clash over talks, arms
Trump calls for Zelenskyy to be replaced as negotiator, while Ukraine’s president says arms shipments delayed.
United States President Donald Trump says someone other than Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy should negotiate on Kyiv’s behalf in talks to end Russia’s war.
“Zelenskyy is a man that should have had settled this war a long time ago. If he would’ve listened to me, he would have made a much better deal a long time ago,” Trump told reporters outside the White House on Monday. “Maybe it’s time for Zelenskyy to get somebody else to negotiate.”
The US president has been verbally swiping at his Ukrainian counterpart for several days as a rift between the leaders deepens.
On Sunday, Trump claimed on Truth Social that Zelenskyy does not want to end the war. Earlier this month, he called for him to be replaced as president, and labelled him a “warmonger” over Ukraine’s attacks on Russian oil refineries.
Trump has also defended sanctions waivers for Russia, saying in the same Truth Social post that he wants to keep Moscow at the negotiating table.
Zelenskyy said the decision “will hurt Ukraine” and strengthen Russian President Vladimir Putin’s war effort.
Trump also announced plans on October 9 for Russia to supply more than 300,000 metric tonnes of diesel to US and global markets to tackle fuel prices that have soared since the US and Israel launched a war on Iran in late February.
The decision has angered not only Kyiv, but also European partners and US officials, who say it rewards Moscow while it continues its four-and-a-half-year war on Ukraine.
Zelenskyy told US senators at a meeting on Monday that decisions taken by the Trump administration “are hard to explain between friends”.
He said arms shipments had been delayed and intelligence sharing restricted.
“We also know that … the Pentagon is delaying the delivery of missiles that our partners have already paid for through the PURL (Prioritised Ukraine Requirements List) programme,” he said.
To his knowledge, he added, one missile package was waiting for the signature of US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.
He also said several European countries were ready to transfer Patriot interceptor missiles from their own stockpiles but were awaiting US approval.
In remarks posted in a video on Telegram, Zelenskyy said that on three occasions in the past week, Ukraine had not received the advance warning of Russian attacks generally provided by its partners.
Last week, Zelenskyy suggested a disruption of Starlink services in Ukraine was “deliberate”. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio rejected the claim.
The sparring comes as Trump’s special envoy Steve Witkoff is set to travel to Norway this week for the next round of negotiations on ending the war in Ukraine, the Reuters news agency reported, citing three people familiar with the matter.
Two of the sources said they expected Zelenskyy to attend the meetings.
The Oslo discussions are expected to include Zelenskyy, Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store, representatives of the E4 – made up of the United Kingdom, France, Germany, and Poland – the European Union, and NATO.

Planning a Christmas getaway? Here’s where flights and hotels could cost less
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
06:22:47 UTC
15:22:47 KST

From the best days to fly to the destinations seeing price drops on hotels, this is where you should be headed for Christmas in 2026, according to a new KAYAK study.
Looking to get away this Christmas, but don’t want to spend an arm and a leg to do so?
Not to worry, because KAYAK has released its Christmas travel trends covering the cheapest destinations to fly to from France, Germany and the UK, plus where hotel prices are falling.
Based on flight and hotel searches made between 1 April and 1 September for travel between 19 December 2026 and 9 January 2027, compared to the same period last year, the results might surprise you.
Here’s what you need to know to save some serious cash.
The cheapest destinations to fly to this Christmas
The cheapest destinations to fly differ by country, with France seeing return flights to Milan from €126, to Brussels from €153, to Venice or Berlin from €161, and to London from €169.
As for Germany, Milan is also a winner, with an average return price of €116, as is Rome (from €169), Vienna (from €170), Paris (from €190) and London (from €192).
For Brits, the cheapest return flights can be found to Dublin (from £127 / €151), Barcelona (from £131 / €155), Milan (from £142 / €169) and Prague or Madrid (from £143 / €170).
Hotel destinations that are getting cheaper
Shockingly, Rovaniemi in Finnish Lapland, better known as the home of Santa Claus, has seen a 22% drop in accommodation prices compared to last year, with an average of €275 per night.
Other cities in Europe you can visit for less include Istanbul, with prices down 12% to an average of €76 per night, Paris (-5%, €140 average per night), Adeje in Spain (-8%, €235 average per night) and York in the UK (-8%, £96/€114 average per night).
Further afield, Thailand could be an option, with Koh Samui prices down 21% to an average of €115 per night and Bangkok prices down 20% to €76 per night. Tokyo prices are down 19%, to €110 per night, while Singapore prices are down 13%, to €164 per night.
Bucket list destination the Maldives is down 10%, to €916 per night, while classic Christmas city New York is down 11% to €273.
In the Caribbean, prices in Fort-de-France, the capital of Martinique, are down 10% to €123 per night.
When to travel and when to book
In general, the best time to book international flights is around 15-30 days ahead of your travels, according to Expedia data revealed earlier this year.
The same is true for Christmas flights from Germany, with decreases seen in December, while those in France will have to play flight price chicken and wait until the week before Christmas.
In the UK, flights should typically wait until six weeks before the big day.
As for when you should fly, for French and British travellers 23 December is the cheapest day, while for Germans, it’s 21 December, according to the KAYAK data.
If you’re staying at home for Christmas but want to delay the January blues, consider flying on New Year’s Eve, which is the cheapest day to fly out across all three countries.
As for booking hotels, France has a similar timeline compared to flights, with domestic accommodation rates around 18% lower than in October the week before Christmas. Internationally, though, rates are around 7% lower from late November to December.
In Germany, the two weeks before Christmas offer rates 9% lower compared to peaks in mid-November, while in the UK, waiting until the fortnight before 25 December can save you 16% internationally and 20% domestically.
The cheapest check-in date for France both domestically and abroad is 21 December, while those in Germany can check in on Christmas Day domestically for the best rates, or 21 December abroad.
Brits will want to check in on 22 December if staying in the UK, or 23 December if heading elsewhere.
Winter sun, without the hefty price tag
The cheapest destinations in general are closer to home, but if the long, winter nights have you down, you’ll need to look long-haul to get a good dose of Vitamin D.
For French travellers, flight prices to Casablanca and Rabat in Morocco are down 19%, as well as 12% to Agadir. Fares to Koh Samui are also down 17%, or you could head to Sri Lanka for 11% less compared to 2025.
Germans can get to Lima in Peru for 29% less than last year, to Cairo for 18% less, and to Port Louis in Mauritius for 14% less, while both Cancún in Mexico and Marrakech in Morocco are down 8%.
Finally, Brits can get their fix in Agadir, Morocco, with flights down 26%, or in Kingston or Montego Bay, Jamaica, with prices down 21% and 18% respectively.
