Palestine weekly: Israeli settlers attack journalist and diplomats
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
06:22:33 UTC
15:22:33 KST

Palestine weekly: Israeli settlers attack journalist and diplomats
Settler olive harvest attacks top 2025 total, journalist and diplomats attacked as Israel halts Gaza commercial imports.
With more than a month left of the olive harvest season to go, United Nations deputy spokesperson Farhan Haq said on Friday that the UN’s Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) had recorded more than 200 Israeli attacks on Palestinian farmers since September 1, eclipsing the 185 that OCHA documented across the entire 2025 harvest season.
The attacks have already killed one Palestinian, injured more than 120 and damaged more than 2,500 trees. The Colonization and Wall Resistance Commission recorded 34 Israeli attacks on Friday that injured at least 19 people, with another 40 on Saturday.
Israeli settlers are carrying out such widescale attacks and thefts with backing from some religious figures. On Friday, Rabbi Dov Lior, spiritual guide of National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir’s Jewish Power party, ruled that settlers may take olives from Palestinian orchards, proclaiming “Jews are permitted to harvest olives even in areas far from Jewish settlements in order to publicly demonstrate our ownership of the land and thereby fulfill the commandment of conquering the land”.
“An olive tree today is more significant in the campaign for Judea and Samaria [the occupied West Bank] than an M16 rifle,” said one post in a settler chat group this week.
“Settlers are stealing the Palestinian olive crop on a vast scale, never seen before in my 22-year history of working on this issue,” said Sarit Michaeli, formerly the international advocacy director of the Israeli human rights group B’Tselem.
Under this ideological push, dozens of attacks on olive harvesters have been reported each day. On October 16, in Abu Falah, northeast of Ramallah, about 80 masked settlers armed with clubs charged at Palestinians picking olives. During the attack, Washington Post photojournalist Heidi Levine, 63, fell and was beaten for more than 10 minutes by settlers, videos and her own account attest. She suffered broken ribs and needed hand surgery, while her camera, phone and passport were stolen. Israeli activist Jonathan Pollak reported that soldiers later shot a village council member, Abdel Jaber Obeid, in the thigh.
Then, on Saturday, masked settlers with clubs attacked a delegation visiting Taybeh, east of Ramallah, that included Belgium’s consul general, French and Polish diplomats, and church representatives. A window of a Belgian consulate vehicle was smashed. French mayor Bernard Baudoux, 78, was kicked and beaten during the attack.
In response to these incidents, United States Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Washington was “very disturbed”, while US Ambassador Mike Huckabee called Levine’s attack “a despicable act of terror carried out by masked cowards”. France demanded arrests and the European Union said it expected “full accountability”.
In response, Israel’s military called the Taybeh attack “severe”, and leader of the Yashar party, Gadi Eisenkot, described settler violence as “Jewish terror under the auspices of the government of Israel”, according to The Times of Israel. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s office, however, offered a conditional condemnation of Levine’s attack, saying questions remained about “who initiated the violence”. After the attack in Taybeh, his office equivocated on the matter, too, remarking that “the more serious the accusation, the stronger the evidence required”.
On Monday, police and the domestic intelligence agency Shin Bet launched “Operation Olive Leaf”, arresting 10 Israelis in raids near Ofra and Shiloh in connection to these attacks on foreign journalists and diplomats.
Attacks across the West Bank
However, no other arrests or investigations have been announced for the dozens of other settler attacks against Palestinians reported this weekend alone. Beyond the headline incidents, masked settlers – often alongside soldiers – targeted farmers, flocks, homes and land.
Attacks included:
- Settlers beat two women in Beit Lid on Tuesday and injured an American citizen, Haytham Tayseer, in Burqa on Thursday, leaving him with deep head wounds.
- Six people, including four women and a child, were injured in Ma’in, in Masafer Yatta, on Saturday, the Red Crescent said.
- Settlers burned four vehicles in Turmus Aya, including a civil defence vehicle, and set fire to a mosque in Mikhmas, the Palestinian news agency Wafa reported.
- Settlers stabbed to death about 20 sheep in Kafr Malek, Mayor Najeh Rustum told Al Jazeera.
- Bulldozers uprooted hundreds of olive trees in Kafr Malek, and settlers cut down 120 olive trees in Kisan, near Bethlehem, Wafa reported.		
Gaza: Halted trade deepens hunger fears
In Gaza, the ever-worsening humanitarian situation is now deteriorating even more rapidly. Israel declared on October 14 that no commercial goods would be allowed to enter Gaza, blaming a dispute between merchants and Hamas over a 10,000-shekel ($3,220) per-truck fee. Gaza’s Government Media Office called that a “blatant disinformation campaign”, saying the sum was a voluntary contribution to a fund for widows and orphans. By Sunday, prices had jumped significantly: a carton of eggs rose in price from 35 shekels ($11.30) to 60-70 shekels ($18-$21), and a sack of flour from 25-35 shekels ($7.50-$10.50) to about 80 shekels ($24), residents said.
Such price increases are taking place just as the World Food Programme announced this week it would cut the number of people it feeds monthly in Gaza from 1.6 million to 1.1 million. Gaza’s Health Ministry said 466 people have died of malnutrition since 2024 and 67 percent of the population faces crisis-level food insecurity or worse through year-end.
Meanwhile, Israeli forces continued to kill Palestinians in Gaza each day. As of October 19, Gaza’s Health Ministry put the toll since last year’s “ceasefire” at 1,522 killed and 5,421 wounded – 27 killed in the past week, against 33 the previous week and 38 the week before. The cumulative death toll has reached 74,480 since October 7, 2023.
Among the Palestinians killed:
- Three children, including Muhammad Riyad Abu Hammad, 14, in Deir el-Balah – the Education Ministry said shrapnel pierced his school bag on his way home from school on Saturday – and Misk Hazem al-Dalu and Tamer Shadi Subh, who were killed in the Maghazi camp and Beit Lahiya, respectively, on Sunday. UNICEF said more than 340 children have been killed since the ceasefire.
- Drone strikes in the past week killed Ahmad Raja al-Shaer and Basel Nabil Qeshta in al-Qarara; Reem Awad in a strike on a Gaza City apartment; Mahmoud al-Madhoun and Ubaida Murtaja in Gaza City; Abdullah and Imad Jaber and Sheikh Majid al-Sabbagh, a Quran school director in Tuffah, on October 17; Amer al-Horani near a Jabalia clinic the same day; and police officer Abd al-Jawad Joudeh in Rafah.
- Shootings killed Saddam al-Za’anin in Jabalia, Hatem Abu Hasanein by quadcopter fire, Huda Abu Adwan, 49, in al-Mawasi and Wijdan Shurrab, 28, in eastern Khan Younis, according to Wafa and local activists.
Israel’s military said several of those killed this week were Hamas members. None of its claims has been independently verified.
Meanwhile, Israeli forces continued advancing the “Yellow Line” deeper into Shujayea on Saturday, placing concrete blocks on al-Qa’qa Street. The line demarcates areas under Israeli control, which now extend across about 65 percent of Gaza, far beyond what was envisaged under last year’s “ceasefire” agreement.

Southeast Asia’s haze crisis will persist until polluters pay
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
06:20:23 UTC
15:20:23 KST

Southeast Asia’s haze crisis will persist until polluters pay
Cheap land clearing imposes enormous costs across borders. ASEAN must change the economic incentives that keep the fires burning.
Across Southeast Asia, the haze has returned with a familiar cruelty. Malaysia has closed schools as air quality deteriorated, Singapore has experienced dangerous levels of air pollution, and even parts of the Philippines have been affected, underscoring how far the smoke has travelled. In Indonesia, meanwhile, forest and peatland fires, a major source of the region’s haze, have threatened communities and livelihoods, particularly in parts of Kalimantan. What begins as land burning in one country can become a public health emergency across an entire region.
The immediate response is predictable: extinguish fires, distribute masks and seek regional cooperation. All are necessary, but none explains why the emergency keeps returning. Malaysian children missing school, Singaporean residents breathing polluted air, Filipino communities exposed to drifting smoke and Indonesian families living near burning land all bear different costs from the same regional failure.
Dry weather and El Nino can intensify fires, but many are deliberately started to clear land for agriculture. The deeper question is why practices that create enormous public losses can remain attractive to those who benefit from them. When the gains from cheap land preparation are concentrated while the costs of smoke are dispersed across communities and national borders, the market signal is distorted and political responsibility becomes easier to evade.
The haze is therefore not merely an environmental emergency or a test of diplomatic goodwill. It disrupts ordinary life, strains public services and exposes how easily environmental costs can be shifted away from those who create them. It is a failure of economic accountability. Unless Southeast Asia changes who pays for the damage, how land-clearing decisions are monitored and what consequences follow proven violations, each dry season will bring another round of emergency measures followed by familiar arguments over blame.
The economics of cheap land clearing
Fire can be an inexpensive way to clear vegetation, especially where land governance is weak, alternative methods are costly and enforcement is uncertain. The private calculation is straightforward: spend less on land preparation and capture the returns. The fires cause respiratory illness, lost working days, school closures and transport disruption, while also damaging ecosystems and releasing greenhouse gases. Those costs are rarely borne in full by those responsible for the burning.
The World Bank’s assessment of Indonesia’s 2015 fire crisis estimated losses of at least $16.1bn, equivalent to 1.9 percent of that year’s gross domestic product (GDP). Government figures put the area burned between June and October at 2.6 million hectares. The bank linked the fires to cheap land preparation, drought and weak enforcement. Its estimate covered agriculture, trade, tourism, transport, healthcare and emergency response, but excluded some long-term health damage and lost ecosystem services.
That figure is not a price tag for the 2026 fires. It shows the scale of losses a recurrent crisis can impose. More recent estimates put the area burned in Indonesia this year at between 637,000 and 900,000 hectares, while Ministry of Health data recorded 283,270 cases of respiratory illness linked to the fires in seven provinces as of October 13. In West Kalimantan province, fires have also threatened communities and livelihoods, underscoring that Indonesians living beside the flames bear costs long before smoke reaches neighbouring countries.
This is the central economic distortion: the cost of burning is not fully reflected in the decision to burn. When benefits accrue privately, but health costs, lost income and ecological damage are borne by society, fire can remain economically attractive even when its total cost is enormous. Small farmers need affordable, practical alternatives to burning; companies must face credible liability when evidence links them to fires; and peatlands need sustained restoration and water management, not emergency attention only when smoke becomes politically embarrassing.
ASEAN’s accountability gap
Smoke travels across borders, but responsibility and enforcement remain largely national. Tracing pollution to a particular fire, identifying those responsible and proving cross-border harm can be difficult. A satellite hotspot is a warning signal, but not by itself proof of who started a fire or whether a company is liable.
The Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) is not without rules. Its Agreement on Transboundary Haze Pollution was signed in 2002 and entered into force in 2003; Indonesia ratified it in 2014. The region also has a Haze-Free Roadmap and a strategy for sustainable peatland management for 2023-30. But agreements cannot substitute consistent implementation, transparent enforcement or incentives that make prevention economically rational.
The challenge is translating these commitments into effective action. Cooperation can improve monitoring and preparedness, but ASEAN’s consensus-based diplomacy has limited leverage when national enforcement is inconsistent or commercial interests resist scrutiny. Its investment framework for haze-free land management aims to mobilise $1.5bn by 2030. Yet money alone will not suffice without transparent spending, measurable outcomes and accountability for repeated fires.
This does not mean every fire is caused by a large corporation or that all pollution in Kuala Lumpur or Singapore originates in Indonesia. Local emissions and weather conditions matter, and fires may involve companies, smallholders or other actors. Accountability requires investigations that identify those responsible and distinguish proven violations from suspicion. Blanket blame lets offenders disappear into arguments about sovereignty, while a lack of transparent evidence erodes trust between neighbours.
Making polluters bear the cost
ASEAN foreign ministers are due to discuss the haze crisis at preparatory meetings before the bloc’s November summit in Manila. Their discussions should be judged by whether they shift the region from managing haze to preventing it.
First, member states should publish comparable data on burned areas, fire recurrence, concessions and enforcement outcomes. Satellite detections should be cross-checked with field investigations, and concession maps should be made available for scrutiny by communities and independent researchers. Greater transparency would make it harder to obscure responsibility through competing claims.
Second, governments should put the polluter-pays principle into practice. Where investigations establish responsibility, penalties and restoration orders should reflect the damage caused, while repeat violations should trigger stronger consequences. Environmental liability must be evidence-based and applied consistently, not used as a political weapon. Penalties must also be substantial enough to deter violations rather than simply become a cost of doing business.
Third, prevention must be economically viable. Smallholders need machinery, technical assistance, credit and access to markets to make alternatives to burning affordable. Peatland rewetting, firebreaks and community-based monitoring require predictable funding before the dry season, rather than ad hoc budgets after fires spread. ASEAN’s investment framework can help mobilise resources, but governments should disclose where funds go and assess their impact on reductions in fires and smoke exposure.
Finally, ASEAN should publish a regional scorecard tied to its 2030 haze-free goal. It should track not only hotspots and hectares burned, but also repeat fires, response times, enforcement, peatland restoration, school closures and population exposure to dangerous air. No regional mechanism can replace Indonesia’s responsibility to prevent fires on its territory. But sovereignty cannot mean that the costs of domestic land-use decisions are ignored once smoke crosses a border. The principle should be simple: those who profit from risky practices must not be allowed to transfer the bill to children missing school, workers losing wages, sick families or neighbouring states.
For more than two decades, ASEAN has had agreements, strategies and roadmaps. The haze’s return does not make these efforts worthless; it shows prevention remains inadequate. If leaders leave November’s meetings with another declaration but no transparent metrics, credible enforcement and funding for alternatives, the region will once again treat the symptoms while preserving the incentives that produce them. Economic accountability is not an add-on to haze policy. It is the condition for making that policy work.
The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

Yasin Gungor
20 October 2026•Update: 20 October 2026
A majority of voters in Canada's western province of Alberta voted to remain part of the country, Canadian broadcaster CBC News projected following a nonbinding referendum.
With 1,480 of 5,587 polling stations reporting, preliminary figures showed 76.2% of voters, or 826,918 people, favored remaining in Canada, while 23.8%, or 257,726 voters, supported initiating the separation process.
The referendum asked voters: "Should Alberta remain a province of Canada, or should the Government of Alberta commence the legal process required under the Canadian Constitution to hold a binding provincial referendum on whether or not Alberta should separate from Canada?"
Around 1.36 million residents cast ballots through advance and special voting mechanisms, according to provincial election agency Elections Alberta.
The ballot included 10 questions, with the first nine addressing immigration and constitutional matters and the final question focusing on Alberta's future within Canada.
The referendum is nonbinding and does not automatically determine whether Alberta leaves the Canadian federation.
Elections Alberta said ballots would be counted by hand, with the separation question counted first.
The agency said unofficial results were expected within 48 hours of polls closing, while official results were scheduled for Oct. 29.

How to reduce utility bills in winter: effective ways to save on payments
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
09:16:52 EEST
15:16:52 KST

How to reduce utility bills in winter: effective ways to save on payments
Kyiv • UNN
Practical tips can help save on heating, electricity, gas, and water. Subsidies and benefits can reduce the financial burden.
In winter, Ukrainians are forced to spend a large portion of their salaries and pensions to pay for heating, water heating, and the operation of electrical appliances. For many, paying their "utility bills" during this period becomes an unbearable burden, forcing them either to borrow money or accumulate debts for services. After all, paradoxically, making an apartment or house energy-efficient also requires considerable funds.
However, the problem can be addressed without expensive home renovations or replacing household appliances. All it takes is to slightly adjust your everyday habits and monitor your consumption of utilities. UNN explains how to do this.
What Ukrainians pay the most for in winter
A large portion of funds is traditionally spent on heating during the winter period. In apartments with central heating, residents receive a single bill for the heat consumed. In apartments or private houses with autonomous heating, however, heating requires paying for a number of services at once: gas, electricity, or the purchase of solid fuel.
At present, electricity for households costs UAH 4.32 per kWh — the government has maintained this tariff until April 30, 2027. Residents of homes with electric heating are charged a preferential price of UAH 2.64 per kWh for up to 2,000 kWh per month. Gas for Naftogaz customers under the "Fixed" plan costs UAH 7.96 per cubic meter until April 30, 2027. The cost of heating and water, meanwhile, varies for Ukrainians in different cities and towns, as it depends on the specific provider.
How to save on heating without sacrificing comfort
First, let us look at the temperature considered safe and comfortable for living rooms in winter. For most regions of Ukraine, it ranges from 18 to 21 °C. However, children, elderly people, and those with health conditions may require a warmer room.
In this regard, the State Agency on Energy Efficiency and Energy Saving of Ukraine advises Ukrainians to lower the heating temperature by one degree wherever this is technically possible. This recommendation is based on information that doing so can reduce heat consumption by approximately 5%. However, it should be noted that this result does not guarantee a comparable reduction in the bill. In addition, for apartments with centralized heating, the financial effect depends on how heat is measured and distributed: without individual metering, reducing the heat output of one radiator will not necessarily lower the charge.
Therefore, to genuinely save on heating without freezing in your own home, we suggest following other tips. For example, radiators should not be blocked by furniture or long curtains, and clothes should not be dried on them. This will help warm air circulate as evenly as possible throughout the room, since there will be no obstacles around the radiators.
A foil-backed screen can also help; it should be installed on the wall behind the heating battery or radiator. The foil will act as a reflector, redirecting heat that would otherwise warm the exterior wall into the room.
Incidentally, living rooms are better ventilated briefly and intensively than by keeping a window partially open for hours. During ventilation, the thermostatic regulator can be temporarily turned down, but ventilation ducts must not be blocked.
Insulating an apartment: inexpensive ways to retain heat
Before spending money on a new, expensive energy-efficient boiler, radiators, or heaters, it is worth checking the windows and doors. In particular, replace worn seals, adjust window sashes, and seal gaps near the threshold and door frame. Such measures may seem insignificant, but it is precisely through gaps in windows and doors that a substantial share of heat is lost. In addition, constant drafts move through the rooms, forcing residents to turn on additional heating devices.
Thick curtains also reduce the feeling of cold coming from the glass, and this can be used to advantage. But, as we wrote above, they must not block the radiator.
But what you should not spend money and time on is heavily advertised products such as thin “insulating” film. Distributors promise that, when applied to windows and even walls, it will help retain heat in homes. In practice, however, the result from such a product is — negligible or altogether nonexistent.
In some households, ventilation is sealed off when cold weather arrives in an effort to retain heat. But this only increases humidity and the risk of mold. In addition, non-functioning ventilation can become deadly if a room fills with smoke or carbon monoxide begins to accumulate in it.
Saving electricity: from water heaters to the night-time tariff
Water heaters, heaters, electric stoves and air conditioners operating in heating mode consume a lot of electricity. For example, a 2 kW appliance will use 10 kWh in five hours, which costs UAH 43.20 at the regular tariff.
Therefore, it is advisable to set the water heater to moderate heating and switch it off when the water temperature reaches 55 °C, rather than heating it to 70 °C. The refrigerator should be kept as far as possible from heat sources. In that case, it will not heat up from the outside and will use less energy to cool its compartment.
To save expensive kilowatt-hours, the washing machine should also be loaded sensibly. There should be some free space in the drum, because a machine overloaded with bed linen and clothes will use more electricity and water to wash the items.
You should also take the opportunity to install a meter with a “day-night” electricity metering function in your home if you have not already done so. Under two-zone metering, electricity costs half as much at night, from 23:00 to 07:00: UAH 2.16 per kWh at the current basic tariff. If 50 kWh per month falls within the night period, the saving compared with single-zone metering is UAH 108. Before replacing the meter, however, it is worth comparing this benefit with the cost of installing it.
How to reduce gas and water consumption from December through March
To save on “blue fuel,” the flame of a gas burner should not extend beyond the bottom of the cookware when cooking. You should also not neglect the lid on a pot, as it helps bring food to readiness more quickly.
The efficiency of a gas boiler depends on proper settings and technical maintenance, which must be carried out by a specialist. It is unacceptable to alter the design of gas equipment or block ventilation yourself.
You can use less water by taking showers instead of baths, installing aerators on taps, using water-saving showerheads, and repairing leaking faucets and toilet cisterns.
An important way to save on “utilities,” which is often neglected, is to submit meter readings within the deadlines set by operators and suppliers. Otherwise, bills may be calculated using estimated volumes, followed by a recalculation that will significantly impact the household budget.
Subsidies and benefits: what assistance is available to Ukrainians in winter
Households for which utility costs constitute an unaffordable financial burden on the family budget may be eligible for a housing subsidy. It is calculated individually based on income, family composition, the cost of services within the social standards, and the amount of the mandatory payment.
According to the Pension Fund, for the 2026–2027 heating season, subsidies for most current recipients will be recalculated automatically, including in cases where the payment was zero during the summer. People applying for the subsidy for the first time must contact the relevant institutions, as must households whose family composition or list of services has changed.
If a person manages to submit an application for state assistance by and including November 30, 2026, the law allows the subsidy to be granted from the beginning of the heating season, provided they are eligible for it. For calculating the heating subsidy, the period from October 16 to April 15 is taken into account.
Documents are accepted by the Pension Fund, Administrative Service Centers (CNAPs), and local self-government bodies. They can also be submitted online via the Pension Fund portal or the administrative services portal "Diia."
It is worth noting that subsidies in Ukraine are available to tenants and internally displaced persons. In addition, certain discounts on utility services are provided for combatants — 75%; persons with war-related disabilities — 100%; and family members of fallen defenders — 50%, within the limits of social norms and subject to the relevant conditions.
How much can be saved on utility services in a one-bedroom apartment
Let us take an apartment with central heating and a gas stove as an example. During a month, its resident used 220 kWh of electricity, 8 cubic meters of gas, and 5 cubic meters of cold water. Electricity would cost UAH 950.40, and gas — UAH 63.68. Let us assume that the combined water supply and wastewater tariff is UAH 40 per cubic meter: this adds another UAH 200. Let us add an assumed UAH 1,500 for heating and UAH 300 for other payments. The total is UAH 3,014.08.
After replacing the light bulbs, reducing unnecessary water heating, and eliminating leaks, consumption fell to 180 kWh, 6 cubic meters of gas, and 4 cubic meters of water. The respective payments would amount to UAH 777.60, UAH 47.76, and UAH 160. With heating and other service costs unchanged, the total would decrease to UAH 2,785.36. The difference is UAH 228.72, or about 7.6% per month.
A reminder
Earlier, we wrote about how to save electricity in the summer and reduce expenses. Experts advise Ukrainians to adjust their appliances and change their habits to cut costs.

Lithuania to switch to winter time this weekend

Unknown Publisher

Lithuania will switch to winter time this weekend, with clocks set back one hour overnight from Saturday to Sunday.
The change will take effect early Sunday and remain in place until the end of March. Under winter time, daylight begins earlier in the morning but also ends earlier in the evening.
Seasonal clock changes were introduced to make better use of daylight hours. However, critics argue that switching between summer and winter time can have adverse effects on health.
Lithuania, like other European Union member states, changes its clocks twice a year under an EU directive.
The European Commission and the European Parliament support ending the seasonal time change, but the proposal has yet to win sufficient support among EU member states to be implemented.

However, he argued that parts of the contemporary Israeli Right no longer represented his values.
"I am not a messianic right-winger. And I am not a racist right-winger. And I am not a right-winger who despises his ideological opponents," Hanegbi wrote.
He also rejected what he described as complacency toward nationalist crime and efforts to undermine law enforcement institutions under the banner of strengthening governance.
His strongest criticism concerned exemptions from military and national service, which he argued had become indefensible following the October 7, 2023, Hamas massacre and three years of military operations.
Hanegbi acknowledged that successive Israeli governments, including those in which he served, had failed to adequately address the issue.
Nevertheless, he argued that continued widespread draft avoidance threatened Israel's existence, particularly given the sacrifices made by regular IDF soldiers and reservists.
He criticized right-wing parties that tolerated coalition partners encouraging young men to disregard military draft notices and declaring that they would rather die than enlist.
Hanegbi praised Liberman's warnings about Hamas, support of West Bank settlement
Hanegbi also pointed to his long personal and professional relationship with Liberman, dating back nearly five decades to their time as students at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem.
The two subsequently worked together in the Knesset and government, including during Hanegbi's tenure as deputy foreign minister under Liberman.
Hanegbi said he had been particularly impressed by Liberman's approach to the threat posed by Hamas during his tenure as defense minister.
He recalled serving in the security cabinet when Liberman repeatedly warned that Israel was failing to give sufficient priority to confronting the terrorist organization in Gaza.
"Unfortunately, all of us, all the cabinet members and all the heads of the security services, did not give his warnings the weight they deserved," Hanegbi wrote.
Liberman resigned as defense minister in November 2018, criticizing the government's approach to Hamas and its decision to accept a ceasefire following an escalation in Gaza.
Hanegbi recalled Liberman warning that the government's policy favored buying short-term quiet at the expense of long-term national security.
He argued that the October 7 massacre demonstrated the gravity of the threat Liberman had identified years earlier.
Hanegbi also praised Liberman's opposition to religious coercion, his support for settlement in the West Bank, and his defense of judicial independence despite years of personal legal scrutiny.
In Hanegbi's assessment, these positions demonstrated that Liberman could remain committed to nationalist principles while respecting political opponents and preserving democratic institutions.

Drone strike in disputed southern Sudan area kills at least seventy, minister says

2026-10-20
06:12:12 UTC
15:12:12 KST

At least 73 people were killed when drones struck a market in the disputed Abyei region along the border of South Sudan and Sudan on Monday, the caretaker information minister for Abyei said, accusing Sudan's army of carrying out the attack.
The minister did not provide evidence for his claim.
Ahmed Wadi, a witness cited by the Guardian, said the strike left "50 bodies who I helped bury, one of them my own brother Mohamed."
A medical source also cited by the Guardian said 30 people died from their injuries following the strike.
"A total of 80 people were killed in the drone strike on Al-Dibab, and another drone strike on Al-Mujlad injured four who are currently being treated," the medical source said. The Jerusalem Post has not been able to verify the numbers the source cited.
Oil-rich area with disputed claims
Abyei is an oil-rich area that is jointly administered by South Sudan and Sudan, which have both staked claims to it. It experiences frequent bouts of violence, with clashes usually involving rival ethnic groups or armed militias.
"Around 73 people have been killed, and 19 have been wounded ... a number of drones were shot yesterday by the Sudanese armed forces," Yohana Akol Ngor, the caretaker minister of information of the Abyei region, told Reuters on Tuesday.
Last year, at least six Bangladeshi peacekeepers were killed, and eight wounded in a drone attack by separatist armed groups on a UN base in Abyei, Bangladesh's armed forces said.
South Sudan's foreign ministry said in a statement late Monday that drones struck a market located north of Abyei town, but did not specify the number of civilian casualties resulting from the attack.
The ministry said it had summoned the Sudanese ambassador to convey the government's "strong protest and deep concern regarding the attack and its implications for the security of civilians and the stability of the Abyei Area."
The medical charity Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) said in a statement that it was treating more than 20 wounded people at the nearby Ameth Bek Hospital.
"So far we received over 20 patients, including several critical cases. Patients with burns were also admitted. We are providing surgical services and wound dressing, along with other emergency care," said Christian Lindauer, MSF medical activities manager at Ameth Bek Hospital.
Sudan has been gripped by war since April 2023 between the Sudanese Armed Forces and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces. The conflict has drawn in local militias and foreign powers, devastated large parts of the country, and created what the United Nations has described as the world's worst humanitarian crisis.

Weapons, millions of shekels in drugs seized by police in major blow to Abu Latif syndicate
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
06:12:11 UTC
15:12:11 KST

A major cache of weapons, explosive devices, and narcotics was uncovered over the weekend in an open area near the village of Rama in the Galilee. According to police suspicions, the stockpile was used by the Abu Latif crime organization, which originates from the local council.
During the operation, 12 firearms, dozens of magazines, hundreds of rounds of ammunition, explosive ordnance, and over three kilograms of a substance suspected to be cocaine - with an estimated value running into millions of shekels - were seized.
The raid was conducted following intelligence pinpointing the location as a central hideout used by members of the criminal organization. Dozens of police officers from the Central Unit (YAMAR) of the Northern District, along with Border Police fighters and the National Guard, conducted hours of searches across complex terrain before locating the items.
Among the seized weapons were eight rifles, including M16s, Kalashnikovs, and a shotgun, as well as four handguns of various types. Additionally, dozens of magazines, hundreds of rounds of ammunition, and spare parts for weapons were found. Alongside the weapons, explosive bricks, a standard IDF explosive device, and dozens of remote triggering systems for explosives were located.
Security forces also seized tactical vests with ceramic plate armor and a vehicle fitted with forged license plates. All findings were transferred to the Israel Police's forensic and explosives labs for further testing and evidence extraction. The tests are intended, among other things, to assist in identifying those involved in hiding the weapons, explosives, and drugs. At this stage, no arrests have been reported following the discovery of the cache.
Latif crime organization linked to murder, extortion cases
The Abu Latif crime organization, which grew in Rama and established its power in the Galilee, has been considered in recent years one of the primary targets for law enforcement. Its activity expanded beyond northern Israel, and it was linked to a series of investigations involving violence, extortion under threat, collecting protection money, and attempts to take over infrastructure projects and public tenders.
In April 2025, an indictment was filed against the head of the organization, Latif Abu Latif, and 11 other defendants in a case involving the takeover of tenders through extortion under threat. According to the indictment, the organization systematically instilled fear in contractors and businesspeople to gain control of high-budget public projects.
Members of the organization were also linked to the murder case of Fatin Kizel in Maghar in March 2024. Kizel, cousin and right-hand man to the mayor-elect, was murdered about two weeks after local elections.
A joint Shin Bet (Israel Security Agency) and police investigation raised suspicions that the murder was carried out to intimidate the mayor and influence his actions. In July of that year, indictments were filed against those involved in the case.
Superintendent Shlomi Asraf, head of the detective branch in YAMAR North, noted that the seizure of the cache constitutes a severe moral and financial blow to the crime organization's infrastructure.
Police stated that the activity is part of the offensive strategy led by Northern District Commander Maj.-Gen. Meir Eliyahu, in line with objectives set by Police Commissioner Inspector General Danny Levy to combat organized crime rings and bolster personal security for residents of the North.

War update: 206 clashes on front line in 24 hours as Russian forces step up attacks on Southern Slobozhanskyi axis
Ukrinform reports this, citing the General Staff’s Facebook post on the battlefield situation as of 8 a.m. on Tuesday, October 20.
Russian forces launched one missile strike and 63 airstrikes, dropping 217 guided glide bombs.
In addition, the enemy launched 8,784 kamikaze drones and carried out 2,607 attacks on populated areas and Ukrainian military positions.
In Sumy region, artillery strikes hit the settlements of Ulianove, Pysarivka, Korenok, Khotin, Mala Korchakivka, Yunakivka, Luzhky, and Velyka Rybytsia. Airstrikes also targeted areas near Pysarivka, Riznykivka, and Sinne.
Ukraine’s Defense Forces used aircraft, missile forces, and artillery to strike a UAV command post and two areas where Russian personnel were concentrated.
In the Northern Slobozhanskyi sector, Russian troops launched four attacks near Tovstodubove, Korenok, Buniakyne, and Rivne.
In the Southern Slobozhanskyi sector, Ukrainian units repelled 26 Russian attacks. Russian troops attempted to advance near Kutkivka, Lyman, Starytsia, Mala Vovcha, Izbytske, Vilcha, Okhrimivka, Zakharivka, Karaichne, Bochkove, Zybyne, and Radkivka.
In the Kupiansk sector, Russian troops conducted no assault operations.
In the Lyman sector, Ukrainian defenders repelled 12 Russian attacks near Kolodiazi, Dibrova, Novomykhailivka, Druzheliubivka, Chervonyi Stav, Zelena Dolyna, and Lyman. Russian attempts to advance were thwarted.
In the Sloviansk sector, Russian troops launched seven attacks near Yampil, Pyskunivka, and Mykolaivka.
In the Kramatorsk sector, Russian troops conducted no assault operations.
In the Kostiantynivka sector, 15 attacks were reported. Russian troops launched assaults near Kostiantynivka, Novoselivka, Druzhkivka, and Novopavlivka.
In the Pokrovsk sector, Ukraine’s Defense Forces repelled 21 Russian attacks. Russian troops attacked near Serhiivka and Molodetske and launched assaults toward Sofiivka, Vilne, Kucheriv Yar, Hannivka, Chernihivka, Dobropillia, and Myrne.
In the Oleksandrivka sector, Russian forces conducted no active offensive operations.
In the Huliaipole sector, Ukrainian troops repelled 11 Russian attacks near Rizdvianka, Dolynka, Hirke, Charivne, and Yehorivka.
In the Orikhiv sector, Ukrainian defenders repelled two Russian attacks near Zarichne and Prymorske.
In the Dnipro River sector, Russian forces conducted no active offensive operations.
In the Volyn and Polissia sectors, the situation remained largely unchanged. No signs of Russian forces forming offensive groupings were detected.
As previously reported, Russia’s total personnel losses since the start of its full-scale invasion of Ukraine on February 24, 2022, are estimated at approximately 1,568,720 troops as of October 20.

Voters reject separation of Alberta from Canada in referendum
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
06:11:53 UTC
15:11:53 KST

Alberta voters reject move toward separation from Canada in referendum
Voters in Canada's oil-rich province of Alberta have rejected a proposal to begin a process toward independence, results showed early Tuesday, delivering a victory for Prime Minister Mark Carney and supporters of Canadian unity amid President Trump's trade war and annexation threats.
The vote was not a direct referendum on independence but would have set oil-rich Alberta on a path toward a future vote on separation from Canada.
With more than 1 million votes counted, about 76% supported remaining in Canada, compared with 23% who backed beginning a process that could lead to separation.
"We are a solid country that's united from coast to coast to coast," Thomas Lukaszuk, a former Alberta deputy premier who led the Forever Canadian campaign against separation, told supporters.
Results were delayed after late openings forced more than 100 polling stations to extend voting hours Monday. More than 1.35 million Albertans, or 43% of eligible voters, cast advance or special ballots. Albertans were deciding whether to remain in Canada or begin a legal process that could have lead to a second vote on separation.
Alberta, home to the world's fourth-largest proven oil reserves, is cowboy country and a conservative stronghold whose political culture has long had more in common with the American West than much of Canada. Resentment toward Ottawa runs deep, but has not traditionally translated into widespread support for independence.
Dustin Degenhardt, a Wainwright voter, said Albertans have long been mistreated by Ottawa.
"Alberta has essentially been treated as, you know, a colony," he said after voting Monday. "They want to take and take and take from us and not return anything."
Taylor MacIsaac, another Wainwright voter, backed separation.
"I think it'll be good for Alberta to separate personally, as a very conservative individual that grew up in rural Alberta," she said.
Dave Malka, 59, of Edmonton, criticized spending money on a "referendum on a referendum" rather than health care.
Despite the proposal's apparent failure, separatist leaders have said they turned a fringe cause into a movement that will not disappear.
Carney earlier urged Albertans to deliver a decisive vote for unity. "Vote like Canada's future depends on it because it does," he told a rally Friday in Edmonton, where he grew up.

2026-10-20

by Vladislava Chugueva
MOSCOW, Oct. 20 (Xinhua) -- Rows of colorful, carefully crafted editions of contemporary Chinese books line the desk of Maria Rudneva, editor-in-chief of Freedom, an imprint of Russia's leading publishing house, Eksmo. Until recently, Chinese web novels appealed only to a niche audience of Asia enthusiasts. Today, however, Rudneva is among the publishing professionals helping bring these works to a mass Russian readership.
"I was simply sobbing at four in the morning. I only had translation up to the 40th chapter, and that was it," Rudneva reminisced about her very first encounter with Chinese web novels. "After such emotional involvement, it is already impossible to walk away from it," she added with a smile.
What started as a fan-driven phenomenon has, over the years, evolved into a publishing strategy. Chinese author Tian Xia Gui Yuan, whose real name is Lu Jing, came to Moscow for the third time this October. A renowned writer of Chinese online romance fiction, she has seen eight of her books translated into Russian, including The Rise of Phoenixes and the Legend of Fuyao series.
"Writing a book, for me, was a very pure endeavour," said Tian Xia Gui Yuan. "I wrote from the bottom of my heart, simply wanting to tell the stories I envisioned. Its journey to overseas readers came as an unexpected and pleasant surprise."
According to publishers and readers, Chinese web novels do more than entertain: they open a door to Chinese culture and classical Chinese literature for Russian readers.
MARKET DEMAND
"First and foremost, I think it was market demand. Interest in ancient China, its aesthetics and culture, had been there for a long time," said Rudneva when asked about the reason behind the current popularity of Chinese literature.
Since Chinese web novels often center on the emotional personal journeys of main characters, readers find much-needed solace as they follow the protagonists' paths.
"What I like is that even in those stories which seem detached from real life, one can find genuine feelings and values that resonate with us in everyday life," said Anastasia, a master's student who attended a fan meeting with Tian Xia Gui Yuan.
Rudneva echoed this sentiment: "Chinese literature delivers a wealth of emotions and adventures all at once." Most readers of Chinese web novels are over 30, and the stories inspire them to overcome the everyday difficulties and challenges of adulthood, she said.
"We feel that the Russian public shows great interest in Chinese literature, including web literature, especially web novels," said Xie Xiaocheng, director of the International Exhibition Center at China National Publications Import and Export Group.
"Many Russians have begun reading Chinese novels. In particular, numerous online novels have gained great popularity after being translated into Russian. This serves as a direct reflection of the steadily warming relations between China and Russia," Xie, also director of the Beijing International Book Fair, told Xinhua.
Indeed, Russian readers have shown a sustained appetite for new stories. In the first nine months of 2026, sales of Chinese books at the Chitai-Gorod national bookstore chain totalled 86,000 copies, with a total revenue of 88 million rubles (about 1 million U.S. dollars).
ADAPTATION JOURNEY
However, Chinese web literature had to travel a long road before finally reaching Russian readers. The greatest challenge was adapting lengthy online novels for print publication.
A key difference came into play -- in China, people are accustomed to reading on their phones, while most Russians regard a literary work as valuable only if it is printed.
"In our country, the digital market is still not seen as a separate, self-sufficient, or serious thing," Rudneva noted. Russian publishers tend to select well-known web novels that already have screen adaptations in China, which makes readers more likely to buy the book, she added.
Accurate translation is another crucial factor in helping readers fully immerse themselves in the vivid fantasy worlds created by Chinese authors. "I want to say that translators are the best people. It's a very hard job, and we must remember that they bear great responsibility," said Anastasia.
As the editor-in-chief, Rudneva pays close attention to selecting translators for her projects. She said the publisher always tries to strike a balance between not overloading the text with complex terminology and faithfully conveying the atmosphere.
For that reason, glossaries explaining key character names and explanations of cultural references have become a vital component of these Chinese books. "Indeed, the task of the translator and editor of an Asian book is, first and foremost, to help readers enter this world," Rudneva said.
Since Russian readers prefer books with character-focused covers, publishers also had to revise the original Chinese cover designs, which tend to prioritise sweeping scenery. Rudneva said each artwork is carefully crafted; often, the covers draw on existing film posters to capture readers' curiosity. "It all comes down to what we expect from Chinese fantasy -- it is aesthetics," she noted.
GATEWAY TO CHINESE CULTURE
In this way, Chinese web novels have become stepping stones for Russian readers to explore Chinese culture. "It definitely serves as a bridge. Literature is undoubtedly the gentlest yet deepest medium for cultural communication. Through authentic characters and vivid plots, audiences grasp the core spirit you wish to convey, the soul and ethos of the Chinese nation," said Tian Xia Gui Yuan.
Readers said they have gradually grown interested in exploring Chinese classics. "Literature reflects the most important historical moments of Chinese civilization, its cultural characteristics, and its worldview," said Daniil Rozhkov, a 10th-grade student who also studies Chinese. He said his favourite authors are Mo Yan and Yu Hua.
"I was never interested in Peking Opera until I read a Chinese web novel. Thanks to that novel, I developed an interest in this art form, went to Beijing to watch a live Peking Opera performance, and began to understand it," said Rudneva. After finishing their favourite novels, readers often travel to China to visit places featured in key plot milestones and forge deep cultural connections, she added.
Modern novels also help Russian readers better understand contemporary Chinese people. "Modern works, including the web literature currently popular on the Russian market, often depict the social landscape of modern China. After reading such books, a Russian reader travelling to China will not face generation gaps or cultural barriers and will be able to integrate naturally and freely into Chinese society," said Xie.
Fascinated by the captivating stories and inspiring characters created by Chinese authors, Russian readers are gradually developing a deeper understanding of Chinese culture. As they turn the pages of Chinese books, they discover common ground with their Chinese counterparts. Such cultural exchange is a valuable bridge, helping deepen the friendship between the two countries and their peoples. ■

Chinese FM highlights trust, friendship, cooperation, partnership on Eurasia tour
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20

Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi, also a member of the Political Bureau of the Communist Party of China Central Committee, and Bulgarian Foreign Minister Velislava Petrova jointly meet the press in Sofia, Bulgaria, Oct. 19, 2026. (Xinhua/Peng Ziyang)
SOFIA, Oct. 19 (Xinhua) -- Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi on Monday offered a four-point summary of his just-concluded Eurasia tour: trust is the cornerstone of peace, friendship is a valuable asset, cooperation is a solid driving force, and partnership is a common goal.
Wang, also a member of the Political Bureau of the Communist Party of China Central Committee, made the remarks while jointly meeting the press with Bulgarian Foreign Minister Velislava Petrova after their talks in Sofia.
Wang said he was glad to visit Bulgaria, during which he met with President Iliana Iotova, Prime Minister Rumen Radev and Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Poulev, and held comprehensive and in-depth exchanges with Petrova, reaching broad consensus.
Both sides agreed that Bulgaria's development has ushered in new hope and that China-Bulgaria strategic cooperation faces new opportunities, Wang said.
China is ready to work with Bulgaria to seize the opportunities and act as strategic partners in development and revitalization, Eurasian connectivity, and the upholding of multilateralism, so as to promote the upward and sound development of China-Europe relations through more proactive, practical and dynamic China-Bulgaria relations, he added.
During his Eurasia tour, Wang, as special representative of Chinese President Xi Jinping, attended the Seventh Summit of the Conference on Interaction and Confidence Building Measures in Asia (CICA), and paid visits to Azerbaijan, Croatia, Montenegro and Bulgaria.
TRUST AS CORNERSTONE OF PEACE
Wang said the world today is intertwined with chaos and changes, and the biggest problem it faces is the deficit of trust. From the Ukraine crisis to the Middle East conflict, resolving conflicts requires trust, and building trust requires communication, he added.
As a responsible major country, China has always worked for peace, Wang said. During the CICA summit, he held separate talks with Israeli and Palestinian leaders, met with representatives of other Middle Eastern countries, and heard Balkan leaders' views on the Ukraine crisis and the regional situation.
Wang noted that the clear message China conveyed to all parties is to remain confident and persistent, pursue dialogue and consultation, show mutual understanding and accommodation, rebuild trust and work together for peace.
China will always stand on the right side of history, fulfill its responsibilities as a major country in bridging the trust deficit and resolving crises and conflicts, and play its due role, he added.
FRIENDSHIP AS VALUABLE ASSET
Wang said that Silk Road relics in Azerbaijan bear witness to the millennium-long friendship between the Chinese and Azerbaijani peoples.
Marco Polo, a household name in China, was born in what is now Croatia. The song "Bella Ciao," sung at the Tara River Bridge in Montenegro, evokes fond memories for a generation of Chinese people. The first Confucius Institute and the first Chinese Cultural Center in the Balkans were both established in Bulgaria.
Wang also said he was delighted to learn that contestants from Montenegro had won the global championship of the "Chinese Bridge" Chinese Proficiency Competition three times.
He noted that these friendly exchanges across time and distance carry forward the spirit of the ancient Silk Road and are vivid practices of mutual learning among civilizations on the Eurasian continent. Such valuable friendships should be given new contemporary meaning and continuously carried forward, Wang added.
COOPERATION AS SOLID DRIVING FORCE
Wang said all four countries he visited during this tour are participants in and beneficiaries of Belt and Road cooperation, and many landmark cooperation projects have played an important role in the development of each country.
Taking the Gobustan solar power plant in Azerbaijan, the Peljesac Bridge in Croatia, the Bar-Boljare highway in Montenegro and China-Bulgaria energy storage cooperation as examples, Wang said that these cooperation projects are based on each country's actual conditions, meet the needs of the people and conform to the trend of the times.
China is ready to tap potential and improve efficiency with the four countries, consolidate cooperation in such traditional areas as economy and trade, investment and infrastructure, actively align the Belt and Road Initiative with the Middle Corridor, and strengthen cooperation in new quality productive forces such as artificial intelligence and green transition, so as to create new engines and inject new impetus into the development and revitalization of each country, he added.
PARTNERSHIP AS COMMON GOAL
Wang said that China's foreign policy is to seek partnership rather than alliance and pursue dialogue rather than confrontation, and China advocates building a new type of international relations and promoting the democratization of international relations.
The three Balkan countries he visited this time are all good friends and good partners of China, and all hope for the healthy and steady development of China-Europe relations and look forward to strengthening China-Central and Eastern European Countries (CEECs) cooperation, Wang said, voicing China's willingness to be an open, solid and trustworthy long-term strategic partner for Balkan countries.
China and these countries believe that state-to-state relations, regional cooperation and China-Europe relations run parallel to and reinforce each other, with the core being partnership, Wang said, adding that the three engines work in concert to achieve win-win outcomes.
The recent progress in China-EU trade and investment consultations shows that China and the EU can properly handle differences through dialogue and consultation, Wang said.
China always believes that openness leads to progress, while isolation only leads to backwardness, and is ready to work with the European side to adhere to the path of multilateralism, practice the concept of free trade, and jointly achieve win-win cooperation between China and Europe at a new and higher level, he added.
Wang noted that China-CEEC cooperation conforms to the trend of the times and the development needs of regional countries, and is an important mechanism conducive to European integration. China is ready to take the opportunity of the 15th anniversary of the China-CEEC cooperation mechanism next year to work with regional countries to advance the cooperation and upgrade its quality, he said.
He added that Bulgaria is known as the Land of Roses, and Chinese people often say, "The fragrance always stays in the hand that gives the rose." China believes that helping others is helping oneself, and stands ready to continue working with Bulgaria and other countries to safeguard peace and stability, promote prosperity and revitalization, and enhance mutual learning among civilizations, making unremitting efforts to build a community with a shared future for humanity, Wang said. ■

UN to slash food assistance to over 700,000 Palestinians
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
06:07:10 UTC
15:07:10 KST

The United Nations World Food Program (WFP) has been forced to slash food assistance to 500,000 Palestinians in the Gaza Strip and 200,000 in the occupied West Bank because of a severe funding shortage, with the agency’s acting head warning that life in Gaza remains “absolutely brutal.”
Carl Skau, acting executive director of the WFP, said the number of people receiving assistance in Gaza was reduced this month from 1.6 million to 1.1 million, while in the West Bank the figure was halved from 400,000 to 200,000.
He urged the international community to provide $450 million immediately so the agency can restore the cut assistance and sustain hot meals and food parcels across both territories for the next six months.
According to the WFP, food rations in Gaza have been cut by half. Families that continue to receive support will get only one food parcel instead of two and a smaller bag of wheat flour.
The number of hot meals distributed daily has fallen from 250,000 to 150,000, with those living in hard-to-reach areas near the so-called “yellow line" now receiving a meal only every other day. Cash assistance has also been reduced for 75,000 families.
The agency said it can still support bakeries covering roughly one-third of Gaza’s bread needs, provide nutrition assistance to about 300,000 women and children, and deliver school snacks to 200,000 children, but these efforts remain under severe strain.
Skau, who had just visited both territories, told UN correspondents in a briefing from occupied Jerusalem that UN teams recorded about 50 attacks per day in Gaza over the past week, according to Press TV.
While the agency has managed to push back on famine since the October 2025 ceasefire, an estimated 1.4 million people, 67 percent of Gaza’s population, continue to face acute food insecurity at crisis levels or worse, with around 200,000 requiring immediate food aid to prevent death from hunger.
He stressed that the cuts are not the result of declining needs or lack of access, but solely of insufficient funding; the WFP received less than half as much money for its Palestine operations in 2026 as in previous years.
The situation is compounded by Israeli restrictions. Last week the Israeli military temporarily halted the entry of commercial goods, including food, into Gaza. While it later said it would resume coordinating commercial trucks, it warned that any reports of merchants paying taxes to Palestinian authorities could lead to the revocation of their licenses.
Skau noted that people closest to the yellow line, along with the sick, mothers, and children at risk of malnutrition, will be prioritized under the reduced program.
In the occupied West Bank, Skau said escalating attacks by Israeli settlers have transformed a long-standing human-rights and protection crisis into a hunger crisis. Food insecurity has more than doubled in the last three years, and nearly one million Palestinians now require food assistance.

Why is landmark UN biodiversity fund nearly empty?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
06:07:00 UTC
15:07:00 KST

Why is landmark UN biodiversity fund nearly empty?
- The Cali Fund was created at COP16 to raise money for biodiversity, but it has collected only US$7,085 (S$9,060) so far.
- It asks firms using digital sequence information to pay 1% of profits or 0.1% of turnover, but contributions are voluntary and few countries have incentives.
- Experts say companies want stronger rules and safeguards, while the UN summit in Armenia will decide if governments can make the fund work.
AI generated
PARIS – Conceived at the 2024 Biodiversity COP, the Cali Fund was meant to raise billions of dollars for nature protection – but has so far collected only US$7,085 (S$9,060).
It is a sluggish start for a fund intended as a showcase for innovative financing that charges companies profiting from the use of genetic data derived from nature.
The trickle of money highlights the difficulties involved in mobilising money for biodiversity.
As a crucial UN biodiversity summit in Armenia running until Oct 30 discusses its future, here is a rundown on how the fund works and reasons for its lacklustre start:
How does the fund work?
Adopted at COP16 in Cali, Colombia, at the end of 2024, the fund began operating in February 2025.
It proposes the payment of 1% of the annual profits of pharmaceutical, cosmetics, biotechnology companies or firms specialising in animal and plant breeding, or 0.1% of their turnover.
In a preparatory document, its designers mentioned the possibility of recovering one billion dollars a year in light of the revenues of the sectors concerned.
However, so far only three companies have contributed: The British firms TierraViva AI (US$1,000) and Prozomix (US$5,000), and the Belgian company E-BIOM (US$1,085).
Two others have pledged an additional US$3,571.
What is its justification?
Digital sequence information (DSI) – data derived from genetic resources such as plants, animals, fungi, viruses and micro-organisms – is freely accessible in digital databases.
Companies draw on this biological heritage to turn it into economic value by developing a medicine, a cream, improving an agricultural plant and so on.
The Cali Fund is based on the idea that those who benefit from this information, directly or indirectly, should in return contribute to the protection of biodiversity and to the local communities preserving it.
The fund is not legally binding but it does invite states to adopt administrative, policy or legislative measures to encourage companies to do so.
Why are companies reluctant?
The main difficulty is the “mechanism still relies very heavily on incentives and voluntary contributions”, according to Juliette Landry from the sustainable development think tank IDDRI based in Paris.
“As long as these incentives are not strong enough and consistent across countries, a company may well ask why it should contribute when its competitors are not doing so.”
Pakhi Das, public policy adviser at the NGO Plant-for-the-Planet, said there were no countries currently with legislation incentivising contributions to the fund, nor are there any where such legislation is under discussion.
Beyond the challenge of drawing enough resources into it, another lies in the actual use of the money collected.
“The main hurdle that companies seem to be raising is ensuring there are safeguards in place for how their funding will be used,” said Vishaish Uppal, a director at WWF-India.
Companies also want to be sure that the Cali Fund’s internationally-accepted certificates – documenting receipt of payment for use of genetic resources – are also accepted nationally, to avoid paying twice.
What does the pharmaceutical industry say?
“The level of participation in the Cali Fund reflects ongoing questions about the design and implementation of the mechanism, rather than a lack of commitment to biodiversity,” said Guilherme Cintra, the director of innovation policy at the International Federation of Pharmaceutical Manufacturers and Associations.
“The current mechanism overlaps with existing law, relies on inaccurate assumptions about how data is used in the discovery of medicines,” he added.
Several major cosmetics companies did not respond to AFP’s requests.
Is success still possible?
The small amount collected “is not enough (on its own) to determine whether the mechanism is a success or a failure,” said Landry from IDDRI.
“In the coming years, the question will be whether governments manage to create the right conditions so that companies marketing products and services based on digital sequence information actually contribute to this mechanism,” she added. AFP

As France erupts, Europe's far right gains from fuel-price anger ahead of elections

As France erupts, Europe's far right gains from fuel-price anger ahead of elections
PARIS/ROME/BERLIN, Oct 20 - The tractors rolling into the town of Gela on the southern tip of Europe are flying the Sicilian flag, emblazoned with Medusa, three bent legs and ears of wheat, a reminder of the island's role as a breadbasket since Roman times.
But the farmers are not bringing in a harvest. They are protesting.
As soaring fuel prices squeeze household budgets and businesses across Europe, cost-of-living pressures are driving unrest and giving fresh momentum to far-right parties ahead of elections next year in countries including France, Italy and Poland.
Parties once considered fringe had already been gaining ground, with voters from motorists in rural France to young men in Germany's former Communist east looking for alternatives.
The US-Iran war, which erupted in February and sent energy prices sharply higher, has compounded the challenge for governments already struggling to contain inflation, support growth and rein in spending.
The discontent has spilled onto the streets.
In France, demonstrations that began over deteriorating school facilities in Paris' northern suburbs have morphed into some of the country's worst unrest in decades, with shops looted, buildings torched and a 19th-century town hall in Limoges set on fire.
"Why am I here? Well, quite simply, I find the current cost of living truly terrifying," said Quentin Leviloux, a 21-year-old protester in Nantes.
"Just think of people who earn barely the minimum wage, when you look at the cost of food, fuel, and everything else. It’s terrifying how incredibly expensive things have become."
The European Commission estimates the Iran conflict has cost Europe roughly €100 billion ($112 billion) through disrupted trade and energy markets. Gas prices have jumped about 140% and diesel prices have doubled.
In a weekend address, French President Emmanuel Macron acknowledged the "legitimate demands" of protesters angered by rising living and fuel costs, while condemning those responsible for violence and looting. "We must never confuse them with those who destroyed, vandalised and looted," he said.
PROTESTS ERUPT ACROSS EUROPE
Violence has also erupted elsewhere. In the wealthy northern Italian city of Milan, police clashed on Sunday with protesters hurling stones and looting stores during demonstrations over poor public services and rising living costs.
In Gela, on Sicily's southern coast, farmers say fuel costs have made operating machinery prohibitively expensive. "We cultivate the land, we harvest debts," said one banner.
"We are completely at a standstill," said Arcangelo Gambino, a farmers' representative in Caltanissetta province. "The (fuel) cost has more than doubled."
Roadblocks by truckers, farmers and steelworkers have disrupted transport across parts of southern Italy, contributing to local fuel shortages and concerns over supermarket supplies.
Tens of thousands marched through Lisbon on Saturday over low wages, housing costs and the rising cost of living, increasing pressure on Portugal's centre-right government.
In Spain, the eviction of an 87-year-old woman from her home sparked nationwide demonstrations over housing shortages and soaring rents, helping trigger a snap election next month.
Belgium has also seen demonstrations, while large rallies in Albania have been driven by anger over perceived government corruption, a lack of jobs and poor education standards.
The protests reflect broader economic anxieties that are increasingly shaping politics across the continent.
Concerns about purchasing power have become "a major driver of populist politics" across Europe, said Gilles Ivaldi, a political scientist at Sciences Po.
Politicians on both the hard right and hard left have increasingly argued that restoring energy ties with Russia would help lower costs, challenging Europe's mainstream consensus on support for Ukraine.
LE PEN MAKES FUEL PRICES A CAMPAIGN ISSUE
The latest energy shock comes after years of economic strain following the pandemic and the fallout from Russia's 2022 invasion of Ukraine.
In France, rising energy costs have provided an explosive backdrop to next April's presidential election. Macron's government is struggling with a ballooning budget deficit and pressure from bond markets.
Frontrunner Marine Le Pen of the far-right National Rally and hard-left veteran Jean-Luc Melenchon have both made fuel prices central planks in their campaigns.
“Rising fuel prices are clearly an issue that boosts Marine Le Pen,” said Ivaldi. “I think this is an issue she has owned for quite some time."
Since the Iran war began, Le Pen's ratings have improved while Macron's have slipped, according to polling by Elabe.
Le Pen's proposal to sharply cut value-added tax on fuel has attracted broad public support. Analysts say the issue resonates strongly with her core voters in rural and semi-rural areas where car travel is often essential.
CALLS TO RESTORE RUSSIA TIES
In neighbouring Germany, the Alternative for Germany (AfD) is leading national opinion polls after strong gains in local elections. The cost of living topped Germans' concerns for a fifth straight year in a survey published this month.
German inflation spiked to nearly a three-year high in September, with energy price inflation rising to 14.9%, handing ammunition to the AfD to attack Chancellor Friedrich Merz.
The AfD is pushing to restore energy ties with Russia, arguing that Berlin’s support for Ukraine is needlessly self-sabotaging at a time when Europe’s largest economy and many of its energy-hungry companies are struggling.
Past experience indicates a link between high energy prices and voter turnout for the AfD, said Jan Steckel, professor for the political economy of climate change at the Technical University of Munich.
“Populist parties often frame energy costs as avoidable and attribute them to government policy choices ... rather than to the underlying geopolitical shocks that drive them," he said.
“These geopolitical shocks are ... much more difficult to explain. And I think this is why incumbent parties often struggle."
The argument is gaining traction elsewhere.
In Italy, Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni faces growing competition from National Future, a new far-right party led by former army general Roberto Vannacci that advocates restoring gas links with Russia.
In Poland, one of Ukraine's staunchest supporters, concern over energy bills is helping boost support for the far-right Confederation of the Polish Crown. Its leader, Grzegorz Braun, has called for a return to buying Russian oil and gas, making the case alongside AfD politicians in Lubmin, where the damaged Nord Stream pipelines land in Germany.
“I love the smell of Russian gas in the morning,” he said. REUTERS

Statue of Soviet dissident and Nobel laureate Alexander Solzhenitsyn removed from waterfront in Vladivostok, Russia, for relocation to a park

Statue of Soviet dissident and Nobel laureate Alexander Solzhenitsyn removed from waterfront in Vladivostok, Russia, for relocation to a park
A monument to writer Alexander Solzhenitsyn has been removed from Korabelnaya Embankment in central Vladivostok. It will be installed in the Park of Faith and Hope in the coming days, city officials told Interfax.
Plans to move the monument to the park became public in early March. The Pacific Fleet’s leadership and veterans proposed the move, saying the monument was “out of keeping with the themes of the memorials and monuments” on the embankment.
Vladivostok officials said the sculpture was not a designated cultural heritage site and that the Council for Culture and the Arts had decided to relocate it.
City officials said there had been “a lot of criticism from historians and local history experts, who pointed out that Solzhenitsyn arrived in Vladivostok by plane and that a monument to him on the embankment among warships was out of place.”
The bronze monument, more than 2.6 meters tall, was unveiled in central Vladivostok on September 2, 2015. Sculptor Pyotr Chegodayev created it. The writer’s son, Yermolai Solzhenitsyn, attended the unveiling.
Solzhenitsyn returned to Russia in May 1994, flying to Magadan and then to Vladivostok before traveling to Moscow by train.

Russia has lost 1,568,720 troops in Ukraine since the beginning of its full-scale invasion on Feb. 24, 2022, the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine reported on Oct. 20.
The number includes 1,560 casualties that Russian forces suffered over the past day.
According to the report, Russia has also lost 12,425 tanks, 25,570 armored combat vehicles, 164,871 vehicles and fuel tanks, 51,359 artillery systems, 2,227 multiple-launch rocket systems, 1,714 air defense systems, 449 aircraft, 356 helicopters, 2,986 unmanned ground vehicles, 35 ships and boats, and two submarines.
Ukraine's General Staff has not revealed its own losses during the full-scale invasion, citing operational secrecy.
Independent Western think-tank reports agree that the Russian casualties significantly surpass Ukraine's losses, with the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) estimating the ratio to be "roughly 2.5:1 or 2:1."
A January 2026 CSIS report said Ukraine has likely suffered between 500,000 and 600,000 casualties from February 2022 to December 2025, of which between 100,000 and 140,000 are thought to be killed in action.
While Ukrainian officials rarely disclose the figure, President Volodymyr Zelensky told France TV on Feb. 4 that at least 55,000 Ukrainian soldiers have been killed in action since the beginning of the full-scale war, in addition to significant numbers who are missing in action.
The intensity of Russian drone attacks and the fighting has made it extremely difficult for Ukraine to retrieve the bodies of fallen soldiers, which are needed for DNA confirmation.
