The EU unveils a strategy to strengthen its position in the Arctic amid pressure from the US and Russia - AFP
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
09:00:57 EEST
15:00:57 KST

The EU unveils a strategy to strengthen its position in the Arctic amid pressure from the US and Russia - AFP
Kyiv • UNN
On October 20, the EU will present a strategy to strengthen its role in the Arctic. The plan includes a cable to Greenland, satellite communications and the expansion of its icebreaker fleet.
The EU will unveil plans on Tuesday, October 20, to strengthen its position in the Arctic, as it grapples with pressure from Russia and the United States in this key strategic region. AFP reports, writes UNN.
Details
From critical raw materials to icebreakers and undersea cables, the bloc wants to strengthen its presence on the geopolitical battlefield, according to a draft of its new "strategy for the Arctic" seen by AFP.
"The new reality in the Arctic requires Europe to be a strong and reliable partner. That is what we aim to achieve with our new strategy," said EU Commissioner for International Partnerships Jozef Síkela.
"It addresses the region's most pressing challenges, from accelerating climate change to growing security and geopolitical tensions, and sets out how Europe should respond," he noted.
Competition in the Arctic is intensifying as global warming causes sea ice to melt. Countries such as Russia, China and the United States are stepping up their activities, competing to gain access to natural resources and new sea routes. With three Arctic countries among its 27 members — Denmark, Finland and Sweden — the European Union has a stake in the region. And repeated threats by US President Donald Trump to take control of Greenland — Denmark's vast autonomous territory — have shaken Europe, the publication writes.
Given that events in the far north also have consequences in the south, the strategy to be presented by European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen aims to establish a common EU approach to the region.
The draft seen by AFP stresses the need to cooperate with "like-minded" non-EU countries such as Canada, the United Kingdom and Norway, and envisages a regular summit of "Northern Neighbourhood" partners.
Until recently, the United States, which was a key ally in the region, is included on the list of those that could take part, but otherwise the country is more notable for its absence from the rest of the document, the publication points out.
Although Trump's tone has cooled since the beginning of the year, eventually leading to the signing of a security agreement with Greenland and Denmark, many in Europe remain wary.
The United States is mentioned only a few times in the 20-page document, compared with nearly two dozen references to Canada.
Some of the initiatives listed in the strategy are clearly aimed at reducing dependence on Washington, the publication notes.
According to the draft, Brussels plans a "sovereign and secure" undersea cable to connect Greenland with the EU mainland, as part of a broader "pan-Arctic" cable project that will also connect Canada, Japan and South Korea.
The bloc is also working to ensure satellite communications in the Arctic through the IRIS² satellite constellation project, which aims to compete with Elon Musk's Starlink.
Also high on the agenda is the question of how to counter an aggressive Russia, as the document points to hybrid threats such as "drone incursions" and undersea cable sabotage.
The strategy envisages better data sharing to monitor Moscow's so-called "shadow fleet" of oil tankers that violate sanctions.
It also emphasizes the importance of expanding Europe's icebreaker fleet, stating that Brussels will develop options for the joint procurement, pooling and shared use of polar vessels with allies.
Among a number of other plans, it also provides for investment in renewable energy and critical raw materials projects.

Israel unveils new IDF ‘Space Force’ to prepare for warfare beyond Earth
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
06:00:52 UTC
15:00:52 KST

The IDF is preparing to establish a new Space Brigade under its Planning Directorate, marking a significant step toward expanding Israel's military capabilities beyond Earth's atmosphere. The unit, expected to be established in the coming months, will oversee the development and operational use of space-based technologies, including orbital surveillance systems and capabilities for future space warfare.
The decision was announced following a senior military appointments meeting Monday chaired by IDF Chief of Staff Lt. Gen. Eyal Zamir. The new Space Brigade will operate as part of the military's multiyear Hoshen program, reflecting a growing recognition within the IDF that space has become an increasingly important dimension of modern warfare.
Brig. Gen. S., whose full name was not released, has been selected to lead the brigade. Two lieutenant colonels, identified as N. and S., have also been designated to head departments within the new unit and will be promoted to colonel. The appointments remain subject to the approval of Defense Minister Israel Katz.
The Space Brigade will be responsible for coordinating the development and operational use of military space capabilities, leading professional training and establishing space operations as a distinct field of military expertise. Unlike traditional combat brigades, it will function as a specialized organizational unit within the Planning Directorate, bringing together technological development, operational requirements and long-term military planning.
According to the IDF, the decision reflects its assessment that space is becoming an active and evolving part of the battlefield, with its military significance expected to increase in the coming years. Over the past year, the military has advanced several projects in the field, including the operation of space-based sensors monitoring Earth and the development of capabilities related to space warfare. The new brigade is intended to consolidate these activities under a dedicated organizational framework.
‘Blue-and-white Star Wars’: Israel's ambitions beyond Earth
Defense Minister Katz welcomed the announcement Tuesday, describing the brigade as a key element of his ambition to transform Israel into one of the world's leading military space powers.
"I welcome the IDF's decision to establish a Space Brigade as part of the policy I am advancing: turning Israel into a military space power, 'blue-and-white Star Wars,'" Katz said.
"The goal set for the IDF and the defense establishment is to make Israel one of the world's leading countries in military space capabilities," he added.
Katz outlined a vision extending beyond traditional satellite-based intelligence gathering and surveillance to future defensive and offensive military operations conducted from space. "The ability to monitor, defend and strike any target from space across vast areas will cement Israel's position as a regional and global power, deter enemies near and far, and ensure our security for generations to come," he said.
The defense minister's comments reflect ambitions to expand the military's role in space from supporting operations on Earth to developing capabilities that could eventually play a more direct role in combat. The IDF, however, has not disclosed which capabilities will be available when the brigade is established or provided a timetable for developing the full range of systems described by Katz. His remarks outline long-term objectives rather than capabilities confirmed to be operational.
Katz also emphasized the potential economic benefits of developing military space technology, arguing that investment in the field could provide a major boost to Israel's technology sector, entrepreneurship and advanced manufacturing. He said the initiative could help position Israel as a leading country in civilian space technology as well, allowing developments originating in the defense establishment to benefit the wider economy.
The establishment of the Space Brigade is intended to provide a dedicated structure for advancing those military ambitions, bringing together projects, personnel and expertise as Israel prepares for a future in which space is expected to play an increasingly significant role in warfare.
New robotics brigade and return of armored unit after 23 years
The Space Brigade was among several major organizational changes approved during Monday's appointments meeting. The IDF also decided to establish a dedicated Robotics Brigade within its Depth Command, with Brig. Gen. Y. selected to lead the new unit. Two additional officers will head departments within the brigade, which is intended to consolidate the military's robotics activities and advance technological capabilities.
Another notable decision was the reestablishment of the 500th Armored Brigade, which was disbanded in 2003. Lt. Col. R. has been selected to command the revived tank formation and will be promoted to colonel, marking the unit's return after 23 years.
The meeting also finalized dozens of senior appointments across the IDF's regional commands, operational units and headquarters. Among them, Lt. Col. Michal Lifshitz was selected to head the Mental Health Department, while Col. Eli Levertov was named deputy military advocate general. New military attachés were also selected for Poland, Germany, Finland, France, Britain and Belgium, alongside a new Ground Forces attaché in Washington. All appointments remain subject to Katz's approval.

France's traditional smoked sausage under threat – but is Brussels really to blame?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
06:00:30 UTC
15:00:30 KST

Political parties across Brittany are up in arms over the French government's failure to defend andouille de Guémené, a traditional sausage suspected of posing a cancer risk.
Anyone who has tried andouille de Guémené knows it is not easily forgotten. Served in a crêpe with sautéed onions, the traditional Breton smoked pork sausage has a devoted following. When I told my French editor I was writing about it, she immediately exclaimed: “L’andouille de Guémené? J’adore!”
But her enthusiasm faded when I explained that the speciality from western France was caught in a regulatory dispute that could threaten its very existence.
The problem lies in EU rules limiting levels of polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs), potentially carcinogenic compounds produced during smoking. Andouille de Guémené is traditionally smoked over beechwood, a process that leaves soot on its surface and increases its PAH content.
The sausage's distinctive flavour depends on this centuries-old method, leaving producers caught between preserving tradition and complying with food safety rules.
A sausage under threat
In the town of Guémené-sur-Scorff, Benoît Rivalan, owner of the century-old Maison de l’Andouille, fears French authorities could shut down his business over the EU's limit of 12 micrograms for certain PAHs.
"We are on their radar," he told Euronews, despite having introduced a special technique to reduce contamination.
“We employ a protective sleeve. It’s like a compression stocking: we put one over each andouille during the smoking process, and it captures 80% of the PAHs while preserving the flavor.”
But Rivalan warns that being forced to adopt further measures could undermine the traditional production method, which relies on smoking over a wood fire.
The story of Brussels bureaucrats threatening a beloved Breton speciality has gained traction in recent weeks among France's EU-sceptic far right.
But is Brussels really to blame? The reality is more complicated.
EU rules allow member states to request exemptions, something the French authorities have never done.
Paul Leguernic, a right-wing local councillor and knight of the Brotherhood of Guémené Andouille Tasters, is furious.
The gastronomic association, founded in 1994, campaigns to protect the traditional sausage from industrial imitations.
“Successive French governments have refused to apply for an exemption for French smoked products,” Leguernic told Euronews, adding that it was easy to blame Brussels when the real issue lies in how Paris has implemented the EU regulation.
For years, producers tested their sausages without the skin to demonstrate compliance with EU limits. But the French Agriculture Ministry subsequently required them to test the entire sausage, arguing that consumers also eat the skin.
The results were dramatic.
"We went from levels ranging between 6 and 8 micrograms to levels of between 120 and 150 micrograms of PAHs," Rivalan said.
Pressure mounts on Paris
Leguernic accused the French authorities of interpreting the European rules too strictly.
"The French authorities adopted an overly zealous interpretation of the European regulation, as the soot generated during the smoking process settles on the skin rather than penetrating the product itself."
He also criticised their refusal to accept a label advising consumers to limit their consumption of the skin.
Loïg Chesnais-Girard, the left-wing president of Brittany’s regional council, wrote to the French government on 28 September, urging it to submit a request for an exemption to Brussels. Last week, all the region’s political parties, except the Greens, adopted a resolution backing the calls made to Paris.
"Consumer food safety must remain an absolute priority, but regulations must also be able to take into account the specific characteristics of traditional production methods and the very limited health risks associated with consuming such a product," the resolution reads.
Several EU countries have already secured exemptions for traditional smoked meats, including Ireland, Croatia, Cyprus, Spain, Poland and Portugal. Finland and Sweden have also obtained derogations for products smoked over smouldering wood or other plant materials.
“It’s crystal clear: France has failed to do its job when it comes to smoked andouille,” Socialist senator Simon Uzenat told Euronews. “It has failed to make the voices of these regions heard.”
A European Commission spokesperson confirmed to Euronews that Paris had not yet requested such a derogation, unlike 10 other EU countries. “France can still request one.”
The derogations apply to smoked meats whose production methods cannot be modified without significantly altering the flavour of the products. “If maximum levels were applied, such traditionally smoked products would disappear from the market resulting in the closure of many small and medium size enterprises,” the EU regulation reads.
Rivalan has cut production by 30%, reducing his workforce in anticipation of a possible closure.
"If the authorities order us to shut down, we’d rather have to lay off 14 people than the 19 we used to employ."
For now, the future of andouille de Guémené remains uncertain. Whether the traditional sausage survives in its current form may depend less on Brussels than on the willingness of the French government to seek an exemption already available under EU law.

‘How green are our valleys?’: in the footsteps of miners on south Wales’s new forest trail
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
06:00:20 UTC
15:00:20 KST

Bracken and heather ripple across the plateau. I exhale into the chill autumn air and my breath mists a view that reaches all the way to Gower and the ochre peaks of Bannau Brycheiniog (formerly the Brecon Beacons). Far below, the Ogmore valley’s terrace houses look like tiny constellations but up here on Tarren y Fforch, it’s just me and a few sheep taking springy steps between tufts of bilberries. If this corner of the south Wales valleys feels a long way from its coal mining past, that is, partly, the point.
I’m hiking the new Llwybr Coedwig Cymru Trail, or Wales Forest Trail. Running from Porthkerry Park, near Barry, to Pont Walby, close to Glynneath, this 50-mile (80km) pilot route is the first section of what the National Forest for Wales hopes will eventually be a trail linking woodlands across the length and breadth of Wales: a sylvan counterpart to the Wales Coast Path.
My father grew up in one of the valleys’ mining villages and, when I visited relatives there as a child, the disconnection of those post-industrial communities from the wild hills that loomed above them was striking. Mountain bikers have long discovered the region’s potential, but walkers still tend to head for the more obvious trails that wind through the national parks or along the coast. This pilot trail seems a good excuse to explore untapped footpaths.
With the sea behind me, I set off from the oak leaf sculpture that marks the trail’s start. The viaduct ahead once carried coal to Barry docks, but today it stands over Caffe Matteo, busy with dog walkers sipping cappuccinos. Leaving them behind, I cross the park between the soft greens of birch and oak trees.
I swerve on to a fern-fringed path and follow a stream to the outskirts of Barry. The next section is less lovely – a long stretch of roadside pavement until I enter Hensol Forest. The sunshine splinters through ancient pine trees and their needles cushion the ground. Weaving in and out of forest and fields, I soak up all the calm this long-distance forest-bathing exercise can offer until the Vale Resort comes into sight.
This vast hotel is popular with golfers, but also holds two trump cards for walkers: a spa where weary hikers can swim, sauna and steam their muscles limber again, and a bar serving energy-boosting Welsh rarebit spiked with ale mustard, Dragon cheddar and charred leeks.
Restored, I rejoin the trail the next morning, dipping along leafy lanes and footpaths as the roar of the M4 gets louder. I cross beneath it to enter Coedwig Gellihir, a small broadleaf woodland, then continue north into Pontyclun, before clambering down to the river at Ynysmaerdy Forest to pick up an old railway path to Coedely.
The trail has been designed to offer stretches for cyclists, pushchair users and horse riders, with more pavement-pounding and, in Thomastown, a reminder of the challenges faced by post-industrial communities. Leaving the village behind, the trail opens out again on to a little rocky path with soaring views of Ogwr Fach Valley.
One of the National Forest for Wales’s aims is to help communities connect with nearby woodlands. In Blackmill, the next village I come to, the trail passes Coed Bach Dimbath, a small community woodland where local groups have come together to build an otter hide, outdoor classroom and accessible paths.
“The woodland there had been inaccessible for decades, and now people can access it,” says Rhodri Hewitt of Natural Resources Wales, the trail’s project lead. “The valleys can feel desperately poor in places, but the River Ogmore is another world entirely.”
Continuing north to Nant-y-Moel, I come to Blaenogwr Farm, a Georgian farmstead marooned in the village, where I’m staying in a homely holiday cottage. I drop off my backpack and head across the road for fish with buttery potatoes and laverbread (made from edible seaweed) and cockle sauce at the Blaenogwr Hotel.
My final day’s walking starts with a climb up to that extraordinary plateau on Tarren y Fforch. Hewitt tells me that parts of the trail follow the paths miners took across these hills to work in pits in neighbouring valleys. I’m glad they had this antidote to the darkness and danger underground. Today’s route feels uplifting. I slip through an ancient gate on to open moorland and pick my way up the escarpment, meadow pipits chirruping around me.
Crossing the plateau, I enter Afan Forest park, a large commercial woodland that’s also home to a forest of wind turbines, a peat restoration project and a network of mountain-biking trails. I have an urge to be inside the forest rather than tracing its edges and detour on to a footpath leading up to the trig point at Craig y Llyn, the highest point of the valleys at 600m.
Continuing beneath branches dripping velvety lichen, I come to another spectacular viewpoint, as the land drops away to the waters of Llyn Fach and Llyn Fawr, with the peaks of Corn Du and Pen y Fan shrouded in soft-focus drizzle behind them. Soon I dip into the loveliest stretch of forest along the whole trail.
The valley of Cwm Gwrelych is a designated geological site of special scientific interest because of the near complete 300m-year-old strata exposed here. But it’s also rainforest-like, cut through with waterfalls, a dark, glossy river and dense, broadleaf woodland. I feel completely enveloped in green as I hike the last couple of miles to the trail’s current end, the Isambard Kingdom Brunel-designed viaduct at Pont Walby. As I continue to Sgwd Gwladys pub with rooms in nearby Pontneddfechan, I remind myself that this is not a finished trail but the beginning of one.
The next morning, I pull on my boots one last time and set out in search of the waterfall the pub is named after. Mist rises from the river, shafts of sunlight turn the leaves amber and a heron glides past in cinematic slow-mo. When we spoke about the trail, Hewitt mentioned an old Welsh proverb: Dod yn ôl at fy nghoed, meaning “To return to my trees”, or finding your way back to a balanced state of mind. As I sit and admire Sgwd Gwladys’ thundering cascade, I realise this leafy trail has delivered exactly that.
The trip was provided by the National Forest for Wales and Natural Resources Wales. Vale Resort has doubles from £104 room-only. The Airbnb cottage costs from £87 a night. Sgwd Gwladys has doubles from £65.55, room only. For trail information, visit gov.wales/llwybr-coedwig-cymru-trail and for region information Visitwales.com

====================================================================================================

The ‘Finger cutter’ and the ‘Brazilian Escobar’: the men accused of bringing cocaine cartels to Europe
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
06:00:19 UTC
15:00:19 KST

In the early hours of 7 September, a convoy of heavily armed police swept through the sleeping streets of central Brussels towards the Haren district, on the city’s north-eastern outskirts. They made their way to 22 Avenue du Bourget, a militarised bunker-like complex that was the former headquarters of Nato.
The modernist complex, with its austere and functional architecture, was hastily built in 1967 and houses the Justitia courtroom, where Belgium’s federal trials are now held. It was here that the perpetrators and accomplices of the 2015 Paris terrorist attacks and the 2016 Brussels attacks were tried in 2022.
Last month, officers armed with assault rifles patrolled the building’s wide corridors, protecting those involved in this decade’s most high-profile trial: the Bressers-Carvalho case.
For a month, judges and a legion of lawyers shared the main courtroom with journalists and the public on one side of a large armoured-glass partition. On the other side were the defendants, 31 in number, flanked by officers with their faces masked to protect them from possible reprisals. It was a scene more typical of countries ravaged by mafias.
During the lengthy hearings throughout the month, two among the many defendants stood out. The first was Flor Bressers, a 40-year-old Belgian born in Lommel, a town of 35,000 in the province of Limburg. Bressers has an unusual profile for criminal circles. A criminology graduate of the Free University of Brussels (VUB), he was often known to his peers as “the professor” or “the academic”.
Yet his most commonly used nickname contradicts the image of a refined and scrupulous man: Bressers is best known as “the Finger cutter”.
Arrested in 2022 at a wine tasting with his wife in a penthouse of the luxury Renaissance Zurich Tower Hotel, Bressers has been facing charges of kidnapping, unlawful detention, extortion involving firearms, and leading a criminal organisation.
The other key figure alleged to be in the criminal organisation is a 68-year-old Brazilian: Sérgio Roberto de Carvalho. In a joint operation involving Interpol, Europol, the Brazilian federal police and the US Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA), Carvalho was arrested on 21 June 2022 at a luxury hotel overlooking the Danube in the Hungarian capital, Budapest.
Based in Mato Grosso do Sul, a Brazilian state in the tri-border region of Brazil, Argentina and Paraguay, which is one of the continent’s centres of organised crime, Carvalho became known in his own country by the nickname “Major”, from his rank when he was a military police officer, a past life in which he blended corruption and crime. In Europe, his moniker was more revealing: “the Brazilian Escobar”.
Together, the Finger cutter and the Brazilian Escobar are the main defendants in a Belgian courtroom bristling with security as the international cocaine trafficking network between Latin America and Europe is put under the spotlight.
Bressers and Carvalho are alleged to have been behind an organisation suspected of transporting up to 45 tonnes of cocaine to Europe.
Prosecutors said they led a lawless multinational operation that moved hundreds of millions of dollars through front companies, one of which, the Antwerp water treatment firm Kriva Rochem, has given the case its alternative name.
The money – allegedly laundered through cryptocurrencies, financial markets and property – financed the complex logistics involved in transporting cocaine produced in Peru and Bolivia along illegal, dusty routes in Brazil, before crossing the Atlantic and being distributed in an unknown number of countries in Europe and beyond.
Bressers had been on Europol’s list of most wanted fugitives since 2021. According to the agency’s notice, he was wanted for kidnapping and unlawful deprivation of liberty, extortion involving a firearm and participation in a criminal organisation.
An earlier case from 2010, in which he was eventually acquitted in 2015 for lack of evidence, alleged that he had ordered a settling of scores, in which the victim had a finger cut off with pruning shears – giving rise to Bressers’ nickname.
In 2020, five years later, he was convicted in relation to another revenge case: kidnapping a Dutch drug dealer who was beaten, threatened with death and cut with a razor blade after being blamed for a missing cocaine shipment. Bressers then became a fugitive, spending two years on the run.
Bressers also appeared as a suspect in at least one other violent case, this time in Guyana, involving the death of a rice wholesaler in the South American country whose seized consignment contained cocaine. His death is believed to have been a cover-up to prevent the gang’s network being dismantled. That case also never went to trial.
Bressers’ partner, Carvalho, is perhaps better known in Europe than in Brazil. According to Brazilian court documents, he led the group that acquired dozens of tonnes of cocaine produced in Peru and Bolivia and transported it through the Brazilian midwest to the ports of Paranaguá and Natal, from where the drugs were shipped to Europe.
Born in 1958 in Ibiporã, in southern Brazil’s Paraná state, Carvalho grew up in Mato Grosso do Sul and became engaged in criminal activity while a police officer in the state. First sentenced to 15 years in prison for drug trafficking in 1998, he was not dismissed from the police until 2010. Rather than continue running his operations from Latin America, the Brazilian Escobar moved to Europe, first hiding in Portugal and then in Spain.
There, according to Spanish police, he took up residence in a €2m mansion in Marbella on the Costa del Sol, using the identity of Paul Wouter, a wealthy Surinamese citizen. From this base in Spain, a known hub of international cocaine trafficking, prosecutors say he coordinated, between 2017 and 2020, an organised crime network spanning Portugal and Spain, specialising in drug smuggling through ports such as Setúbal, near Lisbon, and Leixões in northern Portugal, and through Lisbon airport, as well as the ports of Rotterdam and Antwerp.
Portuguese police suspected that Carvalho had links to the Primeiro Comando da Capital (PCC, or First Capital Command), Brazil’s leading criminal organisation.
Carvalho was cornered – but not arrested – in November 2020 in coordinated raids involving more than 1,000 police officers police from Portugal, Spain, Belgium, the Netherlands, Romania and the United Arab Emirates, as well as Europol. The operation led to 45 arrests and the seizure of more than €13m (£11m) in cash, 70 luxury cars, 37 aircraft and 136 properties.
The court heard that Carvalho is said to have staged his own death in the same year by obtaining a death certificate for Wouter, who was allegedly the victim of Covid-related complications.
He then moved to Budapest, where he was arrested in 2022 while using the identity of Guillermo Díaz Flores, a Mexican national. Carvalho is alleged to have used at least 10 false identities before being detained in Budapest. Extradited to Belgium in June 2023, he was sent to a high-security prison.
In court, he was reunited with the Finger cutter, his alleged accomplice, as they faced charges of orchestrating a transnational criminal organisation. In his trial evidence, Bressers did not admit any of the charges and claimed to be the victim of a media witch-hunt. “I have a strong feeling that all of this was orchestrated by the authorities,” he says.
Bresser’s defence team is contesting the admissibility of the evidence and has requested the case be dismissed. When approached, Bressers’ lead solicitor, Hans Rieder, had not commented by the time of publication. During the trial, the defence accused the press of “painting an absolutely monstrous picture of our client”.
Carvalho, who did not attend all of the proceedings due to health problems, maintained his innocence and claimed to be the victim of persecution by the Brazilian federal authorities. “I have been in prison for five years and nobody is listening to me,” he said at the hearing. “It was a namesake who committed these crimes, not me.”
Carvalho’s lawyers, Frédéric Thiebaut and Renaat Landuyt, were approached for comment but did not respond. The Belgian federal prosecutor handling the case also declined to comment.
The trial hearings wrapped up on 9 October, with a verdict anticipated on 15 December. Bressers could receive up to 20 years in prison, while Carvalho could be handed up to 15 years.
Over the past decade, cases such as the Bressers-Carvalho one have multiplied. During this period, cells of Latin American drug-trafficking groups have been identified by national police forces, Europol and intelligence services in Portugal, Spain, France, Belgium, the Netherlands, Germany, Italy, the Nordic countries, eastern Europe and the Balkans, as well as north Africa.
These criminal offshoots have become embedded in Europe through “brokers” or members of drug cartels that “provide specialised services related to cocaine production in Europe, including extracting cocaine from various carrier materials or the processing of trafficked coca paste”, according to Europol’s Andy Kraag, head of its serious and organised crime centre.
“Latin American criminals are heavily involved in this. We see the presence of Latin American criminals in Europe growing, their activities becoming more and more relevant.
“It used to be the other way around – it’s a two-way street now. We already saw, for decades, European high-level criminals embedded in Latin America, settling down there. And now you see more and more Latin American criminals permanently or semi-permanently active in Europe too,” Kraag says.
High-level sources across Europe and Latin America indicate that these groups are expanding their operations and influence in the real and digital economies, fuelled by cryptocurrencies, gambling companies, and the financial and property sectors.
According to Juan Gabriel Tokatlian, a professor of international relations at Universidad Di Tella in Buenos Aires, and an expert on Latin American organised crime, the “war on drugs”, as waged in Colombia – where he lived for 20 years – made cartels more resilient and dynamic, which explains their ability to adapt and expand internationally.
“Europe has become, in recent years, a place where drug consumption has increased in particular. If you look at the UN reports, it is an important market – in the 1980s, particularly as regards cocaine, it was not relevant,” he says.
“In that context of European demand and an erratic anti-drug policy that militarises but then coexists, we find a series of situations that end up empowering organised crime,” says Tokatlian.
Like Carvalho, dozens of alleged leaders of criminal organisations such as the PCC, Tren de Aragua, the Sinaloa cartel, Clan del Golfo or Los Lobos are being held in prisons across Europe, wanted by national police forces or Europol, or listed on Interpol’s red list of most wanted individuals.
They are sought for links to trafficking cocaine to Europe, trafficking arms and synthetic drugs to Latin America, and ties to European organisations in the Balkans or the Italian ’Ndrangheta mafia.
Gabriel Feltran, a sociologist at Sciences Po university in Paris and director of research at the French National Centre for Scientific Research (CNRS), say groups such as the PCC or Sinaloa are partnering with European crime organisations such as those in Albania or the ’Ndrangheta in “joint ventures”.
He says they buy coca directly from Latin American producers and are capable of delivering directly at the end – so drug ownership no longer passes from hand to hand along the chain.
It is what Feltran calls the “platformisation” of organised crime, in which, like multinational digital platforms such as Amazon, Google and Meta, the cartels integrate their infrastructure and economic models with the aim of controlling the entire drug-trafficking chain, from production deep in Latin America to sale on the streets of Europe.
It means that everything from communications, payments, precursors (chemicals needed to manufacture drugs) and laboratories to logistics is concentrated at the top, with carriers and local operators often unwittingly hired as paid service providers, such as Uber drivers.
Feltran says that, before this platformisation, trafficking was based on routes and several intermediaries who were drug owners in each step of the chain. Now, he says, such “joint ventures get together at the top, buy directly from the producer and deliver directly at the end. They no longer go through intermediaries.”
“Ownership of the drug no longer changes hands. They concentrate everything, optimise a lot and grow very quickly. The more people use their services, the more dependent they become – that’s a network effect.”

The pest I’ll never forget: the maggots that rained down like hail
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
06:00:19 UTC
15:00:19 KST

It was that terrifying summer in 2022 when London reached 40C. I was staying in a friend’s flat while she was away for a year, a former housing association property where the living room ceiling permanently had a hole in it. Each day, the air felt thicker and the leaves looked more limp. Dust clung to every surface. With no wind, the stench of the bins lingered.
I’d nicknamed the guy next door “Techno Guy” because his life’s great pleasure appeared to be sitting in the driver’s seat of a parked red convertible, stereo on full volume, revving the engine but going nowhere. Maybe it was to preserve his car battery, maybe it was to get away from his wife. His music genre of choice, Shazam told me, was Romanian techno (though he was also fond of the Cher megamix). He smoked constantly, each drag like a first breath. The sound of him hawking up phlegm in the morning became a kind of alarm clock.
One Sunday, I was working from home and the smell of the barbecue had been going since breakfast – long rows of sausages, chicken, chops. I popped on my noise-cancelling headphones, thinking the couple next door were settling in for a big party, but later in the afternoon I realised it was just the two of them, having a magnificent feast. “Good on them,” I thought.
A few days later, the heat became unbearable – then record-breaking. I wasn’t alone in taking an umbrella with me if I left the house. It was pressing and cloying. The bins, meanwhile, had reached a crisis state – the smell from next door’s in particular was so heinous I’d learned to hold my breath when I left the front door until I’d cleared them.
The day it happened was alarmingly quiet. No techno, no Cher, not a single rev of the engine. I looked out the window and saw Techno Guy, his torso hidden, elbows-deep in his wheelie bin, groaning like an animal in pain. There was a small but growing pile of bags next to him – all torn and mangled, a brownish sludge seeping out of them – the remnants of the barbecue. At first I thought the sacks were moving, before realising it was a swarm of bluebottles creating a halo. My neighbour disappeared briefly, and returned carrying a jet washer. There was splat, a yell and a blossom of what looked like rice grains were blasted into the air.
With steady horror, I realised what had been breeding in the depths of my neighbour’s bin, and what had compelled him to empty it and – for some incomprehensible reason – attack it with pressurised water. Maggots. Hundreds – maybe even thousands – of maggots, propelled into flight and falling on windows, walls, cars, gardens, hedges, pavements and bins all around. I thanked the universe I’d kept my window closed, as they landed on the windowsill, still wriggling their last wriggle. Some neighbours obviously thought that rain had finally come in the form of hail. They opened their doors to see. And then they too were hit by the unfolding horror.
I’m sure someone yelled, but we were all in a sort of stasis. There stood the neighbour, stray maggots in his hair and on his face, before he went inside to fetch the dustpan and brush.

Googlebook review: Google’s new laptops are woefully underbaked
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
06:00:18 UTC
15:00:18 KST

Google’s attempt to create a new type of laptop to compete with Windows and macOS machines is finally here, combining the best of ChromeOS and Android into the new Googlebook. With advanced links to Android phones and the best of Google built in, can these Googlebooks really compete with a MacBook Air or Surface Laptop? I took two for a spin to find out.
For years, Chromebooks have been the boss of budget laptops, but Googlebooks take a different, far more premium approach. Made by a range of traditional PC makers, including Acer, Asus, Dell, HP and Lenovo, they start at £999 (€1,099/$899/A$2,299) – a far cry from the £160 Chromebooks.
While Google does not make these machines directly, it has set strict hardware quality standards that the laptops must reach. That includes backlit keyboards, haptic trackpads, fingerprint readers, crisp touchscreens, decent speakers and modern fast chips with at least 16GB of RAM.
It is a list of specs you should expect with a premium Windows PC, but those start at a much higher price, primarily thanks to RAMageddon.
As such, the Acer Googlebook 14 and the Asus Googlebook 14 I’ve been testing have excellent hardware with satisfying keyboards, great trackpads and quality screens.
The Acer is a convertible that allows the screen to fold over the back of the device turning into a tablet of sorts. It is 1.14kg and 13.9mm thick, with a glossy 14in 3K OLED screen and a smooth aluminium-magnesium body, costing £999.99.
The Asus is a traditional laptop with a matt 14in 3K OLED screen and a magnesium-alloy body that weighs just 0.99kg and is 11mm thick, costing £1,199.99.
Googlebook OS
Top quality hardware aside, anyone familiar with a Chromebook would be forgiven for thinking it was ChromeOS running on these machines. It has the familiar taskbar at the bottom, Chrome-based web apps and access to Android apps.
But the software is essentially Android underneath, which means getting it up and running is just like setting up an Android phone: scan the QR code with your phone, enter a passcode and transfer your apps and accounts. It is all done and dusted in about four minutes, which is faster than setting up a modern Windows 11 machine even if you know all the shortcuts.
Access to the full gamut of Android apps is the Googlebook’s biggest strength and its greatest weakness. Practically any app you have on your phone can be installed and run on the laptop. But almost all those phone apps are just that, mobile versions, with most not even aware that they are not installed on a phone.
Those that have at least some tailoring to the laptop form come in a few different types, categorised by Google broadly under “compatible with desktop”, which means they should support mouse and keyboard controls; “optimised for desktop”, which means they should scale properly to the laptop’s display; and “made for desktop”, which are a handful of Android apps redesigned with the laptop in mind.
Only the last category really seems to make any difference to the quality of the app, and even then most of them are still not of the same calibre as their equivalents found on Windows or macOS.
Even Google’s apps are a mixed bag. Google Calendar can only show one account at any one time, so you can’t see your personal, work and shared calendars on one screen like you can on Android.
Google Docs starts as its own app, but when you actually open a document it just becomes another Chrome window hidden behind the Chrome logo on the task bar, not the Docs logo.
The Files app shows your Google Drive files, but you can’t pin locations to the side bar to quickly access your commonly used folders, making it a time-consuming dig through endless folders to find things each time.
Even the Chrome browser is not quite up to par with its Windows or macOS counterpart, lacking features such as split-screen tabs, the auto-hiding vertical tab bar or the ability to have multiple profiles, such as a personal and work account.
Google has an app-gap problem and one that will only be solved if developers are convinced Googlebook OS is going to take off and be worth spending time and money making better apps for.
Bring your Android phone into your Googlebook
The other big selling point is deep integration with your Android phone. Google calls this “better together”, which is a collection of features that mirror capabilities of iPhones with Macs or Microsoft’s Link to Windows.
Some of the features are like magic. You can search the files on your phone straight from the Files app on the laptop without plugging it in, see your notifications from your phone, continue tasks on your laptop from your phone and even use apps cast from your phone.
As useful as these features sound, many are not up to scratch. Streaming apps from your phone is so slow that I feel as though I can type entire sentences before they appear on screen in chat apps, and it is restricted to one app at a time. If you click on a synced notification from your phone, it will open in a cast app, even if you have the full app installed on your Googlebook. Even viewing files on your phone from the laptop is irritatingly slow.
The only apps I’ve reliably managed to get to appear with the ability to continue from where I was are Google Docs and Chrome on the phone.
It also took me two hours of troubleshooting to get an up-to-date Google Pixel 11 Pro to actually connect with the Googlebooks, despite using the phone to set them up in the first place.
Gemini
The other big selling point for Google is its Gemini integration into Googlebook OS. The Gemini app is just like it is on macOS and Windows. But it is the Magic Pointer feature, which appears when you wiggle the mouse to click or highlight something on your screen to send it to Gemini, that is the most novel.
You can use it to get Gemini to summarise text, explain something, search for things or generally chat. But I often hit a road block, such as Gemini refusing to generate images or saying it cannot add a date into my calendar in the mode Magic Cursor opens, which oddly isn’t within the desktop Gemini app. Sometimes it works, sometimes it doesn’t, and it is simply not joined up.
Magic Cue has been imported from Google’s Pixel phones, which is meant to pop up with helpful information such as calendar availability or a location in maps when you highlight a date or a place in a chat or email. But unlike on a Pixel phone, I have yet to get it to successfully activate in two weeks of testing.
Google’s super-charged voice dictation system called Rambler, also from the recent Pixels, does at least work as described. Press the dictation key and just speak naturally. Rambler will condense your speech into concise sentences removing filler words and errors.
Verdict
Googlebooks are full of excellent ideas about how a modern laptop should work. The hardware of the Acer and Asus machines I’ve tested is top notch, but the software just isn’t ready for prime time.
When it works it’s great, but it is filled with limitations that might be acceptable on a super-cheap laptop but never on a £1,000 premium machine.
Chrome is not as good as it is on a Mac or Windows PC. Google’s various apps are generally better on an Android phone and the third-party app ecosystem is a mess of poorly optimised mobile apps. Even the best desktop-optimised Android apps pale by comparison to their counterparts on Windows or macOS.
The Android phone-linking system should be the killer feature, but it is partly broken or simply not up to scratch. Even the Gemini integration is flakey.
Most of the Google-specific issues and software bugs are eminently fixable. But the app gap will take serious time, effort and money to convince third-party developers to fix.
Unless you want to spend at least £1,000 to be a beta tester, your money is better spent elsewhere for now.

Who exactly will be affected by the UK review of benefits for young people?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
06:00:17 UTC
15:00:17 KST

Who exactly will be affected by the UK review of benefits for young people?
Around one in eight 16- to 24-year-olds are ‘Neet’ – and Alan Milburn is hinting that the overhaul of their support may be controversial
With nearly 1 million young people not in education, employment or training (a cohort known as “Neets”), the government and its advisers have signalled that welfare benefits may be cut to fund more job support for them. What may change and who will be affected?
Why are politicians talking about Neets?
Ministers are expected to make a major policy announcement in November on plans to tackle what has been called a “generational challenge” and a “moral crisis” – the persistent number of young people in the UK who are out of work, not in college or training, or economically inactive. The head of the government-commissioned review of young people and work, Alan Milburn, has been vigorously preparing the ground in media interviews for what he has hinted will be a major – and potentially controversial – overhaul of employment and benefits support for young people.
Who are Neets?
An estimated 960,000 16- to 24-year-olds are currently classified as Neet according to official estimates – around one in eight young people – with this number forecast to rise to 1.25m by the early 2030s. Although the concept of Neets has been around for more than three decades, Milburn has warned the current cohort are different: not simply jobless but estranged from the world of work. Some 45% of 24-year-old Neets have never had a job. He says urgent action is needed to prevent this group becoming a “lost generation”.
What is the cause of this crisis?
It is partly the labour market: fewer entry-level roles and apprenticeships for young people, a decline in “Saturday jobs” that leave them less prepared for work, and in many areas, few decent job opportunities of any kind. It is also about the failure of state institutions – schools, the NHS, the welfare system – to prepare them for work. And, says Milburn, it is crucially about the increasing number of young people with “work-limiting health conditions” who he says have become economically marginalised because of their anxiety, depression or neurodevelopmental conditions such as autism.
Why is reform of welfare needed?
Milburn says that while the welfare system is not the cause of the Neet crisis, it exacerbates it by failing to provide enough meaningful advice and support to young people, especially those with health conditions. Plenty want to work, but job centre interactions with young people are often limited and “administrative” – paying their cash benefits – rather than providing a springboard for them to participate in work or training. The Department for Work and Pensions (DWP) does have two major employment schemes, the Youth Guarantee and Pathways to Work, with budgets of around £6bn over three years, but Milburn is sceptical about their ability to reach Neets.
Why does the government say it needs to cut benefits for young people?
In theory, ministers could invest in new and improved employment support schemes aimed at Neets without cutting benefits. But they insist benefit savings are needed to fund their vision. They say disability benefit spending on 16- to 24-year-olds – currently £800m a year on universal credit health and £3.2bn on personal independence payment (Pip) – is spiralling out of control. In addition, Milburn is adamant that the design of disability benefits can “trap” young people with incomes of £2,000 a month, while incentivising them not to look for work. For every £1 the DWP spends on employment support for young people, £25 is spent on benefits, says Milburn – a ratio he says must be rebalanced.
What benefits will be cut or reformed, how – and who will it affect?
Ministers and Milburn alike are tight-lipped about any changes, but they are likely to focus on universal credit health and Pip, and the mood music is they will be radical. There is speculation either or both could be cut entirely or dramatically restricted. Some on the right have called for benefits to be removed for young people with so-called “mild” mental health or autism conditions, though because most young Pip claimants have multiple conditions this is unlikely to save significant amounts. A parallel review of Pip by welfare minister Stephen Timms has ruled out means-testing of Pip. Milburn said young people with complex and enduring disabilities will be exempt from any benefit cuts.
What are the risks of cutting disability benefits for young people?
Campaigners say better job support is essential – but cutting benefits for a cohort already on low incomes will simply drive up poverty and hardship, making it harder for them to get a job. They argue that in many areas there simply aren’t the jobs or opportunities, however comprehensive the job support. Around a third of the 1 million Neets are not claiming benefits, so in theory any changes won’t affect them. The political risk for ministers is that changes spark a repeat of last year’s backbench rebellion on disability benefit cuts, which forced a humiliating government U-turn.

The political calculus of peace in Ukraine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
05:57:00 UTC
14:57:00 KST

The political calculus of peace in Ukraine
In Ukraine, calls for peace are testing both public opinion and political ambition.
Emergency services deal with the aftermath of a massive Russian missile and drone attack in Kyiv, Ukraine, on Sept. 8, 2026. (Kostiantyn Liberov / Libkos / Getty Images)
In Ukraine, few words carry as much weight — or as much political risk — as peace.
In early October, several prominent Ukrainian politicians publicly called for an end to Russia's war on terms many considered to be closer to the Kremlin's desires. Their proposals differed, but the public reaction revealed a deep-seated fear: that calls for peace could be a prelude to concessions to Moscow rather than a path to a just settlement.
For years, Ukraine's leadership framed victory, not compromise, as the ultimate goal of the war. But Donald Trump's return to the White House last year changed the political landscape, increasing pressure on Kyiv to negotiate an end to the war while insisting that any settlement must not come on Moscow’s terms.
Now, increasing Russian drone attacks on Kyiv, renewed tensions with Washington and stalled negotiations with Moscow have created fresh uncertainty over how — and on what terms — the war might end.
In these recent statements, critics see more than a desire to stop the fighting. They suspect political maneuvering: populist appeals, and politicians' attempts to position themselves for a future contest for power, or efforts to test how much compromise the public might tolerate.
"The main goal of all these statements is to see how society would react to such a scenario," said Olha Vasylevska-Smahliuk, a lawmaker from the ruling party. "The first is a peace deal with Russia, the second is the removal of the president, and the third is holding elections."
"Of course, we need peace," she added. "The question is under what conditions."
A peace plan backfires
As Ukrainian officials prepared for another round of talks with Washington, Oleksiy Goncharenko, then a lawmaker with the opposition European Solidarity, laid out his own plan for ending Russia's war.
In an Oct. 4 op-ed in one of Ukraine's leading publications, Goncharenko called for seeking an agreement with Moscow, arguing that this wouldn't be synonymous with surrender. He proposed a number of agreements mediated by third countries, with both sides making concessions and with the issue of the eastern Donbas region — the main territorial sticking point — addressed last. His plan also called for Russian to receive the same status as other minority languages in Ukraine and for the Moscow-affiliated Ukrainian Orthodox Church to be allowed to operate.
"Can we destroy Russia right now? No, we can’t. If we accept this objective reality, we can't fight until we cease to exist. We must know when to stop and preserve our state," Goncharenko said.
Critics argued that the proposals came too close to capitulation to Russia, a characterisation the lawmaker rejected.
Mykola Kniazhytskyi, a lawmaker from the same European Solidarity party, said peace depended first and foremost on Russian President Vladimir Putin. Russia has shown no willingness to make concessions or abandon its goal of seizing Donbas.
"Any calls for peace directed at Ukraine, and any accusations against the Ukrainian side in this regard, are clearly playing into Putin's hands and those politicians who seek to portray the victim as the guilty party and absolve the aggressor of responsibility," Kniazhytskyi told the Kyiv Independent.
For Kyiv, accepting a freeze along the current front line would already be a "huge concession," argues Olexiy Haran, politics professor at the Kyiv Mohyla Academy and research advisor at the Democratic Initiatives Foundation.
"Putin has no interest in negotiations or compromise. He wants it all."
"Twenty percent of our territory remains under occupation, where every day brings terror and the destruction of everything Ukrainian," he adds. "These are speculations. Putin has no interest in negotiations or compromise. He wants it all."
Goncharenko has long been a conspicuous figure in Ukrainian politics. One of parliament’s most recognisable lawmakers, he has amassed more than 200,000 Telegram followers.
Before joining former President Petro Poroshenko's team in 2014, he was part of the now banned Party of Regions and promoted pro-Russian narratives, including calls to make Russian Ukraine's second official language.
Since 2025, he has distinguished himself by voting against extending the mobilization in Ukraine, the only lawmaker to do so, and regularly criticized the country's draft policies. His positions have repeatedly put him at odds with his party, prompting questions about why he remained a member.
Several European Solidarity lawmakers told the Kyiv Independent that Goncharenko's views had been debated within the faction before, but expulsion had never been considered. The earlier disagreements concerned his rhetoric rather than the substance of his positions, they said. His peace proposal exposed a deeper ideological divide.
On Oct. 5, the party expelled him from its parliamentary faction.
A false divide
For months, lawmaker Danylo Hetmantsev has drawn a line between what he describes as Ukraine's "peace party" and "war party" — a framing critics say risks depicting those who support the country's defense as those who oppose peace itself.
More cautious in his rhetoric, Hetmantsev, a member of President Volodymyr Zelensky's Servant of the People party and chair of the parliament’s finance, tax and customs policy committee, places himself in the "peace party," which he says is "led by Zelensky."
Hetmantsev hasn't named people he considers part of the "war party." According to him, they "benefit from war" and "want to fight to the last Ukrainian."
Lawmaker Oleksandr Merezhko calls this narrative pro-Russian, arguing that it creates the false impression that Kyiv wants the war to continue. He traces the framing to the Kremlin, which used the term "war party" early after the full-scale invasion to describe Russian officials and businessmen advocating escalation.
Multiple lawmakers from Zelensky's party told the Kyiv Independent that they don’t share Hetmantsev's views. The Servant of the People’s 229 lawmakers hold different positions, they said, and Hetmantsev's viewpoint is not a common position within the party.
Another politician who surprisingly entered the debate was Ihor Terekhov, mayor of Kharkiv, Ukraine's second-largest city. Responding to an op-ed by Valerii Zaluzhnyi, Ukraine's ambassador to the U.K. and former commander-in-chief, Terekhov interpreted it as suggesting that war was Ukraine's inevitable future. Zaluzhnyi's article didn't explicitly say that, arguing instead that ending Russia's war couldn't be treated as a business deal.
"Our ability to endure the war should not be seen as consent to living through it. We strive for peace and prosperity," Terekhov wrote on social media in response.
Terekhov is among the handful of regional politicians regularly featured in nationwide polls. Pollsters have grouped Terekhov and Hetmantsev as potential participants in a joint political project. A spring survey conducted by the Socis sociology center suggested that this hypothetical party could outperform the ruling Servant of the People party.
Terekhov, 59, is among the Ukrainian mayors who reinvented themselves after Russia's full-scale invasion. He has faced criticism for his shifting positions on language and culture, though his public image since 2022 has largely revolved around leading the city battered by Moscow's relentless attacks.
One of Ukraine's best-known mayors, Terekhov is seen as loyal to the central government and has become a familiar face in Kyiv's power circles. During the recent government reshuffle, Terekhov was one of the candidates for the prime minister's post, pro-government lawmakers told the Kyiv Independent.
"(The politicians) are playing to certain sentiments in society, saying what part of the electorate wants to hear," Merezhko says. "That's the problem. We need to put populism aside and stop looking at everything through the lens of the next election. We don't know when a ceasefire will come."
Peace at what price?
Some see the recent flurry of peace proposals as an attempt to see how far public opinion has shifted, as they grapple with intensified Russian attacks and brace for another difficult winter.
"I wouldn’t rule out the possibility that the authorities are testing the waters to see how society reacts," Haran says.
Recent polls showed that despite the hardships that Ukrainians face, public views on ending the war and the means of achieving peace have changed little over the past year.
The latest KIIS poll published Oct. 19 showed around 64% of respondents blamed Russia for stalling peace negotiations and rejected the idea that Ukraine’s government should be more willing to compromise.
The same poll found that around 62% of Ukrainians are prepared to endure the war for as long as necessary.
For those who spoke to the Kyiv Independent, calls for peace overlook a basic obstacle — Putin has shown no willingness to compromise. His demand that Ukraine withdraw from Donbas comes with no guarantee that Russian forces would not advance into neighbouring regions.
"Russia's terms are well known," says Mykyta Poturaiev, a lawmaker from Zelensky's party. "Calling for peace on Moscow's terms is tantamount to calling for the destruction of the Ukrainian state. A country has an electorate, Russian-occupied territories don't."

Russia’s FSB security service publishes dramatic videos of political arrests. A human rights group says roughly a quarter of the arrest scenes it examined were staged.
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
05:56:25 UTC
14:56:25 KST

Russia’s FSB security service publishes dramatic videos of political arrests. A human rights group says roughly a quarter of the arrest scenes it examined were staged.
After Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, the Federal Security Service, or FSB, began posting far more short videos online showing the detention of people facing political prosecution in Russia. The videos are often staged to intimidate government opponents and show off the security service’s effectiveness and power, according to a study by Memorial’s Support for Political Prisoners project. The researchers analyzed 70 criminal cases in which those facing prosecution appeared in such videos.
After Russia invaded Ukraine in 2022, mentions of the FSB on the Telegram channels of the Russian state-run propaganda outlets TASS and RIA Novosti increased two- to threefold, Memorial found. The share of posts mentioning the FSB that included videos also nearly doubled over the course of the war.
Memorial said these videos cannot be treated as reliable accounts of events: Detention footage may contradict detainees’ testimony in criminal case files, and recorded confessions are often obtained through torture. The human rights advocates see them primarily as propaganda videos that reveal a great deal about the security service itself.
Memorial identified five recurring elements in the videos: surveillance footage, the arrest, the results of a search or inspection, the detainee’s transfer, and a confession.
Surveillance footage appears in only six of the 70 cases studied. Filming a suspect committing an alleged crime before detaining them is difficult, and the results aren’t dramatic enough, the human rights advocates said. Memorial emphasized that all six cases using such footage were based on FSB entrapment operations.
Security officers try to make the arrests look as violent and dramatic as possible. They throw suspects to the floor, twist their arms behind their backs, and grab them by the hair. Memorial estimates that roughly a quarter of these scenes are staged. Camera operators often arrive before the officers, and detainees behave unnaturally on camera: For example, they ignore approaching armed officers until the last moment or answer their questions without missing a beat right after hitting the ground.
Filming rarely wraps up in a single take, so officers prefer to film detentions in deserted places. In these videos, suspects can be seen walking past garages or across open fields. Confessions are recorded over and over until the officers are satisfied with the tone and wording.
Officers use both torture and deception to get detainees to take part in filming. Crimean artist Bohdan Ziza said FSB officers filmed at least five versions of his confession and apology. He said they beat him when they felt his remorse was not sincere enough, and that the script was revised each time and cleared again with their superiors.
FSB officers told Donetsk resident Georgy Tabuyev he would get just two years in prison if he unpacked a parcel containing explosives on camera. Tabuyev agreed but ended up receiving a 14-year prison sentence. The video was never published.
The human rights advocates believe these staged videos have become a tool of political repression in their own right. The FSB uses them to try to intimidate government opponents, create a sense that the security services control everything, and impose its own version of events.

“How far does the Truth admit of being learned? … For what a man knows he cannot seek, since he knows it; and what he does not know he cannot seek, since he does not even know for what to seek. Socrates thinks the difficulty through in the doctrine of Recollection, by which all learning and inquiry is interpreted as a kind of remembering; one who is ignorant needs only a reminder to help him come to himself in the consciousness of what he knows. Thus the Truth is not introduced into the individual from without, but was within him.”
– Søren Kierkegaard, Philosophical Fragments

Drone strike in disputed Sudan-South Sudan area kills dozens, minister says
NAIROBI, Oct 20 - At least 73 people were killed when drones struck a market in the disputed Abyei region along the border of South Sudan and Sudan, the caretaker information minister for the jointly administered region said on Tuesday, accusing Sudan's army of carrying out the attack.
The minister did not provide evidence for his claim of who was responsible for Monday's attack.
Abyei is an oil-rich area that is jointly administered by South Sudan and Sudan, which have both staked claims to it. It experiences frequent bouts of violence, with clashes usually involving rival ethnic groups or armed militias.
"Around 73 people have been killed and 19 have been wounded ... a number of drones were shot yesterday by the Sudanese armed forces," Yohana Akol Ngor, the caretaker minister of information of the Abyei region, told Reuters on Tuesday.
Last year, at least six Bangladeshi peacekeepers were killed and eight wounded in a drone attack by separatist armed groups on a UN base in Abyei, Bangladesh's armed forces said.
South Sudan's foreign ministry said in a statement late Monday that drones struck a market located north of Abyei town, but did not specify the number of civilian casualties resulting from the attack.
The ministry said it had summoned the Sudanese ambassador to convey the government's "strong protest and deep concern regarding the attack and its implications for the security of civilians and the stability of the Abyei Area."
The medical charity Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) said in a statement that it was treating more than 20 wounded people at the nearby Ameth Bek Hospital.
"So far we received over 20 patients, including several critical cases. Patients with burns were also admitted. We are providing surgical services and wound dressing, along with other emergency care," said Christian Lindauer, MSF medical activities manager at Ameth Bek Hospital.
Sudan has been gripped by war since April 2023 between the Sudanese Armed Forces and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces. The conflict has drawn in local militias and foreign powers, devastated large parts of the country and created what the United Nations has described as the world's worst humanitarian crisis. REUTERS

Trump administration is holding back supply of missiles for Patriot to Ukraine - WP
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
08:55:03 EEST
14:55:03 KST

Trump administration is holding back supply of missiles for Patriot to Ukraine - WP
Kyiv • UNN
According to WP, Pete Hegseth has not taken steps to approve the transfer of Patriot interceptor missiles to Ukraine. The United States says intelligence sharing is continuing.
The Trump administration has not approved the transfer to Ukraine of interceptor missiles needed to defend the country from Russian missile and drone attacks, officials said on October 19. The Washington Post reports this, UNN writes.
Details
"At least some of the Patriot interceptor missile transfers are coming from countries friendly to Ukraine, which requires Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth's approval of the transfer," a U.S. official and three other people familiar with the situation said. The United States retains control because the weapons are manufactured by it and supplied abroad under an agreement stipulating that transfers to other countries require U.S. approval.
Officials said that "Hegseth has not formally rejected the transfers, but he also has not taken the necessary steps to approve them." "Hegseth has continued to approve certain U.S. assistance to Ukraine," they said.
In recent days, Trump has repeatedly criticized Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, the publication writes. Trump is increasingly blaming Zelenskyy for his problems with high energy prices and worsening political prospects ahead of the midterm elections. Ukraine has been attacking Russian oil refineries for months, one of its main strategies for putting pressure on the Kremlin, the publication writes.
The U.S. war with Iran, the publication notes, has placed enormous pressure on global stocks of Patriot interceptor missiles, and Ukraine has begun facing a shortage. The United States tends to send batches of interceptor missiles in small consignments, often several times, as they are produced, the publication indicates.
Ukraine and its partners are also searching worldwide for other stockpiles, urging countries to offer any interceptors they can afford.
A White House official who wished to remain anonymous to discuss sensitive diplomacy said that the United States "continues to play a constructive role in negotiations with both sides in pursuit of ending the war."
At the same time, Ukraine has experienced repeated disruptions to its early-warning systems for ballistic missile attacks, which rely on U.S. intelligence.
Asked whether the United States was still sharing intelligence with Ukraine, Trump replied on October 19: "We are sharing intelligence. We share a lot. We have given Ukraine a lot. You know what, we have given Ukraine a lot. They have given us nothing."
U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio insisted on October 19 that there had been "no pause whatsoever" in the sharing of U.S. intelligence with Ukraine.
Asked about Ukraine's claims that it had received no early warnings of recent attacks, Rubio said that "a couple of nights ago" there had been a "software issue" that was being investigated by the U.S. European Command.
In his statement, a senior Pentagon official said that "there have been no changes in the War Department's policy regarding intelligence sharing or any capabilities that we allow Europeans to provide to Ukraine."
An official who wished to remain anonymous to discuss sensitive diplomatic matters said that the program under which NATO allies supply Ukraine with U.S.-made weapons (PURL) "continues unchanged."
"Relations between Trump and Zelenskyy have been strained for years. But this month they deteriorated significantly during talks in Miami between representatives of the two governments, when Ukrainian officials rejected the White House's efforts to force them to stop strikes on Russian energy targets, including diesel refineries," U.S. and Ukrainian officials said.
During that meeting, Trump announced that the United States had reached an agreement with the Kremlin that lifted U.S. sanctions on Russian diesel fuel exports.
Oil analysts expressed doubt that the deal would have a significant impact on diesel prices in the United States. They noted that although Ukrainian strikes contributed to the rise in the global price of diesel fuel, a larger factor driving prices higher was the U.S. war with Iran and disruptions to global oil supplies caused by Iran's efforts to block the Strait of Hormuz.
"However, the deal gave Trump a direct interest in ensuring that Ukraine did not strike Russian oil refineries, fueling tensions between Kyiv and Washington and, in effect, bringing the Trump administration partly closer to Putin," the publication said.
"Zelenskyy's public statements that Trump was choosing the other side and that the White House was not on the right \"side of history\" heightened tensions," U.S. officials said.
On Monday, Zelenskyy spoke to U.S. senators during a group telephone call, during which he discussed the challenges facing Kyiv amid a sharp deterioration in relations with Trump.
Several prominent Republicans are increasingly criticizing Trump's recent concessions to Russia, especially his decision on Friday to lift the sanctions established by a bipartisan bill passed in honor of the late Senator Lindsey Graham, a staunch Republican supporter of Ukraine.

US President Donald Trump on Monday used violent unrest in France as an argument against Democrats in his battle to defend a Kansas Senate seat long held by Republicans but in danger of falling to his political opponents.
Trump's rally on behalf of Republican incumbent Roger Marshall was his latest foray into conservative states where Republican candidates are on defense due to voter frustrations over the Iran war and rising prices.
"I love you Kansas, but I'm here for a guy named Roger Marshall," Trump said.

First-term Senator Marshall is in a close fight with Democratic candidate Adam Hamilton, pastor of a Methodist megachurch, who is running against Trump’s tariff agenda and what he calls the president's “erratic leadership.”
“He wants you to repent for being born White,” Trump said of Hamilton.

"We need someone who can sort heifers and steers," he said.

The tightness of the race is emblematic of the challenges looming for Republicans in the November 3 midterm elections as they try to defy political headwinds and retain control of the Senate and the House of Representatives.

US voters' economic concerns

Democrats need a net gain of four seats in both the US House of Representatives and US Senate to overturn Republicans' narrow 218-214 and 53-47 majorities.

Kansans have proven a willingness to cross parties, as voters have elected a Democratic governor, Laura Kelly, for the last two terms. "I don't think it's ever easy to get elected here," said Gina Seman, a Trump voter from Towanda, Kansas, noting that Republican candidates in the past have taken their popularity for granted.

Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
05:50:03 UTC
14:50:03 KST

Voters in Canada’s Alberta have overwhelmingly rejected a proposal to begin a process toward independence, the national broadcaster CBC has projected, delivering a victory for the prime minister, Mark Carney, and supporters of Canadian unity.
With more than 1m votes counted early on Tuesday, about 76% supported remaining in Canada, compared with 23% who backed beginning a process that could lead to separation. About a third of ballots had been counted.
Even though the vote was not explicitly about independence – a point that frustrated separatists – the ballot question nonetheless exposed divisions in Alberta’s politics and raised questions about the durability of national unity.
Delays at roughly 100 of the 1,400 at polling stations across the province pushed results back by more than two hours, but shortly after polls closed on Monday evening the results suggested a decisive win for those looking to remain in Canada.
The separation question – whether to remain in Canada or begin a legal process that could lead to a second vote – was one of 10 put to Albertans on Monday. The others covered issues including immigration, healthcare, education and the province’s constitutional powers. Elections Alberta said the remaining results could take days to count.
In the days leading up to the vote, provincial leaders and federal politicians crisscrossed the province to make the case for a unified country.
Carney, who grew up in Edmonton, warned against a vote from residents of the oil-rich province simply looking to “send a message” to the federal government.
“A vote against Canada is a dangerous bluff that will lead to years of deep uncertainty and lost opportunities for Albertans and Canadians,” he told an energetic crowd last week.
The Conservative leader, Pierre Poilievre, whose parliamentary seat is in the province, told a crowd of supporters that Albertans were not “quitters”.
“To those people who are thinking about taking out their frustration on the current government by voting for separation in the referendum, I say this: Canada is more than a government,” he said. “It is a people, a flag, a land, a history and a promise.”
Data from Elections Alberta indicated roughly 43% of eligible voters – or 1.3 million Albertans – had already cast ballots before Monday’s vote through advance voting and mail-in ballots. That figure pointed to a potentially higher turnout than the province’s last referendum in 2021.
The Alberta premier, Danielle Smith, said publicly that she would vote to remain in Canada but that she would not require elected members of her party to do the same.
Her tenure as leader of the United Conservative party is due in large part to separatists within the party who ousted her predecessor, Jason Kenney. In recent months, Smith has tried to placate both the separatists and federalists in the party, in a province where a majority is not interested in secession.
The referendum has also become a political liability for Smith’s party, which has seen popular support tumble in recent months, including the loss of a one-time conservative stronghold in a byelection.
Still, members of the separatist movement told the Guardian they would continue their push for independence.
In an interview before the results, the Calgary mayor, Jeromy Farkas, a staunch opponent of the independence movement, said the city’s “best future is here, as a Canadian city,” amid fears that uncertainty could lead to capital flight.
“I am Canadian because I’m Canadian, not in a transactional way and regardless of the flavour of prime minister,” Farkas said. “And I’m going to continue to make the case for how our future is strongest together, because no result will permanently put this to bed. “The separatist movement sees this as a long-term project.”

Lavrov reaffirmed Russia’s readiness to help resolve the situation surrounding Iran and briefed Iranian officials on his talks on Sunday in Bahrain with representatives of countries on the Arabian Peninsula.
The two sides stressed the need for close coordination on developments in the Middle East, the Gulf, the South Caucasus and the Caspian Sea, according to the ministry.
They also discussed expanding political, economic and investment ties, including joint transport, logistics and energy projects.
Cooperation would continue through government agencies, parliaments, regional authorities and businesses, the ministry added.

Rare river otter captured on camera at Kazakhstan’s Charyn National Park
                  09:41, 20 October 2026
                
A camera trap has captured footage of a rare Central Asian river otter (Lutra lutra seistanica), listed in Kazakhstan's Red Book of endangered species, at Charyn National Park, Qazinform News Agency reports.
The river otter is a rare mammal whose survival depends heavily on aquatic habitats. It typically lives along rivers and other bodies of water, making the preservation of these natural environments essential for its conservation.
Camera trap footage allows researchers to observe the otter in its natural habitat, study its distribution and develop measures to protect this rare animal.
