"Kind, compassionate, a person of integrity — totally committed to strongly representing the people of that beautiful part of Victoria," he said.
Haines has represented the Indi community since 2019, when she became the first independent MP to succeed another independent in parliament.
Indi had been a Liberal seat for 82 years before Haines' predecessor, Cathy McGowan, was elected in 2013.
Allegra Spender, independent MP for Wentworth, described Haines as an inspiration for the recent wave of independents.
"She doesn’t play politics. She’s actually just really interested in what is best for her community and best for the country, and frankly, you know, a true inspiration, and obviously one of the trailblazers in the independent movement," she told the ABC.

In her maiden speech to parliament, Haines described how her rural upbringing had shaped her.
"I am, like each of you, the sum of my family, my community and the ecology of the places I have lived in," she said.
Haines grew up on a dairy farm in Eurack, near Colac in Victoria's south-west. With her parents and four brothers, she lived next door to her grandmother's farm.
Two of Haines' great-aunts had trained as nurses at St Vincent's Hospital in Melbourne.
"It was they who pretty much predetermined that I should also be a St Vincent's nurse — and so it was," she said.
Working as a former midwife and nurse, Haines has spent decades in Victoria's rural health system. At 26, she became matron of the Chiltern Bush Nursing Hospital. She later worked at Wangaratta Hospital, where some of her constituents first met her.

She now lives with her husband Phil on a cattle farm outside Wangarratta.

She has also been a key figure in the creation of the National Anti-Corruption Commission (NACC), and now serves as the deputy chair of the parliamentary committee on the NACC.

Australian lawmaker Helen Haines has lost a leg after being struck by a car in what Prime Minister Anthony Albanese described as a deliberate attack, local media reported on Tuesday.
Political violence is rare in Australia, but law enforcement have documented a steady rise in threats and abuse directed towards the nation's elected officials in recent years.
Albanese said the attack was a "test of our character" and led an outpouring of support for Haines, widely praised for her efforts to increase transparency in politics and crack down on corruption.
She was hit by a vehicle outside her office in the town of Wangaratta, just over 200 kilometres northeast of Melbourne, at around 3:35 pm (0435 GMT) on Monday.
Witnesses told national broadcaster ABC they heard a bang and saw a woman pinned between two cars.
She was getting things from the trunk of her car when the attack happened, Albanese said.
The driver did a U-turn to get back to her after passing, he added.
"It's clear this was a deliberate act," he said.
'Hero' barber
The 65-year-old was critically injured.
She underwent surgery overnight at the Alfred hospital in Melbourne.
National broadcaster ABC and the Sydney Morning Herald reported she had lost a leg.
"Helen remains in hospital in a critical condition. I spoke with her husband Phil last night, and she underwent surgery last night," Albanese told Australian breakfast show Sunrise.
"All Australians' thoughts are with the family, with her many friends, with her community," he added.
The 43-year-old male driver of the vehicle was restrained by local barber Ricky Jefferies — now widely hailed as a "hero".
Jefferies told journalists his first thought had been: "my wife would be disappointed if I'm injured".
"My family, they're everything, and my community is second to that," a visibly shaken Jefferies told journalists.
"The other people here were just, they did so much more than me... they deserve the credit."
'Devastating'
The driver was then arrested and police found a knife in his car.
Australian media reported that he was known to police and that his name is Brendan Nugent.
An investigation by federal police, the counter-terrorism squad and Victoria state law enforcement is ongoing and he remained in custody on Tuesday morning.
Federal police said they were working with local law enforcement on possible charges, including the offence of causing harm to a government official — which carries a maximum penalty of 10 years' imprisonment.
The alleged attacker's motive remains unknown and Albanese has refused to speculate while the investigation takes place.
But he has bemoaned the fact that political debate in Australia had grown too heated and personal over the past few years and pointed to a significant increase in threats against elected officials.
"It's important in a democracy that people are allowed to have disagreements," he said.
"But that doesn't mean that you have to draw into question people's motivations or their patriotism or who they are."
"We've seen, I think, political discourse go in the wrong direction in recent times," he said.
Haines entered parliament in 2019 after working as a nurse and midwife, becoming known for stances such as supporting stronger climate action.
"This afternoon, our beloved Helen was involved in an incident outside her Wangaratta Electorate Office, and is receiving medical care," her family said.
"We thank the swift assistance of bystanders and the dedicated health workers who assisted her, and police for their response."
Tributes to the independent lawmaker have poured in from across the political spectrum.
Conservative opposition leader Angus Taylor described it as a "shocking day for our nation".
And far-right Senator Pauline Hanson said "violence against any elected representative, whoever they are and whatever they stand for, is never acceptable in Australia".

Witkoff plans trip to Russia after talks with Zelenskyy in Oslo - Axios

Witkoff plans trip to Russia after talks with Zelenskyy in Oslo - Axios
Kyiv • UNN
Steve Witkoff will meet with Zelenskyy and European leaders in Oslo to prepare a peace proposal for Russia. After that he plans to meet with Putin.
U.S. Envoy Steve Witkoff is traveling to Oslo, Norway, on October 20 for talks with President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy and European leaders. After that, Witkoff plans to travel to Russia, where he expects to meet with Kremlin leader Vladimir Putin. Axios reports this, citing a U.S. official, writes UNN.
Details
The talks will bring together Ukraine, its European allies, and the United States, which seek to develop a peace proposal to present to Russia.
The talks in Oslo are expected to be attended by President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy, Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre, representatives of the E4 countries (the United Kingdom, France, Germany, and Poland), and EU and NATO officials.
Kushner and Witkoff plan talks in Norway on the war in Ukraine - Reuters20.10.26, 01:13 • 5592 views
The U.S. official said that after Oslo, Witkoff also plans to travel to Russia, where he hopes to meet with Kremlin leader Vladimir Putin and present ideas developed in close consultation with Ukraine and its European partners.
Trump adviser Jared Kushner has the flu and will not attend the meeting in Oslo in person, but will participate virtually, the U.S. official said.
The planned meetings in Oslo are based on discussions held at Witkoff's Shell Bay club in the Miami area, where Zelenskyy committed to reviewing and advancing a number of proposals aimed at creating a path toward a comprehensive and lasting peace agreement, the U.S. official added.
The U.S. official said that representatives of the United States, Ukraine, and Europe had worked together over the past week to develop proposals.
"Steve and Jared also spoke with President Zelenskyy on Sunday to discuss progress and next steps," the U.S. official said.
The trip is also expected to include efforts to secure the release of Stephen Hubbard, a retired American teacher whom the United States says is being unlawfully detained in Russia.
What the discussions are focused on
The U.S. official said the discussions are focused on two parallel tracks:
-  "securing Ukraine's future: establishing a sovereign, secure, and prosperous future for Ukraine, including credible security guarantees, European integration, and a comprehensive postwar economic structure that meets Ukraine's financial needs and creates opportunities for long-term growth and investment"; 
-  "creating the conditions for lasting peace: developing a comprehensive proposal for Russia that would address the issues necessary to end the war, establish a new and sustainable security architecture between Russia and Europe, and explore opportunities for postwar economic cooperation". 
"President Trump has begun an intensive process of developing a comprehensive peace proposal with Ukraine and Europe, and the next step is to determine whether this work can serve as the basis for serious negotiations with Russia," the U.S. official said.
"These discussions remain dynamic, and substantial work is still underway. President Trump's goal is clear: to stop the killing, end the war, and create the conditions for a lasting peace that benefits Ukraine, Russia, Europe, and the United States," he noted.

Doomsday preacher convicted of mass murder of 190 children, starvation deaths in Kenya cult case
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
05:33:09 UTC
14:33:09 KST

More than three years after Kenyan police unearthed mass graves linked to a starvation cult led by evangelist Paul Mackenzie, the preacher was convicted of murder for the deaths of 190 children and one adult.
Mackenzie's case has gripped the East African nation since officers found human remains in a forest near the Indian Ocean town of Malindi in April 2023, kicking off an investigation that would eventually unearth over 400 bodies, nearly half of them children.
The former taxi driver founded the Good News International Church in 2003, preaching increasingly apocalyptic sermons and urging his followers to starve themselves and their children to death so they could go to heaven before the world ended.
In a March 2023 YouTube video, Mackenzie - who had thousands of followers in person and online - said that he was guided by "the voice of Christ" when he preached messages about the world coming to an end that year.
"I followed the voice that told me I had finished the work," he said.
President said deaths should have been prevented
Videos of the preacher show him dressed in nondescript clothing, speaking calmly to hundreds of people as he recounted his experiences as an exorcist and his victory over "demonic" spirits.
Mackenzie denied charges of murder, manslaughter, child torture and terrorism in a case that highlighted the failings of Kenyan authorities and the lack of oversight governing churches in the predominantly Christian country.
The Kenya National Commission on Human Rights, an independent body, said it was deplorable that Mackenzie could have been first arrested in 2017 and charged with radicalization but continued to operate for years.
"This points to a failure in the investigation and prosecution processes. The arrest should have triggered investigations that would have saved the lives of several people," the KNCHR said in a 2024 report.
Kenyan President William Ruto has said that government agencies should have been able to prevent the deaths, adding that he took responsibility as president.
Dozens of children found living in compound
Mackenzie grew up in Kwale, a rural county in southeast Kenya, and moved to Malindi in the early 1990s to work as a taxi driver.
There, he became increasingly focused on religion, Japheth Charo, who worked as a driver alongside him, told Reuters in 2023.
"He started attacking other faiths like Muslims and Catholics. His preaching started becoming extreme," said Charo, whose family had joined Mackenzie's church but left after his sermons started to alarm them.
In 2012, Mackenzie registered a TV company called Good News Media, and he broadcast sermons on a YouTube channel that had 7,000 subscribers, KNCHR wrote in a report on the case.
Police searched Mackenzie's Malindi compound in 2017 and found dozens of children living there without attending school. He was charged with offering education at an unregistered facility but continued his teachings until 2019, when his church was shut down, and he relocated to the Shakahola Forest.
People were lured there by the promise of affordable arable land but found armed militia who enforced the fasting and eventual deaths of followers, KNCHR found. Those who defied orders to fast or tried to escape were strangled or clubbed to death, it added.
Starve themselves before the world's end
Mackenzie, believed to be in his early 50s, is a domineering figure who forced his followers to cut themselves off from society, forbidding them from engaging with schools or hospitals, institutions he branded as satanic, relatives of victims said.
"He told them to starve themselves ahead of the world's end on April 15, saying he would be the last one and that he would lock the doors," Stephen Mwiti, whose wife and six children were among the fatalities, told Reuters in 2023.
Mackenzie's grip on his followers continued even after the graves in Shakahola were exposed. Prosecutors charged him in connection with the deaths of 52 other people after bodies were exhumed last year in Kwa Binzaro village, some 30 km (18 miles) from Shakahola.
They said he masterminded and oversaw the offenses at Kwa Binzaro while in detention, using radical teachings to draw victims to the remote site. Mackenzie has pleaded not guilty in that case.

14:32:59 KST

Pope Leo will hold a general audience with pilgrims at the Vatican on Wednesday for the first time since undergoing surgery for lung cancer, the Vatican said.
The 71-year-old pontiff had an operation on October 13 to remove the lower lobe of his right lung, fueling speculation about how his illness might change his 17-month papacy.
Leo pledged on Sunday, in his first public event since the surgery, that he would slowly resume his usual activities as the leader of the world's 1.4 billion Catholics.
The pope hosts a general audience with pilgrims on most Wednesdays of the year. It is held in St. Peter's Square when there is good weather, and the pope often tours the crowds, usually in the tens of thousands, in an open-top popemobile.
Leo has been diagnosed with lung adenocarcinoma, the most common form of lung cancer. The diagnosis, for the youngest pope in decades, who was elected only in May 2025, caused shock.
Pope's surgery was a success
The pope's doctors have said his surgery was completed successfully, without complications. They have not yet disclosed the size of the tumor or whether the disease had spread to nearby lymph nodes, key factors in determining prognosis.
The Vatican has provided no indication of Leo's schedule beyond Wednesday.
The pope is due to visit Uruguay, Argentina and Peru from November 6 to 17, on one of the most intense trips arranged for a Catholic leader in decades, but it remains unclear whether that trip will go forward.
Leo's lead surgeon has said the pope could be fully recovered in time for the trip, but the Vatican's secretary of state has indicated the pope may need to adjust the pace of his schedule to aid in recovery.

Researchers use ChatGPT-style technology to predict stroke risk from a person’s DNA
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
05:32:38 UTC
14:32:38 KST

A new AI tool that identifies genetic risk factors for stroke could open the door to more personalised prevention and treatment.
Researchers have developed an AI model that analyses a person’s DNA to catch genetic risk factors for stroke — the second leading cause of death worldwide.
A team at the University of Technology Sydney (UTS) has identified specific genes that show a higher predisposition to ischaemic stroke — the most common type of stroke, in which a blood clot blocks blood flow to the brain.
“When someone has a stroke, particularly at a young age, they often want to know whether other family members are also at risk,” said Kairui Guo, the study’s corresponding author. “These new AI tools will provide the ability to better help families understand that risk.”
Genetics account for roughly 38% of an individual's stroke risk, according to previous research.
“Traditionally, in thinking about stroke risk, genetics hasn’t been a main consideration; however, this study highlights the significant impact of genetic factors,” said Guo, adding that processing that much data at an individual level to provide a personalised assessment would be impossible without AI.
To improve stroke risk prediction, the team created a new AI model based on transformers — the same technology that underpins large language models such as ChatGPT — and trained it on genetic variations to identify links to ischaemic stroke.
The model identified 18 genetic variants associated with ischaemic stroke. It pointed to key genes, such as EDEM2 (active in the brain cortex) and KANK2 (in whole blood), as major contributors to stroke predisposition.
The team tested the model on two major medical datasets, which together included more than 40,000 people.
It successfully categorised individuals into low, medium and high genetic risk groups. Over time, individuals placed in the high-risk group were 21% more likely to suffer a first-time ischaemic stroke compared with those in the low-risk group.
Until now, scientists have estimated genetic risk using polygenic risk scores (PRS) — a statistical tool that estimates a person’s genetic risk of developing a disease, based on the combined effects of many genetic variations. However, this method overlooks how different genetic variations interact with one another or how their specific positions along the DNA sequence affect overall risk.
Towards more personalised medicine
The new model could pave the way for future personalised and targeted treatments.
“AI can be used to find associations between human genes and disease, and build personalised risk assessments, to help prevent a potentially life-changing or fatal event,” said Jie Lu, director of the Australian Artificial Intelligence Institute.
Lu said the next step is a multimodal AI tool that can combine a genetic risk assessment with other types of data, including health and lifestyle surveys, scans and imaging, to better assess stroke risk.
“Genetics are only one part of stroke risk. The ability to combine a genetic score with clinical and lifestyle information, including established risk factors such as blood pressure, age, atrial fibrillation, type 2 diabetes and cholesterol, could enhance monitoring and prevention,” said Lu.

Japan launches uncrewed space mission to become first to gather samples from Mars' moon Phobos
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
05:32:35 UTC
14:32:35 KST

Japan launched an uncrewed spacecraft toward the Martian moon Phobos on Tuesday on a mission intended to become the first to collect samples from the small rocky body and return them to Earth for analysis.
The Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency's Martian Moons eXploration spacecraft lifted off aboard an H3 rocket before dawn from the Tanegashima Space Center in southwestern Japan.
The spacecraft is expected to reach Mars in August 2027 and return samples to Earth in 2031. JAXA hopes the mission will shed light on the origin of the two moons of Mars and deepen the understanding of our solar system's early stages.
Japanese space mission aims to collect at least 10 grams from Phobos
Phobos, the larger of the two Martian moons, orbits the planet three times a day. Phobos has an irregular shape with dimensions of about 27 km by 22 km by 18 km, and orbits roughly 6,000 km above the Martian surface.
JAXA aims to collect at least 10 grams of material from its surface and return it to Earth for analysis.
The launch marked the first interplanetary mission for Japan's H3 rocket. The country's flagship launcher experienced a high-profile failure on its inaugural flight in 2023 when its second-stage engine failed to ignite, but has since completed a series of mostly successful launches.

District heating prices rising across Estonia this winter
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
05:28:00 UTC
14:28:00 KST

District heating prices rising across Estonia this winter
District heating prices are rising across the country this autumn, but vary by region from 1 percent in Tartu in the south to 30 percent in Narva in the east.
The Competition Authority said it is difficult to say how much the cost of heating apartment buildings will rise on average this year.
"Among the larger areas, we can say that prices are on the rise, but again, to very different degrees. In Tartu, for example, the price is rising by about 1.1 percent, in Pärnu by nearly 14 percent, in Tallinn by 8.5 percent, but in Narva by more than 30 percent. And prices also vary because the networks are very different. The Competition Authority publishes these tariffs on its website, where prices range from €53 to €150," said Competition Authority Director General Evelin Pärn-Lee.
Narva uses only natural gas for district heating, which is expensive. The price of heating in the city depends on whether Enefit Power can produce heat for Narva using shale oil.
Narva Mayor Jaan Toots (Center Party) said a conditional special permit has been received from the Environmental Board, but Enefit Power is seeking further clarification "on the precise conditions under which shale oil can be used".
"And if that oil is used, our price per megawatt-hour will fall to around €65. Today, as we know, it is €137 with gas. If the price of gas rises, they will be able to use it. And the average price in winter should then come to somewhere around €90," he said.
Prices of almost all types of heating are set to rise this year.
8.5% rise in Tallinn
Utility and energy company Utilitas has said a rise of up to 10 percent is expected in nearly half of its district heating areas.
At the end of last week, the Competition Authority approved Utilitas' new maximum district heating price in Tallinn at €84 per megawatt-hour.
"We have nevertheless managed to keep the price increase relatively under control. The price in Tallinn will rise by 8.5 percent from mid-November. The price of natural gas has more than doubled over the past year, wood chips have become more expensive, the cost of energy from the Iru plant has risen, and essentially all input costs have increased," said Robert Kitt, chairman of the management board of Utilitas Eesti.
Utilitas hopes to obtain a special permit to use oil shale for heating and to launch the Paljassaare heat pump plant. In that case, the price would not rise any further.
"The current price has been set based on the best information available today, and naturally we expect the large-scale wastewater and seawater heat pump plant in Paljassaare to begin operating. We also hope to replace some of the remaining gas with shale oil," Kitt said.

Israel’s elections 2026 explained in maps and charts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
05:25:31 UTC
14:25:31 KST

Israel’s elections 2026 explained in maps and charts
Israelis vote on October 27 in the sixth election since 2019. Here’s how the system works and who gets left out.
Israelis go to the polls on October 27 to elect the 26th Knesset, in the first general vote since the genocide against Palestinians in Gaza and the wars on Lebanon and Iran.
Benjamin Netanyahu, the longest-serving prime minister in Israel’s history, with 19 years in office, is seeking another term while standing trial on corruption charges. His Likud party and the far-right coalition it leads are locked in a close race with a Jewish-led opposition bloc, with neither side appearing on track to win an outright majority in the 120-seat Knesset, Israel’s parliament.
About 7.3 million people aged 18 and above are eligible to vote, according to Israel’s Central Elections Committee. Most polling stations open from 7am to 10pm, and anyone still queuing when they close is entitled to vote. Election day is a national holiday.
Any party clearing an electoral threshold of 3.25 percent enters parliament, which sits for a four-year term. There are no term limits for a prime minister.
How voting works
Israelis vote for a party, not a candidate.
A majority requires 61 of the 120 seats and no party has ever won that outright. Finishing first does not guarantee power. Parties then have 28 days, with a possible extension of up to 14 days, to assemble a coalition reaching 61. If nobody manages it, the country votes again.
Seats are shared out in proportion to each party’s share of the national vote, so a party winning 30 percent of votes takes roughly 30 percent of seats. The votes for parties failing to secure 3.25 percent are discarded, which explains why small parties routinely merge before every election.
Who can and cannot vote?
About 7.3 million Israeli citizens are eligible to vote in this election, but they are not the only adults living under the government they choose.
Roughly three million adult Palestinians in Gaza, the occupied West Bank and occupied East Jerusalem have no vote in the government that controls their borders, movement and legal status.
Jewish Israelis and Palestinian citizens of Israel, who number about 1.2 million, can vote. So can adult settlers among the more than 750,000 Israelis living in the occupied West Bank and occupied East Jerusalem, who help elect the parliament that legislates over the land they live on.
Most Palestinians in occupied East Jerusalem hold Israeli residency, not citizenship. They can vote for Jerusalem’s city council but not for the Knesset.
The result is a sharp anomaly in the occupied West Bank, where a settler votes and a Palestinian family living nearby, under the same military authority, does not.
Most Israeli citizens living abroad also cannot vote, because Israel has no general absentee ballot and requires voters to be physically in the country on election day. Diplomats and state emissaries are the exception, casting their ballots at Israeli missions on October 20.
What are the main issues?
Israelis are dealing with a series of domestic and international issues this election cycle, including:
- October 7 security failures – Three years on, the government is yet to form a state commission of inquiry into the events of October 7, 2023, when a Hamas-headed attack led to the killing of some 1,200 people, with about 250 taken captive. Israel launched the genocidal war against Palestinians in the wake of the attack, killing at least 74,000 people and leaving most of the besieged territory in ruins.
- Ultra-Orthodox draft exemptions – Supporters of the exemptions say they protect full-time Torah study, but critics argue they place an unfair military burden on everyone else.
- Judicial reform – Netanyahu’s push to curb the Supreme Court’s powers, which sparked mass protests before the war on Gaza, remains a deep fault line. Critics see it as a threat to democracy, while supporters argue that the court has overstepped its authority.
- War and security – The public wants stability but remains wary of concessions in Gaza, the occupied West Bank and Lebanon. Netanyahu promised “total victory”, but Hamas and Hezbollah remain operational.
- Cost of living – High prices and modest wages are being further squeezed by soaring defence spending. Since 2023, Israel’s defence budget has doubled, increasing pressure on public finances.
Israel’s outgoing government
Netanyahu’s coalition held 60 of the Knesset’s 120 seats when parliament dissolved in July. It comprised Likud with 32 seats, Shas with 11, Religious Zionism with seven, Itamar Ben-Gvir’s Otzma Yehudit with six, and New Hope with four. Shas left the government in July 2025 but remained in the coalition and New Hope will merge into Likud for this election.
The opposition held 59 seats: Yesh Atid with 24, Blue and White with eight, United Torah Judaism with seven, Yisrael Beiteinu with six, Hadash-Taal and Raam with five each and Labor with four. Noam’s single seat was unaffiliated.
Who are the main contenders?
Netanyahu is seeking re-election while facing a trial on corruption charges, which he denies.
His far-right coalition is up against a bloc comprising of four major Jewish-led opposition parties, whose leaders have signed a declaration promising not to attack each other ahead of the vote and to join forces in forming a government after the polls.
Former army chief Gadi Eisenkot is viewed as the opposition’s most likely candidate for prime minister, with his new Yashar party evenly matched with Likud in the opinion polls.
The opposition alliance includes the Together list, led by former Prime Ministers Naftali Bennett and Yair Lapid; Avigdor Liberman’s Yisrael Beiteinu and Yair Golan’s Democrats.
Other key players include far-right ministers Itamar Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich, the ultra-Orthodox parties, and the Arab-majority lists Ra’am and the Joint List.
Last month, Israel’s Central Elections Committee voted to bar Ra’am and the Joint List from the election, but the Supreme Court unanimously overturned the bans on October 2, ruling that the evidence did not meet the legal threshold for exclusion.
Sami Abu Shehadeh, a Palestinian citizen of Israel who leads Balad, one of the parties in the Joint List, withdrew from the race after the court signalled that a majority of its judges would uphold his disqualification.
The Arab-led parties could hold the balance of power after the vote, but most leaders of the Jewish-led opposition bloc have ruled out joining forces with them.
Sixth election in seven years
October 27 will be Israel’s sixth national vote since 2019, but the first in 38 years to arrive at the natural end of a full Knesset term.
The instability began in April 2019, when Netanyahu’s Likud party and Benny Gantz’s Blue and White party tied on 35 seats each. A second vote that September produced another deadlock, with Blue and White on 33 and Likud on 32, and neither round yielded a coalition able to reach a majority.
A third election in March 2020 gave Likud 36 seats to Blue and White’s 33, and produced a Netanyahu-Gantz unity government that collapsed within a year. In March 2021, Likud won 30 seats to Yesh Atid’s 17, but an eight-party coalition led by Naftali Bennett and Yair Lapid that also included Ra’am, an Arab party, ended Netanyahu’s 12-year run. It lasted a year.
Netanyahu returned in November 2022, with Likud on 32 and Yesh Atid on 24, at the head of what has been described as Israel’s most right-wing government. Polls now show neither bloc clearly reaching 61.
Israel’s prime ministers
The state of Israel has had 14 prime ministers since its foundation in 1948. Netanyahu is by far the longest-serving, with 19 years in three separate stints: 1996 to 1999, 2009 to 2021 and from 2022 to now
Only David Ben-Gurion, who led the country from 1948 to 1954 and again from 1955 to 1963, comes close.
Whatever happens on October 27, Netanyahu stays on as caretaker prime minister until a new government is sworn in.

From malls to synagogues, Israel's parties battle for every vote with one week until election
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
05:20:59 UTC
14:20:59 KST

With exactly one week remaining before Israelis head to the polls, political parties are intensifying their campaigns, taking to the streets, fighting for every vote and increasingly turning their attacks not only on political opponents but also on rivals within their own ideological camps. The final seven days before the October 27 election may be their last opportunity to sway undecided voters and boost turnout.
Likud: Netanyahu tours shopping malls and steps up media appearances
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has spent recent days coordinating campaign activities with his team, focusing particularly on cities traditionally associated with Likud, where the party believes voter turnout needs to increase. The campaign is emphasizing two central messages. The first, "Right or Palestine," is based on Likud research suggesting that fear of a government formed in partnership with Arab parties is a major factor motivating its supporters to vote. The second, "Netanyahu does not surrender," is intended to signal the prime minister's determination to continue pursuing his policies.
Netanyahu has recently been visiting shopping malls, major retail centers, restaurants and cafes, interacting with the public under strict security arrangements. During these visits, he repeatedly warns that Gadi Eisenkot intends to form a government with Mansour Abbas, leader of the Arab Ra'am party, a claim Likud is also promoting extensively on social media. In a departure from his usual approach, Netanyahu has been granting interviews to media outlets not traditionally associated with him, hoping to attract moderate right-wing voters. Meanwhile, critics have accused the campaign of keeping several senior Mizrahi candidates, Israelis of Middle Eastern and North African Jewish descent, largely out of the spotlight to avoid alienating certain voter groups.
Yashar: Eisenkot targets Likud strongholds
Gadi Eisenkot, leader of the Yashar party, plans to spend the final week campaigning aggressively in Israel's outlying regions and traditional Likud strongholds, seeking to establish his party as the country's largest. The party is conducting an extensive grassroots operation targeting voters who have traditionally avoided parties belonging to the anti-Netanyahu bloc but who, according to internal polling, are considering supporting Eisenkot. Campaign officials have identified approximately 40 cities as priority targets, hoping to win over tens of thousands of undecided voters who could influence the election's outcome and expand the bloc's parliamentary strength.
Eisenkot opened the week with a large rally in Givat Shmuel, visited Eilat on Monday and is scheduled to campaign in Beersheba, Ramla, Modi'in and the Mateh Asher region in the coming days. The party is seeking to capitalize on its diverse candidate list, which includes eight representatives of the religious Zionist community among its top 20 candidates, alongside representatives of Israel's Ethiopian, Druze and LGBTQ communities and immigrants from the former Soviet Union. Particular attention is being directed toward liberal voters, Israelis who serve in the military, younger voters and those casting ballots for the first time. On Sunday, the party plans to hold a major campaign event at Hangar 11 in Tel Aviv under the slogan "Israel sets out on a new path," referencing its ballot designation.
Beyahad: Bennett courts voters through personal discussions and social media influencers
Former prime minister Naftali Bennett, who heads the Beyahad party, is dedicating the final days of the campaign to visits to crowded public spaces and informal political discussion groups, a format he began using several months ago. Bennett meets with former Likud voters, both those disappointed with Netanyahu and those who remain supportive, engaging them in discussions about his own political record and that of the prime minister while responding directly to criticism. In the evenings, he attends rallies in different cities. Most of Bennett's campaign has maintained a positive tone, but he has recently intensified efforts to reach younger Israelis through social media influencers, videos and content specifically targeting first-time voters.
The party is also running a focused campaign among soldiers and others serving in the military, highlighting Bennett's proposal to provide greater benefits to those who serve rather than those who avoid military service. Candidates from his party are holding events across the country every evening, emphasizing the need for political and institutional reform. Bennett repeatedly pledges to establish a state commission of inquiry on the first day his government takes office and to advance a fair military conscription framework immediately upon assuming power.
Yisrael Beytenu: Liberman sends his entire campaign operation into the field
Avigdor Liberman's Yisrael Beytenu party is shifting almost its entire campaign operation into direct voter outreach during the final week. Few staff members are expected to remain at campaign headquarters, with teams instead attending small gatherings in private homes, rallies, panel discussions and personal meetings with activists and undecided voters across Israel. At the same time, dedicated teams are working on digital platforms and social media. The party's central message focuses on Liberman's pledge to enforce military conscription and withhold state benefits from those who refuse to serve, with slogans including "100% for those who serve, 0% for draft dodgers."
"We also speak with people who intend to vote for other parties in the change bloc and encourage them to go out and vote," campaign officials said. "For us, the responsibility is both to the party and to the bloc: to increase the bloc's strength and achieve a decisive outcome at the ballot box. We're fighting for every vote."
The Democrats: memorial ceremony, march and major rally
Tens of thousands of activists and volunteers affiliated with Yair Golan's Democrats party are expected to mobilize across the country ahead of Election Day, organizing tours, public meetings and demonstrations at intersections and bridges, while maintaining a visible presence in cities and towns. Their aim is to promote the party's platform, which includes repealing legislation associated with the government's judicial overhaul, advancing a law barring criminal defendants from serving in government and enshrining the values of Israel's Declaration of Independence in the country's Basic Laws.
On Thursday, the party will hold a memorial ceremony for former Prime Minister Yitzhak Rabin, 31 years after his assassination. On Saturday, tens of thousands of party activists are expected to gather at Rabin Square in Tel Aviv for a "Democracy March" to Habima Square, where a rally will be held together with the October Council. The party is also preparing to recruit 10,000 volunteers to station themselves outside polling places on Election Day, covering approximately 1,000 voting clusters nationwide.
United Torah Judaism: home gatherings and a battle against ultra-Orthodox challengers
The ultra-Orthodox United Torah Judaism party is using the final stretch of the campaign to mobilize its traditional voters while reaching audiences that could defect to rival parties. Although party officials are avoiding public references to the Haredi Public party, led by Moti Leitner, which appeals to working and military-serving ultra-Orthodox Israelis, United Torah Judaism chairman Yaakov Asher has been meeting with precisely those voters. At small gatherings in private homes, Asher has promised to establish religious schools that include secular studies, along with educational frameworks enabling ultra-Orthodox students to pursue vocational training.
At rabbinical gatherings, speakers have emphasized the importance of voting for the party while pushing back against more extreme ultra-Orthodox factions that are encouraging supporters to boycott the election in protest over the absence of a military conscription law or to back new parties challenging the established ultra-Orthodox leadership.
Shas: continuing Rabbi Ovadia Yosef's legacy
Shas is maintaining its focus on defending Jewish religious identity and tradition in the campaign's final week. Rabbi Yitzhak Yosef, the party's spiritual leader, is traveling across Israel to attend rallies and deliver speeches urging supporters to vote for what he describes as the life's work of his late father, Rabbi Ovadia Yosef, the influential former spiritual leader of Shas. The campaign promises to preserve the religious schools and yeshivas established under Rabbi Ovadia Yosef's leadership.
Shas appears to have identified a potential shift among some ultra-Orthodox voters toward Itamar Ben-Gvir's Otzma Yehudit party and the Religious Zionist Party. In response, Rabbi Yitzhak Yosef has increasingly warned against voting for politicians who visit the Temple Mount. In a letter, the rabbi declared that voting for Ben-Gvir was religiously forbidden, writing: "According to Jewish law, it is forbidden to support a party led by someone who ascends the Temple Mount, and may the good Lord have mercy."
Religious Zionist Party: Smotrich campaigns in yeshivas and synagogues
Religious Zionist Party leader Bezalel Smotrich plans to spend the final week persuading voters to support his party rather than Ofer Winter or the Noam party. Smotrich's campaign includes visits to yeshivas aimed at mobilizing the religious Zionist base. 
He is also working to attract more affluent and established voters within the national-religious community. Last Saturday, Smotrich visited several synagogues and communities in Petah Tikva, including neighborhoods whose residents previously supported Bennett and former minister Ayelet Shaked.
Amcha Yisrael: Winter attacks the government's record against Hamas
Ofer Winter, leader of the Amcha Yisrael party, is continuing efforts to distinguish himself from Netanyahu's government following clashes with the prime minister, who has sought to pressure him into withdrawing from the election or attract his supporters back to Likud. 
Winter declared Monday that he intends to remain in the race until the end. His campaign emphasizes that Netanyahu does not have exclusive control over Israel's political right and argues that the current government has failed in its handling of Hamas. At the same time, Winter is using attacks from Netanyahu's political camp to portray himself as a target of political persecution, hoping to turn resentment toward the governing coalition into support among right-wing voters.
The Reservists and the Economic Party: conscription and cost-of-living campaign
Yoaz Hendel expressed renewed confidence Monday following Benny Gantz's announcement that he would not run in the upcoming election. Hendel said internal polling indicated that he was a preferred alternative for some Gantz voters who did not want to align themselves with either major political bloc. In the final week, the joint campaign of The Reservists and the Economic Party is focusing on the confrontation between Netanyahu and economist Yaron Zelekha. The party plans to publish videos showing Netanyahu praising Zelekha in the past, contrasting those statements with his more recent attacks on him. With a limited campaign budget, the party has reserved much of its spending for the final week, planning billboard advertisements centered on military conscription and the cost of living.
Ra'am: mobilizing Bedouin voters in the Negev
One week before the election, Mansour Abbas' Ra'am party is concentrating on maximizing turnout, particularly among the Bedouin community in southern Israel's Negev region, one of the party's most important electoral bases. The campaign emphasizes how Arab voter turnout could influence the composition of the next government. Party officials argue that a stronger Ra'am could help determine the balance of power in the Knesset, promoting the argument that winning eight parliamentary seats could help the anti-Netanyahu bloc secure a 61-seat majority in the 120-member parliament and replace Netanyahu's government.
Its central message is that voting for Ra'am is not merely an expression of support for an Arab political party, but also a means of influencing national leadership and advancing the interests of Arab citizens in housing, land rights, government budgets and the fight against crime.
Joint List: expanding outreach to Russian-speaking Israelis
The Joint List is intensifying efforts to encourage voting among Arab citizens, particularly those who remain undecided or express indifference toward the political process. Its campaign stretches across Israel, including Arab communities in the Triangle region, the Negev and the Galilee, combining political rallies, distribution of campaign materials and videos featuring party candidates and their messages. The central argument is that increasing turnout among Arab voters is essential to translating the community's population size into political influence.
Alongside its traditional outreach to Arab voters, the party is also attempting to broaden its audience through a Russian-language campaign aimed at Russian-speaking Israelis. On Tuesday, the Joint List is expected to present its program for the next Knesset in Haifa, including its vision for establishing a stronger social safety net for Arab citizens.
Otzma Yehudit: Ben-Gvir seeks votes from Likud and rival right-wing parties
As of Monday night, Itamar Ben-Gvir's Otzma Yehudit party was focusing its final-week campaign on drawing voters away from other parties on the right, particularly Likud. Ben-Gvir has intensified a campaign built around the claim that "Netanyahu will not bring Otzma Yehudit into the government," seeking to convince Likud supporters that a stronger Otzma Yehudit would make it impossible for the prime minister to exclude the party from his next coalition. He is also targeting supporters of Moshe Feiglin, who has joined Smotrich's Religious Zionist Party.
During a Facebook Live session, Ben-Gvir said: "I respect Feiglin, but he's already guaranteed a seat. He's number two. Now every vote for them brings in a Smotrich candidate, not a Feiglin candidate. His next candidate is in eighth place." The increasingly aggressive competition among parties on the same side of Israel's political divide reflects the stakes of the final campaign week: For many candidates, winning votes from their closest ideological allies may prove just as important as persuading supporters of the opposing bloc.

Interview: China's technological advances open new opportunities for cooperation, says former British business secretary
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
13:16:50 CST
14:16:50 KST

Former British business secretary Vince Cable speaks during an interview with Xinhua in London, Britain, Oct. 16, 2026. (Xinhua/Zhao Jiasong)
by Xinhua writers Zhao Jiasong, Yu Aicen
LONDON, Oct. 20 (Xinhua) -- China's growing technological strengths are changing the way Western countries approach industrial cooperation with the country, creating new opportunities for investment and technology partnerships, former British business secretary Vince Cable said in a recent interview with Xinhua.
Cable, also an economist, expressed optimism about China's economic prospects and highlighted opportunities for China-Britain cooperation in green technologies and medicine.
"When people from Western countries went to China 30, 40 years ago, China insisted on a transfer of technology into their supply chains," Cable said. "Now China is so well ahead on so many technological areas" that Western countries are increasingly looking to attract Chinese investment and technological expertise.
Cable said the transformation reflects China's remarkable technological progress over recent decades.
Asked about China's economic outlook, Cable said, "I am optimistic," while acknowledging that the country is facing economic challenges.
He welcomed China's ongoing efforts to stimulate economic activity, particularly measures to develop new quality productive forces, which he said are providing alternative sources of demand.
Looking ahead, Cable identified green technology and medicine as two particularly promising areas for China-Britain cooperation. Green technology encompasses solutions to climate change, including cleaner and more efficient energy, batteries and electric vehicles, while medicine is an area where "both countries have strong public health systems and considerable innovation in bioscience," he said.
Cable noted that China has the capacity to conduct large-scale clinical trials and is making progress in developing new drugs, while Britain has considerable expertise in medical research and pharmaceuticals.
"The two countries have complementary strengths that could support closer collaboration," he said.
When it comes to Chinese-made electric vehicles, Cable said Britain and Europe should "take advantage of Chinese advances in electric vehicles" by encouraging Chinese manufacturers to invest locally, transfer technology and support domestic supply chains.
Cable served as Britain's secretary of state for business, innovation and skills from 2010 to 2015 under former Prime Minister David Cameron, and visited China several times.
His engagement with China dates back to the 1990s, when he worked as chief economist for energy company Shell and was involved in planning related to the company's investment in south China's Guangdong Province.
Cable has also become an active user of the Chinese social media platform Rednote, attracting around 180,000 followers.
His interactions with Chinese internet users have given him fresh insights into the country, particularly the openness and curiosity of younger generations.
"A pleasant surprise to find people so open to discussion," he said, highlighting their curiosity and willingness to engage in conversation.
At a time of growing geopolitical divisions, Cable believes personal connections, academic exchanges and direct dialogue can help countries maintain mutual understanding.
He hopes his own engagement with China will encourage more people in Britain to ask a simple question: "Why can't we have good relations with China?" ■

In a speech titled “Secure Indo-Pacific, Resilient Taiwan,” Chung said Beijing was using military exercises, coast guard operations, and other activities short of open warfare to normalize its presence around Taiwan, per CNA.
Chung said Taiwan’s defensive strategy focuses on denying an adversary’s objectives. That requires preserving forces, mobilizing quickly, and sustaining defense capabilities across society, as well as acquiring weapons.
Taiwan plans to speed up procurement, expand domestic defense production, and build secure supply chains with international partners, Chung said. He reiterated the government’s goal of spending more than 5% of GDP on defense by 2030. Its proposed 2027 defense budget is approximately NT$1.1 trillion (US$34.9 billion).
DPP Legislator Chen Kuan-ting (陳冠廷) said Taiwan must prepare for attrition, blockades, and gray-zone coercion as well as a full-scale war, per CNA. He argued that scrambling fighter jets to intercept every Chinese military aircraft consumes resources and burdens pilots, while radar and air defense systems can help track aircraft and inform responses.
Chen urged international defense companies to offer equipment suited to Taiwan’s needs and deliver it more quickly. He said joint production with partners, including the US, could strengthen local manufacturing and reduce reliance on lengthy overseas supply chains.

Taiwanese nationals holding valid car and motorcycle licenses will be eligible to exchange them for local licenses in Australia without taking written or practical driving tests, subject to the requirements of each state and territory, according to the foreign ministry.
The new test-free license exchange arrangement is expected to take effect as early as Oct. 31 this year in Western Australia and Queensland. The arrangement will take effect on Jan. 1, 2027, for New South Wales, South Australia, and the Northern Territory.
Taiwanese will be able to exchange local licenses in Tasmania on Feb. 1, 2027. Dates for the Australian Capital Territory and Victoria have not yet been announced.
The foreign ministry said test-free license exchange means exemption from both the written driver knowledge test and the practical road test. Applicants must still meet local requirements concerning identity, age, health, license validity, and other eligibility criteria.
It added that the arrangement primarily applies to standard car and motorcycle licenses. Other vehicle categories remain subject to the relevant regulations of each state and territory.

Egyptian cucumber farmer helps archaeologists find giant Ramses II statue fragments
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
05:10:23 UTC
14:10:23 KST

A farmer’s discovery has led to the remains of two colossal royal statues and ancient inscriptions in Egypt’s Nile Delta. Archaeologists have identified one as Ramses II and are investigating how the finds fit into the area’s history.
An Egyptian farmer growing cucumbers on his land has helped archaeologists find the remains of two colossal royal statues, including a head of Ramses II measuring 1.6 metres tall.
Khaled Khalil came across a stone bearing ancient carvings on land in front of his home in Behbeit el-Hagar, a village in the Nile Delta’s Gharbia governorate, and alerted antiquities officials.
Officials examined the stone before an Egyptian team from the Supreme Council of Antiquities began a rescue excavation, according to the Ministry of Tourism and Antiquities.
Egyptian news outlet Youm7 reported that Khalil had been growing his crop in a greenhouse on the plot and had not expected to find such a large ancient statue.
“See? Cucumbers bring antiquities,” Gharbia governor Alaa Abdel Moaty joked during a visit to the farmer’s home last week, according to the newspaper.
What archaeologists found
The newly discovered head depicts Ramses II wearing the double crown of Upper and Lower Egypt. Archaeologists also found part of the statue’s back pillar bearing his Horus name, one of the pharaoh’s formal royal names.
Hisham el-Leithy, secretary-general of the Supreme Council of Antiquities, said the head’s proportions suggested the complete statue could originally have stood about 8.5 metres tall, including its base.
The surviving section of the second statue measures about 2.4 metres. Its legs and base are missing, but the face remains well preserved. It wears the royal nemes headdress, part of which is also missing.
Archaeologists think it may depict Ramses II because its facial features resemble those of the first head, although that identification has yet to be confirmed.
A separate pink granite block, about 1.3 metres long, carries hieroglyphic inscriptions including the titles “King of Upper and Lower Egypt” and “Son of Ra”.
Ramses II ruled Egypt for more than six decades, from around 1279 to 1213 BC, during the 19th Dynasty. Colossal statues of the pharaoh still stand at Abu Simbel, one of the best-known monuments of his reign.
Behbeit el-Hagar is known for the ruins of a large temple dedicated to the goddess Isis. Excavations and studies are continuing to establish how the newly found pieces relate to one another and to the surrounding site.
Tourism and Antiquities Minister Sherif Fathy visited Khalil to thank him for reporting the find. The farmer and his wife were awarded a trip to perform Umrah, the Muslim pilgrimage to Mecca that can be undertaken throughout the year.
During the visit, Khalil also asked the governor to help cover the remaining cost of an ambulance for the village. Residents had already raised part of the money, he said, according to local media.

Opposition's motion of no confidence in government fails
A vote of no confidence initiated by the opposition in the Reform-Eesti 200 minority government failed on Monday evening.
Thirty-four members of the 101-seat Riigikogu voted in favor of the motion, with no votes against or abstentions registered. The supporting MPs were from the Isamaa, EKRE and Center opposition parties.
The opposition Social Democratic Party and several independent MPs did not sign the motion and did not vote.
Members discussed the no-confidence motion in the Riigikogu before the vote took place.
Isamaa Chairman Urmas Reinsalu, representing those who initiated the motion, said the question under discussion was whether the government had failed in its duties during Prime Minister Kristen Michal's (Reform) tenure as prime minister.
"Not only because of the wrong decisions it has made, but because it has lost its credibility, its sense of reality and the broader support of society," he said.
The chairman noted that the vote was unlikely to succeed.
"Tactically, this is good news for Kristen Michal: thanks to the support of the Social Democrats, he will remain in office and be able to continue pursuing his agenda in the near future. The bad news for the overwhelming majority of Estonian people is that this government will remain in office for the time being," Reinsalu said.
Michal responded to the accusations and said: "The government's plan is working."
"Estonia's economy is growing twice as fast as the European Union average /.../ Jobs are being created. Unemployment in Estonia has fallen to its pre-pandemic level of early 2020. Inflation has subsided and will fall further," he continued.
He added that the opposition had painted a picture of Estonia that is "unrecognizable in real life."
Political scientist Tõnis Leht told ERR that the vote was primarily an opportunity for parties to position themselves and shape their image.
"Everyone stands to gain a little from this motion of no confidence, and no one really loses much. This is ordinary political theater in which all sides hope to gain something and send messages that appeal specifically to their own voters," he said.

1 Week Without US Intelligence: Russian Ballistics Kill At Least 6 Ukrainians, 21 Injured
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
05:07:20 UTC
14:07:20 KST

Following the US halted the transfer of early-warning intelligence on Russian ballistic missile launches to Ukraine, at least six civilians have been killed and 21 injured in missile strikes, according to a Kyiv Post review of official reports and damage assessments through Monday.
Kyiv residents have suffered the heaviest losses after the White House ordered a halt to sharing missile-launch data gathered by US global satellite networks with Ukrainian military and civil defense authorities. Civilians in Kharkiv and Dnipro were also among the casualties.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
However, senior US officials led by Secretary of State Marc Rubio have denied invoking the cut-off.
“I don’t know where he’s getting these things or why he’s [President Volodymyr Zelensky] saying these things to the press. You should go back and ask him. There’s been no pause,” Rubio told reporters during a Sunday visit to Samarkand, Uzbekistan.
Meanwhile, Zelensky said in an interview with NBC’s Meet the Press on Sunday that US intelligence-sharing “was blocked for some period of time” and that Ukraine “didn’t get it during ballistic attacks during three days,” according to The Guardian.
Speaking to reporters in Kyiv on Monday, Zelensky said the suspension remained in effect and that Ukrainian air-defense forces were still not receiving US-sourced early warnings of Russian ballistic missile launches.
The switch triggering the White House-Pentagon shutdown of data sharing on Russian missile launches detected by US-operated global satellite constellations monitoring hot spots from rocket motor ignitions and tracking missiles on ballistic trajectories was most likely flipped shortly before midnight Kyiv time on Oct. 12 and remains in effect, a Kyiv Post review of early-warning networks found.
Russia Strikes Ukrainian Energy Facility, Damages Church in Overnight Drone Attacks – Two Killed in Khmelnytsky
The number of Ukrainians killed and injured in confirmed ballistic missile strikes from Oct. 12-19, as well as in attacks involving missiles of an undetermined type that may have been ballistic, is probably around 20 dead and more than 100 wounded, based on summed reports from Ukraine’s Interior Ministry during that seven-day period.
The Russian ballistic missile arsenal used against Ukraine includes the modern and relatively accurate Iskander-M, which carries a 480-750 kg (1,058-1,063 lb) warhead; the somewhat less sophisticated North Korean KN-23, typically equipped with a warhead of around 500 kg (1,102 lb); and the relatively inaccurate S-400 heavy anti-aircraft missile, which carries a warhead of about 140 kg (309 lb), repurposed from an air defense role to city bombardment missions.
In Ukraine’s experience, a direct hit from an Iskander-M or KN-23 is sufficient to level a medium-sized apartment building or damage portions of a larger structure, while the explosive force of an S-400 can demolish several apartments or a single family home.
According to Ukraine’s Air Force and media reports, the first confirmed lethal Russian ballistic missile strike following the suspension of US intelligence-sharing occurred at about 10:40 p.m. on Oct. 13, when a missile partially struck a nine-story apartment building in Kyiv’s Desnianskyi district, the capital’s largest and predominantly working-class district. The area is densely built up with Soviet-era residential and business buildings. News reports identified the address of the building as Kubanska Street 24A. The structure, a typical Brezhnev-era apartment block built from pre-fab concrete slabs covered with ceramic tiles, contained about 300 single-family apartments.
The missile was probably launched from Russia’s Kursk region as part of a salvo of 39 missiles launched that night and followed a ballistic trajectory for about four minutes before impact, according to data published by Ukrainian early-warning networks. A review of civilian air-raid monitoring channels showed that the missile struck before networks had reported it airborne.
Blast damage on the central floors caused extensive cracking and wall failures, and ignited a fire that spread through apartments from the ground floor to the eighth floor. Portions of the structure were made uninhabitable, windows in adjacent buildings facing the blast were shattered, and dozens of private automobiles parked in the vicinity were damaged. Media outlets interviewing evacuees reported that no air-raid siren warning had sounded prior to the Russian missile strike.
Most reports identified the weapon as an Iskander-M ballistic missile. There are no major military facilities or government offices in the vicinity of the strike.
As a result of the blast and falling masonry, three women living at the address were killed, aged 35, 58, and 84. Reports of the number of injured ranged from 19 to more than 25 people, including a seven- or eight-year-old girl who suffered cuts and burns to her arm. A reported 16 residents were hospitalized, some in serious condition, and 16 residents were rescued or evacuated from the building.
Later that night, in the early hours of Oct. 14, another Russian ballistic missile struck Kyiv’s relatively upscale Holosiivskyi district in the south of the city, hitting a non-residential building. There was no air-raid siren and no early warning of the strike, according to a Kyiv Post reporter living in the area.
Two civilians were killed by the missile blast and at least one person was injured. According to Kyiv city administration reports, a total of five people were killed and at least 36 injured in the capital that night. Some of the casualties were caused not by ballistic missiles but by drones launched alongside them, the reports said.
From the moment US intelligence-sharing was cut off through Monday, Oct. 19, Russia launched at least five ballistic-missile salvos against Ukraine, according to Ukrainian Air Force and civil defense reports. These included five missiles overnight on Oct. 12-13, 39 missiles on Oct. 13-14, an undetermined number on Oct. 16-17, and 16 missiles on Oct. 18-19.
A conservative estimate of the warhead weight delivered by those missiles, almost all of which detonated in densely populated Ukrainian cities, would be 35-40 tons of high explosives, Kyiv Post calculated based on typical warhead weights.
The most recent ballistic missile-linked casualties occurred in Kyiv overnight from Sunday to Monday. They included a 21-year-old woman who was killed and eight other civilians who were injured when a strike hit, among other structures, a 25-story residential building, educational facilities, a medical facility, a train track, and control systems near a metro station.
In a few cases, early-warning networks reported incoming missiles one to two minutes before impact, but more often the warning came only after the weapon had already struck a building or the ground, according to Kyiv Post reporters in three districts of the city and a review of open-source early-warning data covering the night’s Russian strikes.
In addition to benefiting from the early-warning shutdown, Russian ballistic missile attacks against Ukraine have been made more effective by delays in US deliveries of PAC-3 interceptor missiles for the Patriot air-defense system. Manufactured in the US, the PAC-3 is the only weapon in Ukraine’s arsenal capable of reliably intercepting ballistic missiles.
In comments on Sunday evening, Zelensky said that, despite existing contracts and payments, the United States was supplying Ukraine with only 12 Patriot interceptor missiles per month, a figure an order of magnitude lower than the 100-150 ballistic missiles Russia launches against Ukraine each month.
Zelensky said he “hoped” the US would change what he described as a policy that appeared unbalanced and favorable to Russia. Since the US cut off the sharing of intelligence, independent Ukrainian media have almost unanimously reported that US President Donald J. Trump and the White House are co-operating with the Kremlin in a strategy that aligns with pro-Russian terms.

Myanmar’s ousted leader Aung San Suu Kyi seen in rare photos after receiving gift from King Charles
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
05:07:00 UTC
14:07:00 KST

Myanmar has delivered presents from Britain’s King Charles to Aung San Suu Kyi, releasing rare photos of the imprisoned former leader in what critics said was a stunt by the country’s military to end diplomatic isolation.
A presidential spokesperson said on social media that home ministry officials handed over two gardening books on soil, “along with one sealed envelope and a sealed diplomatic pouch”, from King Charles, who is known to have an interest in planting and the environment.
Photos showed the Nobel Peace laureate smiling in a wood-panelled room, a paper calendar on the wall behind her.
Suu Kyi, 81, the daughter of the assassinated national independence hero Gen Aung San, has spent much of her life in and out of house arrest for leading pro-democracy movements. She is now serving multiple sentences under house arrest at an undisclosed location in Naypyidaw, the capital.
Over her lifetime, the country’s military rulers have been cautious about locking Suu Kyi away in prison due to her beloved domestic status and international prominence, particularly in Britain, where she lived and married an Oxford academic. Most other political prisoners languish in jail.
Despite winning a 2015 election, she was deposed in a military coup in 2021, triggering an ongoing civil war that has killed more than 100,000 people, according to the independent conflict monitor ACLED. Since then, Suu Kyi’s whereabouts and health have been difficult to determine until an International Committee of the Red Cross visit in August.
Coup leader and former junta chief Min Aung Hlaing was installed as civilian president in April after elections that were widely condemned as a sham, and has been making efforts to rebuild regional and international diplomatic ties.
Kim Aris, Suu Kyi’s son who lives in London, said in a statement that he welcomed Charles’s gifts but warned their delivery should not be exploited by the regime.
“We must not allow the military regime to use such selective disclosures to create an illusion of normality or gain international legitimacy,” he said. “My mother’s fundamental human rights continue to be violated.”
Min Aung Hlaing remains under US sanctions for human rights abuses, including the 2016-2017 mass killings and expulsions of Rohingya Muslims that Washington considers a genocide.
The former commander-in-chief has recently conducted several regional visits to rebuild bilateral ties with neighbours, after the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean) regional bloc barred him from its summits for not following an Asean-brokered peace plan.
During his most recent trip to Malaysia this month, the leader was given an official welcome and honour guard. Min Aung Hlaing earlier visited Laos, Thailand, Vietnam and Cambodia.
Phil Robertson, director at the Asia Human Rights and Labour Advocates (AHRLA) group, said the Suu Kyi book photo op was part of Myanmar’s “quest for global legitimacy”.
“The bottom line is Asean has grown tired of arguing with Min Aung Hlaing and Myanmar’s intransigent military leaders and having nothing to show for it, and they desperately want to move the bloc on to other, more cheery issues,” he said.
“So as the Asean dominoes fall to the Myanmar charm offensive, they just want to make their regional capitulation look good – and that requires Myanmar to play its part by trotting out Suu Kyi at occasional intervals to receive their latest beneficence.”
Min Aung Hlaing has also made efforts to reach out to Donald Trump’s administration, saying in a September interview with Time magazine that “it would be ideal if the US could cooperate with us”.
Weeks later, Reuters reported that the US and Myanmar officials had held talks in Naypyidaw and Tokyo, in part to shut down scam centres that target Americans, but which could be broadened to exploitation of Myanmar’s mineral deposits.
The US state department has said it is re-examining “the range of tools the United States has historically leveraged to promote core interests in the country”. China has become Myanmar’s key global partner.
Myanmar has always denied the accusations of genocide, and Suu Kyi, who held the role of state counsellor at the time of the atrocities, defended the country at the international court of justice, disappointing many in her global support base.
Reuters and the Associated Press contributed to this report

From Paris to Tirana, why protests and riots are sweeping across Europe
Soaring rents, dilapidated schools and inflation ignite widespread clashes, fuelling political turmoil across the continent
Rising fuel costs, discontent with the state of schools, declining public services and a housing crisis have created perfectly stormy weather for an autumn of protests in Europe.
Crowds have taken to the streets for weeks in major cities, resulting in arrests, looting, injuries, and violence across France, Italy and Albania. In Spain and Portugal, tent camps have sprung up in protests against unattainable rents and housing costs.
Young Europeans are experiencing “a strong sense of uncertainty and a lack of control,” said Maria Silvestre, professor of sociology at the University of Deusto in Spain. “And when specific situations come together, a spark suddenly ignites that is capable of channelling that discontent and driving people into the streets.”
Cities have turned into battlefields as top EU economies, including France, Italy and Spain, approach pivotal elections, while far-right parties have made electoral gains in Germany and could do so elsewhere. It also comes as Europe faces a critical moment in its support for Ukraine, with President Donald Trump making overtures to President Vladimir Putin even as Russia is blamed for increasingly frequent hybrid attacks in Nato countries.

08:03:33 EEST
14:03:33 KST

Lift and escalator manufacturer Kone is Finland's most reputable company, according to the results of the latest Reputation & Trust survey.
"The company shot straight to the top of the rankings like a rocket. Such a high reputation score indicates that all aspects of the organization’s reputation are at a good or excellent level," noted Riku Ruokolahti, Director of Development at Reputation and Trust Analytics.
The survey asks respondents to rate a company on a five-point scale, with any score above 4.00 considered to be "excellent". A score of 3.50–3.99 indicates a good reputation.
Kone scored 4.01, with forest machine manufacturer Ponsse coming second in the rankings on 4.00, while third place went to food and confectionery company Fazer (3.97).
Aside from Kone, other big movers in the list included grocery chain K-Group, which overtook its retail rival S-Group, as well as Finland's mail carrier Posti.
"Posti has been on an upward trajectory for quite some time now. The company has made one of the biggest gains in brand reputation we've seen in our entire history of tracking," Ruokolahti said.
At the other end of the scale, Chinese discount retail platforms Temu and Shein were once again the least reputable companies in the Finnish market.
The reputations of both firms deteriorated even further compared to last year's results, with Temu now on 2.09 and Shein at the very bottom of the pile on 1.85.
"Temu’s reputation in Finland is even weaker than in the other Nordic countries — in Sweden, Norway, and Denmark, its reputation has actually improved somewhat," Ruokolahti noted. "In this sense, it can be said that Finns are more critical of companies selling ultra-fast fashion and junk than citizens of other Nordic countries."
A total of 11,240 people in Finland responded to the online survey between May and June this year, with a margin of error of 0.92 percent.

How planting a 'rain garden' could help protect your home from flooding
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
05:02:57 UTC
14:02:57 KST

Flooding is expected to grow more extreme due to climate change. Your garden could be your home's first defence.
Heavy rains and flooding hit Spain's Catalonia region last week, claiming at least two lives and submerging homes and roads.
Unfortunately, it’s not the first time. And it won’t be the last: scientists predict an increase in extreme weather events globally, fed in part by human-caused climate change.
When the deluge subsides, people are left to deal with the devastation, shovelling sludge from streets and pumping floodwater from their living rooms.
Gardens may be the last thing people fix, but could they become fortifications against future disasters?
As the threat of flooding and droughts strengthens, so too does the argument for planting a 'rain garden'.
What exactly is a rain garden?
Simply put, a rain garden is a depressed bed planted with native perennials and shrubs selected for their high-water tolerance.
It’s strategically situated in a spot where water – from downspouts, driveways, compacted soil and other sources of runoff – flows downward toward it.
That runoff waters the plants and filters pollutants as the soil absorbs it. And it means the excess water, as well as the road sediment, debris, pet waste pathogens, fertilisers and chemicals it picks up along the way, is kept out of storm drains, watersheds and wetlands.
Rain gardens can also stop water from entering your basement or affecting your foundation.
In dry, drought-stricken regions, too, many gardeners are turning to rain gardens and other methods of collecting rainwater.
How to create a rain garden
You can make a rain garden as big or small as you like, but keep it at least three metres from your house, garage or other structures. Don’t plant it over a septic tank or underground utilities, or near a well that provides drinking water. And avoid sloped areas and those that are soggy to begin with.
Dig the bed in your preferred size and shape (kidney, crescent, round and teardrop are popular). You can either gradually grade the soil toward the centre so it is 15 centimetres lower than the perimeter, or dig everything but the perimeter 15 centimetres deep so a berm that high surrounds the sunken bed.
Direct water toward the bed by installing a gutter extension, creating a downhill slope, digging a trench or connecting a PVC pipe to a distant gutter and running it underground to the rain garden. Slow the flow of water by lining your trench or slope with rocks or small stones.
Some gardeners prefer to keep the centre free of plants and cover the soil there with stones, as well.
The best plantings for a rain garden
Choose native plants best suited to high-water or, if planting the centre, even swampy conditions. Natives are naturally adapted to your region’s environment, so they’ll be easier to grow, require less maintenance and will also provide a habitat for bees, birds, butterflies and other wildlife.
Consider planting flowering perennials alongside sedges and grasses, and incorporating shrubs and small trees, if space allows. Including some evergreens will further help avoid erosion.
FloraVeg.EU is a good resource that lets you search for native vegetation by geographical region and other parameters.
Put plants with the highest water needs at and around the centre of your rain garden, where water will collect and pool for a bit before seeping into the soil. Plant those with moderate water needs along the elevated perimeter of the bed, which will be somewhat drier.
How to care for a rain garden
In the absence of rain, water the plants as necessary throughout their first year, as their roots grow and anchor into the ground. Keep on top of weeds, too, until the plants grow and fill in the bare spots between them.
After you’ve designed, graded and planted your rain garden, there won’t be very much for you to do, except sit back and enjoy your striking natural landscape – and its hidden ecological function.
