These are Europe’s cosiest cities to travel to this autumn, according to a new ranking
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
05:00:57 UTC
14:00:57 KST

From Bruges’ fairytale streets to Lisbon’s sun-soaked cafés, these European cities are perfect for a cosy autumn escape.
As temperatures drop and autumn settles in, it’s the ideal time to explore European cities which seem made for cosy escapes. Think winding cobbled streets, historic cafés and canals lined with colourful leaves.
Now, a new study of Reddit discussions has revealed the continent’s cosiest destinations for autumn 2026, with Bruges taking the top spot.
Amsterdam and Prague follow closely, but the ranking also features some surprising destinations you might not expect – like sunny Lisbon and Athens.
The study, by UK-based holiday home letting agency Big House Experience, looked at cities within continental Europe (and outside of the UK), and analysed Reddit discussions before ranking the destinations according to the number of upvotes they received.
These are the cities to visit to feel the snuggest as it gets chillier and the “-ber” months continue.
Which European cities are the cosiest?
Picture a cosy city, and Bruges will probably come straight to mind, with its cobblestone streets, fairytale-esque medieval architecture and picturesque canals. It’s little surprise, then, that the Belgian city topped this ranking, with more than 15,000 upvotes across relevant Reddit content.
World-famous for its historic buildings and, of course, chocolate shops and quaint cafés, Bruges is the ideal spot for a truly cosy trip. Be sure to wander through the winding streets, which have a real old-world feel, or duck inside a comfy eaterie for a Belgian hot chocolate.
Following closely behind Bruges is Amsterdam, which got 14,477 upvotes. Over the border from Belgium, the Dutch capital boasts historic canal houses, independent coffee shops and tree-lined waterways, which turn beautiful shades of red and orange come autumn.
While Amsterdam is a great city to visit year-round, it’s especially cosy in the chillier months, when hearty dishes are on the menu. Don’t miss the chance to try poffertjes, either. These fluffy, miniature puffy pancakes are served hot with a melting pat of butter and a dusting of powdered sugar and make the perfect autumn treat.
Next up in the ranking are Prague and Kraków, with Reddit upvote scores of 11,098 and 10,117, respectively.
Both of these Central European cities are well known for their historic architecture and atmospheric – and, yes, cosy – old towns, which are home to countless spots for visitors to warm up and wind down after a busy day’s exploring.
In fifth place on the list is a city which may come as a surprise to some: Athens. The Greek capital is usually thought of as a sunny destination and isn’t on many people’s “cosy city break” list, but it did get 9,243 upvotes on Reddit.
Athens proves that cosy doesn’t have to mean cold, with sun-drenched streets, traditional tavernas, tucked-away cafés and lively neighbourhoods offering a welcoming atmosphere throughout the autumn.
It’s followed in the ranking by another famously sunny city: Lisbon, which got 3,243 upvotes.
Lisbon’s tiled streets, historic trams and pastel-coloured buildings give it plenty of charm, while neighbourhood cafés, cosy wine bars and mild autumn temperatures make it ideal for a seasonal escape.
If you’re not a fan of the cold, but love feeling snug, both Lisbon and Athens offer a milder autumn escape, with cosy cafés and atmospheric streets to enjoy without the chill that sets in across much of Europe.
In seventh place, it’s back to chillier climes with Copenhagen. The Danish capital got 2,850 upvotes thanks, in part, to the fact it embraces the country’s concept of hygge, which centres around creating a warm, comfortable and inviting atmosphere, which is easy to find all around the city.
Salzburg and Utrecht complete the ranking, with 2,397 and 1,040 upvotes respectively. Austrian city Salzburg pairs mountain views and properly crisp weather with traditional coffee houses, while Utrecht in the Netherlands offers a quieter city break – and a great alternative to Amsterdam – with leafy canals, historic streets and independent cafés.
The cosiest cities in continental Europe
- Bruges, Belgium
- Amsterdam, The Netherlands
- Prague, Czechia
- Kraków, Poland
- Athens, Greece
- Lisbon, Portugal
- Copenhagen, Denmark
- Salzburg, Austria
- Utrecht, The Netherlands

Ukraine needs another €70 billion, but where will the EU find the money?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
05:00:27 UTC
14:00:27 KST

The EU is searching for another €70 billion to sustain Ukraine's war effort in 2027, but rising borrowing costs and divisions over the Russian assets leave Brussels with few easy options.
The European Union is scrambling to find an additional €70 billion for Ukraine next year, after Russia's escalating assault on the country and its economy rendered the bloc's existing financial support plans insufficient.
At the end of a two-day summit last week, EU leaders heard directly from Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy about the scale of the shortfall.
"The war will cost €155 billion next year. And we need at least €70 billion more from you: for defence, for weapons, and for our resilience. This is a realistic amount. And I ask you to find this support. It will help us hold Russia back," he said.
According to Zelenskyy, the extra injection of cash will help Ukraine ramp up domestic production of its cutting-edge drones to stop Russia's advances on the battlefield, disrupt its supply chains and undercut its war apparatus.
"We really need at least €70 billion additionally for next year," he added.
The appeal struck a chord. EU leaders tasked the European Commission with exploring ways to plug the gap, which is considerably larger than Brussels had anticipated.
Until now, the bloc based its support on the €90 billion loan that leaders signed off last December. The loan was designed to cover two-thirds of Ukraine's financial and military needs for 2026 and 2027 combined, with other allies covering the remaining third.
Crucially, the Commission devised the loan assuming that the war would end sometime in 2026. Instead, Moscow has intensified its offensive, including daytime attacks aimed at crippling Ukraine's already fragile economy.
Kyiv has spent weeks warning that it will need an additional $32.6 billion to support its budget and $45 billion for its armed forces next year – a combined $78 billion, or approximately €70 billion.
Brussels initially declined to comment on the staggering figure. But after several rounds of technical discussions, it has accepted the estimate and concluded that the money must be found if Ukraine is to sustain its war effort.
The €70 billion would come on top of the €45 billion the EU plans to disburse under its existing loan, as well as several billion euros from other programmes.
Faced with a swelling bill, Brussels has been quick to stress that the €70 billion will be a "joint effort" with other allies, such as the UK, Norway, Canada and Japan.
"We always said that we cannot walk this alone. We cannot do this all alone. Therefore, our partners in general must step up," a Commission spokesperson said.
"They have to come forward with pledges, and they have to deliver on those commitments. This is very important."
It is not yet clear how much of the €70 billion the EU will provide, given that the previous split of two-thirds vs one-third has not worked out as planned. Nor is it clear how quickly Kyiv will need the money. What is clear is that the options for raising such a vast sum at short notice are severely limited.
Adding to the pressure, the high-stakes negotiations will unfold in parallel with the bitter fight over the next long-term budget and the lead-up to the French presidential election, where frontrunner Marine Le Pen has vowed to end all aid to Ukraine.
Tapping the markets
Raising fresh joint EU debt on the financial markets, as Brussels is already doing for the €90 billion loan, currently appears the most likely option, according to diplomats and officials. The Commission could increase the existing credit facility, effectively extending the current financing arrangement.
The bloc, with its stable AAA credit rating, has become an in-demand bond issuer since the COVID-19 pandemic, with its auctions often oversubscribed. Mario Draghi, the former Italian Prime Minister and ECB President, has called for large-scale borrowing.
The financial landscape, however, has sharply deteriorated since December, when leaders signed off on the loan. Borrowing costs have soared worldwide in response to surging oil prices, rising public debt and strong demand for AI spending.
European countries have been hit particularly hard, especially those already heavily indebted. Belgium is now borrowing at rates comparable to Greece, while France is paying more than Italy.
This makes the prospect of fresh debt politically sensitive, even difficult, as it would add to the mounting pile of interest payments.
Yield on the bloc's 10-year bond has risen from 2.8% in January to 3.44% in September – a significant increase, although less pronounced than in many other markets.
"This is a dynamic that affects all insurers around the world, and our relative position importantly has not deteriorated," the Commission spokesperson said.
"We remain an extremely competitive issuer."
If joint borrowing emerges as the main option, several countries are expected to opt out.
Hungary, Slovakia and the Czech Republic are already exempted from the €90 billion loan. At last week's summit, Slovak Prime Minister Robert Fico said he and his Hungarian counterpart, Péter Magyar, had agreed to maintain the policy.
"If they (other countries) want to provide a loan to Ukraine, they can do so, but at least two countries are indicating at this point that we will not participate in this financial mechanism," Fico said. "We show solidarity in other ways."
Another country likely to sit it out is Bulgaria, whose new prime minister, Rumen Radev, has repeatedly criticised the bloc's military assistance to Ukraine.
Tapping assets
In recent weeks, several countries have floated an alternative avenue to equip Ukraine with long-lasting financial firepower: the immobilised assets of the Russian Central Bank, worth a massive €210 billion across the bloc's territory.
Sweden, the Netherlands, Spain and Poland revived the debate in August. The Nordics, the Baltics, Germany and Ireland have since expressed support.
These are the same countries that last year pushed the hardest to channel the assets into a zero-interest credit for Ukraine. For the most part, they are the largest bilateral donors to Ukraine and see the assets as a way to ensure genuine burden-sharing.
The project failed when it bumped into Belgium's fierce resistance, which holds €185 billion of these assets in Euroclear, a depository in central Brussels.
Belgian Prime Minister Bart De Wever warned that using the assets would amount to confiscation and have catastrophic consequences for the country. He demanded the total mutualisation of risks and uncapped guarantees against all possible liabilities.
Leaders recoiled at the prospect of bailing out Belgium's banking system and, at the last minute, opted for joint debt to set up the €90 billion loan.
Despite that setback, supporters of using the Russian assets have not abandoned the idea. Ukraine has consistently brought the topic into the conversation.
Zelenskyy said that if Europe does not use them, Russia would seek to retrieve them. (The US has reportedly pitched a plan to partially release the assets as an incentive for Russia to engage in the peace talks, but Europeans shot it down.)
"The main priority is that Russia doesn't have the opportunity to influence later on the discussion on these assets, because we know very clearly they want to bring these assets back," Zelenskyy said last week. "It's one of Russia's aims."
De Wever remains firmly opposed. During the summit, the Belgian premier, on his own initiative, took the floor to tell his peers that his objections remained unchanged, Euronews understands. He argued the money should be kept firmly locked in until the end of the war to prevent external meddling by Moscow or Washington.
The message was received. Officials and diplomats left the summit with the impression that the assets had little chance of succeeding this time around.
The failure of last year's proposal remains fresh in their minds. France and Italy, whose support would be crucial, are still considered reluctant to use the assets.
Belgium's position is even more entrenched. It opposes not only tapping the sovereign funds but also transferring them from Euroclear to an EU-owned custodian, a legal workaround that some have promoted to break the impasse.
"The issue will be coming up over and over. Eventually it may find a resolution. I don't think short-term it's going to be on the agenda, like this month or the next one," Katarína Mathernová, the EU ambassador to Ukraine, told Euronews.
"While the assets remain frozen and they are in Europe and under our regime and now under European jurisdiction, they certainly are for the leaders to discuss in the future. And I think that will happen, but not in the short term."

Don’t be fooled. The AI that was supposed to save us time is doing just the opposite | Gaby Hinsliff
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
05:00:17 UTC
14:00:17 KST

Another morning, another avalanche of emails. Even after a guilty cull, my inbox is sitting at well over 7,000, but lately I’ve started subscribing to the Quentin Crisp theory of housework: why bother, when after four years or so you stop noticing the accumulating dust? Empty inboxes just fill up again anyway.
In theory, email was supposed to save hours of meetings, phone calls and standing over photocopiers. Instead, we just spend hours deleting stuff people wouldn’t have bothered telling us if it had meant picking up the phone, but which they can now spam to their entire database at the click of a button. The glorious ease and convenience of being able to reach the world in seconds came, we now know, with the inconvenience of them being able to reach you right back.
And therein lies the challenge to the government’s hopes of AI helping to transform the machinery of the state on the cheap, saving not only time but billions of pounds in public money. It’s early days, but AI seems not so much to be streamlining public service delivery as gumming it up – partly because, as was once the case with email, the public is using it right back at them.
In a Substack post last week, the former civil servant Sam Freedman noted that governments around the world seem to be experiencing unusual surges in complaints, requests and responses to regulatory and official bodies since the adoption of ChatGPT. It’s the same story in the courts, with employment tribunal cases in England, Scotland and Wales reportedly rising by 39% in a year thanks in part to claimants using AI to draft claims, while magistrates and judges face a wave of people who can’t afford lawyers using ChatGPT to build cases that often don’t make sense. And all of this needs patient disentangling by a human, on the grounds that just because a defendant is citing precedents that don’t exist, it doesn’t mean there isn’t a genuine grievance buried in there somewhere.
Whitehall special advisers complain of departments drowning in AI-generated freedom of information requests, an abuse of a system originally intended to empower individuals. MPs’ offices are similarly swamped by AI-generated letters, all of which need to be read by humans for fear of missing something important from a constituent.
How long before public consultations on changing the law become so spammed by slop that they are in essence useless as a measure of what the country actually thinks? There’s a fine line between the noble aim of making it easier for individuals to interact with an otherwise remote state, and making it so easy that the result is an uncontrollable firehose of meaningless machine-generated guff.
The obvious answer to this kind of AI flooding is getting AI tools to detect or sift it, but that doesn’t always work when dealing with potentially vulnerable human beings. Constituents who use AI to express themselves in more fancy-sounding language when writing to their MP, for example, still have the right to expect a personal response from a human being.
Employers who thought they were being smart by getting AI to sift job applications, meanwhile, are reaping what they sowed, as resentful applicants automate their end of things too and spray-gun applications across the board, rather than concentrating on the jobs they really want. Now neither side can separate the wheat from an avalanche of chaff.
The risk of paralysis is likely only to increase if the public starts adopting agentic AI in the kind of numbers big tech fondly imagines. Early adopters might well find agents save them time and hassle. But shortcuts stop being shortcuts once everyone else is using them too, and risk turning into bottlenecks instead. Think of cars, which have vastly shortened journey times compared with travelling by horseback, except in cities at rush hour when too many other people are also trying to shorten theirs. By 2018, central London daytime traffic was moving on average at just over 7mph – about the same speed as a trotting pony.
Historically, humans have always learned to develop ways around problems of our own making. We have spam filters for email, congestion charges to keep cars out of cities, and in the long term we could well figure out what kind of frictions we need to put back in the system to make it possible to live with the impact of AI.
But for now a useful rule of thumb, if improbable claims start to be made for savings due to AI, will be that more isn’t always better; faster and easier isn’t always more convenient; and time saved in one section of public services has a horrible habit of popping up in another one. Let the Whac-A-Mole begin.
- Gaby Hinsliff is a Guardian columnist

Sami Tamimi’s recipes for lamb meatballs with spinach and chickpea stew, and red rice
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
05:00:17 UTC
14:00:17 KST

This is the kind of meal I love for its generosity and simplicity. A comforting spinach and chickpea stew (sabanekh), scattered with tender lamb meatballs and finished with a bright squeeze of lemon. And, alongside, Iraqi red rice (timman ahmar) brings warmth, colour and a gentle sweetness from the tomato, and soaks up the rich, savoury juices of the stew. Together, they form a hearty meal made for sharing.
Lamb meatballs, spinach and chickpea stew (sabanekh)
Sabanekh is a beloved spinach stew across the Levant, and here I’ve added lamb meatballs to make it a more substantial meal. The combination of cumin, coriander and garlic gives warmth and depth, while a generous squeeze of lemon brightens everything. Serve with rice or warm flatbread to soak up the delicious, fragrant sauce.
Prep 10 min
 
Cook 1 hr
 
Serves 4-6
500g lamb mince
  
Salt and black pepper
 
1 tsp baharat mix 
  
4 tbsp olive oil
  
30g pine nuts
  
1 large onion, peeled and finely chopped (180g)
  
600g frozen whole-leaf spinach 
  
400g tin chickpeas, drained and rinsed
 
500ml water or chicken stock
  
Rice and/or flatbread, to serve
  
2 tbsp lemon juice
 , plus lemon wedges, to serve
For the adha garnish
 
60ml olive oil 
  
5 garlic cloves, peeled and crushed
 
20g fresh coriander, finely chopped
 
½ tsp aleppo chilli flakes
Put the mince in a medium bowl, add a teaspoon of salt, half a teaspoon of baharat and a third of a teaspoon of black pepper, and mix well. Shape the meat into 25 balls (about 20g each) and set aside.
Heat two tablespoons of olive oil in a large saucepan on a medium heat. Add the pine nuts and cook, stirring constantly, for three to four minutes, until golden brown. Spoon the pine nuts into a bowl.
Add the meatballs to the pan in two batches and cook until brown all over. Remove the meat from the pan and add the remaining two tablespoons of oil and the onion, and cook, stirring occasionally, for seven minutes, until soft and translucent. Add the spinach, chickpeas, water/stock, lemon juice, one teaspoon of salt, a good grind of black pepper, and the remaining half-teaspoon of baharat. Bring to a boil and cook for five minutes, until the spinach is soft. Return the meatballs to the pan, cover and cook on a low heat, stirring occasionally, for 20 minutes, until the stew has thickened slightly.
To make the adha garnish, put the oil and garlic in a small frying pan on a medium heat. Cook, stirring often, for two to three minutes, until the garlic is lightly golden, then take off the heat and stir in the coriander and chilli. Pour the adha over the stew, cover and leave for five minutes.
Scatter over the toasted pine nuts and serve hot with the red rice below, or plain steamed rice, and lots of lemon wedges.
Red rice (timman ahmar)
A simple and deeply comforting rice dish, known for its rich colour and savoury flavour. Traditionally made by cooking rice with tomato, onion and spices, it’s the kind of everyday dish that sits naturally at the centre of the Iraqi table. The gentle sweetness of the tomato is balanced by warm spices, while the rice remains light and fluffy. Serve alongside stews, grilled meats or vegetables.
Prep 15 min
  
Soak 20 min
 
Cook 50 min
 
Serves 4–6
300g basmati rice
  
3 tbsp vegetable oil
  
120g vermicelli, broken into small pieces
 
1 medium onion, peeled and finely chopped (120g)
 
3 garlic cloves, peeled and crushed
 
1 green chilli, finely chopped (seeds removed if you want less heat)
 
2 tbsp tomato puree
  
1½ tbsp pomegranate molasses
  
1½ tsp ground cumin 
  
¾ tsp ground allspice 
  
½ tsp ground cinnamon 
  
1 large tomato (140g), finely chopped
 
1 green pepper, stalk, pith and seeds removed, flesh finely chopped (160g) 
  
600ml 
 hot vegetable stock 
  
25g unsalted butter
  
Salt and black pepper
Rinse the rice under cold running water several times, until the water runs clear. Leave the rice to soak in fresh water for 20 minutes, then drain well.
Heat a tablespoon of the oil in a medium saucepan on a medium heat. Add the vermicelli, cook, stirring, for five minutes, until golden brown, then tip on to a plate.
Add the remaining two tablespoons of oil and the onion to the pan, and cook, stirring occasionally, for seven minutes, until soft and lightly golden. Stir in the garlic and chilli, and cook for a minute. Add the tomato puree, pomegranate molasses and spices, and cook for another minute, until fragrant.
Stir in the tomato and green pepper, and cook for three minutes. Add the drained rice and toasted vermicelli, and stir gently for a minute, making sure all of the grains are coated in the tomato sauce.
Pour in the hot stock and add the butter, one and a quarter teaspoons of salt and a good grind of black pepper. Bring to a boil, then cover the pan and leave to cook on a very low heat for 15 minutes. Take off the heat and leave covered for 10 minutes. Gently fluff the rice with a fork, then serve.

New Bradford railway station will ‘transform travel across the north’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
05:00:16 UTC
14:00:16 KST

A new railway station will be built in Bradford to “transform how people travel across the north”, the government has announced.
The station will be at the heart of the Northern Powerhouse Rail (NPR) scheme, built on the current Bradford Interchange site but allowing through trains between Leeds and Manchester.
With the promise of more frequent and faster services, it is expected to support new homes and jobs for the West Yorkshire city, located alongside its Southern Gateway regeneration project and connecting to the proposed tram to Leeds.
Approval of the station, which is expected to be built by the mid-2030s, has been regarded by northern leaders as a critical sign of political commitment to improving rail links across the north, after long delays in delivering pledged upgrades.
The Department for Transport said that NPR would allow a “turn-up-and-go railway” for passengers from Bradford, with sufficiently frequent trains running across the north for people not to need to check timetables.
The transport secretary, Heidi Alexander, said: “Today marks an important milestone for Bradford with a brand-new station that will transform how people travel across the north.”
The new station, along with the proposed West Yorkshire mass transit network – better known as the Leeds tram – will bring more than £1bn in economic benefits, according to Bradford council.
The mayor of West Yorkshire, Tracy Brabin, said: “Bradford has so much untapped potential, and faster, more frequent trains to Leeds and Manchester, and the transformation of the city centre will help to finally unleash it.”
Henri Murison, the chief executive of the Northern Powerhouse Partnership, said the decision to build a new station at Bradford Interchange represented “a long-term commitment to the city and the wider north”. He added: “Confidence is already building here, and this will help build it further.”
NPR was first promised by the Conservatives in 2014 but no firm funded plans emerged for the proposed railway linking cities from Liverpool to Hull.
The government under Keir Starmer announced in January that NPR would be delivered in three stages, with a funding cap of £45bn, which could be topped up by local contributions.
The scheme will start by improving connections on existing lines around Yorkshire. It also includes plans for a new line between Liverpool and Manchester.
As mayor of Greater Manchester at the time, Andy Burnham had championed a new underground station for Manchester Piccadilly as part of the project, which the Treasury did not approve.
The rail industry is also anticipating more work on improving Manchester-Birmingham links to replace the scrapped HS2 northern leg, another transport issue long pushed by Burnham.
Northern transport links could be improved further after the mayor of South Yorkshire and other leaders announced plans to bring Doncaster Sheffield airport into public ownership.
The combined authority and Doncaster city council are set to buy the airport from Peel Land, hoping to restart freight next year and passenger flights by spring 2028.
The airport’s owners shut down operations in November 2022, regarding it as commercially unviable.
However, South Yorkshire’s mayor, Oliver Coppard, said that, subject to formal approval, a deal was now going through that “puts the future of DSA back in our hands and finally gives one of the biggest and best growth opportunities in South Yorkshire the platform for long-term success that it needs and deserves”.
He said the government’s devolution agenda had allowed them to now act to resume flights to the city, adding: “When the airport closed, almost everything was against us; the owners did not want to sell, we had no legal powers to intervene or stop the airport from closing, and no backing from the government at the time. Today, the sky’s the limit.”

Public support for founding principles of NHS is falling across UK population
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
05:00:16 UTC
14:00:16 KST

Public support for the NHS’s founding principles – that it is free to use, available to everyone and tax-funded – has fallen over the last five years, research has shown.
Backing for all three pillars dropped between 2021 and 2025 across the UK population, except for a small rise in millennials’ support for the NHS being funded from taxation.
Experts said the sharp rise in economic hardship and changes in attitudes towards migration during those years could help explain the drop in support.
With healthcare swallowing up ever more public spending as the UK contends with an ageing population, and the government is under pressure to spend more on defence, social care and the special educational needs system, that decline could make it harder for ministers in future to justify raising the NHS budget.
The King’s Fund thinktank analysed British Social Attitudes survey data on attitudes towards the NHS’s founding principles among five age groups: gen Z (born 1997-2012), millennials (1981-1996), gen X (1965-1980), boomers (1946-1964) and those born prewar.
Support for the NHS being free of charge and available to everyone has fallen in recent years across all five groups. While large majorities still agree that it should be available to everyone, the decline in that belief was particularly striking. The proportion of those born before the second world war who think that declined from 87.1% in 2021 to 73.2% last year – a 13.9 percentage point fall. Among boomers it fell from 83.1% to 71.2% – down by 11.9 percentage points.
Support for the NHS being free of charge was also down, but by smaller proportions, and it remains a belief shared by between 85% and 92% of the population.
However, the analysis also revealed the emergence of what the King’s Fund called “a generational fault line in attitudes to NHS funding”, with gen Z holding different views from other age groups.
Support among gen Z for the NHS remaining tax-funded fell by 11.2 percentage points from 2021-2025 – a bigger drop than among gen X, boomers and the prewar cohort. Fewer than four out of five gen Z (74.1%) hold that belief, compared with at least 80% elsewhere.
Danielle Jefferies, a senior analyst at the King’s Fund, said that public backing for the NHS’s underlying principles remained strong 76 years after its creation.
“Nevertheless, politicians and the public should not take that support for granted. Our analysis shows a slight fall in support for the founding principles of the NHS over the last five years, against a backdrop of record low public satisfaction with the NHS and growing divisions across different age groups and political perspectives.
“The public’s longstanding support for the NHS is often wrapped up with the country’s identity, so it is hard to unpick exactly why support for the principles might be falling slightly. While there is no single explanation for the recent shift, wider changes in public attitudes may be playing a role.
“For example, the latest British Social Attitudes survey suggests that changing attitudes towards migration may play a role in declining certainty about the principle that the NHS should be available to everyone.”
Economics probably explains Gen Z’s attitudes, Jefferies added.
“Gen Z are coming of age in incredibly challenging economic climate. Analysis from the Institute for Fiscal Studies suggests that younger adults today are economically worse off than previous generations at the same age. They face high housing costs, significant student debt, years of wage stagnation, and were the first generation to come of age in the aftermath of austerity and during the Covid-19 pandemic.
“Against that backdrop, it’s perhaps unsurprising that younger adults are more hesitant about paying higher taxes to fund public services. Add to that that many younger people might be trying to access [NHS] services like mental health support and dealing with long waits, many could feel short-changed,” Jefferies said.
“When living standards have stalled and many are dissatisfied with public services like the NHS, support for paying more tax cannot be taken for granted.”
Long waiting times for NHS care such as A&E, surgery, cancer treatment and mental health help may influence public opinion too.
Ciarán Devane, the chief executive of NHS Alliance, said: “At a time of huge and sustained challenges for the health service, it is natural that people may question the funding model, though it’s worth noting that even in generation Z, a large majority backed the current approach.
“That said, any erosion of support is a concern. The NHS must keep delivering for the public and for patients, and making the case for continued public backing, including through their taxes.”

EU proposal for security protocol modelled on NATO’s Article 4 draws scepticism
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
05:00:00 UTC
14:00:00 KST

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen has proposed creating a European Union security protocol modelled on NATO’s Article 4 to coordinate responses to hybrid attacks, but the idea has so far received limited support and raised concerns about duplication and political divisions within the bloc.
Von der Leyen raised the proposal amid a series of suspected hybrid threats across Europe, including drone incursions in several EU countries and an attempted attack at Leipzig airport. On the eve of her annual address, a drone was shot down over Lithuania.
“I believe the time has come for a European Article 4 – an emergency security protocol. If one member state activates it, all the others would come together,” von der Leyen said.
NATO’s Article 4 provides for consultations among allies when a member believes its security, territorial integrity or political independence is threatened. It has been invoked nine times.
EU defence ministers have discussed von der Leyen’s proposal, but support appears limited.
“The Commission president has raised the idea, and now we have to work on it,” EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said.
Military officials say they will follow the political decisions made by EU leaders, while warning against unnecessary duplication of existing security arrangements.
“The vast majority of EU countries are also NATO members. I think we should avoid duplication here,” Lithuanian army commander Gen. Raimundas Vaikšnoras said. “We need to find the right balance so that we do not interfere with or overshadow one another.”
Experts are also divided over whether the EU needs a separate protocol.
Marija Martišiūtė, an analyst at the European Policy Centre, said such a mechanism could be useful because NATO allies are not always willing to invoke Article 4. An EU protocol would give a country facing an attack another avenue to seek support, she said.
Under the proposed mechanism, a member state could present its assessment of an incident, explain how it occurred and identify the perceived threat before seeking assistance or a joint decision from other EU members.
The protocol could also provide for potential responses, Martišiūtė said, including an operation, increased monitoring and vigilance, sanctions or financial measures.
But Jacob Funk Kirkegaard, an analyst at the Bruegel think tank, called the proposal a mistake.
“It is a terrible idea. It just diverts attention,” he said.
Kirkegaard argued that NATO’s Article 4 consultations can already risk becoming a forum for empty talk when 32 allies cannot agree on a response. An EU version would be even more difficult, he said, given differences among member states over defence policy and spending.
He pointed to four neutral EU countries and said some members, including Ireland and Malta, were reluctant to engage on defence issues. Austria, he added, was also hesitant to some extent.
The EU already has a treaty provision requiring member states to provide aid and assistance if another member is the victim of armed aggression on its territory. Earlier this year, EU leaders asked the European Commission to draw up an action plan for implementing that mutual-assistance clause.
So far, member states have held tabletop exercises to exchange ideas about what such assistance would mean in practice. It remains unclear when the Commission will present a concrete action plan.

====================================================================================================

Lithuania is nearing tipping point with growing budget deficit, economist warns
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
05:00:00 UTC
14:00:00 KST

The government has already approved the budget, but it still needs parliamentary backing. The debate is expected to be difficult – spending will exceed revenue by €6bn, and the deficit could reach almost 4% of gross domestic product (GDP), above the EU’s Maastricht criteria.
“Security for every individual and security for the state as a whole” is how Finance Minister Taurimas Valys describes the first national budget he has drawn up. It allocates almost €5bn to defence and around another €2bn to families and the most socially vulnerable.
“We are investing in security – both physical security and social security,” Valys says.
The minister has faced criticism even from coalition partners, who say they have yet to hear a convincing explanation for plans to increase the national debt further.
Pensions for older people will rise by an average of up to €88, the minimum wage by around €56, and salaries for teachers and workers in the cultural and scientific sectors by about €100.
Pay for uniformed officers, including police officers and border guards, will increase by around €130.
The country's budget deficit is expected to reach almost 4% of GDP, exceeding the European Union's agreed Maastricht criterion of 3%.
The minister says Lithuania is not the only country in this position, but acknowledges that servicing the national debt will become more expensive.
Next year, interest payments alone could amount to €1bn.
“Unfortunately, we do not yet have an alternative to borrowing and paying interest. So it is natural that these figures are rising. But this is not some supernatural phenomenon. You have to pay interest on debt. That is my comment,” the finance minister says.
Of greater concern, however, is that the deficit is expected to rise further in 2028, approaching 5% of GDP. It will also remain high in 2029.
“It looks as though the Social Democrats are doing nothing to break out of this cycle. The European Commission gave member states the opportunity to borrow additional money for defence over four years, and during that time countries were supposed to do something to avoid constantly living on credit.
“Instead, it seems that in this case we are living for the next government, with the attitude that after us, the deluge,” says former finance minister Gintarė Skaistė, a member of the opposition Conservatives.
According to Rytis Krušinskas, a professor at Kaunas University of Technology, if the outlook for the coming years is as described, tax rises will be unavoidable.
“I would very much prefer that we did not end up in a country governed by the attitude that after us, the deluge. That expression is particularly apt for southern European countries. The impression is that the governing parties, knowing that there is still room to borrow, are not pushing themselves into a corner.
“But Lithuania is approaching a situation in which we will reach what is known as a tipping point. That will inevitably force us to consider the structural reforms that are needed, and then it will be very painful. That is one side of the coin: once we reach that tipping point, we will inevitably be talking about tax increases, and everyone will be affected,” the economist says.
“The fundamental question is whether the measures chosen are effective and whether they will be sufficient. I do not see a clear explanation of the reasoning behind these choices in the government's communication,” he adds.
Coalition partners also critical
“The economy is growing, yet we are increasing the debt. At this point, the figures simply do not add up, either economically or financially,” says former prime minister Algirdas Butkevičius, a member of Democrats “For Lithuania”.
Butkevičius says he cannot recall such chaotic budget planning.
“I have been working on the Budget and Finance Committee since 1996, and I really do not want to subject anyone to severe criticism, but we have never had a situation like this in parliament,” Butkevičius says.
Even a Social Democrat, Algirdas Sysas, has called Valys an “astronaut”, implying that he is out of touch with reality.
Coalition partners say they have put forward proposals to increase government revenue.
The Democrats have called for higher taxes on the gambling industry, while the Farmers and Greens have proposed increasing excise duties on tobacco and alcohol.
However, they say their proposals have hit a wall.
“We asked the finance minister to give us arguments, because we are putting forward our figures. So what are the arguments for saying no?” says Aušrinė Norkienė, a representative of the Farmers and Greens.
“These proposals would generate very little revenue. In some cases, we cannot even consider them because they could bring in less money rather than more.
For example, excise duties on alcohol and tobacco are already higher here than in neighbouring countries, so raising them could have a completely different effect. I think we need sustainable solutions, because these proposals are not sustainable,” says Sysas.
He acknowledges that there are ways to increase revenue, but says they are deeply unpopular.
“Our colleagues, including those in my own party, are very reluctant to talk about tax changes. Take the property tax, which has been completely distorted. Next year, we will collect less than we did the year before last.
“Experts say this needs to be corrected because it does not harm economic growth. It is purely a domestic policy decision,” the Social Democrat says.
Sysas and the Democrats "For Lithuania" have also criticised what is missing from next year's budget. The coalition has decided to improve the country's demographic situation, but some politicians say key measures are absent.
For example, increased childcare benefits are not planned until 2028. Next year, millions of euros are earmarked for a payment to help parents prepare their children for their first year of school, as well as for children's extracurricular activities and summer camps.
The opposition argues that, given the size of the deficit, some of these measures should be reconsidered.
“We need to avoid new spending and, instead, live within our means,” Skaistė says.
Parliamentary approval
The battle over public finances will begin next week.

Canada awaits result in Alberta independence vote

14:00:00 KST

Alberta separatists lose vote on leaving Canada
EDMONTON – Canada’s province of Alberta rejected a plan to hold a binding independence referendum, results showed on Oct 20, a setback for separatists backed by allies of US President Donald Trump.
Public broadcaster CBC and leading private network CTV projected a comfortable victory for the federalist side, with official results showing more than 76% support for national unity with more than a third of ballots counted.
Prime Minister Mark Carney argued the vote had been held “at the worst possible time”, citing the need for national stability as Trump wages a trade war and levels annexation threats.
A sombre mood took over the restaurant in the provincial capital Edmonton where a leading separatist group watched the returns.
Jeffrey Rath, a top leader of the separatist Alberta Prosperity Project, told reporters his push for an independent Alberta will “absolutely” continue, despite the result from the Oct 19 vote.
“We’ve learnt a lot of lessons from this fight,” he said.
Separatist supporter Jour Dain said he was “disappointed in (his) fellow Albertans”.
“Honestly, if this continues down this path of remaining in Canada, I’m just going to move,” the 40-year-old said, expressing a desire to live in the United States.
At the federalist election night party in Edmonton before the results were announced, a band warmed up ahead of an anticipated positive result.
“It was amazing to see the enthusiasm and resolve among Canadians,” said Thomas Lukaszuk, who heads Forever Canadian, the group that campaigned across the province for national unity.
Alberta Premier Danielle Smith, a conservative, said she voted against independence but called the referendum to settle an issue that has divided the province.
She has said a federalists win would close the secession question.
Foreign influence?
Alberta has the world’s fourth-largest proven oil reserves, and much of the separatist momentum has been driven by anger over oil industry management.
Smith has blamed Carney’s predecessor Justin Trudeau for igniting the separatist fire, accusing him of trying to crush oil production to advance his pro-climate agenda.
Alberta’s independence push has also drawn sustained interest from Trump allies.
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent called Alberta a “natural partner” for the United States. Elon Musk, the world’s richest person and a top Trump supporter, posted on X this month that Alberta “should separate”.
Separatist leaders have also held meetings at the US State Department and with Republican political operatives.
‘Rash decisions’
Carney, who grew up in Alberta, has worked to improve relations between the province and Ottawa since taking office in 2025.
He has partnered Smith on advancing a new pipeline to export more Alberta bitumen overseas, a project considered a non-starter during Trudeau’s tenure.
Alberta Prosperty Project leader Mitch Sylvestre told AFP earlier on Oct 19 that had Carney “threatened” the province in the closing days of the campaign.
Carney’s message was “voting against Canada is dangerous”, Sylvestre said, calling that “very unreasonable”.
Haley Erdegard, a 44-year-old who voted in Edmonton, voiced discomfort with the idea advanced by some separatists that Alberta is forced to share too much of its oil revenue with the rest of Canada.
“I think we probably need to put some more work towards cooperation before making rash decisions about trying to start our own country,” she told AFP. AFP

Russian pipeline gas exports to China up 3.7% in January-September
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
04:58:41 UTC
13:58:41 KST

BEIJING, October 20. /TASS/. China increased imports of Russian pipeline gas by 3.7% in value terms in January-September compared with the same period last year, to $7.57 bln, according to data from China’s General Administration of Customs.
The agency traditionally does not disclose the physical volume of pipeline gas imports. According to the published statistics, Russia is China’s largest supplier of pipeline gas. Turkmenistan ranks second ($6.34 bln, down 2% year-on-year), followed by Myanmar ($1.13 bln, down 4.7%), Kazakhstan ($840.34 mln, down 2.3%), and Uzbekistan ($356.09 mln, down 43.9%).
The value of pipeline gas imported by China from Russia in September was estimated at $1.04 bln, roughly the same as in August.
According to the agency’s statistics, China increased its imports of Russian pipeline gas by 25% in 2024, to $8.03 bln. In 2025, the figure rose by 17.1% to $9.41 bln, while supplies via the Power of Siberia pipeline increased by approximately 25% in volume terms to around 38.8 bln cubic meters.
Following Russian President Vladimir Putin’s visit to China in late August and early September 2025, the two countries signed an agreement on annual supplies of 106 bln cubic meters of Russian gas to China.

Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
04:55:46 UTC
13:55:46 KST

The US government has ordered its agencies to stop using artificial intelligence tools from Chinese mainland startup DeepSeek as the two countries race for dominance in the fast-moving sector.
A notice on Monday from the Department of Homeland Security announced the ban on products developed by DeepSeek – and tools created using DeepSeek by third parties – saying they must be removed from IT devices.
The department can issue direction to civilian agencies, but not the military or intelligence services. 
"DeepSeek's models present multiple threat vectors," said a document attached to Monday's notice.
Use of DeepSeek AI tools "may result in the transfer of sensitive data to [China] if used by US government employees or vendors," the department warned.
Its servers are located in China, where the legal system permits the government "extensive authority" to access private company infrastructure, it said.
DeepSeek, one of China's top AI labs, shook up the industry in January 2025 with a low-cost, high-performance chatbot, challenging assumptions of US dominance.
The firm released a long-awaited new model, V4, in April, and this month updated a faster, more lightweight version of V4.
Despite their fierce competition in the field, China and the United States in September agreed to set up a "communication channel" for AI incidents.
The topic is expected to arise again when the countries' leaders meet next month at a summit in Shenzhen. (AFP)

Danish home sales fall 12 percent as higher rates slow market
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
04:54:24 UTC
13:54:24 KST

Denmark’s housing market is showing signs of slowing after a strong start to 2026, according to transaction figures from property portal Boligsiden.
A total of 7,709 homes were sold in September, 12 percent fewer than in the same month last year.
Housing transactions during the first nine months of 2026 were three percent below the corresponding period in 2025.
Apartment sales have fallen most sharply. Eight percent fewer apartments have been sold nationwide this year, while Copenhagen has recorded a decline of 23 percent.
Brian Friis Helmer, personal finance economist at AL Sydbank, said rising mortgage rates could partly explain the slowdown.
Fixed-rate mortgages have recently fluctuated between four and five percent, compared with 3.5 percent at the beginning of the year.
Higher prices for gasoline, natural gas and electricity are also reducing the money households have available, he said.
However, strong employment and rising inflation-adjusted incomes continue to support the housing market.
Sales of houses and terraced homes are also below last year’s level. Holiday home sales, by contrast, have increased by 4.5 percent.
Boligsiden communications director Birgit Daetz said the increase indicates that many households remain financially secure because holiday homes are traditionally purchased during periods of economic strength.
Rising property values and the possibility of rental income may also make such purchases more affordable, she said.

Copenhagen mayor disputes Frederiksen’s claims about meat in nursing homes
Copenhagen Lord Mayor Sisse Marie Welling of the Socialist People’s Party has accused Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen of presenting an inaccurate picture of food policies in the city’s nursing homes.
Frederiksen wrote on Instagram that a Copenhagen proposal could prevent nursing home residents from receiving the meat they want.
“It is a lack of respect for the elderly person’s right to make decisions for themselves,” Frederiksen wrote. “Those people in nursing homes who have toiled and slaved for our country must of course be allowed to eat meat.”
Welling rejected the claim.
“The elderly must naturally have the food they know and like. For many of them, that involves meat,” she wrote.
Welling said individual nursing homes can decide how to plan menus and how much meat to serve. She said residents’ nutritional needs should take priority over climate concerns.
The dispute follows debate over Copenhagen’s food and meal strategy, which aims to make municipal meals more sustainable and reduce purchases of beef.
A consultancy analysis reported that some nursing homes had rejected residents’ birthday requests for beef because of carbon reduction targets.
The study surveyed 200 nursing home residents and 607 people receiving meals at home.
Between 58 and 60 percent were satisfied with the food, while 8 to 13 percent reported little or no satisfaction.
Several nursing home residents criticized meat quality and said beef rarely appeared on menus. The analysis also found that residents wanted greater influence over their meals.
More than half of surveyed Danish teachers feel stressed every week
More than half of teachers in a new union survey said they experience stress daily or weekly, with most attributing it to their working conditions.
The survey by Danmarks Lærerforening, the Danish Union of Teachers, included responses from 1,901 public school teachers and kindergarten class leaders.
Sixteen percent said they felt stressed at work every day, while 36 percent experienced stress weekly and 23 percent monthly.
Nine in 10 of those experiencing stress said workplace conditions were responsible.
“We are facing a working environment problem in the public schools, while at the same time many teachers choose to leave,” union chair Gordon Ørskov Madsen said.
More than one in three respondents said they had taken sick leave from teaching because of stress.
Teachers identified classroom disruption, insufficient preparation time, heavy workloads and difficulty obtaining help for pupils with special needs as major pressures.
Some also reported that parents expected them to resolve conflicts between pupils that occurred outside school.
Nana Vaaben, an associate professor at University College Copenhagen, said teachers can experience moral stress when they know pupils need help but lack the authority to provide it.
Respondents identified fewer teaching hours, more preparation time and better support for pupils with special needs as the measures most likely to reduce stress.
The union plans to raise those proposals in upcoming negotiations with the government and other labor market parties.
Denmark and Vietnam to establish strategic partnership
Denmark and Vietnam will establish a strategic partnership during Vietnamese President Tô Lâm’s state visit to Denmark this week.
Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen of the Social Democrats and Lâm are expected to formally enter into the agreement Tuesday, the Prime Minister’s Office said.
The partnership will build on a 2023 agreement covering areas including climate policy, green growth and the transition to cleaner energy.
The Prime Minister’s Office did not provide further details about the new agreement.
“I am pleased that we, here on the 55th anniversary of Denmark’s diplomatic relations with Vietnam, are now further strengthening Danish-Vietnamese cooperation,” Frederiksen said.
“In an unpredictable world, we need strong partnerships. Both for Denmark and for the EU,” she added.
The agreement is being announced during a state visit by Lâm and his spouse, Ngô Phương Ly.
Independent authority to investigate police strikes against photographers
The Independent Police Complaints Authority will investigate reports that police officers struck two press photographers with batons during demonstrations in Copenhagen on Saturday.
The photographers worked for Danish newspapers Politiken and Ekstra Bladet and were involved in separate incidents during demonstrations for and against remigration.
Copenhagen Police referred the cases to the independent authority, known as DUP, following criticism from both newspapers.
“The Copenhagen Police in no way wish to place obstacles in the way of the press carrying out their work,” police said.
Politiken reported that its photographer was struck several times, had his camera smashed and received treatment at an emergency room.
Ekstra Bladet’s photographer said he was struck on the arm with a baton despite carrying cameras and visible press credentials.
Politiken editor-in-chief Christian Jensen described the incident as a serious attack on press freedom.
“The police make the press their adversary by preventing us from doing our job, which is also about witnessing the police’s exercise of their power,” he wrote.
Ekstra Bladet editor-in-chief Knud Brix also called the reported incident “completely unacceptable.”
The Danish Union of Press Photographers and the Danish Union of Journalists have requested a meeting with the national police commissioner.
They want police leadership to explain how similar incidents will be prevented and how journalists will be protected while covering demonstrations.
Delayed UN climate reports could weaken action before COP33, Danish expert warns
Global climate efforts could face serious setbacks if the UN climate panel does not publish its next assessment reports before the COP33 summit in 2028, a Danish climate expert has warned.
“Without the reports, countries will stand on a basis that is less comprehensive. They will lack crucial knowledge,” said Adrian Lema, head of the National Centre for Climate Research at the Danish Meteorological Institute.
He said countries could spend time debating scientific facts instead of agreeing on action.
“The consequence may be that we set climate action back years, and that uncertainty is created about some of the progress we have achieved,” Lema said.
COP33 will include the next major review of countries’ progress under the 2015 Paris Agreement.
A weeklong meeting of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, known as the IPCC, ended Friday without agreement on a budget or timetable for the reports.
Lema attended as Denmark’s lead negotiator and wanted the reports published well before COP33.
Saudi Arabia, Russia, Iran, India and China argued that publication before the summit was unnecessary, he said.
IPCC decisions require consensus rather than majority votes.
Lema said an agreement remained possible but had become more difficult.
“If we can get enough countries to say it loud and clear, then the few who disagree will be under a different pressure,” he said.
Copenhagen begins separate collection of used diapers for recycling
The City of Copenhagen began installing separate waste bins for used diapers in residential courtyards and municipal day-care centers Monday.
Diapers previously had to be placed with residual waste and were incinerated. They will now be processed at Denmark’s first diaper treatment facility.
“There is a major climate benefit in recycling the diapers instead of incinerating them,” Climate, Environment and Technology Mayor Line Barfod of the Red-Green Alliance said.
The city estimates that between 85 and 94 percent of diaper waste, including liquids and feces, can be converted into new materials.
Cellulose and the contents of the diapers will become biofiber used to produce biogas, electricity and district heating.
Plastic components can be recycled into products such as car interiors. Superabsorbent polymers can become binding material for the construction industry.
Collection will expand to municipal nursing homes, senior housing and other city institutions in February 2027.
Residents of detached houses and members of allotment garden associations will also be able to join the program next year. The scheme is expected to be fully implemented in 2029.
The bins will accept diapers for children and adults, incontinence pads, paper-based cloths and wet wipes without plastic or bamboo. Menstrual hygiene products are excluded.
Diaper waste must be placed in an ordinary plastic trash bag sealed with a tight knot.
Study finds misogynistic TikTok content can appear within minutes
Young male TikTok users can encounter misogynistic content within minutes, even when they do not actively search for it, according to a Danish study.
Researchers from the Center for Digital Pedagogy and Analyse & Tal created eight fictional profiles representing men ages 16 to 19 interested in fitness, dating, investing and gaming.
After the profiles interacted with videos about those subjects, researchers allowed them to scroll automatically for one hour.
Content associated with the “manosphere” appeared after an average of three minutes. In one case, it appeared after 21 seconds.
The manosphere refers to online communities and content that degrade women or support restricting their rights and opportunities.
Researchers also examined one year of viewing data provided by 29 men ages 15 to 22. They identified an average of five to six manosphere videos in each participant’s weekly feed.
The researchers said this was a minimum estimate but emphasized that the 29 participants were not representative of all young men.
Employment and Equality Minister Ane Halsboe-Jørgensen of the Social Democrats called for stronger social media regulation and more discussion in schools and homes.
TikTok said it takes the findings seriously.
“We proactively remove 98.1 percent of the videos that violate our rules on hate and hateful behavior,” Nordic communications director Lukasz Lindell said.
TikTok said it was also working to diversify recommendations and interrupt repetitive content patterns.
Government wants employers to fund Danish lessons for foreign workers
The Danish government wants employers to pay for Danish lessons for workers from countries outside the European Union before they arrive in Denmark.
Social Democratic finance spokesperson Kaare Dybvad Bek announced the proposal Monday during the Folketing’s debate on the government’s 2027 budget bill.
“It provides a saving of 100 million DKK, but first and foremost it sends a clear signal that people who come to the country to work must speak Danish,” he said.
Dybvad Bek said the issue concerned Denmark’s understanding of itself as a society.
More foreign workers have entered the restaurant and service industries in recent years, particularly in Copenhagen. This has led to more customers being served in English rather than Danish, he said.
During the debate, Dybvad Bek also argued that Danes risk losing practical skills when they rely on food delivery services such as Wolt and artificial intelligence for manageable tasks.
He also referred to planned restrictions affecting what he called “underpaid African agricultural workers.”
Dybvad Bek further criticized Nepalese and Iranian nationals who, he said, use Denmark’s education system to enter the labor market while avoiding other requirements.

Regional train services between Odense and Fredericia have been suspended until at least 2 p.m. Monday because of a severed cable.
DSB, Denmark’s national rail operator, has ordered rail replacement buses and updated its journey planner.
InterCity and express trains continue to operate on the route, although passengers may experience longer travel times.
“In Odense and Fredericia, there are staff in orange vests who can assist with guidance,” DSB said.
Banedanmark, the state agency responsible for Denmark’s railway infrastructure, is working to repair the damaged cable.
Train services on the route were expected to return to full capacity Monday after several days of disruptions. The cable damage means that this is no longer possible.
Passengers have experienced longer journeys and fewer trains between the two cities since a fire damaged a relay hut near Aarup in western Funen on October 9.
The hut contained electronic equipment used by the railway’s signaling system. The fire caused signal failures between Middelfart and Odense, disrupting services on Funen and across Denmark.
Even after more trains return, services will continue at reduced speeds near Aarup Station, where trains will temporarily be unable to stop.

Denmark can expect sunshine Monday before rain and stronger winds arrive during the rest of the week.
“On Monday, we have a beautiful autumn day in store,” Danish Meteorological Institute meteorologist Marie Timm said. “There will be some high-altitude clouds in the sky, but otherwise it is a beautiful day where there will be sun for everyone.”
After overnight temperatures fell close to freezing in some areas, daytime temperatures will rise to between 9 and 13 degrees Celsius.
Winds will generally be light to moderate, although coastal areas could experience fresher conditions.
Tuesday will begin dry with some sunshine before clouds and rain move across Denmark from the southeast.
The islands will receive rain during the morning and early afternoon, while northern Jutland will be affected later.
Timm said the amount of rain and strength of the wind remained uncertain because forecasts continued to change.
Another weather front will bring rain from the west Wednesday, with only brief dry periods expected.
Widespread rain is also forecast Thursday, followed by stronger southerly winds and further rain Friday.
Daytime temperatures from Tuesday through Friday will range from 8 to 13 degrees, while nighttime temperatures will remain between 5 and 10 degrees.
Timm advised people to bring rainwear rather than umbrellas because of the expected wind.
One in three Danish teachers reports verbal abuse from pupils
One in three Danish public school teachers experienced rude or abusive language from pupils during the previous week, according to a new survey.
Four in 10 teachers said such incidents occurred daily or several times a week, education trade publication Folkeskolen reported.
The survey was completed by 1,901 teachers and kindergarten class leaders between August 26 and September 14, 2026.
Teachers reported comments including “You fucking bad teacher,” “You are a damn idiot” and “You don’t boss me around.”
Lars Peter Sønderbo Andersen, a senior researcher in occupational and environmental medicine at Regional Hospital Gødstrup, said the language damages teachers’ working environment and undermines their authority in classrooms.
He said the problem has worsened in recent years.
In a similar survey conducted almost 10 years ago, one in four teachers reported being called derogatory terms such as “bitch,” “idiot” or “whore” at least once a month.
Danmarks Lærerforening, the Danish Union of Teachers, described the new findings as concerning.
“Some of these statements are quite severe, and we can hear from the inquiries we receive that it affects the teachers when they are spoken to like that,” union representative Thomas Andreasen said.
He called for schools to establish clear, shared rules for acceptable language. He also said having more permanent teachers in classrooms could help.
Denmark contacts more than 25 countries seeking prison spaces
Denmark has contacted more than 25 European countries about potentially renting prison spaces as its correctional system faces record overcrowding.
“The Danish Prison and Probation Service is in a serious situation,” Justice Minister Nicolai Wammen of the Social Democrats said. “We must do everything we can to resolve the capacity challenges in Danish prisons.”
Denmark already has an agreement to rent 300 prison spaces in Kosovo for foreign nationals sentenced to deportation. However, delays mean the renovated prison is not expected to begin accepting inmates until late 2027 or early 2028.
The original plan expected inmates to begin serving sentences there in early 2023.
Wammen called the Kosovo agreement important but said additional measures were needed to relieve Denmark’s prisons.
The Justice Ministry declined to identify the countries it contacted or disclose the correspondence. It said publication could risk damaging Denmark’s foreign policy interests.
Estonia’s Justice Ministry confirmed that Denmark had not entered discussions with it. Estonia is concentrating on an existing agreement under which it began receiving inmates from Sweden in 2026.
At the end of September, Denmark had about 4,650 inmates but only 4,300 prison spaces, according to the Prison Officers’ Union.
The union calculated the average occupancy rate at 105.4 percent, the highest recorded level. It stood at 102.7 percent in 2025.
Denmark rejects Russian proposal for maritime and air security agreement
Russia has urged Denmark to enter into a security agreement intended to prevent incidents at sea and in the air, Danish broadcaster TV 2 reported.
The Russian Embassy in Denmark said Russia had previously made the same proposal.
“Today, one can only note that Russia’s initiative for de-escalation has not been met with understanding,” the embassy wrote.
The appeal follows a September incident in which the Russian frigate Soobrazitelny fired two flares toward a Danish military helicopter in international waters near Gedser.
According to the Danish Armed Forces, the flares were fired without warning while the Fennec helicopter was photographing the frigate during a routine mission.
Russia’s ambassador to Denmark, Vladimir Barbin, later accused the helicopter of acting “provocatively.”
The embassy said an agreement could provide a legal framework for preventing similar incidents.
Defence Minister Jeppe Bruus of the Social Democrats rejected the proposal.
“Russia’s aggressive behavior clearly and deliberately violates the international rules by which the country is already bound,” he said. “As long as that is the case, entering into more agreements that are not complied with does not solve the problem.”
The embassy said Russia had protested through diplomatic channels over similar incidents in 2025 and 2026.
Eight arrested during demonstration and counterprotests in Copenhagen
Eight people were arrested Saturday in connection with a demonstration organized by the movement Det Danske Folk in central Copenhagen.
Three arrests occurred before the demonstration began at 2 p.m. in Kongens Nytorv, Copenhagen Police Deputy Inspector Jakob Hansen said.
Two people were arrested after being “in disagreement about some things,” while another was arrested for refusing to provide their name to police.
Five more people were arrested around 5 p.m. as the demonstration ended at Højbro Plads.
“As the demonstration is dispersed, there are smaller groups that begin putting on masks and initiating confrontations with others,” Hansen said. “We have to prevent that, and that leads to a clash with the police.”
Officers drew their batons during the confrontation.
Police did not disclose why the five people were arrested or how many people were involved. It was also too early to specify possible charges against any of the eight people.
The demonstrators marched from Kongens Nytorv toward Christiansborg Palace Square. Counterprotesters gathered at several locations along the route.
Det Danske Folk promoted the demonstration with slogans supporting what it called “fair and realistic remigration” and opposing Islamization, Sharia law and social control.
The counterprotesters gathered under the slogan “No to remigration.”
Electricity’s share of Danish energy use rises to 23.4 percent
Electricity accounted for 23.4 percent of Denmark’s total energy consumption in 2025, an increase of 1.5 percentage points from the previous year.
Green Power Denmark, an industry organization representing the Danish energy sector, said the increase was driven mainly by electric vehicles and the district heating sector’s use of electric boilers and heat pumps.
The organization said growing electrification is gradually reducing Denmark’s reliance on oil and natural gas.
“We are freeing ourselves from what is happening in the Middle East and American politics,” Green Power Denmark chief executive Kristian Jensen said.
He said Danish energy prices remain affected by developments abroad because the country still relies on prices set by global markets.
Denmark’s electrification rate rose by only 3.8 percentage points in total from 2016 through 2024, making the 1.5-point increase in 2025 significant.
Green Power Denmark wants electricity to account for 60 percent of total energy consumption by 2035.
Jensen said achieving that target would require industrial companies to replace natural gas with electricity and heat pumps.
He pointed to iron foundries and food producers, including dairy group Arla, as examples of industries already using heat pumps.
Such changes could reduce companies’ carbon dioxide emissions and energy costs while improving their competitiveness, Jensen said.
Figures for Denmark’s electrification rate in 2026 are not yet available.
The 21-year-old singer has gone from posting piano videos on TikTok to becoming one of Denmark’s biggest pop stars. On Friday, she received the top prize at DR’s annual P3 Guld music awards.
Danish singer Annika has won P3 Prisen, the main award at one of Denmark’s most prominent annual music events, P3 Guld.
The 21-year-old received the award Friday evening at DR Koncerthuset in Copenhagen, a year after being nominated for the same prize but losing out to Danish band Aphaca.
P3 Guld is the annual music awards show organised by P3, the youth-oriented music and entertainment radio station run by Danish public broadcaster DR.
The event celebrates artists who have made a significant impact on Danish music over the past year, with P3 Prisen regarded as its main award.
Annika, whose full name is Annika Wedderkopp, was selected by a P3 jury ahead of fellow nominees Zar Paulo and producer Anton Westerlin, who is also her boyfriend.
“With an authentic foundation in her own life, Annika creates massive hits about breakups and infatuations, about doubt and a steely belief that everything will naturally work out,” the jury said.
From TikTok to the Danish charts
Annika’s rise has been rapid.
She began by posting videos of herself singing at the piano on TikTok before breaking through with “Knuser hjerter” in 2024.
She followed it with several successful releases, including “Så længe jeg er sexy”, and won P3 Talentet, the event’s talent award, that same year.
Last year, she released her debut album “AW”, which includes “Stolt”, a collaboration with Danish rapper Lamin. She also opened Roskilde Festival’s Orange Stage, the festival’s largest and most prestigious stage.
Previous recipients of P3 Prisen include some of Denmark’s best-known contemporary artists, including The Minds of 99, Tobias Rahim, Artigeardit, Lamin, Tina Dickow and Jada.
Other winners
Several other awards were presented at Friday’s ceremony.
Guldimund and Saveus won P3 Lytterhittet – the listeners’ choice award – for their song “Vil du noget?”.
Zar Paulo received P3 Live, an award recognising an artist who has distinguished themselves on Denmark’s live music scene. The award returned this year after previously being presented in 2001 and 2009.
Danish-Faroese artist Friða Saiya won P3’s Næste, a new award that has replaced P3 Talentet and highlights emerging artists.
Criticism over lack of women
This year’s P3 Guld also faced criticism before the ceremony over the gender balance among its performers.
Twelve men and two women were scheduled to perform during the evening.
Ditte Christiane Jensen, head of editorial at DR Ung, defended the lineup in a written response to Ritzau.
“Talent, creativity and artistic quality are not about gender,” she said.
“This year’s lineup was put together based on the artists and bands that have left a significant mark on the music year and in P3’s universe.”

Trump: Greenland deal biggest real estate deal ever
The US president says he “got it for nothing” after signing a new defence agreement with Denmark and Greenland that expands the American military presence on the island.
US President Donald Trump has described a new defence and security agreement with Denmark and Greenland as potentially “the biggest real estate deal that has ever been made”.
Speaking at a Republican campaign rally in Dalton, Georgia, Trump portrayed the agreement as a major achievement for the United States.
“What do you think of the deal I made on Greenland? Got it for nothing,” Trump told supporters.
“It is probably the biggest real estate deal that has ever been made.”
Trump was campaigning ahead of the US midterm elections on November 3.
His comments come after months of tension over Greenland, an autonomous territory within the Kingdom of Denmark. Trump has repeatedly said that the United States wants control and ownership of Greenland, arguing that the island is crucial to American national security.
Two new US military bases
The United States, Denmark and Greenland signed a new security and defence agreement on Greenland at the end of September following lengthy negotiations.
The agreement was signed at the United Nations in New York shortly after Trump addressed the UN General Assembly.
It allows the United States to establish two additional military bases in Greenland.
The US currently operates Pituffik Space Base in northwestern Greenland, which plays an important role in missile warning, space surveillance and Arctic security.
The new agreement also opens the possibility of deploying parts of the planned US Golden Dome missile defence system in Greenland. The system is intended to protect the United States against threats including missiles and drones.
Despite Trump’s description of the agreement as a “real estate deal”, it does not transfer ownership of Greenland to the United States.
Trump’s comments came as Republicans campaign to retain control of Congress in the November midterm elections. Democrats are currently polling more strongly in the race for the House of Representatives, while control of the Senate remains more uncertain.
Republicans currently hold majorities in both chambers.

Denmark’s shift from fossil fuels to electricity is accelerating
Electric cars, heat pumps and electric boilers are driving a sharp increase in the share of Denmark’s energy consumption covered by electricity.
Denmark is becoming increasingly electrified as electric cars, heat pumps and electric boilers replace fossil fuels.
Electricity accounted for 23.4 percent of Denmark’s total energy consumption in 2025, according to figures highlighted by industry organisation Green Power Denmark.
That was an increase of 1.5 percentage points in just one year.
The increase is significant. Between 2016 and 2024, the share of electricity in Denmark’s total energy consumption rose by only 3.8 percentage points.
The acceleration is being driven particularly by the growing number of electric cars and by district heating companies investing in electric boilers and heat pumps.
Kristian Jensen, CEO of Green Power Denmark, says the development will gradually make Denmark less dependent on imported oil and natural gas – and therefore less exposed to international energy prices and geopolitical developments.
“We are freeing ourselves from what is going on in the Middle East and American politics,” Jensen told Ritzau.
“When Danes experience that gasoline, diesel and electricity have become more expensive than they were a year ago, it is because we are still dependent on the price set in the rest of the world.”
Target: 60 percent by 2035
Green Power Denmark wants electricity to account for 60 percent of Denmark’s total energy consumption by 2035.
Reaching that level will require a much faster transition in Danish industry, according to Jensen.
He points to heat pumps as one of the technologies that can help companies replace natural gas with electricity. Iron foundries and food producers, including dairy group Arla, have already demonstrated that large heat pumps can be used in industrial production.
Jensen argues that other companies should follow their example.
“It will not only reduce the companies’ CO2 emissions, it will also reduce energy expenses and thereby improve their competitiveness,” he said.
Figures for Denmark’s electrification rate in 2026 are not yet available, but Green Power Denmark expects the shift towards electricity to continue.
