The ultimate safety net: why joining an a-Kasse could be your smartest career move
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
04:49:44 UTC
13:49:44 KST

Flexicurity and the role of the a-Kasse
The cornerstone of the Danish labour market is “flexicurity”, helping employers to adapt, and empowering employees with robust financial and professional security.
Unlike many countries where unemployment insurance is managed entirely by the state, the Danish system relies heavily on an unemployment insurance fund, or a-kasse.
As an expat, joining an a-kasse early is arguably the smartest career move you can make. It provides a reliable financial safety net if you lose your job or decide to follow a new career path, offering a predictable income while you transition between roles.
Beyond financial peace of mind, an organisation like Akademikernes A-kasse gives you access to targeted career counselling, legal safety and deep market insights that can help you fast-track your next breakthrough.
Resources for members at Akademikernes A-kasse.
Deciphering the Danish workplace
Once inside a Danish company, the informal atmosphere can be refreshing but confusing. 
Ulugbek Bekmukhamedov is a Copenhagen-based data analyst from Uzbekistan, who wrestles with some of the cultural differences.
“The use of first names is standard and managers sit with everyone else,” he says, “but informality is not the same as simplicity. It can be confusing because so much is left unsaid.”
It’s worth noting then, you would be wise to proactively master a few essential unwritten rules. This is a society that heavily relies on trust and autonomy, where traditional micromanagement and strict reporting lines are minimal.
You might find that Danes take lunch much earlier than usual. “11:30 am seems to be the average lunchtime,” laughs Ulugbek. But taking these shared, informal moments seriously is precisely where professional trust is built.
In Denmark, work-life balance is a reality. Booking meetings late in the afternoon – especially on Fridays – is highly discouraged, as employees head home early.
Soft Skills matter
Khurshid Sultan is Senior Career Consultant at Akademikernes A-kasse. “Navigating a career can become isolating in a new country,” he warns. “Build a small network around your search. Talk to career consultants, professional groups, and peers.”
Ultimately, Danish employers hire for team fit just as much as technical capability. “Employers may look for independence, collaboration, curiosity and the ability to take initiative,” adds Khurshid.
“Show these through examples, not claims.”
Finally, he recommends that you don’t ignore the native language completely. “You do not need to be fluent to begin, but learning the language can widen your options and help you understand the culture around work.”
By engaging with the collaborative culture, combined with securing your baseline with an a-kasse, you can turn a challenging transition into an empowering career leap.

Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner is also expected to participate in the talks remotely because of illness, one source said.
The schedule remains tentative and could change.
The planned talks with Putin are also expected to address the release of American citizen Stephen Hubbard, who had reportedly been serving with a Ukrainian territorial defense unit in the town of Izium, in Kharkiv Oblast. Hubbard was detained by Russia in 2022.
The planned negotiations follow an Oct. 18 phone call between Zelensky, Witkoff, and Kushner, during which they discussed possible next steps toward a peace agreement.
Zelensky also told Bloomberg that he had proposed suspending Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil infrastructure in exchange for additional American-made Patriot interceptor missiles to defend against Russian ballistic missile attacks.
The proposal comes as Washington presses Kyiv to stop targeting Russian oil refineries, amid growing tensions over U.S. military support for Ukraine.
Ukrainian officials told the Kyiv Independent that Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has yet to approve the transfer of a significant batch of Patriot interceptor missiles already paid for by Kyiv's allies, raising concerns in Ukraine that Washington is withholding the weapons as political pressure.
NATO officials told the Kyiv Independent that deliveries under the purchasing initiative were continuing, including air defense equipment, while a U.S. government official disputed Ukraine's allegations.

Unique evacuation: Kharkiv military hospital tells how wounded soldier was rescued by heavy-lift drone
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
04:39:00 UTC
13:39:00 KST

Unique evacuation: Kharkiv military hospital tells how wounded soldier was rescued by heavy-lift drone
The hospital announced this on its Facebook page, according to Ukrinform.
"The first-ever aerial evacuation of a wounded soldier from the battlefield in the history of the war was carried out by Ukraine's Defense Forces in the Kharkiv region. A 49-year-old soldier who had lost both legs was lifted from a position in the Kupiansk sector by a large drone," the post said.
The report says the soldier had been holding an observation post when Russian forces killed his comrade with explosive drops from drones. Kostiantyn was wounded in both legs and left alone at the position. Several attempts to evacuate him using different means, including unmanned ground vehicles, failed as the enemy did everything possible to thwart the missions.
"Although the Russians urged me to surrender, I couldn't allow myself to do that. They dropped either a loudspeaker or a gramophone and tried to put psychological pressure on me. I remember it all word for word because the recording kept playing over and over: 'Buddy, we know you're here. Your comrades won't help you. Did you hear that explosion? The next one could hit you. A white light will lead you out. And then it's captivity, an exchange, and home!'
"They knew I was wounded and had already been left without my comrade, holding the position alone. I simply shouted: 'Russian warship, go f... yourself!' And that was it. After that, they dropped two anti-tank mines on me...
"I'm very grateful to my command, especially my company commander, who kept everything under control. They kept dropping medicines for me along with food and water: Betadine, antibiotics, painkillers and other things," said the soldier, now a patient at the Kharkiv hospital.
Soldiers from several brigades and even army corps joined forces to save him. The Ukrainian military had never before carried out an evacuation operation of this complexity, said Artem Bohomolov, commander of the 10th Army Corps.
"There was no other way to save him. What was done had absolutely never been done before in Ukraine. I cannot say whether similar operations have been carried out elsewhere in the world. The planning was lengthy and meticulous. Dozens of people worked to save one man. The planning involved Unmanned Systems Forces, artillery units, electronic warfare units and air defense units. But every life saved is worth many, many hours of work," Bohomolov said.
The serviceman underwent several operations at the Kharkiv hospital. Before that, it took several days to stabilize his condition.
"Since medicines and food were dropped at his position by drones, he managed to avoid severe complications, suppuration, gangrene and other problems. By the time he reached us, his wounds were already granulating, which showed that he had received antibiotic therapy and anti-inflammatory medication. Without that, he would not have survived," said Volodymyr Kupriianchuk, head of the hospital's Department of Surgical Infections and Thermal Injuries.
The soldier was evacuated using a Ukrainian-made Ayudag-6 hexacopter, also known as Heavy Shot. For this mission, engineers from Gurzuf Defence worked with the military to add certain components and make modifications to the drone.
"This is the first mission in the history of the war in which a person has been evacuated by an aircraft. I think everyone understands how challenging it was: you weren't carrying someone one or two kilometers, or even 10, but more than 15 kilometers. And you knew that aerial combat was ongoing and electronic jamming was constant. That entails enormous responsibility," said Ivan, one of Gurzuf Defence's directors.
"No one fights alone, and unconventional thinking usually leads to success. We knew that an aircraft like this was being built for one of the brigades. We contacted the manufacturer and the brigade – the 92nd – and they agreed to help, sending both the aircraft and their specialists to assist us," said Taras Maksimov, commander of the 14th Mechanized Brigade named after Prince Roman the Great.
"An incredible number of people and various units were involved in providing cover for the aircraft's flight. It was like 'Star Wars' – a huge operation, a real buzz!" said a serviceman known by the call sign "Vader" from the Unmanned Ground Systems Company of the 92nd Assault Brigade.
The day before the operation, a video was recorded on a phone for the wounded soldier, explaining how to put on his equipment and secure himself to the aircraft. A camera was also installed on the drone so the team could see whether he was ready for the flight, explained a pilot from the 30th Mechanized Brigade, who uses the call sign "Chornyi."
"They are all my angels now, especially the pilot. He came to visit me in the hospital. The general came too, and the drone manufacturers brought me gifts...
"Where did I find the strength, and how did I hold on? I don't know. God helped me. The support from my command kept me going. I have a very good company commander and very good guys, my comrades. They were all deeply worried about me. And it was precisely this – knowing that someone was thinking about me and that no one had abandoned me – that kept me going all this time," Kostiantyn said.
The hospital added that he now faces prosthetic fitting and rehabilitation, as well as psychological support.

US Supreme Court to hear case on race in school admissions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
04:38:07 UTC
13:38:07 KST

US Supreme Court to hear case on race in school admissions
A group of parents claims local admission policy boosts Black and Latino students while constraining Asian applicants.
The United States Supreme Court has agreed to hear a case about the role of race in admissions to selective Maryland middle schools after a group of parents claimed policies discriminated against Asian students in favour of Black and Latino students.
The Supreme Court agreed on Monday to hear the parents’ plea on four academically rigorous “magnet” schools in Montgomery County, a suburb on the outskirts of Washington, DC, in the neighbouring state of Maryland.
The high court said it would weigh whether the parent group has enough evidence of discrimination for the case to move forward.
Lower courts previously dismissed the case because Asian-American students were not underrepresented at the specialised-curriculum schools compared with the pool of students that applied.
If the Supreme Court rules for the parent group, the Association for Education Fairness, it could revive the lawsuit.
The court is expected to hear arguments in the coming months and rule by June.
‘The Pandemic Plan’
The Montgomery County school district’s selection process was introduced in the 2021-2022 school year during the COVID-19 pandemic.
It screens all students for academic potential, and then implements a lottery to randomly assign students from that pool to receive enriched instruction at either a magnet school or a local school.
The suit alleged that the screening process makes it harder for Asian-American students, who the challengers said are clustered in “high-performing, low-poverty elementary schools”, to enter the lottery pool.
Part of the process ranks a student’s performance by comparing the student’s test scores against those of other students whose family incomes are at a similar level.
“Under the applicant pool benchmark, the government can set specific racial targets, hit them, and avoid even an inquiry into discriminatory intent,” so long as it has not explicitly called out race in its process, they wrote in their appeal to the Supreme Court.
Previously thrown out
The case was thrown out in 2022 by US District Judge Paula Xinis. She noted that the percentage of admitted Asian-American students exceeded the percentage of Asian Americans among all applicants to the magnet schools.
Xinis also found no evidence that the lottery policy was implemented with discriminatory intent.
The school system has consistently argued the new admissions policy, called the “Pandemic Plan” due to the timing of its release, is race-neutral.
“The Pandemic Plan is a colorblind lottery,” lawyers wrote in a brief asking the Supreme Court not to take up the case. “Nothing about the Pandemic Plan, its history, or its purpose is offensive to the Constitution.”
Supreme Court justices will now consider whether a group claiming to be targeted by a race-neutral policy must show it was disproportionately harmed to prove intentional discrimination.

Country diary: A species brought to the edge of extinction, recovering in the fens | Mark Cocker
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
04:30:15 UTC
13:30:15 KST

In keeping with this region’s summer of torrid heat and drought, the field by the path was an expanse of burnt, dead thistles. What was totally unexpected were the 13 great egrets among it. Ironically, the birds may well be here as a consequence of the climate crisis, but their appearance in a parched brown expanse felt strange.
First, they are creatures of freshwater marsh and routinely hunt fish. Second, great egrets are the size of grey herons, but pure white, aside from lemon eyes and dagger-like beaks of pale autumnal orange. What was weirdest of all was the gestalt whole; the way they threaded through that horizon of brown, long necks extending and retracting like winding snakes, and all this gleaming intensity focused on catching voles. Then a bird would fly, the white rope of its neck rising, followed by a ragged cloak of wings, turning eventually to the stolid beat of heavy flight.
What is perhaps strangest of all – although birdwatchers have long since normalised those developments – is that here’s a species that was brought to the edge of extinction by the Victorian trade in feathers for haute couture. The species slowly recovered and expanded massively in Europe until it colonised our shores at the beginning of the century. It started to breed in 2010, and by 2019 there were 24 nesting pairs. But the winter total may reach four figures.
Great egrets hunting in a Cambridgeshire field of dead vegetation might be a good news story. Yet the wider tale of Ouse Fen is astonishing. In an innovative partnership between a gravel-extraction business and the RSPB, the whole floodplain has been gradually converted from low-quality agricultural land into one of the richest, most dynamic wetlands in Britain, whose total area will be 3,000 hectares (7,410 acres).
It is already hoaching with wetland wildlife such as water voles and bitterns, spined loaches and marsh harriers. Extensive archaeological work on the other parts of the site has revealed that its most abundant bone material from the Neolithic is remains of beavers and dalmatian pelicans. Given this evidence of its past, who would dare predict what its future might be?

Japan launches world's first mission to collect samples from Martian moon
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
04:29:09 UTC
13:29:09 KST

Faisal Mahmud
20 October 2026•Update: 20 October 2026
Japan successfully launched a spacecraft Tuesday on the world's first mission to collect rock and sand samples from a Martian moon, according to the country's space agency.
The Martian Moons eXploration (MMX) probe separated successfully from an H3 rocket and entered its planned orbit, the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA) announced, according to Kyodo News Agency.
The rocket lifted off from the Tanegashima Space Center in southwestern Japan at 4.41 am local time (1941GMT Monday).
JAXA project manager Makoto Arita said the spacecraft had reached its planned orbit with "exceptional precision."
The 4,480-kilogram spacecraft will travel to Phobos, the larger of Mars' two moons, and is scheduled to enter Martian orbit in August 2027.
A French-German rover will first land on Phobos, followed by two planned landings by the Japanese spacecraft to collect samples.
The probe will subsequently observe Mars' second moon, Deimos, before departing Martian orbit in November 2030. It is expected to return samples to Earth in July 2031.
Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi welcomed the launch, expressing hope that the historic mission would succeed.
The launch was originally scheduled for 2024 but was delayed following the failure of the H3 rocket's maiden flight in 2023.
The international MMX mission seeks to determine how Mars' moons formed and advance technologies for future planetary exploration.

WELLINGTON, Oct. 20 (Xinhua) -- New Zealand exporters can start using the country's free trade agreement with India from Tuesday, with tariffs removed on more than half of New Zealand's exports to the South Asian country as the deal went into effect, a senior New Zealand official said.
Almost 57 percent of New Zealand exports to India are now tariff-free, rising to 82 percent over time, while tariffs on 95 percent of current exports will eventually be removed or reduced, New Zealand Trade and Investment Minister Todd McClay said in a statement.
The agreement removes tariffs on sheep meat, wool and coal, and on more than 95 percent of forestry and wood exports. It also provides preferential quota access for apples, kiwifruit and milk albumins, the statement said, noting that a second round of tariff cuts will take effect on Jan. 1, 2027.
Tariffs on New Zealand wine exports to India, previously as high as 150 percent, will fall to 25 or 50 percent over 10 years, McClay said.
New Zealand and India launched talks in March 2025 and concluded them in nine months, according to the minister. The agreement entered into force 19 months after negotiations began.
The agreement would help New Zealand exporters diversify their markets and support the country's goal of doubling the value of exports over 10 years, he said, adding that New Zealand Trade and Enterprise is running a program to help exporters use the agreement through advice, market insights and connections in India. ■

====================================================================================================

Japan launches unprecedented mission to bring back samples from Mars’ moon phobos
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
04:19:34 UTC
13:19:34 KST

NASA has landed nine spacecraft on Mars over the past 50 years, and China touched down in 2021, but no one has returned samples from Mars, let alone its moons.
Japan has launched a spacecraft on a first-of-its-kind journey to Mars, where it will try to land on the planet’s moon Phobos and bring a piece of it back to Earth.
The Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency, which is leading the effort, launched the spacecraft before dawn on Tuesday from the main spaceport on Tanegashima Island, with officials declaring success an hour later, when the spacecraft separated as planned from the rocket’s upper stage.
Flight controllers burst into applause, shaking hands and embracing each other.
Five space agencies are backing the five-year mission, which will put a robotic sample collector and a small rover on Phobos, the larger and nearer of Mars’ two tiny moons.
A first for Mars and its moons
The $578 million mission, known as MMX for Martian Moon Exploration, centres on a 5-tonne spacecraft expected to reach Mars by late next summer. It will match Phobos’ tight orbit before releasing Idefix, a French-German rover named after the white terrier in the Asterix comics.
No bigger than a microwave oven, Idefix will drop onto Phobos on its own, bouncing for several minutes before stopping in the moon’s extremely low gravity.
“There’s a lot of adrenaline and a lot of excitement and a lot of wow,” said NASA astrophysicist Tom Statler, who is involved in the project.
NASA has landed nine spacecraft on Mars over the past 50 years, and China touched down in 2021, but no one has ever ventured onto Phobos or its companion, Deimos, and no one has returned samples from Mars, let alone its moons. If successful, dust, soil and rock from Phobos will reach Earth in 2031.
Analysts believe Japan has an edge, having already completed two asteroid sample returns.
Phobos is a lumpy, potato-shaped rock about 22 kilometres across. Studying it could explain how Mars’ moons, and possibly moons elsewhere, formed.
What happens after Idefix the rover lands?
The four-wheeled rover is designed to right itself if it lands upside down. All bets are off, though, if it sinks into soft soil or gets wedged between rocks, said the French Space Agency’s Julien Baroukh. Once the rover’s solar panels are deployed, the vehicle can no longer right itself, he added, which is why it will move at a glacial 1 millimetre per second (0.04 inches per second).
Idefix will serve as a “scout for safety,” according to Baroukh, as it prowls around Phobos for 100 days. Japanese flight controllers want to avoid powdery soil and rough terrain when the mothership — a four-legged stationary lander — descends to the surface to gather samples in late 2028 or 2029.
The lander will spend just two hours on Phobos, drilling and vacuuming up at least 10 grams (one-third of an ounce) of material before launching back into space. It will then study Deimos during a series of flybys, leave the Martian neighbourhood in 2030 and hurry back to Earth to deliver the samples in the Australian desert in 2031.
It is a treacherous undertaking, with wreckage littering the path. The moons’ names are hardly comforting: Phobos is Greek for 'fear', and Deimos means 'dread'. They are the twin sons of Ares, the god of war, known as Mars in Roman mythology.
Scientists hope to learn how Mars’ two moons formed
Russia failed in all three of its Phobos attempts, as well as in many other Mars endeavours. In its only other Mars mission, Japan failed to get a spacecraft into orbit around the red planet. Even NASA has had its share of flops in the quest to answer the burning question: did life ever exist on Mars?
By studying the moons, scientists hope to learn whether Phobos and Deimos formed in the aftermath of an ancient collision between Mars and a battering space rock. The moons might also be stray asteroids that were captured by Mars’ gravity.
Either way, scientists expect to find traces of Mars on Phobos, making the samples an irresistible two-for-one that should help demystify how planets and moons form, and perhaps even the recipe for life. The findings will help shape future Mars missions, including crewed ones, said Lindsay Hays, NASA’s acting planetary science director.
“It is a once-in-a-lifetime chance. We are part of the first sample return mission from the Martian system,” said Markus Grebenstein, the German Space Agency’s rover chief.
Japan is not alone in seeking the scientific riches in the Martian system’s rocks and dirt. China plans to launch its own Mars sample return mission in 2028. NASA, meanwhile, is still debating how to retrieve the more than 30 sample tubes collected by its Perseverance rover, the new champion of off-Earth driving.
Japan and China could end up neck and neck in returning samples from the Martian system, as both are targeting 2031.
Japan is investing $350 million (€308 million) in this mission. NASA is contributing $87 million (€77 million), the French Space Agency about $68 million (€60 million), the German Space Agency about $56 million (€49 million) and the European Space Agency some $17 million (€15 million).

European tech investment in Q3 2026: from growth capital to public markets
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
04:16:24 UTC
13:16:24 KST

For two quarters, the story of European tech funding has been about where money was flowing and how it was organized. It focused on a few strategic sectors, with capital flowing through new funds, public programs, and credit. Q3 extends that story by showing some of those efforts in action.
According to Crunchbase, European startup funding edged up from $24 billion in Q2 to $25 billion in Q3. The more significant change came at the later stages, where investment rose from $12.1 billion to $17.3 billion. This suggests that the quarter’s momentum was concentrated in larger, more mature companies rather than spread evenly across the market.
Europe’s growing tech companies are facing a common challenge. Access to capital still lags behind ambitions and financing needs. The €3 billion raised by French AI company Mistral shows how international that funding has become, with investors from Europe, the US, and Asia. But there is progress on the European side, too. The new Scaleup Europe Fund helped lead the round and has backed other major companies, including Fever. As more businesses mature, some go beyond private investors, such as Italian software group Bending Spoons, which completed a $1.68 billion Nasdaq IPO, and two European quantum computing firms, IQM and Pasqal.
The Q3 investment story isn’t only about companies raising hundreds of millions. Other deals point to changes in established industries. AI businesses are starting to compete directly with traditional professional service providers. New tech is also addressing administrative burdens in healthcare.
In this edition, Zubr Capital, a growth equity firm investing in global tech companies, revisits the question Q2 left open: can Europe’s tech companies scale on European terms?
Who Leads Europe’s Biggest Funding Rounds?
In our Q1 digest, we saw funding clustering in fewer, larger rounds. By Q3, the focus shifted to who could lead these rounds as financing needs reached hundreds of millions or even billions of euros.
The previously mentioned €3 billion Series D for Mistral, described by the company as Europe’s largest tech equity round, was led by South Korea’s Samsung, with the Scaleup Europe Fund and US-based PSG Equity as co-leads. Lovable did something similar in Sweden by raising $400 million in a round led by US investor Menlo Ventures and co-led by the European fund. German autonomous systems developer Quantum Systems raised $1.2 billion in a round co-led by Blackstone, Advent, and European investors Noteus Partners and Airbus.
Most of these deals combined VC with corporate investors, private equity, and institutions looking for long-term commitments. That doesn’t mean European funds could only follow. Kembara led a $175 million round for German energy tech company Reverion. DTCP Defence led a $175 million raise for Britain’s maritime-defense company Kraken Technology. But leadership should not be confused with ownership or control. Defense-tech company Helsing raised $1.8 billion internationally, but said it remained predominantly European-owned.
How the Scaleup Europe Fund is Scaling
The fund’s first publicly announced investment came in August when it disclosed a co-lead role in Finnish satellite company ICEYE’s financing (originally announced in June). The fund is targeting €5 billion to address late-stage growth-financing shortages for European tech companies.
Within weeks, the fund’s portfolio reached six companies: ICEYE, Mistral, Lovable, The Exploration Company, Tandem Health, and AI-chip developer EUCLYD. In September, Fever became its seventh portfolio company following a $250 million round. The fund led or co-led several deals, rather than merely participating.
The portfolio is diversifying quickly, spanning satellites, AI, semiconductors, healthcare software, and consumer-facing digital platforms. Fever is a good example. It helps event organizers reach new audiences, sell tickets, and optimize pricing internationally. This suggests the fund’s unifying criterion is global scale, not a single strategic industry.
September also saw CriteriaCaixa and Dutch pension fund ABP committing €250 million each, with Allianz participating. That creates a route for institutional capital into European scaleups at a stage when their funding needs may exceed conventional venture-fund capacity. It is too early to judge the impact: €5 billion is a fundraising target, individual investments are not always disclosed, and entire financing rounds cannot be attributed to the fund. But Q3 showed that the initiative moved from an announced financing vehicle to an active participant in some major international transactions. Growing businesses, however, will eventually need alternatives to large private rounds.
Where European Tech is Finding Different Ways to Go Public
Mature tech companies often look to public markets for both fresh financing and an exit route for early investors. In Q3, these goals were pursued in different ways, showing that a listing’s size doesn’t always equal the fresh money a company receives.
Bending Spoons from Italy completed a $1.68 billion Nasdaq IPO in July. About $954 million from the initial offering went to the company. Proceeds from shares sold by existing holders went to those shareholders.
Quantum computing companies IQM of Finland and Pasqal of France went public on Nasdaq through SPAC mergers rather than conventional IPOs. IQM received approximately €198.7 million in net proceeds from its transaction and related private investment. Pasqal had about $360 million in cash available at closing.
IQM also listed in Helsinki. Smaller European offerings ranged from German defense-antenna manufacturer SMAG (€30 million in Frankfurt) to French industrial-tech company D.A.T.E. (€12.6 million on Euronext Growth Paris). These reflect varying paths and funding scales, not evidence that European exchanges cannot support larger companies. It raises a question for the next stage of European growth: where will Europe’s biggest tech businesses choose to list?
Professional Services and How AI is Changing the Game
Most of Q3’s investment story centers on access to capital, but some deals reveal changes in where and what investors back. Beyond the headline deals, some smaller investments pointed to changes in established industries. Not just in the technologies used, but in how services are delivered and businesses are organized.
Professional services are an excellent example. AI companies are not limited to selling tools for accountants, recruiters, or other specialists. Some are evolving to offer the services themselves. Others focus on acquiring established firms, then changing how those firms operate. Belgian startup Spott takes the tool-provider approach. It raised €18.3 million in Series A funding for an AI-native platform used by recruitment agencies. By contrast, London’s Jack & Jill secured $40 million to develop AI agents connecting jobseekers directly with employers.
Accounting offers an especially clear contrast, with Berlin-based mika AI raising €6 million for AI-powered bookkeeping and tax filing for smaller businesses, bypassing traditional firms for routine tasks. Limetax secured €36 million to acquire tax and accounting practices and integrate them through a common AI platform (€6 million in equity and €30 million in acquisition debt from German banks).
For property management, Britain’s Dwelly raised $170 million to buy independent letting agencies, then connect them to an AI-driven platform. That combined $95 million in equity with $75 million in debt. Debt accounted for about 83% of Limetax’s announced package and 44% of Dwelly’s. Unlike subscription software businesses that primarily fund product development and customer acquisition, firms focused on consolidating traditional providers need capital to buy operating businesses. That is why the financing mix is so central to consolidation.
There is an opportunity to capture service revenue, not just software fees. That means more responsibility for staff, service quality, and regulatory compliance, especially when established businesses are combined with unfamiliar AI-driven processes. Q3 showed competing approaches, but it’s still unclear which will scale best.
The Operational Challenge of Healthcare
Some healthcare investments focus on how services operate, rather than only on new treatments. That means more focus on documentation, scheduling, insurance checks, and billing. Sweden’s Tandem Health raised €86.5 million in a Series B led by the Scaleup Europe Fund. The AI assistant prepares patient summaries before consultations, supports clinicians during appointments, and handles documentation and coding afterwards.
London’s Penelope Health announced a $100 million funding commitment for technology that turns complex US health-insurance rules into structured information that providers and insurers can access automatically. Dutch startup Clementine secured €1.7 million for patient inquiries and appointment management in hearing-care clinics.
This focus on reducing administrative friction has commercial promise: less time spent on administrative work and more capacity for patient care. Adoption still depends on workflow integration, data security, professional oversight, and measurable savings.
How Zubr Capital Sees Q3
Q3 offered a partial answer to the question left by Q2. International investors remain essential for Europe’s largest rounds, but European capital, like the Scaleup Europe Fund, took meaningful lead roles. At the next financing stage, Bending Spoons, IQM and Pasqal used Nasdaq, while IQM also listed in Helsinki and smaller companies raised money on European exchanges.
Investors also backed AI businesses taking on traditional service providers and healthcare startups automating administration. The appeal of these models is clear, but the commercial results are yet to be proven. Nor is one quarter enough to establish whether Europe’s growth-capital gap is closing.
From Zubr Capital’s perspective, two developments are particularly relevant for growth equity investors. The first is the growing role of European capital in large funding rounds, giving companies more options as their financing needs increase. The second is the emergence of AI-driven business models that combine established service operations with technology and acquisitions.
The test ahead is whether European funds can continue to lead large deals, whether European public markets can attract larger issuers, and whether new service models can sustain growth. Scaling on European terms doesn’t necessarily mean excluding international capital. What matters is whether European companies have more ways to finance their growth — and can turn that capital into sustainable business value.

In ruby-red Kansas, Trump contemplates the possibility of a Democratic win in the state
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
04:13:28 UTC
13:13:28 KST

The fact that Donald Trump was here at all said more about a looming electoral disaster facing his Republican party next month than anything contained in his dark and discursive 98-minute stump speech.
On Monday, amid raucous chants of “USA! USA!”, the president held his first campaign rally in Kansas for eight years. No Democrat has won a US Senate seat in this ruby-red state since 1932, the year Herbert Hoover was president, Amelia Earhart was the first woman to fly solo across the Atlantic and the Nazis became the biggest party in the German Reichstag.
Since then Republicans in the state have built one of the longest winning streaks in Senate history, but such is the collapse in public esteem of the president that the midterms on 3 November could be the night that a blue wave engulfs the heart of Trump country.
“You’re really sort of – I hate to say it – you’re sort of tending toward the purple,” the president told about 5,000 supporters in a multipurpose arena outside Wichita, acknowledging that Kansas already has a Democratic governor in Laura Kelly. “That’s why I have to be sure that we get this guy.”
The “guy” concerned was Roger Marshall, a first-term Republican senator facing an unexpectedly strong challenge from Democrat Adam Hamilton, a Methodist megachurch pastor. Opinion polls show them running neck and neck. In the third quarter, Hamilton reportedly raised $11m while Marshall managed just $800,000.
Marshall, 66, is an obstetrician-gynaecologist and ex-congressman who has proved a staunch Trump ally, including by embracing his debunked claim that the 2020 presidential election was stolen. Hamilton, 62, founded the 24,000-member Church of the Resurrection, the biggest United Methodist congregation in the country. He opposes Trump’s tariff agenda and what he calls the president’s “erratic leadership”.
Despite Hamilton’s background as a pastor and former Republican, Marshall insisted on Monday that Hamilton was “too woke for Kansas”. Accompanied by Chuck Berry’s Johnny B Goode as he walked on stage, Marshall said: “This is a guy that participates in protests against police. He supports drag shows. He tells us to apologise for the colour of our skin. And in a state with more cattle than people, he tells you to stop eating beef.” The crowd jeered each time.
Trump, 80, is barnstorming the country in what some have called a “desperation tour” aimed at rescuing Republicans from the hole he has dug for them. Critics suggest he might actually be making life harder by nationalising races that candidates would prefer to keep focused on local issues.
By imposing himself in Kansas, at a rally that was disrupted by several protesters, Trump underlined the election as a referendum on his presidency, with the potential to cost Republicans control of both the Senate and House of Representatives just two years after they swept into power.
Farmers in Kansas, a heavily agricultural state, have been hit hard by the consequences of the Iran war: a gallon of diesel costs nearly $6. The president upset cattle ranchers with a plan to reduce import tariffs to lower the price of beef and with aggressive immigration raids that prompted some agricultural workers to stay at home. On Monday Trump announced a new program to provide farmers with $8bn in support to offset diesel costs during the harvest season.
The election will test whether the old playbooks that fuelled his presidential campaigns – hurling insults, stirring bigotry and telling lies – can still work among an electorate weary of the cost of living, foreign wars and government corruption.
Trump launched a tirade against Hamilton, dismissing him as a “radical left lunatic” and a “phoney who’s pretending to be a moderate”. Trump claimed the Democrat supports flooding Kansas with refugees who “go around killing people”, that he used church money to fund “transgender crap”, that he “openly mocks Jesus” and that he believes America is systemically racist.
“He wants you to repent for being born white,” Trump said.
The president also sought to weaponise the recent upheaval in France, pushing the baseless nativist claim that the violence is being led by immigrants. “We’re not going to let that happen to this country,” he said. “When you see burning steeples and raging fires in France, just remember that is what the radical Dumocrats want to do to America.”
Trump unleashed bitter attacks on three Muslim politicians: Abdul El-Sayed, Ilhan Omar and Rashida Tlaib. When Tlaib’s name was mentioned, members of the crowd yelled: “Deport her!” Trump falsely claimed that both El-Sayed and his sister are members of the Muslim Brotherhood, an Islamist opposition group in Egypt. He mockingly warned that, should El-Sayed be elected and sit on the Senate intelligence committee, he would leak information to the enemy.
Supporters roared their approved, thrilled by what they saw as Trump’s transgressive daring. The president, who won Kansas by 16 percentage points against Democrat Kamala Harris in 2024, showed he can still draw a crowd in one of the most surprising battleground states in the country.
Earlier, in warm sunshine, a long line of people snaked through fields outside the arena. There were sights that have become familiar over more than a decade: giant Trump flags, tables full of “Make America great again” caps, spangly “DJT” and “Trump the golden age” jackets, “Alligator Alcatraz” merchandise, “We are all Charlie Kirk now” sweaters and T-shirts that said “Stand for the flag, kneel for the cross”.
One woman wore a sweater that said: “0% liberal.” One man wore a T-shirt that declared: “I love Trump because he pisses off all the people I can’t stand.”
For these supporters, Trump rallies are galvanising and still the best way to get out the Republican vote. Cybersecurity worker Justin Nelsen, 44, said: “It fires us up, it gets us all excited for the cause and allows us to put out there what we want here as the state of Kansas. That’s why I’m here.”
Attendees were aware of the danger posed by Hamilton. Brittany Jones, a 33-year-old lawyer wearing a Stars and Stripes sweater, said: “If you know Adam Hamilton at all you know that he’s a problem and a chameleon and good at saying what he thinks people want to hear, even if he doesn’t believe it. He has shown himself to be not only a turncoat to things that matter to Christians, he has wholly given himself to the local agenda. Even though he claims to be a moderate, there’s nothing moderate about him.”
A Democratic victory here would represent a political earthquake, Jones acknowledged. “It’s seismic. It would be sad for most Kansans when they realise what happened, and some people just aren’t thinking through the consequences, but he has a built-in audience of people who are highly motivated.”
Jones, who had her friend’s three-month-old baby, Hannah, tucked under one arm, said she mostly welcomed Trump’s second term. “Overall I care about the social issues and he’s done a lot to protect girls’ sports, he’s done a lot to protect kids from being put through harmful gender transition procedures. Those things matter to me, they matter to the future of girls all across Kansas and America, and so I’m excited about those things.”
Construction worker Thad Snider, 42, who attended wearing a red “Make America Great Again” T-shirt alongside his mother, said he was not overly worried about the Senate seat falling to the Democrats.
“I don’t think Adam’s as strong a candidate as what the media is trying to sell him as,” he said, pointing to Hamilton’s past political donations to Democrats including Hillary Clinton. “I don’t think it’s going to happen but, if it did happen, it would be very shocking.”
Snider argues that voters faced a stark choice between political parties, describing the Republicans as the “least bad” option because “at least they’re not socialists or communists”. He added that he disagreed with foreign wars and wished Trump had done more on election integrity, but remained loyal to the president. “Any time you turn around a battleship, it takes time.”
That sentiment was echoed by Darrell Claphan, 72, a retired sales worker, who said of Trump: “He’s doing fantastic. He’ll go down in history being the number one president at what he’s done for the country in my lifetime.”
Claphan dismissed opinion polls showing a close race, stating: “Polls have been wrong ever since I’ve been alive.”
Asked how he would react to a Democratic Senate victory in Kansas, Claphan said: “I’d be shocked. But I don’t think it’s going to happen.”

South Korea orders stern response to any North Korean provocations amid border tensions
Unknown

13:13:24 KST

Faisal Mahmud
20 October 2026•Update: 20 October 2026
South Korea's top military officer on Tuesday ordered troops to respond decisively to any North Korean provocations a day after Pyongyang threatened additional weapons deployments and renewed propaganda broadcasts along their heavily fortified border.
Joint Chiefs of Staff (JCS) Chairman Gen. Jin Yong-sung issued the directive during a visit to a central front-line military unit, according to Yonhap News Agency.
Jin rejected North Korea's accusation that Seoul was responsible for escalating tensions following a Sept. 21 landmine explosion that injured three South Korean soldiers.
He said Pyongyang's attempt to portray legitimate South Korean military operations as provocations was unacceptable.
He ordered troops to respond firmly to further provocations and violations of the armistice agreement, including incursions across the Military Demarcation Line.
On Monday, Kim Yo Jong, the sister of North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, warned that Pyongyang could resume loudspeaker propaganda broadcasts and deploy additional tactical strike weapons along the border.
She accused Seoul of using warning shots and broadcasts to obstruct North Korea's border fortification work.
Jin described the September explosion involving North Korean-planted antipersonnel mines as a clear provocation and armistice violation.
The incident has heightened tensions around the Demilitarized Zone which separates the two Koreas, which are technically still at war, as the 1950–1953 Korean War ended with an armistice rather than a formal peace treaty.

Why pharma giant Roche is putting German investments on hold
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
04:07:21 UTC
13:07:21 KST

Germany’s bid to revive its struggling economy faces a fresh setback as a major pharmaceutical player raises concerns over the country’s business climate.
Swiss pharmaceutical giant Roche said on Monday it would put expansion in Germany on hold, dealing a blow to Berlin as a government-backed investment summit got underway.
"We have put all future investment decisions in Germany on hold for the time being," Daniel Steiners, head of Roche Germany, told Die Welt newspaper.
"As far as the pharmaceutical sector is concerned, I can say that political decisions have recently destroyed a great deal of trust."
German lawmakers in July passed a bill forcing pharmaceutical companies to cut prices as part of a bid to control costs in the country's statutory health insurance system.
Drugmakers have to grant a 15.5% rebate on most branded medicines from next year, up from a current rate of 7%.
The United States in June cited the reforms when it launched a tariff probe into Germany over what it said was Berlin's "persistent underpayment for innovative pharmaceutical products".
Asked about Steiners' comments, Economy Minister Katherina Reiche said the measures were necessary to keep a lid on social security contributions.
Nevertheless, she also praised "the enormous contributions of the pharmaceutical industry".
But Roche's criticism comes at an awkward time for the government, which is hosting a summit in Berlin on Monday and Tuesday aimed at drumming up business interest in Europe's top economy.
Suffering from subdued demand at home as well as US tariffs and increasingly fierce Chinese competition abroad, Germany's economy has posted little growth since a burst of pent-up pandemic demand at the end of 2022.
Speaking alongside Reiche at a press conference, Roland Busch, head of industrial giant Siemens, said Roche's announcement was a signal.
"Companies are saying: if the investment conditions in Germany aren't right, then they'll simply invest elsewhere," he said. "That's understandable."

Voting ended Monday in Canada's western Alberta province in a consequential referendum that could set it on a path toward leaving the country.
Polling stations were originally scheduled to close at 8 pm local time (0200GMT Tuesday), but voting was extended at some locations due to delayed openings.
Around 1.36 million residents had already cast ballots through advance and special voting, according to Elections Alberta.
The ballot contained 10 questions, with the first nine addressing immigration and constitutional matters.
The final question asked whether Alberta should remain in Canada or whether its government should begin the legal process toward a second, legally binding referendum on separation.
The vote itself is nonbinding and does not directly determine whether Alberta leaves Canada.
Elections Alberta said ballots would be counted by hand, with the separation question counted first.
Unofficial results are expected within 48 hours of polls closing, while official results are scheduled for Oct. 29.
