How to catch the peak of the Orionid meteor shower this week
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
04:00:15 UTC
13:00:15 KST

The Orionid meteor shower peaks this week. Here's how to see it from Australia
Sometimes it's good to sit back, find a dark, quiet spot, and stare at some stars.
This week provides a great excuse, with the Orionid meteor shower peaking on Thursday morning, showering stargazers in meteors produced by Halley's comet.
In good, dark sky conditions, experts suggest you may be able to see a meteor every 4–5 minutes.
But with a bright Moon in the sky and the shower only being visible in certain hours, you will need to pick your time to see the best of the Orionids.
When can I see the Orionids?
The Orionid meteor shower started earlier this month and will continue until early November.
But according to amateur astronomer Ian Musgrave, it's worth making the effort to get out of bed early this Wednesday, Thursday and Friday morning from about 4am.
The very best time will be Thursday morning at the meteor shower's peak, when the most meteors will be visible in the sky as the Earth passes through the thickest part of a debris trail.
Unfortunately, this year the peak in the Orionids corresponds to an almost full Moon, so earlier in the night the meteor shower will be washed out by the bright Moon.
But by the early morning, the Moon will go below the horizon and this will make the sky darker and the Orionids easier to see.
"Between 4am to 5am under dark skies, you should see about a meteor every 4 to 5 minutes or so," Dr Musgrave said.
The debris for the Orionids and the Eta Aquarids meteor shower — in April to May — is caused by the trail of Halley's comet.
The comet orbits around the Sun but is only visible to the naked eye from Earth every 74 to 79 years. It will make its next pass in 2061.
How to see the most meteors
The first thing to do is to be in an area with as little light pollution as possible, ideally a dark sky site.
From about 4am local time on the east coast and 6am local time on the west coast, look towards the northern sky.
Meteor showers always come from a single point in the sky, called the "radiant point", so keep an eye out for meteors coming from just below Orion's belt.
University of Southern Queensland astronomer Jonti Horner says the Orionids overlap with another meteor shower called the Taurid meteor shower.
"Neither of them on its own is the best shower of the year," he said.
"But one shower [Orionid] has fairly swift meteors … and the other [Taurid] very slow meteors … and so they add up and put on a better show."
A better meteor shower is coming soon
Dr Horner says that the Orionids can be thought of as a warm-up act for the Geminid meteor shower, which peaks in mid-December.
"The Geminids are a better one to guarantee that you will get a good show if the skies are clear," he said.
"They are a much better bet if you're somebody who's not an astronomy tragic like I am."

====================================================================================================

‘The last bastion is gone’: the US right idolised Orbán’s Hungary. Can they recover now he has fallen?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
04:00:15 UTC
13:00:15 KST

Espresso Embassy, a third-wave coffee shop in Budapest’s diplomatic and governmental quarter, is where visiting reporters and academics come to talk politics. On the way in for my morning coffee on 18 March, I passed a poster for Viktor Orbán’s Fidesz party that had been vandalised with a marker pen: “the safe choice” had become “the certain way to get fucked”. From across the cafe, I spotted the American journalist and historian Anne Applebaum locked in conversation, possibly with a source. I heard someone exclaim: “Just like Mussolini!” It was election season in Hungary.
It was also a couple of days before Cpac Hungary, a satellite event of the US-based conservative conference. As members of the international right arrived in town, the notorious Orbánist thinktank known as the Danube Institute was hosting an event called On Censorship, Tolerance, the Left and God. The official line would be: bad, good, bad, good.
After dark, I walked along the walls of Buda castle and past the Jesuit stairs to the institute. The featured speakers were Dave Rubin, an American podcaster from the so-called “intellectual dark web”, and Eva Vlaardingerbroek, a Dutch provocateur who claimed the title “shieldmaiden of the far right” on her X profile. “You don’t realise how good you have it” in Hungary, Rubin said. “So many things are wrong across the west.” After the panel, an American man introduced himself to me and asked how long I’d been in Budapest. Had I ever considered dual citizenship? If so, he could help. “My friends,” he said, “call me the Harriet Tubman of white people.”
For the previous few months, I’d been hanging around the Danube Institute and other state-subsidised gathering places, trying to pass as yet another member of the rightwing intelligentsia making his pilgrimage to Budapest. Founded in 2013 with state funds redirected by the Orbán government, the institute had become known as the central hub in the emerging “postliberal” movement, a loose coalition of heterodox conservative thinkers frequently associated with the idiosyncratic American blogger and self-styled Christian dissident Rod Dreher. During Dreher’s first fellowship term at the Danube Institute in 2021, he helped arrange Tucker Carlson’s weeklong press junket in Hungary, which featured a fawning Fox News interview with Orbán. Since then, liberal publications such as the New York Times, the New Yorker and the Atlantic have dispatched journalists to grill Dreher about the institute and his relationship to Orbán’s autocratic regime. This produced a series of breathless reports that showcased the small thinktank as a clearinghouse for dangerous illiberal ideas. As Applebaum wrote in her book Twilight of Democracy: “The Danube Institute exists, in practice, to make the Hungarian government presentable to the outside world.”
In Applebaum’s view, the Orbán regime had “created a political system in which no opposition party could possibly win”, and the foreign intellectuals at the Danube Institute were either cynical propagandists or naive stooges for Orbán’s anti-democratic project. But soon, Orbán would be out of power, ousted in a landslide election in April, and in June the new Hungarian parliament would pass a constitutional amendment dismantling the patronage system that funds the Danube Institute, as well as MCC Brussels, a training ground for Fidesz elites.
It was end times for the postliberals in Budapest, even if they didn’t know it yet. What will survive the demise of the so-called Budapest scene is a fractured group of rightwing thinkers who, whatever their fate in Hungary, will continue to hold a frightening level of influence over US political culture. If they were ever Orbán’s puppets, they aren’t any more. But reducing them to the unthinking servants of one particular strongman has made it more difficult to confront the real threat of postliberal ideas – or the crisis to which they are responding.
Officially, I was in Budapest to write a book about the western intellectuals who travelled to Hungary to meet the dissident opposition during the final years of the communist era. My family and I were guests of the Institute for Advanced Study, which had once been called the Collegium Budapest before it was effectively closed by the Orbán government in 2011. Now reopened, it was part of the rump of Central European University that still remained in Hungary. The rest of the institution was forced to move to Vienna during a prolonged campaign against George Soros and Hungary’s independent civil society.
At the start of this year, I made it my half-ironic mission to infiltrate the Danube Institute. I really did want to see what was actually going on inside this thinktank that had become known as the headquarters of the international postliberal project. Reaching it was not hard. It is housed in the Lónyay-Hatvany Villa, a refurbished building that had briefly served as an SS casino during the second world war and now housed a high-end restaurant on its main floor. One evening, I climbed a steep staircase dimly lit by iron sconces, the yellow light reflecting off wet stone, until I reached a narrow passage closed in by two high walls. Up ahead, I noticed a doorway marked only by a floor lamp on a small red carpet. I hesitated, then entered.
Straight in front of me was a dining room with a commanding view of the Danube. I snapped a few photos with my phone until I heard someone behind me on the stairs. I hurried into the basement annexe and reached a check-in table. I gave a young assistant my name, and she pointed towards a coat check. It turned out that infiltrating the Danube Institute just required online registration.
In the brightly lit basement, a shelf offered complimentary issues of glossy rightwing journals such as The European Conservative and Hungarian Review. I picked up a copy of the then state-subsidised Hungarian Conservative with a painting by Tivadar Csontváry Kosztka on the cover; its title was Mysterious Island.
The other guests were beginning to arrive, and I was immediately worried I’d been misled by a New Yorker piece on Dreher, in which he told a journalist that “the Danube Institute had a casual dress code” and he “could usually leave the suits at the apartment” even when meeting with ministers from Orbán’s Fidesz party. But here was a parade of male intellectual fashion: ribbed turtlenecks; crocheted ties and silk cravats; blazers of tweed, linen and corduroy. I looked down at my rumpled blazer – the only one I own – and felt underdressed.
In the months to come, I would jot down scraps of overheard conversation. Much of it was unsurprising, especially for anyone who had spent time on X: “We’re going to interrogate him with truth serum”, “No one is linking except Tucker”, “Hitler would have gone broke on her OnlyFans”, “Do you have a contact for Vance?”
All the knowing gossip and memes were part of a game of one-upmanship among intellectuals who styled themselves as insiders. Still, there was something jarring about seeing this very online culture in the flesh. Most of the names they dropped were exactly the ones you’d expect. What did catch me off guard was how often I also heard them mention the names of the liberal journalists who had alerted me to the existence of the Danube Institute in the first place. If Hungary looms large for people like Applebaum, she, in turn, haunts the postliberal imagination; these guys all clearly read the Atlantic.
“Anne Applebaum, I think she’s great,” I overheard one of the institute’s fellows wisecrack at the bar. “I really respect her.” At the very first event I attended, a debate on How Non-Liberal Regimes Rule Through the Good Life, the main speaker referred to Applebaum as “persona non grata” at the Danube Institute. The postliberal economist Philip Pilkington responded: “I do find the descent into Applebaumism hilarious.”
Pilkington was referring to Applebaum’s stubborn tendency to divide the world between liberal democracies and illiberal autocracies, between virtuous and corrupt elites. This “moral purity test” was not only hypocritical, he pointed out, it was intellectually unserious. According to Pilkington, it prevented liberal elites from accurately seeing themselves. The “crude” Applebaum analysis, he said, doesn’t “have a good explanation of why liberalism is falling apart”.
Part of the appeal of postliberalism is that it does provide an account of why it feels as though everything is falling apart: a liberal world order could never have turned out otherwise. At least this is Pilkington’s view, as expressed in his 2025 book, The Collapse of Global Liberalism. Born in Ireland, Pilkington is a millennial former leftist who took a job in finance and then moved to Hungary, where until June he was employed at the Danube Institute and the Hungarian Institute of International Affairs, then another Fidesz-aligned thinktank. For him, “liberalism is, in the final analysis, a dark and uncivilised philosophy of life that will destroy any civilisation it touches”.
Equally comfortable making sweeping claims about “Marxian historical materialism” and offering hot takes about yoga pants as a symptom of civilisational decline, Pilkington argues that the drive to demolish all hierarchies is “self-undermining” and “self-destructive”: “The reality is that equality does not exist in most spheres.” Liberal capitalism, according to this line of thought, only ever appeared stable because it was built on a foundation of pre-liberal hierarchical structures, such as the church, family and classical legal traditions. Now it has become a victim of its own self-undermining success. As Pilkington puts it, “liberal capitalism” became “far too aggressive in its promotion of work and consumption and is undermining the building blocks on which the stability of society rests”, namely “the family and the ability to reproduce the species”.
The postliberal movement’s foundational text is 2018’s Why Liberalism Failed by the philosopher Patrick Deneen, another visitor to the Danube Institute. The title of Deneen’s book captures the shared premise of all postliberal thought: that the historical period in which western societies were governed by a “regime of liberalism”, as he put it elsewhere, has already reached a calamitous end. Whether that period began in 1989 with the fall of communist regimes in central and eastern Europe or 500 years ago with the Protestant reformation remains a matter of some obfuscation.
For postliberals, the collapse of liberalism was an inevitable outgrowth of its first principles: its anti-hierarchical commitment to formal equality, its faith in human progress and, above all, its emphasis on individual autonomy. In practice, Deneen argues, these values actually produced extreme economic inequality, spiritual debasement and a profound sense of unfreedom. “Liberalism has failed,” he writes, “not because it fell short, but because it was true to itself.”
At least initially, the postliberals seemed more solicitous of the populist masses than of the Republican old guard: they supported Donald Trump, who was then styling himself as a champion for a new working-class coalition against the elite establishment. Deneen and other postliberals claimed their goal was to transcend the toxic left-right divide in US politics by positioning themselves as both allies of social democracy and enemies of corporate progressivism. Indeed, they insisted the only way to defeat the disastrous post-cold war alliance between neoliberal economics and neoconservative foreign policy was through a novel fusion of social-conservative values and left economic ideas.
After postliberalism relocated to Hungary it became more true to itself. The year after its publication, Why Liberalism Failed was translated into Hungarian, and Deneen met Orbán in Budapest. In the years after 2018, the Danube Institute and other regime-supported institutions hosted nearly every major American postliberal intellectual in Budapest. Many are now familiar figures on the so-called New Right. To use a basketball analogy, if Deneen was the philosopher-coach and Dreher was the veteran point guard on this postliberal squad, the rest of the starting five might include the Catholic integralist Adrian Vermeule; the national conservative Yoram Hazony; the censorious culture warrior Christopher Rufo; and the shapeshifting opinion columnist, UnHerd editor and Compact magazine cofounder Sohrab Ahmari, with the political theorist Gladden Pappin coming in off the bench.
Back in the US, Pappin had been a junior academic before he began writing blog posts for the Journal of American Greatness under the pen name Manlius Capitolinus. By now, all of Pappin’s posts as Manlius Capitolinus have been taken down, but he subsequently published a series of revealing essays under his own name in another journal. In Toward a Party of the State, from 2019, Pappin argued that the “liberal conservatism” of the old Republican establishment had failed precisely because it became a handmaid to the “governing ideology of neoliberalism”, a form of statecraft without a moral vision of the good life.
Drawing on left thinkers such as Nancy Fraser, Pappin suggested that neoliberalism maintained its fragile legitimacy by “redefining itself as progressive”, creating an unholy alliance between pro-corporate and socially liberal constituencies. To overcome the “neoliberal ideological hegemony”, according to this theory, we need a national unity government with a strong, activist party-state led by intellectuals, among them, presumably, Pappin himself.
At the time, postliberals could still squint and see Trump as a vessel for this project. After Trump’s defeat in 2020, Pappin visited Budapest for the first time, and before long, he had relocated to Hungary. In 2023, he was appointed president of the Hungarian Institute of International Affairs, a highly unusual position for a foreign national. Pappin now had the opportunity to learn from the Fidesz party-state and start putting his ideas into practice.
To postliberals, Orbán’s governing programme looked like a dream come true. As Rufo, coming off his stint at the Danube Institute, put it in 2023: “Hungary’s leaders are serious people combating the same forces confronted by conservatives in the west: the fraying of national culture, entrenched leftwing institutions and the rejection of sexual difference.” But, compared with the contemporary Republican party, Orbán seemed exhilaratingly willing to use the power of the state to pursue a conservative vision of the good life.
Orbán was the great defender of the postliberal trinity: “strong families, strong borders, strong industry,” as Pappin said in an interview with the Atlantic. “Orbánomics” consisted of a series of interventions to build up Hungary’s car manufacturing capacity, ensure access to less expensive Russian energy and increase work requirements for welfare recipients, raising taxes on banks and even nationalising some.
Defying the EU, the Orbán regime also pursued a so-called “zero migration” policy. But the postliberals were perhaps most enamoured of Orbán’s efforts to encourage traditional family formation and raise the birthrate. Since 2022, Hungary has spent about 5% of its GDP every year on a suite of welfare initiatives offering generous maternity leave, childcare support and tax breaks for mothers.
As Rufo explained, these seemingly “progressive” policies were meant to serve “conservative ends”: first, “to incentivise traditional marriage and family formation”; second, to help ward off “foreign ideologies, such as critical race theory and gender ideology”; and, third, because “raising the native Hungarian birthrate obviates the need for foreign immigration”. Hungary’s student debt policy also allowed new mothers to suspend, reduce or ultimately erase their debt entirely, depending on how many children they had given birth to. In 2023, Pappin pointed to Hungary’s student debt programme as a model for the kinds of policies the Republican party should pursue.
During the Biden years, the postliberals yearned for the kind of power and stability in the US that Orbán enjoyed in Hungary. In Deneen’s 2023 book Regime Change: Toward a Postliberal Future, the philosopher was no longer just diagnosing the problem with liberalism; he was suggesting a radical solution. Deneen now called for a revolutionary turn to “aristopopulism”, in which a cadre of elites would act as “class traitors” to help socially conservative workers depose the liberal-meritocratic ruling class in the US, and take control of a newly integrated state and civil society. “What is needed, in short,” he wrote, “is … the peaceful but vigorous overthrow of a corrupt and corrupting liberal ruling class and the creation of a postliberal order in which existing political forms can remain in place, as long as a fundamentally different ethos informs those institutions and the personnel who populate key offices and positions.” As an example of what he had in mind, Deneen pointed to Hungary.
By the time I arrived in Budapest in late 2025, Trump was back in power, with the postliberal darling JD Vance as his vice-president. The new administration was armed with a blueprint for Deneen-style regime change. In 2023, the Heritage Foundation, a conservative US thinktank, had released a report titled Project 2025, “75% of which is being implemented”, as Heritage’s’s Paul McCarthy, who’d been involved in drafting the chapter on US foreign aid, claimed at a Danube Institute event this February. (The Danube Institute and Heritage had established a formal collaboration in March 2023, a month before the Project 2025 report was released.)
For Applebaum and other post-cold war liberal intellectuals such as the historian Timothy Snyder, the direction of the US right was yet more evidence that “America’s future is Hungary”. According to Snyder, Trump and Vance are “Orbán’s pupils”, and many of their policy decisions “arise in whole or in part from Hungarian sources”.
But in Hungary, a funny thing was happening: Orbán’s own government was no longer popular. Péter Magyar, a former Fidesz insider who had broken with the party, was leading Orbán by double digits in independent polls. One of two things was about to happen: either Fidesz would be out of power for the first time in 16 years, or Orbán would prove himself a genuine dictator. The Applebaum theory of Orbán’s regime was about to be put to the test, and so was postliberalism.
On the national holiday of 15 March, I joined masses of supporters of Magyar’s new Tisza party as they filled the streets all the way up to Heroes’ Square, where Orbán had made his first major political speech in June 1989. Later that year, Orbán raced back to Budapest from his Soros-funded scholarship at Oxford to participate in the unfolding regime change as a representative of Fidesz, founded as the Federation of Young Democrats. Now, my Hungarian friends were joking that Orbán resembled one of the corpulent bureaucrats he had once sought to replace.
In the Hungary of 2026, postliberalism was not working out as planned. Inflation and house prices had risen faster than anywhere else in the EU. Orbánomics was crashing out. Industrial development hadn’t resulted in the promised economic growth, and Fidesz had been rocked by a massive pollution scandal at an electric vehicle battery plant. Though migration was effectively halted, Chinese guest workers streamed in to work in the newly created car industry jobs. After creeping up marginally, the fertility rate seemed to be flattening.
Corruption throughout Orbán’s patronage system was so rampant that Hungary was being widely labeled a mafia state. Fidesz had rewritten the constitution, installed party loyalists in key judicial roles, gerrymandered electoral districts, changed election laws to inflate their parliamentary majority, put much of the higher education sector under the control of boards stacked with party members and overseen the sale of media companies to regime-friendly oligarchs. Already, the regime had granted that women with at least four children did not have to pay income taxes for the rest of their lives. In the run-up to the election, they reduced the number of children required to three, and then two. But that wasn’t going to be enough to win an election, let alone replace the global neoliberal economic order.
Both Trump and Vance had been rumoured guests at Cpac Hungary, but neither showed up in the end. The event chair still claimed that the “biggest stars of the sovereigntist right” were all on the way to Budapest. Javier Milei, the president of Argentina, was a last-minute addition. They also advertised an appearance by the Czech prime pinister, populist billionaire Andrej Babiš, but he pulled out at the last minute. Maybe they had all been scared off by Orbán’s tanking poll numbers.
Lingering outside the gate on the day of the event itself, I saw Pappin walking toward the VIP entrance. I ducked behind a Cpac banner reading “FEL GYŐZELEMRE!” (“ON TO VICTORY!”).
I wondered how he was taking the polls. A little over a week earlier, I had run into Pappin after an event at which he had joked that the liberal Canadian prime minister, Mark Carney, sounded a lot like a “dangerous postliberal” when he prominently declared that the crisis in the rules-based international order was “a rupture, not a transition”. I was grabbing a coffee at a Scruton cafe – part of a chain named after the conservative English philosopher and Orbán ally Roger Scruton. Exposed lightbulbs hung from the ceiling in front of a stencilled cartoon of a hip, young Scruton in a double-breasted suit, with a speech bubble: “The greatest treasure of Hungarians is their national identity.” When I spotted Pappin at the next table, I decided to introduce myself, playing up the extent to which Scruton himself figures into my research. We talked about life in Budapest, the city he had referred to elsewhere as “Scrutopia”, and he scoffed at the impression of the Danube milieu put forward by the western press. “You know, all these people show up in Budapest looking for some kind of conservative intellectual utopia,” he said. Though the scene had been influential, he added, “There are only like five of us.”
Five intellectuals in close proximity to power can do a lot of damage. Take it from Deneen in Regime Change: “Even if relatively small, an elite cadre skilled at directing and elevating popular resentments, combined with the political power of the many, can bolster populist political prospects as a working governmental and institutional force.” But this wasn’t what was happening in Hungary, at least not any more. The political power of the many was no longer cooperating. Though Vance had finally flown in for support, the polls still weren’t moving in Orbán’s direction.
On 11 April, the night before the election, I heard Orbán’s voice echoing from the castle during a final torch-lit rally. The next day, the city was all nerves. The final turnout, nearly 80%, would set a national record. After polls closed, I gathered with friends to stream the independent Partizán media feed on YouTube. The first results, released just after 8pm, put Fidesz slightly ahead. Then, at 9.16pm, a new banner crossed the bottom of the screen: Orbán had called Magyar to concede. The convoluted Hungarian election machine had backfired, and Tisza had defeated Fidesz in a landslide. “Looks like the last bastion is gone,” Eva Vlaardingerbroek posted on X.
My friends and I rushed to Batthyány Square, where Magyar was set to give his victory speech. The crowd throbbed with expectation; drones circled above us. Techno music drifted across the Danube from a dance party next to the floodlit parliament. We eavesdropped on two childhood friends who hadn’t seen each other in years as they embraced and looked deeply into one another’s eyes in wonder. Their meet-cute was interrupted by someone vomiting on the cobblestone at their feet.
It slowly dawned on me that what we were witnessing was not a change of government but a regime change. Throughout the campaign, Magyar had used the Hungarian term rendszerváltás, literally “system change”, once reserved for talking about the democratic transition from communism in 1989, and now, somehow, Tisza had made it happen.
If Pilkington is right that post-cold war liberals don’t have a good understanding of why their world is falling apart, neither did the postliberals after Magyar’s win. For them, the fact that Orbán had conceded gracefully was proof that he had always been committed to democracy – and that liberal critics such as Applebaum and Snyder had misunderstood him all along. On election night, Rod Dreher responded to news that Orbán had conceded with a sarcastic post on X: “But … but … but, I was told by so many experts and journalists in the west that this would never happen, that Orbán is a fascist dictator who would never surrender power!”
It’s true that Applebaum’s work often relied on a reductive binary between democracy and autocracy that, in this case, had obscured the fact that democratic change was still very much possible in Hungary. But the postliberals were trapped in their own binaries, too: because Orbán wasn’t a dictator, their logic went, Hungary must have ultimately been a democracy. This allowed them to dismiss all the ways Fidesz had held on to power by changing election laws, packing the judiciary, attacking civil society and higher education, and consolidating control over the media.
There was one thing that Applebaum and the postliberals could agree on after the election: the demise of the so-called Hungarian model. Applebaum’s post-election column marked the passing of one of her own stock narratives. Orbán’s Hungary would no longer serve, she wrote, “as a model for Americans or Europeans who want to capture their own states, or take apart their own checks and balances, or impose their own illiberal ideologies on people who don’t accept them”. In his own postmortem, Dreher reached a similar conclusion: “As a model for Maga and other nationalist conservatives in the west, Hungary is over.” But it would be a mistake to think that Orbán’s defeat, or the potential closure of state-supported institutions such as the Danube Institute, means the end of postliberalism.
“We are all postliberals now,” Pilkington argued on Postliberal Order, the Substack newsletter he shares with Deneen, Pappin and CC Pecknold, a historian of theology. As he pointed out, Magyar shared many of Orbán’s views on core issues. “From the standpoint of domestic politics, Magyar effectively ran on Fidesz’s own platform,” Pilkington argued in a different post-election column, “promising to keep migration low, maintain Hungarian cultural nationalism, and keep the generous family support system that Fidesz built in place.” But Pilkington wasn’t just making a narrow political point. Postliberalism as an intellectual project was not tied to the fate of any particular political party. “No doubt, Fidesz has been an incubator of alternative thinking in transatlantic conservatism, but these ideas are in the ether and are unlikely to go away any time soon.”
In the narrow, descriptive sense, it’s true that there is no going back to the liberalism of the brief, post-cold war interregnum, circa 1989-2015. Still, postliberals are terrible at predicting what comes next. On X, Pilkington posts regular prophecies of western civilisational catastrophe with the swagger of a former finance guy. “There is an old phrase in investment,” he writes in The Collapse of Global Liberalism, “it is better to be wrong for the right reasons than right for the wrong reasons.”
But if Pilkington is right about our new postliberal era, it is for the wrong reasons. Clearly, the world of post-cold war liberalism is over. But the idea that all the challenges brought on by its collapse can be answered by the postliberal programme is a farce. As Hungary has shown, postliberal policies don’t produce a life good enough to win over voters. In the end, Hungary was a false model for our authoritarian future. Now the model we have to worry about is US-made.
In all my time in Hungary, there was one person I had never seen at the Danube Institute or at any of the other events I attended: Rod Dreher, an alleged mainstay of the Budapest scene. After a few failed attempts, we finally met on a spring afternoon in early May, the day before Magyar was sworn in as prime minister. Over rosé spritzes and nicotine pouches, I made my confession to Dreher: I told him I had been attending events at the Danube Institute, about all the wild conversations I had overheard, and about how I was just trying to understand what attracted American intellectuals to the dissident right. We both agreed that Hungary was a strange place to look for lessons about the US. But here we both were.
“I was never part of any scene here, although I kind of thought I would be,” he told me. Like Pappin, he noted that only a handful of conservative anglophone intellectuals lived in Budapest; most of their companions were only there temporarily, to check out what it was like when their side was in power. But the Scruton cafes were “phoney”, more Ikea than English country house. The Danube Institute, though it was never the Orbánist propaganda factory it was rumoured to be, was overseen by overcautious Hungarian managers, he said, who had held it back from becoming a truly stimulating intellectual environment. “There was a scene,” he admitted, “but it was very superficial.”
And now the Budapest scene, however superficial, was coming to an end. Over the next few months, the new Tisza-led parliament would pass a series of laws and constitutional amendments aimed at dismantling the Fidesz party’s system of funding thinktanks and other intellectual institutions. At the end of July, Pappin would resign from the Hungarian Institute of International Affairs, and the MCC foundation would be formally dissolved. Already, Magyar had promised not only to end government funding of the organisation that runs Cpac Hungary, but to investigate the former funding through the newly created National Asset Recovery and Protection Office. As Dreher would later put it: “The unsettling atmosphere of vengeance that has overtaken Hungary since Péter Magyar became prime minister [sic] likely means the end of the Danube Institute.” (The Danube Institute did not respond to requests for comment.)
I asked Dreher what he would do next. He told me he had briefly considered moving to Vienna, but then he had had a change of heart. It was time to give up the good life in central Europe and return to the American south. My own temporary resident permit was about to expire. As the sun set behind Károlyi-kert, one of the oldest gardens in Budapest, Dreher and I downed our last rosé spritzes. Postliberalism was finally coming home, and so were we.

Singapore, Hong Kong take different paths in race for stablecoin dominance. Who will win?
Singapore is boosting infrastructure while Hong Kong is betting on banks – but ultimately, practicality will decide the winner, experts say
Both approaches reflect different priorities in the race to build global cryptocurrency centres: Hong Kong is linking stablecoins to its existing financial system, while Singapore is looking to strengthen the infrastructure for circulating and settling tokenised assets.
Analysts said the ultimate test would be whether either regulatory framework could support practical, commercially viable uses.
HSBC, one of Hong Kong’s largest banks, revealed the name of its stablecoin, RedCoin, last month. The Hong Kong dollar-pegged token is expected to launch in the second half of this year and be integrated into the bank’s mobile banking platforms.

China’s new 0.1-nanometre electron microscope ready to challenge US and Japan
Model marks shift from R&D to commercialisation and aligns with country’s effort to cut reliance on imported tech
China is ready to commercialise a 200-kilovolt transmission electron microscope with an information resolution down to 0.1 nanometres that could introduce a new challenger into a market long dominated by the US and Japan.
Developed by Hefei-based manufacturer CIQTEK, the microscope features a point resolution of 0.25nm and an information limit of 0.1nm – on par with leading workhorse models on the market.
This marks a shift for the country’s expanding advanced electron microscopy industry from research and development to commercialisation, according to a report by the official ministry newspaper Science and Technology Daily on Monday.
It also represents the latest achievement aimed at reducing the country’s reliance on imports of the technology used in vital advanced industries like chip manufacturing.

WASHINGTON, October 20. /TASS/. US Presidential Special Envoy Steve Witkoff hopes to visit Russia and meet with Russian President Vladimir Putin after holding talks with Vladimir Zelensky in Oslo on Tuesday, Barak Ravid, a correspondent for Axios and Israel’s Channel 12, said on X, citing sources.
According to the sources, Witkoff is currently flying to Oslo for a meeting with Zelensky scheduled for Tuesday. Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store, as well as representatives of the United Kingdom, Germany, Italy, France, the European Union leadership, and NATO, are expected to take part in the talks.
"The objective is to continue aligning on a comprehensive proposal that can form the basis for renewed negotiations with Russia," Ravid said.
According to one of his sources, Witkoff hopes to visit Russia after Oslo, where he intends to discuss with Putin the proposals developed jointly with Ukraine and European partners. Last week, representatives of the United States, Ukraine, and Europe worked on developing these proposals at the technical level. They include the release of Stephen Hubbard, a 72-year-old US citizen convicted in Russia of fighting on the side of the Ukrainian armed forces.
"President Trump has directed an intensive process to develop a comprehensive peace proposal with Ukraine and Europe, and the next step is to test whether that work can form the basis for serious negotiations with Russia", a US official told Ravid, adding. "These discussions remain fluid, and substantial work remains. President Trump’s objective is clear: to end the killing, bring the war to a close, and establish the conditions for a lasting peace that benefits Ukraine, Russia, Europe, and the United States."
Jared Kushner, a special envoy and son-in-law of the US president, will not accompany Witkoff in person this time because he has the flu. He will participate in the consultations remotely.
On October 1, Putin said Russia would like to end hostilities in Ukraine through a peaceful settlement as soon as possible. Moscow is ready for negotiations but sees no willingness on the part of the Kiev government to engage in talks, the president added.

Rubio India visit: Bilateral with Jaishankar, Jamnagar refinery tour &amp; trade deal - whats on agenda
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
03:46:06 UTC
12:46:06 KST

External affairs minister S Jaishankar will meet US Secretary of State Marco Rubio in Mumbai on October 20 to discuss ways to enhance the Comprehensive Global Strategic Partnership between India and the US. (File photo)
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio will begin a three-day visit to India on Tuesday, with talks on a proposed bilateral trade deal, energy security and strategic cooperation expected to feature prominently during his meetings with External Affairs Minister S Jaishankar and other engagements in Mumbai and Gujarat’s Jamnagar.Rubio is scheduled to arrive at Mumbai’s Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj International Airport at 2.15 pm on Tuesday, according to the Ministry of External Affairs (MEA). He will lay a wreath at the Taj memorial to honour the victims of the 26/11 terror attacks before holding bilateral talks with Jaishankar at the Taj Mahal Palace hotel.The two leaders are expected to discuss the India-US Comprehensive Global Strategic Partnership, including energy, trade and investment, defence, critical and emerging technologies, and the situation in West Asia. Rubio will later attend the “Freedom 250 Reception” at the Jio World Convention Centre to mark the 250th anniversary of US independence. Jaishankar will be the guest of honour.
Trade deal and energy security in focus
The visit comes as both countries seek to advance negotiations on a proposed trade agreement amid friction over tariffs, energy imports and immigration policies.Speaking in Uzbekistan ahead of his India visit, Rubio said the two sides were close to finalising the agreement.
"We're trying to finalise a trade deal with India right now. We're very close to doing that."Rubio also linked the negotiations to Washington’s decision to grant a temporary waiver on certain sanctions related to Russian energy purchases. He said India’s energy requirements and its importance as a US partner were among the factors being considered."These sanctions were not just sanctions on Russia. They include tariffs on a number of countries—India, for example, and others. And so I think the president wants to take the 60-day period of time to sort of analyse what imposing both sanctions and tariffs will mean to the global economy and even to the U.S. economy," Rubio said.He added that India had diversified its energy sources but continued to rely on Russian supplies because shifting to alternatives could not happen overnight."You've got countries like India, for example, that have voluntarily diversified their energy portfolio, but are still getting a substantial amount of energy from Russia because it's hard to pivot from one day to the next. But they're also an important ally and partner of the United States. So we need that period of time to sort of study all this and figure out what the right combination is," he added.India and the US have been negotiating the proposed trade pact since early 2025, seeking to address tariff disputes, reduce non-tariff barriers and improve market access. Jaishankar recently said the negotiations were nearing a "landing point".
Jamnagar visit and meeting with Ambani
Rubio will travel to Jamnagar in Gujarat on Wednesday, where he is expected to visit Reliance Industries’ oil refining complex and meet chairman Mukesh Ambani before returning to Mumbai. The Jamnagar leg of the visit is expected to last around nine hours.The visit comes as Reliance Industries prepares for a planned investment in a Texas oil refinery, bringing energy cooperation and private-sector investment into focus. Officials have not confirmed reports that Rubio may also visit the Vantara animal rehabilitation centre in Jamnagar.Rubio is also expected to engage with Indian business leaders during his visit, although meetings with industrialists Gautam Adani and Tata Sons chairman N Chandrasekaran have not been officially confirmed.
Rubio’s trip is his second visit to India this year, following his May visit, when he met Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Jaishankar and attended a Quad foreign ministers’ meeting.Bilateral relations have faced strains following US tariffs on Indian goods, disagreements over Washington’s claims about its role in de-escalating the India-Pakistan military conflict in May 2025, and changes to US immigration policies, including higher H-1B visa fees.The two sides are also expected to exchange views on the West Asia crisis and regional stability. Rubio’s visit follows his meetings with Central Asian foreign ministers in Uzbekistan, where he promoted US trade, security and investment ties with the region.

Christiane Amanpour to leave CNN after 43 years

Christiane Amanpour to leave CNN after 43 years
October 20, 2026
Veteran journalist Christiane Amanpour on Monday said she was leaving her role at CNN after 43 years at the network.
"After thinking carefully for several months and experiencing a few sleepless nights, as you can imagine, I've decided to separate from CNN," Amanpour, 68, said in a statement.
"This daily show on CNN and PBS will come to an end at the end of this year. But CNN and I have worked out a smooth transition where we continue doing Amanpour once a week through to June," she said in a video message posted on social media.
Amanpour, who became famous for her on-the-ground reporting from major war zones, did not give a reason for her departure.
That said, her move to resign comes weeks after CNN's parent company, Warner Bros. Discovery (WBD), was formally taken over by Paramount Skydance.
After a yearlong process, Paramount closed its merger with WBD on October 6, uniting two giants in TV news — CBS and CNN — under one roof.
The merger has drawn concerns over the independence of the newsroom at CNN as the merged company's owners, the Ellison family, are close allies of US President Donald Trump.
"You know I've always been fiercely independent, and I will continue to be that for you as long as I am here and beyond. That's especially important today as we face unprecedented pressures from all sides, political, financial, and also from the rising dangers in the field," she said, without directly referring to the deal.
What to know about Amanpour's career
Amanpour, who was born in London to an Iranian father and British mother, joined CNN in 1983 as an assistant. In the next few years, she went on to cover major wars in the 1990s, including the Gulf War and the Bosnian War.
Amanpour has interviewed many world's leaders, reported from conflict sites and interviewed newsmakers from hotspots such as Iraq, Afghanistan, Pakistan, Somalia, Rwanda and the Balkans.
She said she "looks forward to interesting new projects down the line, and will always be rooting for CNN and maintaining its history of independent journalism. Remember: always be truthful, not neutral."
In a memo, CNN Chief Executive Mark Thompson praised Amanpur for "43 extraordinary years of remarkable journalism, loyalty and friendship."
"Like so many CNNers who will hear the news today, I'm very sorry to see her go, but I've come to accept that this is the right time for her, both personally and professionally," Thompson said.

This is MiTAC Computing’s second application under the reshoring program, which was launched in 2019. The agency said the program has attracted 368 companies, with about NT$1.55 trillion in planned investments and 97,136 jobs expected.

The legislature held a committee hearing Monday to discuss the proposed amendments.
At the hearing, KMT Legislator Lai Shyh-bao (賴士葆) said no one opposed freezing oil prices to mitigate the potential impact on the cost of living, but argued that the policy had become a subsidy for big businesses' energy consumption, per CNA. He also suggested that CPC's proposed capital increase of NT$233.8 billion (US$7.18 billion) might include NT$140 billion for the Alaska project.
Lai Chien-hsin rejected that characterization, saying the capital increase aimed to address accumulated losses stemming from the COVID-19 pandemic, Russia's invasion of Ukraine, and the US-Israel war with Iran, per UDN. He stressed that without government intervention, CPC would be unable to absorb energy price shocks while continuing to invest in Taiwan's energy infrastructure.
Regarding the energy research fund, the Directorate-General of Budget, Accounting and Statistics warned that the amendment would significantly weaken funding, per Liberty Times. The agency noted that Taipower contributed NT$3.49 billion to the fund's NT$4.57 billion budget for 2026.
Chung-Hua Institution for Economic Research Associate Research Fellow Chen Jong-shun (陳中舜) said most energy researchers at the nation's leading institutions rely on the fund. He added that Taipower's deficit was roughly 80 times the fund's 2026 budget.
On the reasons behind the financial losses at CPC and Taipower, Chen said both government interference in pricing and energy policy had contributed to the companies' difficulties, per NOWNews. He noted that Taiwan was the only country to rely on natural gas for more than 40% of its electricity generation while depending exclusively on shipping for supplies.
Chen proposed allowing market forces to determine energy prices while using tax revenue to assist lower-income households and struggling businesses.
DPP Legislator Chung Chia-pin (鍾佳濱) supported the proposed capital infusion, suggesting that funding could come from tax revenue generated by the AI industry. General Chamber of Commerce of the Republic of China Secretary-General Liu Shou-jen (劉守仁) also backed the move, urging the government to provide funding to prevent utility price increases in December.
However, some experts were less supportive of the proposal. Chung-Hua Institution for Economic Research Assistant Research Fellow Hsu Chia-sheng (許家勝) called for conditional capital infusions after determining how much of Taipower's losses resulted from the government's price stabilization policies.
National Tsing Hua University professor Yeh Tsung-kuang (葉宗洸) opposed the capital infusion, saying the public should not have to tolerate the government allocating billions of Taiwan dollars annually to bail out Taipower and CPC when the companies had other means of addressing their financial losses. He called on the government to consider reopening nuclear power plants.
In related news, Taiwan Gas Appliance Manufacturers Association Chair Lai Fang-chuan (賴芳泉) warned that Taiwan could face natural gas shortages this winter if supply issues and negotiations remain unresolved following Taiwan Plastics Group's decision to decouple its natural gas prices from CPC’s, per Liberty Times.
Lai said CPC's maximum monthly output of liquefied petrolium gas was 90,000 tonnes, while Taiwan's winter demand reached 100,000 tonnes. He said Taiwan Plastics Group could assist CPC if the state-owned company failed to meet demand, but urged CPC to ensure it operated at maximum capacity.
Lai added that CPC might already be facing a supply shortfall of thousands of tonnes and called on the company to address the issue.

Organoid pioneer named chair professor at Taipei Medical University
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
03:36:34 UTC
12:36:34 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taipei Medical University announced Monday that Dutch scientist Johannes (Hans) Clevers, a pioneer of organoids — miniature, three-dimensional tissue models grown from stem cells — will become a chair professor at its College of Medicine.
Widely known as the “father of organoids,” Clevers is a member and former president of the Royal Netherlands Academy of Arts and Sciences. His research has helped scientists develop models that reproduce some structural and functional features of human organs. Researchers use them to study diseases and test potential treatments, per LTN.
Tsai Kun-chih (蔡坤志), director of TMU’s Institute of Clinical Medicine, said Clevers helped pioneer organoid technology in 2009, when his research team demonstrated that intestinal stem cells could grow into organized, miniature intestinal structures in the laboratory. The findings opened new possibilities for studying human biology and disease outside the body.
Researchers can develop organoids from healthy or diseased tissue, including patient-derived tumor cells, to investigate disease mechanisms and assess how different treatments affect individual tissues. The models do not, however, reproduce every feature of a complete human organ or organism.
Tsai said organoid biobanks could improve preclinical drug testing by helping researchers assess treatment responses before clinical trials. The technology could be used to study cancer, inflammatory conditions, metabolic disorders, and genetic diseases.
TMU President Wu Mai-szu (吳麥斯) said the appointment would create opportunities for cooperation in research methods, talent development, and clinical applications, per LTN. He said the two sides aim to develop organoid models that more closely represent human diseases and patients’ responses to treatment, while training biomedical researchers in Taiwan.
According to TMU, Clevers will provide guidance in four areas: technical exchange, talent training, academic research, and clinical applications. The university said faculty members and technical personnel would have opportunities to learn about organoid technologies and research approaches at the Hubrecht Institute for Developmental Biology and Stem Cell Research in the Netherlands.
Clevers will also share his expertise and provide technical consultations to TMU and its affiliated hospitals as they explore clinically relevant organoid models and potential clinical studies.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The Institute for Information Industry said Monday that it helped the National Chung-Shan Institute of Science and Technology’s Propellant Research and Manufacturing Center obtain US cybersecurity certification.
The US Department of Defense has tightened requirements for protecting controlled unclassified information, which contractors must meet to qualify for certain defense work, according to an institute press release. The institute’s Cyber Security Technology Institute helped the NCSIST center obtain Cybersecurity Maturity Model Certification (CMMC) Level 2, following its work with NCSIST’s Aeronautical Research Institute on a drone project.
CMMC Level 2 assesses 110 security requirements, including incident response, access control, risk management, and cybersecurity awareness. An accredited third-party assessment organization conducts the audit to check how defense contractors protect sensitive information.
The Cyber Security Technology Institute helped NCSIST’s Information Security Center incorporate CMMC requirements into its procedures. It also helped the propellant center review how controlled unclassified information moves through its systems and who can access it. The center prepared for the audit while continuing its existing research work.
The institute said its experience with US defense cybersecurity requirements helped the two NCSIST units obtain certification within a year. The Aeronautical Research Institute passed its assessment on Nov. 5, 2025, followed by the propellant center on Oct. 19, 2026.
Cyber Security Technology Institute Director-General Lee Jung-san (李榮三) credited cooperation among NCSIST’s information security center, propellant center, and other staff. He said the institute plans to help other industries, including semiconductor and electronics manufacturing, meet CMMC and related cybersecurity requirements.

====================================================================================================

Asia-Pacific Community: Chinese-developed perennial rice takes root in Malaysia's Sarawak, offering hope for food security
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
11:35:22 CST
12:35:22 KST

MIRI, Malaysia, Oct. 20 (Xinhua) -- "When I saw the rice fields turn golden, I was so excited (that) I couldn't sleep. Words cannot describe how I felt," Hii King Chiong said.
Months after the first harvest of perennial rice on what was once swampy land in Malaysia's Sarawak state, Hii, executive chairman of Borneoland Paddy Sdn Bhd, still speaks of the moment with excitement.
When Xinhua visited the experimental field in Miri, a city in eastern Sarawak, on Oct. 15, lush green rice plants filled the plots, with a second harvest expected in just over a month. Nearby, seedlings of several varieties were growing in further trials. It was hard to imagine that the land had once been a swamp.
On Aug. 6, the field yielded its first crop after months of joint work by China's Yunnan University and Borneoland Paddy. At the harvest ceremony, Sarawak Premier Abang Johari Openg said that if the technology could be widely adopted, the state could significantly improve its rice self-sufficiency and potentially become a rice exporter.
Sarawak currently meets only about 21 percent of its rice needs through domestic production, and the state government aims to raise that share to 60 percent by 2030. Boosting local production and reducing dependence on external supplies have become important priorities for strengthening food security.
To explore possible solutions, Sarawak turned to China. Yunnan Province and Sarawak are sister regions, while Yunnan University and Universiti Malaysia Sarawak have maintained long-standing academic exchanges. Building on these ties, the two sides began working together in 2025 to test perennial rice varieties developed by Yunnan University in Sarawak.
"I have faith in the Chinese team and in Chinese technology," Hii said.
Before the cooperation with the Chinese team, Hii had invited several teams of experts to assess the land, but the challenging conditions of the swampy terrain left many doubtful about the prospects for cultivation.
The breakthrough came when he approached a team led by Hu Fengyi, dean of Yunnan University's College of Agriculture. While other experts had advised him to abandon the idea, Hu's team inspected the site and offered a different answer.
For the researchers, bringing rice varieties to Malaysia was only the first step. The real challenge was to help the plants adapt to local climatic, soil and water conditions while equipping the Malaysian team with the skills needed to grow perennial rice.
In March, 30 perennial rice varieties entered the trial phase. The Chinese researchers provided hands-on guidance throughout the process, from preparing the fields and building bunds to setting up irrigation and drainage systems, sowing seeds, raising seedlings and transplanting them. They also helped with water and fertilizer management and pest control, monitoring plant growth through field visits and remote follow-ups and adjusting cultivation practices when necessary.
After the first harvest, the team selected five varieties that showed promising adaptability to local conditions. Among them, "Yunda 28" performed particularly well, yielding more than 500 kg per mu (one mu is approximately 667 square meters), compared with around 200 kg per mu for traditional local rice varieties.
The preliminary results have encouraged both sides to explore the technology's potential for wider application in Sarawak.
One distinctive feature of perennial rice is its ability to regrow after harvest. Buds on the underground stems can sprout into new shoots, potentially reducing the need to sow seeds, raise seedlings and transplant rice plants for every new crop, Hu said.
But the first harvest is only an initial milestone. Whether the rice can deliver consistent yields over successive seasons in Sarawak, and which varieties can adapt to the local environment over the long term, will require further observation and testing.
Agricultural technology cannot simply be transferred from one place to another without adjustment, Hu said. It must be refined in response to local conditions and needs.
"We need to keep improving the technology so that it is easier to use, produces higher yields and better-quality rice, and better meets Malaysia's needs," he said.
Cooperation is already moving into its next phase. Abang Johari has expressed interest in deepening ties with Yunnan University and establishing a perennial rice research center in Sarawak. In early October, the Malaysian team visited Yunnan University to learn about its research facilities and equipment.
As the partnership progresses, the Malaysian team is gaining a more direct understanding of China's agricultural technology. For Hii, the experience has also highlighted the value of sharing scientific advances through international agricultural cooperation.
Hii's trial field has gradually become a local attraction. "Many people have come to visit after hearing that we have introduced new perennial rice varieties developed in China," He said. ■

====================================================================================================

Z.AI founders worked on research funded by China institute that UK tied to spies
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
03:35:00 UTC
12:35:00 KST

Z.ai founders worked on research funded by China institute that Britain tied to spies
- Four Z.AI founders worked on a 2018 to 2021 AI project partly funded by CGTRI, which MI5 said had “very strong ties” to China’s spy agency.
- The project, worth 2.94 million yuan, aimed to analyse social media, spot events and map people’s links, including a knowledge base of “China-related key persons”.
- The report links Z.AI to wider US scrutiny, including tech access limits, data extraction claims and concerns over its vulnerability ledger being shared with Chinese state databases.
AI generated
Four founders of one of China’s most promising artificial intelligence companies, Z.ai, worked on research in a joint project with a technology institute that the British government accused of having “very strong ties” to China’s main spy agency, according to publicly available research papers from China and an “espionage alert” from Britain.
The nearly four-year AI research project, which overlapped with the company’s start in 2019, was co-funded by Beijing-based China General Technology Research Institute (CGTRI) and the National Natural Science Foundation of China, according to a previously unreported 78-page report that the project’s leaders compiled to detail their findings.
A CGTRI engineer and one of Z.ai’s founders were among the project’s leaders, and three other Z.ai founders contributed to the research, according to the report.
The report was published on a Chinese government website that provides research funding records.
Britain’s MI5 intelligence service, in the Sept 30 espionage alert, accused CGTRI of primarily existing to fund academic research that directly improves China’s main spy agency’s “technical capability for espionage”.
The first-of-its-kind bulletin said the institute has “very strong ties” to China’s Ministry of State Security and warned of potential criminal consequences for “any institution or individual continuing to conduct research ultimately funded by CGTRI following publication of this espionage alert”.
A spokesperson for China’s embassy in Britain called MI5’s allegations against CGTRI “baseless”.
The Z.ai founders’ work on research partially funded by an alleged Chinese intelligence front highlights the risks cited by some US officials regarding China’s growing prowess in AI – and could add to further scrutiny of Z.ai in particular. The two countries are racing to develop a technology that is transforming the global economy and could give their military services an advantage.
The US restricted Z.ai’s access to American technology in 2025 based on allegations that the company aided the military with AI research. More recently, US officials accused the company of systemically extracting proprietary knowledge from American rivals.
It is not clear what, if anything, any of Z.ai’s founders may have known about CGTRI’s alleged relationship with Chinese intelligence. The MI5 alert did not mention Z.ai.
Z.ai did not respond to e-mailed requests for comment, nor did the four founders involved in the research project. The company previously said the US decision to restrict its access to technology “lacked factual basis” and would not have a substantial impact on its business.
Reached by phone, a CGTRI representative said the institute does not do any external communication with anyone. Efforts to e-mail CGTRI for comment were unsuccessful.
Liu Chang, a spokesperson for the Chinese embassy in Washington, declined to address specific questions about Bloomberg’s report.
“I’m not familiar with the specifics,” he said. “The development of AI in China comes from greater self-reliance and strength in science and technology. China advocates AI for good. We firmly oppose attempts to throw mud at China by distorting facts.”
A White House spokesperson referred questions about Z.ai to the Commerce Department, which declined to comment.
In an indication of the importance of AI to US intelligence, President Donald Trump in October appointed Jay Clayton, the director of national intelligence, as his new AI czar. In-Q-Tel, an independent non-profit investment firm set up by the Central Intelligence Agency in 1999, has made AI-related investments as part of its focus on start-ups used by the military and intelligence agencies.
Chinese AI models have gained in popularity because they are cheaper than US rivals and are closing the performance gap.
In the last year, however, US AI labs OpenAI and Anthropic have raised concerns about Chinese rivals including Z.ai, DeepSeek, Moonshot and MiniMax allegedly extracting data from American models to try to reproduce some of those capabilities through a technique called distillation.
It is a practice that is common across the industry, but violates terms of service when used to create a competing technology. OpenAI and Anthropic have warned that models created through this method often lack safeguards designed to block misuse of cyber and biological capabilities.
The Chinese companies have not responded to the allegations, though China’s Ministry of Commerce denied intellectual property violations and threatened to take all necessary measures to respond to actions that harm its interests.
The project involving CGTRI and the Z.ai founders ran from January 2018 through December 2021 and had a total approved project budget of 2.94 million yuan (S$563,000), according to the researchers’ report.
It sought to develop AI tools to analyse social media posts, spot key events and map peoples’ connections, according to the researchers’ report.
A key goal of the project was developing a knowledge base of “China-related key persons”, according to the report, which did not elaborate on who such people would be.
James Mulvenon, who leads intelligence research and analysis at Virginia-based Pamir Consulting, a national security contractor, reviewed the researchers’ report at Bloomberg’s request. He said the project involved research with both military and civilian uses that seeks to revolutionise how people use AI to identify and track specific individuals.
China’s Ministry of State Security “had an obvious interest in funding this research and reaping the targeting benefits”, said Mulvenon, co-author of a book on Chinese industrial espionage.
Z.ai, also known as Zhipu, was spun out of research done at China’s elite Tsinghua University. The company has received backing from local governments in China, as well as tech giants including Alibaba Group and Tencent, Bloomberg has reported.
In January, Z.ai became the first major Chinese generative-AI start-up to go public with its Hong Kong listing. Its shares have outperformed Hong Kong’s Hang Seng Index, rising more than 300% since its initial public offering versus a 6% decline in the benchmark. Z.ai’s current market capitalisation is about US$32 billion (S$40.9 billion).
In an interim financial report filed in September, Z.ai listed five founders as “key persons” who are part of the company’s “single largest group of shareholders”. Four of them are listed as participating in the AI research project, which was jointly conducted by CGTRI, Tsinghua University and Southeast University, according to the researchers’ report. Neither university responded to requests for comment.
Z.ai co-founder Li Juanzi, a professor in the computer science and technology department at Tsinghua University in Beijing, led the research project alongside CGTRI’s Cao Weibing and another professor from China’s Southeast University, the researchers’ report says.
It describes the three as being “jointly responsible for the design of the overall technical plan, coordination of tasks among the three participating institutions, and the overall research progress of the project”.
That report lists three other founders of Z.ai – Tang Jie, Xu Bin and Zhang Peng, who is the company’s chief executive officer – as co-authors of papers, co-inventors on patents, or holders of software copyrights in a directory of all the project’s research achievements. The report explicitly states that non-participants cannot be included.
Only one person identified in Z.ai’s interim report as a company founder and “key person” was not named in the project’s documentation, chairman Liu Debing.
Z.ai’s recent handling of a ledger it posted online detailing vulnerabilities it had found in other companies’ software also raised alarms, according to a report by the China-focused consulting firm Garnaut Global. The company is run by John Garnaut and Matt Pottinger, former national security officials from Australia and the US.
Garnaut Global said its analysis of Z.ai’s ledger, which was established on Aug 14, showed that Z.ai found 2,436 vulnerabilities in software from Microsoft, Intel, Alphabet’s Google and other leading Western companies.
Microsoft declined to comment, while Intel and Alphabet did not respond to requests for comment.
In the last year or so, some of the more advanced AI models have proven adept at finding flaws in software, some of which hackers might be able to exploit.
In some instances, the companies or computer researchers who find vulnerabilities alert the affected parties so they can be fixed before a hacker exploits them – sometimes for a cash reward.
But Z.ai chose to leave most of the affected vendors in the dark, disclosing just 5% of the vulnerabilities to the companies, according to the Garnaut Global report, which was reviewed by Bloomberg.
Ten days later, Z.ai took the ledger down, replacing it with a notice that the Chinese government would be managing vulnerabilities discovered by the company’s AI models through several databases, including one run by the Ministry of State Security, the Garnaut Global report said.
“Rather than sharing vulnerability details with the affected companies, Zhipu has given China’s peak cyberespionage agency access to these vulnerabilities,” said the report. BLOOMBERG

This surge successfully surpasses the 940,000 tons exported during the entirety of 2025, fulfilling a national strategic target originally established in 2010.
"Now, we have officially broken the historical record for rice exports," MAFF Undersecretary of State and Spokesperson Khim Finan said in a statement shared with the media. "This stands as a brilliant achievement for the nation and the entire agricultural sector."
Thong Mengdavid, deputy director of the China-ASEAN Studies Center at the Cambodia University of Technology and Science, said that the milestone marks a structural shift for the country, signaling Cambodia's evolution from a raw paddy producer into a highly competitive, high-value agro-exporter on the global stage.
He attributed the growth largely to strong consumer preferences and expanded logistics networks, noting that China remains a major consumer of Cambodia's fragrant and premium rice varieties.
"Crucially, trade architecture like the Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership and the Cambodia-China Free Trade Agreement has provided a powerful catalyst," Mengdavid told Xinhua. "By drastically cutting trade barriers, streamlining customs rules, and granting preferential tariff access, these FTAs effectively lower transaction costs for Cambodian exporters while enhancing brand visibility across Chinese and regional supply chains."
According to the Cambodia Rice Federation, the nation's primary export varieties consist of premium fragrant rice and white rice, with major shipments heading toward the Association of Southeast Asian Nations, the European Union and China. ■

From Syria's border to Gaza: The secret mission of fallen Druze IDF commander Ehsan Daxa
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
03:33:00 UTC
12:33:00 KST

Two years after Col. Ehsan Daxa, commander of the IDF's 401st Armored Brigade, was killed in combat in the northern Gaza Strip, details are emerging of a military campaign he led along the Syrian border. Under the name "Date Harvest," Daxa oversaw a series of strikes aimed at pushing Syrian military infrastructure away from Israel's border at a time when many considered the sector relatively quiet.
Officers who served alongside him and his widow, Huda, describe a commander who refused to wait for threats to intensify, his concern for Syria's Druze community and the operational legacy he left behind.
Some commanders look at a border and see the situation as it is. Ehsan Daxa looked at it and saw what might happen 10 years down the road. For him, the relative calm along the Syrian border was not a reason to lower the level of alertness, but an opportunity to act before a potential threat became real.
In November 2021, the Kapiyot and Nachshon military posts were attacked. In August 2023, the 'Migraine' outpost was targeted in the deepest strike of the campaign. Between those operations, a clear operational doctrine took shape: Rather than wait for military infrastructure to become an active threat, it was necessary to act against it while it was still being established.
A complex reality along the 'Barrel Line'
For years, the prevailing assumption was that the border fence served as the main line of defense. But between the fence and the Alpha Line, in an area known as the "barrel line," the reality was more complicated.
Syrian forces had crossed the line and erected tents and structures in the demilitarized zone near the Israeli border. At the time, a Syrian presence in the area was effectively permitted. Daxa believed that situation could not be allowed to continue.
Although the Syrian regime had been weakened by years of civil war, he understood that circumstances could change and that military posts that appeared insignificant could eventually become positions from which threats against Israel could be launched.
"He always thought at least 10 steps ahead," says his widow, Huda Daxa. "He knew how to put himself in the other side's shoes, understand how they thought and then piece together the entire picture. He was a strategist, and his time in the Golan Heights was when he was at his best."
Maj. S., who served as the intelligence officer of the 474th Brigade under Daxa's command, remembers a commander who refused to settle for conventional assessments of the situation. According to S., Daxa toured the sector and personally sought out Syrian positions that had encroached on the area. In his view, responsibility for defense did not end with identifying threats beyond the fence. It required a thorough understanding of the terrain and the infrastructure that could endanger Israel in the future.
The campaign developed gradually. Initially, strikes targeted positions established inside the demilitarized zone that had crossed the line defined by the IDF. The operations were subsequently expanded to additional outposts between the Alpha Line and the barrel line, and eventually deeper into Syrian territory.
The operations included ground raids, tank deployments and the use of Gil anti-tank missiles. Their objective was to push Syrian forces back and prevent them from establishing infrastructure that could eventually also be used by other hostile groups, including Hezbollah.
"The goal was to create a substantial security zone, clear and open for the movement of our forces," says Lt. Col. S., deputy commander of the Golan Brigade, who served alongside Daxa. According to him, the campaign strengthened defenses in the sector and improved the forces' preparedness for a possible escalation.
For Daxa, thinking ahead was not limited to military considerations. He also carried a deep concern for the Druze community in Syria, particularly the residents of Sweida. His connection to his Druze roots and to the State of Israel existed side by side, shaping his understanding of the complexities beyond the border.
"He was always worried about the situation of the Druze there," Lt. Col. S. recalls.
Huda says that concern also surfaced at home, although Daxa did not share details of the operations he was leading.
"At the time, I didn't always understand why he was so worried. Today, after what happened in Sweida, many things take on a different meaning. He understood things that not everyone could see."
Bringing humanity to a difficult reality
In July 2025, following the fall of the Assad regime, a deadly massacre of members of the Druze community took place in Sweida. It is impossible to say that Daxa foresaw those specific events, but the concerns he had expressed earlier reflected the way he considered future scenarios and his unwillingness to assume that circumstances would remain unchanged.
Those who knew Daxa say his operational determination was only one side of his personality.
Lt. Col. S. recalls their first meeting, shortly after he took up his position. He expected a demanding professional discussion, but Daxa brought out some halva, a sweet he particularly loved, and the conversation turned to family, life and their connection to the Druze community.
Maj. O., operations officer of the 401st Brigade, who accompanied Daxa during the fighting in the Gaza Strip and was beside him in his final moments, also remembers his ability to bring humanity into difficult circumstances.
On the day O. assumed his position, during a particularly painful period of combat operations, Daxa greeted him with a smile, invited him to sit with the commanders and helped him settle into the role despite the difficult events unfolding around them.
Two years after his death, Daxa's legacy is reflected not only in the memories of those who served alongside him, but also in the doctrine he advanced: Rather than merely responding to a threat that has already reached the border fence, identify the danger while it is still distant and act to prevent it from developing.
For Huda, this was the essence of his character. "He always tried to understand what would happen next and what needed to be done today to be ready for tomorrow," she said.
At an observation point overlooking the sector, facing the landscape where he served, that legacy takes on additional meaning. Behind the operation and the positions that were attacked stood a commander who believed that the responsibility to defend begins long before the enemy reaches the fence.
