France's riot damage doubles: Who will pay for thousands of wrecked shops?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
03:32:42 UTC
12:32:42 KST

At least 3,000 French shops were hit over the weekend. Insurers say they are mobilised, but lost trade may not be covered. Here is who pays the riot bill.
The number of shops damaged during France's weekend riots has reached at least 3,000, twice the figure reported just a day earlier.
Yet insurers, who are expected to pick up much of the bill, still have no estimate of what the destruction will cost them.
France Assureurs, the country's insurance federation, told Euronews that its members were "fully mobilised to support affected policyholders".
It could not provide an initial estimate of losses or say how many claims had been already filed.
Its crisis team is now working with public authorities across France following what the federation described as "extremely violent events".
French markets underperform as damage bill rises
On Sunday, Carrefour chief executive Alexandre Bompard, who also chairs the FCD retail federation, estimated that around 1,500 shops had been affected.
He put the industry's losses at several hundred million euros.
By Monday, the government's count had reached 3,000.
Carrefour alone reported damage at 50 stores, including 20 that had been looted.
Financial markets were also under pressure on Monday. France's CAC 40 closed 1.1% lower, underperforming the broader Euro STOXX 600, down 0.9%.
Carrefour shares lost 2.2%, while luxury group LVMH fell 1.8%. A Louis Vuitton boutique in Marseille was among the stores broken into over the weekend.
Insurance stocks declined too. AXA shed 1.3% and reinsurer SCOR lost 0.9% in Paris. In Milan, Generali fell 2.3% and Unipol dropped 3.2%.
French government bonds also came under selling pressure on Monday.
The yield on the country's 10-year bonds rose by around eight basis points to 4.94%. Germany's equivalent yield increased by less than four basis points.
That widened the difference between French and German borrowing costs to approximately 148 basis points.
What the 2023 riots tell us about the cost
France has a recent benchmark for what a weekend like this can cost.
The riots that swept the country in June and July 2023 resulted in €793 million in insured losses, France Assureurs told Euronews.
Insurers handled around 17,000 claims, averaging roughly €46,600 each.
Two-thirds of the total, about €523 million, went on shops and business premises. A quarter, close to €200 million, went to local authorities whose town halls, schools and buses had been attacked.
Cars made up the remaining 7%.
Even those figures did not capture the full extent of the destruction.
A subsequent French Senate inquiry estimated property damage at closer to €1 billion. Some losses had never been declared, while others were only partly covered by insurance.
The comparison is particularly relevant now because the number of shops affected appears to be higher.
CCI France counted around 2,500 vandalised businesses during the 2023 unrest. This weekend's government tally has already exceeded that figure.
France's new riot insurance scheme is not ready
France sought to address the insurance problems exposed by the 2023 riots in its 2026 budget law.
The legislation makes riot damage cover compulsory in certain property insurance policies and creates a national fund to help insurers absorb major losses.
Insurers would finance the fund through contributions of up to 1.5% of relevant premiums, while the state would provide guarantees of up to €4 billion a year.
But the scheme has yet to take effect. It still needs European Commission approval and a government implementing decree.
For businesses hit by this weekend's violence, that means compensation will depend on their existing insurance contracts.
Insurance may cover the damage, but what about lost sales?
Most French policies for shops and buildings include “riot and civil commotion” cover, according to France Assureurs.
That usually pays for fire, theft, vandalism and smashed shopfronts. It also tends to cover the plywood boards and security guards a gutted store needs in the days afterwards.
Lost trade is where many shopkeepers will come up short.
Compensation for a full or partial closure depends on optional business interruption cover.
It pays on lost gross profit, not lost sales, and normally only when physical damage covered by the policy forced the shop to shut.
Some contracts go further and pay out even if the premises were untouched. That applies only “in the circumstances expressly specified in the policy”, the federation said.
Policyholders generally have five days to notify their insurer, and filing a police complaint is a prerequisite for some types of cover.
The state’s share of the bill
Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu said on Monday that businesses hit by the unrest would be able to put staff on activité partielle, France’s state-funded furlough scheme, from Tuesday.
He also asked local officials to impose targeted curfews, and said a state of emergency would follow “if necessary”.
President Emmanuel Macron refused the resignation of Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez, as the number of arrests passed 2,400.
Every euro of support lands on a budget expected to post a deficit of 5.4% of GDP this year, with public debt at 119% of GDP.
And while the final bill for the riots is still unknown, one thing is becoming clear: the cost will extend well beyond the shops that were attacked.

‘Deliberate’ car ramming of Australian MP an isolated incident, police say
A 43-year-old man accused of deliberately hitting Helen Haines outside her office remains in police custody.
The Australian Federal Police (AFP) have said the alleged targeting of independent lawmaker Helen Haines appeared to be an “isolated incident” and there were no known further threats associated with the attack.
Haines was struck by a Toyota Land Cruiser SUV outside her office in Wangaratta, about 200km (124 miles) northwest of the state of Victoria’s capital, Melbourne, on Monday, in what Prime Minister Anthony Albanese called a “deliberate” act.
The 65-year-old underwent surgery overnight, with Australian media outlets reporting on Tuesday that she has lost a leg and remains in critical condition in a Melbourne hospital.
The suspect is in police custody, an AFP statement released on Tuesday said. Local media identified the driver as a 43-year-old man from Tarrawingee, Victoria.
Federal and state police were working “to identify potential charges”, including “the offence of causing harm to a Commonwealth public official which carries a maximum penalty of 10 years’ imprisonment”, the statement said.
The prime minister said on Tuesday that the vehicle had performed a U-turn before hitting the MP.
“It’s clear that there was a deliberate act here. This wasn’t an accident, someone just skidding off the road,” Albanese told the ABC national broadcaster.
The prime minister said the alleged attacker’s motive remained unknown.
Bystander intervened
A former nurse, Haines is an independent federal MP for the Victorian seat of Indi and is known for her socially conscious policy positions on the environment and transparency.
Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke told ABC Radio that witnesses said Haines was struck twice by the vehicle before a bystander intervened.
Ricky Jefferies ran from his barber shop, restrained the attacker and removed a knife from him after initially believing the incident was a car accident, Australian media reported.
“I heard a loud bang with no brakes. It was crazy; I just ran out to the front to see what’s happening,” Jefferies told reporters outside his shop.
“I didn’t realise the seriousness of the situation initially, and once it became relevant, I just did what I could and what others were already trying to do.”
Threats and abuse
Foreign Minister Penny Wong said she was shocked by the “deeply disturbing attack” and wished Haines a full recovery in a post on X.
The attack comes after the federal police documented a steady rise in threats and abuse directed towards the nation’s politicians in recent years. Politicians have historically been highly accessible to the public and usually go about their business without security.
Albanese said on Monday that “the temperature has increased in recent times”.
Haines entered parliament in 2019 after working as a nurse and midwife, becoming known for stances such as supporting stronger climate action.
She has been praised for her efforts to increase transparency in politics and crack down on corruption.

Review finds Kumanjayi Little Baby subject to 'extensive failings'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20

12:16:09 KST

IN BRIEF
- An independent review into the Northern Territory's child protection system has been tabled with 45 recommendations.
- The NT Children and Families Minister described 'unforgiveable' mistakes and pledged "considerable structural reform".
WARNING: This article contains references to an Aboriginal person who has died.
An independent review prompted by a five-year-old girl's alleged outback murder has found "extensive failings" by a territory's child protection department.
The body of Kumanjayi Little Baby was found five days after she was allegedly abducted from Alice Springs' Old Timers camp in April, sparking widespread outrage and vigils across Australia.
Jefferson Lewis, 47, has been charged with her murder and is awaiting trial.
The Northern Territory government initiated an independent review of the child protection system by former NSW police commissioner Karen Webb and longtime public servant Greg Shanahan.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
The review, tabled in the NT parliament on Tuesday, found child protection officers repeatedly failed to adequately assess safety threats to Kumanjayi Little Baby and her family.
The government had accepted the review's 45 recommendations in full to prompt "considerable structural reform" of the child protection system, NT Children and Families Minister Robyn Cahill told reporters on Tuesday.
She said the mistakes made were "unforgivable", with a disconnect between what the legislation required officers to do and the policies put in place under the previous Labor government.
Cahill said she had directed her department to audit existing safety frameworks and have all people involved assessed to make sure they would be safe around children.
"Anyone to be considered must have a working with children clearance which requires a national criminal history check," she said.
Cahill said having somebody independent verify her concerns and provide a pathway forward was critical.
The report said the department had received 14 notifications over six years about Kumanjayi Little Baby's exposure to domestic and family violence, largely involving her father.
The offences included verbal and physical violence, breaches of domestic violence orders and coercive and controlling behaviour.
Cahill said despite "the escalating pattern of violence that she was being exposed to" a domestic and family violence risk assessment was never done.
Webb and Shanahan called for a "system-wide reset" of the department, saying it needed to move away from a predominantly reactive model of responding to notifications of harm.
In July, the NT government passed new child protection laws that explicitly state that safety must be the top priority in child welfare decisions.
The reforms were criticised for placing less emphasis on maintaining cultural connection and potentially making it easier for Aboriginal children to be placed with non-Indigenous carers.
Children's ministers of every state and territory except the NT and Queensland joined federal Families Minister Tanya Plibersek in releasing a statement supporting the Aboriginal child placement principle.
The principle says an Indigenous child who needs to be removed from their parents must first be placed with a family member, and only placed with a non-Indigenous carer as a last resort.

Gen Z is becoming the least happy generation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
03:11:29 UTC
12:11:29 KST

Gen Z is becoming the least happy generation
The decline accelerated during the COVID-19 pandemic, when the figure dropped to 39% in 2020. Although it recovered to 51% in 2023, it has since fallen again.
The trend also affects adults aged 30 to 44. Their thriving rate stands at 45% in 2026, down from a peak of 62% in 2016 and 2017. Among Americans aged 45 to 64, the rate is 46%, matching the lowest level recorded for this group in 2008.
In contrast, Americans aged 65 and older are reporting better life evaluations. Their thriving rate has risen from 38% in 2008 to 53% in 2026, matching the record high reached in 2021.
What is behind the decline?
Gallup's analysis points to several factors associated with the decline in well-being among younger adults, including rising depression rates, weaker close relationships, less daily enjoyment and a reduced sense of productivity.
Since 2019, the share of young adults reporting that they experience significant enjoyment every day has fallen, while satisfaction with living standards and confidence in the future have also weakened. The report also identifies difficulties in achieving personal goals and declining enthusiasm about the future as contributing factors.
Economic uncertainty is another concern. Younger Americans face challenges related to housing affordability, job market pessimism and fears that artificial intelligence could replace their jobs. Concerns about the future availability of Social Security and Medicare benefits may also add to their financial uncertainty.
Loneliness and declining trust in political and social institutions are further concerns. According to Gallup, only 14% of Americans aged 18 to 34 said they were extremely proud to be American, down 10 percentage points from 2025.
Why are older Americans doing better?
The improving life evaluations among Americans aged 65 and older are partly associated with greater financial security.
In this age group, 59% said they had enough money to do everything they wanted, while 67% reported not worrying about money during the previous week. Food insecurity has also declined, with 6% saying they had experienced it at least once in the past year.
The report also points to improvements in some health indicators, including lower reported rates of high blood pressure and diabetes compared with seven years ago. Older adults are also visiting dentists more frequently, another factor associated with better well-being.
The 2026 findings are based on three quarterly web surveys conducted in February, May and August, involving a total of 15,156 U.S. adults.
Gallup classifies respondents as thriving based on their assessments of their current lives and expectations for the next five years. Participants must rate their current lives at least 7 out of 10 and their anticipated lives in five years at least 8 out of 10 to meet the criteria.

Japan launches world's first Mars moon sample-return mission
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
03:11:27 UTC
12:11:27 KST

Japan launches world's first Mars moon sample-return mission
The spacecraft, part of the Martian Moons Exploration (MMX) mission, was carried into space aboard the H3 rocket No. 10. It successfully separated from the rocket and entered its planned orbit, JAXA said.
“I believe we were able to place it into the planned orbit with exceptional precision,” said Makoto Arita, JAXA’s H3 project manager, at a press conference. He also expressed satisfaction at the successful launch of a project that has attracted worldwide attention.
The rocket lifted off from the Tanegashima Space Center on the island of Tanegashima in southwestern Japan at 4:41 a.m.
The spacecraft will travel to Phobos, the larger of Mars’ two moons, which orbits around 6,000 kilometers from the planet’s surface and has an estimated diameter of 20 to 30 kilometers. The mission aims to collect samples, including rocks and sand, and return them to Earth in July 2031.
Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi welcomed the successful launch in a post on X, expressing hope that the historic mission would achieve its objectives, collect samples and safely return them to Earth.

The launch was initially scheduled for 2024 but was postponed following the failure of the H3 rocket’s maiden flight the previous year.
The MMX mission is an international collaborative project designed to investigate the origins of Mars’ moons and develop technologies for future space exploration.
According to the mission plan, the spacecraft is expected to enter orbit around Mars in August 2027. A rover jointly developed by French and German teams will then land on Phobos, followed by two planned landing attempts.
After completing its investigation of Phobos, the spacecraft will observe Deimos, Mars’ smaller moon, before departing the planet’s orbit in November 2030.
During its return journey, the spacecraft will release a capsule containing the collected samples.
If successful, the mission will provide scientists with valuable material for studying the formation and evolution of Mars’ moons and gaining new insights into the history of the Martian system.

US Justice Department charges 28 California residents in alleged election fraud scheme
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
03:08:39 UTC
12:08:39 KST

Diyar Güldoğan
20 October 2026•Update: 20 October 2026
The US Department of Justice on Monday charged 28 foreign nationals living in California with alleged federal election-related crimes, including falsely claiming US citizenship on voter registration forms and in many cases casting ballots in elections.
Federal authorities announced that 11 of the defendants were arrested as part of “Operation Protect the Vote,” a coordinated effort involving all four US Attorney’s Offices in California to investigate suspected election fraud.
According to the Justice Department, all 28 defendants are lawful permanent residents, commonly known as green card holders. Although permanent residents may legally live and work in the US, they are not US citizens and generally are prohibited from voting in federal elections.
The criminal complaints include allegations of making false statements in naturalization applications, with some defendants also charged with fraudulent voter registration. The Justice Department said the offenses carry maximum potential penalties of five years in federal prison.
The charges remain allegations, and the defendants are presumed innocent unless proven guilty in court.
“Every illegal vote cancels out the vote of a lawful American citizen,” Acting Deputy Attorney General Trent McCotter said in the statement.
“Each of the 28 defendants charged today appears on the list of more than 20,000 likely noncitizen registrants we provided to California election officials last week,” he added.
Last week, the Justice Department, working with the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), filed a complaint against California for its voter-registration lists, alleging that more than 20,000 people who are likely noncitizens are registered to vote in the state.

“If he can cause Ukraine to fail, he delivers Ukraine to Putin,” Clark said.
The retired general suggested Trump might be seeking Putin’s assistance in pressuring Tehran over its nuclear program, while Moscow could demand concessions on Ukraine in return.
“This is a very, very corrupt, dangerous bargain,” Clark said. “The President of the United States is supposed to be the leader of the free world. He’s got to act like it and not cozy up to Putin.”
Asked whether he believed Putin was offering to help Trump resolve the war with Iran in exchange for Ukraine, Clark replied: “Exactly. That’s exactly what’s coming across.”

‘Almost No Patriot Missiles Left’ – Zelensky Offers 30-Day Pause on Russian Oil Strikes in Exchange for US Interceptors
‘We’ve seen this play before: 1938 Munich’
Clark drew a stark historical parallel between the possible Trump-Putin arrangement and the 1938 Munich Agreement, when Britain and France agreed to Nazi Germany’s annexation of Czechoslovakia’s Sudetenland without Czechoslovakia’s participation.
“We’ve seen this play before: 1938 Munich. The great powers met with Adolf Hitler,” Clark said.
“They gave up Czechoslovakia, and it didn’t stop World War II.”
Clark argued that ending a war at the expense of an invaded country’s sovereignty would undermine the international principles the United States has historically defended.
“The basic rule of this is you’re the leader of the free world. You go against aggressors,” he said.
“You don’t say the most important thing is to stop a war. It isn’t. The most important thing is to maintain the rights of nations to be free of invasion.”
He also compared the situation to US negotiations over the Vietnam War, arguing that agreements reached without adequately protecting an ally’s interests could lead to disastrous consequences.
Clark warns US restrictions are leaving Ukraine exposed
Clark’s warning came amid growing tensions between Kyiv and Washington over Trump’s decision to ease Russian energy sanctions, reported restrictions on satellite communications and delays in delivering critical air defense missiles.
President Volodymyr Zelensky has accused Washington of failing to provide advance intelligence on recent Russian ballistic missile attacks and slowing satellite services used by Ukrainian forces.
During Monday’s interview, Clark said he had witnessed growing concern among European security officials during a recent visit to Warsaw.
“When they realized that we’d cut off the use of Starlink and cut off the intelligence, and missiles were falling, 38 missiles in one night hitting around Kyiv,” Clark said, describing the reaction to the reported disruptions. “They know that President Trump is not the leader of the free world. They think he’s in a corrupt bargain with Vladimir Putin… It really hurts me as an American to have people say that about our president.”
As Kyiv Post previously reported, restrictions affecting Starshield satellite capabilities have disrupted Ukrainian military operations, including the use of interceptor drones against Russian aerial attacks.
Zelensky raised those concerns during a bipartisan congressional call Monday, warning that delays in urgently needed weapons and intelligence were undermining Ukraine’s defenses.
The Trump administration has denied deliberately suspending intelligence-sharing with Kyiv, while US officials have disputed claims that Washington ordered satellite restrictions.
‘How can you decide the fate of Ukraine without Ukraine?’
Clark also condemned the possibility of a three-way summit involving Trump, Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping, which could take place during next month’s Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen, China.
The proposed meeting has prompted concerns in Kyiv that the leaders of the US, Russia and China could discuss a settlement to Russia’s war without Ukrainian participation.
“Why is China at the table to decide the fate of Ukraine? And why isn’t Ukraine at the table?” Clark asked.
“How can you decide the fate of Ukraine without Ukraine there?”
Clark suggested that Beijing and Moscow could use such a meeting to pressure Washington into withdrawing further support for Kyiv, presenting Ukraine’s capitulation as a path toward ending the war.
Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha has similarly warned that a summit between Trump, Putin and Xi without Zelensky would encourage Moscow to continue its invasion.

Bomb threats, attempted hijackings must not become new norm for Israeli travelers - editorial
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
03:03:56 UTC
12:03:56 KST

After four alarming incidents involving flights to and from Israel in just three weeks, questions now abound, beyond aviation security, about the realities for Israelis even wishing to travel abroad, to anywhere.
For the 51 passengers aboard Austrian Airlines flight OS82 from Tel Aviv to Vienna on Sunday evening, what should have been a routine journey became another alarming episode in an increasingly troubling few weeks for international aviation connected to Israel.
Somewhere above southeastern Europe, a suspected bomb threat forced the aircraft to abandon its planned route and divert to Sofia, Bulgaria, where emergency services awaited its arrival, and a Bulgarian fighter jet had been scrambled to escort it to safety.
The passengers and six crew members were evacuated while the aircraft was searched, and Austrian Airlines eventually confirmed that no danger had been found. The passengers were able to continue their journey to Vienna that same night.
But the relief of another incident ending safely cannot hide the growing questions around the security of flights carrying Israelis and those traveling to and from the Jewish state.
This was no isolated occurrence.
Israel-bound flights increasingly face security threats
Last week, a Delta Air Lines flight arriving at Ben-Gurion Airport from New York was subjected to an emergency security response after an anonymous report claimed that a bomb had been placed in the aircraft’s cargo hold. The same procedure was carried out – passengers were evacuated, the aircraft was isolated, and security personnel conducted their inspections before declaring the threat false.
Later that day, another Delta flight preparing to depart New York for Tel Aviv was held at John F. Kennedy International Airport following a similar warning. American authorities searched the aircraft before granting clearance for departure. Once again, authorities found no bomb.
So in the space of several days, we had three false bomb threats against flights flying to or from Israel.
And barely two weeks before those incidents, on September 30, came the attempted terror attack aboard flydubai flight 1073 from Dubai to Tel Aviv. The actions of the captain and passengers that day are well known and do not need repeating here, but that day could have ended very differently.
International aviation has always been vulnerable to threats, and Israel has decades of experience confronting terrorism directed at civilian aircraft. The security procedures developed at Ben-Gurion Airport and aboard Israeli airlines are, unfortunately, the result of years of experience when inadequate precautions led to tragic circumstances.
But Israeli travelers increasingly depend on foreign airlines that operate under different national jurisdictions and security arrangements. After years of war and regional instability, the gradual restoration of international air links has been an important step toward normality for Israelis.
Malicious threats may undermine Israeli confidence in aviation
Indeed, Delta resumed its New York-Tel Aviv service in September after reviewing the security environment. Its return was a welcome sign of renewed confidence in Israeli aviation. The latest incidents threaten to undermine that confidence at precisely the moment when it is needed most.
Those responsible for making malicious threats must understand that such actions carry serious criminal consequences. Investigations should establish who made the warnings, how they were communicated, and whether any connection exists between the incidents.
In parallel, Israel must continue working closely with international airlines and foreign aviation authorities to ensure that security standards, whether in intelligence sharing or crew-vetting procedures, remain appropriate to the threats they face. Airlines also have a responsibility to communicate clearly with passengers and maintain confidence in the effectiveness of their safety procedures.
Israelis have grown accustomed to extraordinary circumstances becoming part of everyday life. Sirens, security checks, disruptions, and uncertainty have all become familiar features of a reality that few other populations experience with such regularity.
But boarding a commercial flight should still come with the reasonable expectation of arriving safely and without unnecessary fear.
Four incidents in three weeks do not yet establish a new pattern of coordinated attacks against Israeli aviation. They do, however, provide sufficient reason to examine how the threats facing travelers are changing and whether existing security arrangements are keeping pace.
For Israeli passengers who simply want to visit family, travel for business, or take a holiday abroad, the prospect of emergency landings and bomb scares becoming an accepted part of air travel is deeply unsettling.
Governments and airlines must ensure this extraordinary series of incidents remains an exception and does not become the new normal.

A case of Newcastle disease, which attacks the respiratory, nervous and digestive systems of birds, was identified at a turkey producer that supplies livestock exclusively to MBRF, said the people who did not want to be identified as details are not public. The producer supplies MBRF’s Chapeco plant, which is a unit that produces poultry targeting export markets.
The company declined to comment, saying: “As this is an industry-wide matter, we are redirecting inquiries on the subject to the Brazilian Animal Protein Association (ABPA).”
The news risks hurting poultry sales for Brazil, as key importing countries have in the past restricted purchases after news of outbreaks. Still, the extent of impacts will depend on decisions from buyers, who may limit imports from the entire country or from the specific regions. In a previous outbreak of Newcastle in 2024, Brazil had to halt shipments to China and the European Union.

Cyberangriffe kommen nicht nur zu Bürozeiten
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
03:00:00 UTC
12:00:00 KST

An diesem Vormittag wartet die IT-Abteilung von Babor auf einen Cyberangriff. Genauer gesagt auf das Ergebnis eines Cyberangriffs, den sie selbst in Auftrag gegeben hat: Ein Penetrationstest soll zeigen, wie gut die Systeme des Kosmetikherstellers geschützt sind. Denn die Bedrohungslage verändert sich. Künstliche Intelligenz verändert nicht nur, wie Unternehmen arbeiten, sondern auch, wie sie angegriffen werden. Phishing-Mails lassen sich heute in Sekunden auf ihre Opfer zuschneiden, Schadsoftware kann sich automatisiert an Abwehrmechanismen anpassen, und Angriffsmuster entwickeln sich schneller weiter, als klassische Sicherheitskonzepte nachziehen können. Für Unternehmen werden damit zwei Fragen immer wichtiger: Wie schnell erkennen sie einen Angriff und wie reagieren sie darauf?
Ein Härtetest für die IT-Sicherheit
Gemeinsam mit den Expertinnen und Experten von Vodafone und SITS hat das Team die eigene IT-Infrastruktur einem kontrollierten Cyberangriff ausgesetzt. Die Frage ist, wie gut die Systeme einem echten Angreifer standhalten würden und vor allem, wie früh ein solcher Angriff erkannt wird. „Das Ergebnis haben wir mit Spannung erwartet“, sagt Mirella Fiebes, Teamlead Systemadministration bei Babor. Für die IT-Abteilung ist der Test mehr als eine technische Übung. Babor betreibt rund 200 Server am Hauptsitz in Aachen, dazu kommen weitere Rechenzentrumsstrukturen an unterschiedlichen Standorten. ERP-Systeme, Datenbanken und Kollaborationstools bilden die Grundlage der täglichen Geschäftsprozesse. Weltweit vernetzte Standorte mit Tochtergesellschaften in Europa und Nordamerika sowie mehr als 1000 Mitarbeitern machen die Infrastruktur zusätzlich komplex. Entsprechend hoch sind die Anforderungen an ihre Absicherung. Die bisher eingesetzte Sicherheitslösung stieß zunehmend an ihre Grenzen. Gesucht war ein Ansatz, der nicht nur automatisiert auf verdächtige Aktivitäten reagiert, sondern die gesamte Infrastruktur rund um die Uhr im Blick behält und bei Bedarf Security-Expertinnen oder -Experten hinzuzieht. Inzwischen ist ein solches Security Operations Center (SOC) bei Babor im Einsatz. Der Penetrationstest sollte deshalb auch zeigen, wie gut die neue Sicherheitsarchitektur im Ernstfall funktioniert.

Nighttime curfews came into effect in cities across France, including parts of Paris, Bordeaux, Nice and Lyon, as French police attempted to crack down on rioting and looting during protests. Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu said further curfews would be imposed Tuesday evening "wherever required". Follow our liveblog for the latest updates.
Weekend rioting and looting heightens scrutiny of police tactics
Prime Minister Lecornu has defended police handling of the unrest, saying that “despite scenes of severe violence and extensive property damage, no one was killed, and that is a miracle”.
Interior Minister Laurent Nunez offered his resignation on Sunday evening but President Emmanuel Macron refused it “given the need for continued command of law enforcement in the current context,” his office said.
Macron instructed Nunez “to take all necessary steps to ensure full transparency about the failures in planning and intelligence-gathering that led to the violence,” the statement said.
The president also asked for the introduction of “new policing tactics on the ground as quickly as possible” to put an end to the violence.
French unrest sparks fears for critical tourism industry
The weekend unrest in Paris has left visitors scrambling to navigate the City of Light as marches, traffic delays and wafting tear gas snarled the French capital's 14-billion-euro ($16-billion) tourism industry.
On Monday, a small group of protesters was blocking the entrance to the Louvre's famous glass pyramid, leading to sometimes tense confrontations with frustrated tourists hoping to tour the world's most visited museum.
Targeted curfews helped keep the peace overnight, says French PM
The targeted curfews imposed in parts of Paris and other cities helped keep the peace overnight, French Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu has said in a post on X.
He added that local authorities on the ground will be able to impose targeted curfews again on Tuesday night where they deem necessary.
Which cities had nighttime curfews?
Paris
The curfew ordered for parts of Paris ran from 11:00 pm (2100 GMT) Monday to 6:00 am Tuesday.
It applied to two areas that were the focus of looting on the weekend: the République square in the centre-east of the capital, and the very central Chatelet-les-Halles zone where many shops are located.
Additionally, a ban on public gatherings taking place in those two zones came into effect from 8:00 pm on Monday.
Lyon
France's third-biggest city of Lyon had a curfew for its very central zone, where a tourist office was torched in the protests on Saturday.
The ban on public movement in the zone applied from 9:00 pm Monday to 6:00 am Tuesday.
A public-gathering ban was also in force in parts of Lyon from 6:00 pm Monday.
Nice
Nice, the biggest city on the French Riviera, had a curfew for its centre running from 9:00 pm to 6:00 am, under order of the mayor. But its curfew applied only to unaccompanied minors.
Lille and northern towns
Lille, France's fourth-biggest metropolitan area, and the towns of Douai, Wattignies and Denain, all located in the north of France, declared curfews for unaccompanied minors from 8:00 pm Monday to 6:00 am Tuesday. The measures applied only to certain zones.
France asks online marketplaces to prevent sale of looted items
As thousands of French shop owners reel from the weekend violence and looting, listings of apparently stolen items have been popping up online.
The French government has asked major second-hand marketplaces such as Vinted, eBay and Amazon to crack down on suspicious adverts.
France stunned by scale of unrest
Mass protests in France are often tainted by violence on the fringes of otherwise peaceful marches, leading to clashes with police.
Saturday’s unrest recalled the riots that followed the fatal police shooting of a teenager in 2023, when authorities imposed local curfews, and violence during the Yellow Vest movement that began in 2018 over fuel prices and broader economic grievances.
Trump exploits France riots to warn US voters over immigration
US President Donald Trump used the protests roiling France to score some quick political points Monday, as the upcoming midterm elections force his Republican party to face strong headwinds.
At a rally in Kansas, the US president launched into a lengthy tirade about France, which he said was being "conquered, looted, and burnt to the ground by migrants, jihadists, and communists."
"And we're not going to let that happen to this country," he added.
While speaking with reporters previously in the day, Trump recalled an exchange with his French counterpart Emmanuel Macron: "I told him a long time ago, you're making a big mistake in France. You're letting everybody from the world come in...Paris is going to be a Muslim city very soon."
Earlier Monday, the 80-year-old president wrote on his Truth Social platform: "The migrants have taken over France. They must CLOSE THE BORDERS, FAST!"
Paris imposes overnight curfew after France's worst rioting in years
Paris police issued an overnight curfew on Monday in two areas of the French capital, after a weekend marred by France’s worst rioting in years that targeted city halls, other public buildings and thousands of businesses across the country.
The order aims to protect “people and property from the violence and looting,” the Paris police statement said.
The curfew prohibits anyone from entering or remaining on the Place de la République, where rioting took place Saturday, and the shopping neighbourhood of Les Halles, which has been subject to looting.
The curfew will be in effect from 11 pm Monday until 6 am Tuesday. In addition, gatherings and demonstrations are banned from 8 pm, the Paris police said.
Earlier Monday, Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu had called for “very limited” and “localised” curfews.
In northern France, local authorities imposed a curfew for children and teenagers under age 18 in several cities, including Lille, starting from Monday and for the next two days from 8 pm to 6 am. Nice, on the French Riviera, also imposed an overnight curfew for minors from 9 pm.
Lecornu defended police handling of the unrest, saying that “despite scenes of severe violence and extensive property damage, no one was killed, and that is a miracle.”

Pregnancy discrimination remains widespread in Australian workplaces
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
02:50:34 UTC
11:50:34 KST

IN BRIEF
- Nearly half of mothers report discrimination during pregnancy, parental leave or returning to work.
- An Australian Human Rights Commission report found pregnancy discrimination hasn't decreased over the last decade.
After being passed up for an associate principal role at a school, a woman went on maternity leave to have her first baby.
When she returned to work, she expected to go back to her role in leadership.
Instead, her principal told her she would come back as a music teacher.
"He just said, the school no longer needed my role," the Perth woman told AAP.
"I don't have any formal music qualifications ... He gave me the job he considered to be the least important."
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
The mother-of-two, who spoke on the condition of anonymity as she still works in the state school system, considered taking action against her principal.
She spoke to the Fair Work Ombudsman and her union, but decided not to pursue a claim.
"My life was already so full, I didn't want to take more time away from being with my kid," she said.
"And it would just be rough to work for someone that you had legally fought with to have that job."
In another case, Alana, from Melbourne, worked at a hydrotherapy service for babies and tried to take time off to be with her one-year-old when he was hospitalised.
"I gave a few days' notice, and she [the manager] got really, really angry and lost it, and said it's unacceptable, if your son is sick, you have to call your mother or a babysitter," she said.
"Another time he was sick ... she said that I had to have my husband take him, or I wouldn't have a job."
Almost half of mothers, 49 per cent, experienced discrimination during pregnancy, parental leave or return to work, a 2014 Australian Human Rights Commission (AHRC) study found.
About 91 per cent did not lodge formal complaints out of stress, fear of retaliation or lack of legal awareness.
Little has changed, with pregnancy, breastfeeding and family responsibility discrimination remaining "a significant and widespread workplace issue" in 2026, an AHRC report released on Tuesday found.
The number of alleged pregnancy discrimination complaints the AHRC received rose from 54 in 2021 to 72 in 2025.
The AHRC met with 84 stakeholders, including industry, community, advocates, lawyers, unions and academics.
Recurring patterns of discrimination were identified, including "sham" redundancies and job loss during pregnancy or parental leave, diminished duties when returning to work, and refusal of flexible work arrangements.
Harms were amplified for First Nations, migrant, racially-marginalised, disabled, and LGBTQI+ communities, who experienced intersecting forms of discrimination.
"It was really clear that pregnancy discrimination, and discrimination on the basis of carers' responsibility, is widespread and hasn't changed significantly in the last 12 years," Sex Discrimination Commissioner Anna Cody said.
She said employers needed to change how they conceptualise work, with flexible working arrangements made a presumption unless an employer rebuts, and the 12-month service requirement to access unpaid parental leave eliminated.
The AHRC made 18 recommendations, including amending the Sex Discrimination Act to ban indirect discrimination based on family responsibilities, and limiting redundancies during or immediately after parental leave.

Thailand and Cambodia have agreed to dial down the rhetoric and use a hotline between their navy commanders to avoid flashpoints over a vast contested patch of energy-rich seas in the Gulf of Thailand, according to a UN-backed mediation panel at The Hague tasked with helping to settle the dispute between the neighbours.

While an uneasy ceasefire agreed in December holds along the frontier, relations between Bangkok and Phnom Penh have plunged to a nadir, with both accusing the other of targeting civilians during the conflict and intermittent breaches of the truce.
Amid the rancour, competing claims have escalated over the Gulf seabed which holds oil and gas reserves worth an estimated US$300 billion.

BEIJING, Oct. 20 (Xinhua) -- Chinese border authorities handled 192 million entries and exits in the third quarter of 2026, up 7.9 percent from a year earlier, officials said on Tuesday.
Foreign nationals made 23.27 million border crossings from July to September, up 15.6 percent year on year, according to the National Immigration Administration.
Visa-free entries by foreign nationals reached 8.99 million, accounting for 77.5 percent of all entries by foreign nationals, a 24.1 percent increase year on year.
Since December 2023, when China launched a trial policy granting unilateral visa exemptions to visitors from six countries, it has expanded unilateral visa-free entry to travelers from 50 countries as of September. The policy allows eligible visitors to stay for up to 30 days.
It also extended the visa-free transit period for certain countries from 72 or 144 hours to 240 hours in December 2024. There are 57 eligible countries so far. ■

Four dead as torrential rain batters eastern Spain

Unknown Publisher

Four dead as torrential rain batters eastern Spain
Cars swept away, roads submerged, residents isolated in parts of Spain’s Mediterranean coast.
Four people have been killed as torrential rainfall sweeping eastern Spain triggered severe flooding, evacuations and shelter-in-place orders for tens of thousands of people, authorities said on Monday.
The downpour from Storm Adam, which started on Saturday, dumped as much as 700 litres of rain (185 gallons) per square metre in 24 hours in some areas of the Valencia region.
Floodwaters have since isolated several towns along the Mediterranean coast, while rivers have burst their banks and streets have turned into torrents, leaving scenes reminiscent of the catastrophic flooding that killed more than 230 people in the Valencia region two years ago.
The storm is confirmed to have killed four people: two in the coastal resort of Oliva, a third at a beach in Sagunto, and a fourth who fell into a swollen stream in Catalonia.
Winched to safety
On Monday morning, 800,000 residents were under shelter-in-place orders, but that was reduced to 87,000 in eight municipalities by late afternoon.
Security forces carried out more than 400 rescues in the Valencia region, according to government representative Pilar Bernabe.
People stranded on rooftops have been winched to safety amid widespread evacuations.
The storm, which also lashed the Balearic Islands and Catalonia, prompted authorities to order about 100 municipalities to remain indoors for several hours on Monday.
Most restrictions were lifted by early afternoon as conditions improved, the regional government said.
‘It’s a disaster’
In Els Poblets, northeast of Alicante, cars and vans were piled on top of one another from the force of the water, as residents tried to salvage what they could from their homes.
“The village, well, it’s a disaster. Some people have lost everything all over again, just like in 2007, when exactly the same thing happened,” resident Javier Fornez said.
More than 2,000 people were evacuated, mainly in Oliva, and authorities carried out nearly 100 rescues in Valencia and Alicante on Monday, the Civil Guard police said.
The mayor of Pego, Enrique Moll, told public regional broadcaster A Punt radio on Monday that several people were still waiting to be evacuated by helicopter from their roofs. All access routes to the town were blocked, he added.
The deputy mayor of Oliva, Salvador Llopis, told state broadcaster TVE on Monday that emergency services were rescuing trapped residents, particularly elderly people stuck inside their homes with water up to their waists.
National weather agency AEMET announced on Friday that last month was mainland Spain’s hottest September on record, after registering its warmest summer between June and August.

But responsibility for Israel's future requires us to see the bigger picture and make decisions like this, even when we believe our vision and our path are right. She added: "First and foremost, I want to say to everyone who is calling, texting, writing and worrying about me: I simply love you. I love this nation, and I am not giving up on it, or on the things that need to be fixed here. Because a beautiful and good Land of Israel is, above all, a just and equal one that sees and recognizes everyone."
"During my years of partnership with Benny, I saw his integrity, dedication and love for the country and its people up close. Every time he said 'Israel before everything,' he meant it and stood behind those words. I meant it too. Even during difficult times, Benny continued to carry the banner of unity and work to bring the different parts of our society together. He understood, especially after October 7, just how much our resilience, security and future depend on our ability to stand together."
Tamano-Shata continued: "It was this belief that led me to continue walking with him and standing by his side, even when the road was difficult, even when colleagues abandoned ship, even when other paths were offered to me, and out of gratitude and appreciation for the man and our partnership. I value Benny and thank him for his trust and for the journey we shared. I never doubted that Israel always came first for him. The decision he made today reflects the very commitment with which we began this journey."
Tamano-Shata added that once it became clear that votes cast for the party would be wasted, its leaders decided to withdraw.
"When there is concern that the party list will not cross the electoral threshold, our responsibility is to allow those who place their trust in us to vote for candidates who can represent them in the Knesset, even at the cost of giving up our own candidacy this time," she said.

In search for Amelia Earhart’s plane, tantalising clue turns out to be tree debris
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
02:35:00 UTC
11:35:00 KST

In search for Amelia Earhart’s plane, tantalising clue turns out to be tree debris
- US explorers searching Nikumaroro for Amelia Earhart’s plane found the satellite “visual anomaly” was likely washed-up trees, not wreckage.
- The US$900,000 Purdue-backed mission said it found no “smoking gun”, after a week on the Kiribati island and earlier failed searches.
- The “castaway hypothesis” still has support, with claims of radio calls, artefacts and bones, but the official US view says Earhart crashed at sea near Howland Island.
AI generated
LOS ANGELES – US-based explorers who voyaged to a tiny South Pacific island seeking to solve conclusively the 1937 disappearance of famed American aviator Amelia Earhart have determined that an object they suspected was wreckage from her plane was a cluster of washed-up trees.
Leaders of the mission made the announcement on Oct 19.
The team set out in October from Los Angeles for the archipelago nation of Kiribati on a US$900,000 (S$1.15 million) expedition backed by private donors and Indiana’s Purdue University, long affiliated with Earhart and her legacy.
The objective was to learn whether an elongated, multi-pronged object detected by 2020 satellite imagery in the island’s lagoon was a remnant of Earhart’s long-missing twin-engine Lockheed Electra 10-E airplane.
Such a finding would have decisively proven some scholars’ hypothesis that Earhart and her navigator, Fred Noonan, crash-landed on or near the coral-ringed atoll and perished as castaways there, hundreds of kilometres from their intended refuelling stop.
‘Adventure is worthwhile’
“Unfortunately, we weren’t able to find that smoking gun,” Purdue general counsel and team member Steve Schultz said in a video message recorded on the island of Nikumaroro, part of the Phoenix Islands in Kiribati.
Quoting Earhart, he added: “You know, Amelia herself said, ‘Adventure is worthwhile in itself’.”
After a week at the island, the team ultimately concluded that the “visual anomaly” picked up by satellite “was likely a collection of large trees” wedged in the sand at the lagoon, the expedition said in a statement.
Much of that debris had fragmented and washed away since it was first spotted, leaving a smaller Y-shaped segment whose reflective surface – suggestive of metal – turned out to come from “its carbonate veneer”, the team said in a statement.
Two previous attempts to locate the aircraft’s wreckage in the ocean around Nikumaroro also proved fruitless, and a plane-shaped sonar image captured elsewhere on the sea floor turned out to be a pile of rocks.
Earhart and Noonan were last seen taking off in the Electra on July 2, 1937, from Papua New Guinea, during her multi-stage attempt to become the first woman to pilot a plane around the world, and the first aviator to circumnavigate the equator.
Radio contact with the flight was lost the next day after Earhart, 39, reported “gas is running low”, followed by her final known transmission giving her navigational line of position.
Castaway hypothesis ‘remains very strong’
The disappearance spawned one of the largest air-sea searches ever undertaken, and endures as one of the great unsolved mysteries of the 20th century and aviation history.
The expedition’s leader, Richard Pettigrew, head of the Archaeological Legacy Institute of Eugene, Oregon, said evidence supporting the “castaway hypothesis”, suggesting Earhart and Noonan died while marooned on Nikumaroro, “remains very strong”.
He cited the body of evidence collected during the past 30-plus years by veteran Earhart explorer Ric Gillespie, co-founder of The International Group for Historic Aircraft Recovery and author of the 2024 book One More Good Flight: The Amelia Earhart Tragedy.
His case includes multiple radio distress calls picked up in the days immediately after Earhart vanished, with bearings that converge on Nikumaroro, and a 2018 forensic analysis of human bones recovered on the island in 1940 showing they belonged to a woman of Earhart’s build and stature.
Gillespie’s investigation also encompassed such artefacts from the island as a woman’s shoe, a compact case, a freckle cream jar and medicine vial, all dating to the 1930s, as well as remnants of a jackknife like the one Earhart carried on the plane.
Yet another piece of evidence is a photograph taken of the island’s shoreline months after Earhart vanished, showing an object that appears to be the Electra’s landing gear.
The Purdue expedition in October said it uncovered a number of other artefacts, including a steel tube about 75cm long found in the lagoon, that may yield more evidence when studied.
According to Gillespie, the plane has been lost to history, eventually swept by tides off the coral flat where it had landed and carried into the sea to sink and break apart in the surf.
The official US government view of Earhart’s fate has long been that her plane ran out of fuel and crashed at sea near its refuelling destination of Howland Island, another dot of land about 640km north-west of Nikumaroro. REUTERS

China increases LNG imports from Russia by 44.3% to 7.19 mln tons in January-September
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
02:30:33 UTC
11:30:33 KST

BEIJING, October 20. /TASS/. China’s imports of Russian liquefied natural gas (LNG) increased by 44.3% year over year in January-September, reaching 7.19 mln metric tons, according to data from China’s General Administration of Customs.
According to the statistics, the value of LNG supplies from Russia to China rose by 38.5% to $3.92 bln. Russia ranks second among China’s leading LNG suppliers.
Australia was China’s largest LNG supplier in January-September, although its exports to China declined by 1.1% compared with the same period in 2025 to 15.01 mln metric tons. Malaysia ranked third with 6.2 mln metric tons, up 26.1%.
Qatar followed with 4.88 mln metric tons, down 65.5%, followed by Indonesia with 2.46 mln metric tons, a decline of 22.8%. The United States exported 231,180 metric tons of LNG to China over the nine-month period, down 11%.
In September, China doubled its LNG imports from Russia compared with August to 1.85 mln metric tons. In value terms, supplies increased 2.2-fold to $1.18 bln.
According to official statistics, China increased its LNG imports from Russia by 3.3% in 2024 and by 18.2% in 2025, reaching 9.79 mln metric tons.

Ukrainians in US to retain temporary protected status for now
The US Department of Homeland Security (DHS) said this, Reuters reported, according to Ukrinform.
A DHS spokesperson said an announcement regarding TPS holders from Ukraine and Sudan would be made “at the appropriate time,” while their immigration protections would remain in effect.
Temporary Protected Status allows foreign nationals already in the United States to remain in the country and work legally when armed conflicts, natural disasters or other extraordinary conditions are occurring in their home countries.
This is the second extension in recent months for certain groups of immigrants holding TPS, despite the Donald Trump administration’s stepped-up efforts to crack down on illegal immigration.
In September, his administration allowed Salvadoran nationals to retain their protection. Meanwhile, decisions have previously been made to terminate TPS for nationals of Haiti, Venezuela, Somalia, Yemen, Syria and other countries.
The decision regarding Ukrainians comes amid deteriorating relations between the Trump administration and Ukraine. In recent days, the US President declined to step up sanctions against Russia over the war and lifted restrictions on Russian diesel fuel exports.
According to Reuters, around 240,000 Ukrainians who fled the war have registered for TPS in the United States. The status is also held by approximately 6,800 Sudanese nationals, as the war between the army and a paramilitary group has triggered one of the world’s worst humanitarian crises.
As reported by Ukrinform, Moldova is ready to accept a new influx of Ukrainian refugees if Ukraine faces a severe humanitarian situation this winter.

Kazakhstan and Azerbaijan present Trans-Caspian Route opportunities to Japanese investors
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Kazakhstan and Azerbaijan present Trans-Caspian Route opportunities to Japanese investors
On Monday, October 19, Tokyo hosted a conference on strengthening transport connectivity between Japan, Central Asia and the Caucasus through the development of the Trans-Caspian International Transport Route (TITR) and the launch of a direct air service between Tokyo and Almaty, Qazinform News Agency reports.
The event, aimed at attracting Japanese investment in the TITR’s infrastructure, brought together approximately 100 participants, including representatives of relevant government ministries, the Japan International Cooperation Agency (JICA), the Business Association ROTOBO, and Japan’s logistics sector, the press service of the Kazakh Foreign Ministry said.
Ambassadors of Kazakhstan, Yerlan Baudarbek-Kozhatayev, and Azerbaijan, Farid Talibov, presented the countries’ transport development strategies, highlighting efforts to improve the efficiency of logistics chains and expand international transport cooperation.
In his remarks, Yerlan Baudarbek-Kozhatayev highlighted the official commissioning of the Trans-Caspian Fiber-Optic Communication Line in Baku on October 15, 2026, in the presence of presidents Kassym-Jomart Tokayev and Ilham Aliyev. The project is expected to expand international data exchange capacity and enhance the resilience of digital communications.
Japan’s State Minister of Economy, Trade and Industry, Kei Takagi, emphasized the strategic importance of the TITR for Tokyo in the context of diversifying international transport and logistics routes. He noted that the development of the Middle Corridor offers additional opportunities to strengthen Japan’s trade and economic ties with the countries of Central Asia and the Caucasus.
Mieko Koyanagi, Director of the International Logistics Office at Japan’s Ministry of Land, Infrastructure, Transport and Tourism (MLIT), briefed participants on the results of trial shipments conducted by Japanese companies along the Middle Corridor. These trials made it possible to analyze key parameters of the route, including delivery times and costs, the specifics of customs clearance procedures, and the quality of transport and logistics services.
Particular attention was given to Japan’s support for improving the efficiency of customs administration at the Port of Aktau. The project, valued at up to JPY 719 million, includes the installation of a fixed, large-scale X-ray scanning system at the port, which is expected to reduce cargo inspection times by a factor of three.
As part of the event, Adel Dauletbek, Air Astana’s Senior Regional Manager for the Republic of Korea and Japan, provided an overview of prospects for strengthening transport connectivity in light of the planned launch of direct scheduled flights between Almaty and Tokyo’s Narita Airport in December, 2026.
Earlier, Qazinform reported that Kazakhstan and Azerbaijan signed an agreement on the Middle Corridor development.

'Phenomenon of a Qurultay’ book presented in Ankara
The book "The Phenomenon of a Qurultay," which explores the history of Kazakh statehood and traditions of governance, has been presented in the Turkish capital, Qazinform News Agency correspondent reports.
The 400-page scholarly work was previously presented to readers in Almaty and Astana. The book has been published in Kazakh, Turkish, Russian and English. It draws on historical manuscripts examining the origins of a Qurultay and its role in the region’s political life.
The Turkish-language edition was published with the assistance of the ruling Justice and Development Party (AK Party) of Türkiye, through its Directorate of Relations with Turkic States.
The event brought together members of the diplomatic corps, Turkish scholars and Kazakhstanis residing in Ankara. The presentation was followed by an expert discussion on the historical significance of a Qurultay and its relevance to contemporary political processes.
Kürşad Zorlu, Vice Chairman of Türkiye’s Justice and Development Party, noted that a Qurultay represents an important part of ancient Turkic history and traditions of state governance. According to him, renaming Kazakhstan’s parliament the Qurultay symbolizes a return to historical roots and underscores the continuity of the country’s political institutions.
One of the book’s authors, public figure Omarkhan Oksikbayev, emphasized the importance of reviving this tradition. He also highlighted President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev’s initiative to establish the National Qurultay in 2022 and the subsequent development of the institution into a Parliament.
The authors plan to continue studying historical sources and prepare further research. The book is currently being presented at several higher education institutions across Kazakhstan. Future presentations in Azerbaijan and European countries are also under consideration.
According to the authors, the project aims to draw international attention to the history of Kazakh statehood and the evolution of traditions of public representation.
Earlier, Qazinform reported Turkic world scholars discussed cultural heritage preservation in Bishkek.

Moldova denies sending protest note to Ukraine over border guards' Dniester crossing
Moldova's Foreign Ministry denied sending a diplomatic protest to Ukraine over an incident involving two Ukrainian border guards, contradicting an earlier statement by a senior Moldovan lawmaker.
On Oct. 19, the chair of Moldova's parliamentary national security committee, Lilian Carp, said protest notes had been sent to Ukraine's embassy and authorities after Ukrainian border guards crossed into Moldova.
Moldova's Foreign Ministry subsequently denied issuing a protest note and indicated that the matter was being addressed through established channels between the two countries' authorities.
The two Ukrainian border guards had entered Moldova in a motorboat on Oct. 15 while attempting to detain a Ukrainian man crossing the Dniester River near Holosnita, along the Vinnytsia Oblast border. Moldova's Border Police detained the officers, and prosecutors opened criminal proceedings over the alleged illegal crossing, an offense under Article 362 of Moldova's Criminal Code.
Ukraine's State Border Guard Service spokesperson Andrii Demchenko said the man resisted detention and evaded capture, and that low water levels and an engine failure caused the border guards' boat to drift onto the Moldovan bank.
The two guards were returned to Ukraine after discussions between authorities. Ukraine's border service said an internal investigation remained underway. The man they were pursuing remained in Moldova.
The Ukrainian man, a 49-year-old from Kyiv, told Moldovan media that he was trying to reunite with family members who had left Ukraine for Bulgaria because of the war. According to PRO TV Chișinău, he has remained in hospital, and is requesting asylum.
The incident happened during a time of heightened security concerns in Moldova related to Russia's war against Ukraine.
On the night of Oct. 15–16, four Russian drones violated Moldovan airspace before returning to Ukraine, prompting condemnation from Moldova's Foreign Ministry.

Zelenskyy accuses US of delaying Patriot missile shipment

The accusations come as Ukraine-US relations are strained. US President Donald Trump has eased sanctions on Russia and directly criticized Zelenskyy, calling for someone else to take his place.
What did Zelenskyy say?
The Ukrainian president said that the US was holding back interceptor missiles, with one shipment only waiting for the signature of US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth before it could be sent to Ukraine.
He also said that Ukraine's European allies had agreed to transfer some of their own Patriot missiles but that this too was pending the green light from the US .
"The missiles are ready, and they could already be in Ukraine," Zelenskyy said. "But unfortunately, there is still no approval."

There are also growing concerns over restrictions affecting Starshield, a military satellite communications network developed by Elon Musk's SpaceX. Ukrainian military communications and drone operations depend on using Starshield data.
The US government controls access to Starshield, but Trump has denied ordering any restrictions.
US says it's not withholding intelligence
The accusations come as Ukraine faces renewed Russian attacks on its energy infrastructure. In the night between Sunday and Monday, several Russian ballistic missiles struck the Ukrainian capital and its surroundings, cutting off electricity to more than half a million households.
"Another Russian ballistic missile attack came in several waves overnight, and once again, there was no early warning from our partners," Zelenskyy wrote on Telegram about the attack.

On Monday, Trump doubled down on his previous complaints about alleged ingratitude from the Kyiv administration.

Kiev condemned the agreement, accusing Washington of making concessions to Moscow behind Ukraine’s back.
US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner reportedly reminded Ukrainian negotiators during talks in Miami that Washington is supplying Kiev with weapons and intelligence and that Ukraine should not pursue attacks that hurt American consumers. Ukrainian officials interpreted the remarks as a threat to suspend the assistance unless the refinery strikes stop.
The Trump administration has denied issuing any ultimatums. Secretary of State Marco Rubio has rejected claims that the administration deliberately restricted intelligence sharing or Starlink access. The Pentagon has likewise denied changing its intelligence-sharing policy.
Yet Zelensky continued to challenge the administration, telling senators that SpaceX’s Starlink and the US military’s Starshield satellite systems remain partially restricted and that Ukraine missed US early warnings about Russian ballistic missile attacks on three occasions over the past week.
He also accused Secretary of War Pete Hegseth of holding up Patriot interceptor missiles and AIM-9X missiles that NATO countries already purchased for Kiev.
The Washington Post reported that the Pentagon has yet to authorize certain transfers of Patriot missiles from third countries.
Following the meeting, Blumenthal pledged further congressional action, saying bipartisan support for Kiev remains “clear and unequivocal.”
Trump lashed out at Zelensky on Monday, accusing him of obstructing efforts to end the conflict and suggesting that someone else should negotiate on Ukraine’s behalf.
“Zelensky doesn’t know what he’s talking about,” Trump told reporters. “Maybe it’s time for Zelensky to get someone else to negotiate… We’ve given a lot to Ukraine, they’ve given nothing to us.”

In 2024, China reduced its oil imports by 1.9%, although supplies from Russia increased by 1.3%. In 2025, China’s oil imports rose by 4.4% to 577.72 mln metric tons, while purchases from Russia declined by 7.1% to 100.72 mln metric tons.

French riots lay bare risks and opportunities for 2027 election candidates
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
02:00:00 UTC
11:00:00 KST

Police officers stand near a fire during an unauthorized demonstration marked by riots and clashes with law enforcement at Place de la Republique in Paris on October 18, 2026. | Gauthier Bedrignans/Hans Lucas/AFP via Getty Images
PARIS — Looting and rioting across France over the weekend are threatening to reshape the contours of the French presidential race.
Far-right frontrunner Marine Le Pen is seizing on the crisis to cast herself as the candidate of law and order, but there are risks for her too. Many voters see her as a highly divisive leader whose 2027 victory would only deepen the societal fault lines exposed by the riots.
Far-left firebrand Jean-Luc Mélenchon, widely tipped to challenge Le Pen in the second round next year, is also treading carefully as rivals accuse him of encouraging the rage on the streets that has morphed into pillaging and arson.
Advertisement
For the flailing centrists, there is now an opportunity to finally make an impression in the contest — but only if they can distance themselves from President Emmanuel Macron, who is seen as fluffing his response to the nationwide wave of vandalism.
Overall, it’s pushing the election into uncharted waters.
“If there’s a real crisis, you don’t know where it could lead,” said one conservative who holds regular talks with officials from the far-right National Rally and was granted anonymity to discuss the subject.
Where does that leave the candidates? POLITICO takes a look at the strategic calculus for the leading runners across the political spectrum.
Marine Le Pen, on the up
Le Pen is receiving an immediate boost. Even her rivals admit it.
This Saturday’s unrest “benefits the far right,” said center-right European Member of Parliament Nathalie Loiseau. “They are circling around the violence like vultures,” she said in an interview.
Advertisement
Le Pen has already cast herself as the alternative president, delivering a sober address to the nation Sunday and pitching herself as the candidate of a “pacified France.”
Jordan Bardella, president of her National Rally party, upped the ante on the protests and pitched his party as the only one able to restore order, dialing up fears about the pillaging. The rioters “will soon be breaking into people’s homes,” he said at a press conference in Paris. “The authorities are collapsing.”
But excessive, prolonged chaos could backfire on a party long seen as instigating civil unrest. And the topic is already becoming a talking point inside the National Rally.
Far-right party Rassemblement National candidate in France’s 2027 presidential election Marine Le Pen holds a press conference on the sidelines of a meeting of Patriots parliamentary group on the eve of an EU Summit in Brussels on October 14, 2026. | Nicolas Tucat/AFP via Getty Images
“Some say that this shows that there will be riots if the National Rally comes to power,” said Charles-Henri Gallois, one of Bardella’s advisors. “But I don’t believe it.”
According to the conservative quoted above, periods of instability can lead the French to turn their backs on anti-establishment figures and prefer traditional veterans.
“You could end up with [Charles] De Gaulle on the Champs-Élysées,” the official said, referring to how the first president of the Fifth Republic emerged with extra powers after the 1958 crisis that roiled the nation.
Advertisement
Jean-Luc Mélenchon, on the defensive
Far-left leader Mélenchon is in a bind as he walks a tightrope between supporting protesters and distancing himself from violence.
The France Unbowed party supported the school protests in the run-up to last weekend’s riots, and far-left elected officials have played a prominent role in the blockades, either in decrying alleged police violence or in support of the protesters.
In the battle for leadership between Mélenchon and center-left MEP Raphaël Glucksmann, the former grabbed the limelight.
Jean-Luc Melenchon, during the October 17 demonstration in Paris on October 17, 2026. | Augustin Pasquini/Hans Lucas/AFP via Getty Images
But the violence this weekend could end up marginalizing the far left, especially with the government and political rivals accusing them of fueling the unrest. “They tried to aggravate the situation,” Loiseau said.
On Monday, Mélenchon tried to turn the tables, firing back at the government, saying the prime minister was fomenting “disorder” with his accusations that ultra-left groups were trying to disrupt the election.
Advertisement
Edouard Philippe, looking for a reset
For the center-right presidential hopeful Philippe, the riots aren’t good news either. He has to work hard to distance himself from his old boss, President Emmanuel Macron, who is seen as failing to respond sufficiently to the crisis. (Philippe was Macron’s first prime minister.)
But the protests could also be his opportunity to show some character, and rebut critics who think his campaign lacks energy and panache. Philippe, the best-placed centrist candidate to beat the far-right, has seen his poll ratings stall in recent months and has struggled to cut through the campaign noise.
Edouard Philippe gives a speech during a meeting between the Alliance for General News Press and several presidential candidates in Paris on October 14, 2026. | Dimitar Dilkoff/AFP via Getty Images
A break with Macron might just be what he needs.
Philippe came out hard against the president after he failed to announce any measures during his primetime television address Sunday. “I would have preferred… decisions and initiatives to restore order,” he wrote online. “This country needs someone in command.”
But the former PM will need to stick his neck out more if he’s going to make an impact.
“He’s very presidential, and it’s a posture that suits him,” said one of Macron’s ministers, who, like others cited here, was granted anonymity to speak candidly.
Advertisement
“But he’s not saying anything. What’s his measure? Why doesn’t he say we need to call a state of emergency? “
Raphaël Glucksmann, on the offensive
For the MEP Raphaël Glucksmann, the protests are a trial by fire after he won the Socialist Party primary contest earlier this month and became the center-left’s presidential candidate.
On Monday, Glucksmann tried to strike a very different note from Mélenchon, telling reporters that “it’s unbearable … that hordes of looters should attack symbols of the state.”
Raphaël Glucksmann, Member of the European Parliament, co-chair of Place publique, and winner of the left-wing primary for the 2027 presidential election, speaking after his victory during the first-round results night at the Solaris in Paris on October 11, 2026. | Benjamin Vodant/Hans Lucas/AFP via Getty Images
Sensing a chink in the far-left leader’s armor, he accused the leader of France Unbowed of being “a springboard” for Le Pen, who would be “the beneficiary of the chaos.”
Glucksmann has seen his poll ratings go up since he won the Socialist Party primary outright, reaching 15% to 16.5% according to a recent Elabe poll — in a similar territory to Mélenchon and Philippe.
But the minister quoted above expected Glucksmann to peak soon.
Advertisement
“He can only take voters away from Mélenchon,” the minister said. “A left-wing voter may vote for the right, but a right-wing voter won’t vote for the left anytime soon,” the person said.
Emmanuel Macron, on the skids
Macron is being roasted for going on television to address the nation and announce … absolutely nothing.
On Sunday, Macron promised that rioters who “destroyed” things would have to pay the price and called for “clear answers” on why the protests turned violent.
“Fucking hell, it’s rubbish,” said one former senior government official.
Macron has cultivated an image of being above the fray and went on a trip to the Middle East on Monday. But his failure to respond to the violence risks damaging his final months in power. “It’s out of touch,” a regional official said.
According to the minister quoted above, Macron should have let his prime minister do the talking but instead was encouraged to make “a speech to calm” the situation.
Advertisement
On Monday, Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu tried to get a grip on the situation, announcing localized curfews, movement restrictions, and bans on public demonstrations.
But another day of demonstrations has already been announced for next Saturday, sparking fears the protests will snowball into sustained protests similar to the Yellow Vests movement in 2018 and 2019.
If so, this chaos will be a defining element of the 2027 campaign.
