Spanish left-wing chaos dampens Sánchez’s hopes of election miracle
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
02:00:00 UTC
11:00:00 KST

MADRID — Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez’s chances of staging a poll-defying election comeback have suffered a serious dent.
Spain’s notoriously fragmented far left has failed to unite on a single ticket ahead of November’s election, which many Sánchez supporters had hoped would mobilize voters, capitalize on the country’s electoral system and increase the prime minister’s hopes of forming a new government.
The left-wing disarray leaves Spain’s conservative People’s Party, led by Alberto Núñez Feijóo, on track to claim power after eight years of socialist rule in Madrid, as a broader tilt to the right reshapes European politics.
Advertisement
With negotiations stuttering, an exasperated Mónica García, health minister and candidate for the left-wing Broad Front, warned on social media that the left risked getting “trapped in egos, worries, internal disputes and electoral and/or personal calculations that are good for nobody except the right.”
The Broad Front took shape shortly after the election was called in order to bring together several parties to the left of Sánchez. But after several days of frantic discussions, prominent left-wing party Podemos did not join the united ticket — except in the Canary Islands and the Valencia region — hampering the far left’s overall electoral prospects.
“The only way for [Sánchez] to be able to govern again is for there to be a strong presence to the left of the Socialists,” said Kiko Llaneras, polling analyst for media outlet El País, who pointed out that “the Broad Front isn’t actually that broad.”
He added, “The big question is whether this new movement will be strong enough to allow the left to form a majority — and that’s going to be very difficult.”
Defying the odds
The Broad Front is made up of Sumar, the junior partner in the current Socialist-led government; the Catalan Comuns; the communist-led United Left (IU); Más Madrid; and an array of regional left-wing parties. The lead candidate of the ticket will be Ada Colau, the former mayor of Barcelona.
Spain’s electoral system rewards united platforms, and the Broad Front is not as inclusive as a similar alliance — created in 2023 and including Podemos — which helped Sánchez defy the odds and form a new administration after the last election.
Advertisement
Sumar, the dominant force in the 2026 alliance, has seen its vote share more than halved since 2023 to 5%, according to POLITICO’s Poll of Polls.
“Junior partners in any coalition tend to suffer because it’s difficult for them to implement their agenda and they tend to be less visible,” said Pablo Simón, a political scientist at Madrid’s Carlos III University.
Sumar has been lacking a high-profile figurehead. Yolanda Díaz, the labor minister and deputy prime minister who was once touted as a potential prime minister-in-waiting, is not running in the election.
Ada Colau prepares to cast her ballot during local and regional elections in Barcelona, Spain on May 28, 2023. | Pau Barrena/AFP via Getty Images
The Broad Front ticket, Simón said, “is better than if there had been no agreement at all, but it’s still looking tough for them.”
Amid a last-minute scramble leading up to Friday’s midnight deadline for the registration of electoral alliances, hopes that Podemos, polling at around 3%, might join the ticket were dashed as talks ran aground over candidacies and the left-wing party’s concerns about being subsumed by the alliance.
Speaking the next day, Colau apologized to voters on the left for the lack of a deal with Podemos and, referring to the fraught negotiations, said that “if someone doesn’t want to sit down at a table, you can’t force them.”
Advertisement
‘We have failed’
Sánchez is banking on a solid performance by his socialists and a resurgence by Sumar and its fellow parties to prevent what most polls suggest is a virtual inevitability: The People’s Party forming a coalition government with the far-right Vox, which has enjoyed a surge thanks to its aggressive stance on immigration.
But there was further disappointment on the left last week — beyond Podemos not appearing in the Broad Front — when hopes of an even wider ticket were dashed.
Gabriel Rufián, the charismatic parliamentary spokesperson for the Catalan Republican Left (ERC), had led a debate in recent months on the need for unprecedented unity on the left going into the next election in order to prevent the far right from entering government. The prospect of Rufián, who has a strong appeal outside Catalonia, leading a joint ticket had stirred excitement among voters.
However, restricted by his own pro-independence ERC, Rufián said he would be running only for that party, ruling him out of involvement in the kind of ambitious, nationwide ticket he had raised hopes of leading.
“We have failed and, specifically, I have failed,” he said.
Juan Carlos Monedero, a co-founder of Podemos and former senior figure in the party, told POLITICO that “there is no one who has the authority to make a success of [a united left]. Rufián flirted with it, but in the end his loyalty to ERC was more important.”
Advertisement
Polling analyst Llaneras said that, as well as potentially mobilizing voters, greater unity would have provided a boost to the parties to the left of the socialists because of the country’s electoral framework.
“When it comes to converting votes into seats in Spain it’s very hard to do that with less than 10% of the vote,” he said. “Because the electoral districts in Spain are small, dividing the vote means losing a lot of representation. In districts where there are six or seven seats, you can miss out on all of them.”

Saudi Arabia postpones ‘Davos in the Desert’ summit to 2027 after deadly attacks
The flagship event was scheduled for October 26 to 29, but the kingdom has faced repeated missile and drone strikes from Yemen’s Houthis
Saudi Arabia has decided to postpone its flagship investment conference until next year, organisers confirmed in a statement on Monday, following deadly attacks which rocked the kingdom in recent weeks as the Middle East conflict widens, disrupting business.
The Future Investment Initiative, or FII, was planned for October 26 to 29, but will now take place in 2027, with a new date to be announced “very soon,” the organisers said. Reuters reported earlier Monday that the in-person event had been scrapped and organisers were weighing postponing the event.
The conference, set for its 10th edition, has become a must-attend event for some of the world’s top financiers. Informally dubbed “Davos in the Desert”, in a nod to the World Economic Forum’s annual meeting in Switzerland, the state-backed annual event has showcased the kingdom’s ambitious investment plans in a bid to attract billions of dollars needed to fund its economic transformation away from hydrocarbons towards tourism, sports and technology.
Expected speakers for this year’s event included Goldman Sachs CEO and Chairman David Solomon, Standard Chartered CEO Bill Winters and Citi’s CEO Jane Fraser, according to a draft programme.

The human cost of surging US air strikes in Somalia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
01:52:32 UTC
10:52:32 KST

The human cost of surging US air strikes in Somalia
Families recount deaths, injuries and displacement as Trump accelerates US strikes against armed groups in Somalia.
Mogadishu, Somalia – Nearly a year after a suspected US strike in southern Somalia left shrapnel embedded in her son’s body, Maryam Haji Abdi Guled still feels compelled to accompany him to school.
She fears another child might push him while playing, disturbing a fragment of metal lodged near his hip. Doctors have warned that removing it could leave him paralysed.
“I hold his hand, take him to school, and I bring him back myself. I watch over him,” she told Al Jazeera.
Her son, Abdiqadir Salah, was seven when he was injured during a November 2025 military offensive involving United States air strikes and Somali ground forces around Jamaame, in Somalia’s southern Jubaland state.
Maryam is among several survivors interviewed by Al Jazeera in recent months who say family members were killed or seriously injured during the offensive. Their accounts describe deaths, displacement, lost livelihoods and injuries that continue to shape their lives.
Their testimonies come as US air operations against armed rebel groups in Somalia have intensified sharply under President Donald Trump.
Public records from the US Africa Command (AFRICOM) listed 84 strikes in Somalia through September 2026, while the New America Foundation, which independently tracks the campaign, documented 88 over the same period.
The US military has acknowledged conducting air strikes in the area on November 14 and 15, 2025. But it disputes allegations that its aircraft caused civilian casualties.
AFRICOM told Al Jazeera it had completed an assessment of reports that US operations killed between 10 and 12 civilians and destroyed homes and businesses in Jamaame. It concluded that the information reviewed did not meet the military’s “more likely than not” threshold for determining that US air strikes had caused the reported harm.
That finding does not establish that US strikes caused no harm. Rather, AFRICOM said the evidence did not establish that US operations were more likely than not to have caused the reported casualties and damage.
Al Jazeera asked whether investigators had spoken to survivors, relatives of those killed, hospital staff, local authorities or other witnesses. AFRICOM did not say whether they had done so.
The command said the assessment could be reopened if new information emerged that might change its findings.
The conclusion contrasts with accounts from families who say they witnessed the bombardment and with independent monitoring reports documenting civilian deaths and mass displacement during the offensive.
For those who lost loved ones or were left caring for seriously injured relatives, whether they will ever obtain justice remains unresolved.
A morning of bombardment
Maryam remembers the morning aircraft appeared over Jamaame. She was preparing breakfast after her children returned from school when they heard a roar overhead. Aircraft had become so common that the family no longer regarded the sound as unusual.
“The aircraft never leave us, night or day, and we have become accustomed to them,” she said.
Her children ran outside towards the noise. Maryam followed, intending to bring them back inside before the family fled. Then a munition struck nearby, followed by another explosion near the front door. More bombardment followed around the house.
Maryam believes the attack on her home was carried out by US drones that had been circling over the town before the bombardment.
Ugaas Ahmed Ugaas Said Ali, a Bimaal clan chief who had been in contact with families affected by the attacks, said the suffering extended far beyond those who had managed to leave Jamaame.
“Maryam is one of the fortunate people who has been able to obtain medical care. There are many injured people left in the town from that offensive who haven’t been able to make it to Mogadishu,” he said.
The costs that remain
Maryam recalled one munition hitting the ground without exploding, while other strikes killed people nearby. Amid the explosions, she became separated from her children. Three of her six children were wounded, including Abdiqadir, who suffered the most serious injuries.
It took her a day and a night to reach medical care in Mogadishu. During the journey, which lasted more than 24 hours, her son bled and struggled with pain.
Her experience was one of several reported during days of fighting in and around Jamaame.
According to Jubaland authorities, Somali government and regional forces, including the US-trained Danab commando unit, launched operations against positions held by the armed group al-Shabab in villages surrounding the town.
The authorities said at least 56 al-Shabab fighters were killed and 20 captured. Al Jazeera could not independently verify those figures.
AFRICOM declined to disclose how many strikes were conducted or which munitions were used, citing operational security.
Witnesses interviewed by Al Jazeera said the bombardment came without warning. Three people – two who said they had lost family members, and another whose home was destroyed – declined to speak on the record, citing concerns about their safety.
Ali said residents were afraid to discuss losses caused by air strikes and government offensives because they feared reprisals.
A monitoring network led by the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) documented 12 civilian deaths during fighting and air strikes around Jamaame between November 16 and 18, 2025.
The figures cover different phases of an offensive involving both air strikes and ground fighting, making it difficult to establish which forces were responsible for individual deaths.
The UNHCR-led network also recorded 22,800 people fleeing Jamaame and surrounding villages between November 16 and 18, describing the displacement as “rapid and widespread”.
It reported damage to shops and storage facilities, restrictions on civilian movement in al-Shabab-controlled areas, and signs of psychological distress among those who had escaped.
For Ali Aden Borrow, a 52-year-old farmer from Jamaame, the offensive devastated his family. He was away from home when he received a telephone call telling him that his wife had been hit.
She was nine months pregnant and trying to gather their children to escape the fighting when debris from what Ali described as an air strike struck her neck. She and her unborn child died.
Their three surviving children, two girls and a boy, eventually went to live with their grandmother. Ali has since moved between villages and Kismayo, Jubaland’s de facto regional capital, searching for work and trying to support them.
The cost of food, transport and other necessities has left him in debt. He said the family had received little outside assistance.
Another farmer, Nuur Ali Nuur, was working his land when his wife was injured during the same period of fighting. He told Al Jazeera that debris from an air strike struck her lower body and right hand, leaving her paralysed from the waist down.
Their youngest daughter, who was still breastfeeding, was also slightly injured. Neighbours helped transport his wife to hospital while Nuur struggled to care for their five children.
He said he could not afford to take her promptly to better-equipped medical facilities and still owed money for her treatment. Even the journey towards Kismayo depended on persuading a driver to accept payment later.
Anna Zahn, the US-based archive lead at Airwars, said the consequences of air strikes could last for years. Injuries were often under-reported in Somalia, where treatment could be costly and prolonged.
“In fact, the medical care that is needed may not even be available because the very same strikes that caused the injuries could’ve damaged the infrastructure needed – roads, cars, hospitals, factories – to provide advanced and sustained medical care,” Zahn said.
Earlier research in Jubaland by the peace organisation PAX documented chronic injuries, lost livelihoods, displacement and psychological trauma following alleged US air strikes. Researchers said they could not establish the target status of those involved in most of the cases examined.
What did the US investigation establish?
Al Jazeera presented AFRICOM with the accounts of Maryam, Ali and Nuur, including the reported deaths of Ali’s pregnant wife and unborn child, the injuries that left Nuur’s wife unable to walk, and the shrapnel wounds suffered by Maryam’s children.
AFRICOM did not provide the underlying evidence supporting its assessment. It said its investigations draw on intelligence and operational reporting, much of which is not publicly available. It also did not say whether investigators had obtained testimony directly from the affected families.
Zahn said some strikes announced by AFRICOM generated no local reporting that researchers could find. In other cases, witnesses described harm that could not be confidently attributed to a particular force.
She added that AFRICOM had largely stopped routinely disclosing the number of fighters killed or injured in individual strike announcements from early 2025, reducing the information available for independent comparison.
AFRICOM has previously revised its findings on civilian casualties in Somalia, acknowledging deaths caused by its operations after initially reporting that no civilians had been harmed.
The command said that when an assessment establishes that US military operations more likely than not caused civilian harm, it considers appropriate and feasible responses, alongside measures intended to prevent similar incidents.
Those responses may include acknowledgement, an apology or compensation, depending on the circumstances. US legislation makes up to $3m available annually for discretionary payments to people killed or injured, or whose property was damaged, during US or coalition military operations.
Decisions also take account of factors including advice from the host government and potential risks associated with distributing payments.
Speaking in Mogadishu in July, AFRICOM commander General Dagvin Anderson said there had been occasions when US forces made mistakes and “provided reparations”. He also said the command investigated all credible reports of civilian harm.
Questions over targeting
On September 13, 2025, AFRICOM carried out a strike near Badhan in northern Somalia that it said killed Omar Abdullahi, a local clan elder travelling as part of a convoy. The command later identified him as an al-Shabab arms dealer.
Puntland’s Criminal Investigation Department subsequently said Abdullahi had no criminal record and was not under investigation.
Somalia’s Defence Ahmed Moallim Fiqi contested the killing in parliament, saying Abdullahi could have been questioned rather than targeted.
AFRICOM told Al Jazeera that its civilian-harm assessment of the strike did not meet the “more likely than not” threshold for attributing civilian harm to US operations.
Asked whether it still considered Abdullahi an al-Shabab arms dealer, what evidence supported that claim and whether the targeting decision had been reviewed, AFRICOM did not directly answer.
AFRICOM distinguishes between deliberate strikes, which are subject to multiple layers of review, and defensive strikes against imminent threats.
AFRICOM’s targeting criteria for deliberate strikes can extend beyond those directly involved in hostilities to include people deemed to provide material support. This raises questions about how such determinations are made and how the criteria affect the risk of civilians being targeted.
The US says its strikes are conducted in coordination with Somalia’s federal government. Somalia’s Defence Ministry did not respond to Al Jazeera’s request for comment.
That cooperation has become increasingly important as Washington expands its air campaign against al-Shabab and the ISIL (ISIS)-affiliated armed group in northern Somalia.
An expanding air war
Zahn said the number of strikes during Trump’s second presidency had nearly reached the total carried out throughout his first term, at roughly four times the rate recorded under former US President Joe Biden.
Airwars data analysed for a separate investigation documented at least 216 civilians killed or wounded in US strikes in Somalia between 2007 and the end of May 2025.
That figure represents only the casualties the organisation was able to document, not an estimate of the full toll. It also predates the offensive around Jamaame.
US air operations in Somalia date back nearly two decades, when Washington began conducting strikes against suspected al-Qaeda-linked fighters in 2007. The campaign has since expanded into sustained military support for Somali forces fighting al-Shabab and, more recently, the ISIL affiliate in Somalia.
Under Trump, the US has loosened restrictions on who can authorise air strikes. The administration’s 2026 “counterterrorism” strategy says greater approval authority was returned to military commanders shortly after Trump took office, reversing the more centralised procedures used under Biden.
Anderson has welcomed the increased operational flexibility, saying it allows faster responses and more rapid air strikes as additional US military assets become available.
Somalia’s President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud also acknowledged the change during an appearance at the Council on Foreign Relations in September 2025.
“During the era of President Trump, it is bigger and much easier than before,” he said of US military support.
US officials argue that al-Shabab remains a direct threat to American interests. During his US Senate nomination process in 2025, Anderson described the group as al-Qaeda’s largest, wealthiest and most lethal affiliate. He said both al-Shabab and Somalia’s ISIL affiliate aspired to attack the United States.
Yet the expansion of US air operations has not eliminated al-Shabab, which has repeatedly regained territory after offensives by Somali and allied forces.
David Sterman, a senior policy analyst at the New America Foundation, said US operations under Trump initially concentrated on the ISIL affiliate in northern Somalia in early 2025, but gradually shifted back towards the south during 2026, historically the main focus of the campaign against al-Shabab.
Ahmed Suleiman Hussein, a national security official, wrote on X in May that government research had found that civilian harm from air strikes could generate grievances that al-Shabab and the ISIL affiliate might exploit for propaganda and recruitment.
Somalia has since adopted a national civilian-protection policy, which Hussein said needed to be consistently incorporated into “counterterrorism” operations.
A family unable to return
For Maryam, the Jamaame offensive has reshaped almost every part of her family’s life. After her children were injured, she initially fled into the countryside, but there was no hospital capable of treating Abdiqadir.
She eventually made the roughly 24-hour journey to Mogadishu, at times carrying him against her body because his injuries left him unable to sit or stand without severe pain.
“He was bleeding in the car and it was a rough road,” she said.
Once in the capital, Maryam moved between hospitals, searching for treatment. Doctors warned that removing the shrapnel lodged near Abdiqadir’s hip could kill him or leave him paralysed, she said.
At several hospitals, she was asked to sign documents absolving medical staff of responsibility if surgery caused further harm.
“I said, ‘No, I will not sign. Bring my son out to me,’” she recalled.
At another hospital, doctors recommended amputating his leg, which she also refused. In September 2026, after a fundraising campaign by the British newspaper The Guardian helped cover his treatment, Abdiqadir underwent surgery in Mogadishu.
Doctors removed two pieces of shrapnel but left another in place because of the risk of paralysis.
“He is currently able to play and move, and we can’t take this risk,” Maryam said.
She has remained in Mogadishu to keep him close to medical care, unable to resume the farming and livestock work that once supported her family in Jamaame.
“I cannot return there now. This child will not get medical care there, and the situation that we fled yesterday is still there, it is even possible that something worse could happen,” she said.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The Army will demolish three piers of the damaged Mingli Bridge in Fuli Township, Hualien County, on Tuesday as part of a combat engineering exercise.
Lieutenant General Chiu Chih-feng (邱之峯), commander of the Hualien Defense Command, recently inspected preparations for the demolition, according to Liberty Times. He urged troops to sharpen their engineering skills through practical training and test their ability to impede enemy movement.
Mingli Bridge connects Fuli and Zhuoxi townships in Hualien County. It was damaged by an earthquake in September 2022 and further affected by Typhoon Haikui the following year, which caused the bridge deck to sink.
The Hualien County Government has allocated approximately NT$350 million (US$10.75 million) to rebuild the bridge, per Liberty Times. The old structure must first be dismantled.
The Army will demolish three of the bridge’s seven piers on Tuesday morning. Traffic and access to surrounding areas will be restricted from 9:30 a.m. to 10:30 a.m., Liberty Times reported. The riverbed within 300 meters of the bridge will also be a restricted area.
The Army has conducted two bridge demolition exercises this year. The first took place at Shanjin Bridge in Yunlin County in March, though some results fell short of expectations. On Sept. 22, the Army’s 53rd Engineer Group demolished Xizhou No. 3 Bridge in Yuanshan Township, Yilan County.

Car allegedly did U-turn and struck Helen Haines twice with bystanders rushing to help MP

The man accused of attacking Helen Haines allegedly made a U-turn before ramming the independent MP twice in an alleged targeted attack near her electorate office, causing her to lose one of her legs.
The member for Indi was airlifted from Wangaratta in northern Victoria to Melbourne’s Alfred hospital for emergency surgery on Monday night.

A 43-year-old Tarrawingee man alleged to have driven the Toyota LandCruiser was arrested at the scene. The alleged attacker has been named as Brendan Nugent, Guardian Australia has confirmed.
Police were expected to interview the suspect on Tuesday, Acting Supt Ashley Mason said.
Anthony Albanese confirmed authorities believed the attack was deliberate.
“Helen Haines represents the best of our political representatives,” the prime minister said on Tuesday afternoon.
“Kind, compassionate, a person of integrity, totally committed to strongly representing the people of that beautiful part of Victoria.”
Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter here
The home affairs minister, Tony Burke, said witnesses alleged the driver completed a U-turn before the incident.
“What witnesses have described is the driver doing a U-turn to get into the car park and to ram Helen against a vehicle, then to reverse and do it a second time,” he told ABC radio.
“A bystander ran towards the scene, got the driver out of the vehicle and held the driver until police arrived.”
Ricky Jefferies, whose barbershop is next door to Haines’ office, ran from his shop to help after hearing the crash.
“I had no choice but to take him out of the car because it was the right and safest thing to do,” he told reporters on Tuesday morning.
Jefferies, who returned to work on Tuesday morning, alleged the driver had a knife on him. “He didn’t pull it out,” he said. “Basically just … took it out of his pocket and threw it away.”
Burke said: “I think every Australian is grateful for those moments when a hero like this runs towards the most dangerous place.”
The home affairs minister said the nation’s security agencies and police would be working through what more could have been done to prevent the alleged attack and to help keep others safe.
On Monday, Burke reported that there had been 1,067 reports of harassment or threats against high office holders in Australia in the last financial year, an increase from 951 the year before.
“We already knew that we needed to do more to be able to keep people in public office safe and we have been,” he said.
“While we don’t make public the dollar figures and the exact provision of security for obvious reasons … we had a very significant uplift in the budget.
“There is a direct line between the temperature of debate and things willing people will say, and then when people are willing to take action.”
Albanese has been joined by leaders and parliamentarians from across the country in calling for a calming of political discourse.
The mayor of Wangaratta, Irene Grant, expressed gratitude to Jefferies for stepping in to stop the man.
“I spoke to the barber this morning and he just shrugged his shoulders. He seemed to just take it in his stride. This was something that he had to do and he did it,” she said.
“He was extraordinarily modest about the very brave action that he took yesterday … he did an amazing job.”
Wangaratta, the rural city in which the incident occurred, is a tightknit community in north-east Victoria. At the last census it had a population of about 20,000 people, while the broader local government area had just under 30,000.
Haines was elected to federal parliament in 2019 and has been key to the establishment of the National Anti-Corruption Commission, as well as campaigning for rural health services, telecommunications access and pushing back on misuse of taxpayer funds, or pork barrelling.

Beyond money: Why young Tunisians are considering emigration
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
01:47:42 UTC
10:47:42 KST

Beyond money: Why young Tunisians are considering emigration
For many young Tunisians, the question is no longer simply how to make a living, but where they can build a future.
Tunis, Tunisia – For Maher Qassem, the phrase “beyond money” sums up why he is considering leaving his country.
After years of working in the media and trying to secure a stable life for his family, he is now thinking of starting over abroad. Buying a home and planning for a better future have given way to more immediate concerns: covering monthly expenses and meeting mounting financial commitments.
Speaking to Al Jazeera, Qassem says almost his entire salary goes towards loan repayments, rent and his son’s education. At times, he adds, he has been unable to help his sick mother pay for medication and treatment.
Qassem is among many young Tunisians who see little meaningful change in their daily lives. Seven years into President Kais Saied’s rule, he worries about his son’s prospects and the quality of life the country can offer future generations.
Others, however, continue to trust the president.
Tunisians remain divided between those who believe the past several years have failed to deliver the change they hoped for and those who still believe reform is possible. These contrasting views unfold against a backdrop of persistent economic difficulties.
No change
Ghaith remembers the excitement surrounding the 2019 presidential election and the expectations raised by Saied’s victory. He was 19 at the time, had little interest in politics, and did not vote. But he recalls the hope that accompanied the president’s election.
Seven years later, Ghaith says, little has changed in his own life.
The cost-of-living pressures that existed then remain, he tells Al Jazeera, while ordinary citizens continue to face recurring difficulties obtaining some essential goods and services.
He is also frustrated by the authorities’ communication with the public. Tunisians want clearer answers about government policies and the results they are expected to deliver, he says. They also want accountability and a clear vision for the future.
For Qassem, the reasons for leaving extend beyond economic hardship. He believes working as a journalist has become more difficult, too.
Not everyone has lost faith in the president.
Mohamed Amine, a taxi driver in his 30s, voted for Saied in the most recent presidential election and remains convinced that he can improve the country’s situation.
The president is “sincere in his intentions” and wants change, Amine tells Al Jazeera. He believes, however, that various obstacles have hindered Saied’s reform programme.
It is too early to judge the outcome, he says. The president should be given more time.
Unemployment and emigration
Unemployment, particularly among young people and university graduates, remains a major challenge in Tunisia.
According to the National Institute of Statistics, the unemployment rate stood at 14.9 percent in the second quarter of 2026, with approximately 622,000 people out of work.
The situation is more severe among younger Tunisians. Unemployment among people aged 15 to 24 reached 35.4 percent, while the rate among university graduates stood at 26.6 percent. Among female university graduates, it was 35.6 percent, compared with 14.2 percent among men.
The desire to leave is widespread. A study by Afrobarometer, an independent African research network that conducts public-opinion surveys across the continent, found that around two-thirds of young Tunisians had considered emigrating.
The proportion who said they thought about leaving “a lot” rose from 38 percent in 2018 to 51 percent in 2024. Among young people considering emigration, 59 percent cited better job opportunities as their main motivation.
The findings point to frustration among a section of Tunisia’s youth and growing concerns about the prospects for professional and social stability at home.
The loss of skilled workers
The desire to leave extends beyond young people seeking their first jobs. Tunisia is also losing qualified professionals trained in the country.
Kamel Sahnoun, head of the Tunisian Order of Engineers, said at a press conference organised by the professional body that approximately 6,500 engineers left Tunisia in 2022 alone. The figure compares with an annual average of about 3,000 in 2013 and 2014, highlighting the scale of the departure of skilled workers.
The healthcare sector is also losing professionals.
Figures from the Tunisian Agency for Technical Cooperation show that 1,839 healthcare and paramedical professionals were recruited to work abroad in 2023. Another 1,022 were recruited during the first nine months of 2024, followed by 1,244 in 2025.
The figures, alongside international demand for Tunisian expertise, reflect the search for better working and living conditions abroad.
Beyond the economy
Hamza, a 26-year-old software engineer working for a foreign company, earns what he describes as a good income. Yet he is seriously considering leaving Tunisia.
“It’s no longer just about money,” he tells Al Jazeera.
His decision is shaped by several factors, including his lifestyle, his dealings with the administration, uncertainty about the future and the country’s broader economic situation.
Ramadan Ben Omar, a researcher specialising in migration, says the reasons people leave Tunisia have become more complex.
The motivations are no longer purely economic, he tells Al Jazeera. They also include the search for greater freedom, opportunities to participate in public life and the chance to build a better future.
Increasingly, he says, young people see emigration as a life project in its own right, rather than simply a way to improve their income.
Ben Omar also points to border areas such as Ben Guerdane, where accumulated economic and social pressures have prompted more young people to consider leaving through regular or irregular migration routes.
The question of the future
Maher has packed his bags for a new beginning in France. Hamza is weighing the decision despite his professional success. Ghaith is disappointed after years of waiting, while Mohamed Amine continues to believe in the possibility of reform.
Their contrasting experiences reflect a country grappling with economic difficulties and political uncertainty. For some, the prospect of a better life lies abroad; for others, hope for change at home remains.
The question facing Tunisia is whether it can offer its young people enough reason to stay.

CANBERRA, Oct. 20 (Xinhua) -- More than 1 million Australians have accessed free health advice through the federal government's 1800MEDICARE service since its launch 10 months ago, Minister for Health and Ageing Mark Butler said on Tuesday.
The service, which provides round-the-clock health advice by phone and digital platforms, aims to ease pressure on hospital emergency departments and improve access to healthcare across Australia.
According to a government statement, one in 10 callers were diverted from visiting an emergency department or calling emergency services, while another one in 10 were referred to urgent care services.
Nearly 60,000 callers received free virtual consultations with general practitioners, while one in five callers were from rural and remote areas.
New South Wales recorded the highest number of calls at over 471,000, followed by Victoria with more than 352,000 and Western Australia with over 133,000.
Butler said more than 170,000 people had been diverted from busy emergency departments or emergency calls through the service.
The Australian government has invested more than 200 million Australian dollars (about 141 million U.S. dollars) in 1800MEDICARE to expand access to urgent and after-hours healthcare.
The service allows Australians to speak with registered nurses and access further medical care, including after-hours telehealth consultations, when needed. ■

Japan launches H3 rocket carrying Mars moon sample-return probe
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
09:45:40 CST
10:45:40 KST

TOKYO, Oct. 20 (Xinhua) -- Japan launched an H3 rocket carrying a spacecraft to explore a moon of Mars early Tuesday, beginning a five-year sample-return mission, according to the country's space agency.
The Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA) launched the unmanned Martian Moons eXploration (MMX) spacecraft aboard H3 rocket No. 10 at 4:41 a.m. local time from the Tanegashima Space Center in southwestern Japan.
The flagship rocket released the spacecraft approximately 71 minutes after liftoff, placing it onto a trajectory toward Mars.
The MMX spacecraft is designed to land on Phobos, the larger and closer of Mars' two moons, collect at least 10 grams of surface material and return the samples to Earth, according to JAXA.
The spacecraft is expected to reach the Martian system in 2027 and conduct detailed observations of Phobos, including from a quasi-satellite orbit. It will also observe Deimos, Mars' other moon, during the mission.
The mission includes deploying a small rover named Idefix to explore Phobos' surface and support the landing and sampling operations.
JAXA aims to return the samples to Earth in 2031, potentially providing new insights into the origin of Mars' moons and the evolution of the Martian system. ■

Jury members evaluate entries for TOI’s Ideas for India contest in Delhi
NEW DELHI: Three separate juries evaluated entries in the three categories for the award and the panel members acknowledged at the end of the day that the quality of applicants was excellent. In each of the categories, bulk of those shortlisted for evaluation by the jury were very young, either still in college or just out of it, though there were some older innovators too.Over 14,000 applications were received, which were filtered down by Techgig to 1,000 and Grant Thornton shortlisted it to 35 finalists that were split between three juries. While first was on sovereign technology for India handled 14 entries, second on Inclusive Innovation for Bharat met a dozen applications and third on Sustainable & Resilient India dealt with nine entries.
-
The juries followed a pattern of a short presentation by the applicants, followed by questions from jury members and then a brief discussion between the members before scoring the applicant. Several jury members admitted that they were pleasantly surprised by how well thought through the presentations were, especially given the age of most applicants.Even where some aspect of the road to implementation may have not occurred to the applicants — say, a compliance issue or consent to be obtained — it was striking how eager the innovators were to learn from the experience of those who had worked in the real world for decades and knew what it takes to translate brilliant ideas into real solutions.
The maturity to take hard questions as essential inputs rather than as harsh criticism was quite remarkable.
Ideas For India
The diversity of the presentations was also a striking aspect. In the technology sovereignty category, for instance, the ideas ranged from closing a felt gap in middle sized drones to faster and more efficient identification and countering of cyberattacks to dealing with ships that go ‘dark’, which may not always be for innocent reasons.
But these were not just ideas. The drone entry had already done some testing in the field with army units, the dark ships idea had been explored with a port and so on.Such was the overall quality of the applicants that at least in two categories some of the jury members voiced the opinion that perhaps the awards need not be restricted to two in each category. There was, after all, no compulsion to stick to a bell curve, they pointed out. Most left the venue feeling satisfied that they had done their bit to encourage a cohort whose innovative mindset was matched by its enthusiasm to do good for society and for India.

Participants included representatives of ethnocultural organizations, government institutions, civil society, diplomatic missions and international partners.
Moldovan President Maia Sandu also attended the event. She emphasized the importance of mutual respect, social cohesion and the preservation of cultural diversity.
The main topics included preserving cultural and linguistic identity, strengthening public trust and the country’s European future. Participants discussed equal opportunities for different communities to participate in public life, access to education and information, and language rights. Particular attention was paid to the practical implementation of minority rights. As Moldova moves closer to EU membership, it is important not only to declare equality and non-discrimination but also to create conditions in which people can exercise their rights and participate in decision-making.
Participants also discussed the 2017–2027 Strategy for Strengthening Interethnic Relations, reviewing progress made, existing gaps and priorities for future policy documents.
Another session focused on information resilience among minorities. Participants stressed the importance of reliable information and media in minority languages, as well as media literacy, support for quality journalism and the ability to distinguish verified facts from manipulation.
The NCUM noted that these issues are also important for Moldova’s Ukrainian community. The different experiences of these groups call for a thoughtful approach. According to the organization, preserving language and identity, ensuring access to education and information, and participating in civic processes are essential to Ukrainians’ full participation in society.

Getting More From Less: Rethinking Structure Through Form
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
01:30:00 UTC
10:30:00 KST

What happens when structure is treated not as something added to architecture, but as something the architecture itself provides?
Throughout architectural history, form has provided structure. Arches, trusses, and other structural geometries used the arrangement of material to achieve strength, often allowing individual elements to serve multiple functions. Today, however, building envelopes often rely on a hierarchy of separate elements: a primary frame carries loads, secondary supports hold panels in place, brackets connect the pieces, and additional layers provide enclosure or finish. Together, these components require added material, weight, fabrication steps, and on-site coordination.
Some of the most significant advances in architecture emerge from eliminating unnecessary or redundant components. Reducing secondary structures, simplifying connections, and assigning multiple functions to individual elements can result in more efficient building systems. BŌK Modern approaches these complexities by revisiting that older principle through modern engineering and fabrication: simplifying a system by asking one component to do the work of several. By folding and forming metal to create strength through geometry, their idea remains on looking for opportunities to reduce supporting structure while getting more performance from the material itself.
Related Article
Exploring Façade Cladding Systems in Modern Architecture
In what might be called a self-reinforcing system, geometry, material, connections, and architectural function are designed together. Removing a part can change how the remaining assembly performs, how it is made and installed, and ultimately how the architecture is experienced.
Through the development of contemporary metal envelope systems, reducing redundant components can make assemblies lighter, more adaptable, and easier to install. It can also reduce material consumption, streamline construction, and create opportunities to explore new architectural expressions. The following three BŌK Modern projects show what that looks like in practice.
Moscone Convention Center: Reducing the Supporting Structure
At the Moscone Convention Center, BŌK Modern reconsidered the secondary structure typically required to support large facade systems. A conventional solution would have relied on cantilever field welded steel HSS supports and Z-girts behind the architectural panels. Instead, the practice developed an integrated assembly in which formed aluminum panels took on 68% more structural loading capability than the conventional approach, reducing the required structural steel support behind it by 83%.
The shift toward an integrated assembly affected the project well beyond material quantities. Sections of the facade could be assembled at ground level and lifted into position, reducing work at height and changing the installation sequence. Compared to the conventional cantilever support and Z-girt system, this integrated approach required half the labor. The efficiencies were interconnected: eliminating structural components also reduced the work needed to fabricate, connect, and install them. At Moscone, simplification became not only an aesthetic decision, but a strategy for reducing cost, labor, material, and construction complexity.
1500 Mission: Making the Material Do More
The 1500 Mission Canopy applied the same principle in a different way. Rather than relying on a conventional system of steel trusses, aluminum cladding, and welded connections back to the façade, BŌK Modern employed modular triangular trusses made from formed aluminum sheets. The solution applied one of the simplest structural principles—the truss—through contemporary materials and fabrication technologies. Brake-forming aluminum sheets into triangular panels allowed the geometry of the formed aluminum to give relatively lightweight material the rigidity necessary to support itself and other canopy components.
This shifted the relationship between architecture and structure. The truss was no longer simply a framework hidden behind the architectural surface; the structural logic became part of the metal assembly itself. It also changed how the canopy was constructed. Panels could be installed progressively or assembled into sections and lifted into place, while bolted connections replaced field welds.
According to a project comparison, the approach reduced labor costs by 30% relative to a conventional truss system and resulted in 23% less embodied carbon. The project demonstrated that using less did not mean asking less of the system. By rethinking the geometry of the material, it was possible to get more performance from it.
Bolt-On Balcony: Consolidating the Assembly
BŌK Modern's Bolt-On Balcony applies this simplification strategy to an assembly made up of numerous individual parts. A conventional balcony might require a perimeter frame, joists, wall supports, tie rods, anchor forks, railing posts, front-cladding supports, and a separate finished floor. Instead of accepting each component as necessary, the design examined which of those functions could be combined.
The resulting formed-sheet design incorporates several roles into a single assembly, including the structural floor, finished surface, and patented Plate Truss™ technology. This system creates an integrated truss supported by two vertical attachment points at the facade. Those points connect to existing structural elements, removing the need for steel cantilevers, extensive welding, and the rod-and-fork suspension systems of the conventional approach.
Bolted construction eliminates the need for field welding, avoiding the risk of damaging nearby finishes during the final stages of construction. Its comparatively lightweight design can often be lifted into place with equipment such as a forklift rather than a crane, further simplifying logistics. According to installers familiar with both methods, a single Bolt-On Balcony can be assembled in less than a day, roughly twice the pace of a conventional rod-and-clevis-supported system.
Because this approach allows prefabricated assembly in a controlled shop environment, much of the work can be completed before arriving on site, shifting labor away from field conditions and reducing installation complexity. In this case, simplification comes through consolidation. By designing the floor, structure, connections, and finished architectural surface as parts of a single system, the Bolt-On Balcony reduces the number of separate components—and the operations associated with them—without reducing what the assembly is asked to do.
Moscone, 1500 Mission, and the Bolt-On Balcony addressed different architectural challenges, but each led to a similar question: what can be removed if the remaining elements are designed to do more?
That question shifts simplification away from minimalism for its own sake. Less structure is valuable not simply because there is less of it, but because eliminating unnecessary components can reduce material, connections, fabrication, welding, labor, and coordination while creating a cleaner architectural result. The tools are distinctly contemporary—engineered aluminum, digital modeling, precision forming, and modern fabrication—but the underlying idea is much older. Architecture has long used geometry to extend the capabilities of material. BŌK Modern's approach brings that principle into contemporary metal systems: simplify the assembly, use form to create performance, and get more from every piece that remains.

Japan launches mission to explore Mars' moons and bring back samples
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
01:29:41 UTC
10:29:41 KST

Japan launches mission to explore Mars' moons and bring back samples
Japan launched a spacecraft on Tuesday on a five-year mission to explore Mars' mysterious moons, Phobos and Deimos, and bring back samples for the first time. The $578 million project aims to deliver dust, soil and rocks to Earth in 2031, potentially shedding light on how the moons formed and the origins of life.
A Japanese spacecraft rocketed towards Mars on Tuesday on an unprecedented quest to explore its mysterious moons and bring back samples.
Five of the world’s space agencies joined forces for the five-year mission that will attempt to land a robotic prospector plus a rover on Phobos, the larger and closer of Mars’ two pint-sized moons.
The Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency, which is leading the bold sampling effort, launched the spacecraft before dawn from the country's main spaceport on Tanegashima Island. Officials declared success an hour later when the spacecraft separated as planned from the rocket's upper stage. Flight controllers burst into applause and jumped to their feet, shaking hands and embracing.
While NASA has successfully landed nine spacecraft on Mars over the past 50 years and China scored a 2021 touchdown, no one has ever ventured onto Phobos or its sidekick Deimos. And no one has managed to fetch samples from Mars, let alone its moons.
If successful, bits of dust, soil and rocks from Phobos will arrive on Earth in 2031.
“There’s a lot of adrenaline and a lot of excitement and a lot of wow,” said NASA astrophysicist Tom Statler, who’s involved with the project.
Read moreFrench, US and Russian astronauts return to Earth after eight months in space
Japan has an edge going in, with two asteroid sample returns already under its cosmic belt.
Phobos is a lumpy, potato-shaped rock just 14 miles (22 kilometres) or so across. Examining pieces of it can explain how Mars’ moons – and possibly moons elsewhere – came to be.
Dubbed MMX for Martian Moons Exploration, the $578 million mission features a hefty 5-tonne spacecraft that should reach Mars by late next summer. It will sync up with Phobos’ tight orbit around the red planet, before ejecting the French-German rover that’s named Idefix after the white terrier in the Asterix comics.
No bigger than a microwave oven, Idefix will plop onto Phobos by itself, bouncing for several minutes before coming to a halt in the moon's extraordinarily low gravity.
The four-wheeled rover is designed to right itself if it lands upside down. All bets are off, though, if it sinks into soft soil or gets wedged between rocks, said the French Space Agency’s Julien Baroukh. Once the rover’s solar panels are deployed, the vehicle can no longer right itself, he added, which is why it will move at a glacial 1 millimetre per second (0.04 inches per second).
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
Idefix will serve as a “scout for safety,” according to Baroukh, as it prowls around Phobos for 100 days. Japanese flight controllers want to avoid powdery soil and rough terrain when the mothership – a four-legged stationary lander – descends to the surface to gather samples in late 2028 or 2029.
The lander will spend just two hours on Phobos, drilling and vacuuming up at least one-third of an ounce (10 grams) of material, before launching back into space. It will study Deimos during a series of flybys before leaving the Martian neighbourhood in 2030 and hustling back to Earth for a 2031 sample delivery in the Australian desert.
It’s a treacherous undertaking, with wreckage littering the path.
Read moreNASA finds a 'once in a century' lunar crater, bigger than the Roman Colosseum
The moons’ names aren’t exactly comforting: Phobos is Greek for fear and Deimos means dread. They’re the twin sons of the god of war Ares – Mars in Roman mythology.
Russia stumbled in all three of its Phobos attempts as well as many other Mars endeavours. In its only other Mars mission, Japan failed to get a spacecraft into orbit around the red planet. Even NASA has had its share of flops in a bid to answer the burning question: Did life ever exist on Mars?
By studying Mars’ moons, scientists hope to learn whether Phobos and Deimos formed in the aftermath of an ancient collision between Mars and a battering space rock. It’s also possible that the moons might be stray asteroids that became ensnared in Mars’ gravity.
Read more'All human emotions': French astronaut Sophie Adenot returns to Earth
Either way, scientists anticipate finding traces of Mars on Phobos, making the samples an irresistible two-for-one that should help demystify planetary and moon formation, and perhaps even the recipe for life. The findings will help shape future Mars missions – including those by astronauts – said NASA’s acting planetary science director Lindsay Hays.
“It is a once-in-a-lifetime chance. We are part of the first sample return mission from the Martian system,” said the German Space Agency's rover chief Markus Grebenstein.
Japan isn’t the only one looking to claim the scientific riches packed into the Martian system’s rocks and dirt. China plans to launch a sample return mission to Mars in 2028, while NASA is still debating how to retrieve the more than 30 sample tubes collected by the Perseverance Mars rover, the new champion for off-Earth driving.
Japan and China could be neck-and-neck in getting samples back from the Martian system. Both are targeting 2031.
Japan is investing $350 million in this mission. NASA is contributing $87 million, the French Space Agency about $68 million, the German Space Agency about $56 million and the European Space Agency some $17 million.
(FRANCE 24 with AP)

Israel revokes visa of French journalist tasked with covering election
Israel's Population and Immigration Authority canceled last week an entry visa issued to Sylvain Mercadier, a journalist for the L'Humanité daily newspaper, which is affiliated with the French Communist Party. The visa was revoked days after it was issued by Israel.
In a statement, the outlet said that Mercadier was meant to cover Israel's election, and that this is the first time in the paper's 122-year history that a reporter was barred from entering a country. The statement added that Israel provided no justification for the decision, and that requests for an explanation "have gone unanswered."
The Population and Immigration Authority did not respond to Haaretz's request for comment.
Mercadier is the fourth foreign correspondent who has been barred from entering Israel in the past week.
Election workers say they weren’t told to enforce court ban on voter-tracking apps
Many Israeli election poll workers responsible for ensuring the integrity of the vote were not instructed to enforce a court ban on voter-tracking apps such as Elector, according to interviews with poll workers. The apps, widely used by Likud, Shas and United Torah Judaism, allow parties to track who turns out to vote in real time and take steps to boost turnout.
The Central Elections Committee said its training materials for poll workers did not include the ban because they were printed before the Supreme Court ruling last month, which found that the use of voter-tracking apps violated privacy rights.
The committee said the ruling was emphasized in in-person training sessions, but many poll workers told Haaretz they had not received such instruction.
The High Court of Justice overturned last month a Central Elections Committee decision to allow the real-time transfer of voter information from polling stations, ruling that such data cannot be shared even through popular voter-tracking apps.
Explained: How do Israeli elections work?
There are 120 seats in Israel's Knesset, and voters choose a party rather than an individual candidate. To govern with a majority, a party must receive at least 61 seats.
To enter the Knesset, a party must pass an electoral threshold of 3.25 percent of all valid votes cast. Votes for parties that fail to meet the threshold are discarded when seats are allocated.
If a single party fails to win 61 seats, a coalition must be formed. No party has ever won an outright majority in Israel's history: The most seats ever held by a single party was in 1969, when Golda Meir's center-left Alignment party won 56 seats, with over 46 percent of the vote.
Following the election, Israel's president meets with members of the Knesset who recommend a party leader to form a coalition. The president then gives a mandate to the leader who can most likely create a coalition of at least 61 seats.
The designated candidate has 28 days to form a government, with a possible extension. If no coalition emerges, the mandate may pass to another lawmaker or the Knesset may dissolve, triggering another election.
Don't dismiss Gantz's last-minute exit: Even a handful of votes can change history | Analysis
In 1996, when Israel was experimenting with directly electing the prime minister, Shimon Peres lost to Benjamin Netanyahu by 14,000 votes. In the 2019 election, The Hayamin Hehadash party headed by Naftali Bennett and Ayelet Shaked fell short of making it into the Knesset by 1,450 votes. In November 2022, Meretz was left out of the Knesset due to 4,000 missing votes, and Israel embarked on the bloodiest and most horrific four years in its history.
A few thousand votes, a fraction of a percent of the total vote, can change history. It can definitively destroy a wounded country or breathe new life into it and save it from ruin.
Consequently, nobody should make light of Benny Gantz's decision to withdraw from the race. Even if he did so belatedly, it's good that he is gone. The votes that, according to the polls, would have gone to his Kahol Lavan party – anywhere from thousands to tens of thousands (between 0.7 and 1.4 percent of the expected total vote) – could play a critical role in the election, which currently seems to be a tight race.
Hegseth meets Netanyahu in unannounced visit to Israel, Axios reports
Exactly a week away from the Israeli Knesset election, U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth made an unannounced visit to Israel on Monday, during which he met with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, Axios reported, citing two sources with knowledge.
Reuters could not immediately confirm the meeting, but Hegseth said in a social media post that he had visited U.S. service members in the Central Command area of responsibility, which covers the Middle East, northeast Africa and parts of Asia.
The Pentagon and Israel's embassy in Washington did not immediately respond to requests for comment. According to the report, the visit comes against the backdrop of discussions between the two countries regarding the possibility of resuming the war against Iran.
News of Hegseth's trip also comes a day after U.S. President Donald Trump endorsed Netanyahu in next week's parliamentary election in Israel - its first vote since the Hamas attack on October 7, 2023, that shook the country and plunged the Middle East into turmoil, as Israel went to war in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran.
U.S. Vice President JD Vance, however, declined to endorse Netanyahu in an interview earlier on Monday, saying he was not getting involved in Israeli elections.
"I endorse American candidates, and that's where I'm focused on is the midterms," Vance, who traveled to Budapest and endorsed Viktor Orban in Hungarian election earlier this year, said in an interview with digital media outlet 2WAY.
"I'm not anti-endorsing him, but I'm not pro-endorsing him, I'm not getting involved in Israeli elections." Vance said.
Q: Trump endorsed Netanyahu. Do you endorse Netanyahu? JD Vance: I endorse American candidates. I'm not getting involved in Israeli elections.

Political hate speech can have real-world fallout. After the alleged attack on Helen Haines, our leaders must act | Paul Daley
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
01:18:28 UTC
10:18:28 KST

If the increasingly vituperative tenor of our public discourse, online and verbal, has fully trailed America’s into the murky dungeon of political violence with the appalling alleged attack on Helen Haines, Australia’s political class has only itself to blame.
Amid outpourings of concern from across the political spectrum (including from people who have fostered considerable vicious personal animus online and in the parliament) for the gravely injured and much-respected member for Indi, it is blindingly evident that the political square has long been utterly incapable of self-regulation.
There are no consequences for the abuse hurled across the chambers by Australia’s elected representatives beyond brief parliamentary suspension amid the invariably blokey guffaws. There are no consequences for political operatives here – students of the US experts of weaponising political hatred – who pursue their opponents and critics online with the most vicious, cruel and offensive personal attacks, sometimes under the purported guise of humour.
The ongoing traditional political race-call, for all of its marketability of conflict, meanwhile, reports both the anguish of the attack targets and the dismissive calls for them to effectively harden TF up. It’s just a bit of a joke, don’t you know, snowflakes? All’s fair in the tinderbox of politics. It’s not for the faint-hearted, after all.
Do the worst public excesses of personal invective by elected representatives seep into the broader community and license them to do the same? Undoubtedly. But do they transmogrify into actual political violence?
What has happened to Haines is still being investigated but has of course given elected representatives pause to stop and think. The question is, how will they act to change things?
The last fortnight or so in Australian politics is a particular a case in point – a burning example of the need to “turn the temperature down” in line with the prime minister’s repeated entreaties to parliamentary colleagues.
There have been verbal evocations of violence (of public execution) in the House of Representatives (defended by senior mainstream politicians) and (of a murder fantasy) at a major conference of purportedly “conservative’’ leading thinkers.
Social media echo and amplify the worst excesses of what passes for public/political discourse. It also too often contorts it into ideations and outright threats of violence against politicians and sometimes their staff, too often gendered and sexual. Security authorities have been consistently warning about the increasing threats to MPs, especially women.
Meanwhile media – old and new – have their own onerous responsibilities in this increasingly polarised space. Too many outlets are far from immune to picking sides and fomenting polarisation, given the marketability of political hate and division that drives the internet in times of news media convergence.
The federal government has shown a world-leading willingness to take on the major tech companies (albeit with limited efficacy, perhaps) to protect children from the worst excesses of social media. But is there a willingness to take on the same powerful forces to curb the no-less-insidious pervasion of political hate speech, whether from the elected or the hordes of nameless trolls and bot-factories swamping the online world?
The extremities of left and right will converge where there is any real – or perceived – threat to what passes as political speech freedom but too often lands into the purview of hate and violent threat.
Regardless of whether the hate speech which evokes or potentially spurs violence emanates from the extreme left or right – it is virulently pervasive in both – now is not the time for inertia.
Actions speak louder than words. And in coming weeks and days there will be a lot of words spoken by politicians about the tragic violence inflicted on perhaps federal parliament’s most respected and loved lower house member.
In times of crisis our federal and some state parliaments do national introspection well. But too often nothing comes of it. Now, amid all the calls for determined countermeasures to the hate and evocations of violence that have inveigled almost every medium of our body politic, it is time for leaders to act.
It’s impossible to legislate tolerance and kindness – although that is what’s needed most right now as more and more heat, more opinions and more anger flood the national discourse in the wake of this national tragedy.
If Haines’ terrible experience represents the moment of “national reckoning’’ that our political class and media insist it is, then it’s truly time for the paradigm shift to redemptive action.

Former UN torture expert accuses colleagues of ignoring Hamas sexual violence on October 7
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
01:15:30 UTC
10:15:30 KST

Alice Jill Edwards, who served as the UN special rapporteur on torture from August 2022 to July 2026, has sharply criticized her colleagues at the organization. In a personal opinion column published Monday in Britain's Daily Telegraph, she accuses them of an obsessive focus on one side of the Gaza conflict, undermining the UN's credibility in the process.
Edwards describes her visit to Kibbutz Kfar Aza, about 14 months after the October 7 massacre, as one of the most difficult moments of her tenure. Mandy Damari and Simona Steinbrecher, the mothers of hostages Emily Damari and Doron Steinbrecher, guided her through their daughters' destroyed homes, where bullets had struck everyday objects, including a microwave and refrigerator. 
"I had a knot in my stomach as the desperate mothers of the two young women taken hostage led me through the shattered glass and rubble of their daughters’ modest, small single-floor houses," she wrote.
UN officials failed to document sexual violence
The visit led Edwards to conclude that hostage-taking should be recognized as a form of torture: "I tried to remind myself that I needed to avoid feeling too emotional. After all, I was a neutral observer – the role each United Nations special rapporteur is supposed to fulfill. Yet the suffering of these mothers made me realize that we must consider hostage-taking as a form of torture."
She argues that the victims also include the hostages' family members, who are forced to endure agonizing uncertainty over the fate of their loved ones and consequently suffer psychological torture. She adds that videos released by Hamas, including one showing hostage Evyatar David digging what appeared to be his own grave while speaking Hebrew, were intended to pressure Israel through the hostages' families, constituting another form of torture.
Edwards said that families and released hostages felt the UN had not done enough for them. She criticizes Francesca Albanese, the UN special rapporteur on the occupied Palestinian territories, and Reem Alsalem, the special rapporteur on violence against women, who "never formally documented these horrors, despite the growing body of evidence which to most of us is indisputable, but which they dispute."
According to Edwards, the two continued publishing reports she characterizes as one-sided and hateful, while offering explanations for their failure to address the issue that she found difficult to justify. Alsalem cited Israel's refusal to grant her entry and access as the reason she could not expand her investigation. Edwards argues that even after the hostages were released, neither official gave sufficient weight to their testimony about the torture and deprivation they had endured.
When Edwards published a report on the events of October 7, including the massacre of more than 370 young people at the Nova music festival, only one other special rapporteur agreed to sign it. Others refused, and some attempted to have material removed from the report. She said one of the significant achievements of her tenure, stemming largely from her visit to the kibbutz, was a UN General Assembly resolution requiring countries to define hostage-taking as a form of torture.
"But I feel strongly that during the Gaza-Israel war, the UN has been doing itself no favors by obsessively focusing on only one set of abuses – especially as neutrality, independence and impartiality are the cornerstones of a trustworthy UN," she wrote.
'No pro-Israel bias'
Edwards stresses that she was not influenced by pro-Israel bias. In her previous role as chief legal adviser to the UN High Commissioner for Refugees, she defended Palestinians against discrimination and heard testimony concerning Israeli violations. She drafted the UN's position on Palestinian refugees and led proceedings before Europe's highest court to protect them. This year, she published a second, detailed report on the mistreatment of prisoners in Israeli jails.
Edwards also describes a series of systemic failures within the UN, including an extremely limited budget, unpaid positions, excessive workloads and funding from individual countries. According to Edwards, the budget provides enough money for only one assistant and one field mission per year. She paid for her own trip to Israel and the Palestinian territories.
Edwards also raises concerns about the ability of individual countries or groups of countries to fund specific rapporteurs. Such funding, she said, could be an innocent gift or an attempt to exert influence, but at the very least it creates suspicions of political interference. Lawyers representing victims are reluctant to share confidential information with rapporteurs funded by governments accused of committing abuses.
Edwards argues that the solution would be to channel all contributions into a single central budget and distribute the money equally among rapporteurs. "However, despite these problems, and many others, there appears little appetite to fix the system – not even by the UN secretary-general, Antonio Guterres, (who, incidentally, was my former boss as UN High Commissioner for Refugees)," she wrote.
Guterres recently said in an interview that the rapporteurs were independent and that many were therefore beyond his control. "Independence is both the strength and the vulnerability of these positions, but when misused to dogmatically pursue political agendas, the UN as a whole is weakened," Edwards wrote.
Edwards sees the contest to select the next UN secretary-general as an opportunity for change. "With more wars today than at any time since the organization’s founding in 1945, the next secretary-general needs to take a more decisive role and exercise a greater amount of the power that is actually at his or her disposal.
"Guterres has in my view failed to carry out the original mandate of the UN – to step in efficiently and fairly as a mediator to dampen down international conflicts. While the blame for today’s wars can’t be laid at his feet, it’s disappointing that he has adopted a rather fatalistic posture – as though he has no sway other than to convene meeting," she wrote.
Edwards also criticizes the process of selecting the secretary-general, in which candidates must take care not to antagonize the United States, China or Russia. 
She continues that she was surprised by the scale and nature of torture carried out by Russian security forces against captured Ukrainian soldiers and civilians in occupied areas of eastern Ukraine.
According to Edwards, people released in prisoner exchanges described a "system of torture" involving separate supervisors, interrogators and torturers, designed to extract information and instill fear. She compared Russia's invasion of Ukraine to the Soviet Union's invasion of Finland, which led to the Soviet Union's expulsion from the League of Nations.
Edwards also describes several personal achievements, including bringing together torture survivors from different conflicts and developing a "Survivors' Charter," written largely by the victims themselves. She said her most moving moment came when Shireen Khudeeda, a young Yazidi woman who survived captivity, sexual slavery and abuse by ISIS in Iraq and Syria, told her she had received a scholarship and passed her examinations.
Attorney Ayelet Razin Bet-Or, who works to document and secure recognition of the sexual violence committed on October 7 and during captivity, responded to Edwards' remarks.
"Dr. Edwards' clear, honest and courageous voice stands in sharp contrast to the silence and conduct of other officials within the UN's human rights mechanisms, who failed to fulfill their fundamental duty toward the victims of sexual violence and torture perpetrated by Hamas.
"Edwards' testimony is particularly important because it comes from within the system itself, from someone who has devoted her life to defending human rights, regardless of the national identity of the victims or the identity of the perpetrators. She reminds us of a truth that should have been self-evident: Human rights are not a matter of political position, and the protection of women who have suffered sexual violence cannot be selective.
"When officials entrusted with protecting women from violence choose not to give proper recognition to the testimony and suffering of Israeli victims, this is not merely a moral failure. It is a profound blow to the credibility of international institutions and to the trust that victims around the world place in the system that is supposed to protect them.
"Edwards' courage should not be the exception. It should be the standard. It is time for the UN to engage in genuine soul-searching, ensure accountability among its officials and put victims of violence, rather than political agendas, back at the center of its work."

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu fell further behind former Army Chief of Staff Gadi Eisenkot in a new opinion poll released Monday, with the opposition politician widening his lead in public perceptions of who is better suited to head the government.
The Channel 12 survey found that 45% of respondents considered Eisenkot better suited to serve as prime minister compared with 33% for Netanyahu, widening the gap to 12 percentage points from 10 in the previous poll.
The findings come just eight days before Israel’s Oct. 27 parliamentary elections, with Eisenkot’s Yashar party also projected to emerge as the largest in the 120-seat Knesset.
Yashar was projected to win 24 seats, ahead of Netanyahu’s Likud with 21, according to the survey.
Former Prime Minister Naftali Bennett’s Together party followed with 14 seats, while Yair Golan’s Democrats and the Arab-led Joint List were projected to secure nine each.
Avigdor Lieberman’s Yisrael Beiteinu party, the ultra-Orthodox Shas party and National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir’s Jewish Power party were each projected to win eight seats.
The poll put Jewish-led parties opposing Netanyahu at 55 seats, up two from the previous survey, compared with 51 for his governing coalition.
The two Arab parties were projected to secure another 14 seats, bringing the total for parties outside Netanyahu’s bloc to 69, although their inclusion in a future governing coalition remains uncertain.
In a separate question on suitability for prime minister, Bennett also led Netanyahu, with 39% favoring the former prime minister against 34% for Netanyahu. Another 22% considered neither suitable.
The survey also examined the impact of US President Donald Trump’s public endorsement of Netanyahu ahead of the elections.
Some 64% of respondents said Trump’s backing would make no difference to their vote, while 17% said it made them less likely to support Likud.
Only 12% said the endorsement strengthened their support for Netanyahu’s party.
Trump endorsed Netanyahu on Sunday, praising his leadership and partnership with Washington, particularly in confronting Iran.
