The annual event was due to start next week on October 26 and run through October 29, with a date next year to be announced “very soon”, the statement released on Tuesday said.
FII Institute chief executive officer Dr Maha Bint Mishari Al Saud said the decision “comes from a deep commitment to our partners, members, speakers and delegates”.
“Because this is our landmark tenth edition, we want to ensure it delivers the full scale, extraordinary quality, and unforgettable impact that our community has come to expect and truly deserves,” she said.
Informally dubbed “Davos in the Desert”, a nod to the World Economic Forum’s annual meeting in Switzerland, the state-backed conference showcases the kingdom’s ambitious investment plans in a bid to attract billions of dollars needed to fund its economic transformation away from hydrocarbons towards tourism, sport and technology.
Expected speakers included: Alphabet & Google’s president and chief information officer, Ruth Porat; Goldman Sachs Group chairman and CEO David Solomon; and BlackRock chairman and CEO Laurence Fink, according to the FII website.
Fighting between a Saudi-led coalition supporting Yemen’s internationally recognised government and the Iran-aligned Houthis has escalated in recent weeks.
The Houthis, also known as Ansar Allah, have hit military, energy and civilian infrastructure across Saudi Arabia, including Riyadh’s international airport, killing at least 18 people and injuring hundreds more.
Government staff to work from home
Government agencies in the Saudi capital, Riyadh, have told employees to work from home, one worker and two consultants told the AFP news agency, as the city comes under repeated attack from the Houthis.
The Kingdom Centre, a 99‑storey tower in downtown Riyadh that houses the International Monetary Fund’s regional office, also requested workers stay away until further notice.
On Sunday, an employee of a government agency in the capital received a message saying, “It has been decided to implement remote work from Monday to Thursday this week”. The message added: “We ask everyone to continue their activities as normal.”
Companies based in the King Abdullah Financial District, which hosts offices of major United States firms, have also asked employees to work from home, according to other sources.

The evolution of China’s active defence doctrine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
01:00:06 UTC
10:00:06 KST

Advertisement
Opinion
The evolution of China’s active defence doctrine
As the PLA approaches its centenary, it must execute a modern Long March to ensure the doctrine remains decisive in this hi-tech era
4-MIN READ4-MIN
1
 Listen
Chow Chung-yan began his journalistic career at the South China Morning Post and rose to become editor-in-chief in 2025. 
The British Army’s miraculous escape from Nazi Germany’s encirclement at Dunkirk is considered by some to be the greatest military retreat in modern history and a prime example of snatching victory from the jaws of defeat.
Yet years before Dunkirk, the military retreat by the Chinese Red Army, known as the Long March, was more impressive and consequential.
While the Dunkirk evacuation remains in Hollywood fare and a staple of World War II folklore, the Long March is taught at military academies worldwide as a foundational case study in asymmetrical warfare, insurgency and strategic political-military integration.
It was a baptism of fire that did more than resurrect Mao Zedong’s political career and mark his ascent to primacy. It also firmly established “active defence” as the Chinese Communist military’s core doctrine, which continues to guide the nation’s strategic planning to this day.

Video footage shared across social media networks showed local residents and a backhoe evacuating bodies from the collapsed mine onto a wooden canoe along an adjacent river.
Safety hazards
Emergency response teams faced severe impediments reaching the remote disaster site due to rugged geographical terrain and the active presence of illegal armed organisations, the governor's office said.
Narino represents an established hub for illicit mining, where armed groups exert control over the clandestine gold trade alongside narcotics trafficking and extortion rackets.
Residents in Santa Barbara de Iscuande have reported targeted killings by armed gangs over suspicions of stealing gold or collaborating with state security forces and rival factions.
Mining accidents remain frequent across rural Colombia, where unregulated operations consistently lack basic structural reinforcement and emergency safety infrastructure.
The tragedy follows a similar collapse in August in the Narino town of Policarpa, which claimed 13 lives.

Albert Heijn owner files police report over cyberattack

Albert Heijn owner files police report over cyberattack
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
Ahold Delhaize, the parent company of Dutch supermarket chain Albert Heijn, filed a police report on Monday over the cyberattack that forced it to take systems offline more than a week ago.
The company said in a statement on Monday that its investigation had confirmed the suspicious activity in its IT systems was caused by “the malicious actions of others”. Until now it had described the problem only as a “cybersecurity incident”.
Police and the public prosecution service (OM) urged the company to file a report last week, because a criminal investigation cannot start without one.
It is not clear why Ahold Delhaize has now decided to do so, broadcaster NOS reported.
The company did notify the National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC), the justice ministry’s cybersecurity agency, within 24 hours of discovering the attack, as required under a new cybersecurity law that came into force on August 15.
Albert Heijn’s website and app are back online and home deliveries are expected to resume on Friday, October 23, the company said. The websites of drugstore chain Etos and drinks chain Gall & Gall, also owned by Ahold Delhaize, are available again.
Ahold Delhaize said it had so far found no evidence that sensitive data belonging to customers, staff or business partners had been taken. It declined to give further details while the investigation continues, saying they could compromise its security.
The Albert Heijn hack is one of the first major incidents since the new reporting law came into force. It covers some 8,000 organisations seen as vital to the country, from healthcare, drinking water and banks to the food sector, including supermarkets.
The problems began on Sunday, October 11, when Albert Heijn switched off part of its IT systems, halting home deliveries and work at its distribution centres and leaving empty shelves in some stores.
Security sources told NOS last week that servers in the US, Poland, Moldova and Turkey had been used in the attack. Sector insiders told the Financieele Dagblad that the outage was costing the company “tens of millions” of euros a day.

BRUSSELS, October 20. /TASS/. The European Union intends to counter Russia and China in the Arctic and seek unrestricted access to the Northern Sea Route, EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said in an interview with The Times.
Earlier, Vladislav Maslennikov, director of the Russian Foreign Ministry’s Department of European Affairs and Russia’s senior Arctic official at the Arctic Council, said the European Union was showing an intention to pursue escalation in the Arctic and was unwilling to stop politicizing cooperation in the High North.
In the interview, the EU foreign policy chief argued that the West must stop Russia and China from moving toward dominance in the Arctic. The Northern Sea Route, which is already actively used by Russia and China, is of particular concern to Brussels. The Times noted that the route allows ships to travel between Asia and Europe one-third faster than the traditional route through the Suez Canal. It is becoming increasingly important amid growing instability in the Middle East.
According to Kallas, the EU should work with Canada and the United States, ostensibly to prevent "Russia and China from gaining full control" over the route. She said EU and NATO countries would seek to ensure that the Northern Sea Route remains open to all ships.
Kallas also confirmed that the European Commission would present its new Arctic strategy on Tuesday, the last update having been made in 2021. The new strategy will include investments in the construction of new icebreakers, the establishment of a military center to monitor Russian activity in the Arctic, and provisions to ease the EU’s existing ban on offshore oil and gas extraction in the Arctic. The European Commission hopes that the prospect of developing offshore oil and gas reserves off Norway will increase investor interest in the region and help alleviate the EU’s energy supply problems.
Bloomberg previously reported that the European Union plans to launch an Arctic surveillance program in 2027. The program is expected to use the EU’s Copernicus and Galileo satellite systems to detect threats on land and at sea.

More wet weather ahead for an already drenched Queensland
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
00:51:20 UTC
09:51:20 KST

In Brief
- A blocking high and inland trough are bringing heavy rainfall across Queensland.
- The BoM expects drier weather to start around Tuesday next week.
Queensland residents are being warned to prepare for more heavy rain and storms, after a wet start to the week.
The Bureau of Meteorology's (BoM) senior meteorologist David Crock says two interacting weather patterns are bringing heavy rain to the state.
A high-pressure system sitting over the Tasman Sea and an inland trough over western Queensland are bringing showers, rain and some thunderstorms.
"This time last week, most of the catchments across southern and south-eastern and central Queensland were very dry following little rainfall in recent months," Crock said.
"Rivers and creeks are now starting to fill up after several days of rain."
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
The Sunshine Coast was among the wettest areas, with Sippy Downs receiving 127mm in less than 24 hours from Monday morning.
Other parts of the north tropical coast have already recorded 50 to 90mm rainfall.
The remote Middle Percy Island recorded 121mm last Friday, nearly 10 per cent of its annual average rainfall.
Inland rivers in some parts of the Maranoa and Warrego regions have started to fill up after several days of rain.
The BoM has no flood warning at present, but has warned residents to stay vigilant.
"Even where catchments remain dry, heavy rain with thunderstorms can lead to rapid flash flooding," Crock said.
He said there is a risk of severe thunderstorms with heavy rainfall through central and western Queensland on Tuesday and Wednesday.
Towards the end of the week, a cold front could also bring storms to southern and south-eastern Queensland.
While blocking highs can bring the same kind of weather to an area for an extended time, the BoM is predicting drier weather from midway through next week.
"There's a fair bit of uncertainty still with this forecast as the blocking high can be very stubborn and can slow down an approaching cold front, but it looks like by this time next week we will see much drier weather," he said.
It's the start of Queensland’s severe weather season, according to the BoM, as October to April is the peak time for storms, tropical cyclones and floods across the state.

Cuba accuses US of letting terrorists operate with impunity after speedboat raid
HAVANA, Oct 19 - Cuban law enforcement officials on Monday alleged that the US was allowing terrorists to operate with impunity on American soil, citing details of an investigation into a February speedboat incursion that led to a gun battle at sea, deaths and injuries on both sides.
On February 25, 10 Cuban exiles attempted to infiltrate the island nation by boat from the Florida Keys, armed with nearly 13,000 rounds of ammunition, 11 rifles, 15 handguns, Molotov cocktails, a VHF radio and Starlink satellite communication equipment, according to the Cuban investigation that was described by state-run media on Monday. Five were killed; the rest, including some who were wounded, are in custody and face terrorism charges, authorities said.
Cuba said on Monday that its investigation, which included confessions from those detained by its authorities, found that some of those involved in training insurgents remain at large in the US.
"It is also important to highlight ... the crimes still being committed today by individuals and organizations that, from within the United States, provided the property used to carry out these acts, arranged and secured land and maritime transport, and facilitated the purchase and stockpiling of weaponry," said Cuban prosecutor Edward Roberts.
Cuban authorities accused Maritza Lugo Fernandez, a Cuban national residing in Florida, of helping to organize the alleged plot. Some of those detained confessed they had trained on a farm property in Florida owned by Lugo Fernandez, who leads the Florida-based "Partido Democrático 30 de Noviembre," or the Democratic Party of November 30.
Lugo Fernandez denies the allegations.
"For more than 40 years, that regime has accused me of being a terrorist - of everything they can possibly come up with ... ," she said in a clip included in the state-run media report. "Personally, I live with peace of mind; I’m not concerned about what they say because I am very clear - fully aware - that it is all a lie."
Neither the US Embassy in Cuba nor the US Department of Justice responded to a Reuters request for comment on the Cuban government's allegations.
Cuba and the FBI previously said they were cooperating on the investigation.
According to Cuban authorities, several of those detained in February said they planned simultaneous attacks on police and border guard units in Matanzas, a province just east of Havana, with the goal of inciting an armed uprising and triggering a US military intervention.
The accusations come as the US has piled pressure on Cuba's government, including a nine-month de facto fuel blockade and reinforced sanctions that have led to an unprecedented economic crisis on the island.
The US has called the Cuban government corrupt and says it is seeking a change in leadership there. REUTERS

“We are also going to file a complaint in the United States because there must be protection for human rights,” Sheinbaum said during her morning press conference.
Emiliano Andrade-Covarrubias, 56, died in US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) custody at the Rio Grande Processing Center in Laredo, Texas.

The death brings to 18 the number of Mexican nationals who have died in ICE custody or during immigration enforcement operations since US President Donald Trump returned to office on Jan. 20, 2025, according to Mexican media reports.
The cause of Andrade's death has not been officially established. Mexican authorities have called for transparency and accountability as investigations proceed.
The case adds to diplomatic tensions over the treatment of migrants in US detention facilities, with Mexico seeking stronger safeguards for its citizens abroad.

Space Forces Central Poised for ‘Fivefold’ Growth in Coming Years
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
00:49:57 UTC
09:49:57 KST

The general in charge of the Space Force’s component to U.S. Central Command said Oct. 19 he expects that in about three years his small team of Guardians will be five times the size it is today—growth he said is needed to meet the military’s demand for space capabilities in Middle East operations.
Space Forces Central was activated in December 2022 with a small staff of about 30 personnel split between Shaw Air Force Base, S.C., and Al Udeid Air Base, Qatar. Brig. Gen. Todd Benson, SPACECENT commander, said during an event at the Mitchell Institute for Aerospace Studies that while his team has had an outsized impact during operations against Iran, it needs to grow.
“It doesn’t matter what service you’re with or what component, the expectations are the same: You have to present combat-credible forces, and you have to lead joint forces in combat,” he said. “That takes size to do that. It doesn’t matter what service you’re with. So, we have to get to that point, and I think we will in the next few years.”
Benson declined to offer an exact number of personnel he wants to reach, but said his goal for the component is to have a “steady-state” headquarters staff that’s at least somewhat comparable to other service components—though he noted that even a fivefold increase won’t put SPACECENT in the ballpark of the others due to the smaller size of the Space Force.
“Our peers have thousands, so we would not be anywhere near that as a smaller service,” he said. “But I would expect that we’d be about fivefold the size we are today, which is not a large number, but that’s what we need to make sure that we have the requisite staff to do planning cycles, all the intelligence that we need.”
The Space Force today has components within every geographic combatant command and just this month added its newest component earlier, U.S. Space Forces Special Operations, or SPACEFOR-SOC. Each component is charged with presenting space expertise to commanders in the field, and that includes deploying to the front line to generate space effects like electronic warfare, satellite communications, navigation and timing, and missile warning.
Because the Space Force’s components are still small in size, balancing the day-to-day needs of their headquarters staff with their deployed forces is a challenge—particularly for SPACECENT amid ongoing operations in Iran.
Benson offered a glimpse into the component’s daily operations, which include daily planning sessions with headquarters staff and meetings with CENTCOM leadership. At the same time, SPACECENT is supporting 24/7 operations in the Middle East.
“There are no days off, really, downrange,” Benson said. “Everybody’s working as hard as they can, and just trying to deal with things like the elements of weather and ops tempo, making sure everything’s maintained.”
Benson said building SPACECENT’s team of intelligence professionals is a priority, especially when it comes to providing inputs into the joint force’s targeting processes, which involves inputs from the services components to select and prioritize military targets. At one point, SPACECENT had only two Guardian representatives in a process that includes more than 1,000 personnel.
Benson said operations over the last year have shown the need for more of everything, from personnel to space systems on the ground—like jammers—and on orbit. Also, having Guardians downrange and supporting from their home station has both cemented the importance of space effects and changed the way the joint force thinks about space in operations.
“Space will forever be a part of every military operation going forward,” Benson said. “There is no going backwards on that.”

UN Security Council adopts resolution on digital threats to children in conflict
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
00:34:48 UTC
09:34:48 KST

Merve Gül Aydoğan Ağlarcı
20 October 2026•Update: 20 October 2026
The UN Security Council unanimously adopted a resolution Monday addressing how digital technologies are used to commit violations and abuses against children in armed conflict.
The resolution, penned by Greece, also stressed the need to provide children with digital literacy so they can identify online risks and help prevent violations before they occur.
The measure urged member states to improve domestic compliance with their obligations under international law to end and prevent violations and abuses against children, including those committed, facilitated or amplified through digital technologies.
Greece chaired the Working Group on Children and Armed Conflict in 2025.
Speaking before the vote, Greece's UN envoy Aglaia Balta said the Council must not stay silent on the digital dimension of grave violations.
"The question before us is not whether the Council should address the digital dimension of grave violations, but whether it can afford to remain silent while others exploit it," she said.
Balta stressed that the resolution reinforces the existing framework by ensuring it captures violations regardless of the means used.
"Recruitment through a smartphone is still recruitment. A mandate that cannot see where violations begin is a mandate that falls behind," she said.
Describing the text as a starting point, Balta said: "This resolution does not close the chapter on this urgent issue; it opens it. It is a seed, one that must grow as digital technologies reshape every aspect of human life, and above all, the lives of children."
"Thirty years ago, the international community resolved that children caught in war would no longer be invisible. Today, we must make sure they do not vanish in the digital space," she added.

Kennedy’s vaccine plan could cause surge in hepatitis B, study finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
00:23:00 UTC
09:23:00 KST

Kennedy’s vaccine plan could cause surge in hepatitis B, study finds
Apoorva Mandavilli
- Ending routine hepatitis B shots for newborns could raise chronic infections sharply and leave more than half of Americans at risk by age 20, a study found.
- Researchers led by Amir Mohareb modelled 3.6 million births a year. Delaying vaccination to two months would lift chronic cases by 19%, from 255 to 303.
- A shared decision-making policy could raise chronic infections by 83% to 467 cases a year. A federal judge has temporarily blocked Kennedy’s December and January vaccine changes.
AI generated
Ending the practice of immunising all newborns against hepatitis B, as Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr has recommended, would sharply increase the number of chronic infections and put more than half of Americans at risk of the disease by age 20, according to a new study published on Oct 20.
Hepatitis B is a highly contagious virus that can lead to cirrhosis, liver failure and liver cancer.
To prevent infections, doctors in the United States have for decades administered the first dose of the hepatitis B vaccine to all babies within 24 hours of birth – and within 12 hours to infants whose mother is known to be infected.
But in December 2025, a panel of advisers chosen by Kennedy recommended that parents should decide whether, or when, infants should get the shot if they were born to mothers who test negative for hepatitis B. In those cases, the group said, parents should decide “no earlier than two months of age”.
Kennedy and his associates have argued that hepatitis B is primarily a sexually transmitted disease and that babies do not need the protection unless their mothers are infected.
But the virus can be spread by people who do not know they have it, as well as by household objects used by an infected person.
In January, Kennedy proposed a new childhood vaccination schedule in which the vaccine would be offered under a shared clinical decision-making approach – that is, after consultation with a healthcare provider.
In March, a federal judge temporarily blocked the implementation of the December and January recommendations. But the lawsuit continues.
Amir Mohareb, an infectious diseases physician at Massachusetts General Hospital and Harvard Medical School who led the study, and his colleagues modelled the potential impact of changing hepatitis B vaccination policy on the estimated 3.6 million infants born in a single year.
Immunising babies at two months of age rather than at birth would increase chronic hepatitis B infections acquired by age 20 by 19%, from an average of 255 cases per year to 303, the study found.
Switching to a shared decision-making policy would increase chronic infections by 83%, to an average of 467 cases, and would result in more than 50% of children born each year entering adulthood susceptible to infection. The findings were published in the journal Annals of Internal Medicine.
The Department of Health and Human Services did not provide comment. NYTIMES

United States Representative Rashida Tlaib has called for her government to arrest the commander of an Israeli military unit believed to be responsible for the killing of five-year-old Palestinian girl Hind Rajab in Gaza.
In a social media post on Monday, Tlaib pointed to reports that Israeli soldier Sean Glass was present in the US. She emphasised that the US had a legal responsibility to probe his involvement in Rajab’s death.
“As a party to the Genocide Convention and the Geneva Conventions, our government is obligated to arrest and investigate him for these war crimes and acts of genocide,” she wrote.
As part of her post, Tlaib shared a report from the Hind Rajab Foundation (HRF), which tracks Israeli soldiers suspected of war crimes in Gaza.

“Sean Glass commanded the ‘Vampire Empire’ Company implicated in the killing of five-year-old Hind Rajab, members of her family, and the medics sent to rescue them. HRF’s investigation places him and his troops in the direct vicinity of Hind’s vehicle during the killing,” the group said in a statement.
“Today, Glass walks free in the United States. HRF demands that the US authorities arrest him and bring him to justice.”
The five-year-old’s killing on January 29, 2024, triggered global outrage and became a symbol of Israel’s targeting of Palestinian civilians and children during its genocidal war on Gaza.
Rajab and her family were attempting to leave Gaza City when their vehicle came under Israeli fire.
Her family was killed in the gunfire. Rajab called emergency services, appealing to rescuers, “I’m so scared. Please come!”
Recordings of her telephone call made international news. But both Rajab and the rescue team that tried to reach her were ultimately killed by Israeli forces.
The car Rajab was in was riddled with 335 bullet holes, which Israeli authorities initially blamed on a firefight with Palestinian fighters.
An investigation by the group Forensic Architecture found no evidence of an exchange of fire and concluded that only Israeli forces had been present in the area at the time of the incident.
Israel has opened a probe into the killings, but such investigations are seen by Palestinians as a means of dodging accountability and buying time until outrage over an incident dissipates.
Experts at the United Nations and other human rights watchdogs have declared Israel’s assault on Gaza to be a genocide. At least 74,000 Palestinians have been killed, including at least 21,000 children.

Collingwood captain Ruby Schleicher will leave the struggling AFLW club to return to her native Western Australia.
Schleicher informed the Magpies of her decision on Tuesday after suffering a season-ending shoulder injury in their round 9 loss to St Kilda.
The 28-year-old inaugural Collingwood player is expected to land at West Coast, with the Eagles reportedly offering a four-year contract.
A two-time All-Australian, Schleicher's departure is a massive blow to perennial competition strugglers Collingwood, who have only won one game after 10 rounds this season.
"This has been a really tough decision for me to make but one that is ultimately the best for where I am in my life and career," Schleicher said in a club statement.
"Collingwood has been my home for my entire adult life … I'll always consider myself a Collingwood person.
"I'm excited for my next chapter, but also for the club's next chapter."

Schleicher reportedly turned down a one-year deal to remain at the Magpies after strong interest from the Eagles.
Joining the Magpies ahead of the inaugural AFLW season in 2017, the defender-turned-midfielder has played 82 games for the club and took over as captain from Bri Davey in 2025.
Schleicher was moved to the forward line this season under coach Sam Wright and kicked 10 goals before fracturing her shoulder against the Saints.
"While we are disappointed to see Ruby depart our Club, we respect her decision to return home," Kelly said in a statement.
"We thank Ruby for everything she has given to Collingwood and wish her all the very best for the next chapter."
Like Schleicher, Davey is among several senior leaders set to come off contract at the end of this campaign, while vice-captain Jordy Allen's contract runs until the end of the 2027 season.

Italy’s government will dispatch 500 army troops to “defend Milan” after two days of unrest that saw demonstrators clash with police, loot shops and vandalise property, deputy prime minister Matteo Salvini said on Monday.
The deployment is expected to be included in a package of security measures to be approved at a cabinet meeting expected on Tuesday, and comes as shops in central Milan closed early and boarded up their windows, fearing a fresh outbreak of violence in Italy’s financial capital.
“From words to action: 500 more troops to defend Milan,” Salvini, head of the co-ruling right-wing League party, wrote on social media.
Most stores in Milan’s Via Montenapoleone luxury shopping district, home to brands including Chanel, Tiffany and Dior, had removed merchandise from their windows as a precaution, while police patrolled the street and a handful of tourists looked on.
Several hundred hooded protesters, many believed to be minors, set bins ablaze and looted shops in the city centre over the weekend after an initially peaceful demonstration on Saturday over poor public services and rising costs.
Among the stores ransacked were sports retailers Decathlon and Arc’teryx and mobile phone operator Vodafone, television footage showed. Clothing brands Levi’s and Under Armour, as well as Decathlon, covered their shop windows with cardboard and wooden panels.
Italian prime minister Giorgia Meloni, who faces a national election next year, condemned the violence and chaired a meeting with ministers and security chiefs on Monday to discuss the situation.
“The government will respond firmly to these attacks on the state, including through measures aimed at curbing violence by minors,” foreign minister Antonio Tajani, who also serves as deputy prime minister like Salvini, wrote on X.
As part of the planned crackdown, the Corriere della Sera newspaper said Meloni was considering extending preventive detention for minors and cracking down on youth gangs, while bringing forward some provisions contained in an existing security bill currently being examined by parliament.
Italian police said it had detained 271 young people during unrest in Milan on Sunday. Of those taken to police stations, 32 were arrested, including 23 minors and 13 foreign nationals, police said on Monday. A further 28 people were reported to judicial authorities.
The unrest followed clashes on Saturday in other northern cities including Bologna, Brescia, Bergamo and Turin, where 28 protesters were arrested, according to a police report released on Sunday.
The disturbances echoed unrest in neighbouring France, where hundreds of thousands of people angered by rising living costs and declining public services took to the streets on Saturday in some of the country’s most violent protests in years.

Exiled critic of Rwandan president found beheaded in Uganda
Ugandan police say a male body has been found in a village near Kampala, and his head has yet to be located.
An exiled vocal critic of the Rwandan government has been found decapitated near Kampala, south-central Uganda, according to a police spokesperson, in a case which remains under investigation.
Ugandan police said on Monday they were investigating the “murder of a male adult (around 50), whose head was cut off, and up to now, the head has not yet been recovered”, spokesperson Kituuma Rusoke told reporters, adding that the body had been identified by relatives as Robert Kabera.
The body was found in Luwala, a village near Kampala, and the killing likely took place late on October 16 or early on October 17, police added.
Robert Kabera, a former sergeant who fled Rwanda several years ago, was living in Uganda. The former soldier was not critical of the government during his time with the military, but grew increasingly opposed to Rwandan President Paul Kagame.
Kabera had a YouTube channel, “Major Robert TV”, with 144,000 subscribers. He featured a song praising opposition figure Victoire Ingabire, a rare voice of dissent in Rwanda who had been repeatedly imprisoned.
‘A witch-hunt’
In Uganda, “Robert had no issues with anyone”, his brother, Victor Agaba, told the AFP news agency.
“Our problem comes from home… The army created a criminal case against him. It was a witch-hunt,” he said.
Kabera was declared a fugitive after leaving Rwanda and accused of corrupting a minor, charges he denied.
Rwandan authorities have been accused of assassinating opponents of President Kagame, who has governed the country since coming to power in 2000. The Rwandan president took the reins in the aftermath of the 1994 genocide in which 800,000 people were killed, primarily from the minority Tutsi community.
Kabera is not the first opposition figure in exile to be assassinated.
In 2021, a former lieutenant in the Rwandan army, Revocat Karemangingo, was shot dead in Mozambique, where he was suspected of secretly supporting an opposition force.
Outspoken opponent Seif Bamporiki was shot dead in South Africa the same year, while a former Rwandan intelligence chief turned critic, Patrick Karegeya, was strangled in his South African hotel room in 2014.
Former general Faustin Kayumba Nyamwasa, who co-founded the Rwanda National Congress (RNC) opposition party with Karegeya and lives in exile, has survived several assassination attempts.

Israel Air Force welcomes Apache helicopter deal amid bureaucratic delays
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
00:04:54 UTC
09:04:54 KST

Israeli Air Force officers welcomed progress in the Apache helicopter deal following a series of delays, but warned that despite the breakthrough, other procurement deals remain stalled, primarily due to government bureaucracy.
The officials stressed that these purchases are critical to the IDF's readiness amid the growing Iranian threat. "An across-the-board government budget cut will not solve all the problems. We must reduce bureaucracy and implement the large defense budget approved by the government," an officer familiar with the procurement deals said.
"The damage is already being felt. We can see it in operational capability gaps, not only in the Air Force," he added.
Among the critical purchases currently under consideration are the seventh and eighth aerial refueling aircraft. After years of delays and foot-dragging, a decision was made to upgrade the Air Force's refueling fleet through the purchase of Boeing KC-46 Pegasus aircraft, which would extend the range and operational capabilities of Israeli fighter jets.
The American refueling aircraft that served as flying gas stations during Operation Roaring Lion demonstrated beyond any doubt the need for Israeli-owned aerial refueling aircraft in a future independent IDF campaign against Iran.
The KC-46 is intended to replace Israel's aging Re'em tanker fleet, which has undergone several upgrades over the years. The new aircraft can refuel multiple fighter jets in midair at once and is equipped with advanced communications and defense systems.
Air Force officers emphasized that if the deal is signed in the coming months, the aircraft could be delivered as early as 2030. Any further delay in the procurement process would push back their arrival by years.
IDF wants to replace Yasur helicopters
Another issue under consideration is the purchase of helicopters numbered 12 through 18 in the Pereh helicopter program, which are intended to replace the Air Force's aging Yasur helicopters. The new helicopters are expected to extend the IDF's operational range and increase its capacity to transport combat troops and military equipment.
Senior defense industry officials have also warned of shortages of munitions and missiles. They stressed that procurement agreements must be signed to expand production lines in Israel and accelerate manufacturing.
Senior IDF officials have similarly warned of shortages of advanced munitions for the Navy and Air Force, which are preparing around the clock for a potential multi-front conflict.
Senior Ground Forces officials have also warned that the IDF still needs to replenish its stocks of tank ammunition and artillery munitions, including those used by its rocket forces.
In the area of ground mobility, Ground Forces Commander Maj. Gen. Nadav Lotan is working to accelerate procurement processes for various types of jeeps and trucks, as well as armored combat vehicles, including tanks, Eitan armored personnel carriers, and Namer armored personnel carriers.
"This is a force that has suffered tremendous wear and tear over the past three years, and we need not only vehicles but also spare parts, and quickly," a senior Ground Forces officer said.
IDF Data Division looking for maintenance of old systems
Another critical capability gap, one that officials have been less willing to highlight, involves technology for the IDF Military Intelligence Directorate's new Data Division, including the maintenance of older systems.
The IDF's C4I and Cyber Defense Directorate, which has made significant advances in digital capabilities, also requires critical technology and infrastructure.
Advancing these projects will require larger budgets, which were approved by the IDF General Staff more than a year ago, partly to support the military's artificial intelligence transformation.

Trump open to idea of joint meeting with Xi, Putin next month
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
00:04:20 UTC
09:04:20 KST

US President Donald Trump said on Monday he is open to three-way arms-control talks with the leaders of China and Russia as soon as next month, raising the prospect of an unprecedented meeting and a major diplomatic gambit for the US president.
"We would have it to talk about nuclear weapons and denuclearization," Trump told reporters outside the White House. "If President Xi wants to have it, I'd have it. I'm sure we'd talk about other things like trade too."
Trump has tried to thaw frosty relations with Beijing and Moscow as those non-Western powers grow closer. A three-way meeting would also raise alarm from Europe to Asia over private deals that weaken Washington's transatlantic and Indo-Pacific alliances.
But a deal struck between the three countries could also lower global tensions. An end to Russia's war in Ukraine could resolve the biggest threat in decades to European security, and a deal on arms would bind the three nations with the biggest stockpiles of nuclear weapons.
In recent days, Trump has moved to warm ties with Russian President Vladimir Putin, announcing a diesel-fuel deal and signing an order on Friday waiving key sanctions on Moscow. Trump has also sought stable relations with Chinese President Xi Jinping, who in turn has nurtured close ties with Putin.
So far, Trump has not delivered on a campaign promise to quickly end the war in Ukraine.
The White House has been discussing for weeks a possible meeting between the leaders focused on denuclearization on the sidelines of the November 18-19 Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in China, according to a person familiar with the matter.
Putin later pitched using such a meeting to negotiate an end to the four-year-old Ukraine conflict in a manner that would favor Moscow, the Wall Street Journal reported on Sunday, citing people familiar with the discussions. Putin's suggestion came during an October 9 phone call with Trump that yielded the deal on Russian diesel.
Earlier on Monday, the Kremlin said that the potential meeting had come up in talks.
The three leaders have met separately but never held formal talks together.
The White House did not respond to a Reuters request for comment. The Russian and Chinese embassies in Washington also did not reply to requests for comment.
Trump's diesel deal with Putin and the executive order waiving sanctions on Moscow have drawn criticism from Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy, who has warned they would embolden Putin and prolong the war.
Speaking about the possible meeting on Monday, Trump said, "I would do it, not so much for Ukraine because Russia, frankly, has been fine on Ukraine." He added that "Zelenskiy is not helping matters much," and that "it's time for somebody else to negotiate on behalf of Ukraine."
Moscow launched one of its broadest air assaults in months overnight, cutting power to more than half a million households and damaging energy infrastructure across Ukraine. Ten people were reported killed.
Trump seeks nuclear talks
Last week, Trump told reporters he thought a denuclearization deal with Russia and China was possible, but that it "doesn't have to be this year." It's not clear how advanced any talks between the countries are.
Russia has the most stored nuclear warheads, followed by the United States and China, according to the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute.
The Strategic Arms Reduction Treaty expired earlier this year. The New START treaty, signed in 2010, allowed a single extension, which Putin and former US President Joe Biden agreed to for five years. Any new extension would require an executive decision to voluntarily extend the limits of the treaty.
China's foreign ministry said last week that its "nuclear strength is by no means at the same level with that of the US and Russia" and that it would be "neither fair, reasonable nor realistic to ask China to join the so-called trilateral nuclear disarmament negotiations at this stage."
Trump has already agreed to attend the APEC summit in Shenzhen next month, marking his second trip to China this year and his third visit with Xi over the same period. China, Russia, and the United States are all APEC members.
On Monday, Trump downplayed the idea of another high-profile meeting in China with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un.
"I get along with him very well, and I'm not sure that anybody's asking for a meeting," he said.
Trump previously said he planned to meet with Kim this year. North Korea has publicly indicated that it is not open to talks aimed at convincing Pyongyang to give up its nuclear weapons.

Mahmoud Khalil takes deportation fight to the US Supreme Court
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
23:56:32 UTC
08:56:32 KST

Mahmoud Khalil takes deportation fight to the US Supreme Court
Lawyers for the former student leader seek to overturn an appeals court decision that would allow for his removal.
Pro-Palestine activist Mahmoud Khalil has petitioned the United States Supreme Court to review a court ruling that could pave the way for his re-arrest and deportation.
On Monday, Khalil’s lawyers filed an emergency application to the high court, seeking an immediate stay of a decision from Philadelphia’s 3rd Circuit Court of Appeals.
That court had ruled that federal law should have prohibited lower courts from ordering Khalil’s release from immigration detention in June 2025.
Instead, the appeals court said that Khalil’s detention should have been weighed first in an immigration court — a system overseen by the executive branch of the US government — and not in district court, which is part of the judicial branch.
In March 2025, Khalil became the first student protester known to be targeted for his pro-Palestinian views under the second administration of President Donald Trump.
A permanent US resident and former Columbia University graduate student, Khalil was arrested inside the student housing complex where he lived with his wife, a US citizen.
The push to deport Khalil has become a flashpoint in the debate over free speech on US campuses.
His petition to the Supreme Court could result in a major legal showdown that determines whether federal courts can intervene when noncitizens face retaliatory detention for speech protected under the First Amendment of the US Constitution.
Khalil’s lawyers have asked the Supreme Court to rule that noncitizens do indeed have the right to sue if immigration officials detain them as a reprisal for exercising free speech.
“If the Trump administration can punish someone for their pro-Palestine speech, this or any future administration can punish anyone for any speech,” Khalil said during a news conference on Monday.
Trump campaigned for re-election in 2024 in part on a pledge to crack down on the pro-Palestinian student protest movement, which had erupted in 2023.
Columbia University in New York became an epicentre for such activism. Khalil, who was born in a Palestinian refugee camp in Syria, had served as a spokesperson for the protest groups.
The Trump administration, however, has characterised pro-Palestinian activism as a threat to US foreign policy interests. It has argued it has the legal right to deport noncitizens who engage in such protests as a result.
After his arrest, Khalil was quickly moved to immigration detention centres in New Jersey, then Louisiana, where he remained in custody for more than three months.
Khalil faces deportation to Algeria or Syria if the 3rd Circuit Court’s decision holds.
In May, the 3rd Circuit narrowly voted six-to-five against reconsidering his case, but its decision will not go into effect until Khalil has exhausted his appeals.
He has fought his deportation both in the immigration court system and in the federal district court system, where he has filed a habeas corpus case. Both cases remain ongoing.
In April, the Board of Immigration Appeals denied his appeal in the immigration court system and issued a final order of removal in his case.
On Monday, faculty and staff at Columbia University held a silent vigil outside one of the school’s gates to protest what they described as “abducted students”, taken by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE).
Placards with portraits of Khalil and fellow student protester Mohsen Mahdawi, among others, were hoisted into the air. Demonstrators called for solidarity with the students facing deportation and pushed for Columbia University to reopen its gates to the public after their closure during the protest movement.

Colombia illegal gold mine collapse kills 14 people
The collapse of an illegal gold mine in southwestern Colombia killed 14 people and injured seven others, local authorities said on Monday.
The accident took place in the rural Chambero sector of the Santa Barbara de Iscuande municipality, located in the department of Narino.
Search and rescue operations have concluded, Narino Governor Luis Alfonso Escobar said.
Jorge Tovar Castillo, a disaster response official in Narino, said that an additional 12 to 15 miners have been reported as missing following the accident.
He said that municipal authorities were handling the response but added that communication had been difficult.
Santa Barbara de Iscuande is surrounded by dense rainforest and can only be reached by boat or small aircraft.
In a message on X, Escobar said the gold mine was an “informal” mine.
Informal and unregulated mining is common in rural parts of Colombia, where operations often lack adequate safety infrastructure, leading to frequent fatal accidents.
“At this moment our priority is to save lives, accompany families and guarantee an opportune response to this painful tragedy,” Escobar wrote.
In August, 13 people died in a similar mining accident in the municipality of Policarpa, also in Narino.

a tiny backpack for your phone? this expandable case hold anything from cards to airpods and keys
ninja labs’ magsafe flex pouch snaps onto the back of your smartphone, turning it into a stretchy, compact pocket that can hold everyday essentials, from airpods and car keys to other small personal items.
prefer designboom on google
a tiny handbag for your smartphone
There’s now room for your AirPods, chapstick, and car key fob on the back of your phone, thanks to a stretchy silicone pocket by Los Angeles-based Ninja Labs. The company has introduced a MagSafe version of its Flex Pouch, a small, expandable compartment that attaches magnetically to compatible smartphones. It can be pulled off whenever you want, turning an ordinary phone into a tiny, stretchy handbag that’s ready to hold all the little things that tend to disappear into our pockets.
The pouch can accommodate anything from a single credit card to a thick stack of twenty, according to the company. Lip gloss and wireless earbuds can be squeezed inside, along with a handful of loose change. The contents press against the soft silicone, creating a lumpy silhouette that changes depending on what’s packed inside. Empty it out, and the pocket shrinks back down.
memory silicone stretches to twice its original size
The design relies on Ninja Labs’ proprietary silicone blend, which can stretch to twice its original size before returning to its familiar shape. Its naturally grippy surface wraps around the contents, keeping objects in place without a zipper or clasp. The pouch expands outward from the flat surface of the phone, making room for surprisingly bulky objects while leaving them accessible from the top.
The company says the material retained more than 90 percent of its original stretch after 10,000 stretching cycles. The silicone can accommodate objects with irregular shapes, although the company advises against storing ordinary house keys or anything with sharp edges that could puncture the material. A car key fob, on the other hand, fits inside the soft pocket.
ninja labs gives its flex pouch a magsafe update
The magnetic attachment is the latest development in Ninja Labs’ existing Flex Pouch collection, which originally incorporated the stretchy pocket directly into an iPhone case. With the new MagSafe version, the storage compartment becomes an independent accessory. It snaps onto the back of a compatible phone or case and can be removed in seconds, allowing users to keep their existing protective case.
The $58 USD MagSafe Flex Pouch is available in pink, baby blue, lavender and black, with translucent silicone and a sparkling pink option among the finishes. It works with MagSafe-compatible iPhones and can also be used with Android devices fitted with a suitable magnetic case. The accessory provides storage without any additional protection for the phone itself. And while it might be an unusual sight to see a phone bulging with cosmetics or a bundle of cards, the ability to leave the bag at home could be tempting.

What is celebrated on October 20 in Ukraine and around the world
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
02:53:11 EEST
08:53:11 KST

What is celebrated on October 20 in Ukraine and around the world
Kyiv • UNN
In Ukraine, Breast Cancer Awareness Day is observed, while around the world, Statistics Day, World Osteoporosis Day, and International Chefs Day are marked. The faithful honor Saint Artemius.
On October 20, Ukraine observes the All-Ukrainian Day of the Fight Against Breast Cancer, while around the world, under the auspices of the UN and international organizations, World Statistics Day, World Osteoporosis Day, and International Chefs Day are observed.
According to the new calendar, the church calendar honors Saint Hieromartyr Artemius, while according to the old calendar, it commemorates Saints Sergius and Bacchus the Martyrs, writes UNN.
World Statistics Day
An official international UN date established by the United Nations Statistical Commission and observed for the first time in 2010. By decision of the UN, the date is observed once every five years, beginning in 2010; however, national statistical agencies around the world hold thematic events every year on October 20.
The day highlights the crucial role of reliable, objective, and high-quality data in government decision-making, the development of economic reforms, and ensuring transparency in society.
World Osteoporosis Day
A global observance established in 1996 by the National Osteoporosis Society of the United Kingdom with the support of the European Commission and later endorsed by the World Health Organization and the International Osteoporosis Foundation.
The event seeks to raise public awareness of the "silent epidemic"—a systemic disease of the skeleton that leads to reduced bone density and an increased risk of fractures—and also promotes a balanced diet enriched with calcium and vitamin D, as well as regular physical activity.
International Chefs Day
Established in 2004 at the initiative of the World Association of Chefs' Societies, which brings together more than 10 million professional chefs from around the world.
The event is dedicated to promoting culinary excellence, preserving national gastronomic traditions, teaching children the basics of healthy nutrition, and charitable initiatives during which chefs prepare meals for orphanages and socially vulnerable groups.
Usyk prepared a burger together with a former White House chef04.05.26, 18:29 • 6753 views
International Day of the Air Traffic Controller
A professional observance for air traffic controllers and air traffic management specialists. The date was chosen to commemorate October 20, 1961, when the International Federation of Air Traffic Controllers' Associations was founded in Amsterdam.
The observance draws attention to the great responsibility, psycho-emotional strain, and exceptional professionalism of controllers, who ensure around the clock the safety and regularity of flights by thousands of civilian and military aircraft in the planet's airspace.
All-Ukrainian Day of the Fight Against Breast Cancer
An official national observance established by Decree No. 42/2005 of the President of Ukraine dated January 17, 2005.
The event forms an integral part of Breast Cancer Awareness Month worldwide and aims to unite the efforts of government bodies, medical institutions, and public organizations to expand free screening programs, introduce modern diagnostic protocols, and remind every Ukrainian woman of the critical importance of undergoing an annual mammogram or ultrasound examination.
According to the new calendar, Orthodox and Greek Catholic believers honor the memory of Saint Artemius the Great Martyr of Antioch—a prominent Roman military commander and duke of Egypt during the reign of Emperor Constantine the Great.
When Emperor Julian the Apostate came to power and renewed the persecution of Christians, Artemius openly denounced the emperor for paganism and heresy. For this, the saint was subjected to severe torture, imprisoned, and executed by beheading in 362.
According to the old calendar, believers honor the memory of Saints Sergius and Bacchus the Martyrs—high-ranking soldiers and noble dignitaries at the court of Emperor Maximian Galerius.
Having professed their Christian faith, they refused to take part in a pagan sacrifice, after which they were stripped of their military ranks, dressed in women's clothing as a mockery, and sent to stand trial in Syria, where, after brutal torture, Bacchus was beaten to death with whips, while Sergius was executed with a sword.

University of North Carolina settles federal probes by Trump administration
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

University of North Carolina settles federal probes by Trump administration
WASHINGTON – US President Donald Trump’s administration has reached a settlement deal with the University of North Carolina (UNC) at Chapel Hill to close 18 federal probes over alleged race discrimination and anti-Semitism at the university.
Trump has targeted universities with probes and funding-suspension threats over pro-Palestinian protests against US ally Israel’s assault on Gaza, diversity initiatives, transgender policies and climate programmes, leading to free speech, due process and academic freedom concerns.
The voluntary settlement agreement released by both parties does not require a monetary settlement payment and will remain effective until the end of 2028.
UNC did not admit to any wrongdoing or liability and the deal maintained its eligibility for federal funding.
The agreement said UNC will appoint an internal administrator and establish a coordinator position in its compliance office to address discrimination, including anti-Semitism.
The agreement asks UNC to provide mandatory anti-Semitism training to students, faculty and staff.
The university said Elizabeth Hall, associate vice-chancellor for university compliance, was appointed to serve in both roles while being the point of contact for the Justice Department and overseeing UNC’s reporting obligations under the deal.
The agreement prohibited face masks or coverings concealing an individual’s identity during protests. It said student groups “shall be subject to discipline for anti-Semitic discriminatory conduct”.
Trump has alleged pro-Palestinian protesters are anti-Semitic and support extremism.
Protesters, including some Jewish groups, say opposing Israel’s occupation of Palestinian territories and its assault on Gaza is not anti-Semitic and advocacy for Palestinian rights does not imply supporting extremism.
A former Justice Department attorney said in a whistleblower complaint in August the Trump administration’s probes of universities over anti-Semitism accusations lacked evidence and had predetermined outcomes.
The settlement deal said UNC will adopt and maintain “non-discriminatory” admissions policies and “not use any racial proxy”.
It does not prevent UNC from considering how applicants overcame adversity at a personal level, and it may consider facets of family background like poverty if those considerations are applied consistently, the deal said.
The Justice Department said that on a quarterly basis, UNC will send any anti-Semitism and race discrimination complaints it has received to the US Justice and Education departments.
The Supreme Court rejected affirmative action at colleges in 2023 when it struck down race-conscious admissions programmes at Harvard and UNC.
Trump has cracked down on diversity initiatives, casting them as discriminatory against white people and men.
Civil rights advocates say they help marginalised groups like ethnic minorities, LGBT communities and women.
The government has also settled with some other schools.
In 2025, Columbia University agreed to pay more than US$200 million (S$256 million) to the government to resolve probes and Brown University said it would pay US$50 million to support local workforce development under a settlement.
Harvard has yet to make a deal. REUTERS

Trump approval falls to record low of 31% as midterms near, Reuters/Ipsos poll finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

08:50:45 KST

US President Donald Trump's approval rating fell to a record low as Americans worried about high gasoline prices and appeared ready to punish his Republican Party in the November 3 congressional elections, according to a Reuters/Ipsos poll that closed on Monday.
Some 31% of Americans approve of Trump's performance in office, down a percentage point from two weeks earlier and the lowest level in either of his presidential terms, the four-day poll showed.
Asked which party they would vote for if the congressional elections were held today in what is known as a "generic ballot" question, some 47% of registered voters in the nationwide poll picked Democrats, and 35% chose Republicans. The 12-point Democratic advantage was the widest over the current election cycle and could bolster Democratic hopes of seizing control of the US House of Representatives and the US Senate.
Loss of power could complicate Trump's agenda
For Republicans, losing control of either chamber could complicate Trump's agenda in the last two years of his term.
Generic ballot polls are national polls that provide an overall view of which party poll respondents want to see in charge in Congress. While these polls provide a view of national public sentiment, they do not capture all the nuances of the state-by-state and district-by-district contests that determine control of the Senate and House, contests in which Republicans hold some structural advantages.
A Reuters/Ipsos poll two weeks earlier showed Democrats leading Republicans by 7 points, 44% to 37%.
Much of the drop in support for Republican congressional candidates was due to a larger share of women saying they would pick Democrats. Some 50% of female voters said they would vote Democratic, compared to 32% eyeing Republican candidates. Men also favored Democrats, but by a smaller margin.
Trump's popularity has suffered since he ordered military strikes on Iran in February alongside US ally Israel. The war triggered a surge in gasoline prices, hitting household finances. Some 68% of Americans disapprove of Trump's handling of the economy, including 37% of self-identified Republicans.
Voters in the poll picked Democrats over Republicans as the better stewards of the economy, by 40% to 33%.
The survey, which was conducted online, gathered responses from 1,679 US adults, including 1,279 registered voters. The poll's results had a margin of error of 2 percentage points for all respondents and 3 points for registered voters.

AI tool predicts cancer survival chances with single face photo, study finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
23:50:00 UTC
08:50:00 KST

AI tool predicts cancer survival chances with single face photo, study finds
- Researchers say an AI tool can predict cancer patients’ survival chances from a single face photo, using risk scores to separate higher- and lower-risk groups.
- The model was trained on more than 40 million face images and over 30,000 cancer patient photos, and it estimated age with about five years’ error.
- Experts said it is not ready for clinical use and must be tested against doctors’ judgement, but the team says it may give doctors “one more piece of information”.
AI generated
Researchers built an AI tool that can predict cancer patients’ survival chances by using a single photograph of their face, complementing doctors’ gut instincts to potentially guide treatment decisions, especially when medical data is scarce.
The new model was trained to estimate a person’s age or, for those with cancer, their survival chances. The artificial intelligence was trained on more than 40 million images of people’s faces as well as photographs of more than 30,000 cancer patients, many of whom had already died.
The tool gave patients risk scores – those with the highest scores were more likely to die within 90 days, according to the research published in The Lancet Digital Health on Oct 19.
The scientists say the findings are a first.
Doctors are trained to assess patients just by how they look, said Raymond Mak, a radiation oncologist at Mass General Brigham Cancer Institute and one of the study’s authors, but they are “in general not very good at estimating end-of-life expectancy”.
“We think that using AI, we can capture some of that physiological reserve, risk for mortality, just from a face photo,” Mak said in an interview.
The AI tool showed it could estimate age with a margin of error of about five years and reliably allocate patients to higher- or lower-risk groups, which subsequently had different risks of death. The model worked across different ages, races, genders and types of cancer.
AI tools are increasingly being tested for cancer detection and treatment, from helping to diagnose patients by reading scans to predicting the risk of a patient developing cancer by analysing genetic and lifestyle risk factors.
Despite the promising results, Miroslaw Bober, professor of video processing and machine learning at the University of Surrey, said the tool is not ready for clinical use.
“Predicting an outcome is not the same as explaining it,” said Bober, who was not involved in the research. “It has not shown that these predictions add clinically useful information beyond doctors’ assessments of a patient’s general health and fitness, which were not measured in the study,” he said.
Bober added that the tool needs to be tested against doctors’ own judgment as well as across different hospitals and patient groups.
Mak, who developed the tool with his team, said he was stunned by how well it worked for survival. The algorithm focused mostly on the bridge of the nose and the area just beneath the eyes to make its assessment, they found.
He did some digging and found that Hippocrates was first to describe how sunken eyes and temples as well as a sharp nose were among the early physical signs of impending death.
The tool is unlikely to be used to deny or limit patients’ access to medicine, according to Mak. “We know that doctors at the end of life tend to overtreat,” he said. He views it as “a way for doctors to have one more piece of information”. Bloomberg

Mali has grappled since 2012 with a multi-front security crisis pitting the national armed forces and paramilitary allies against militant groups, Tuareg separatist groups, and criminal networks.

Tottenham Hotspur claimed their first Premier League victory of the season on Monday, defeating newly promoted Coventry City 3-1 in London in the final match of Week 7.
Roberto De Zerbi's side entered the match at the bottom of the standings with just three points from six games, having endured one of their worst starts to a league campaign.
Coventry created the first dangerous opportunities, with Tatsuhiro Sakamoto delivering a threatening cross in the seventh minute that nearly resulted in an own goal before goalkeeper Antonin Kinsky gathered the ball.
Two minutes later, Sakamoto saw his shot deflected over the crossbar after combining with Brandon Thomas-Asante.
Despite the visitors' early pressure, Tottenham broke the deadlock in the 14th minute through James Maddison.
Mohammed Kudus raced down the right flank, beat his marker and laid the ball off to Maddison, who curled a powerful right-footed strike from outside the penalty area into the top left corner beyond goalkeeper Carl Rushworth.
The goal was Maddison's first in the Premier League since February 2025, ending a 610-day league scoring drought during which he endured a lengthy injury-related absence.
Coventry responded five minutes after the interval when Jack Rudoni capitalized on a series of deflections inside the Tottenham penalty area before firing a shot past Kinsky to level the score at 1-1.
However, the hosts regained the lead in the 58th minute through Omar Marmoush, who scored his first goal for the club.
The Egyptian forward turned his defender near the left edge of the penalty area before curling a powerful effort into the far right corner, leaving Rushworth with no chance.
De Zerbi introduced Ben Davies in the 69th minute after Andrew Robertson suffered an injury.
Tottenham also welcomed back Dejan Kulusevski late in the second half, with the Swedish international replacing Marmoush to make his first appearance in 526 days following a lengthy absence through a knee injury.
Substitute Mathys Tel nearly extended the lead in the first minute of second-half stoppage time, curling an effort narrowly wide of the post.
Davies sealed Tottenham's victory in the sixth minute of second-half stoppage time after Coventry failed to clear Tel's cross, with Dominic Solanke touching the ball into the defender's path.
Davies struck with the outside of his left foot from outside the penalty area, and his low effort slipped under goalkeeper Rushworth's glove and into the net.
The result lifted Spurs to 16th place in the Premier League standings with six points, while Frank Lampard's Coventry dropped to 17th, also with six points.

The judge released three of the suspects under restrictive conditions but extended the fourth suspect's detention by three days, explaining that "there is reasonable suspicion that the offenses were committed."
The police operation, dubbed "Olive Leaf," began Monday morning in cooperation with the Shin Bet security agency, supported by Border Police units operating in the West Bank and IDF forces. Ten suspects were arrested during the operation.
Separately, a resident of Samaria was arrested Sunday on suspicion of involvement in other incidents of extremist violence. Prosecutors submitted a declaration of intent to indict him Monday, with an indictment expected as early as Tuesday.

“I would do it, not so much for Ukraine, because Russia, frankly, has been fine on Ukraine. They haven’t been doing much,” Trump told reporters when asked about a possible summit with Putin and Xi.
“We would have it to talk about nuclear weapons and denuclearization,” he added.
Asked whether he would discuss Ukraine at such a meeting, Trump said he would do “whatever I can do to end the war.”
The US president also defended his controversial deal involving Russian diesel exports and his decision to waive new sanctions against Moscow, measures Zelensky has criticized as benefiting Putin while Russian forces continue attacking Ukrainian civilians.

Russian Strikes Kill 2 in Kryvyi Rih as Dnipropetrovsk Region Braces for Winter Blackouts
Trump’s remarks came hours after a Russian drone struck a public park in the Kharkiv region, killing six civilians, including two children, and injuring 15 others, seven of them children.

“We ask that sanctions on Russia stay in place as long as the killings continue. We ask America to be strong,” he said.
Kyiv Warns Three-Way Summit Would Encourage Putin

Ukraine has rejected that argument, pointing to its constitutional and legal provisions governing elections during martial law, imposed following Russia’s full-scale invasion in February 2022.
Trump’s willingness to consider meeting Putin and Xi comes amid growing tensions between Washington and Kyiv over Russia sanctions, intelligence-sharing and military assistance.
Zelensky has criticized Washington’s decision to ease restrictions on Russian diesel exports, warning that additional energy revenues could help Moscow finance its invasion.

US agents arrest 11 in California on alleged illegal voting
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
23:40:00 UTC
08:40:00 KST

US agents arrest 11 in California on alleged illegal voting
Federal agents across California on Oct 19 arrested 11 non-citizens who were charged with crimes including fraudulently registering to vote in US elections, part of a dragnet that the government says bolsters its lawsuit against the most populous state in the run-up to the Nov 3 midterm elections.
The 11 are among 28 green card holders who are in the country legally but have been charged with various voting-related crimes – part of a coordinated effort by the federal government in California “to combat and root out fraud in US elections”, the office of First Assistant US Attorney Bilal Essayli in Los Angeles said in a statement.
The individuals came to the US from countries including Mexico, Belize, India, Georgia, Tonga and the Philippines.
Many of them went on to cast ballots illegally in several elections, the US says.
The arrests are part of a broader stand-off between the Trump administration and California’s top elected officials over the accuracy of the state’s voter rolls.
The US Justice Department last week sued California for allegedly failing to join an effort to remove 20,000 suspected non-citizens identified by the federal government from the state’s voter rolls.
“California refused to look at that list,” Acting Deputy Attorney-General Trent McCotter said in the statement. “Today’s charges show exactly what that refusal puts at risk. California must verify the citizenship of those more than 20,000 registrants before mail-in ballots are counted.”
California Attorney-General Rob Bonta, a Democrat who is defending the state in court, has said that any allegation of voter fraud “should be taken seriously and investigated”, his spokesman Walter Garcia said.
“The 28 individuals charged this morning represent a tiny fraction – approximately 0.0001% – of California’s more than 23 million registered voters,” Garcia said. “That’s not evidence of widespread voter fraud, even if the allegations are true.”
The Justice Department on Oct 19 asked the court handling its lawsuit against California to issue a temporary order requiring the state to set aside mail-in ballots from the 20,000 people on the list and take steps to verify their citizenship status before the votes are counted.
A hearing on the request has not been set.
Los Angeles County Supervisor Janice Hahn issued a statement calling the arrests “voter intimidation” and a “blatant attempt to undermine trust in our midterm elections” 15 days before election day, which is on Nov 3.
“These arrests are being used to paint a picture of widespread voter fraud when we know that is not the case,” Hahn said. “California has laws in place to protect the integrity of our elections, and LA County is fully abiding by them.”
The US Justice Department has ramped up arrests for alleged non-citizen voting or voter registrations in the weeks leading up to the midterm elections, filing more than 100 new criminal cases since the start of September, court records show.
US President Donald Trump has claimed without evidence that illegal voting by non-citizens swayed the election against him in 2020. Such cases are relatively rare in the US, studies of past elections have shown.
California officials including Bonta have blasted the Trump administration effort as a baseless attempt to interfere in the election and sow doubt about its potential outcome.
The list of suspected non-citizens is also likely inaccurate, the officials have said, and violates privacy rules. BLOOMBERG

====================================================================================================

‘Once-in-a-lifetime chance’: Japan launches historic mission to collect rocks from Mars’s moon Phobos
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
23:37:57 UTC
08:37:57 KST

Japan has successfully launched a spacecraft on an unprecedented mission to bring back samples from one of Mars’s moons that scientists hope will shed light on the origins of the solar system and life on Earth.
The Martian Moons Exploration (MMX) spacecraft, propelled by Japan’s flagship H3 rocket, lifted off before dawn from Tanegashima island in the country’s far south-west, the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (Jaxa) said.
The spacecraft is expected to reach Mars’s orbit in August next year and collect at least 10g of soil and rock from the surface of Phobos, one of two small, potato-shaped moons orbiting the planet. It is scheduled to return in 2031, Jaxa said.
The pock-marked moon, which has a diameter measuring 14 miles (22.5km), orbits Mars three times a day about 6,000km above its surface.
The flagship H3 rocket carrying the unmanned probe blasted off into a pitch black sky from Tanegashima Space Centre at 4:41am, witnessed by thousands of people who had woken up early to follow a livestream.
An hour later, Jaxa scientists declared the launch a success when the spacecraft separated from the rocket’s upper stage, prompting scenes of celebration in the flight control room.
Nasa has landed nine spacecraft on Mars over the past half a century, while China landed on the Martian surface in 2021, but this is the first time anyone has attempted to land on Phobos or the planet’s smaller moon, Deimos.
“There’s a lot of adrenaline and a lot of excitement and a lot of wow,” said Nasa astrophysicist Tom Statler, who is involved in the Japan-led project to collect samples.
Five space agencies are collaborating on the five-year mission, which will attempt to land a robotic prospector and a rover on Phobos, the larger and closer of the two moons.
The $578m mission features a five-tonne spacecraft that will sync with Phobos’ tight orbit around Mars when it arrives next summer. It will then eject a small French-German rover, named Idefix after the white terrier in the Asterix comics.
If all goes according to plan, the four-wheeled rover will bounce (due to gravity on Phobos being 1/1,000th as strong as Earth) for several minutes on Mars’s surface before coming to a halt. It will spend 100 days surveying the planet’s surface to find safe landing and sampling sites ahead of the arrival of the main craft, a four-legged stationary lander that will gather the samples.
The lander will spend only two hours on Phobos drilling and vacuuming up material, before launching back into space. Officials said it would observe Deimos during several flybys before leaving Mars’s orbit in November 2030.
“It is a once-in-a-lifetime chance. We are part of the first sample return mission from the Martian system,” said the Germany Space Agency’s rover chief Markus Grebenstein.
Scientists hope the samples will help them establish how Phobos and Deimos were formed and even offer clues about the origins of life. MMX’s findings will also help shape future Mars missions, including crewed expeditions, Nasa said.
According to one theory – the “giant impact” hypothesis – the two moons formed after a celestial body collided with Mars. A second proposition, known as the “capture” hypothesis, suggests that the moons are asteroids pulled in by Mars’s gravity.
Determining which theory is correct will help reveal “how a habitable environment for life might have arisen on the terrestrial planets”, Jaxa said, referring to the four planets closest to the sun: Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars.
The US and China are in a race to be the first to return rock samples from the surface of Mars. Nasa’s Perseverance rover, which has been roaming across Mars since 2021, has already collected samples, but its return to Earth was halted by the Trump administration after a congressional vote in January this year.
China’s Tianwen-3 spacecraft is scheduled to launch around 2028 and could bring back Mars samples as early as 2031, potentially before the Japanese moon mission’s return.
