US says immigrants from Sudan can keep protected status for now
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
22:23:37 UTC
07:23:37 KST

Breadcrumb
US says immigrants from Ukraine, Sudan can keep protected status for now
Immigrants from Ukraine and Sudan can keep their temporary protected status in the United States for now, the Department of Homeland Security said Monday, the day protections were set to expire.
In a statement, a DHS spokesperson said that announcements on Ukrainian and Sudanese TPS holders would "be made at the appropriate time" and that their immigration protections would remain in place.
Temporary protected status allows people already in the US to stay and work legally if their home countries are affected by natural disasters, armed conflict, or other extraordinary conditions.
The temporary respite is the second in as many months for certain immigrants under the TPS program, even as US President Donald Trump has moved to expel other foreign nationals as part of an aggressive immigration crackdown.
In September, his administration allowed TPS holders from El Salvador to retain their protections after earlier moving to revoke them from Haitians, Venezuelans, Somalis, Yemenis, Syrians and others.
The latest allowance comes as Trump has pivoted away from Ukraine in recent days, declining to impose tougher sanctions on Russia over the four-year-old war and lifting sanctions on Moscow's diesel exports.
Some 240,000 Ukrainians who fled the conflict have registered for TPS status in the United States.
There are an estimated 6,800 TPS holders from Sudan, where a war between the army and a rival paramilitary has created one of the world's worst humanitarian crises.
Global Refuge, a faith-based, refugee-focused nonprofit, welcomed the respite for Ukrainians and Sudanese enrolled in TPS but urged an official decision to give enrollees, their dependents, and employers certainty.
"The appropriate time to act was weeks ago. Families who depend on this status to stay safe and keep working deserve a formal decision in writing," Krish O'Mara Vignarajah, president and CEO of the group, said in a statement.

News Analysis: How West Bank settler violence is testing Israel ahead of elections
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
06:20:57 CST
07:20:57 KST

JERUSALEM, Oct. 20 (Xinhua) -- Israeli police on Monday arrested 10 suspects as part of an investigation into violent incidents involving foreigners in the West Bank over the weekend, including separate attacks targeting a Washington Post photographer and a European diplomatic delegation.
The rare move follows growing international alarm over settler attacks on Palestinians in the West Bank.
With national elections scheduled for next week, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu now faces growing international demands for accountability while managing tight political dependencies at home.
ATTACK ON DIPLOMATS DRAWS PRESSURE
The European diplomats were there to assess the situation in the West Bank amid escalating attacks by Israeli settlers on Palestinians trying to bring in their olive harvest, media reports said.
Though police have not identified the suspects, local media said they were Israeli settlers.
Netanyahu's office responded to the incident by noting the diplomats' visit hadn't been coordinated with the Israeli military and questioning how the event unfolded.
The European Union condemned the attack, called for accountability, and urged a halt to settlement expansion.
An Israeli official familiar with Israel-EU relations told the Israeli news website Ynet that Brussels' reaction was partly restrained due to Israel's upcoming election, as the EU seeks to avoid accusations of interference.
Monday's arrests marked a rare step, with critics questioning whether it was merely a temporary move under diplomatic pressure.
NETANYAHU'S ELECTORAL DILEMMA
Political calculations remain central to the Israeli government's approach. Netanyahu's ruling coalition relies heavily on far-right partners, including National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir and Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich, both strong advocates of settlement expansion.
Netanyahu therefore faces a delicate political balancing act. On one hand, he seeks to avoid alienating right-wing voters who favor expansion policies in the West Bank. On the other hand, failing to address attacks on foreign nationals risks alienating Western allies.
Political tensions have surfaced internally. Ben-Gvir alleged that Netanyahu assured European governments to shut him out of the next coalition.
Unverified or not, the claim highlights friction within the coalition. With polls showing a tight race for a 61-seat parliamentary majority, keeping Likud as the biggest bloc will be Netanyahu's opening bid for any post-election deal.
A TEST OF INTERNATIONAL STANDING
The arrest came as Western allies pile on diplomatic and economic pressure on Israel.
A coalition of 12 nations recently announced coordinated trade restrictions targeting Israeli settlements in the West Bank. Britain imposed a formal import ban on goods originating from the settlements, while the Netherlands implemented a trade ban on settlement products.
The moves mark a pivot from symbolic rhetoric to binding trade restrictions, though questions remain about whether they can exert meaningful pressure on Israel.
In a joint warning letter, 61 Israeli economists, including former central bank governors and finance ministry directors, cautioned that unchecked violence and settlement expansion pose a grave economic risk to Israel, warning that it could trigger wider restrictions and corporate divestment from Israel's banking and tech sectors.
Similarly, experts from the Israel Democracy Institute warned that unaddressed settler violence undermines Israel's international standing, noting growing friction in defense procurement, export markets and academic exchanges.
According to the institute's survey data, nearly two-thirds of Jewish Israelis, including a majority of right-wing voters, agree that violence against Palestinians damages Israel's international legitimacy. ■

Bulgarian PM meets Chinese FM, voices willingness to expand cooperation with China
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20

Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev meets with visiting Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi, also a member of the Political Bureau of the Communist Party of China Central Committee, in Sofia, Bulgaria, Oct. 19, 2026. (Xinhua/Peng Ziyang)
SOFIA, Oct. 19 (Xinhua) -- Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev met with visiting Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi here on Monday, expressing willingness to elevate the positioning of bilateral relations and expand cooperation with China across the board.
Asking Wang, also a member of the Political Bureau of the Communist Party of China Central Committee, to convey his sincere greetings to Chinese leaders, Radev said that Bulgaria cherishes its traditional friendship with China, admires China's tremendous development achievements, and regards China as an important stabilizing force for safeguarding peace in today's world.
Radev said that Bulgaria firmly adheres to the one-China principle and will not conduct any official exchanges with Taiwan. Bulgaria-China relations have a long history and bright prospects, and Bulgaria is ready to further elevate the positioning of bilateral relations and expand cooperation with China across the board, he said, adding his belief that Wang's visit will inject new impetus into this endeavor.
He also said that Bulgaria warmly welcomes Chinese enterprises to invest here, and will increase government support, ensure policy stability and provide a sound business environment.
Radev said that, historically, Western countries actively supported economic globalization and trade liberalization and viewed China as somewhat conservative and closed, but today China has become a staunch supporter of globalization and free trade.
He also said Europe has concerns about its trade deficit with China, but Chinese goods with high quality and competitive prices have helped curb inflation in Europe; in reality, neither side can do without the other. Bulgaria-China cooperation on connectivity enjoys good prospects, and Bulgaria is willing to serve as a gateway and bridge connecting Eurasia and linking Europe and China, Radev added.
For his part, Wang conveyed Chinese leaders' warm greetings to Radev, saying that forging a new future for China-Bulgaria relations requires consolidating the political foundation and deepening political mutual trust so as to create better conditions for bilateral cooperation in various fields.
China appreciates Bulgaria's continued adherence to the one-China policy and its understanding and support for China's legitimate position of safeguarding national sovereignty and territorial integrity, Wang said.
Noting that China and Bulgaria enjoy traditional friendship, with bilateral relations on a solid foundation and having broad prospects, Wang said that upgrading the positioning of bilateral relations is a natural and logical step.
Wang said China is ready to deepen political mutual trust, expand practical cooperation and achieve mutually beneficial and win-win results with Bulgaria, and that China will be Bulgaria's most reliable and long-term strategic partner in its development and revitalization.
He stressed that China is committed to advancing modernization and building a community with a shared future for humanity together with all countries. China is willing to work with Bulgaria to advocate multilateralism and free trade and promote the democratization of international relations.
Wang noted that the Belt and Road Initiative and the China-Europe Railway Express have boosted transcontinental and trans-regional connectivity, and these, together with Europe's Middle Corridor vision, can complement and reinforce each other, rather than exclude or offset one another.
China is ready to strengthen strategic alignment with Bulgaria, support Bulgaria in playing a bridging role in Eurasian connectivity, and achieve mutually beneficial and win-win outcomes for China and Bulgaria as well as for China and Europe, Wang said. ■

NEW YORK, Oct. 19 (Xinhua) -- U.S. state of Florida's Attorney General James Uthmeier on Monday issued an arrest warrant for Cuban Revolution leader Raul Castro on charges of conspiracy to commit first-degree murder linked to the 1996 downing of two civilian aircraft.
In May, Castro was indicted, along with five others, on U.S. federal charges related to the incident.
The prosecutors accused Castro of ordering the downing of two planes operated by Brothers to the Rescue, the Miami-based Cuban exile group, on Feb. 24, 1996.
Born in 1931, Castro served as Cuba's minister of the Revolutionary Armed Forces at the time of the incident.
Uthmeier said the arrest warrant will restrict Castro's ability to leave the island nation and prevent him from traveling to any place with an extradition agreement with the United States.
However, he acknowledged that Castro, now 95, is unlikely to willingly fly to Florida to face legal proceedings.
Earlier this year, Cuban President Miguel Diaz-Canel condemned the U.S. charges against Castro as a "political maneuver" with no legal basis whatsoever.
He said the indictment against Castro reveals "the arrogance and frustration" of U.S. officials in the face of the Cuban Revolution and is intended to "enlarge the file" Washington is building to justify possible military aggression against Cuba.
Castro is the youngest brother of the late Cuban Revolution leader Fidel Castro. A guerrilla fighter along with his brother, Raul Castro served as a military and political leader after the triumph of the revolution in 1959.
Since the beginning of 2026, the United States has announced new measures against Cuba, including restrictions targeting countries that supply oil to the island and additional sanctions against Cuban entities and officials.
In June, the United States imposed sanctions on five Cuban state-owned entities and a member of the extended family of Castro. In May, the U.S. government sanctioned 11 Cuban officials. ■

Yemen has been mired in conflict since late 2014, when the Houthis seized the capital Sanaa and much of the country's north. A Saudi-led coalition intervened in 2015 in support of the internationally recognized Yemeni government. ■

"OCHA is also deeply saddened by the killing of a Sudanese Red Crescent volunteer while providing first aid at a health center in the town of Um Darfa, in Blue Nile State, last week, following a drone attack on the facility," the office said. "Since the conflict began in April 2023, 25 Sudanese Red Crescent volunteers have reportedly been killed while on duty."
The office said international humanitarian law requires the protection of civilians and civilian infrastructure, including medical facilities and humanitarian personnel.
OCHA said rising food prices further challenge families struggling to meet their basic needs.
The World Food Programme said the cost of its local food basket rose by 24 percent in September compared with August. Currency depreciation, fuel shortages and conflict-related disruptions to markets and supply routes are driving up costs.
"Despite immense challenges, the United Nations and its humanitarian partners continue to deliver life-saving assistance," OCHA said. "In Central Darfur State, partners recently rehabilitated a water facility in the locality of Zalingei, restoring access to safe water for some 2,500 people. More than 2,000 families also received water, sanitation and hygiene assistance across several localities."
However, the humanitarian office said underfunding threatens relief operations.
With less than three months left in the year, Sudan's humanitarian response plan is just over 43 percent funded, with 1.2 billion U.S. dollars of the nearly 2.9 billion required received so far, OCHA added. ■

Feature: Shahla's basket -- the Lebanese daily struggle to make ends meet
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
06:20:25 CST
07:20:25 KST

BEIRUT, Oct. 19 (Xinhua) -- Moving between supermarket shelves in the eastern Lebanese city of Zahle, Joumana Abou Shahla compares prices carefully, weighing similar products to stretch her household budget.
Every item in her basket has become a calculation: what her family needs, what it can afford, and what must wait until another day.
"What matters now is whether I can afford to meet my family's needs with an income that no longer keeps pace with rising expenses," Shahla told Xinhua.
Choosing cheaper products, she said, has become a way to ease the daily burden, a struggle shared by many Lebanese households as rising costs make food, healthcare, and education harder to afford.
Lebanon's consumer price index rose 16.66 percent in August from a year earlier and 1.4 percent from July, according to the Central Administration of Statistics.
For Layla Abou Amer, a woman in her 50s living in Baalbek, eastern Lebanon, the strain is measured by how quickly the family's money runs out.
Her husband's monthly salary of about 600 U.S. dollars is exhausted within the first week of the month, Amer told Xinhua.
The family rations food, buys vegetables and fruit in small quantities, and occasionally borrows from local shops.
Jalal Saleha, who owns a food shop in the town of Bar Elias, said customers increasingly focused on necessities, shopping mainly during the first week of the month.
The strain extends far beyond grocery bills. An assessment, titled "An Enduring Nightmare" and released by the United Nations Children's Fund on Sept. 30, found that four in five households in Lebanon struggled to afford necessities.
Some 22 percent of surveyed households reported that their children had gone to bed hungry during the preceding two weeks, while 31 percent said their children had gone without needed healthcare, mainly because of financial constraints. 46 percent had reduced education spending, while 17 percent said their children had stopped attending school.
Job losses and declining earnings have further eroded families' ability to cope.
A July report by the International Labour Organization, based on a May survey of 2,485 private-sector workers employed in Lebanon before the conflict resumed in March 2026, found that 33 percent of respondents were no longer working. Among those still employed, average labor income had fallen by 14.8 percent. Accounting for both job losses and reduced earnings, average labor income across the surveyed population was estimated to have declined by 40.4 percent.
The impact was particularly severe in conflict-affected southern areas, with unemployment reported among 76.5 percent of surveyed workers from Nabatieh Governorate and 43.2 percent from South Lebanon Governorate.
As winter approaches, transportation, electricity, and heating costs add to the burden.
Samer Ayoub, an employee at a private commercial company earning about 550 dollars a month to support a family of four, told Xinhua that school bus fares had risen by 40 percent from last year, with schoolbooks, stationery, and other necessities also more expensive.
Economy and Trade Minister Amer Bisat attributed price pressures partly to fluctuations in global oil prices and market disorder, saying the ministry was conducting inspections and taking action against violators, while acknowledging that enforcement alone would not resolve the problem.
Lebanon's General Confederation of Labour called on Sept. 21 for an economic state of emergency, urging wage and transportation allowance adjustments and stronger oversight of fuel and food prices.
Meanwhile, the gap between needs and assistance remains stark. According to the Lebanon Response Plan, a unified humanitarian and stabilization framework co-led by the Lebanese government and the UN, over 2.3 million people needed food assistance during the first half of the year, while nearly 350,000 people had received assistance by the end of June.
For families like Shahla's, cheaper food can stretch a limited budget but cannot bridge the widening gap between earnings and essential expenses. The crisis is measured not only by inflation and lost earnings, but also in the quiet arithmetic of everyday survival: what families put in their shopping baskets, what they leave on the shelves, and what their children must do without. ■

News Analysis: Egypt's pledge to help defend Saudi Arabia centers on shared interests, balanced deterrence
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
06:20:14 CST
07:20:14 KST

CAIRO, Oct. 19 (Xinhua) -- Egypt's National Defense Council, at a meeting chaired by President Abdel Fattah El-Sisi on Sunday, decided to provide Saudi Arabia with "all necessary and possible forms of support" to safeguard the kingdom's security, while pledging to intensify diplomatic efforts to ease tensions between Riyadh and Yemen's Houthi group.
Egypt's decision, analysts say, stems from concerns that regional insecurity could spill over to its interests, and Cairo may offer defense support to Riyadh while steering clear of direct involvement in the conflict.
SHARED SECURITY INTERESTS
El-Sisi on Saturday asked parliament to authorize Egypt to defend Saudi Arabia if requested, while stressing he meant "defense," not war.
The development came amid escalating Houthi missile and drone attacks on Saudi Arabia, including strikes targeting King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh as well as oil facilities, highlighting the growing threat to critical infrastructure in the kingdom.
The Houthi group, which controls much of Yemen's Red Sea coastline, has also imposed a "maritime ban" on Saudi shipping and attacked Saudi tankers.
"No one can now separate Gulf security, Saudi security, the security of the Red Sea and Bab al-Mandab, and the future of the conflict in Yemen," said Abu-Bakr Al-Desouky, an Egyptian political analyst and expert on Gulf affair. "All these issues are interconnected and intertwined, and each affects the others."
Disruptions to Red Sea shipping have affected traffic through Egypt's Suez Canal, a major source of foreign currency for Egypt.
"Egypt seeks to protect navigation in the Red Sea and the Suez Canal, while remaining committed to defending a fellow Arab country," Al-Desouky told Xinhua.
The planned military support for Riyadh has apparently drawn domestic debate. Egypt's parliament on Monday postponed a vote on authorizing the move until Oct. 26 after several lawmakers reportedly requested to speak.
The Houthi-controlled parliament in Sanaa has warned Cairo against military involvement, with its speaker writing his Egyptian counterpart on Saturday to oppose any Egyptian military backing for Riyadh, Houthi-run al-Masirah TV reported.
DEFENSE SUPPORT, DIPLOMACY PUSH
Egypt has not disclosed details of any planned military support to Riyadh.
Hani Al-Gamal, deputy director of the Cairo-based Tafkir Center for Strategic Studies and Research, said any aid would focus on protecting Saudi airspace and borders, intercepting drones and missiles, and safeguarding Red Sea shipping, rather than offensive operations inside Yemen.
Pakistan and Türkiye on Oct. 5 agreed to deploy forces and capabilities in Saudi Arabia in accordance with their commitments under the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement, though no tangible action has been taken.
Al-Desouky said countries supporting Saudi Arabia seek to help protect the kingdom without joining the fight in Yemen, as a deeper entanglement could bring financial, security and political costs, including possible Houthi strikes on their own interests.
However, growing regional support for Riyadh, he said, could "provide leverage to push all parties to the crisis toward negotiations, provided the aim is to protect Saudi Arabia and defend its territory, rather than to subdue the Houthis."
Egypt, Pakistan and Türkiye could combine defensive cooperation with broader crisis-management efforts to help reduce cross-border attacks, facilitate talks, and safeguard freedom of navigation, he added.
"Negotiations, not military escalation, are undoubtedly the solution, the main solution to the crisis," Al-Desouky said. ■

"We are aware of an incident which targeted the property of a Leonardo employee last weekend," a company spokesperson said in a statement sent to AFP on Monday.
"We are also assisting Counter Terrorism Police with their ongoing investigation into this incident," they added.
Police Scotland confirmed officers were called on 11 October to a "report of vandalism to a property and cars" in Dunfermline, north of Edinburgh, where Leonardo has a site.
A video on the group's website appears to show someone tagging vehicles and a building wall with red paint.
The Sunday Times reported that The List had targeted three locations, including in Hampshire in southern England, where they reportedly slashed the tyres of a car belonging to an executive at Ultra Intelligence & Communications.
The List claimed on its website that it targeted Ultra's chief operating officer, whom it accused of working with Israeli arms company Elbit.
"We were called on Saturday, October 10, to a report of a criminal damage incident in Fleet," Hampshire police said in a statement quoted by the Times.
"It was reported that red paint had been thrown across the front of the house and two car tyres had been damaged," the police force added.
The group also said it targeted the home of Keysight's director of technology manufacturing.
The Palestine Action group was proscribed as a "terrorist" organisation by the UK government last year after a series of attacks targeting defence companies, including Elbit and Leonardo.
On its website, The List said it "escalated our actions against the home addresses of some of the most highly complicit companies in the ongoing genocide of our brothers and sisters in Palestine."
"Our list of complicit actors remains long, compiled through leaks, hacking and whistleblowers. If you work with Elbit, expect us," the group added.

Explosive-laden Ukrainian drone crashes in NATO state

Explosive-laden Ukrainian drone crashes in NATO state
An explosive-laden Ukrainian attack drone crashed in Lithuania on Sunday, damaging a passenger car, Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevicius confirmed on Monday.
The drone triggered a high-level air alert in several Lithuanian regions before crashing in the northern Pasvalys district, near the Latvian border. Debris from the UAV damaged a passing car, but no one was injured, according to National Crisis Management Center head Vilmantas Vitkauskas.
Sinkevicus said the response to the incident was different from standard procedures because the drone arrived from a fellow NATO nation.
“The drone entered from the Schengen Area, crossing the border with Poland, so the response was slightly different. Fighter jets were, of course, scrambled and tracked the moving object, but they were unable to see it visually due to adverse weather conditions,” the prime minister said.
On Monday, Sinkevicus confirmed that the UAV was identified as a Ukrainian strike drone. “There is no doubt that it was carrying an explosive payload.”
According to Lithuanian Defense Minister Robertas Kaunas, the drone was likely a part of a major Ukrainian attack on St. Petersburg, Russia.
“Some of the drones were diverted off course by Russia’s electronic warfare systems and ended up in our territory. This particular drone is a consequence of the attack on St. Petersburg,” the minister told the LRT broadcaster. He also identified the drone as a Ukrainian FVP-1 model.
The Ukrainian drone attack on St. Petersburg on Sunday night killed one person and injured five others, according to Governor Aleksandr Beglov. It also damaged more than a dozen apartment buildings and sparked a fire at an oil terminal.
Moscow has condemned the Ukrainian strikes on Russian civilian and energy infrastructure calling them terrorist attacks aimed at compensating for setbacks on the battlefield, where Russian forces have continued to advance.
Despite identifying the drone as Ukrainian, Lithuania blamed Russia for the incident. The case will be investigated as part of a Lithuanian probe into “Russia’s aggression against Ukraine,” a police official told Elta news agency. Kiev said it regretted the drone incident, while calling Russia’s actions “the root cause of the security threats in our region.”
Kiev has been ramping up its long-range UAV attacks on energy infrastructure in Leningrad Region, Russia, which surrounds the country’s second-largest city, St. Petersburg, since spring. The campaign resulted in a number of incidents where explosive-laden drones crashed in nearby NATO member states – Latvia, Lithuania, and Estonia – while on their way to Russia.
In July, Deputy Foreign Minister Sergey Galuzin said Russia has “verified data indicating that Latvia and other Baltic republics have already provided air corridors for Ukrainian drones that have attacked our country’s civilian infrastructure.”
The Baltic nations and Finland, which have been among the staunchest backers of Kiev in the EU amid the Ukraine conflict, previously denied any involvement in the drone attacks on Russia.
Russian Security Council Secretary Sergey Shoigu previously warned that if it turns out that the Baltic states and Finland “deliberately provide their airspace” to Ukrainian UAVs, Russia will have the right to self-defense in response to an “armed attack” under Article 51 of the UN Charter.

Qatari electricity lifeline for Lebanon includes 2 power plants
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
22:04:33 UTC
07:04:33 KST

Breadcrumb
Qatari electricity lifeline for Lebanon includes two power plants, LNG supply deal
Qatar plans to build two power plants in Lebanon over the next three years and sign a 20-year liquefied natural gas supply deal as part of a proposal to revive the ailing Lebanese power sector, Reuters said.
Lebanon's energy sector is at the centre of the country's financial and economic malaise, contributing tens of billions of dollars to the national debt since the country's 1975-1990 civil war even as it failed to deliver 24/7 power.
The state power company currently supplies just a few hours of power per day, with the rest coming from expensive private diesel generators that spew toxic exhaust often seen forming a yellow-grey layer of smog above Beirut.
Qatari Prime Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman al-Thani visited Lebanon last week and publicly promised to help revitalise the country's power sector. Few details were then presented to reporters.
But according to a proposal drafted with input from the Lebanese and Qatari governments, dated October 2026 and seen by Reuters, the programme "covers gas-fired power generation, LNG supply and regasification, renewable energy, battery storage, and regional electricity interconnections".
"The program aims to attract private/project financing without upfront Lebanese public-budget capital expenditure; payment obligations and guarantees remain subject to negotiation," the document said.
The blueprint, called the National Integrated Energy Investment Programme, still requires approval from both governments and remains subject to amendment, a person familiar with the matter said.
They set the implementation timeframe at three years if approvals come swiftly.
Qatar has long backed Lebanon financially and politically, stepping in multiple times over the last decades during political and economic crises.
The Qatari Foreign Ministry did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the proposed plan. Lebanon's energy minister also did not respond to a request for comment.
Proposal follows growing Qatari presence in Syria
According to the document, the plan includes two new combined-cycle plants at Deir Ammar in northern Lebanon and at Zahrani in the south, each at a capacity of 825 megawatts.
QatarEnergy would also enter a 20-year LNG supply agreement with Lebanon, using a floating storage and regasification unit with a capacity of 3.5 million cubic meters per day and the Arab Gas Pipeline via Syria with a capacity of 4.5 million cubic meters per day.
The proposal also includes plans for 800 MW of solar and 440 MW of wind, battery capacity and power imports from Syria, beginning with 300 MW via two separate routes.
Numerous proposals to reform Lebanon's power sector and provide electricity through the national grid have repeatedly stalled due to political bickering and the vested interests of senior politicians in the fuel and energy sectors.
The proposal would build on a growing Qatari presence in neighbouring Syria, where Qatari conglomerate Power International Holding has secured contracts for 5,000 MW of power generation, as well as oil and gas extraction and pipelines.

Elbit secures $235 million contract with European country for PULS launcher and EXTRA-MR rockets
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
21:57:18 UTC
06:57:18 KST

Elbit Systems has secured a $235 million government‑to‑government deal to supply EXTRA‑MR (Medium Range) rockets and PULS (Precise & Universal Launching System) launchers to an undisclosed European country, the company said Monday, marking another significant expansion of Israeli rocket‑artillery systems across Europe.
The three‑year contract, signed between Israel’s Defense Ministry and that of the unnamed country, covers delivery of the medium‑range variant of Elbit’s EXTRA supersonic rocket, along with PULS launchers, related platforms, and integrated logistics support.
Elbit Systems’ PULS provides a comprehensive and cost-effective solution capable of launching unguided rockets, precision-guided munitions, and missiles with various ranges. The PULS launcher is fully adaptable to existing wheeled and tracked platforms, enabling significant reductions in maintenance and training costs.
The EXTRA‑MR is a precision‑guided rocket with an 80‑km. range, designed for mid‑range strike missions against high‑value targets. It is fully compatible with the PULS launcher and existing C4I networks, positioning it as a flexible, lower‑cost option for armies seeking rapid‑response firepower without committing to full ballistic‑missile inventories.
The deal adds to a growing list of European militaries adopting PULS, which has gained traction among NATO members looking to expand long‑range fires after Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. Close to a dozen European countries including the Netherlands, Denmark, Greece, and Germany, have already selected the system in recent years.
The announcement underscores Israel’s accelerating defense exports into Europe, where demand for long‑range precision fires continues to surge amid shifting continental security requirements.
"This contract award further strengthens Elbit Systems’ position as a global leader in rocket artillery systems and reflects the growing international demand for our advanced rocket and launcher capabilities,” Bezhalel “Butzi”Machlis, president and CEO of Elbit Systems, said.
“The PULS systems and precision rocket solutions are recognized among the leading systems in their category and have been selected by a growing number of customers worldwide, including European and NATO member states. We remain committed to delivering advanced operational capabilities that support our customers’ evolving defense requirements," Machlis noted.

Laura Gamba Fadul
20 October 2026•Update: 20 October 2026
Venezuela's main opposition party, Vente Venezuela, on Monday announced a nationwide mobilization scheduled for Oct. 22 to demand safe passage for the party leader and 2025 Nobel Peace Prize laureate Maria Corina Machado to return to the country.
Speaking at a press conference in Caracas, national party leader Carlos Fernandez said the demonstrations will span all 23 states and unite a broad coalition of civil society, trade unions, youth groups and opposition parties.
“On Oct. 22, mothers, teachers, young people who want a prosperous future, all social sectors, the Plataforma Unitaria and political parties across the spectrum will take to the streets,” Fernandez said. “Set aside your fears. Maria Corina is coming to unite Venezuela and accelerate the transition.”
Beyond demanding Machado’s return, the opposition outlined three other core demands driving the street action.
In the first place, establishing a definitive date for presidential elections under the slogan “Election Day is Liberation Day!” Vente Venezuela endorsed a proposal originally put forward by US Congressman Bernie Moreno to set the presidential vote for July 24, 2027, a timeline publicly supported by Machado.
The party also demands the immediate and unconditional freedom of all detained opposition activists and political dissidents.
“Enough of keeping our brothers and sisters behind bars! Their families cannot take it anymore,” Fernandez emphasized.
The third demand is giving full political rights and the lifting of administrative disqualifications targeting opposition leaders.
Fernandez framed the Oct. 22 mobilization as the “spearhead for peaceful mobilization” amid worsening socio-economic conditions and infrastructure failures across Venezuela.
“Venezuela is going through one of the hardest times in its history,” he said. “Not only do we face persecution, torture and exile, but today we are dealing with a country in darkness, without water, and where our people are starving. We are living through it every single day.”
The protest call comes amid a third round of political transition talks between representatives of the government and a sector of the opposition. The negotiations resumed shortly after Washington lifted sanctions against Jorge Rodriguez, the chief negotiator for the administration and brother of interim President Delcy Rodriguez.
A central point on the negotiation agenda remains the lifting of political bans following Machado’s formal demand for the immediate removal of the administrative disqualification imposed on her in 2023 which barred her from appearing on the ballot during previous presidential election cycles.

World Food Programme cuts aid to 500,000 Palestinians in Gaza
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
21:54:42 UTC
06:54:42 KST

Breadcrumb
World Food Programme cuts aid to 500,000 Palestinians in Gaza, cites funding shortages
The UN World Food Programme has said funding shortages are forcing major cuts to its aid programme in Gaza, leaving about 500,000 people without monthly food support in a territory where two-thirds of the population struggle to get enough to eat.
The WFP said it was reducing the number of recipients of its monthly assistance from 1.6 million to 1.1 million.
In addition, food rations have been halved, cash assistance has been cut for 75,000 families, and daily hot meals for those unable to cook have fallen to 150,000 from 250,000, with some families in hard-to-reach areas now receiving a hot meal only every other day.
The WFP said about 1.4 million people, or two-thirds of Gaza's population, face crisis levels of food insecurity or worse, including roughly 200,000 people in emergency conditions.
Last year's US-brokered Gaza ceasefire calls for the eventual reconstruction of the territory. But little progress has been made towards implementing a deal to end the conflict that includes terms for Hamas to disarm and Israel to withdraw its troops.
Life is still brutal in Gaza, says acting head of WFP
"It's a year into the agreement of this ceasefire. Well, life is still brutal here. There is no proper shelter...There are no basic services. There is no safety, no security," acting Executive Director of the WFP Carl Skau told Reuters in Gaza.
"These cuts are happening just as we are facing the fourth winter. You know, I've been through the winters here, absolutely brutal," he added.
The WFP said it urgently needs $450 million over the next six months to maintain critical operations in Gaza and the Israeli-occupied West Bank.
"We tell the world now is not the time to look away. This is the time to step up to sustain this support, to protect the progress that has been made, but also to push for early recovery," said Skau.
Israeli forces still hold more than 60 percent of the territory and conduct almost daily airstrikes, while Hamas controls most of the area where more than two million Palestinians live, mostly in temporary shelters with what aid agencies call inadequate aid supplies.
The Gaza government media office described the WFP announcement as "catastrophic" and said it might accelerate famine in the enclave, calling for more fund to aid agencies to prevent it.
"On top of the circumstances and the difficult life, you want to make it even harder on us," said Palestinian woman Sabrine Kuhail, standing by a tent shelter at a displacement site in Nuseirat refugee camp in central Gaza Strip.
"You made us hungry for three years with war, destruction, siege, and the bloodshed that is not stopping. What do you want from us? Enough, enough, we are tired."

Elon Musk has quietly forked out more than $400 million to Republican organizations since July, making him the largest known donor of the 2026 midterm elections. But can money alone buy the midterms?
The windfall represents a change in tune from May 2025, when Musk, in the middle of a political feud with President Donald Trump, grumbled, “In terms of political spending, I’m going to do a lot less in the future.”
The donations come at a critical time for the Republicans who are struggling in the popularity polls amid a sluggish economy, political infighting, and an on-again, off-again war with Iran, a potential quagmire that has the MAGA crowd furious. Nevertheless, the slush fund is helping Republicans, who currently control both the House of Representatives and the Senate as part of the 119th United States Congress, to purchase pricey late-campaign advertising. Meanwhile, the Democrats have no billionaires in their corner who can match Musk’s financial power.
The biggest Musk payout was awarded to the Senate Leadership Fund, the primary super PAC that supports Republican Senate candidates. Musk lavished the organization with nearly $200 million over the summer, which was a quarterly record for one donor at the group and more than its Democratic counterpart raised from all sources in the same quarter.
At the same time, America PAC, the political action committee which Musk founded in 2024, got around $75 million from him over the same period. His federal committee contributions for the 2025-26 cycle now total around $400 million, including $90 million given before July. Musk previously gave around $290 million during the 2023-24 cycle.
America PAC spends most of its midterm budget on door-to-door canvassing and intensive field operations. PAC officials said nearly 3,000 paid canvassers worked across the country last month, and knocked on 6.5 million doors in seven Senate battlegrounds and nearly three dozen House races. The mission focuses on registering and turning out conservative voters, especially those who vote irregularly, a more difficult objective in a midterm year without Trump leading the ballot.
The PAC’s messaging focuses on socialism and transgender policy, hot button topics for their Democratic rivals. Its canvassers are focusing on connections between Democratic candidates to New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, two highly controversial figures who are members of the Democratic Socialists of America. Never before have socialists held such high positions in the US and that has many Americans vexed. At the same time, its best-known advertisement in Texas features Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico, who remarked in 2021 that God is “nonbinary.”
“If Democrats take control of Washington and win key gubernatorial and attorney general races this November, then America risks becoming a socialist, woke and borderless country,” America PAC spokesman Andrew Romeo told reporters in a recent interview. “These robust investments have allowed the G.O.P. apparatus to get its message out so Republicans can have a fighting chance to defy history.”
In other spending sprees, from July through September, Musk gave $20 million to the Congressional Leadership Fund, $10 million to the Republican Governors Association, and $2 million to the Republican Attorneys General Association.
Meanwhile, Texas, which accounts for more than a third of America PAC’s disclosed spending, has received more of Musk’s cash than any other state. He forked over $10 million to Lone Star Liberty PAC, which backs Republican Senate nominee Ken Paxton, at a time when Democrats were seriously outspending Paxton.
The Republicans, especially Trump, owe a lot to the world’s first trillionaire. Musk endorsed Trump for the 2024 presidential election and became one of his largest political donors, reportedly spending hundreds of millions backing him and other Republican candidates. Trump returned the favor by putting Musk in charge of the Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE) to slash federal spending.
The seemingly unbreakable relationship between Trump and Musk collapsed after the US president pushed through his One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which Musk has called a “disgusting abomination,” “debt slavery,” and “political suicide.” The fracture between the two men was so serious that Musk went on to create the America Party to challenge the two-party system.
Today, Musk, apart from funneling massive amounts of money into Republican campaign coffers, has remained on the sidelines of the political process to devote more time to his various business ventures. His dream of a third party has also been put on hold as he did not file formal registration paperwork with the Federal Election Commission to legally establish the America Party.
In the meantime, the native of South Africa will have to wait and see if his vast funds can make a difference in one of the most momentous midterm elections in history.

What we know so far about the attack on Helen Haines

In brief
- Independent MP for Indi Helen Haines has undergone surgery after being struck by a vehicle outside her office.
- Haines was airlifted to Melbourne's Alfred hospital where she remains in a critical condition.
Independent MP Helen Haines remains in a critical condition in a Melbourne hospital after she was allegedly deliberately struck by a four-wheel drive outside her electorate office in Victoria's north-east.
A 43-year-old man is in custody and counterterrorism authorities have joined Victoria Police in investigating the incident.
The suspect arrested can been named as Brendan Nugent.
A senior security source confirmed the man's identity to SBS News.
The 43-year-old from Tarrawingee, a town in north-eastern Victoria, was arrested at the scene on Monday afternoon and spent the night in custody.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
He was being questioned by police on Tuesday morning.
Witnesses say the driver made a sharp U-turn before striking Haines outside her Wangaratta office on Monday afternoon.
A bystander who intervened and restrained the alleged attacker has since been praised as a "hero" by Prime Minister Anthony Albanese.
Authorities are still working to establish a motive.
Here's what we know so far.
What happened?
Haines, 65, was struck by a Toyota LandCruiser outside her electorate office in Wangaratta shortly after 3.30pm on Monday.
According to eyewitness accounts relayed by Albanese, Haines was retrieving something from the boot of her car when the vehicle carried out a sharp U-turn and struck her.
"This wasn't something with a car just going off the road. This is something that is very clear was aimed at causing harm to Helen Haines," Albanese told ABC News24 on Tuesday.
Witnesses told media outlets they saw Haines trapped between vehicles outside her office after the impact.
Haines suffered critical injuries and was airlifted to Melbourne's Alfred Hospital, where she remains in a critical condition.
A knife was allegedly found inside the vehicle after a bystander intervened and performed a citizen's arrest.
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese praised Wangaratta resident Ricky Jefferies, who allegedly restrained the suspect after the incident, describing him as a "hero" whose actions may have prevented further harm.
Authorities have not publicly identified a motive and have not said whether the suspect had any prior connection to Haines.
Albanese has repeatedly described the incident as a deliberate attack.
"This wasn't an accident. There was a deliberate act, it would appear," he told ABC's 7.30 on Monday night.
"We don't know what the motivation is. So that is the work that's being undertaken."
What's the latest?
The crime scene outside Haines' electorate office has now been cleared, but investigations are continuing.
Victoria Police are leading the inquiry, supported by the Australian Federal Police, ASIO and Victoria's Joint Counter Terrorism Team.
Speaking on Tuesday morning, Albanese said authorities were still working to establish why the attack occurred.
"The police have a suspect in detention, and the police are going through their investigation," he told Sunrise.
"It's being led by Victoria Police, but in conjunction with the Australian Federal Police and ASIO, through the counterterrorism task force.
"It's important here that people allow that process to take place, that we deal with facts rather than speculation, and at this stage, it's not clear what the motivation of this attack was."
Haines underwent surgery on Monday night and remains in a critical condition at Melbourne's Alfred Hospital.
In a statement issued on Monday evening, her family thanked bystanders, emergency workers and police who responded to the incident.
"We thank the swift assistance of bystanders and the dedicated health workers who assisted her, and police for their response," the statement said.
The family said they would make no further comment and asked for privacy to be respected.
The prime minister said he was due to receive further briefings on the investigation on Tuesday.
What does it mean for politicians' safety?
The attack has prompted renewed concerns about the safety of elected representatives and the increasingly hostile nature of political debate in Australia.
Albanese said the political climate had become increasingly hostile over recent decades.
"There has been too much shouting, not enough discourse, not enough polite conversation and disagreement," he said.
"We want to encourage people to participate and to have their say and to do so in a way, though, that doesn't create tension and in a way that is respectful."
Asked whether additional security measures may be introduced for parliamentarians, Albanese said the government would follow the advice of security agencies.
The attack is one of the most serious incidents involving an Australian parliamentarian in recent years and has raised fresh questions about how MPs engage with their communities.
Nationals MP Sam Birrell, whose neighbouring electorate borders Indi, said regional MPs may need to reconsider aspects of that engagement.
"Many of us in regional communities go and advertise that we're going to be in a certain place," he told the ABC. "The idea is in Australia, you represent your people. You want to hear from them."
"I don't want to see that lost, but obviously we need to understand what's happened here and whether there are things that we need to do."
Independent senator David Pocock said the attack should serve as a reminder that violence against politicians could never be accepted.
"It's clearly time to come together and make sure we don't go down a path where violence against parliamentarians or any form of political violence is tolerated here in Australia," he said.
Bridget McKenzie said female politicians in particular continued to face threats and abuse.
"It seems female MPs in particular are fair game, with sexually violent threatening commentary," she told ABC Radio Melbourne.
How have politicians reacted?
Political leaders from across the spectrum have condemned the attack and wished Haines a recovery.
Albanese said there was no place for political violence in Australia.
Opposition Leader Angus Taylor described the incident as a "shocking day" for the nation.
"No one should be targeted in this way," he said.
"Our nation cannot become a place where violent attacks are normalised.
"I've spoken with the Prime Minister, and we are united in our view that political violence must never be accepted as part of public life."
One Nation leader Pauline Hanson also condemned the attack.
"Violence against any elected representative, whoever they are and whatever they stand for, is never acceptable in Australia," she said.
"Members of parliament and their staff must be able to serve their communities without fearing for their safety."
Greens senator David Shoebridge said he was "horrified" by the incident.
"Helen is an extraordinary human being and brings people together like few others," he said.
Nationals leader Matt Canavan described Haines as "a lovely lady" who worked "tirelessly" for her local community.
"The world just isn't fair, is it, that somebody like that can have something so traumatic occur to her," he told ABC News24.
Albanese said Haines was widely respected across parliament and in her electorate.
"Helen was a kind, caring advocate," he said.
"There's a reason why Helen Haines is so loved and admired, because she's someone of integrity. She's someone who treats everyone with respect."

Egyptian parliament delays vote on military support for Saudi Arabia
Lawmakers adjourn second session as one party tells members to abstain over unclear commitment.
Egypt’s parliament has delayed a vote on authorising its armed forces to support Saudi Arabia, which has come under increasing attack from the Iran-aligned Houthis in Yemen.
The vote has been adjourned to October 26, the House of Representatives said on Monday. The move prolongs the debate over Egypt’s role in the Yemeni conflict.
The opposition Egyptian Social Democratic Party said it had told its lawmakers to abstain.
The party said parliament had not been given enough information about the mission’s objectives, duration, cost, or the risks to Egyptian troops.
However, the party, which holds nearly a dozen seats, said most of its lawmakers support the measure, according to two members of parliament who spoke to the AFP news agency.
The parliament has been tasked with authorising President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi to approve any request from Saudi Arabia for defence assistance amid attacks on the kingdom by Yemen’s Houthis.
The call for support came after the Iran-backed rebel group attacked Riyadh’s international airport and the state oil company Saudi Aramco last week. Saudi authorities say 13 people were killed in the October 10 attack on the airport.
El-Sisi said on Saturday that Egypt would take “any measure” needed to protect its Gulf allies.
“I’m not talking about confronting or attacking anyone,” el-Sisi said. “We’re talking only about defence.”
After approval from the National Defence Council, chaired by el-Sisi, Egypt’s constitution requires a two-thirds parliamentary majority to send troops on a combat mission abroad. The council gave its approval on Sunday.
Egypt’s rocky economy
The Grand Imam of al-Azhar urged Arab and Muslim leaders on Sunday to mediate Egypt’s parliamentary decision and avert further bloodshed.
Saudi Arabia holds an important role in financing Egypt’s rocky economy. It is due to deposit $5.3bn into Egypt’s central bank this month, plus $267.39m in interest.
Egypt’s EGX30 stock index fell early on Monday amid concerns about possible military involvement but recovered to close 0.4 percent higher.
Nematallah Choucri, head of research at HC Securities, told the Reuters news agency that geopolitical developments are the main driver of recent market losses.
Egypt is also affected by the shortage of oil and gas exports from the Middle East due to the United States war on Iran and fighting in Yemen.
Egypt’s economy is heavily dependent on remittances from Egyptians working in the hydrocarbons industry in Saudi Arabia.
Suez Canal threat
Political analyst and Gulf studies expert Thomas Bonnie James told Al Jazeera that the Houthi security threat to Saudi Arabia also threatens the Suez Canal, which Egypt’s foreign minister says has lost about $11bn since the Houthis launched attacks in the Bab al-Mandeb strait in solidarity with Gaza in 2023.
James also said Egypt does not want to be seen as the regional ally that “stood aside while others defended the kingdom”.
Turkiye and Pakistan have made their own pledges after activating the Mecca defence pact with Riyadh, signed in August, amid the deteriorating security situation in the Middle East.

Japan launches ambitious robotic mission to Martian moon Phobos
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
21:42:23 UTC
06:42:23 KST

Japan launches ambitious robotic mission to land on Martian moon Phobos, return samples to Earth
Japan launched an ambitious $350 million mission to Mars on Monday to study the red planet's two moons in unprecedented detail, dropping a small rover on the largest — Phobos — before the mothership touches down to robotically collect soil samples for return to Earth.
The primary goal of the Martian Moons Exploration mission, or MMX, is to determine whether Phobos and the smaller moon Deimos were created by the impact of a large body early in the solar system's history or whether the two are asteroids that once passed close enough to Mars to be captured by the red planet's gravity.
The Martian moons are much smaller than Earth's, with Phobos measuring just 17 miles across at its widest while Deimos is less than half that size. Both are irregularly shaped and similar in appearance to asteroids. But size and shape alone are not enough to answer the question of their origin.
"One of the most intriguing questions about Phobos and Deimos is simply why these two little moons are there in the first place," said Thomas Statler, who helped oversee development of two NASA instruments aboard the MMX spacecraft.
"In some ways, they resemble asteroids from the outer part of the asteroid belt ... but there (are) other lines of evidence pointing to these moons being remnants of a giant impact early in Mars' history."
The collected samples, expected to be returned to Earth in 2031, should answer that question one way or the other.
"By going to the Martian moons, studying them up close and bringing samples back to Earth, we'll be able to determine whether Phobos material is more consistent with an asteroid composition or with debris created by a collision involving Mars," Statler said.
The mission got underway at 3:41 p.m. EDT (4:41 a.m. Japan time) with the sky-lighting launch of a Japanese H3 rocket from the picturesque Tanegashima Space Center operated by the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency, or JAXA.
Four solid-propellant strap-on boosters and two hydrogen-fueled first stage engines powered the rocket out of the dense lower atmosphere before the H3's second stage took over to continue the climb to space.
One hour and 11 minutes after liftoff, following two firings of the upper stage engine, the 9,900-pound MMX probe was released to fly on its own.
If all goes well, the spacecraft will brake into orbit around the red planet in September 2027 on a trajectory that will allow it to circle the planet in lockstep with Phobos.
MMX will spend three years in that orbit, training a battery of instruments on Phobos and its surrounding environment, studying its chemical and mineral composition, assessing its possible use as a staging base for future astronauts and dropping a small rover, supplied by the German and French space agencies, onto the moon's surface in early 2029.
The 55-pound rover is not equipped with braking rockets or anything else to slow its descent. Given the gravity of Phobos is just 1/1,000th as strong as Earth's, the rover is expected to bounce down on the surface, tumbling gently to a stop.
It is designed to right itself regardless of how it ends up after coming to rest and then to begin its surface exploration. It is equipped with cameras for navigation and to study the soil as it rolls about, an instrument to fire laser beams into the ground to determine what minerals might be present and another that will monitor soil temperatures.
About a year after the rover's landing, in the 2030 timeframe, the MMX spacecraft itself will touch down on Phobos once and possibly twice to collect a tiny amount of soil using two devices, one built by JAXA and the other supplied by NASA.
The official mission requirement is to capture at least 10 grams, or less than half an ounce, of material. Depending on the nature of the soil, however, the sample size could be larger.
The MMX then will lift off and, after wrapping up remote observations of Deimos, head back to Earth, putting the Phobos samples into an aerodynamic, heat-resistant capsule that will re-enter the atmosphere over Australia, where a recovery team will be standing by.
The samples will be studied by an international team of researchers.
"There's a lot of adrenaline, a lot of excitement, and a lot of wow," said Statler. "MMX will be the first spacecraft ever to return to Earth from the Mars system. That says a lot."
But "the most exciting thing of all," he said, "will be watching the sample return capsule re-enter Earth's atmosphere and opening that capsule and seeing those materials for the first time. There is absolutely no lack of excitement and adrenaline on this mission."

Torrential rain battered eastern Spain, unleashing severe flooding that left at least four people dead in recent days, inundated streets and forced many residents to stay indoors, authorities said Monday.
The downpours, which pummelled parts of Spain's Mediterranean coast particularly hard, dumped as much as 700 litres of rain per square metre (155 US gallons per square yard) in just 24 hours in some areas of the Valencia region.
Floodwaters swept away parked cars, submerged roads and cut off residents, some of whom had to be airlifted to safety by emergency crews.
"We are talking about three deaths," Valencia regional president Juan Francisco Perez Llorca told reporters Monday, while urging caution as authorities assessed the damage.
Two of the victims were found in the coastal resort of Oliva, one of the areas worst hit by Sunday night's storms.
One was a 79-year-old woman found in her home, while another was a man who suffered a fatal heart attack at a local campsite.
The third victim was a man who drowned Sunday while swimming at a beach in Sagunto.

Firefighters in neighbouring Catalonia had on Sunday also reported the death of a woman who fell into a rain-swollen stream.
Security forces carried out more than 400 rescues in the Valencia region, both by air and land, according to government representative Pilar Bernabe.
The heavy downpour, which also lashed the Balearic Islands and Catalonia, prompted authorities to order around 100 municipalities to remain indoors for several hours.

Scientists say human-driven climate change is intensifying the Mediterranean storms that typically hit eastern Spain in autumn as the sea absorbs heat during the summer, leading to increased evaporation and heavier rainfall.
National weather agency AEMET announced Friday that last month was mainland Spain's hottest September on record, after the country registered its warmest summer between June and August.

Colorado wildlife overpass cut vehicle-animal collisions by 91%, report finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
21:39:09 UTC
06:39:09 KST

Colorado officials have tracked herds of elk, bears, pronghorn and even northern leopard frogs ambling across its new wildlife overpass. According to a newly released report, the overpass, which acts as a bridge over a busy stretch of interstate, has helped cut wildlife-vehicle collisions by 91% since its completion 10 months ago.
The overpass is the centerpiece of a larger system built by the state to assist wildlife crossing the highway, which also includes miles of 8-ft tall fencing and five large wildlife underpasses.
“One of the most heartwarming moments for me was when [Colorado department of transportation] sent me a picture of an elk mama taking her calf under [Interstate-25],” Brandon Marette, a wildlife biologist for Colorado parks and wildlife, told CBS News. “All came to fruition in that one moment. That elk with her calf was just standing there in safety.”
The Colorado department of transportation said before the overpass system was built, there was an average of one wildlife-vehicle crash a day in this corridor.
Such wildlife crossings are popping up across the country as a way to protect wildlife habitat and reduce collisions, which can result in injuries and deaths in humans and animals. Research has shown that overpass systems are successful in “nearly eliminating” these accidents and that such infrastructure buildouts often “pay for themselves” by preventing costly crashes.
Nearly 20 wildlife crossings are under way in the US, with the structure in Colorado currently the biggest. The overpass, which sits between the state’s two biggest cities, Denver and Colorado Springs, spans six lanes of traffic and connects 39,000 acres of habitat on both sides of the interstate. The bridge is covered in grass and measures 200ft wide and 209ft long with gradually sloped entrances to ease crossings for animals.
This region of Colorado is known for high movement of large game. State officials say that wildlife underpasses and tunnels often don’t work for big animals, such as bull elk, because they restrict mobility and don’t accommodate their antlers.
“Elk and pronghorn like these big open structures where they can see for miles in each direction,” Chuck Attardo, the environmental manager for Colorado department of transportation, told CBS News. “For decades, pronghorn going from Trinidad to Greenland were looking for a place to cross on I-25. And when we open this up, we have pronghorn on video using the overpass, and for the first time in decades they’re coming over here to the west side.”
While large game animals have been taking advantage of the crossing, officials have also tracked smaller wildlife using the corridor, including mule deer, coyotes, rabbits, frogs and the threatened Preble’s meadow jumping mouse.
The project received $22m in federal funding and $8m from the state, but officials say they were able to complete it for just $15m. Now, the Colorado department of transportation says it is hoping to build other wildlife crossings across the state.

160 people reported killed in escalating drone attacks across Sudan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
21:38:46 UTC
06:38:46 KST

160 people reported killed in escalating drone attacks across Sudan
Rights groups warn increasing attacks by unmanned aircraft are targeting civilians and infrastructure.
Sudan army accused of drone strike on livestock market
A wave of drone attacks across Sudan has killed more than 160 people in recent days, according to medics and rights groups.
Drone attacks on Khartoum killed three children on Monday, according to Emergency Lawyers, a group that monitors violence against civilians in Sudan’s civil war, while more than 160 were reported to have been killed in western regions since Friday.
The attacks were blamed on both the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) and government forces, They have been fighting since 2023, but the increasing use of drones in recent months has caused growing numbers of civilian casualties.
The deadliest recent attack was near a market on Sunday evening in Al-Dibab town in the southwestern state of West Kordofan, which is controlled by the RSF. Residents and medical workers said a drone attacked a transport hub where villagers had gathered after a market day to find rides home, killing 80 people.
Another 47 wounded people were taken to the nearby town of Al-Mujlad, where 30 later died from their injuries, a medical source said, according to the AFP news agency.
The RSF’s self-declared administration, known as Tasis, and Emergency Lawyers accused the army of carrying out the attack.
Dams attack
In eastern Sudan, a military source said on Sunday that air defences intercepted several RSF drones targeting the Atbara and Setit dams in Gadaref state, about 420km east of Khartoum. There was no immediate comment from the RSF.
Early on Monday, another drone attack hit the RSF stronghold of Nyala, the capital of South Darfur. Medical and RSF sources said 17 people, including seven RSF officers, were killed and 23 wounded.
An RSF drone attack on Friday hit a gathering of displaced people in Sudan’s Blue Nile province on the border with Ethiopia, killing 41 people, Emergency Lawyers said.
The group condemned the attack, calling it a humanitarian tragedy.
The United Nations condemned the deadly attacks on Monday.
“We are alarmed by the continued deadly drone strikes across the country that are killing civilians, including children, and that are disrupting central services,” Stephane Dujarric, spokesperson for UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres, told reporters.
At least 59,000 killed
The current war in Sudan began in April 2023 when the military leader, Abdel Fattah al-Burhan and RSF leader Mohamed Hamdan Dagalo, also known as Hemedti, fell out over plans to fold the paramilitary into Sudan’s army.
In June, Hemedti was sentenced to death in his absence for war crimes.
However, the fighting, now in its fourth year, continues and has killed at least 59,000 people, according to conflict monitor ACLED. Aid groups say the actual toll is likely higher.
The UN says about 13 million people have been forced from their homes, creating what aid groups call the world’s largest humanitarian crisis.
Across Sudan, 33.7 million people, including 17.3 million children, urgently need food support this year. An estimated 825,000 children face severe, acute malnutrition, according to the UN.
The United States on Friday urged the UN Security Council to push for a humanitarian truce and expand an arms embargo on Sudan, but China and Russia opposed widening the embargo.

DHS officials urged secret purchase of voting machine for hacking test after Trump took office: Report

Merve Gül Aydoğan Ağlarcı
20 October 2026•Update: 20 October 2026
Political appointees at the US Department of Homeland Security (DHS) pressed the country's cybersecurity agency to quietly buy a voting machine and try to hack it shortly after President Donald Trump began his second term, ProPublica reported Monday.
Two former administration officials told the outlet that the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) was to pass its findings to the White House and keep any discovered vulnerabilities from the machine's manufacturer, a break from normal procedure.
Career staff saw the request as a possible step toward political interference, as one former official told the outlet that "my thought was they could keep it in their back pocket to invalidate any (election) results they don’t like."
CISA employees repeatedly said the task could not be done, partly because the specialists able to carry it out had been dismissed under billionaire Elon Musk’s Department of Government Efficiency. The appointees eventually dropped the matter, according to the report.
Since Trump returned to office, more than 1,000 CISA employees have been laid off or pushed out, cutting the agency by roughly a third. His 2027 budget proposal seeks another $700 million reduction, which could mean 900 further job cuts.
Several state election offices said they received no help from CISA while planning for the midterms.
"There is a difference between deprioritizing and being nonexistent," Ryan Macias, an election security expert who has consulted for the agency, said in the report.
States also say the administration's release of declassified 2020 election records, which included sensitive information they had given CISA in confidence, has damaged trust.
Arizona Secretary of State Adrian Fontes said he told acting CISA Director Nick Andersen in an August call that he did not trust him.
"What they’ve done is basically cut us off and left us on our own," Fontes said.
CISA released a 13-page election security plan on Sept. 24. Maine Secretary of State Shenna Bellows said the offer of support came "too little, too late."
White House spokesperson Lauren Bis said Trump "has done more than any other president to ensure we have free and fair elections."

Andy Burnham outlines new rules to outlaw ‘rip-off’ private parking fines
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
21:30:07 UTC
06:30:07 KST

Drivers will get a guaranteed five minutes to decide whether to park and 10 minutes to leave after their parking session ends before they face a fine under new rules for private car parks that Andy Burnham said were designed to outlaw “rip-off” charges.
In the latest in a series of “everyday fixes” to ease the cost of living and give consumers a “fairer” deal, the prime minister said a new official code of practice for the industry meant motorists in England, Scotland and Wales would enjoy a range of new rights.
The consumer body Which? said the “long overdue” rules appeared to fall well short of what was needed to help drivers fight back against private parking “cowboys”, however.
Each year in the UK, private firms dish out millions of parking tickets, and the number has been climbing. In August, the RAC said the number issued rose 17% in a year to reach a record 16.9m in 2025-26.
Complaints about poor behaviour by some operators are rife, and campaigners say reform is years overdue. Legislation was passed in early 2019, and an official code of practice was unveiled by the then government in early 2022 – but lasted less than six months after legal challenges by several parking firms forced it to be withdrawn.
In a fresh push, a new private parking code of practice is due to be laid in parliament on Tuesday, though it is unclear when this will take effect. Ministers said they would look to bring the code into force “as soon as possible”.
New rights for drivers include “a guaranteed five minutes to decide whether to park, and 10 minutes to leave once their session ends”.
The government is sticking with the existing industry maximum parking charge of £100 despite calls to halve it. Which? said: “It is particularly concerning that the government has shied away from a £50 price cap.” The consumer body had called for a maximum £50 fine, and this was also the amount at which some charges were capped under the withdrawn code.
Meanwhile, fines will be scrapped on appeal for “honest mistakes”, such as stopping briefly to check directions, and for situations such as a medical emergency, vehicle breakdown or broken ticket machine.
For “smaller slip-ups”, such as forgetting to display a parking permit or entering the wrong vehicle’s registration, the government said drivers would face a maximum charge of £20 on appeal. This appears to be a less generous system than under the original rules: the code that was withdrawn required the cancellation of a parking charge “in all mitigating circumstances”.
Which? said the government had also shied away from an independent appeals body “that could rein in the industry’s worst practices” and had failed to take action on private parking debt recovery fees, which it said were regularly added without motorists’ knowledge and pushed unfair charges even higher.
On the latter point, the government has promised to consult on these fees – which are added when a fine becomes overdue – “as soon as possible next year”. These fees are currently capped at £70, and the consultation will look at whether they should be cut or scrapped altogether.
Burnham said: “Being a few minutes late back to your car or typing one digit of your number plate wrong shouldn’t end with a hefty fine landing on your doormat.
“These charges leave people feeling ripped off and out of pocket, so I’m putting a stop to them. We are introducing clearer rules, longer grace periods and lower charges for genuine mistakes.”

Asian Para Games | Gabbasov's long road to gold leads past a friend
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
05:25:06 CST
06:25:06 KST

TOYOTA, Japan, Oct. 19 (Xinhua) -- Yerkin Gabbasov from Kazakhstan knew that South Korea's Park Jinho was his friend and the arch rival on the shooting range at the 2026 Asian Para Games.
The 43-year-old fired a Games record 249.1 points in the men's 10m air rifle standing SH1 final on Monday, edging Park Jinho by 0.6 points and reversing their finish at the Paris Paralympics two years ago.
"I was preparing for two years because I wanted to beat my opponent and friend from Korea," Gabbasov said after securing Kazakhstan's first gold of the tournament.
"We are friends in real life, but I wanted to beat him."
Park took gold in Paris, where Gabbasov's silver made him Kazakhstan's first Paralympic shooting medallist.
The Kazakh had already won the same event at the World Cup in Changwon, South Korea, earlier in 2024.
But his route to the international shooting stage had been a long one.
In 2007, Gabbasov fell from a building under construction. He spent two years confined to bed and had to learn to sit in a wheelchair.
He later found work at a public service centre in Kokshetau and tried several sports before taking up shooting seriously in 2021.
Three years later, he was on the Paralympic podium.
His wife Shynar supported him throughout his recovery and sporting career.
Gabbasov has described how she turned him in bed, tended to his medical needs and made plans for their future while he struggled to recover.
She accompanied him to Paris. Asked whether he could have competed without her, Gabbasov said he could not have let his country down.
In Japan, he went one better.
His victory also secured Kazakhstan a shooting quota place for the Los Angeles 2028 Paralympics. Under the qualification rules, the berth is allocated to the national Paralympic committee.
But qualification had not been on Gabbasov's mind during the final.
"I'm happy. I didn't think about it during the competition. I just shot." Gabbasov has turned the tables for now. With Los Angeles on the horizon, the two friends could yet meet again with Paralympic gold at stake. ■

Meanwhile, a medical source at a hospital in eastern Khartoum said that a man aged around 50 was killed in a strike targeting a civilian building in the same neighborhood.
Earlier in the day, a military source told Xinhua that the ground-based air defenses of the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) shot down two suicide drones targeting the area around Khartoum International Airport in the eastern part of the capital.
Falling debris from the interception killed a person inside a civilian building in eastern Khartoum, the source said, adding that neither drone had hit its intended target.
The Imtidad Nasir area lies east of Khartoum, near Khartoum International Airport and the headquarters of the SAF's General Command.
Khartoum International Airport resumed operations in February 2026 after being out of service since fighting broke out between the SAF and the RSF in April 2023. ■
