Roundup: African leaders urge local mineral processing to retain value
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
05:24:59 CST
06:24:59 KST

by Justice Lee Adoboe
ACCRA, Oct. 19 (Xinhua) -- African leaders urged greater local mineral processing to retain more value on the continent at the opening of a mining summit in Accra on Monday.
Ghanaian President John Dramani Mahama, who opened the three-day Mining in Motion Summit in the Ghanaian capital, said Ghana, for instance, is working to phase out the export of unprocessed mineral ores completely by 2030 and promote local processing to retain more economic value from the country's mineral resources.
He said the government would introduce the necessary legal measures, mineral-specific requirements, and clear implementation timelines to support the proposed reforms.
This is the line African mining countries should adopt, Mahama urged, calling for investments by African countries in processing facilities, reliable energy, haulage infrastructure, technology, skills, and financing.
"For generations, my country, Ghana, has been shipping a lot of our manganese and bauxite through the port in Takoradi. Much of this material has supplied industries in other parts of the world, while we have imported the finished products made from these mineral ores," Mahama said.
He said that Ghana, therefore, seeks to move beyond extracting and exporting minerals in their raw form to processing them locally and using them to drive industrial development.
On his part, Liberian Vice President Jeremiah Koung said Africa needs to embrace common values on mineral development while respecting their individual national circumstances.
Koung said that African countries need to cooperate in establishing regional infrastructure, reliable geological information, clear mineral agreements, community benefits, and responsible artisanal and small-scale mining.
Francisca Tatchouop Belobe, African Union commissioner for economic development, trade, tourism, industry and minerals, singled out Ghana's mineral sector reforms being spearheaded by the Gold Board (GoldBod) as an example of how reforms in the mineral sector could help African countries strengthen foreign exchange reserves, support currency stability and build more resilient economies.
"The establishment of the Ghana GoldBod illustrates how mineral sector reform can serve broader national development objectives by improving foreign exchange, strengthening international reserves, supporting currency stability, and macroeconomic resilience," Belobe noted.
Belobe said that Ghana's efforts to strengthen local content, domestic enterprises, and mineral value addition provide important lessons for other African countries.
She advocated for stronger implementation of the African Mining Vision, the African Green Minerals Strategy, and the African Continental Free Trade Area to support regional value chains.
Belobe, therefore, urged the continent to move away from mineral extraction alone to processing, manufacturing, and the development of competitive African businesses.
The Mining in Motion Summit is a continental platform advancing Africa's mineral future through policy alignment, coordination, and implementation. ■

Namibia's mining outlook worsens amid diamond slump, rising costs
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
05:24:52 CST
06:24:52 KST

WINDHOEK, Oct. 19 (Xinhua) -- Namibia's mining sector is projected to contract by 6.2 percent in 2026, a sharper decline than previously forecast, the Chamber of Mines of Namibia said Monday.
In its September 2026 Monthly Mining Update, the chamber said the Bank of Namibia had revised its forecast from a contraction of 2.2 percent, reflecting weaker mining output so far this year.
The country's mining production composite index fell 4 percent month on month in August, driven by a 12 percent drop in diamond output. Production of uranium, zinc and gold rose 8 percent, 27 percent and 4 percent, respectively, but the gains were insufficient to offset the decline in diamonds.
Rising fuel prices were also squeezing profit margins at profitable mines and deepening financial pressure on loss-making operations, the chamber said. Continued fuel inflation could keep operating costs elevated in the coming months, particularly for mines facing weaker commodity prices.
Despite these challenges, minerals accounted for about 72 percent of Namibia's domestic exports in August, generating 6.69 billion Namibian dollars (about 408 million U.S. dollars) out of a total of 9.33 billion Namibian dollars.
Uranium export earnings surged 438 percent month on month to 3.36 billion Namibian dollars.
The increase followed the resumption of full production at the Husab mine in July after a planned maintenance shutdown in June, according to the report.
However, mineral prices were mixed in September, with gold and tin recording monthly declines, although prices remained supportive of the sector overall, the chamber said.
The medium- to long-term outlook remained positive, supported by firm gold and uranium prices, as well as new mining projects and planned expansions, it added. ■

Feature: Traditional Chinese medicine broadens rehab care in South Sudan
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
05:24:46 CST
06:24:46 KST

JUBA, Oct. 19 (Xinhua) -- William Deng Deng, a 52-year-old employee of the South Sudan Revenue Authority, relied on a wheelchair after suffering a stroke in August. After beginning treatment at Juba Teaching Hospital, he says he can now get around without one.
Deng is receiving care from Jiang Tao, a doctor with the 14th Chinese (Anhui) medical team to South Sudan, whose work at the hospital's Physical Therapy Department combines traditional Chinese medicine (TCM), including acupuncture, with targeted physiotherapy.
The 16-member team, dispatched by the health commission of China's Anhui Province, arrived in South Sudan on Sept. 6 for a 53-week mission.
TCM is expanding rehabilitation options in the country, where treatment at the hospital is being used to address conditions ranging from stroke and traumatic brain injury to osteoarthritis.
"I was moving on the wheelchair, but now I am able to move around freely with the support of a walking stick. What is now left is only my hand, but I think also when my leg becomes better and my hand will be okay also," Deng told Xinhua in Juba, the capital of South Sudan, on Monday.
Omer Jadhallah, a 66-year-old Sudanese refugee living in Juba's Atlabara suburb, came to the department in mid-July with severe muscle stiffness and persistent pain in the stump of a leg amputated in 2024. His surgeons had recommended a prosthesis, and he sought physiotherapy to ease the pain and regain movement.
"When I came here, I had muscle stiffness, but due to the physiotherapy I am receiving, I am recovering. When I came here, I found many other patients who have been treated well. The staff here are very cooperative and helpful; we felt like a family," Jadhallah said.
"I came here in a worse condition, but now I am gradually recovering," he added.
Issa Ibrahim, a 50-year-old Sudanese national, said he believes he would still be paralyzed had he not received the treatment. He suffered a stroke brought on by high blood pressure.
"The stroke left me completely paralyzed on one side. I was in an extremely poor, exhausted state and unable to move my arm, read, or do anything for myself," he noted.
Ibrahim said that upon checking into Juba Teaching Hospital, he received all necessary medical care directly on-site, eliminating the need to seek specialized treatment abroad or at outside facilities.
"Everything from medical tests and physical therapy to specialized nutritional support was provided right inside the hospital. The therapy sessions were fully accessible," Ibrahim said.
"After two and a half months of care, I have fully regained my health and mobility. I am no longer hindered from doing anything, and I am now in the final stages of care, getting ready to be discharged," Ibrahim added.
Jacob Pitia Hillary, deputy head of the Physical Therapy Department, explained that core TCM techniques, including acupuncture, are proven highly effective in delivering rapid pain relief for patients suffering from lower back pain and various other ailments.
"Some of our patients who come here are usually afraid of the needles, but when we counsel them, they get to know the importance of acupuncture," Pitia said.
Jiang said his team treats about 20 patients a day, for conditions including stroke, paralysis, joint pain and chronic back pain.
Elizabeth Denya Joseph, a 27-year-old physiotherapist who completed specialized TCM training in China in April, emphasized the clinical value of acupuncture. She noted that the practice significantly alleviates pain while promoting blood circulation to stimulate nerve recovery.
"We work as a team, we join hands together with the Chinese medical team to help our patients recover faster," Denya said.
Jiang said that his team focuses primarily on neurological and osteoarticular conditions, treating post-stroke sequelae, facial paralysis, knee osteoarthritis, cervical spondylosis, lumbar disc herniation, and scapulohumeral periarthritis.
He added that the department routinely conducts comprehensive rehabilitation assessments and provides targeted therapeutic care for patients experiencing restricted limb mobility resulting from physical trauma.
"In clinical practice, we fully leverage the advantages of TCM- simple, convenient, economical, and effective. We standardly apply a variety of appropriate TCM techniques such as acupuncture, moxibustion, cupping, acupoint pricking blood therapy, tuina and bone-setting, and cutaneous needle therapy," Jiang said.
Jiang further highlighted the distinct approach of TCM compared to Western practices, explaining that TCM emphasizes holistic regulation and proactive disease prevention.
He noted that because the discipline operates largely without heavy pharmaceutical reliance, it offers a high safety profile and remains widely accessible to a diverse patient population. ■

Roundup: Africa seeks to promote RMB settlement to align with zero-tariff treatment
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-20
05:24:36 CST
06:24:36 KST

ACCRA, Oct. 19 (Xinhua) -- African governments and financial institutions have been gradually promoting diversified trade settlement and expanding RMB settlement, as China fully implemented zero-tariff treatment for 53 African countries with which it has diplomatic relations in May.
Ecobank Group, a Togo-based pan-African banking group, has recently signed a memorandum of understanding with the Cross-Border Interbank Payment System (CIPS) to strengthen RMB payment connectivity between China and Africa.
From late July to August, Stanbic Bank, the subsidiary of South Africa's Standard Bank Group in markets including Kenya, Tanzania, Uganda, Ghana, and Namibia, officially connected to CIPS.
Bank of Kigali, Rwanda's largest commercial bank, announced in late September that it had officially become a direct participant in CIPS.
Ghana's GCB Bank PLC, the country's largest indigenous bank, and Banco de Fomento Angola, Angola's second-largest commercial bank, also planned to join CIPS to meet customers' growing demand for direct RMB settlement.
Bill Blackie, chief executive of business and commercial banking at Standard Bank Group, said in September that China's zero-tariff treatment is helping African businesses lower export costs, while growing RMB settlement capacity is further facilitating trade between Africa and China.
He said Standard Bank currently provides RMB payment connectivity in 10 African markets, enabling some cross-border payments to be settled within minutes rather than days.
Johnson Asiama, governor of the Bank of Ghana, said recently that authorities will work with their Chinese counterparts to eliminate third-party currency settlements in transactions between Ghanaian traders and Chinese suppliers.
China has been Africa's largest trading partner. In 2025, China-Africa trade grew by 17.7 percent year on year to reach 348 billion U.S. dollars, while Africa's exports to China exceeded 123 billion dollars.
"CIPS is beginning to offer Africa a different route," said Gerald Mbanda, a Rwandan researcher and publisher on China-Africa development and cooperation.
He told Xinhua that this is more than a technical banking development and could become an important financial component of the expanding economic ties between African countries and China.
According to Mbanda, CIPS provides infrastructure for cross-border payments and settlement in yuan. As African banks increasingly connect to the system, businesses can gain more direct access to RMB-denominated transactions with Chinese counterparts.
Jonas Atingdui, a Ghanaian economic and policy analyst, said that the internationalization of the RMB could be understood as part of the gradual diversification of the international monetary and payments system. There is a gradual decline in the proportion of U.S. dollar reserves held by central banks, globally, in favor of gold and other currencies.
"For African economies, greater use of the RMB can provide an additional option for settling trade with China," he said.
He said direct RMB settlement through CIPS can not only reduce unnecessary currency conversions, lessen reliance on multiple correspondent or intermediary banks, improve transaction efficiency and lower foreign exchange risk, but also improve business relationships with Chinese suppliers.
With the official implementation of the zero-tariff measures, China's imports from Africa reached 193.8 billion yuan (about 28.96 billion U.S. dollars) in May and June, up 23.5 percent year-on-year. Imports of avocados, apples and oranges surged by 130 percent, 89.6 percent and 27.9 percent, respectively.
Atingdui said that to better use the zero-tariff dividends, financial development needs to keep pace with trade. If Ghanaian exporters sell to China and receive RMB, the development of RMB payment infrastructure gives them an opportunity to receive and manage those proceeds more directly.
He also noted that the market depth of the RMB in Africa is currently limited, and therefore, financial infrastructure needs to be complemented by financial education.
"The next stage should ensure that this channel is not used exclusively by large enterprises. Banks, government agencies and business associations should educate smaller importers and exporters about RMB settlement, foreign exchange risk, documentation requirements and opportunities related to direct trade with China," he added. ■

Pan Gongsheng, governor of the People's Bank of China, China's central bank, said the central bank has actively promoted the transformation and improvement of China's monetary policy framework, further enriched its monetary policy toolkit, and made the market-based interest rate regulation mechanism clearer.

Pan also unveiled that the central bank will join with other financial authorities to introduce a number of policy measures.

Other policy measures to be introduced include pilot measures to facilitate foreign financial institutions' RMB purchase and sale business in the onshore foreign exchange market, and issuing guidelines regarding financial support for building international science and technology innovation centers in Beijing (Beijing-Tianjin-Hebei region), Shanghai (the Yangtze River Delta), and the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area, according to Pan.

According to him, China will facilitate cross-border investment and financing by enhancing the convenience of investment operations through the Qualified Foreign Institutional Investors scheme.
Foreign-funded entities are encouraged to leverage their parent companies' professional expertise and strengths to further refine their product portfolios and participate in innovative business areas in China, Wu added.
Fu Hua, president of Xinhua News Agency, said at the opening ceremony that creating a favorable public opinion climate for financial reform and development is an important part of building a new ecosystem for financial development, adding that Xinhua stands ready to make an effort toward that end.
Zhu Hexin, head of the State Administration of Foreign Exchange (SAFE), said a batch of incremental measures will be rolled out to better support enterprises in engaging in international cooperation and competition.
These include facilitation measures for the current account to better meet the diverse settlement needs of foreign trade enterprises and support the development of new forms and models of trade, and measures to optimize foreign exchange management under the capital account to better meet enterprises' needs for cross-border investment, financing and fund allocation, and expand two-way investment cooperation.
Zhu revealed that China intends to expand its pilot program that allows securities companies to conduct foreign exchange settlement and sales business, and support financial institutions in providing exchange rate risk management services to enterprises.
The annual conference, which runs from Oct. 19 to 22, is jointly hosted by the Beijing Municipal People's Government, the People's Bank of China, the NFRA, the CSRC, Xinhua News Agency and the SAFE. ■

President Volodymyr Zelensky pressed US lawmakers on Monday, Oct. 19, for answers Washington has yet to provide about Ukraine’s restricted satellite links and the missing allied warnings of incoming Russian ballistic missiles.
Speaking during a virtual meeting with Republicans and Democrats from both the Senate and the House, Zelensky said neither problem had been explained by the US side. The meeting, Zelensky said in a statement, was arranged by Democratic Senator Richard Blumenthal and Republican Sen. Thom Tillis.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“The American side has not given Ukraine any explanation for either of these two problems,” Zelensky said, adding that “Our teams will continue working on all the issues we discussed today.”
Unanswered questions for Washington
Both issues have weighed heavily on Ukraine’s air defense in recent days, as tensions between Kyiv and Washington continue escalating their public feud.
Zelensky told the lawmakers that Kyiv had again received no advance notice from partners before the first wave of Russia’s overnight ballistic missile strike. Earlier on Monday, he said such warnings had failed to come three times recently.
At the same time, Starlink and Starshield terminals are still losing connection at higher speeds on parts of the front line.
The restrictions, which began overnight on Oct. 13-14, have crippled several types of drones Ukraine uses – the interceptor drones against Russia’s jet-powered Shaheds and mid-strike drones against Russian oil refiners.
Bulgaria Seeks Arrest of 2 German Nationals Over Arson Attack on Starlink Antennas
Neither SpaceX CEO Elon Musk nor the White House accepted responsibility for the disruptions, which came without a prior warning.
‘This is how Russia responds’
To show lawmakers what exactly was at stake, Zelensky brought photos from Russia’s strike on a central park in Nova Vodolaha, Kharkiv region, that killed six people – including three children – earlier on Monday.
Among those killed was an infant named Angelina, who was just over a year old and lying in her stroller.
“Her mother’s name was Inna; she died in the hospital… The other girl who was killed was 11 years old. My condolences to their families and loved ones,” Zelensky said in a separate statement on Monday.
According to local authorities, 15 other civilians were wounded; half of them children. Russian forces struck a park and its cafe, both full of people, including families.
Zelensky tied the attack to Washington’s recent decision to ease pressure on Moscow. “This is how Russia responds to the lifting of sanctions and the easing of pressure,” he said.
His remarks came as US President Donald Trump signed an executive on Oct. 16, waiving sweeping Russia sanctions and tariffs set to take effect just two days later.
The decision suspends 500% tariffs on Russian imports and 100% duties targeting major buyers of Russian oil and gas, and follows Trump’s latest diesel deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin that drew criticism from the Congress, the EU and Ukraine.
Instead of enforcing the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026, signed into law on Sept. 18, Trump lifted sanctions on Russian diesel exports through April 2027.
Led by Blumenthal, a total of 12 senators – six Republicans and six Democrats – signed a joint letter on Oct. 14 urging Trump to rescind his deal with Putin, calling it a gift to Moscow and a betrayal of Ukraine.
On Monday, US Representative Brian Fitzpatrick, a Pennsylvania Republican, vowed investigations, public hearings and budget cuts for anyone who restricted Ukraine’s Starshield access.
Ukraine seeks more Patriots ahead of winter
Hours before the virtual congressional meeting, Zelensky hosted a delegation from Lockheed Martin in Kyiv.
The US defense giant produces both the Patriot air defense system and the F-16 fighter jets – the two weapons Ukraine leans on most against Russian ballistic missiles and jet-powered drones.
“Both areas are difficult right now,” Zelensky said. “We discussed how we can expand and increase deliveries.”
As the company expands production of ballistic missile interceptors, Kyiv hopes to purchase a part of the new output. The move is particularly important because, as of Oct. 15, Ukraine had reportedly exhausted its Patriot stocks completely.
“Almost all the ballistic missiles from the last strike were not intercepted due to lack of the [interceptor] missiles,” a source, speaking on the condition of anonymity, told CNN.
Currently, PAC-3 interceptors cost roughly $4 million per missile, which makes their high cost compounded by the rate at which they are expended during sustained operations. Still, they are in short supply worldwide as countries among the world seek to rearm amid the war in Iran and Russia’s escalating rhetoric towards Europe.
As of Oct. 1, Lockheed Martin is in advanced talks over PAC-3 production outside the US as demand triples.
Dan Tenney, the company’s senior vice president for global business development and strategy, told Kyiv Post that the company is investing up to $9 billion through 2030 to expand missile production, strengthen supply chains and bring new factories online.
On July 20, Lockheed Martin introduced the PAC-3 ACE, a Patriot interceptor designed to deter air and missile threats at less than half the cost of the PAC-3 MSE variant. Initial production was expected to start within 36 months.
German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius said Germany would deliver PAC-2 missiles to Ukraine from its own Bundeswehr stocks on Sept. 8, while Ukrainian Defense Minister Yevhen Khmara said contracts are being signed with partners for about 1,000 Patriot missiles.
Late in September, Zelensky met with Trump on the sidelines of the 81st United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) in New York, where the US president told him he made a “final decision” to grant Ukraine the licenses to produce Patriots domestically.
The idea was initially floated during the NATO summit in Ankara, Turkey July 7-8, but Trump later backtracked on the promises, saying Washington must exercise caution when sharing sensitive military technology.

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz on Monday reiterated the need to press ahead with his reform agenda, citing the reduction of bureaucratic hurdles, the digitalization of public administration, and reforms to social security systems.
“We invest in rebuilding and modernizing our infrastructure and our defense capabilities,” Merz said in an address to business leaders at the Invest in Germany summit on Monday evening, with closed-door talks to continue on Tuesday.
“Germany is embarking on the biggest modernization drive in its recent history. In the coming years we are on top of our annual efforts, channeling half a billion euros into rebuilding and modernizing our infrastructure as well as into green energy and climate initiatives,” he added, urging investors to take part in this modernization drive.

Most Germans say Merz’s reform drive is headed the wrong way, and the conservative leader has fallen to a personal low, a survey published on Oct. 8 found.
The poll for public broadcaster ZDF found that 59% of respondents believe the coalition’s planned and partly adopted changes to pensions, health care, and long-term care are going in “the wrong direction.”
Only 30% said the measures are on the right track. Supporters of Merz’s conservative CDU/CSU alliance were the only party camp with a majority in favor, at 66%.
Most voters were angry about what they saw as an unjust distribution of the costs. Some 80% said the burdens are distributed unfairly, versus 12% who called the distribution fair. On social insurance changes, 77% said they do not believe the government will make important contributions to solving the problems.

Quick hits: Renshaw floored by miracle grab as Bavuma's six stops traffic
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
21:16:34 UTC
06:16:34 KST

Matt Renshaw has been shocked by his own miracle grab, while Temba Bavuma's soaring six has stopped the Gqeberha traffic on a day when a soggy outfield threatened to ruin it all.
Here are the quick hits from day two of the second Test between Australia and South Africa.
1. A soggy outfield almost ruins it all
Things did not look good as the scheduled start of play approached on day two. Dark skies and pouring rain meant a delay was inevitable.
But within two hours, the rain had ceased, and another hour after that, the sun was beating down in Gqeberha.
The St George's outfield, however, just wasn't playing ball. Three surface inspections came and went, with the umpires and ground staff determining the soggy turf too treacherous for play on each occasion.
The two areas of particular concern, both deep in the outfield, were simply refusing to drain.
It was Test cricket at its exasperating, excruciating worst, and the threat of an entirely lost day loomed on the horizon.
But five hours after the scheduled start of play, and more than three since the last downfall, the officials finally determined the field fit for purpose.
By the time the Australian bowlers were going through their warm-ups, it was a glorious day in the Eastern Cape.
2. Hazlewood the latest to succumb to sickness
But when the Australians finally got on the field for a 30-over evening session, they were without one of their most dangerous weapons.
Josh Hazlewood was battling sickness and nowhere to be seen at St George's Park, leaving just the — admittedly serviceable — trio of Pat Cummins, Mitch Starc and Scott Boland for the South African batters to contend with.
A day earlier umpire Chris Gaffaney was forced to withdraw from the Test with a bout of food poisoning, the saga no doubt leaving those in attendance wondering if there might be a dish to avoid at the St George's canteen.
Hazlewood is expected to return on day three.
3. Carey poised for 200
It was typically outstanding stuff from Boland as day two belatedly began.
The Victorian had Temba Bavuma swinging and missing dramatically with the first ball of the afternoon. He only had to wait until his second set of the day to claim his third wicket of the match, luring Marques Ackerman into a drive and nicking off the debutant for six.
Meanwhile, behind the stumps, Alex Carey was nearing a major milestone.
And when Mitchell Starc had Matthew Breetzke edging through to the Australian wicketkeeper only moments later, Carey was one take away from becoming the fifth Australian gloveman to take 200 catches in Test cricket after Adam Gilchrist, Ian Healy, Rod Marsh and Brad Haddin.
Carey will hope to join that group on day three.
4. Bavuma interrupts traffic with massive six
It was an absolutely massive six, and it came from absolutely nowhere.
Bavuma had been so composed and diligent in steadying ship after the losses of Ackerman and Breetzke, and looked set to defend his way to stumps.
But the South Africa captain absolutely exploded in hooking Cummins over the backward square leg boundary.
The ball sailed over the rope, out of the stadium and then rolled onto the road, where a security guard was forced to weave through the Gqeberha traffic to collect it.
5. Renshaw stunned by own miracle grab
With only a matter of minutes remaining in the day's play, Australia was pushing for the one final wicket that would put them well on top in the game.
Shadows were lengthening, light was fading quickly, and Marnus Labuschagne had just put down a relatively simple catch at leg slip.
Visibility clearly wasn't great but, somehow, Matt Renshaw produced something remarkable.
It was definitely Carey's catch, but the Australian wicketkeeper was rooted to the spot as Ryan Rickleton edged towards the men behind the wicket.
The ball looked destined to fly between the keeper and slip, but there he was, Renshaw, diving at full stretch and managing to get his right hand between ball and turf.
The Queenslander looked absolutely stunned to have taken the catch that had South Africa rocking at 5-97 at stumps.

Helen Haines was chatting with locals at a dog park on Monday morning. By the afternoon, she was fighting for her life
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
21:14:37 UTC
06:14:37 KST

Victorian independent MP Helen Haines was at the opening of a dog park in Mansfield on Monday, out and about in her sprawling electorate of Indi, talking to locals and moving freely.
Later in the afternoon, at 3.35pm, she was unpacking a car outside her electorate office in Wangaratta when a man understood to be known to authorities struck her with his car. He allegedly completed a U-turn when he saw Haines.
What happened will urgently change how MPs assess their personal safety, not least because local settings are no longer free from danger.
The prime minister, Anthony Albanese, says the government will act on the advice of security officials but an increase in protection feels inevitable.
There is much we don’t know about what has happened, including the motivation of the alleged attacker.
But a dark tide of threats and abuse has been rising.
For years, federal politicians have had an ominous sense that something was shifting in Australia’s national life.
Monday’s alleged attack on Haines saw that tide turn into reality, with a much-loved local member critically injured in the street outside her electorate office.
Long having warned against the growing intensity of political debate, Albanese reflected the grave shock of the country in the hours after the incident.
Along with the home affairs minister, Tony Burke, Albanese revealed that recorded threats against politicians numbered more than 1,067 last financial year, as the cohort of office holders requiring around-the-clock close personal protection grew.
Those responsible for protecting federal politicians in Australia often take their cues from overseas. When a gunman opened fire at the Canadian parliament in 2014, the Abbott government built a fence around Parliament House. Amid threats stemming from Covid-19 lockdowns, and the souring of social media discourse, the Asio director general, Mike Burgess, cautioned in 2025 that the warning light for political violence was “already flashing red”.
Albanese was evacuated from The Lodge in February and a blast-resistant facility was added to his Sydney residence. December’s antisemitic massacre at Bondi was only the latest wake-up call, along with incidents overseas such as the alleged murder of British politician Ann Widdecombe.
Here, local MPs have been changing their behaviour. Many no longer publicise where they will be for community events ahead of time, and some MPs’ local electorate offices have been closed for months at a time.
But the alleged attack on Haines shows something rapidly being lost in our politics. The shift in sentiment can no longer be dismissed as social media noise or harmless comment.
A review of politicians’ offices last year found a sharp rise in politically motivated hostility, with 85% reporting high levels of abusive or violent behaviour from constituents. This behaviour included verbal threats, intimidation, spitting and throwing of objects.
The risk to individuals – especially women in politics – has not been taken seriously enough. Whether security services could have done more will be considered in the weeks and months to come.
But dismissing overheated political rhetoric and petty attacks as woke or overly sensitive will not cut it now, as Haines remains in a critical condition after undergoing surgery.
More needs to be done to stop a normalisation of violence and gratuitous insults. That includes the importation of rhetoric from the US and Europe, like calls for politicians to be locked up or harmed for their decisions. The politicians dishing out verbal attacks themselves, or inciting individuals to hate online, must be held accountable.
The alleged attack on Haines could prove a turning point for Australian politics, but hard questions about safety and the culture of debate must be answered.
- Tom McIlroy is Guardian Australia’s political editor

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz and Huang are set to unveil a joint AI pact intended to speed up the integration of AI products across German industry.
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang warned that Germany is falling behind in the artificial intelligence race as he spoke to members of the media in London last week.
Despite its strong potential and wealth of talent, Huang believes progress in Europe is being blocked by too much hesitation and analysis and has called on policymakers to be quicker to put AI into practice.
In response to concerns about the country's technological competitiveness, the German government has been planning closer cooperation with the US company.
At the Invest in Germany investment summit in Berlin this week, Chancellor Friedrich Merz and Huang are set to unveil a joint AI pact intended to speed up the integration of AI products across German industry.
The German government is preparing to commit hundreds of millions of Euros to the initiative.
Alongside start-up Black Forest Labs, around 10 established German companies including Siemens and Audi are expected to take part.
The partnership builds on the Sovereign Open Source Foundation Models initiative, an alliance dedicated to developing powerful open-source AI systems.
The funding is to be used primarily to buy computing capacity in Deutsche Telekom's Industrial AI Cloud, which is equipped with Nvidia's latest Blackwell hardware.
The government hopes the investment will make Germany a more attractive destination for innovation and technological development.
On Tuesday, senior international executives, investors and government officials at the Invest in Germany summit will discuss new investment in Germany, focusing on artificial intelligence, energy and infrastructure, as well as the competitiveness of the German economy.

Poland has detained and expelled 15 Russians and Belarusians who tried to take part in youth world karate championships that were taking place in the Polish city of Bielsko-Biała.

The announcement came one day after the karate world championships in the cadet, junior and U-21 categories had finished in Bielsko-Biała.

Since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, Poland has been one of Kyiv’s closest allies, providing military and humanitarian support while also pressing for tougher international sanctions against Moscow.
Meanwhile, Poland has become the primary target in Europe for sabotage operations carried out by operatives working on behalf of Russia, including arson attacks and an attempt to derail a train. Russia has also repeatedly violated Polish airspace with drones, missiles and, most recently, a helicopter.
In response to Russia’s aggressive actions, Poland has successively shut down all Russian consulates on its territory. Moscow responded by likewise closing all Polish consulates that it previously hosted. In January, Russia warned its citizens against travelling to Poland due to “Russophobia”.

Kenyan starvation cult leader found guilty of killing 191 people
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
21:10:00 UTC
06:10:00 KST

The leader of the Kenyan "starvation cult" Paul Mackenzie alongside 28 others were declared guilty of murder by a Mombasa court on Monday over the deaths of 190 children and an adult in one of the world's worst cult-related tragedies in recent history.
The preacher was arrested in 2023 after police received a tip-off, and weeks later authorities began uncovering bodies in shallow graves in the Shakahola Forest near the coast in southeastern Kenya.
Prosecutors say Mackenzie and his Good News International Church organized a Christian doomsday sect in which they ordered followers to starve themselves and their children to death to go to heaven before the world ended.
The case has gripped Kenya since the discovery of the mass graves.
It raised questions over how Mackenzie was able to continue to operate despite having been on the radar of the authorities since 2017, when his premises were searched by police.
In 2019, authorities shut down Mackenzie's church and he relocated to the Shakahola Forest, police said.
Mackenzie denied murder charges, saying he did not force the victims to starve, but the court rejected that argument.
He and the others convicted will be sentenced on Nov. 6. Defence lawyer Lawrence Obonyo, who represents Mackenzie and almost all of the others convicted, said he had been instructed to appeal.
Francis Wanje, 62, lost eight family members, including two grandchildren to the cult. He told Reuters that the judgment made him happy and gave him confidence in the judiciary.
"So many are going to learn from what has come up today. ... You find churches everywhere, but they've got ill reasons for the churches. So it is good for members of the public to be very careful," Wanje added.
In total, more than 400 bodies have been recovered from the Shakahola Forest.
Many of the children's bodies were severely decomposed, with only 26 able to be identified, and investigations into the other deaths are ongoing.
Justice Diana Kavedza Mochache said in a hearing lasting more than eight hours that, in some cases, children were isolated and denied food while their parents watched.
The director of public prosecutions, Renson Ingonga, told reporters afterwards at the Mombasa High Court: "That is the best judgment we would ever get."
Mackenzie was in court, wearing a striped polo shirt and red trousers, sitting alongside his wife, one of the co-accused.
When his name was read out by the judge he was silent, staring into space.
The case has led to calls for tougher oversight of churches and other religious organizations in a country where religious faith plays a prominent role in public life.
Kenyan President William Ruto said in 2023 that government agencies should have been able to prevent the deaths. He said he took responsibility as president.

US, Cuba trade barbs at UN ahead of sanctions vote
UNITED NATIONS, Oct 19 - The United States and Cuba traded accusations at the United Nations on Monday after US diplomats hosted an event featuring Cuban dissidents ahead of next week's annual UN vote on a resolution calling for an end to a US embargo on the island.
Cuban ambassador to the UN, Ernesto Soberón Guzmán, and other representatives yelled at the US ambassador to the UN, Mike Waltz, as he left the event at the UN building, which focused on allegations of human rights abuses by the Cuban government.
The tensions between the two nations are rising before the vote on the non-binding resolution, which has passed in the UN General Assembly by wide margins every year since 1992, and amid mounting strain from a US-imposed oil blockade on Cuba.
"I hope you...noted the so-called diplomats from the Cuban embassy here that we allow here by dint of treaty, harassing, yelling, intimidating, and filming not only our just released former political prisoners but others," Waltz told reporters in New York.
"Year after year, the Cuban regime comes to the General Assembly and propagates a lie through its annual resolution...It uses excuse after excuse to justify its oppression, to justify the misery of the Cuban people, and what we are doing here at the US mission to the UN is exposing those lies," he said.
The vote is expected to take place on Oct. 27-28, officials said.
The US has maintained a trade embargo on Cuba for more than 60 years and US President Donald Trump's administration has been stepping up the pressure, after using the military in January to remove Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro.
The UN vote can carry political weight, but only the US Congress can lift the Cold War-era embargo.
Cuba has blamed US sanctions for the crisis the country is mired in, the worst economic downturn in decades characterized by shortages of basic goods, collapsing infrastructure and runaway inflation.
"The US is acting as an international delinquent, enforcing collective punishment on the people of Cuba. They are inflicting immense suffering upon the whole population of a peaceful nation," Guzmán, the Cuban ambassador, said at an impromptu gathering outside the US meeting with dissidents.
Last month, Trump said at the UN that Cuba was a failed state and freedom would be coming to the island nation.
Cuba's electrical grid suffered a total collapse last month, plunging it into darkness and leaving millions without power. REUTERS

Milan riots expose Italy's youth gang crisis as Meloni vows crackdown
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
21:02:13 UTC
06:02:13 KST

The disturbing images from France and the shock over the scale of violence there have, over the past 24 hours, diverted some attention from equally disturbing scenes in another major European city: Milan. On Saturday and Sunday, thousands of young people rioted in the city center, clashing violently with police officers who were vastly outnumbered, hurling concrete blocks and stones, vandalizing property, and looting and destroying numerous luxury stores in the heart of the city.
Italy was left in shock Sunday by the scenes of destruction and, above all, the extreme violence and rampaging of the rioters. Police were forced to fire tear gas and deploy water cannons in an attempt to regain control as they confronted hundreds of masked demonstrators. Among the well-known stores completely looted were Decathlon's flagship store, a Vodafone mobile phone store and one of the country's best-known bookstores, Feltrinelli.
Italian police announced Monday that they had arrested 271 young people involved in Sunday's unrest. Dozens of police officers were injured. Clashes similar to those in Milan also took place in Bologna, Brescia, Bergamo and Turin, all in northern Italy, resulting in dozens of arrests. But it was the scenes in Milan that left many Italians angry, outraged and, above all, bewildered, as the level of violence stunned both the authorities and the political establishment.
An extraordinarily high proportion of those arrested, nearly 80%, were minors, according to Italian media reports. Of the 32 suspects brought before a court for detention hearings, 23 were minors and 13 were foreign nationals. According to Corriere della Sera, an astonishing number of those detained were children as young as 11 to 14. Reports and police accounts indicated that radical left-wing activists and students also participated in the riots, including the looting and clashes with police. However, many managed to escape as the violence escalated. Those who were caught were predominantly children who had traveled into the city from Milan's suburbs. A large proportion came from immigrant backgrounds, including families originating in North Africa, Eastern Europe and elsewhere. Some were born in Italy to immigrant families that had lived in the country for decades.
Immigrant parents who built lives in Italy: 'I'm ashamed'
Corriere della Sera described remarkable scenes Monday outside Milan's central police station, where distraught and embarrassed parents stood waiting for their detained sons to be released. Some had lived in Italy for many years and were well integrated into society, while others barely spoke the language. Many waited in tears, visibly ashamed.
"If my child took part in these riots, I will punish him severely," one father was quoted as saying.
"I break my back every day to earn a living, and I'm ashamed. If my son did what they're saying, he'll pay dearly for it. I'm deeply disappointed in him," said another father of Tunisian origin.
"Where were you? What did you do? I'll tear you apart!" another father reportedly shouted after arriving to collect his arrested son.
"I wish someone had smashed your head in! I'll smash your head in!" one father, tears in his eyes, reportedly shouted at his son after he was released from custody.
Italian media reported that many of the teenagers had flocked to central Milan after seeing the demonstrations begin on Saturday. The protests had originally been planned around the rising cost of living, but as images spread on Instagram and TikTok, young people began traveling into Milan from surrounding towns and cities.
Many of these teenagers, or children, belonged to groups known as "Maranza." The term, Italian slang for groups of children and teenagers who move around together, often dressed in fashionable clothing but displaying aggressive, anti-establishment attitudes, has become increasingly familiar across Italy in recent years, particularly in the Milan area. These groups have become a significant part of the city's problem with violence and crime, fueling racist sentiment because many of their members are second- or third-generation immigrants, often from Arab or Eastern European backgrounds.
Masked 10-year-olds with clubs and stolen scooters
Many of the children arrested Saturday and Sunday were reportedly associated with these groups. Italian media outlets spoke with some of them, who said they had decided to join the "party" and film everything for TikTok. Some openly boasted about the looting and clashes with police.
Many parents of those arrested said they learned their children had traveled to Milan to participate in the riots only after they were detained. One couple said they initially heard their son had not arrived at school, only to discover later that he had been arrested. Other parents tracked their children's locations through an app and discovered they were at a police station.
The young age of the rioters has shocked many Italians. Journalists covering the unrest documented masked children as young as 10 and 11 riding electric bicycles or scooters, wearing stolen helmets and carrying clubs and metal objects. Some were seen leading groups of teenagers into confrontations with police or raids on stores, stopping along the way to upload footage of the incidents to social media.
Italian media also reported Monday that police had identified members of the organized radical left, associated with Milan's social centers, among the demonstrators. However, many of these activists reportedly left when police began using force to disperse the crowds and restore order.
Authorities are still struggling to determine who was behind the riots, who organized the gatherings, if anyone, and whether the violence was coordinated at all.
One widely circulated hashtag, "Italy in the Squares," called on Italians to join the demonstrations, echoing events in France. But authorities have yet to identify any organization or individual responsible for orchestrating the unrest.
Investigators are also examining the possibility that a foreign organization was behind the incitement to violence and the mass gatherings, a suspicion frequently raised in Europe in recent years following outbreaks of anti-establishment unrest. So far, however, Italian authorities have found no evidence to substantiate such suspicions. The prevailing assessment is that many of the young people who rioted in Milan were driven simply by a desire to vent their frustrations, "break things" and "destroy things."
By Monday evening, stores in central Milan were again closing amid fears that the riots could resume spontaneously. Large numbers of police officers were deployed throughout the city.
The Italian government, led by Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni, announced that it would convene Tuesday to advance emergency legislation aimed at preventing similar incidents. The proposed measures would authorize preventive detention of violent youths, ban gatherings by the youth groups known as Maranza and allow police to establish surprise checkpoints on roads outside cities and at the entrances to major urban centers, in an effort to prevent criminal elements seeking to create chaos from entering.

Hepatitis B Cases Could Surge Under New Vaccine Guidelines, Study Finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
21:00:03 UTC
06:00:03 KST

Hepatitis B can be a silent killer. It can pass from mother to child during birth and can spread through contact with infected blood or semen. Among babies infected before they turn 1, up to 90% develop a chronic, potentially lifelong infection, for which there are treatments but no cure. People may not even know they have the virus until their liver fails or they develop cancer, years later. Early-in-life hepatitis B infections, left untreated, lead to a 1 in 4 lifetime chance of developing liver cancer.
In the U.S., hepatitis B vaccination became routinely recommended for all infants in 1991; later guidance specified that the first dose should happen within 24 hours of birth. However, in Dec. 2025, the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) under the Trump Administration moved to cease recommending this practice for babies born to mothers who test negative, instead advising a shared decision-making model where parents and clinicians decide together what is medically appropriate: a dose shortly after birth, or a first dose "no earlier than 2 months of age." (For babies born to mothers who test positive or whose status is unknown, the CDC continues to recommend a dose shortly after birth.)
A new study, published today in Annals of Internal Medicine, uses computer modeling to simulate the hepatitis B infection status of an entire year’s worth of children born in the U.S. under the new recommendations over their first 20 years of life. The researchers find that if only about 26% of children are vaccinated—an estimate of what would occur under shared decision-making—chronic hepatitis B cases would rise by 225%.
When should kids get the first dose of hepatitis B vaccine?
The American Association of Pediatrics continues to recommend vaccination at birth against hepatitis B for all infants, and 15 states have sued the Trump Administration over vaccination schedule changes.
“It's been challenged in many states and by professional societies, but we wanted to add some evidence to the conversation about what the potential impact of those changes could be,” says Dr. Amir Mohareb, an infectious-disease researcher at Harvard Medical School and Massachusetts General Hospital who is an author of the new study.
The simulation modeled how many of 3.6 million children, born the same year in the U.S., would develop hepatitis B under a number of scenarios, including if the former CDC recommendations continued to be followed, if the initial dose (also called a “birth dose”) was delayed, and if a shared decision-making scenario was employed.
The model suggests that if the first dose is delayed until 2 months old, and only 75% of infants get it, then there would be a 19% increase in chronic cases compared to if every child received their first dose at birth. With a 26% vaccination rate at 2 months, the number climbed to 225%.
This study modeled only at a single year of births, notes Mahoreb. “Imagine that happening year after year after year after year. That could quickly become thousands and thousands of new infections, and even a small number of new infections could result in lifelong chronic infection that could be detrimental to families, lead to more cases of cancer, and [become] costly to the health care system,” Mohareb says.
Two other recent modeling studies have looked at the impacts of changing hepatitis B vaccine recommendations. One found that if vaccination no longer occurred at birth, a substantial increase in screening pregnant women for the virus would be necessary to keep infection numbers in infants down. Another, looking at the economic ramifications, found that even if every child eventually received the vaccine, delaying the first dose by 2 months yielded an additional $16.4 million in health care spending on new infections.
“All three of these studies complement each other, in a good way, and provide some modicum of evidence so that we don't need to risk doing a clinical trial or testing this on people,” Mahoreb says. “We have done those experiments.” Decades ago, he continues, clinical trials already proved the efficacy of the existing approach, “so that we would have the benefit now of advancing medical progress and not needing to reopen that question.”

Trump approval hits record-low 31 percent, polls show Republican struggles
A Reuters/Ipsos poll reveals Democrats are leading by 12 points in generic US congressional ballot surveys against Republicans.
United States President Donald Trump’s approval rating has fallen to 31 percent – another record low in his political career, according to a new Reuters/Ipsos poll.
The same poll found Trump’s Republican Party also at a major disadvantage: when respondents were asked whether they would rather vote for a generic, unnamed Democrat or Republican, Democrats led by 12 points.
The percentage of Americans who disapprove of Trump has grown steadily in recent months, especially since the February 28 launch of the US-Israel war on Iran, which has driven up petrol and diesel prices and had knock-on effects across the economy.
Several recent polls have documented the growing problems facing Trump and his party ahead of midterm elections, set for November 3, which could determine control of the House and Senate.
An NBC poll released Sunday found 71 percent of Americans said the country was on the “wrong track” and 55 percent would vote for the Democratic Party if an election were held that day.
A Washington Post/ABC/Ipsos poll, also released on Monday, found Trump had a record-low approval rating of 33 percent, with 7 out of 10 saying petrol or gasoline was becoming unaffordable.

Mississippi attorney general rules fatal police shooting of one-year-old as ‘justified’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
20:58:26 UTC
05:58:26 KST

On Monday, the office of the Mississippi attorney general, Lynn Fitch, announced that the police shooting of Kohen Wiley, a one-year-old, as he sat in his mother’s lap “was justified”. The statement came four months after the baby was killed in Senatobia, Mississippi.
On 14 June, officers in Senatobia, a small city near Memphis, were responding to a shoplifting call alleging Vellesiya Wiley, the baby’s mother, and Latoya Ferrell, a friend, had stolen a pack of diapers. Neither woman has been charged with a crime. Officials have not released any evidence of shoplifting.
According to police reports, on the day of the shooting, the women and child exited the store, entered their vehicle and began to leave the parking lot when officers arrived.
The police drew their weapons. Wiley lifted the baby up to indicate that there was a child in the car. An officer, identified by other records as Sgt Hunter Foster, fired into the vehicle, killing Kohen Wiley and wounding Ferrell. Foster is white; both Wileys and Ferrell are Black.
The Mississippi bureau of investigation, which investigated the shooting, alleged that the driver “drove in the direction of the officers, almost striking one”. But the civil rights attorney Ben Crump, who is representing the family, released an independent autopsy that indicated Wiley was shot from the side of the car, not the front, which contradicted officers’ statements that Ferrell headed towards them.
“ I watched my baby take his first breath, and I watched my baby take his last breath,” Kohen’s mother said during a press conference after the shooting.
It is not yet clear if or when law enforcement officials will release footage from the incident.
The shooting was just the most recent in a series of incidents involving Senatobia’s police force. The town is about 40% Black.
In September, Senatobia fired its police chief, who reportedly used racial slurs. And in 2023, the town made national news after an officer arrested and placed in a cell a 10-year-old Black boy who had urinated in public. That child was later sentenced to three months’ probation.
Last year, the town’s aldermen voted to replace the police chief who was serving at the time of the 10-year-old’s arrest with Harold Vanderford, who served when Wiley was killed. He has been replaced with Angelica Maze, who is Black.
“A one-year-old was shot and killed by an officer of this department, and nearly three months later his family still has not been allowed to see the footage,” Crump said at the time. “The racist language that cost Chief Vanderford his job is exactly why this family cannot simply be told to trust the process. MBI has the footage. Release it, finish the investigation into Sgt Foster, and give this family the facts they have been owed since the day Kohen died.”

Midterm Ad Spending Has Surpassed $10B. Where Is the Money Coming From?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
20:57:58 UTC
05:57:58 KST

Political advertising spending for the midterm election cycle this year has reached a record high, surpassing $10 billion as of last week. It is projected to reach $11.6 billion by Election Day, according to the media tracking group AdImpact. The previous midterm spending record was set in 2022 at $8.9 billion, the organization reported, and the 2024 presidential cycle saw some $11.2 billion spent on ads.
The figure does not capture other campaign expenses, such as staffing, travel, and voter outreach. But it does measure one of the more influential political campaign tools: Research published in the American Political Science Review in 2021 estimated that a Senate candidate with a $2 million television advertising advantage over an opponent could gain about 10,000 votes—potentially enough to tip a close race.
Spending the most, however, does not guarantee electoral success, experts tell TIME.
“It is important to keep in mind that having the most, and spending the most, does not guarantee you wins,” says Brendan Glavin, the director of insights at the research group OpenSecrets, which tracks money’s effect on U.S. politics, policy, and elections. “You need to have enough to compete, and you need to be able to get your name out, and people need to know who you are. But it’s not always about having the most.”
That has not deterred both parties from digging deep into their piggy banks this cycle—although their spending has been uneven.
Republicans have significantly outspent Democrats in Senate races, at $233 million to $121 million on broadcast television ads across nine of the tightest upper-chamber races last month, according to AdImpact. In races categorized as “toss-ups” by the Cook Political Report, AdImpact data attributes $947 million to Republicans and $625 million to Democrats, including ads that have not yet been aired. A large portion of the funding comes from a small number of deep-pocketed individuals bankrolling super PACs.
The spending gap is much narrower in House races, where Republicans have outspent Democrats by $14 million across 21 toss-up races.
Democratic Senate candidates, however, have substantially outraised their Republican opponents in many competitive races.
Here’s where some of that money has come from and a look at how it’s being spent.
Texas Senate race: $500 million
Texas is one of the most closely watched Senate races. October polling shows that James Talarico has the chance to become the state’s first Democratic Senator since 1993. A win in the state would deal a critical blow to Republicans’ grip on the upper chamber of Congress. He’s at 51% against Republican Ken Paxton according to CBS/YouGov polling from Oct. 8-16.
Combined ad spending and airtime reservations have surpassed $500 million, according to AdImpact, making it only the second non-presidential race to cross that threshold. The Ohio Senate race in 2024 reached $542.7 million.
Elon Musk, who has given $369 million to Republicans since the start of 2025 and is the biggest individual donor to federal elections this cycle, gave $158 million last month to Senate Leadership Fund, which transferred matching amounts to Texas PAC, the group supporting Paxton. Musk gave an additional $10 million to Lone Star Liberty PAC in August to support the candidate.
Glavin says that these donations, although not funneled to Paxton’s campaign directly, “essentially went directly into supporting Paxton” and appear to have “helped stabilize things” for him.
Talarico has outraised his opponent by roughly $50 million from July through September—but large donors and super PACs have given Paxton the edge when it comes to broadcast ads.
Ohio Senate race: $460 million
Over $450 million in combined ad spending has gone toward Ohio’s Senate race, according to AdImpact.
Republicans have spent nearly $270 million to support Jon Husted, while Democrats have spent over $180 million in support of Sherrod Brown. Ohio gives Democrats another chance to flip a Republican-held seat, with Husted leading by less than a point as of Sunday, according to an ActiVote poll.
Husted was appointed to replace Vice President JD Vance in 2025, meaning that the winner of this special election would need to win again in 2028 to serve a full six-year term.
Through September, Republicans spent $41 million more than Democrats in aired election ads, making it the second-largest GOP dollar advantage among nine identified battleground states, behind Texas, according to AdImpact.
Maine Senate race: $200 million
Maine is home to the most expensive Senate race per capita this cycle, with a combined ad spend of roughly $200 million.
In Maine, Democrats are vying to flip a red seat. Republican Sen. Susan Collins is seeking her sixth term, but she’s closely contested by logger and former Maine Senate President Troy Jackson.
Republicans have spent or committed almost $114 million on advertising since January, compared with almost $81 million for Democrats, according to AdImpact.
What are the donation limits for PACs and super PACs?
The Federal Election Campaign Act sets limits for individual donations to congressional races.
The limit for an individual donation to a candidate’s campaign is $3,500 per election for the 2025-2026 election cycle. These caps are adjusted for inflation every two years.
A traditional political action committee (PAC) pools contributions to support or oppose candidates. Individuals may contribute up to $5,000 to a traditional federal PAC per year. The limit is higher for contributions to a national party committee, at $44,300 per committee per calendar year.
Super PACs, unlike traditional PACs, cannot donate directly to candidates’ campaigns or coordinate their advertising with those campaigns. Those restrictions are intended to prevent unlimited outside donations from becoming a way around limits on contributions to candidates.
There is no limit to how much an eligible person or entity can donate to a super PAC, as demonstrated by Musk's steep contributions in Texas.
Several other billionaires have also contributed to Republican super PACs: Shipping industry moguls Elizabeth and Richard Uihlein donated $138 million in the current election cycle, while Jeff Yass, who founded Susquehanna International Group, and his wife, Janine, contributed $110 million. The top donor to a Democratic super PAC is George Soros, who is linked to the entities responsible for contributing $102 million to Democracy PAC, which he founded in 2019.
Two court decisions in 2010 helped establish today’s super PAC system. The Supreme Court’s Citizens United ruling protected independent political spending by corporations and unions, while a subsequent federal appeals court ruling removed limits on individual contributions to groups making only independent expenditures.
Critics argue that the system gives wealthy donors disproportionate political influence and allows money to flow through nonprofits that conceal its original sources, using what’s referred to as “dark money.” Super PACs must disclose their donors, but those donors can include organizations that do not identify their own funders.
The legal rationale for allowing unlimited contributions rests on the premise that prohibiting individuals or entities from contributing directly to campaigns prevents corruption.

Tech stocks had a nice oversold bounce on Monday. Earnings this week will determine if it's for real
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
20:57:14 UTC
05:57:14 KST

This week's major earnings hold the key to whether this technology comeback has legs, investors said.
The S&P 500 and Nasdaq Composite rallied Monday, largely due to a rebound in artificial intelligence companies. Chip stocks surged, with the iShares Semiconductor ETF (SOXX) on pace to snap a nine-day slump. The Magnificent Seven outperformed, as did memory chip makers. The iShares MSCI South Korea ETF (EWY), dominated by SK Hynix and Samsung Electronics, surged 4% after also suffering steep declines over the past week.
That comes after the S&P 500 fell nearly 2% last week, its worst weekly decline since late June. The Nasdaq Composite dropped 4.5% over the same five-day span.
Monday looked like a bounce from oversold conditions, but a bigger move will depend on this week's big tech earnings — which include results from major names such as Meta Platforms and Tesla — to clear some of the recent worries about the sustainability of the AI trade. SpaceX reports after the bell Tuesday.
"Tech earnings are key this week. Fundamentals are unchanged, but given fragile price action, we turn neutral [on] risk assets and stay neutral duration," wrote Ajay Rajadhyaksha, global chairman of research at Barclays.
This week will be especially crucial for the S&P 500 and Nasdaq, which need to hold support so as not to confirm a further breakdown, Katie Stockton, founder of Fairlead Strategies, said in a Monday note. For the time being, however, widespread, short-term oversold conditions suggest support can hold, she said.
Earnings test
Of the 47 S&P 500 companies that have reported their third quarter thus far, 85% have beaten expectations, and the broad market index is on track to post a blended earnings growth rate of 29%.
But the bulk of tech results are still to come, and they have a high bar to clear.
"Investors are going to need proof statements from any company that is considered part of the AI trade that they can deliver on the earnings growth expectations being built into their pricing," said Ron Albahary, chief investment officer at LNW. "We don't have a valuation-potential bubble here like we had in the internet bubble. We have an earnings-expectation-potential bubble in this cycle."
As a result, the market will take a "more discriminating" approach to tech, which Albahary views as a healthy move that will lead to "more of a dispersion of winners and losers within the AI trade universe." In that environment, some AI beneficiaries may continue to rise, while others like the neocloud platforms may sell off due to the amount of debt they're taking on to finance the build-out, he said.
"Previously, the AI headlines would drive the bulk of the AI universe stocks up or down," the CIO said. "I don't think we're going to see that kind of uniformity going forward."
As it stands now, action in the AI trade appears to be more of a "reality check" than a "full-blown unraveling," according to Wells Fargo Investment Institute's Sameer Samana. But he still believes there may be more pressure in the days and maybe even weeks ahead.
"We recently downgrade[d] tech because we thought expectations had gotten too optimistic, and while the recent selling has taken some of that optimism out of the equation, we don't think it's fully done and may last through the midterms given the politicization of AI/data centers," the Wells Fargo head of global equities and real assets told CNBC.

Zelensky holds online meeting with bipartisan delegation of U.S. Congress

Zelensky holds online meeting with bipartisan delegation of U.S. Congress
The Office of the President announced this, Ukrinform reports.
The Head of State briefed them on the brutal Russian drone attack in the Kharkiv region, which killed six people, including a mother and her child, who was just over a year old.
“This is how Russia responds to sanctions waivers and reduced pressure,” Zelensky stressed.
He also updated the delegation on the situation on the front, where Ukraine is reclaiming more territory than Russian forces are able to capture, and on offensive operations carried out by Ukrainian troops.
“I am grateful to America and to all our partners for their support. We fully understand that our success depends on the support of our partners. And without America, things would be much harder for us,” the President emphasized.
According to Zelensky, Ukraine continues to face restrictions on the operating speeds of Starlink and Starshield services in various sectors of the front.
“We still have no explanation for this. Just different strange stories we’re hearing, unfortunately,” he noted.
The restrictions on Starlink and Starshield speeds, he explained, undermine frontline logistics, Ukraine’s medium-range strike capabilities and its ability to defend against Russian drones.
“The hardest to shoot down are the jet-powered Shaheds. That’s exactly why we need Starlink and Starshield to work at higher speeds,” the head of state stressed.
He said Russian attacks had become more brutal and insidious, and that Ukraine had received no warning from its partners about the first wave of ballistic missile strikes the previous night.
“I’m talking first of all about the American early warning of missile threats. This is already the third time in a short period that we’ve had no such warning about ballistic missiles. And we have received no clear explanation from our partners, our strategic partners, from Washington – why this is happening,” Zelensky said.
The meeting also focused on strengthening Ukraine’s air defenses, including accelerating the delivery of missiles for Patriot systems under the PURL initiative.
The Ukrainian President also briefed the delegation on his contacts with U.S. President Donald Trump’s envoys, Steven Witkoff and Jared Kushner.
He separately thanked the delegation for supporting Lindsey Graham’s sanctions bill.
“This is an extremely strong bill that was supposed to take effect – but unfortunately, it has not. We hope this will change,” he said.
According to the Office of the President, members of the U.S. Congress assured Ukraine of their support for efforts to bring Russia’s war of aggression to an end.
Zelensky said Russia had no intention of ending the war and was preparing new attacks for the winter. According to him, Ukraine supported U.S. President Donald Trump’s proposal for an energy ceasefire, but Russia continued attacking Ukraine’s energy infrastructure.
The President stressed that the Russian leader had rejected a proposal to halt strikes on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure in exchange for Ukraine stopping attacks on Russian oil refineries.
“We also offered another option – and I want to thank the members of the U.S. Congress who raised this idea. We could stop striking Russian oil refineries for 30 days. And in return, we would expect America to help us protect our skies for those same 30 days – just 30 days – specifically with Patriot interceptors. That would be fair. I’m sure. But unfortunately, we have not heard any willingness to help with this option either,” Zelensky said.
The Office of the President added that the teams would follow up on all the issues discussed during the meeting.
As Ukrinform reported, Zelensky met in Kyiv with a team from U.S. defense company Lockheed Martin to discuss expanding supplies of ballistic missile interceptors and the possibility of servicing and repairing F-16 fighter jets in Ukraine.

Gokhan Ergocun
19 October 2026•Update: 19 October 2026
Women hold 30.3% of managerial positions in Germany in 2025, falling well below the EU average of 35.9%, official data showed on Monday.
According to data from Eurostat released by the Federal Statistical Office (Destatis), around 1.3 million men held management roles in Germany in 2025, compared to 569,100 women.
Sweden took the top spot in the EU comparison with women filling 44.4% of leadership positions, followed by Latvia at 43.8% and Estonia at 43.1%.
Over a 10-year period, the proportion of female executives in Germany rose by one percentage point from 29.3% in 2015, while the EU average increased by four percentage points over the same timeframe.
Malta saw the highest increase over the decade at 13.9 percentage points, followed by Estonia at 12 percentage points and Austria at 7.5 percentage points.
The low share of women in leadership in Germany comes despite high female employment, with women making up 47.1% of all employed persons in 2025, slightly above the EU average of 46.5%.
Meanwhile, women made up 42.6% of government members in Germany in the third quarter of 2026, exceeding the EU average of 33.5%, according to the European Institute for Gender Equality.
Finland recorded the highest share of women in government across the EU at 56.7%, while Denmark reached 52.4% and Sweden achieved gender parity at 50%.
