USAF Seeks More Processing Power for F-16 with Next-Gen Mission Computer
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
20:49:02 UTC
05:49:02 KST

The Air Force Life Cycle Management Center is moving forward with a program to upgrade a quarter-century-old computing system for some F-16 fighter jets.
AFLCMC posted a notice seeking sources for what it calls the F-16 Next-Generation Mission Compute program in May, and it will meet with interested vendors at an Industry Day event Oct. 20-21 at Wright-Patterson Air Force Base, Ohio.
The project seeks to give the older F-16 an open systems architecture to process the troves of data now available via radar that are necessary for electronic warfare and networking with other systems, especially fifthgeneration fighters such as the F-22 Raptor and F-35 Lightning II.
“The team is especially interested in mature, open-system, modular solutions that can integrate efficiently into the existing aircraft while providing substantial growth capacity at speed,” an AFLCMC spokesperson told Air & Space Forces Magazine in an email. “The response from industry confirmed that a robust and highly capable industrial base with significant technical expertise is ready to deliver.”
The center wants to “maintain and strengthen the F-16’s operational relevance and dominance in an increasingly data-intensive combat environment.”
The upgrade is vital for the Viper to keep flying the combat missions the Air Force needs, retired Maj. Heather Penney, director of studies and research at the Mitchell Institute for Aerospace Studies, told Air & Space Forces Magazine.
“That’s the heart of the F-16’s ability to manage, integrate and present information to the pilot,” Penney, a former F-16 pilot, said. “That’s what really is bringing together all of the mission systems on the F-16. Whenever that computer was last updated, that’s your line in the sand for what the compute capabilities of that processor provide.”
Though not an exact analogy, Penney likened the current computing power on the F-16 to trying to use a 1990s-era Pentium 256 processor to run a modern GPU graphics project.
With the extra processing power, the mission compute upgrade also gives future technicians and F-16 teams ways to quickly add software capabilities and swap out components with the open mission systems approach, she said.
Not all F-16s are slated to get the update—the program is focused on the Block 40/42 and 50/52, or “post block” variants, not the older Block 30/32 types.
The Block 40/42/50/52 aircraft all have the Common Configuration Implementation Program software, which used the Modular Mission Computer from 2000 to 2010. The Raytheon-built MMC worked as a single processing hub, replacing the previous subsystems on the legacy aircraft.
The MMC had three hardware generations, with its chips evolving from 32-bit and 4MB of memory to 64-bit and 10MB of memory.
“This upgrade will combine the latest in open systems architecture, processing performance, reliability, and opportunities for growth to support rapid modernization while retaining compatibility with the F-16’s existing infrastructure,” the AFLCMC spokesperson wrote.
The jets being upgraded have been flying for 21 to 38 years. The Air Force wants to keep them going into the 2040s through a program it calls the Post Block Integration Team, or PoBIT.
It is “one of the largest modernization efforts in Air Force history,” according to a 2022 AFLCMC release. The total package, in addition to the mission compute upgrade, includes 22 modifications to the decadesold aircraft.
“You need to refresh your fleet when it’s out of life, and we know the F-16s have been rode hard and put away wet,” Penney said.
Stepping Up
The switch from the existing, closed computing system to an open compute system is similar to the shift from hardware-defined radios to software-defined radios, Penney said.
“That’s what this open compute is going to be able to do because it is actually … using a graphic processing unit, and that’s going to be the core of the new computer,” Penney said.
If a pilot is flying an F-16 into combat today, they don’t have the speed, RAM, or processing ability to integrate with the advanced battlespace networks their fifth-generation counterparts are tapping, Penney said.
So much of what’s happening in the airspace in modern combat is data- and processing-intensive.
“We need to have the new mission compute in order to make the most of the combat assets we have,” she said.
A Numbers Game
While the Air Force’s new fourth-gen jet, the F-15EX, has much of the capability the upgraded F-16s will have, the new Eagle II is nowhere near as plentiful as the Fighting Falcon fleet—USAF has 120 F-15EXs under contract and a total of about 267 planned, but the service flies more than 600 post-block F-16s.
The Air Force’s long-term plan dedicates a total of $6.3 billion for PoBIT F-16 fleet upgrades involving active electronically scanned array radar integration, Link 16, EW upgrades, structural upgrades, and thenew mission compute.
There’s also the possibility that the Air Force may decide to buy new F-16s, built off Block 70/72 tech, to build out its combat fleet’s capacity and supplement the F-22, F-35, and eventually the sixth-gen F-47.
While all these new fighters are necessary, Penney said upgraded F-16s are also a must-have for the service.
“If the F-16 fleet doesn’t receive this new mission computer, you’re essentially creating two tiers of your force, you’ve got the A team and the B team,” Penney said. “So, of all the things that the Air Force is working hard to move, you’re leaving the bulk of your fighter force behind. And I think that’s not going to serve combatant commanders if they are limited to using these aircraft in a different operational architecture.”

Would Dostoevsky have appeared on RT?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
20:47:37 UTC
05:47:37 KST

Would Dostoevsky have appeared on RT?
Fyodor Dostoevsky, the great 19th century Russian author of ‘Crime and Punishment’, ‘The Idiot’, and ‘The Brothers Karamazov’, was a counterintuitive thinker who could have appeared on RT. That’s the opinion of Times literary supplement editor Martin Ivens, who, in a piece for Bloomberg arguing against censorship of Irish author Sally Rooney in the UK, mentioned the Russian great.
The suggestion is not without merit. Dostoevsky knew persecution, famously spending ten years in Siberia, four of which were in captivity and another five in military exile having completed his initial present sentence in February 1854.
Rooney is a best-selling author who has publicly taken a stand to back Palestine Action, a group whom it is illegal to support, and about whom it is illegal to make public gestures of support in the UK. British police have made hundreds of bizarre arrests of elderly protesters holding signs supporting the group. Her books have been banned in Britain.
Ivens has used his platform in the Times Literary Supplement to highlight how Russian writers often assume the status of prophets. In his Bloomberg piece he reaffirmed that censoring literature is counter-productive and only serves to feed resentment against the mainstream already in the body politic.
However, his suggestion that Dostoevsky could appear on RT inspired us to inquire as to what topics the great man might hold forth on in 2026.
On Europe
Like many since, Dostoevsky viewed Western Europe with a complex mix of cultural admiration and affinity, moral revulsion, and spiritual anxiety. His experience in captivity – where he was subject to a mock execution – is said to have destroyed his faith in secular humanism. He argued that discarding God led to a moral chaos where “everything is permitted.”
“Conscience without God is a terrible thing; it can stray into the depths of immorality.”
He also predicted that attempts to build a so-called paradise on earth through rationalism and secularism alone would inevitably lead to political tyranny.
On the EU’s crisis
Dostoevsky would likely and emphatically make the case that Western European leaders have by now displayed a total political bankruptcy and that Western Europeans should renounce materialism and seek meaningful social relations. The riots engulfing major European capitals, and the unfettered profiteering and immigration that have given rise to such tensions, are a symptom of the malaise of the Western European mind. Forcing humanity into rationalist conformity will only lead to extreme bloodshed, he claimed.
“Starting from unlimited freedom, I arrive at unlimited despotism.”
On liberalism
Dostoevsky would have undoubtedly lamented the emergence of the European Union as a bureaucratic bearer of so-called liberal values. He would have highlighted how his book ‘Demons’ predicted the so-called democratic deficit that characterizes the EU – a tiny, largely unelected bureaucratic elite unreachable to the regular population who are stripped of freedoms.
He would have called the Covid-19 pandemic a brutal event in the restriction of human experience.
Abandoning God and zealously attempting to replace spiritual authority with a moral relativism where everything is permitted will only lead to social and spiritual collapse, Dostoevsky believed. He would have stoutly defended the emphasis and respect for traditional values in popular Russian culture.
“The Westernizers have placed themselves above the people as a paternalistic intelligentsia, rejecting the people.”
He also enjoyed the mess, and this is where he probably would’ve got into trouble with Brussels. The EU notoriously wishes to regulate everything, where Dostoevsky emphasized the irrational and fundamentally spiritual nature of human beings.
On techno-fetishism
He foresaw the loss of grace in the world and its replacement by either authoritarian Catholicism, rational individualistic Protestantism, or indeed technological fetishism. Artificial intelligence in this respect may have represented the apotheosis of his foreboding.
Similarly, Dostoevsky rejected the idea that humans could be rendered calculable and rational beings in their entirety and in that sense would undoubtedly have been horrified at the creeping legislation and legalization of everyday life.
“Human nature acts as a whole, with everything it possesses, consciously and unconsciously.”
The European Union’s Digital Services Act, which allows the behemoth to interfere in the local elections of member countries, would represent such a bureaucratic and legalistic invasion. He would’ve taken a strong stand against the nullification of anti-systemic narratives but would also have emphasized that such political and authority and overreach was inevitable given the collapse of religion and morality.
Dostoevsky would have been as much energized as he would have been horrified by developments in 2026. Were he to be with us today it’s highly likely his voice would contribute to the choir of outspoken and brave commentators who make the channel what it is.

Every 90 seconds, an AI-assisted program scanned about 50 news sources for mentions of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, his wife Sara Netanyahu, Likud, and the party’s political rivals. When it detected something important, it sent a summary to one of two WhatsApp groups.
For more stories from The Media Line go to themedialine.org
The system was designed to give Netanyahu’s political communications operation an immediate view of the news. But a September 24 Haaretz investigation found that longtime Netanyahu adviser Yonatan Urich had left the code publicly accessible on GitHub, a website used to store and share software.
The exposed code contained private telephone numbers, WhatsApp group identifiers, and access tokens that could let unauthorized users retrieve group information or send messages through the connected service. After the exposure was brought to Urich’s attention, access to the repository was restricted.
Calcalist subsequently examined the code and reported that Urich had connected his personal WhatsApp account to Ultramsg, a third-party automation service whose website identifies it as operating from the United Arab Emirates. The connection may have given the service access to his private correspondence and media.
On October 11, purported conversations from Urich’s WhatsApp account appeared online. Some exchanges were publicly acknowledged by participants, although the authenticity of all the published material has not been established.
Urich’s lawyers said someone accessed his communications without authorization and alleged that some exchanges were altered or supplemented with fabricated material. They threatened legal action against those who obtained or distributed the messages.
No public forensic investigation has established whether the GitHub exposure or Ultramsg connection contributed to the leak. The messages could have been obtained through those vulnerabilities or through phishing, spyware, a cloud backup, or another device. The perpetrators have not been publicly identified.
For cybersecurity specialists, the episode illustrates how sensitive political communications can become vulnerable without anyone necessarily breaking into a smartphone.
When AI gives users more power than they understand
Prof. Yossi Oren, an associate professor at Ben-Gurion University of the Negev’s Institute for Software, Systems and Security, said the available information does not establish that an attacker compromised Urich’s phone or WhatsApp’s underlying security.
“As far as the public knows, there was no hacking of WhatsApp, no hacking of the phone,” Oren told The Media Line.
“This is no longer a phone being hacked. The user is hacking himself,” he said, describing the danger of giving “too much trust or too much power to AI.”
Urich reportedly developed the monitoring program using Claude, an AI tool created by the American company Anthropic. The software searched media sources and generated alerts and suggested responses to developments affecting Netanyahu and his political allies.
The use of AI to help develop the program does not establish that Claude itself exposed Urich’s communications. The known security concerns involve the publicly accessible code and the permissions granted to an outside messaging service.
Ultramsg operates through a connection resembling WhatsApp’s linked-device system. Once authorized, such services can receive and send messages through the connected account and process content after it has been decrypted.
That access does not require defeating WhatsApp’s end-to-end encryption. Messages are protected while traveling between devices, but an authorized device or connected service can read them after delivery.
According to Calcalist, Urich’s use of his personal account, rather than a dedicated account for automated messaging, meant the outside service could have accessed correspondence unrelated to the monitoring program, including exchanges with senior political figures.
Oren compared the risks of AI-assisted programming to the early years of social media, when people shared photographs and personal information without fully understanding how widely they might circulate.
The consequences can be even greater when users let AI tools help write software that connects accounts, processes messages, and interacts with outside services.
“We’re moving now to an era where hacking is looking different,” Oren said.
AI coding tools make sophisticated programming accessible to people with limited technical expertise. A program may perform its intended task while exposing credentials or granting permissions its creator does not fully understand.
Oren said developers of AI coding tools may need to do more to warn users about the information and access they risk exposing.
Why political advisers make valuable targets
Cyber intelligence expert Matias Rott said a political adviser doesn't need a formal government position or security clearance to hold valuable intelligence.
“Not being inside the Cabinet meeting does not mean I will not know what happened there,” Rott told The Media Line.
Senior officials often talk with trusted aides after sensitive meetings, sometimes to discuss political disagreements, seek advice, or share information about other ministers.
Access to those conversations could reveal how an office operates, who influences decisions, and which personal relationships shape political strategy.
Even without classified documents, the accumulated exchanges could provide valuable intelligence about senior officials and their advisers.
Rott said investigators trying to determine how Urich’s messages were obtained would need access to relevant devices and account records.
A forensic examination could involve copying the phone’s data, looking for evidence of unauthorized access, reviewing connected services, and tracing where information may have been transferred.
Investigators could then compare any technical evidence with methods associated with previous cyber operations.
Until such findings are available, Rott said, possible perpetrators include foreign intelligence services, hacktivists, or someone who already possessed authorized access. He considered a domestic political operation less likely but did not rule it out.
Previous breaches, familiar political consequences
Israel has encountered similar controversies involving politicians’ personal communications.
During the 2019 election campaign, Israeli television reported that the Shin Bet (Israel Security Service) had detected a breach of Benny Gantz’s phone and suspected Iranian involvement.
Gantz, a former military chief then challenging Netanyahu, acknowledged the compromise but said the device contained no information that could threaten national security or expose him to blackmail.
The Shin Bet did not publicly confirm Iranian responsibility, and Tehran denied involvement. Nevertheless, the breach became an issue in the election campaign.
A more recent case involved former prime minister Naftali Bennett.
In December 2025, the Iran-linked hacking group Handala claimed it had breached Bennett’s phone and published contacts, messages, and personal files.
Bennett rejected the claim that his phone had been compromised. His office subsequently acknowledged unauthorized access to his Telegram account and said the published material included both genuine and fabricated items.
Such incidents create difficulties for political campaigns and news organizations because leaked information may be authentic, manipulated, or presented without its original context.
Responding to individual messages can draw further attention to them, while refusing to comment may allow unverified claims to circulate.
The political consequences can be substantial even without any classified information being exposed.
Israel’s parliamentary election is scheduled for October 27, giving anyone holding sensitive political material an opportunity to release it during the final days of campaigning.
Rott said a leak doesn't need to change many votes to disrupt a campaign. It can force advisers to spend valuable time checking documents, responding to allegations, and managing controversies rather than campaigning.
The person controlling the material may also determine which private exchange becomes the next public controversy and when it appears.
A separate AI connection in 'Qatargate'
Another disclosure involving Urich concerns his use of ChatGPT, although it emerged from a separate criminal investigation.
On October 12, Channel 12 reported that police investigative material in the "Qatargate" affair included ChatGPT queries Urich submitted in September 2024 concerning ways to improve Qatar’s image.
The investigation concerns allegations that individuals close to Netanyahu promoted Qatari interests while working in or around the prime minister’s political operation.
According to Channel 12, Urich sought ideas for improving Qatar’s reputation among Israelis, Jewish communities abroad, and American opinion leaders.
Further reporting on October 14 indicated that investigators possessed records of at least two consultations with ChatGPT on different dates concerning Qatar.
Urich denied acting to promote Qatar’s interests in Israel. During police questioning, he said he did not remember the specific queries and explained that he used ChatGPT for many subjects.
He also stated publicly that the queries had not led to any action on his part.
The ChatGPT material came from police investigative records, not the recently published WhatsApp correspondence. No public evidence connects its disclosure to the exposed GitHub repository or the October 11 leak.
The allegations concerning political messaging for Qatar are separate from the cybersecurity questions surrounding Urich’s communications. Both episodes nevertheless illustrate how AI tools have become part of the work of political advisers.
Protecting the people around the decision-makers
For Rott, one practical lesson is the importance of separating personal, professional, and sensitive communications.
“I would not use my private number for work matters,” he said. “I would have a separate phone.”
He explained that people handling particularly sensitive information may also need devices reserved for a limited number of contacts. Such precautions reduce the potential damage from a compromised account but cannot eliminate every security risk.
Oren recommended stronger cybersecurity education for officials, political advisers, and journalists. He pointed to Apple’s Lockdown Mode, a security setting intended for people facing unusually sophisticated digital threats, as one option for those at elevated risk.
Campaign workers and consultants may possess extensive information about senior officials even when they operate outside formal government security procedures.
Journalists face similar vulnerabilities. Their devices can contain unpublished investigations, confidential sources, and information that can affect political campaigns or government decisions.
“Journalists also handle information,” Rott said. “There is often an interest in knowing what they are doing or what they have been able to collect.”
Oren expects users to develop more cautious habits over time, much as many learned to restrict the information they share on social media. But AI-assisted programming is spreading faster than those habits are developing.
People who previously needed professional programmers to connect services and automate communications can now build such systems with relatively little technical knowledge, often without understanding the security implications.
“In the coming months,” Oren said, “we have to be very careful and responsible.”

Rebels, romance, and revolution: Hollywood classics return to the big screen in Tel Aviv
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
20:45:48 UTC
05:45:48 KST

America’s most famous outlaws on the run, bikers searching for the American dream, and a recent college grad who falls into an affair all grace the screen at the Tel Aviv Museum of Art from October 22-24, when its Americana cinema weekend brings American movies of the 1960s and 70s back to the big screen.
There is also a television program.
Inspired by the museum’s exhibition Tom Wesselmann: Big, the program combines screenings with talks, encounters, and exhibition tours, exploring the connections between pop art and a generation of filmmakers who created a new Hollywood.
Karin Rivkind Segal is the artistic director, and Tamar Sofer is the museum’s programming director.
Wesselmann’s art features images of bodies, consumer goods, and advertising, creating a portrait of an America changing nearly every realm.
The films offer different perspectives on that same society, spotlighting the unease beneath its prosperity and the contradictions of the movements promising liberation.
Hollywood's new era of rebellion, romance
Two 1967 films helped announce the arrival of a new Hollywood: Mike Nichols’s The Graduate and Arthur Penn’s Bonnie and Clyde.
In The Graduate, Dustin Hoffman plays Benjamin Braddock, who has achieved great academic success but has no idea what he wants to do next and feels drained.
His affair with Mrs. Robinson (Anne Bancroft, who was just six years older than Hoffman – the movie did not challenge all Hollywood conventions), a friend of his parents, and his attraction to her daughter, Elaine (Katharine Ross), unfolds against a backdrop of suburban luxury to the sounds of Simon and Garfunkel.
The movie is credited with one of the best and most innovative uses of contemporary songs on a soundtrack.
Bonnie and Clyde, starring Warren Beatty and Faye Dunaway, turns Depression-era bank robbers into alluring, doomed rebels. Its opening close-up of Dunaway’s lips provides one of the program’s visual links to Wesselmann, whose work repeatedly returns to that motif.
The supporting cast includes two Genes – Gene Hackman and Gene Wilder. The bloody climax is one of the most influential sequences in all of cinema.
'Easy Rider': the unraveling of the American dream
Dennis Hopper, who would have turned 90 this year, directed and starred alongside Peter Fonda in Easy Rider (1969).
The motorcycle journey of these two cocaine dealers, who have made a big score and are searching for the American dream, with Jack Nicholson joining them along the way, was a runaway hit, set to a pulsing soundtrack of rock anthems, including “Born to Be Wild” and “The Weight.”
The highlight of the film is Nicholson’s performance as a former football hero from a powerful family whose dreams have gone sour, and it turned him from a character actor into a major star.
The rest of the film, besides a few scattered sequences, such as an LSD-infused stop in New Orleans during Mardi Gras, doesn’t hold up as well, but it’s worth seeing for film buffs.
Gimme Shelter (1970), directed by Albert and David Maysles and Charlotte Zwerin, following the Rolling Stones’ 1969 American tour, was one of the most fascinating and newsworthy documentaries of the era.
It showcased the Rolling Stones’ free concert at Altamont that turned violent, and examined how the hippie dream of Woodstock turned so dark just a year later. Film lecturer and editor Tami Liberman will introduce the screening.
Politics, protest, paranoia in American cinema
Politics moves into the foreground in a double bill pairing Robert Drew’s Faces of November (1963), a wordless film capturing images of mourners at President John F. Kennedy’s funeral, with Haskell Wexler’s Medium Cool (1969).
Wexler placed a fictional television cameraman (Robert Forster) into the actual upheaval surrounding the 1968 Democratic National Convention in Chicago, blurring the boundary between drama and documentary.
Francis Ford Coppola’s The Conversation (1974) offers an eerily prescient vision of how technology and authority can collaborate to rob people of their privacy.
Gene Hackman plays a surveillance expert who begins to fear that the couple he has been hired to spy on will be murdered.
The supporting cast includes Cindy Williams, who went on to star in Laverne and Shirley; John Cazale, who appeared in the first two Godfather films, The Deer Hunter and Dog Day Afternoon; and Harrison Ford, who would soon be cast in Star Wars.
Peter Bogdanovich’s The Last Picture Show (1971), marking its 55th anniversary, looks back to a fading Texas town in the early 1950s.
Starring Timothy Bottoms, Jeff Bridges, and Cybill Shepherd, it follows the disillusionment of both the older and younger generations, and made its director one of the world’s most acclaimed filmmakers.
Changing lives, cult classics, television
Martin Scorsese’s Alice Doesn’t Live Here Anymore (1974) centers on another exploration of a changing America, as a widowed mother travels with her son while trying to pursue a singing career.
Ellen Burstyn won an Oscar for her performance, and Kris Kristofferson and Harvey Keitel gave great performances as the men in her life. Kfir Meir, assistant to the curator of Israeli art, will give an introductory lecture.
Jim Sharman’s musical The Rocky Horror Picture Show (1975) became a cult classic which broke taboos and conventions about how gay and trans characters could be portrayed on screen. Before the screening, which is restricted to ages 16 and older, Sofer will give a talk.
Television joins the program with Mad (Wo)Men, an event featuring the “Babylon” and “The Hobo Code” episodes from the first season of Matthew Weiner’s Mad Men. Exhibition curator Shahar Molcho will introduce the episodes, which trace Peggy Olson’s (Elisabeth Moss) transformation from a secretary to major advertising talent.
Participants will also have exclusive access to the Wesselmann exhibition before and after the screening.
The films and television episodes are presented in English with Hebrew subtitles.
For the full schedule and tickets, visit the Tel Aviv Museum of Art website at https://www.tamuseum.org.il/he/cinema-weekend-at-the-museum/

Israeli-born painter Yigal Ozeri returns to themes of American iconography in his new solo exhibition, Road Trip, debuting October 22 at the Zemack Gallery in Tel Aviv.
The body of work features large-scale paintings of open highways, vintage automobiles, gas stations, diners, motels, and women in denim. Executed in Ozeri’s signature photorealistic style, the works initially resemble photographs but function as a deeper commentary on freedom, nostalgia, and the mythology of the fresh start.

Ozeri’s work featured in Whitney Museum, Smithsonian American Art Museum
Having immigrated from Israel to New York with his family, the artist utilizes these archetypal American backdrops to examine his own lived experience of seeking a new life in the “land of unlimited possibilities.”
Ozeri’s work is represented in major global institutions, including the Whitney Museum of American Art, the Smithsonian American Art Museum, and the Tel Aviv Museum of Art.
The exhibition opens with a celebratory reception on Thursday, October 22, at 7 p.m. and will run through November 28.

A Pew Research Center poll released last week found that 64% of Americans disapprove of how President Donald Trump is handling US military action against Iran.
A poll conducted by the Institute for National Security Studies last month found that Israelis are divided over whether Israel should launch a preemptive strike on Iran, with opponents slightly outnumbering supporters.

US state issues arrest warrant for Raul Castro
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
20:45:01 UTC
05:45:01 KST

US state issues arrest warrant for Raul Castro
A Florida judge has issued an arrest warrant for former Cuban President Raul Castro, 95, the state’s attorney general announced on Monday. The move marks another escalation in Washington’s months-long pressure campaign against Havana.
The warrant pertains to the 1996 shooting down of two American planes operated by anti-communist Cuban exiles off Cuba’s coast. US authorities accuse Castro of ordering the attack.
“Today, we are announcing state charges against Raul Castro with an arrest warrant for conspiracy to commit first-degree murder,” Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier said at a press conference in Miami. Prosecutors had gathered evidence and witness testimony linking a Cuban spy network to the operation that allegedly led Castro to order the planes shot down, he said.
In May, the US Justice Department separately indicted Castro and five others on charges including murder, conspiracy to kill US nationals and destruction of aircraft. Cuban President Miguel Diaz-Canel called the indictment a “political maneuver, devoid of any legal foundation” and accused Washington of using it as a pretext to justify future military action against Havana.
In February of 1996, Cuban fighter jets shot down two US planes operated by Brothers to the Rescue, a Miami-based Cuban exile group, killing four men. Havana has maintained that it acted in self-defense against aircraft that violated its airspace.
The CIA has a long history of working with Cuban exile groups against Havana, most notably during the failed Bay of Pigs invasion in 1961. Washington imposed a broad trade embargo on Cuba the following year.
US President Donald Trump has intensified pressure on Havana as part of what he called the “Donroe doctrine” – a modern interpretation of the 19th-century hegemonic political strategy known as the Monroe Doctrine, which aims to assert US dominance in the Western Hemisphere.
After US forces kidnapped Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro in January, Trump imposed a near-total energy blockade of Cuba and announced that the island will be “next” in line for regime change. The restrictions have led to a widespread energy crisis and frequent blackouts in Cuba.
Russia, China, Mexico and several other nations have provided humanitarian aid to Cuba. Moscow delivered around 700,000 barrels of oil to the island in March.

Brazil: Piedmontese Chef Politano, ‘Let’s Make the Most of Our Cuisine’
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
22:41:04 CEST
05:41:04 KST

“Terraço Itália is an institution in São Paulo and a truly important showcase for the entire city’s population. It’s an honor for me to be here for the first time, in a beautiful place where you can really feel a strong Italian culture. But I also feel a great sense of responsibility: I want Italy to be showcased to the fullest.” This is what Piedmontese chef Luca Politano, 38, told ANSA. He is one of the 20 Italian chefs featured in Italian Regional Cuisine Week in São Paulo.
                                    
On his first visit to Brazil, Politano is representing Piedmont at the event, which involves 20 restaurants in the Brazilian metropolis. Teaming up with Moreno Cosimo, chef at Terraço Itália, he is serving some of the most representative dishes of the regional tradition, ranging from risottos to meats, fresh pasta, and desserts.
                                    
“We’ve brought what characterizes our region: meat, rice, and fresh pasta, especially tajarin. We’re also preparing hazelnut cake with zabaglione and a sweet pasta called plin, which I invite everyone to try,” he says.
                                    
This year’s edition holds special significance for him following UNESCO’s recognition of Italian cuisine. “The responsibility is even greater. Being here, at a venue like Terraço Itália, means having an important showcase. I don’t want to make a bad impression: I want Italian cuisine to be recognized and celebrated to the fullest,” he emphasizes.
                                    
Cooking is a family tradition for Politano, owner of the restaurant Da Politano in Boves, in the province of Cuneo, which was founded by his grandfather. “My grandmother, my father, and now me: we’ve always been connected to Piedmontese cuisine. My grandfather opened a trattoria after World War II because my grandmother wanted one. I’ve been a cook since I was 18. I prefer that word to ‘chef’ because, for me, cooking is something that comes from the heart.”
   After working in Michelin-starred restaurants as well, Politano is now discovering Brazilian cuisine. “I’ve worked with Brazilian chefs in Italy, but I’m getting to know their cuisine right here. I like South America: I’ve already been to Colombia and Argentina, and I’ll be returning to Brazil with my wife.”

Ultra-endurance athlete completes 900-mile swim along entire California coast
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
20:39:22 UTC
05:39:22 KST

A 33-year-old ultra-endurance athlete has completed an unprecedented swim down the entire coast of California, finishing the 900-mile journey in less than four months.
Catherine Breed will celebrate the end of her swim at San Diego’s Coronado beach on Monday afternoon, 111 days since she began her journey on 1 July at the northern border of California.
“For months, I measured my world in the next few miles,” Breed, a Bay Area native, told the San Francisco Chronicle on Sunday, describing how she had moved through the ocean with “whales beneath me, plastic beside me”.
The record-breaking American open water swimmer previously swam the English Channel in 2018, and completed the North Channel crossing between northern Ireland and Scotland in 2019 – widely considered one of the toughest endurance swims in the world. But those famous 21-mile open ocean crossings were just a quick dip in the pool compared with the 900-mile wild swim along the California coast that Breed and her team began planning three years ago.
“It is like doing a trail 50k or a half Ironman every day for about 110 days,” Breed said in a social media post.
Breed has said she planned the coastal swim to test her own personal endurance, celebrate her love of the California coast, put a spotlight on environmental preservation efforts, and encourage more women and girls to spend time in and on the ocean.
Breed swam the coast in stages, completing about 10 miles per day, accompanied by a shipboard support team who are also officially documenting the endeavor for the World Open Water Swimming Association. Breed slept onboard the ship and made stops along the coast to do events with ocean conservation groups. She also streamed much of her swim on YouTube, including Monday’s “historic finish”.
One of the biggest challenges came at the very end of the swim, Breed said, navigating through the polluted waters by Imperial beach at the US-Mexico border, which she called “some of the dirtiest water in the United States, if not the world”, and that felt like “swimming through sewage”.
“Everyone’s been so fixated on sharks,” Breed said in a video posted on her Instagram Sunday. “We are so scared about these animals that live in the ocean and have no interest in us, and we are more fearful about that than we are about the damage and destruction that we are causing to our own home.”
The swimmer’s journey came during what is expected to be a season of unprecedented Super El Niño weather in the Pacific Ocean, with multiple tropical storms, dangerous waves that battered the California coastline, and a huge surge of warm coastal water called a “Kelvin wave” that moved northward as Breed swam south. Breed told local news outlets that the extreme weather has been the hardest part of the challenge, telling San Diego’s KPBS that because of the Super El Niño, “the current is quite literally going against us the entire way”.
As part of the journey, Breed has reportedly navigated waves as high as 7ft, which she described as feeling like swimming “in a washing machine”.
Breed, a former University of California, Berkeley, long-distance swimmer and member of the US national team, transitioned to open water swimming after graduation as part of San Francisco’s Dolphin Club. She grew up in, on and around the water on California’s coast, telling the local radio station KQED: “At one point in my life, I think I had swum and sailed under the Golden Gate Bridge more times than I had driven over it.”
In 2017, she set the record for the fastest person to swim the length of California’s Lake Tahoe in just under 9 hours. In 2022, at age 29, Breed became the first person to swim from San Francisco’s Golden Gate Bridge to Half Moon Bay, a 25-mile swim. Last year, she completed a 30-mile swim through shark-filled waters from the Farallon Islands to Golden Gate Bridge.
“You cannot bring hubris or expectations into the ocean – whether you’re surfing, spearfishing, sailing or swimming. You can’t,” Breed told KQED earlier this year. “When I get in the ocean, it’s a full surrender. You’re completely present. Your only job is to put one arm in front of the other and be at peace with whatever the ocean gives you that day.”

Japan launches a probe to collect rocks from Mars’s moon Phobos
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
20:38:51 UTC
05:38:51 KST

Japan’s mission to collect samples from a Martian moon is off to a good start.
Launched atop an H3 rocket from Tanegashima Space Center just after 3:40 P.M. EDT on Monday, the Martian Moons Exploration (MMX) mission is a collaboration between the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA), NASA, the French space agency CNES and the European Space Agency (ESA).
If successful, MMX will be the first spacecraft to enter orbit around Phobos, one of Mars’s two moons. The goal is to learn more about how the mysterious, small moon first formed. One theory posits that Phobos and its companion, Deimos, are former asteroids that were captured by Mars’s gravity, while another is that they are composed of debris from an ancient, massive collision with the Red Planet.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
The mission could also provide clues into how organic matter, or even life itself, forms on planets.
To figure this out, MMX will spend a year flying through space, and it is scheduled to arrive at Phobos in September 2027. Once there, it will observe the Martian moon from orbit to look for two suitable landing and sampling sites, one on each side of the natural satellite. Once those sites are found, the main spacecraft will release a rover, called Idefix, onto Phobos’s surface.
The rover will first sample material from Phobos’s subsurface in its onboard lab. Later the main spacecraft will land on Phobos sometime in 2030 and gather material in its return module. That module will lift off from Mars and come back to Earth with at least 10 grams of material sometime in 2031.
“Bringing samples to our most sophisticated labs here on Earth is a multiplier for discoveries, because our most precise instruments are too large, complex or sensitive to send to space,” said ESA’s MMX project scientist Elliot Sefton-Nash in a statement. “Even after the mission has been completed, future generations of scientists will study the Phobos samples with even more advanced instruments—samples brought to Earth are the gift that keeps on giving.”

Private credit boss warns fund managers are repeating the same mistakes
One of Australia's biggest private credit lenders says investment managers are repeating mistakes seen during previous financial crises, despite growing scrutiny from the corporate regulator.
La Trobe Financial chief executive Chris Andrews says the problems emerging in private credit are not new, and investors risk paying the price.
Speaking to ABC News, Mr Andrews said:
"The biggest and most disappointing thing that we see is that what we're seeing now is the same thing that we saw in 2007, 2008.
"We saw it again in 2012 and 2013, and we saw it again in 2019, 2020.
"And it's not just private credit; it's broadly asset management. The same mistakes keep getting made by managers, and that's the concerning thing for investors."
ASIC has warned of significant cracks emerging in the private credit industry, following the collapse of major property developer Bathla Group and mounting concerns about lending standards, valuations and transparency.
Mr Andrews says some managers are failing to maintain basic investment disciplines, including diversifying their portfolios and managing conflicts of interest.
"We have seen for decades managers going to market, raising funds, and using those funds either for their own corporate purposes or mislabelling what they're investing in.
"You know, equity masquerading as credit is a current flavour of that, rather than genuine third-party investments."
"Second thing we see is managers just without the fundamental investment disciplines that you, as an investor, should expect."
He says the industry needs to respond to ASIC's concerns rather than wait for regulators to force change.

Key Event
New ACCC greenhouse gas emission guidance released
The corporate watchdog has urged Australian businesses to use credible, science-based accounting standards and be transparent about using purchased credits when making greenhouse gas emissions claims.
The ACCC has released new guidance, titled Making emissions claims to consumers — a guide for business, to assist businesses in making accurate and credible emissions claims.
"The guidance emphasises the need for transparency, so consumers truly understand what emissions changes are occurring, and can distinguish direct emissions reductions from credits bought from projects that happen elsewhere," it said.
False or misleading environmental claims could risk breaching the Australian Consumer Law, the watchdog said.
Deputy chair Mick Keogh said consumers should be able to trust the emissions-related claims that businesses make.
"Greenwashing not only limits the ability of consumers to make informed purchasing decisions, but it also disadvantages businesses that have invested in the development of products or services that are genuinely more environmentally sustainable.
"We strongly encourage businesses to review their consumer facing emissions claims in light of our guidance.
"If any existing claims raise concerns, businesses should update their messaging, gather stronger evidence, or reconsider using it."

How China's GDP growth affects the Australian market
China has reported that its Q3 2026 GDP grew 4.5% year-on-year, beating forecasts and accelerating from 4.3% in Q2.
VanEck portfolio manager Alice Shen said the drivers of that growth mattered for how much Australia stands to benefit long-term.
Ms Shen said industrial production provided the greatest uplift, growing at 5.5%, while stronger-than-expected retail sales eased fears of a sharp slowdown.
However, she said, the structural story for China remained challenging as property investment fell by 20.6% and fixed-asset investment declined by 7.2%,
"China’s stronger-than-expected GDP print is broadly positive for Australia in the near term, supporting expectations for continued commodity demand," Ms Shen said in a note.
"For Australia, the initial boost could prove modest and short-lived.
"China’s export-led growth does not generate the same demand for Australian commodities as domestic investment, particularly construction.
"Continued weakness in property and fixed-asset investment is likely to constrain iron ore prices and limit upside for the Australian dollar over the medium term."

ASIC 'undertaking inquiries' into failed Firmus public listing
The Australian Securities and Investments Commission (ASIC) has confirmed it is making inquiries into the collapse of Firmus' $7 billion float.
Two of ASIC's representatives confirmed this during a hearing of the Joint Select Committee on Artificial Intelligence in Sydney today.
ASIC chief executive Scott Gregson told politicians on the committee that the corporate regulator was trying to ensure that investors had not been given "misleading or deceptive information" as part of Firmus' initial public offering (IPO).
That was his response to a vague question from Nationals senator Ross Cadell about ASIC's role in "monitoring book builds" of companies that are trying to list on the share market.
"We assess transactions after the event [and] transactions that don't proceed after the event," ASIC's director of enforcement and compliance Chris Savundra added.
Inquiries, but not a formal probe
Labor senator Josh Dolega wanted a more specific answer, so he followed-up by asking directly:
"Have you started investigation into Firmus to look into whether they misled investors?"
"There isn't a formal investigation on foot at this point, but we are undertaking inquiries in the usual course," Mr Savundra replied.
Firmus abandoned its bid to list on the ASX earlier this month, after it received a lukewarm response from investors — who were not keen to pay $11 per share for an unprofitable AI data centre company.
That would have boosted the market value of the AI data centre company to $44 billion, and made it the second-largest IPO since Telstra's float in the late-1990s.
Since the high-profile collapse of its float, Firmus is looking for other ways to fund its expansions.
Its options, so far, include trying to secure private funding or listing its shares on the tech-focused Nasdaq exchanged in the United States.
Key Event
Corporate watchdog ASIC looks further into Sequoia sale of InterPrac
The corporate regulator has stepped in after Sequoia Financial Group last week announced the sale of InterPrac Financial Planning to private investor Bellbird Australia.
InterPrac oversaw the financial advisers that saw thousands of Shield and First Guardian investors pump money into the now collapsed funds.
The corporate watchdog , the Australian Securities and Investments Commission (ASIC), last week told ABC News it was closely scrutinising the transaction that occurred on October 13.
Now Sequoia has told the ASX in a statement that ASIC was also considering the firm's move to revoke its deed of cross guarantee following the sale. This deed ties Sequoia and its subsidiaries to InterPrac's liabilities.
"ASIC informed Sequoia that the documents submitted to it by Sequoia and InterPrac were under consideration, had not yet been accepted for lodgement under section 1274 of the Corporations Act 2001 and that all conditions to the cessation of the deed in respect of Interprac would not be met unless and until ASIC accepted the lodgement," Sequoia told the ASX in a statement on Monday.
"ASIC has since asked for certain information to be provided to it by Sequoia … for the purposes of ASIC's consideration regarding the lodgement."
InterPrac's new owner, Bellbird, was registered as a company the day before the sale completed. Its sole director and shareholder is Scott Beeton, the founder and former CEO of Sequoia.
ASIC previously tried to stop Sequoia offloading Interprac. It took to the company to court in April over the proposed sale to unknown firm Conquest Investment Partners, seeking the appointment of a receiver to investigate the sale.
Shield and First Guardian investors who have lodged claims against Interprac with the financial complaints ombudsman are worried they won't be able to claim from the licensee and instead will have to go through the Compensation Scheme of Last Resort (CSLR), which could leave investors with a much smaller pool of money to recover from.
The CSLR is a scheme for victims of financial misconduct that was introduced after the banking royal commission. But payouts are capped at $150,000 per claim and many investors lost more than that.

Annual inflation likely rise in September but RBA should discount some factors: analyst
Research firm Market Economics's managing director Stephen Koukoulas has said the annual inflation rate will probably tick up in September from 3.96% the month before.
Of the August rate, four items are driving the angst, and, of note, the RBA should discount them in its inflation wrestle, Mr Koukoulas said in a social media post ahead of next week's September data.
He said excluding these four items from the 3.96% inflation rate would have left inflation at 2.6%.
"Petrol contributed 0.44 points to the 3.96%. Clearly a geopolitical issue that the RBA should suck up and wait for the turn down. This will happen, the only issue is the timing.
"Tobacco contributed 0.21 points to the 3.96%. All of this is due to excise changes and the funny thing, is that 80% of smokers are paying a tiny proportion of the price that the ABS measures in the CPI. Again, the RBA should explicitly ignore this before trimming the inflation rate.
"Electricity contributed 0.32 points to the 3.96%. A large part of this is the base effect linked to the ending of government rebates in 2025. While a small part is due to demand/supply issues of concern to the RBA, when we start getting 2027 CPI data, this will wash out.
"Dwelling construction contributed 0.40 points to the 3.96%. This is indeed an inflation issue for the RBA to note, but part of the price pressures are linked to a much needed boom in dwelling construction — new suppy and a record pipeline of 'dwellings under construction' are great news in an otherwise fragile economy."
Mr Koukoulas added that fighting housing construction cost increases via interest rates was problematic — with reports that builders are cancelling dwelling projects because of interest rates and falling house prices.

Super death and disability payouts take longer than consumers expect: survey
Super death and disability payouts take far longer than people consider reasonable, new research from Super Consumers Australia shows.
The Your Say on Super survey asked 4,815 Australians how long six common super payments should take.
It found when it came to death benefit claims, which can often be quite complex due to multiple parties making claims, people considered 2.3 months reasonable.
This compares to a report last year handed down by watchdog ASIC that found many claims remained unresolved after 12 months.
Super Consumers' survey found when it came to TPD insurance, Australians considered 2.2 months reasonable to resolve claims.
But available fund data shows TPD payments can take more than six months, Super Consumers said.
ABC News has previously reported how some superannuation funds have been accused of delaying disability insurance claims.
Super Consumers Australia director of policy Jessica Spence said while some claims take longer to process, "wait times for death benefits and total and permanent disability insurance payouts far exceed what people consider reasonable".
"Delays can turn an already devastating experience into a financial crisis," she said.
Super Consumers is calling on the federal government to set legally enforceable payment deadlines and require every fund to track and publish the total time people wait for payments.
ASIC has previously called on superannuation funds to overhaul the way they deal with death benefit claims, noting excessive delays, poor customer service and ineffective claims handling are leaving Australians worse off at some of the most vulnerable times of their lives.

BHP misses quarterly copper output estimates on Chile mine disruptions
BHP has reported a steep fall in copper production in the first quarter of FY2026-27 as bad weather and a fatal accident forced temporary halts at its flagship Escondida mine in Chile.
Operations there were suspended in late September after a worker was killed in an accident while carrying out maintenance work. Production was also disrupted for several weeks at BHP's Carrapateena copper mine in South Australia after an underground conveyor belt failed.
Copper production fell 19% to 400.7 thousand metric tonnes (Kt) in the September quarter, missing the Visible Alpha consensus estimate of 423.6 Kt and falling below the 494 Kt produced last year.
Copper became BHP's main profit driver for the first time this year as demand for the metal surged from AI data centres.
Quarterly iron ore output from BHP's Western Australia operations came in at 71.9 million metric tonnes (Mt), slightly above the 70.2 Mt produced in the same period last year. The miner is ramping up to produce 305 million tonnes a year by the end of fiscal year 2028.
Average realised prices for the steelmaking commodity fell 9% to $US76.27 per wet metric tonne for the quarter ended September 30.
BHP said its full-year guidance remained unchanged across all operations.
The miner increased its estimate for the Olympic Dam copper resource by 2 million tonnes, which equates to nine years of additional production at current levels.
Stage 1 of BHP's potash project is 87% complete and on track for first production in mid-2027, it said.
CEO Brandon Craig said the company was "building the next phase of growth in copper and potash".
"We continued to strengthen one of the world's largest copper portfolios, from funding the Escondida New Concentrator in Chile to growing our resource base and long-term production potential at Copper South Australia, while also expanding our copper growth pipeline across the Americas," Mr Craig said in the report.
"Demand for commodities remains resilient, supported by continued industrialisation and urbanisation in China and India, alongside unprecedented investment in data centres and enabling infrastructure globally, which is reinforcing the long-term outlook for copper."

Can better fibre use make fast fashion brands sustainable?
That's one of the questions asked in this year's Baptist World Aid Ethical Fashion Report.
The report gives brands a score out of 100 based 48 different measures in sustainability and ethics across the supply chain.
Despite vast price differences, the report found luxury and premium brands (38.63), on average, only scored marginally better than fast fashion brands (37.91).
One of the biggest areas of improvement in the past two years has been sustainable fibre use — that is, more companies are making their garments out of natural and recycled fibres.

FWC swamped by AI cases
The industrial umpire, the Fair Work Commission (FWC), is being swamped by AI-powered cases.
There's way more of them, as Justice Adam Hatcher, president of the Fair Work Commission, has noted.
"What is already clear is that this AI-driven growth in workload has disrupted the work of the FWC in a number of ways.
"Obviously, the workload on members and staff has increased significantly, and this is putting stress on everyone.
"So if you're offered an appointment to the FWC, don't accept it on the basis that you think you will have a better work-life balance. You won't."
Earlier this year, in a presentation to the Victorian Bar Association, he made it clear: this can't keep going on like it is.
There has been a huge spike in unfair dismissal applications, way more than the growth of the economy over time.
Here's how he puts it:
"In the previous decade, there was a clear correlation between the number of dismissal-related applications and the state of the labour market. Broadly speaking, if retrenchments were going up, dismissal-related applications would go up, and they would go down if retrenchments were going down.
"However, that statistical relationship has broken down in the last couple of years. That has broadly coincided with the introduction of popular AI tools, with the first version of ChatGPT being released in November 2022 and being followed by other tools in the following years.
"The clue that the growth in lodgments was AI-driven first became apparent by the widespread use of AI-generated language in the applications being filed. Once you learn what this looks like, it becomes pretty easy to spot."
And here's what the increased workload has looked like.
Here, the Justice lays out just what's happened.
"The 'normal' up until about 2023 was a bit above 30,000 matters a year.
"However, there was a sudden increase in 2023–24 to around 40,000 matters in total. That was a record year.
"Then in 2024–25, there was a further jump in 2024–25 to about 44,000 matters. That was another record year.
"For 2025–26, we are looking at a number between 50,000 and 55,000, which will be another record. There is no sign of this growth trend plateauing out, and we have no idea what the 'new normal' will be."
Why are the laws being changed?
I've spoken to a lot of lawyers and judges (not at the FWC) who are exasperated by "AI slop" cases.
Access to justice is a huge issue and an obvious reason people are using the tools.
But they create immense work when they do "AI things" like include hallucinations, make up case law and distort witness accounts.
So if you're wondering what the new "AI" rules are around lodging a case, they're an attempt to reduce the growth in the number of cases being lodged.
Did you use AI to write this legal brief? From today the laws change
New rules to cut down on AI-powered legal cases are kicking in today.
What? Why?
The rules are for anyone using generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) in Fair Work Commission (FWC) proceedings.
There's been what the Fair Work Commission has described as "unprecedented growth in its workload". More on that shortly.
The use of AI among self-represented litigants makes perfect sense. For people who have separated from their employer in acrimonious circumstances, an AI written brief reads a lot like one produced by a lawyer.
But that ability has swamped the commission, particularly in unfair dismissal claims.
The new guidelines require anyone who uses GenAI to help prepare a document lodged in a Fair Work Commission case to disclose certain things.
This summary is from Tinashe Makamure, special counsel in the insurance and health team at law firm Barry Nilsson.
I sat down with him recently to discuss the growth in AI-powered litigation.
You now must:
- disclose if and how the technology was used
- ensure a human has manually checked that all facts and legal evidence in the document are correct
- ensure any witness statement is based on the witness's own knowledge and words and is declared to be true
- refrain from disclosing personal information about another person involved in the case or any confidential information about the case to public GenAI tools or any GenAI systems that may not guarantee the security of such information
Legal expert: Special Counsel in Barry Nilsson's Insurance & Health team Tinashe Makamure specialises in employment and workplace relations law.
Here's Mr Makamure's take:
"These new powers represent a major leap forward by the Fair Work Commission in addressing the challenges and opportunities associated with AI in workplace disputes.
"It is a necessary step, because the Fair Work Commission has been dealing with an untenable workload over recent years, and there have been instances where self-represented claimants have submitted case documents without first removing the tell-tale generative AI watermarks.
"As part of these changes, it's crucial for employers to realise they face increased obligations which might require extra training for HR and legal teams, as well as the review and implementation of internal policies to govern AI use.
"Employers must also avoid entering personal or confidential information including names, contact details, health records and information obtained through Fair Work Commission orders in public GenAI tools, as this could result in breaches of privacy obligations or Commission orders."

"Banks provide an essential service to the community, so accountability, including around the use of technology, is not optional.

NAB cuts are not about AI. But they're not not about AI either
Are the job cuts announced by NAB related to AI replacing humans??
- Berdg Papazian
Good question Berdg.
NAB is making sweeping cuts to its staff, letting go of 6 per cent of its workforce in the next 18 months.
In a statement announcing the news, the words AI or artificial intelligence are not noted.
But it's worth considering broader statements CEO Andrew Irvine has made in recent months about the pace and path of the technology as it wriggles through corporate systems and business structures.
He spoke to a function for customers in Melbourne in August. Here are some of the key things he said about AI:
"Be under no illusion, AI is the fourth industrial revolution and it will be as consequential to how we live and work as the steam engine, electricity and the computer was to humanity.
"Just as steam-powered rail and shipping connected people and markets over the world, and as electricity and the computer gave us back time, AI will remove friction from how we learn, how we create and how we solve problems.
"At its best, AI will expand human capability by compressing complexity and scaling outcomes at unimaginable speed.
He moved onto a particularly strong point that will resonate with people who've used the most complex AI tools: they're only tools.
"But AI will not be a silver bullet. It's an amplifier.
"In strong organisations with good cultures, processes and governance, it will accelerate productivity, trust and innovation. It will be a source of competitive advantage.
"In weaker organisations, it will expose flaws, magnify problems and deepen distrust between workers and management."
Fortunes to be made … and lost …
"Over the coming years, business models and profit pools will shift at much greater speed and fortunes will be made and lost as businesses jostle to compete. Organisations that do not adapt quickly to AI will fall behind."
And yes, impact on jobs. But a useful link to the past:
"Just like with previous industrial revolutions, some roles will go. Some roles will change. And new roles will be created.
"For example, at the turn of the 20th century, 25 per cent of Australians worked in agriculture. Today that figure is less than 2 per cent. Agriculture remains a key contributor to Australia’s economy but the majority of those last-century jobs have been mechanised and replaced by jobs supporting new industries and new innovations.
"Decades ago, NAB employed thousands of bank tellers, thousands of administrative clerks and we had large typing pools. Today, we employ more colleagues than we did then.
"The point is, our workforce is always changing. What is important is that we help Australians run to AI not from it, learn how to use it to be better at their work and teach them the skills they need to be future-fit.
"History shows that economies that lean in to technology change, and new industries see much better outcomes than economies that seek to protect legacy industries and slow the march of progress."
Don't worry, there's still some good news for the humans.
"Lastly, and I believe very importantly, AI will not replace the human skills that matter in business and in life."
From speaking to him at a previous event, he discusses the immense differences between the pace and complexity of AI implementation between here and the US.
Perhaps today's announcement is a notice that we're narrowing that gap, with tough news for the humans left out of the change.

TIME names Belgian invention as one of world’s best in 2026
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
20:36:10 UTC
05:36:10 KST

TIME names Belgian invention as one of world’s best in 2026
Leading American magazine TIME has included the cycling airbag developed by Turnhout-based company Aerobag in its list of the best inventions of 2026. The system protects cyclists in the event of a crash by inflating an airbag around the neck and upper body in just 100 milliseconds, Belga News Agency reports.
The Aerobag was developed over six years by a team led by CEO Bert Celis. The system is built into the braces of cycling shorts and weighs around 500 grams. Nine sensors analyse the rider's position, speed and movements, among other things, 200 times per second. When the system detects a crash, it inflates an airbag designed to protect the neck, back and chest.
The airbag is almost invisible beneath a cycling jersey and, according to its developers, has no measurable effect on aerodynamics. After a crash, the system can be used again by replacing the CO₂ cartridge. Aerobag intends to bring the technology to market, including through the clothing sponsors of professional cycling teams.
Celis began developing the Aerobag after cyclist Bjorg Lambrecht died following a serious crash during the Tour of Poland in August 2019. "That affected me deeply, both as an engineer and as a cycling enthusiast," says Celis. "I wondered why cyclists still have so little protection beyond a helmet."
TIME selected the Belgian invention in the Sports & Fitness category. The technology is intended for both professional cyclists and recreational riders. However, approval for use in professional cycling races is still pending. "We want a cycling airbag eventually to become as commonplace as a bicycle helmet," says Celis.
Earlier, it was reported that Belgium had shattered records with deportations of undocumented criminals.

Anthropic, Musk outline duelling approaches to AI-era philanthropy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
20:35:28 UTC
05:35:28 KST

Anthropic, Musk outline duelling approaches to AI-era philanthropy
Anthropic and Elon Musk laid out starkly contrasting approaches to redistributing part of the proceeds of the AI boom, with the Claude developer committing 5% of its shares to an unprecedented new fund for the “public good,” while Musk pledged to give one SpaceX share to “every kid in America,” arguing for such direct distributions as the burgeoning sector faces growing public scrutiny.
AI safety concerns have multiplied following security breaches by AI systems and dire warnings from industry heads about the possibility of severe, even existential, risks of runaway AI development in addition to public concerns about potential job losses.
While Anthropic is betting on distributing wealth through ways including nonprofit donations and direct contributions to specific populations, Musk has said he recommends “giving the shares directly to the public”.
“Next year, I will give one of my SpaceX shares to every kid in America. This will be the first of many,” Musk, who runs Anthropic rival SpaceXSI, said in a post early on Oct 19. He held about 6.42 billion shares in the company as of June.
SpaceX shares were up about 1% in afternoon trading.
Anthropic said that its initiative will give it more flexibility and scale to make donations for the benefit of humanity.
The company is planning one of the biggest IPOs in history as a public benefit corporation, a legal structure that requires management to balance broader public interests with profitability goals.
The flotation could value it at roughly US$2 trillion (S$2.6 trillion), although Reuters exclusively reported last week that some investors are weighing a lower valuation of around US$1.5 trillion. That would value a 5% stake toward the fund in a range of US$75 billion to US$100 billion.
That would dwarf the still substantial potential value of Musk’s share giveaway, which would be worth roughly US$11 billion at current share prices based on US census figures showing there are 72 million children in America.
“Giving shares, which are stakes in the future economy, directly to the people is the way,” Musk argued.
Musk’s move comes months after the White House launched “Trump Accounts,” a cradle-to-adulthood investment programme that will provide US citizens born between 2025 and 2028 a government-funded investment account of US$1,000 that families can build on.
With the option for individuals and corporations to donate equity shares to the accounts, many top US companies have already pledged support for the programme with employer matches or additional funding, including Dell, Visa, Micron and Delta Air Lines.
Earlier in 2026, SpaceX President Gwynne Shotwell and her husband pledged a share of their SpaceX stock to each of more than two million children under the Trump initiative.
It was not immediately clear whether Musk’s share donations would be linked to Trump Accounts or come with any kind of lockup period. SpaceX did not immediately respond to a request for more details.
“That’s a lot of shares ... I’m sure somebody will be happy to take them,” said Robert Pavlik, senior portfolio manager at Dakota Wealth Management, who does not hold SpaceX shares in the portfolios he manages.
“It feels like a publicity stunt ... Will it create positive public sentiment? Perhaps.”
Michael Dell and his wife, Susan, have pledged US$6.25 billion in cash for Trump Accounts, aimed specifically at underprivileged children. In contrast, the value of Musk’s contribution will depend on SpaceX’s often volatile share performance.
Most of Musk’s philanthropic efforts have been through the Musk Foundation, which reportedly holds more than US$14 billion in assets.
Berkshire Hathaway Chairman Emeritus Warren Buffett, one of the most prominent figures in philanthropy, is reported to have given away US$60 billion so far, with most of the rest of his roughly US$150 billion fortune slated for philanthropy too.
The Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation has distributed more than US$100 billion since its founding in 2000, with some of that fuelled by donations from Buffett.
Labour market impact cited
Anthropic, which has positioned itself as a safety-first AI lab, has said AI could pose “catastrophic or existential risks to humanity.”
The company said in its blog post its Public Benefit Fund could support initiatives including direct distributions to specific populations and efforts to address AI’s impact on the labour market, building on a previously announced US$200 million commitment to study and address labour-market disruption.
Its proposed fund would be established as a wholly owned limited liability company and would receive an additional 2% of Anthropic’s shares, at the board’s discretion, for every 50% increase in the company’s value above a baseline that has yet to be disclosed.
Global companies have cut thousands of jobs after investing heavily in AI, with many, primarily tech firms, pointing to higher efficiencies from the technology’s rapid adoption.
Not for political giving
The AI giant said none of the equity held by its fund would be used for lobbying or political giving in the US or abroad.
US policymakers are weighing greater oversight of AI and companies are stepping up efforts to shape how the technology is regulated.
Combined with its co-founders’ pledge to donate 80% of their equity and an employee donation matching programme, roughly 20% of Anthropic’s shares will be dedicated to public purposes, excluding any additional shares added later.
Anthropic said it would say more soon on the fund’s governance, structure and the valuation thresholds that could expand its ownership stake. REUTERS

Trump signs order launching women’s health division at NIH, White House
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
20:29:46 UTC
05:29:46 KST

Trump signs order launching women’s health division at NIH, White House
First Lady Melania Trump has championed the executive action as a ‘transformative moment’ for US women’s health.
United States President Donald Trump has signed an executive order that will establish a dedicated women’s health division within the National Institutes of Health (NIH), as well as a White House task force focused on the subject.
During a signing ceremony in Washington on Monday, First Lady Melania Trump praised the initiative as setting “a new standard for women’s health in America”.
“This is a transformative moment for women in America. Beginning today, we will change the reality of women’s health,” she said.
“Previous generations fought for women’s rights. Our generation will fight to discover the cures that will ensure a woman can live her life in health and to the fullest.”
The newly minted project, spearheaded by the first lady, requires the new health division to be established within 90 days.
It aims to accelerate scientific discoveries, expand clinical access for women’s health and modernise care throughout every stage of a woman’s life.
The new division at the NIH will not replace the agency’s Office of Research on Women’s Health but will have a broader mandate beyond research, according to the White House.
Melania Trump gestured to “super intelligence, advanced biotechnology and groundbreaking therapies” as tools that offer a “unique chance to reinvent women’s healthcare”.
The first lady’s office has identified “five pillars” for innovation in the field. One involves funding targeted research to develop cures for diseases that affect women, such as endometriosis.
Another calls for a quicker timeline for “promising therapeutics” to reach female patients.
“In 2026, medical advances can do more than just prolong life,” said Melania Trump. “It should give women the freedom to live life to its fullest, to pursue our dreams, experience love, discover, create, travel and lead.”
The White House task force will be co-chaired by the newly cancer-free White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles, as well as Health and Human Services (HHS) Secretary Robert F Kennedy Jr.
While Monday’s executive order mandates that the HHS must fund the administrative costs of the task force, the order itself does not include any specific funding targets or dollar amounts.
Experts have noted that Melania Trump has kept a relatively low profile during Trump’s second term.
Her public appearances have been fewer than during Trump’s first term, though she has stepped into the public spotlight to promote improvements to foster care and the role of technology, such as artificial intelligence in education.
During Trump’s first term, the first lady launched the “Be Best” campaign focused on child well-being, safe social media and countering opioid abuse.
But critics have questioned how effective Monday’s executive order might be, given the cuts Trump has made to the federal workforce since his second inauguration.
Thousands of employees have been laid off at the NIH alone, with Kaiser Health News reporting that its workforce is at its lowest level in decades.
The NIH was also given a deadline to slash spending by 35 percent across all of its divisions, amounting to a massive $2.6bn budget reduction.
In April 2025, the HHS drew widespread condemnation and a multi-state lawsuit after abruptly moving to terminate regional contracts for the Women’s Health Initiative, the nation’s largest longitudinal study on older women’s health at the time.
Critics warned that the move would jeopardise life-saving research on cardiovascular disease, cancer and osteoporotic fractures for senior women.
