Anti-Netanyahu bloc plots swift Knesset takeover after election, but internal divisions threaten plan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
19:56:05 UTC
04:56:05 KST

The anti-Netanyahu bloc is preparing to move quickly to seize control of key Knesset positions immediately after the October 27 election, with plans to replace the parliamentary speaker and block controversial judicial overhaul laws from taking effect. But even before voters head to the polls, disagreements within the opposition are raising doubts about whether the parties can secure the votes needed to carry out their plans.
Representatives of the parties have been holding a series of meetings to coordinate their strategy for the first days after the election, drafting legislation and identifying parliamentary moves that could be carried out even before a new government is formed. Their most pressing concern is a set of laws passed by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's coalition that are scheduled to take effect after the election, leaving little time for opponents to intervene.
The plan begins with gaining control of the Knesset's Arrangements Committee, which oversees parliamentary business during the transition to a new government. Opposition officials believe that controlling the committee could allow them to replace the Knesset speaker within days and begin advancing legislation to repeal or delay the coalition's laws.
But the strategy depends on cooperation from lawmakers across several parties, and that is where concerns are emerging. At a recent meeting, some representatives warned that candidates on certain opposition lists had previously supported elements of the judicial overhaul and might refuse to vote for their repeal.
The legislation at the center of the dispute includes measures concerning the attorney general, changes to the Police Internal Investigations Department that would place it under the Justice Ministry, and a law altering the composition of the Judicial Selection Committee. The latter is scheduled to take effect immediately after the election.
The latest meeting brought together Oded Forer of Yisrael Beytenu; Shaul Meridor and Orit Farkash representing Gadi Eisenkot's Yashar! party; Liran Avishar Ben-Horin and Gili Haushner from Naftali Bennett's Beyahad party; and Ram Shefa of the Democrats.
Some participants raised concerns about the decision-making process within Eisenkot's Yashar! party, particularly after its representatives asked for time to consult before providing answers on certain legislative proposals. Others pointed to previous statements by candidates on opposition lists who had publicly supported some of the coalition's judicial changes.
"Some people on these lists promoted and publicly supported the judicial overhaul laws," one source in the anti-Netanyahu bloc said. "And that's where the problem lies."
A senior figure involved in the discussions said the absence of clear positions from some parties was making it difficult to reach binding agreements before election day. "Some parties are not stating their positions clearly," the official said. "There are parties with a range of opinions, and we don't know what their guiding position is. Certain issues came up in the meetings, and there was hesitation. Not everything can be taken for granted, and there is a lack of clarity on some matters."
Despite the disagreements, working groups have begun preparing legislative proposals aimed at reversing existing laws and advancing measures they believe must be approved quickly. The goal is to complete as much of the groundwork as possible before the election, rather than spend the first days afterward negotiating over legal language and parliamentary procedure.
The preparations also account for a possible election outcome in which neither political bloc emerges with a clear majority, but the anti-Netanyahu parties hold a narrow parliamentary advantage. Under that scenario, they hope the president would give their bloc the mandate to attempt to form a government, a development they believe could also help them secure control of the Arrangements Committee.
"Our goal is for the president to give the mandate to our bloc," opposition officials said. "The importance of receiving the mandate is not only the ability to try to form a government, but also gaining control of the Arrangements Committee. If we control the committee, we can replace the Knesset speaker within a day or two, or at the beginning of the following week."
The officials stressed that the timetable would be tight, making advance agreements essential. Closer to election day, the parties intend to assess how individual candidates are likely to vote, with particular attention to those whose positions on judicial legislation remain unclear.
That effort is also intended to prepare the bloc for political pressure from Likud. Opposition officials believe Netanyahu's party will try to persuade individual lawmakers to withhold support from efforts to repeal the coalition's legislation, potentially depriving the anti-Netanyahu camp of a majority on critical votes.
"There is legislation that must be advanced as soon as possible after the election," a senior opposition official said. "If the people we're concerned about don't vote with us, we may not be able to repeal the coalition's laws. We're certain Netanyahu will apply enormous pressure, and we need people who can withstand it."
Those concerns follow an earlier report by ynet and Yedioth Ahronoth that Likud had established a dedicated team to examine new candidates on opposition party lists, including their family connections, social circles and influential associates. The reported aim is to identify potential avenues of influence that could prevent lawmakers from voting against Likud after the election.
For the anti-Netanyahu bloc, the parliamentary battle is therefore taking shape before the election itself. Its parties are preparing to move rapidly against the outgoing coalition's legislative agenda, but their ability to do so will depend not only on the number of seats they win, but also on whether they can maintain unity when the first crucial votes are called.

One man down and on a flattening pitch, Boland and Starc continue to shine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
19:55:32 UTC
04:55:32 KST

As the afternoon meandered on and the stubbornly soggy outfield of St George's Park threatened to waste another day of the second Test at Gqeberha, South Africa had good and bad fortune to ponder.
The good news was that upon the game's long-awaited resumption at 3:45pm local time, Australia would be without one member of its intimidating quartet of fast bowlers due to illness. The bad news, with no disrespect to the others, was that it wasn't Scott Boland.
Sure enough, within 10 minutes of the restart, the Victorian had struck again to remove debutant opener Marques Ackerman — Boland's third wicket in five typically compelling overs.
Worse still for the Proteas, Mitchell Starc, who'd been a little out of sorts in his brief spell on day one, was hitting his straps too. Bowling with fluency and at speeds nudging towards 150km/h, the left-armer soon struck as well thanks to a lazy waft outside off stump from Matthew Breetzke and a smart catch from Alex Carey.
At that stage, South Africa was 4-40 and staring into the abyss.
What transpired in the hour that followed was heartening for South Africa, though perhaps not enough to shift the course of this truncated contest.
The pitch — whose lack of hessian coverings during the worst of the downpours was said to be predictive of imminent mayhem — seemed to flatten out and not behave so treacherously at all.
The batting, circumspect but not unadventurous, started to look less fragile as Proteas skipper Temba Bavuma got going with South Africa's recast number six, Ryan Rickelton. And the missing bowler, Josh Hazlewood — who Cricket Australia says will return on day three — was suddenly looking like a real hole in the bowling rotation.
Loading Twitter content
Indeed, a bubbly 50-run partnership later, and with stumps not far away, Bavuma could have permitted himself some satisfaction that he and Rickelton had pulled things out of the fire so calmly. He might also have felt his side's bad luck was starting to turn when a sun-blind Marnus Labuschagne put down Rickelton at leg slip.
As ever, though, Boland had other ideas. Well, one idea, to be honest: hammer away on a patch of the pitch roughly the size of a Wisden cricketers' almanac and wait for the ball to seam either way.
The burly right-armer duly took Rickelton's outside edge and Matt Renshaw, at first slip, took a catch that could be charitably described as fortunate; it looked like Carey's, but the keeper didn't move a muscle; Renshaw did, on a significant delay, grasping it in one hand when the ball was past him and then slowly mouthing some easily-made-out words of relief: "Oh. My. God."
Thus, from a relatively promising position, the Proteas finished the day 5-97 from the 43 overs that have been possible so far. Boland, with 4-31 from 14 overs, was not simply the pick of the bowlers but a one-man show who single-handedly lifted the contest out of its torpor, his every delivery imbued with potential.
Now that he is ranked in the world's top 10 Test bowlers without commanding regular selection, it is often said that Boland is unlucky. Another way of looking at it is that, at 37 — an overripe age for a fast bowler of any kind, let alone one so vigorous and impactful — he simply knows his own virtues and limitations better than he did as a younger man, and can conserve and channel his energies in ways the regulars cannot.
It is also, surely, a minor triumph of man management. That Boland and, perhaps more so, Starc continue to glide to the crease in such prolonged spells and with such devastating impact is not a matter of luck. Today, again, Starc, who is also pushing 37, was a genuine menace: a 148km/h bouncer to Bavuma was as scary as anything he bowled in his 20s.
We talk often of Starc's eye-popping strike rate of 45 — six better than Dennis Lillee and Mitchell Johnson, seven better than Glenn McGrath and Jeff Thomson, 12 better than Starc's old sparring partner Shane Warne — but it is now his longevity that is so unusual to the point of freakishness.
Playing in his 109th Test, Starc is bowling at a level that history suggests should be impossible. Jason Gillespie and Brett Lee, the express quicks of preceding decades, were done with Test cricket at 31 and 32 respectively; like Johnson, they'd strung together 70-something Tests between the inevitable injuries.
Touch wood, Starc will feasibly play 50 or 60 more Tests than that — a coda of similar length to Merv Hughes's entire Test career. The way Cricket Australia has balanced Starc's financial and physical preparation requirements for the last decade is an organisational triumph that should be studied. If only it, and Starc himself, were replicable.
As for South Africa, what they can replicate remains to be seen, but it's very unlikely, as in Durban, that promising 50-partnerships will get this one done.

"Zelenskyy doesn't know what he's talking about. Zelenskyy is a man that should have had this war settled a long time ago. If he would have listened to me, he would have made a much better deal a long time ago," Trump told reporters before departing the White House to campaign for the Nov. 3 midterm congressional elections in the state of Kansas.
"I think it's time for somebody else to negotiate on behalf of Ukraine because what's happened? A tremendous number of people are dead. They're losing their male population," he said.
"Maybe it's time for Zelenskyy to get somebody else to negotiate," Trump added.
"Zelenskyy is not helping matters much. I think he doesn't want to stop it, but I want to see people not die."
"We've given a lot to Ukraine. They've given us nothing," he added.
 
Possible talks with Putin, Xi on Ukraine

"No, but I would do it. Not so much for Ukraine because Russia, frankly, has been fine on Ukraine," he said.
Trump indicated that nuclear disarmament would be a priority in any such meeting.
"We would have it to talk about nuclear weapons and denuclearization," he said.
"We have more nuclear weapons than anybody. Russia is second, China is third, but catching up. China was way behind, and now they're catching up. It'll take about probably five years," Trump added.
Asked whether he would meet Putin and Xi to discuss ending the war without Zelenskyy present, Trump said he would do "anything I can do to end the war, whether somebody's there or not."
The Wall Street Journal reported Sunday that Putin had proposed a trilateral meeting next month with US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping to discuss the war in Ukraine and seek an end to the conflict on terms favorable to Moscow.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told the Journal that discussions were underway but there was no clear understanding yet on the meeting or its agenda, though all three sides acknowledged the “hypothetical possibility” of such a meeting.
The report came on the heels of Trump announcing a deal to buy Russian diesel fuel and later signing an executive order waiving key sanctions on Moscow, a move Zelenskyy criticized.
"Any easing of sanctions against Russia without a clear and lasting de-escalation agreement with Russia is an obvious weakness," Zelenskyy said.
 
Russia, China, and Iran
Trump also said Russia and China had provided limited support to Iran despite their close relations with Tehran.
"Russia could have done a lot more to help Iran. Russia's done very little for Iran. China could have done a lot more for Iran," he said.
"I view that as being a very positive thing," Trump added.

The incident happened about 3.35pm and involved a four-wheel drive, which allegedly U-turned before striking Haines. The independent federal MP is in a critical but stable condition at Melbourne’s Alfred hospital and has lost one of her legs.
A 43-year-old man has been taken to Wangaratta police station for questioning.
‘Violence has no place,’ says human rights commission
The Australian Human Rights Commission has expressed shock and sadness at the attack on Helen Haines. In a post to social media, the commission said:
Everyone should be safe at work and in life. Violence has no place in our society.
Everyone should be treated with respect, irrespective of their political opinions, gender, faith, race or background.
Parliamentarians must be able to carry out their duties safely. This attack happened against a backdrop of increasing polarisation and threats against politicians. We must address intimidation, hatred, threats and violence that undermine our democracy and democratic institutions.
Zoe Daniel: ‘It was obvious … someone would get physically hurt’
The three-time ABC foreign correspondent and former independent member for Goldstein, has written a comment piece after the alleged attack.
It was obvious to those of us who work in and around politics, that eventually, someone would get physically hurt.
The fact that it’s Helen Haines, arguably the best of all of us, not just as a politician but a person, is unbearable.
Some of us community indies have T-shirts that say, “What would Helen do?”
They were a gift from the member for Kooyong, Dr Monique Ryan, a few years ago.
And while it was a bit funny at the time, it’s not a joke.
Helen is the one you go to when you’re grappling with the moral quandaries that arise frequently as an MP, in a job when a binary yes/no vote sometimes feels impossible. With intelligence, warmth and deeply held ethics, she represents the very backbone of the parliament.
‘Don’t send that nasty comment’: Hastie joins calls to turn the temperature down
Liberal frontbencher Andrew Hastie said he’s shocked and saddened by the alleged attack on Helen Haines, and also had concerns about his own safety and of others in Parliament.
“It’s always in the back of my mind”, he said, “which is why I stay fit and I take precautions”. Hastie was recently given extra security by the government due to threats on himself and his family, and says more broadly that the temperature needs to be turned down, particularly on social media.
Speaking to ABC radio this morning, Hastie said:
Be a better steward of Australian democracy. The worst thing we can do right now is point fingers at our political opponents and say, see, it was something that they posted or something that they said. How can we each be better? Maybe don’t like that nasty post or don’t send that nasty comment or don’t trash someone when you don’t even know who they are.
Despite their political differences, he said he held Haines in “very high regard” and called her one of the gentlest and friendliest MPs. It echoed the tributes from other politicians across federal and state parliaments who described her as “the best of us”.
Albanese praises Haines, as MP remains in critical condition
Anthony Albanese is speaking at an event organised by The Age in Melbourne. He says Helen Haines is still in a critical condition in the Alfred Hospital.
Albanese said:
Helen Haines represents the best of our political representatives.
Kind, compassionate, a person of integrity, totally committed, strongly representing the people of that beautiful part of Victoria.
I was asked earlier today when someone suggested ‘could we do a vigil somewhere? What can we do to show our support and solidarity between fellows at this difficult time?’
My response to them, when I thought about it, was just ‘be like Helen: kindness, compassion, caring.’
Light will win over darkness: PM reiterates praise for barber who rushed to help
Prime minister Anthony Albanese is speaking in Melbourne and has again praised Rick Jefferies, the local barber who stepped in during the alleged attack against MP Helen Haines.
He says Jefferies’ actions represented the best of the Australian character.
“This is just a bloke,” Albanese said.
He said it was just the right thing to do, but he did run into danger, not knowing what the consequences could potentially be for him.
Just running to help someone else. A great example of the Australian spirit and the best of the Australian character.
So I think that even in dark times we see light. What Ricky represents is light, and light will be over darkness each and every time.
The independent member for Indi has lost her leg and remains in a critical condition after being rammed by a vehicle, in what has been labelled an allegedly targeted attack.
Haines was allegedly hit by a Toyota LandCruiser outside her electorate office in Wangaratta, northern Victoria, at about 3.35pm on Monday afternoon.
She was airlifted to a Melbourne’s Alfred hospital and is fighting for her life after undergoing surgery overnight, with sources confirming to AAP the MP had lost one of her legs.

Rubio puts Trans-Caspian trade and critical minerals at centre of Central Asia talks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
19:53:16 UTC
04:53:16 KST

The US and five Central Asian governments backed closer transport and industrial cooperation at a C5+1 meeting in Samarkand. Rubio also held bilateral talks, while Uzbekistan signed the Artemis Accords.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio and the foreign ministers of five Central Asian countries agreed to deepen cooperation on transport, critical minerals and security at a C5+1 meeting in Samarkand on Monday.
The talks brought together the United States, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan and Uzbekistan. In a joint statement, they backed investment in the Trans-Caspian trade route, closer industrial cooperation and simpler customs procedures.
A trade route to Europe
The Trans-Caspian route, also known as the Middle Corridor, connects Central Asia with European markets through the Caspian Sea, the South Caucasus and Turkey, bypassing Russia.
"We're going to enhance the infrastructure of the Trans Caspian trade route and give our partners more ways to reach American and Central Asian markets," Rubio said.
Washington also wants to diversify supplies of critical minerals used in energy technologies and advanced manufacturing. The six governments identified mineral processing, energy cooperation and cybersecurity among their priorities, but the joint statement gave no figures for new infrastructure funding.
Uzbek Foreign Minister Bakhtiyor Saidov proposed cooperation extending from mineral exploration to processing and local industrial clusters. He also called for closer links between the C5+1 diplomatic forum and the B5+1 business platform to involve companies in identifying projects.
The US push comes as the five Central Asian states maintain extensive economic ties with Russia and China. Speaking separately to Euronews in Samarkand, Rubio said Washington was seeking competition, not exclusivity.
"This is not about coming here to say, stop talking to somebody else or stop working with some other country," he told Euronews.
Bilateral talks with the five ministers
Rubio also held separate meetings with each of his Central Asian counterparts.
Kazakhstan's Foreign Minister Mukhtar Tileuberdi discussed trade, energy, critical minerals and technology with Rubio. Kazakhstan's Foreign Ministry said the US Secretary of State expressed interest in visiting the country after the G20 summit in Miami in December, although no date was announced.
The US State Department said they also discussed Kazakhstan's commitment to join the Abraham Accords, a US-backed framework for normalising relations with Israel.
Rubio also met Kyrgyzstan's Foreign Minister Jeenbek Kulubaev to discuss bilateral cooperation. Tajik Foreign Minister Sirojiddin Muhriddin raised trade, investment and regional security, according to his ministry.
Rubio held talks with Turkmenistan's Rashid Meredov, with the two countries preparing another round of political consultations in Ashgabat in November.
Uzbekistan and the US held the first session of their Enhanced Strategic Partnership Dialogue, covering trade, energy, technology and security. Following the talks, Foreign Minister Saidov signed the Artemis Accords in Rubio's presence, making Uzbekistan the 77th country to join the international framework for peaceful space exploration.

US charges 28 in California sweep targeting alleged non-citizen voting
Trump administration seeks emergency order over mail ballots, while state officials dismiss allegations as baseless political theatre
US federal authorities charged more than two dozen foreign nationals Monday in California as part of a statewide sweep targeting people who officials say have illegally registered or voted in US elections.
The arrests are part of a Trump administration effort to root out non-citizen voting ahead of next month’s midterm elections, even though data shows that the problem is incredibly rare, difficult to prove and has not been shown to change the outcome of races.
The charges escalated a simmering voter roll fight that came into focus last week when the Justice Department sued California and warned that local election workers who knowingly process or tabulate ballots submitted by non-citizen voters are at risk of investigation and potential prosecution.
The Justice Department said the 28 people who were charged as part of a sweep dubbed Operation Protect the Vote are lawful permanent residents – but not US citizens who are permitted to legally vote. They are charged with crimes including making false statements on a naturalisation application and submitting fraudulent voter registrations.

Trump approval falls to record low of 31% as midterms near, Reuters/Ipsos poll finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
19:51:01 UTC
04:51:01 KST

Trump approval falls to record low of 31% as US midterms near, Reuters/Ipsos poll finds
WASHINGTON - President Donald Trump’s approval rating fell to a record low as Americans worried about high gasoline prices and appeared ready to punish his Republican Party in the Nov 3 congressional elections, according to a Reuters/Ipsos poll that closed on Oct 19.
Some 31% of Americans approve of Trump’s performance in office, down a percentage point from two weeks earlier and the lowest level in either of his presidential terms, the four-day poll showed.
Asked which party they would vote for if the congressional elections were held today in what is known as a “generic ballot” question, some 47% of registered voters in the nationwide poll picked Democrats and 35% chose Republicans.
The 12-point Democratic advantage was the widest over the current election cycle and could bolster Democratic hopes of seizing control of the US House of Representatives and the US Senate.
For Republicans, losing control of either chamber could complicate Trump’s agenda in the last two years of his term.
Generic ballot polls are national polls that provide an overall view of which party poll respondents want to see in charge in Congress.
While these polls provide a view of national public sentiment, they do not capture all the nuances of the state-by-state and district-by-district contests that determine control of the Senate and House, contests in which Republicans hold some structural advantages.
A Reuters/Ipsos poll two weeks earlier showed Democrats leading Republicans by 7 points, 44% to 37%.
Much of the drop in support for Republican congressional candidates was due to a larger share of women saying they would pick Democrats.
Some 50% of female voters said they would vote Democratic, compared to 32% eyeing Republican candidates. Men also favoured Democrats, but by a smaller margin.
Trump’s popularity has suffered since he ordered military strikes on Iran in February alongside US ally Israel. The war triggered a surge in gasoline prices, hitting household finances.
Some 68% of Americans disapprove of Trump’s handling of the economy, including 37% of self-identified Republicans.
Voters in the poll picked Democrats over Republicans as the better stewards of the economy, by 40% to 33%.
The survey, which was conducted online, gathered responses from 1,679 US adults, including 1,279 registered voters. The poll’s results had a margin of error of 2 percentage points for all respondents and 3 points for registered voters.

Zelensky said he and the pope discussed the humanitarian emergency unfolding in Oleshky, including the Vatican's diplomatic efforts with Russia.
"We are working to help our people there and are preparing solutions," Zelensky said. "His Holiness informed me about his contacts with the Russian side regarding this issue."

Ukraine and Russia are currently discussing a ceasefire proposal and are nearing an agreement to evacuate residents from Oleshky, Human Rights Ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets said on Oct. 18.
The sides are negotiating a local ceasefire to allow residents to be evacuated directly to Ukrainian-controlled territory, rather than having to travel first through Russian-occupied areas and then through Russia and Belarus, Lubinets said.
No final agreement has been publicly announced, and it remains unclear when an evacuation could begin. It is not clear to what extent Pope Leo's intervention impacted the agreement.
Oleshky has been under Russian occupation since the early days of the full-scale invasion. Residents face severe shortages of food, water, and electricity, while mined roads, constant drone attacks, and interrogations by Russian troops at checkpoints make safe evacuation virtually impossible.
Despite the escalating emergency, Russian forces have been preventing Ukraine and international humanitarian organizations from accessing occupied regions to provide aid.
Zelensky said he also spoke with Pope Leo about Russia's intensifying attacks — and the failure of Kyiv's partners to provide advance warning of missile launches.
"Of course, we also discussed all the security challenges and threats we are currently facing, including the recent instances where we did not receive advance warning from our partners about Russian ballistic missile attacks, which has happened three times recently," he said.
The night before, Russia launched 16 ballistic missiles at Kyiv and the surrounding region, killing at least one person and injuring eight others. Ukrainian officials said they received no warning from the U.S. or other partners until after the first missiles struck.

OpenAI Engineer Accused of Spying on Executives Ordered to Remain in Custody
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
19:49:17 UTC
04:49:17 KST

The former OpenAI engineer accused of bugging a company conference room must stay in custody while he awaits trial, a federal judge ruled on Monday after expressing concerns about his ties to Saudi Arabia.
US prosecutors alleged Abdulrahman Alfozan is a flight risk because the Saudi Arabian government has offered to support him with no strings attached. They cited, for example, the Saudi consulate’s offer to work with a bail bonds firm to help fund Alfozan’s release.
Federal magistrate judge Alex Tse questioned whether Alfozan is an “asset” for the kingdom and how a bond backed by the government could keep him in the country. “I find that problematic,” Tse said. “It seems like a blank check. ‘We’re going to pay whatever the court wants to get him out.’ I’m more interested in people from his family wanting to put up assets.”
William Pernik, an attorney for Alfozan, dismissed the flight risk worries as baseless. But he failed to convince the judge that Alfozan was committed to his life in the US. “There is a real threat here that once he leaves the case is over,” Tse said.
Aflozan appeared in an orange prison uniform and a medical face mask pulled down over his neck on Monday in Tse’s San Francisco courtroom, which was filled to capacity with journalists, students on a field trip, and about 20 people supporting Alfozan.
Employee attempts to steal confidential company information are common in Silicon Valley. But Alfozan’s case has drawn international attention for the alleged amateur spycraft and geopolitical tensions at the center of it. Authorities haven’t offered a potential motive but have noted Alfozan has worked for a Saudi venture capital firm, offered consulting services to Saudi companies, and is supposedly friendly with people high up in the Saudi government.
Pernik said there is no evidence of Alfozan spying for Saudi Arabia or engaging in something covert. “It’s not as if he sneaked in under the covers of darkness,” he said of the OpenAI conference room. “This was an open room where anybody could work in.”
After the hour-long hearing, Pernik told reporters he was disappointed with the custody ruling and would continue to try to fight it.
While Alfozan is a US permanent resident who had been on the path to obtaining citizenship, his ties to his native Saudi Arabia have come under scrutiny. Prosecutors allege that Alfozan was “in frequent communications via WhatsApp” with a member of the Saudi royal family throughout 2025 and 2026.
The Saudi royal, who is not identified, was allegedly recruiting Alfozan to return to the country for a job working on a forthcoming AI initiative, according to a court filing. “Saudi needs you more then [sic] the US!” the individual wrote to Alfozan this past May, per the filing. Alfozan allegedly “responded ‘100,’ indicating he agreed.”
US authorities also allege that the Saudi government bought Alfozan's wife and infant son a ticket to return to the country a few days after his arrest. She ended up leaving sooner on another flight booked by her sister’s husband, who works for the Saudi navy, according to attorneys for both sides.
Alfozan's wife has not been accused of wrongdoing, and the FBI last week declined to comment on whether she would face any charges.
Alfozan was at OpenAI for just over a year when the AI lab discovered a covert audio recording device hidden in a wad of toilet paper behind a TV in an executive conference room used for confidential business meetings. OpenAI found the device in late September, connected it to Alfozan, and then fired him earlier this month just before the FBI arrested him.
Alfozan faces five years in prison on a single count of using a device to intercept communications, but prosecutors say additional charges are possible. Included among the government’s evidence are alleged conversations between Alfozan and an AI chatbot in which he asked for help setting up listening devices. Prosecutors also produced a photo taken of Alfozan looking behind the TV after OpenAI had removed the recorder. It’s unclear what, if anything, was recorded, because the device’s data was encrypted, according to authorities.
Authorities say they also found components for recording devices at Alfozan’s home and photos of other OpenAI monitors and another OpenAI conference room on his phone. OpenAI previously said it recovered a second listening device in a bag Alfozan brought to the office and left unattended.
Pernik claimed the electronics at Alfozan’s home were for home monitoring projects, including trying to improve a smart litter box for their cat. “This is a gentleman who spent 15 years of life immersed at this intersection of technology and personal life,” Pernik told the judge.
Authorities said ahead of the hearing that they believed Alfozan had the means to flee. They cited the $385,000 salary and $2.2 million profit-sharing package he received while working at OpenAI as well as other funds he earned from previous gigs at Meta and other US tech companies.
According to Alfozan's attorneys, his wife needed to leave the US to renew her American student visa. Alfozan had planned to accompany her on the trip before being arrested. They had a one-way ticket to Riyadh, which Alfozan’s attorneys said was typical for him because he sometimes had to return earlier than planned for work.
Nas Yasin, another attorney for Alfozan, said his wife’s flight was booked by her sister’s husband in his personal capacity. Yasin added that Alfozan’s wife had just secured a visitor visa from the US and planned to return to California from Saudi Arabia as soon as Tuesday. Alfozan’s next court date is scheduled for November 6.

Florida issues arrest warrant for Cuban leader Raul Castro
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
19:48:53 UTC
04:48:53 KST

Florida issues arrest warrant for Cuban leader Raul Castro
The state-level announcement mirrors a federal indictment from May as the US steps up pressure on the Cuban government.
Florida, in the southeastern United States, has issued an arrest warrant for 95-year-old former Cuban leader Raul Castro.
The move comes as US authorities step up pressure on the government in Havana.
State Attorney General James Uthmeier said on Monday that the warrant was based on criminal charges over Castro’s alleged role in ordering two unarmed aircraft to be shot down in 1996.
The aircraft were affiliated with Brothers to the Rescue, a Florida-based group that helps Cubans fleeing the country. Four people were killed in the attack.
Castro faces state-level charges of conspiracy to commit first-degree murder in Florida.
“Raul Castro ordered the murder of four Floridians in cold blood, and Florida will never stop pursuing accountability for that communist conspiracy,” Uthmeier wrote in a news release.
He said the arrest warrant was necessary accountability for the lives lost. “Thirty years later, we are still fighting for justice for Carlos Costa, Pablo Morales, Mario de la Pena, and Armando Alejandre Jr.”
The decision to shoot down the two small twin-engine planes has been the subject of renewed controversy over the last year, as Republican President Donald Trump seeks to oust Cuba’s communist leaders.
The attack took place on February 24, 1996. US authorities say the planes were flying over international waters and received no warning before they were shot down.
Cuban officials, meanwhile, have argued that previous Brothers to the Rescue flights had breached the country’s airspace, despite warnings to stay away.
Castro, now 95 years old, was Cuba’s defence minister at the time of the attack. A key figure in the Communist Party of Cuba, he later became president of the island in 2008, replacing his brother, the late revolutionary leader Fidel Castro.
Though he retired from the presidency in 2018, Raul Castro and his family remain powerful figures in Cuba’s government.
Since the start of the year, the Trump administration has signalled it would like to see regime change in Cuba.
To trigger such change, the administration has tightened US restrictions on the island, including by imposing a de facto energy blockade in January.
By threatening steep tariffs against any country that supplies Cuba with oil, the US has effectively barred fuel exports to the country, according to experts.
That, in turn, has caused deteriorating conditions on the island and strained the country’s already meagre power system, which relies heavily on fossil fuels. Only 40 percent of Cuba’s oil is produced domestically.
Additional sanctions have been placed on Cuba’s economy, limiting its state-run industries.
But in May, the Trump administration unveiled a superseding indictment also targeting Raul Castro for the 1996 plane downings.
It charges Castro with federal crimes including conspiracy to kill US nationals, destroying aircraft and four counts of murder.
The Trump administration issued a statement in support of Florida’s actions against Castro on Monday.
“We’re committed to pursuing every lawful, prosecutable avenue to bring accountability, including parallel federal and state prosecutions,” US Attorney Jason Reding Quinones said.
“Our historic federal indictment laid the groundwork, and James [Uthmeier] and his team have now taken the important step of bringing charges under Florida law.”
Trump has previously used indictments to justify military operations targeting government leaders that are at odds with the US, including former Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro.

Florida issues arrest warrant for Raul Castro over 1996 shootdown of civilian aircraft
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
19:46:34 UTC
04:46:34 KST

Maryam Ashalem de Andres
19 October 2026•Update: 19 October 2026
Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier announced Monday that authorities had secured a state arrest warrant for former Cuban President Raul Castro over the 1996 shootdown of two civilian aircraft that killed four men.
“Raul Castro ordered the premeditated, state-sanctioned murder of four Floridians in cold blood,” Uthmeier said in a post on US social media company X.
The warrant charges Castro with conspiracy to commit first-degree murder over the Feb. 24, 1996, incident involving aircraft operated by Brothers to the Rescue, a Miami-based Cuban exile group.
Uthmeier vowed that Florida would continue seeking accountability for Carlos Costa, Pablo Morales, Mario de la Pena and Armando Alejandre Jr., the four men killed in the incident.
Florida’s Office of Statewide Prosecution and investigators secured the warrant after authorities reopened the case at Uthmeier’s direction last year, according to the Florida Department of Law Enforcement.
On Feb. 24, 1996, Cuban fighter jets shot down two of three unarmed Cessna aircraft operated by the group over international waters, killing all four people aboard.
The aircraft had departed from Opa-Locka Airport in Miami-Dade County and were flying away from Cuba, according to the Florida Department of Law Enforcement.
The warrant was signed by Chief Judge Ariana Fajardo Orshan of Florida’s 11th Judicial Circuit Court, which ordered that Castro be held without bond.
The state-level action follows a federal indictment announced in May against Castro over the same incident. Federal charges include conspiracy to kill US nationals and destruction of aircraft.
The 1996 shootdown remains a source of tension between Washington and Havana. Cuba maintained that the aircraft had violated its airspace, while US authorities said they were flying over international waters.
Castro, 95, served as Cuba’s president from 2008 to 2018, succeeding his brother Fidel Castro.
Florida authorities said the investigation would continue as they seek to hold those responsible for the deaths accountable.

Last week, Apple and Meta teamed up to bring a large open-weight model, developed by Meta, to multiple high-end Mac Studios.

Mercedes unleashes new EV era in South Korea with next-gen CLA and GLC SUVs
Mercedes-Benz Korea on Monday launched all-electric versions of its CLA sedan and GLC sport utility vehicle (SUV) in South Korea as part of its push to expand its electric vehicle lineup, Yonhap reports.
The German luxury automaker unveiled the all-new electric CLA and GLC, both built on its next-generation, in-house-developed electric vehicle platforms.
"Together with these two models, we marked a very important turning point in our electrification journey as the first representatives of a new generation of purpose-built electric architectures," Mercedes-Benz Korea CEO Shirin Emeera said during a launch event in Seoul.
The electric CLA comes in two variants: the CLA 250+ electric with an 85 per kilowatt hour (kWh) nickel-cobalt-manganese (NCM) battery and the CLA 200 electric with a 58 kWh lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery.
Both models use batteries supplied by Chinese battery maker Contemporary Amperex Technology Co. Ltd. (CATL).
The CLA 250+ electric and CLA 200 electric offer driving ranges of 474 kilometers and 342 kilometers, respectively, on a single charge under South Korean certification standards.
Both support fast charging, allowing their batteries to charge from 10 percent to 80 percent in about 22 minutes and 20 minutes, respectively.
The electric GLC, the first fully electric version of Mercedes-Benz's popular SUV, comes with an 85 kWh NCM battery and offers a driving range of up to 448 kilometers. Its battery, also supplied by CATL, can be charged from 10 percent to 80 percent in about 22 minutes.
The electric CLA is available in five trims, priced between 52.9 million won (US$39,759) and 67.7 million won, while the electric GLC comes in two launch editions priced at 90 million won and 94.8 million won.
Mercedes-Benz said the electric CLA has received about 1,000 preorders since September, while the electric GLC has drawn more than 2,500 since July. Deliveries of both models are set to begin in mid-November.

“Bones covered by skin”.
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
19:42:41 UTC
04:42:41 KST

Photo: screenshot from a video distributed for the press by the court
In July 2025, Russian soldiers took 68-year-old Halyna Bekhter from her home in the Russian-occupied part of Ukraine’s Zaporizhzhia region. She was soon convicted of treason: according to investigators, she had transferred money to the Ukrainian army.
In their letters, Bekhter’s cellmates say she can no longer eat or care for herself, and they suspect she has progressive dementia. Despite this, prosecutors secured a harsher sentence. Bekhter is now being transferred to a penal colony.
Mediazona looks at what is known about her case.
Halyna Bekhter and her husband lived in the village of Reichenfeld (called Plodorodne until 2025) in Ukraine’s Zaporizhzhia region, according to Lyudmila Huseynova, founder of the human rigths group Numo, Sestry (“C’mon, Sisters!”). The village was occupied at the very start of Russia’s full-scale invasion. In the summer of 2022, Bekhter’s daughter fled to the part of the country under Ukrainian control, but her elderly parents stayed behind.
Huseynova told Novaya Gazeta Europe that the Bekhters never hid their pro-Ukrainian stance, which led to conflicts with some of their pro-Russian neighbors. As a result, the Russian military took the couple in for questioning in November 2024, but later released them.
In July 2025, Halyna Bekhter was detained. Huseynova, who is in touch with the family, says a neighbor who had spoken in support of Putin reported her. Bekhter had told the neighbor: “Our people will be back soon. Let’s see what you have to say then!”
According to Numo, Sestry, Bekhter was first held in Melitopol, then in the village of Yakymivka in the Zaporizhzhia region. She spent some time in Donetsk before being moved to Pretrial Detention Center No. 1 (SIZO-1) in Simferopol, Crimea. Her husband died in their home village in January 2026.
In March 2026, the occupational administration’s Zaporizhzhia Regional Court sentenced 68-year-old Bekhter to 11 years in prison on charges of “treason.” According to investigators, in July 2023 she used a Ukrainian banking app to send money to an account linked to the Armed Forces of Ukraine (the amount was the equivalent of 1,240 rubles, or about $15).
Prosecutors found that sentence too lenient and appealed, asking for 16 years instead. In July, the First Appellate Court of General Jurisdiction increased Bekhter’s sentence to 12 and a half years. By the time of the appeal, it was already known that she had developed symptoms of dementia in custody.
In May, two months after the sentencing, the human rights organisation ZPCh (“For Human Rights”) published excerpts from a letter written by Bekhter’s cellmate in Simferopol:
In a subsequent letter dated July 2026 and quoted by Novaya Gazeta Europe, the cellmate wrote that Bekhter, who is 176 centimeters (5’9”) tall, weighed 50 kilograms (110 lbs). “[She] lies in bed all the time, doesn’t change her clothes, doesn’t understand what to do in the shower, and has no control over her bodily functions. She suffers from fecal incontinence,” the woman wrote, asking for adult diapers to be sent.
Bekhter is currently being transferred from the detention centre to a penal colony. And, according to Mediazona’s sources, the transfer has already taken more than three weeks. Her destination is still unknown.
Shortly before the transfer, a cellmate described Bekhter’s condition as follows: “Her bones are covered only by skin, no muscle at all. She soils herself, and the girls wash her and do her laundry. She’s completely lost her mind; they spoon-feed her and mash everything up for her since she doesn’t have a single tooth left. She won’t survive the transfer. What kind of justice can we even hope for?”
The most recent letter about Halyna Bekhter was received on October 12: it was written from Penal Colony No. 15, a transit prison in the Samara region by her former cellmate Larisa Belyaeva, who was convicted of purchasing Ukrainian military bonds:
Belyaeva wrote to Russia’s human rights commissioner, Yana Lantratova, describing everything happening to Bekhter, but has received no response.
Russian occupation courts regularly convict elderly Ukrainians of financially supporting the Ukrainian army, and hand them double-digit prison terms.
In July, Vitaliy Ilyin, 63, was sentenced to 12 years in prison. In September, Natalya Nadeina, 69, received the same sentence. In August, a 74-year-old woman was sentenced to 14 years in a penal colony; almost nothing is known about her.

Trump open to Putin, Xi trilateral summit but would focus on nuclear arms

Trump open to Putin, Xi trilateral summit but would focus on nuclear arms
WASHINGTON - President Donald Trump said he would be willing to meet with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping but indicated his focus would be on denuclearisation efforts rather than ending the war in Ukraine.
“I would do it – not so much for Ukraine, because Russia, frankly, has been fine on Ukraine,” Trump told reporters Oct 19.
“We would have it to talk about nuclear weapons and denuclearisation,” he added. “We would schedule a meeting based on the denuclearisation, and that’s a very positive thing for the world.”
The Wall Street Journal reported earlier on a push by Moscow to bring the three leaders together at a summit.
The Journal reported that the summit would be about negotiating an end to the war in Ukraine, and didn’t mention if denuclearisation would be on the agenda.
But Trump has long pushed for China to join talks between the US and Russia on nuclear arms control given that Beijing is rapidly building its stockpile of warheads.
But Beijing has so far pushed back against the idea given that its arsenal is so much smaller than those held by the US and Russia.
While there are no finalised plans for such a meeting, Trump suggested that it could happen in China.
He is slated to visit the country in November for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit and for talks with Xi on the sidelines.
“If they’d like to have it, I think it would be held in China. He just left here,” Trump said, referring to Xi’s recent visit to Washington. “If President Xi wants to have it, I’d have it. I’m sure we’re talking about other things like trade too, but yeah, I would do that.”
Trump has courted Putin as he seeks a resolution to a war he once vowed to end on his first day in office.
He’s faced criticism from Ukraine and its allies over a diesel deal with Russia that critics cast as an economic bailout for Moscow with questionable legal standing. Energy analysts have said the deal does little to help alleviate fuel costs for US consumers.
Trump has ratcheted up pressure on Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, casting the leader of the country Russia invaded as the main obstacle to peace.
Zelensky has charged that the US has been pulling back on intelligence it provides to Kyiv, as the two leaders grow farther apart.
Holding a meeting with Putin and Xi to discuss Ukraine is likely to infuriate Kyiv and its allies who have long insisted that the country have a seat at any table to decide its future.
Trump indicated to reporters on Oct 19 that he would be willing to meet without the Ukrainian president, saying his focus was doing “anything I can do to end the war.”
The US leader also claimed Russia has done little to support Iran in its eight-month conflict with the US, and said he didn’t want to disrupt ongoing negotiations with Putin, which he said include talks about freeing a hostage.
“Russia could have done a lot more to help Iran,” Trump said. “Russia has done very little for Iran. China could have done a lot more for Iran.” BLOOMBERG

Larry David kvetches about Democratic Socialists of America, takes aim at their antisemitism
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
19:37:29 UTC
04:37:29 KST

Larry David, the famously cranky creator of Seinfeld and Curb Your Enthusiasm, has just penned a “modest proposal” skewering the hypocrisy and antisemitism of the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) in the online publication Air Mail.
David’s piece, titled “The View from Here,” was published over the weekend and featured the subhead, “A comedian’s modest proposals for the Democratic Socialists of America.” He opens the piece by saying that he recently attended a DSA meeting and joined the group.
The DSA counts New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani among its members, and Mamdani has endorsed DSA candidates for public office, including Darializa Avila Chevalier, who is running for US Congress as a Democrat.
The DSA promoted and urged its members to attend the notorious rally in Times Square in New York City on October 8, 2023, that celebrated the Hamas massacre the previous day. Multiple DSA chapters condoned and gave explanations for the massacre.
Since then, they have doubled down on accusing Israel of genocide and apartheid.
Tackling this issue head-on, David writes, “The DSA has great respect for religious traditions. Because of our burgeoning Muslim population, we want to take all measures to give these people a strong sense of belonging in America.
“Along those lines, we’ll require that all Caucasian women wear a hijab on weekends in solidarity with their Muslim sisters. In addition, Jews will no longer be allowed to refer to themselves as ‘the Chosen People.’ Henceforth, their new nickname will be ‘the Bagel People.’”
His proposal continues: “We strongly believe in a two-state solution. To this end, we propose that Palestinians should be given all the land currently occupied by Israel and that Israel should be given Pitcairn Island in the South Pacific, where the weather is beautiful, and grapefruits are aplenty. We think the Bagel People will be very happy there.”
Larry David mocks DSA with outlandish proposals on housing, pets, reparations
David includes his trademark irreverent shtick in the proposal, ribbing the group by suggesting that all homeowners be forced to leave their doors open and host any and all strangers; that people be granted bereavement leave when their pets die and maternity and paternity leave when they adopt pets; and that as a form of reparations for slavery, whites be enslaved to Black families for a year.
Towards the end, he writes, “We Democratic Socialists love to laugh … but not at the expense of others. The last thing we want is for any person to be offended by a joke that targets them or someone they know. No one should ever have their feelings hurt.
“Consequently, any comedian who is responsible for causing emotional discomfort in any way will be sent to a facility where they will be re-programmed and hopefully emerge with a greater awareness of the sensitivities of their fellow citizens.
“If, however, the re-programming is unsuccessful, the repeat offender will be sent to Pitcairn Island to live with the Bagel People.”
Air Mail, co-founded by former Vanity Fair and Spy editor Graydon Carter in 2019, tends to feature articles on entertainment, celebrity gossip, and the high life rather than politics, but its editors made room for David’s DSA piece.
Larry David's DSA satire sparks criticism and confusion online
The New York Times wrote an article on the piece and reported that DSA representatives did not respond to their request for comment. Some actual DSA members and sympathizers, not known for their sense of humor or satirical acumen, slammed the piece online, while others seemed merely bewildered by it.
On a Reddit thread, one user wrote, “It’s still pretty weird, but I would need more context before jumping to the conclusion that this is supposed to be read as disparaging DSA rather than making fun of its naysayers…
“I just can’t bring myself to believe that Larry David doesn’t know the difference between personal and private property. Isn’t Bernie [Sanders] like his first cousin or something?”

The illusion of truth: Why the press is wrong about settlers - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
19:37:28 UTC
04:37:28 KST

We live in a media-driven world, and we know not everything we’re told is true.
Yet, when something is repeated often enough, it can be very persuasive. This is why people fall for daily smears against Israel, and one of the strongest examples of this is the intensifying demonization of the settlers.
Take the recent violent confrontations involving settlers and Palestinians in the West Bank. European diplomats were caught up in one incident, foreign journalists in the other. In both cases, the cameras were already there before the trouble began. What unfolded was trial by media, and as usual Israel never stood a chance.
For the international press, these were stories made for television: violence, vivid pictures, and villains.
Media reporting on recent attacks lacks essential details
Now, I don’t know much about the intricacies of olive harvesting, but it was a surprise to me that the peaceful Palestinians of Abu Falah had reportedly come armed with fireworks. What could they have been there for, to blow olives off the trees? Or attack Jews? Media hasn’t really reported that, nor that foreign activists who record themselves provoking settlers were with them, because it would spoil the narrative.
Then there were the European diplomats visiting Taybeh in a show of solidarity with Palestinians. We know they did not co-ordinate their trip with the IDF. Had they arranged appropriate security the outcome would almost certainly have been different. But they preferred to waltz in of their own accord and complain when something happened (although they could not have wished for better headlines). Perhaps an Israeli delegation should wander into the streets of Paris during violent riots, without co-ordinating with the French authorities, and then express outrage if things turn ugly?
Now consider the numbers.
There are approximately 500,000 settlers and, if you’re the UN, there are an additional 250,000 in east Jerusalem. That’s a total of 750,000. According to the Shin Bet, only a few hundred are involved in violence. A few hundred out of three quarters of a million! European cities have their own hoodlums, but nobody seriously suggests that they define the rest of the population.
In the real world, practically every settler is peaceful and has nothing to do with the kinds of scenes we see on the news. I myself have property in Gush Etzion, and family who live there. Does that suddenly make me a violent settler? Of course not. Same goes for all the others.
Incidents of settler violence blown out of proportion by Western media
These incidents are vastly blown out of proportion. The UN says that in the past 12 months there were just over 2,000 settler attacks (its definition includes non-violent acts); the Shin Bet says there was twice that amount of Palestinian violence - stone-throwing, petrol bombs, shootings, stabbings, and more. Why do we never hear about those on the BBC and CNN, or in the Washington Post or New York Times?
Netanyahu was right when he told the UN last month that there was an eighth front to the wars Israel is fighting. He called it “the war for truth”.
This is true of the treatment of the settler movement, reinforced almost daily by an anti-Israel media, by the UN, by Israel’s enemies and even by many of its allies with much worse problems of their own. And there is a psychological explanation for why this kind of reinforcement can be so powerful. In 1977, three American university professors demonstrated what became known as the Illusion of Truth Effect. It means that people become more likely to believe something is true simply because they have heard it repeatedly, even when it is false.
Repeat a falsehood often enough and, before long, people accept it as fact.
The same principle applies to the vilification of the settlers. A distorted image, cemented by relentless repetition, becomes the illusion of truth.
Just don’t be fooled.

Russian forces are attempting to exploit the autumn inclement weather to launch breakthroughs in the Huliaipole sector.

The corps’ units are facing the Russian Federation’s 5th, 29th, 35th, and 36th Combined Arms Armies, as well as the invaders’ 68th Army Corps.
The enemy’s primary tactic remains deep infiltration.

The Russians have also been attempting for some time to amass armored vehicles within a 20-kilometer zone from the front line.
Over the past week, amid deteriorating weather conditions, the enemy began conducting localized assaults using infantry, motorcycles, and armored vehicles.

According to intelligence reports, units of the Russian Federation’s 5th Tank Brigade, 37th Motorized Rifle Brigade, and 64th Separate Motorized Rifle Brigade have completed training at military ranges and are ready to deploy military equipment along the direction of the enemy’s main offensive.
The 7th Corps of the Air Assault Forces moved into the Huliaipole sector in September of this year.
The corps’ mission is to stabilize the situation on a designated section of the front and reduce the offensive capabilities of Russian forces.

Bulgaria Seeks Arrest of 2 German Nationals Over Arson Attack on Starlink Antennas
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
19:30:34 UTC
04:30:34 KST

Bulgarian authorities have issued European arrest warrants for two German nationals aged 19, accused of setting fire to Starlink antennas near Sofia, the latest in a series of suspected sabotage attacks on satellite infrastructure that Ukraine relies on to defend itself against Russian jet-powered drones.
The Sofia City Court granted the request from the Sofia City Prosecutor’s Office, which is seeking to have the pair held in custody, Bulgaria’s state news agency BTA reported.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Both men were charged in absentia on Oct. 14 and could face from three to 12 years in prison if convicted. The ruling can be appealed within three days.
Under German privacy rules, the suspects have been identified in German media only by their initials, S.I. and T.B.
German authorities, however, say the suspects’ current whereabouts are unknown.
A 6-hour visit turns into 8 burned antennas
The pair, according to the prosecutors, set eight Starlink antennas on fire at a site in Plana, a village 30-40 kilometers (18-25 miles) southeast of the Bulgarian capital, on Oct. 9.
They entered Bulgaria from Serbia through the Kalotina border checkpoint at 5:37 p.m. local time on Oct. 9 in a German registered car, telling border officers they were visiting as tourists.
Wearing gloves and masks, they allegedly set fire to the antennas at the Plana Teleport facility (a modern ground-based satellite communications station) at about 10:25 p.m.
According to BTA, three antennas were completely destroyed, two were partially damaged and three others were affected as well.
Kyiv Metro to Resume Full Service Past Damaged Chernihivska Station
Around 11:55 p.m. local time, the pair reportedly crossed back into Serbia through the same checkpoint.
Defense disputes identification
The suspects’ court-appointed lawyers argued that investigators had identified the car, but not the men inside it.
“It may ultimately turn out that these are not the people who committed the criminal act,” said Zhanet Manasieva, a court-appointed lawyer for one of the defendants.
The court rejected those objections, finding reasonable grounds to suspect the two were involved. However, both lawyers said they would appeal.
Plamen Tonchev, head of Bulgaria’s State Agency for National Security (DANS), has told lawmakers he believes the fire was sabotage and warned that further attacks cannot be ruled out, German news outlet dpa reported.
Political row in Sofia
According to BTA, the attack became public only on Oct. 12, when opposition lawmaker Ivaylo Mirchev of Democratic Bulgaria revealed it on Facebook.
He put the damage higher than the prosecutors did, saying two masked men had set fire to 11 of the site’s 17 antennas.
Prime Minister Rumen Radev, who repeatedly rejects accusations of being pro-Russian, told the parliament on Oct. 14 that Bulgaria was working with partner services and asked security chiefs not to disclose details.
After Monday’s ruling, Mirchev demanded that Radev explain what had been achieved and who bore responsibility. “Need we remind everyone that for three days the Interior Ministry and the security services kept silent and concealed the incident,” he wrote on Facebook, BTA reported.
A wider campaign of sabotage
On Sept. 23, a fire damaged antennas and a generator at a Starlink ground station in Wola Krobowska, south of Warsaw, RMF reported. The facility, run by Polish state operator Exatel, helps provide internet access across both Central and Eastern Europe, including Ukraine.
The suspects, according to dpa, were arrested in Nürtingen, near Stuttgart in Germany, on Oct. 13.
Warsaw suspects Russian intelligence was behind the attack.
On Oct. 17, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk reiterated his previous warning that Russia may escalate hybrid attacks, sabotage, and border provocations against Poland and the Baltic states before Christmas.
According to him, the risks would be particularly acute around borders and railway lines used to transport essential supplies to Ukraine, including gas, oil and food.
Lithuanian Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevičius said on Oct. 18 that someone had tried overnight to set fire to a company storing Starlink equipment, but failed because security services had warned the company in advance.
“Our services are very closely monitoring the activities of hostile states and are taking measures to protect people and their property,” he wrote on Facebook.
The attacks come as Ukraine’s access to the network is already under strain by the escalating tensions with the US.
Overnight on Oct. 13-14, aerospace giant SpaceX tweaked the parameters for Ukraine’s Starshield, disrupting the country’s drone operations. Around the same time, Ukrainian authorities also reported that they hadn’t received a partner warning about Russian ballistic missiles.
Although SpaceX CEO Elon Musk claimed that the US military and US President Donald Trump set speed limits on the terminals, not the company, Trump denied that account.
“I don’t know if it was somebody, because it wasn’t me, and I don’t think it was Elon,” Trump told reporters. “And, as far as I understand, everything is the same as it’s always been.”
On Monday, President Volodymyr Zelensky reiterated that Ukrainian units were still losing satellite connections, adding that the equipment stopped working at 130-160 km/h (81-100 mph) along various parts of the front.
On that same day, US Representative Brian Fitzpatrick, a Pennsylvania Republican, warned that anyone who tries to restrict Ukraine’s use of Starshield will face accountability, including a full investigation, public hearings and steep budget cuts.

Türkiye launches massive data centre project in digital hub push
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
19:30:31 UTC
04:30:31 KST

A groundbreaking ceremony was held on Monday for Ankara’s data centre complex, located in the Baskent Organised Industrial Zone, marking a significant milestone in Türkiye’s efforts to become a regional digital hub.
The new facility is the result of a joint venture between Ronesans Holding and global data centre operator Digital Realty.
Turkish Industry and Technology Minister Mehmet Fatih Kacir said at the ceremony that the initial facility will require a $450 million investment in basic infrastructure and building construction, while an additional $900 million will be allocated to cooling systems and IT infrastructure.
“Once all phases are complete, this facility will represent a fixed capital investment of $4.1 billion in the Ankara Temelli Baskent Organised Industrial Zone,” he said.
Kacir referred to data processing and cloud computing capabilities as “the oil of the 21st century,” highlighting the growing importance of technology in the modern global arena.
“The total installed capacity of data centres worldwide is expected to rise from around 103 gigawatts last year to 200 gigawatts by 2030,” he noted, adding that over one-fifth of the total value of new global investments has been made in data centres.
Kacir stated that Ankara launched the HIT-30 programme to allocate $30 billion in incentives through 2030 to attract high-tech investments and support the cloud computing and technology that AI applications require.
He noted that Türkiye started a new chapter in technology development and production through its National Technology Initiative, which highlights digital sovereignty as integral to independence.
“We implemented a comprehensive support framework to develop data centre and cloud computing capacity and attract global investments,” he said.
“We have benefited more than 8,900 researchers to date through the Turkish Science e-Infrastructure (TRUBA), enhancing the country’s high-performance computing infrastructure with over 80,000 processor cores, 504 graphics processing units (GPUs) and 26 petabytes of data storage capacity.”
The minister mentioned that the HIT-30 programme, the largest-scale incentive package in the nation’s history, includes the “HIT-Data Centre Call” scheme, dedicating a $1.4 billion budget to supporting the construction of data centres of at least 30 megawatts, while the “HIT-Artificial Intelligence Call” mobilises $1.6 billion to accelerate the establishment of domestic cloud-based infrastructure.
“And through the HIT-Quantum Call, we aim to build a quantum infrastructure of our own, the technology of the future, to further cement Türkiye’s position as a regional hub for data processing and storage,” he added.
Ankara’s broader strategy was also detailed in the 2026-2030 Türkiye Artificial Intelligence Action Plan, which aims to expand installed data centre capacity, with a national goal of at least 1 gigawatt by 2030.
“We will facilitate access to high-performance chips for entrepreneurs and researchers through the ‘GPU for Everyone’ programme to bring together scientists, tech startups and investors within a comprehensive AI ecosystem supported by strong infrastructure,” the minister noted.
Kacir added that Ronesans Holding and Digital Realty are expected to play a key role in reaching this goal, as the two firms plan to lead a combined investment of more than $10 billion in Ankara and Istanbul to establish a projected data centre capacity of 200 megawatts, making up one-fifth of the national goal.

According to the report, which Urich did not deny, he said he saw no moral problem with the work and estimated that he had received hundreds of thousands of shekels for the project.

Ukrainian Drone Operators Logged Over 3 Million Strike Missions Since March, DELTA Data Shows
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
19:30:12 UTC
04:30:12 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Ukrainian Drone Operators Logged Over 3 Million Strike Missions Since March, DELTA Data Shows
Ukraine’s DELTA combat system recorded more than 3 million strike missions by UAV operators between March and October 1, as the Mission Control module rapidly expanded across the Defence Forces, Ukraine’s Ministry of Defence reported on October 19.
In September alone, service members recorded more than 1.8 million completed mission results in Mission Control. At the beginning of 2026, the system processed around 196,000 records per month, meaning monthly usage increased more than ninefold in nine months.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Mission Control is a module within the DELTA combat ecosystem that allows service members to record completed missions, analyze their results, and use that data to plan subsequent operations.
The Ministry of Defence explained that the module effectively continues the combat cycle after a weapon or unmanned system has been used: results are recorded, analyzed, and incorporated into future planning.
Mission Control is currently used to track unmanned systems and artillery missions. Air defense units, Army Aviation, and other components of Ukraine’s Defence Forces are also gradually adopting the system.
Since the active rollout began in March, UAV operators have submitted:
- nearly 3.6 million reconnaissance mission reports;
- more than 3 million strike missions against enemy targets;
- more than 1.02 million UAV logistics missions;
- nearly 168,000 logistics missions using unmanned ground vehicles;
- nearly 500,000 missions to intercept aerial targets;
- nearly 370,000 remote mining missions using UAVs.
The growing volume of data gives Ukrainian forces a more complete picture of combat activity and allows commanders to compare different approaches and use the results in future planning, the Ministry of Defence noted.
Mission Control is therefore developing from a reporting tool into part of a continuous digital cycle within DELTA covering planning, combat employment, analysis, and subsequent decision-making.
The latest figures build on DELTA’s rapid expansion across Ukraine’s battlefield operations. By July 2026, the Ministry of Defence had already reported that the system was recording more than 6,600 confirmed enemy targets hit each day.
DELTA’s expanding role follows its use during NATO’s REPMUS 2026 exercise, where Ukrainian forces integrated aerial, surface, and underwater drones, as well as radars, into the system. Ukraine also used DELTA to coordinate reconnaissance, maritime monitoring, maneuvering, escort missions, and simulated strikes alongside allied forces.

'We will fight' — We asked Ukrainian soldiers about Trump's latest outburst

'We will fight' — We asked Ukrainian soldiers about Trump's latest outburst
A soldier from a separate task force rifle battalion of the National Police of Ukraine in Donetsk Oblast, Ukraine, on Oct. 16, 2026. (Dmytro Smolienko / Ukrinform / Future Publishing via Getty Images)
U.S. President Donald Trump on Oct. 18 claimed his approach to ending the war in Ukraine is "very simple."
In a post on Truth Social, Trump explained that his decision to ease sanctions on Russia while simultaneously piling pressure on Ukraine was to avoid "foolishly (driving) Russia away from the bargaining table."
For many of Trump’s critics in Ukraine, his recent decisions are viewed in similarly simple terms — Trump is helping Russia win the war.
Trump also doubled down on his criticism of President Volodymyr Zelensky, and appeared to suggest that Ukraine's position in the war was untenable.
"He could have made a better deal two years ago than he can now. His country is in shambles, a large portion of his land is lost, his oceans and seas are gone, and his male population is low, wounded, and/or dead. I WANT THIS WAR END!"
But as Russia escalates its aerial bombardment of Ukraine's cities, its forces remain largely stuck on the front lines.
And as Operation Vivaldi has shown, in some sectors Moscow's troops are actually going backwards.
The Kyiv Independent asked Ukrainian soldiers what they thought about Trump's latest outburst.
Some soldiers asked to be identified by callsign or first name only for security reasons.
Bohdan, 
a serviceman
The enemy has not achieved any successes that would suggest a victory on their part. Civilians are the most susceptible to a decline in morale — especially lately, as Russia has been launching mass strikes against civilian infrastructure.
I wouldn't take Trump's words seriously.
He is a media-focused, overly talkative, choleric, elderly, and unwell man.
Artem Kariakin, 
soldier and former partisan
In my opinion, Trump is seeking to bring the fighting in Ukraine to an end by any means necessary, including through Ukraine’s capitulation. He confidently declared to the entire world that he would stop the war in Ukraine, yet year after year he has failed to do so. People no longer believe these claims, and consequently, his slogan that "this war would never have happened under my presidency" is also raising more and more doubts.
It is absolutely clear to me that he is concerned primarily with his own image and approval ratings. That is why he has repeatedly threatened Ukraine — a country that is defending itself against aggression and fighting for its own land. I do not think Trump is genuinely interested in the actual situation on the battlefield. He can easily take Putin’s claims at face value when Putin says that Russia controls certain Ukrainian towns and cities that Russian forces have been unable to reach for years.
I never thought I would see the day when the Russian population, living under the constant influence of propaganda, would be more skeptical of Putin’s claims than the American president.
As for morale at the front, we are not giving up. By now, we have grown accustomed to Trump’s statements and his constantly shifting attitude — from threats against Putin one day to threats against Zelenskyy the next. But when it came to the situation with Starlink, for example, most of us were stunned.
Any restrictions affecting the main communication tool we rely on at the front are not a way of forcing us into a ceasefire at any cost. They are a shove in the back of every one of us, putting our lives at risk. When our hands are tied and we are prevented from defending our own lives and the lives of our loved ones, it hits us hard psychologically. It is not merely a slap in our faces; it is a slap in the face of the entire civilized world.
read also
I hope Trump abandons the idea of using our lives as leverage and understands that we will continue fighting to the end regardless. Otherwise, he risks going down in history as the president who betrayed the entire civilized world.
Returning to the situation on the battlefield, Russia has clearly become bogged down along the front line and is retreating in some sectors. And, as if by some cruel law of nature, every time Russia begins to lose the initiative on the battlefield, those whom we thought were our allies start putting obstacles in our way.
It is especially painful to watch this happen at a time when Putin, faced with the hopelessness of Russia’s situation on the battlefield, has shifted almost entirely toward a strategy of terror against Ukrainian civilians. He is no longer betting on victory at the front — having realized that he cannot defeat the Ukrainian army — but instead on breaking and defeating our civilian population.
But President Trump, and the international community as a whole, must understand one thing — in February 2022, I picked up a weapon and went out to defend Kyiv without even having a helmet or proper body armor. All I had was a Kalashnikov light machine gun, while massive columns of the Russian army were advancing toward our district of the capital. There were many of us like that.
Back then, there was no talk of Starlink or Tomahawks. We went into battle fully aware of how slim our chances were, prepared to fight off an enormous enemy army with little more than our bare hands.
Today, we have a massive army of our own, our own weapons and strike capabilities, and technologies that many countries around the world cannot replicate.
Even if the entire world turns its back on us, we will still stand and fight for our country — because we are Ukrainians.
Illia,
a serviceman in an air assault brigade
In my opinion, the best option is to achieve peace along the current line of contact. The main priority is to stop the bloodshed and save lives.
Morale is dropping every day.
Those who have been fighting since the very beginning are exhausted, and few have any desire to continue. Especially when faced with such injustice.
Trump acts in his own country's interests; for them, it is better if this war ends, as it yields nothing positive. In this situation, neither side — neither us nor Russia — will win, so it is difficult to discuss any clear outcome.
As for why he is pressuring us rather than Russia — I suspect it is simply because we are the weaker party.
