Kazakhstan tops FIE men’s team épée world rankings for the first time
The Kazakhstan men’s épée team has reached the No. 1 spot in the International Fencing Federation (FIE) World Rankings for the first time in the country’s history, Qazinform News Agency reports.
The historic milestone follows a run of international titles over the past twelve months, culminating in a gold-medal performance at the 2026/27 FIE World Cup season opener in Casablanca, Morocco.
Kazakhstan's rise to the top of the FIE rankings caps an impressive winning streak. The team secured consecutive gold medals: at the Islamic Solidarity Games in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, in November 2025; the Asian Fencing Championships in New Delhi, India, in June 2026; the World Fencing Championships in Hong Kong in July; and the Asian Games in Aichi-Nagoya, Japan, in September.
Long dominated by traditional fencing powerhouses such as France, Italy, Hungary, and Switzerland, as well as Asian heavyweights Japan and South Korea, the men’s team épée rankings are now led by Kazakhstan. Kazakhstan arrived in Casablanca ranked third behind Switzerland and France, but its victory at the Moroccan event pushed the squad past both rivals to take the No. 1 spot.
Kazakhstan achieved the top ranking with a revised lineup featuring Kirill Prokhodov, Vadim Sharlaimov, Alexandr Fedotov, and Kirill Pavlov. En route to the title, the squad defeated France — a 23-time world champion in men's team épée.
Qazinform reported earlier that President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev congratulated Kazakhstan’s men’s épée fencing team on their triumph in Morocco.

The strike came as Saudi Arabia canceled a major international investment conference following repeated Houthi attacks on its territory.
The missiles struck a camp in Shabwa province operated by forces loyal to Yemen's internationally recognized, Saudi-backed government. According to a Yemeni military official, the attack occurred as newly recruited soldiers were lining up for a training session. The provincial government warned that the death toll could rise as authorities assessed the casualties.
The Shabwa authorities condemned the strike as a major escalation, saying it had targeted recruits undergoing training and preparation. They called on Yemen's presidential leadership and the Saudi-led coalition to accelerate the deployment of air defense and early warning systems to protect the province against further attacks.
Rashad al-Alimi, chairman of Yemen's Presidential Leadership Council, promised a "firm response," accusing the Houthis of resorting to terrorist attacks when facing military pressure. The rebels acknowledged carrying out the strike, claiming that the camp was operated by Saudi officers and that some had been killed. They provided no evidence to support that assertion, and Saudi authorities did not immediately comment.
The attack marks another escalation in Yemen's civil war, which has intensified since the broader conflict involving Iran began in February. The renewed fighting shattered a ceasefire established in 2022 that had largely halted major hostilities between the Houthis and government forces.
The Houthis, who control Yemen's capital, Sanaa, and much of the country's north, have expanded their military operations in recent weeks, targeting Saudi airports, oil infrastructure and military facilities while also capturing territory along the Red Sea coast near the strategically important Bab el-Mandeb Strait.

Saudi Arabia announced Monday that it was canceling an international investment conference scheduled for the following week, which had been expected to attract senior executives from Wall Street and other international financial institutions. The decision underscored the growing consequences of the Houthi campaign for Saudi Arabia's economy and international business activities.
The latest escalation follows a series of deadly incidents inside Yemen. On Sunday, the Houthi-run Health Ministry accused Saudi-led forces of carrying out an airstrike in the rebel-held northern province of Saada that killed at least nine people, including five children and two women. The rebels said additional strikes over the weekend had left more than 30 people dead or wounded. Saudi Arabia did not immediately respond to those allegations.
Saudi Arabia entered Yemen's civil war in 2015 after the Houthis seized Sanaa and large areas of northern Yemen. Riyadh has long viewed the movement's military capabilities and its ties to Iran as a threat to its security. According to U.N. experts, Iran and allied groups in Lebanon and Iraq have provided the Houthis with military expertise, training and advanced weapons, although Tehran denies supplying arms to the rebels.
The conflict has taken on renewed strategic importance as Houthi forces advance near Bab el-Mandeb, a vital maritime chokepoint connecting the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden. Earlier this month, the Saudi-led coalition launched a major offensive aimed at removing the rebels from recently captured territory along the coast.
Meanwhile, the U.S. State Department renewed its demand Monday for the release of more than 20 Yemeni employees of the American Embassy in Sanaa, marking five years since their detention by the Houthis. The embassy suspended operations in 2015, but local employees continued providing security and maintenance services. Washington called for their immediate and unconditional release.

Will Trump's endorsement enhance Netanyahu's standing in the eyes of Israeli voters? - analysis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
17:51:50 UTC
02:51:50 KST

In June, US President Donald Trump reportedly told Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu he would be in prison if not for him. On Sunday, he told Israelis to give the prime minister another term.
What happened?
How did Trump go from acknowledging that he had called Netanyahu “f**king crazy” during their June conversation to praising him on Truth Social as “strong, brave, and brilliant” and giving him his unequivocal endorsement?
That is one question.
Another is whether this endorsement, the first explicit, written endorsement of this type in the country’s history, will matter.
US presidents have made their preferences in Israeli elections crystal clear before. Usually, however, they have left Israeli voters to connect the dots.
Previous US presidents set precedent for expressing views on Israeli elections
In March 1992, three months before an Israeli election, then-president George H. W. Bush announced that he would not approve $10 billion in long-sought housing loan guarantees to help absorb immigrants from the former Soviet Union unless prime minister Yitzhak Shamir froze settlement construction.
Shamir lost to Yitzhak Rabin, who signed an agreement with Bush for the guarantees two months after his victory. Aaron David Miller, an administration official at the time, later wrote that the perception that Shamir had mismanaged relations with Washington hurt him badly, and that the Bush administration helped orchestrate that perception.
In 1996, president Bill Clinton went to extraordinary lengths to boost Shimon Peres over Netanyahu, later acknowledging as much in a television interview. He also tried to help Ehud Barak stave off defeat at the hands of Ariel Sharon in 2001. Neither effort produced the desired electoral result.
Barack Obama pointedly refused to meet Netanyahu when he came to address Congress in 2015, just weeks before that year’s election. And Joe Biden’s 2022 visit, after another election had been called, gave then-prime minister Yair Lapid an opportunity to look prime ministerial alongside an American president.
Trump's explicit support for Netanyahu deviates from past presidents
So American involvement in Israeli elections is nothing new. What distinguishes Trump’s intervention is how little he has left to interpretation.
In April 2019, Trump helped Netanyahu through policy decisions, foremost among them the recognition of Israeli sovereignty over the Golan Heights. This time, he dispensed with the need for voters to infer his preference from his policies. He endorsed Netanyahu much as he might endorse a favored candidate for Congress.
“Please let this Letter serve to represent my Complete and Total Endorsement of Bibi Netanyahu in his upcoming Race for Re-Election as Prime Minister of Israel,” he wrote. “BIBI NETANYAHU WILL NEVER LET YOU DOWN!”
Blunt? Certainly. Surprising? Given Trump’s previous interventions in Israel’s domestic affairs, less so.
In June 2025, Trump took to Truth Social to demand an end to Netanyahu’s corruption trial, calling it a witch hunt and a travesty, and invoking American military support for Israel in what sounded like a veiled threat.
“It is terrible what they are doing in Israel to Bibi Netanyahu,” he wrote. “The United States of America spends Billions of Dollars a year, far more than on any other nation, protecting and supporting Israel. We are not going to stand for this.”
Sunday’s endorsement also came with a warning. Trump suggested that an Israeli government headed by anyone else could leave the US to confront Iran alone – something he said he was reluctant to do.
“If Israel has the wrong Leader, which would be anyone other than Bibi, America will have to do this work [attack Iran] ourselves, and I am not inclined to do so,” he wrote.
The message went beyond saying that Netanyahu was his preferred candidate. It suggested that the choice Israelis make could affect Washington’s willingness to act against Iran.
That is a considerable weight to place on the Israeli voter.
Trump recently hesitated to endorse Netanyahu
But why intervene now? In a Newsmax interview as recently as Thursday, Trump stopped short of an endorsement and, when asked whether he trusted Netanyahu, said he trusted no one in politics. By Sunday, those reservations were gone.
One explanation is straightforward: Trump always intended to endorse Netanyahu and was waiting for the moment when he thought it would have the greatest impact.
The final stretch before an election is when parties roll out the big guns they were saving for maximum impact. Trump, in campaign terms, is a very big gun.
Netanyahu’s opponents offered less flattering explanations.
Lapid, number two on the B’Yachad list, said in a radio interview that Netanyahu had begged Trump for an endorsement instead of pressing him to act against Iran.
Yashar head Gadi Eisenkot offered his own explanation: Netanyahu had “lied” to Trump about Eisenkot’s willingness to attack Iran. Throughout the campaign, Netanyahu has portrayed Eisenkot as reluctant to take aggressive military action against Hamas, Hezbollah, and Iran.
Another theory being floated is that Trump had seen private polling suggesting Netanyahu was faring considerably better than the public polls indicated. According to this theory – and without access to the polling supposedly driving this decision, it is only a theory – Trump, having backed Viktor Orban’s losing bid in Hungary earlier this year, was reluctant to risk another unsuccessful endorsement. Once persuaded that Netanyahu had a chance to win, he felt comfortable backing him.
Trump-Netanyahu disagreements may remain after endorsement
The endorsement also makes a broader point about the Trump-Netanyahu relationship, which has been marked by growing disagreements and tensions in recent months, as seen in Trump’s expletive-laden June phone call to the prime minister.
The president’s endorsement does not mean that those disagreements have disappeared. It means that, despite them, Trump still prefers Netanyahu to the alternatives. Frustration with a prime minister and support for his reelection are not mutually exclusive.
But Trump’s preference is one thing. The weight Israeli voters give it is another. This brings us to the second question: will his endorsement make a difference at the ballot box?
Is there really a substantial pool of voters in the anti-Netanyahu camp – Yashar or B’Yachad voters, for instance – who will read Trump’s endorsement, suddenly see the light, and switch to Likud?
Unlikely.
Trump’s endorsement might have carried greater weight in March, following the first week of the war with Iran, when Israeli confidence in him was running high. Since then, that confidence has diminished.
The Israel Democracy Institute found that the share of Jewish Israelis who believed Israel’s security was a central consideration for Trump fell from 64% in March to 26% in a survey published in early July.
That measures something different from personal popularity, but it is directly relevant to the argument Trump is now making: that Israelis should take his preference into account when deciding who can best protect them.
Still, converting Netanyahu’s opponents is only one way an endorsement could matter.
Its more plausible effect is within the right-wing camp: reassuring wavering Netanyahu supporters, encouraging them to turn out, or persuading voters considering smaller right-wing parties that Likud is the safest bet for their vote.
It also gives Netanyahu a fresh answer to those questioning his management of Israel’s most important relationship. After months in which the disagreements with Trump were on public display and his opponents charging that he has badly mismanaged Israel’s relations with the US, he can now point to an unequivocal endorsement from the president himself.
The campaign message practically writes itself. Whatever the arguments, whatever the tensions, Netanyahu is still the man Trump wants across the table.
Whether that moves enough votes to change the coalition arithmetic is another matter. American presidents have tried to influence Israeli elections before, only to find the Israeli voters an independent lot determined to reach their own conclusions.
Trump, in his inimitable style, has made his choice clear. The question now is whether Israeli voters will agree that his choice should also be theirs.

Syrian university restriction on female enrollment deepens concerns over women’s rights
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
17:51:43 UTC
02:51:43 KST

Two newly established Syrian state universities specializing in defense and security have barred women from enrolling in most courses, in admission policies condemned as discriminatory by Human Rights Watch (HRW), according to reports and statements from Damascus.
Syria’s Higher Education Ministry announced on September 30 that admission to law, economics and management, and social sciences programs at the National University of Defense Sciences would be restricted to men. At the Syrian University for Security Sciences, women may apply only to cybersecurity programs. Meanwhile, several public universities specializing in kindergarten education, midwifery, and nursing are now admitting only female students.
Applications closed on Monday, and the admission rules are unchanged despite the controversy.
HRW warns of 'concerning pattern' of discrimination
HRW warned that the restrictions violated Syria’s Constitutional Declaration and its international legal obligations, forming part of a “concerning pattern” of state actions restricting women’s roles in Syrian society and reinforcing gender stereotypes.
“Syria’s authorities are rebuilding the army and the security forces without women,” said Hiba Zayadin, senior Syria adviser at HRW. “Women can’t train as officers, and they can’t even study to be the army’s lawyers or administrators. This is discrimination, plain and simple.”
Although the September announcement has sparked international criticism, a former Higher Education Ministry official told Agence France-Presse last month that some gender-based admission policies had long been in place. However, excluding women from defense and security universities is a new development.
Many of the newly established defense universities, including the National University of Defense Sciences, require male students to commit to military service. This requirement does not apply to female students in the limited number of courses open to them.
Women effectively denied pathway to joining army
Human Rights Watch noted that, despite the opening of the Women’s Police Institute, whose first class graduated in September, restrictions on women’s admission to most defense university courses have effectively denied them a pathway into the army.
The exclusion follows an August decision by Syrian authorities to bar members of the Women’s Protection Units (YPJ), the all-female component of the Kurdish-led Syrian Democratic Forces, from joining the army.
Restrictions extend beyond the defense and security sectors. State technical institutes specializing in oil and gas and railway studies also admit only male applicants.
The new Syrian authorities have also repeatedly raised questions about women’s roles in public life. In December 2024, a government spokesperson suggested that women might be biologically unsuited to certain political roles and said their ability to serve as judges “could be an area of study and research for specialists.” The following month, the governor of Latakia banned female state employees from wearing “excessive” makeup, threatening legal action against those who failed to comply.
“Women are underrepresented in parliament, the police, and some public offices, and are now shut out of the army,” Zayadin said. “The authorities have promised to respect women’s rights, but their actions directly contradict those promises. Women’s full participation, in all roles and sectors, is essential to building a brighter future for Syria.”
Sally Obeid, a founding member of the Syrian Christian Congress, condemned the admission rules on X, insisting that Damascus’s “goal” was “to kill women’s minds, clone Taliban policies, and confiscate Syrian women’s right to seats in engineering and law.”

Global Jewish life profoundly reshaped by impact of Israeli-Palestinian conflict, INSS report shows
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
17:51:40 UTC
02:51:40 KST

A new report published by the Institute for National Security Studies (INSS) on October 10 contends that the ongoing Israeli-Palestinian conflict has evolved past a localized Middle Eastern affair to profoundly reshape everyday Jewish life across diaspora communities.
The report, titled “No Longer on the Sidelines: How the Israeli-Palestinian Conflict Impacts Diaspora Jews,” was authored by INSS senior researchers Theodore Sasson, a professor at Middlebury College, and Avishay Ben Sasson-Gordis, head of the US-Israel field.
Drawing on six months of discussions between an INSS Joint Working Group and leaders of major Jewish organizations across the US, Canada, France, the UK, and South America, the authors note that local fallout from Israel’s conflict choices makes global Jewry genuine stakeholders in Israeli policy. They have identified four major impacts: normalizing hostility, dividing communities, diminishing political influence, and fueling antisemitism.
The authors explain that hostility toward Israel has normalized across Western societies due to interpretations of the IDF’s conduct in Gaza and the West Bank.
The report highlights that a March 2026 Pew poll showed 60% of Americans view Israel unfavorably, up from 53% in 2025 and 42% in 2022, with 75% of young adults (18-29) holding negative views. Israel’s US standing now mirrors hostile nations like Iran, China, and Russia rather than allies like the UK and Germany.
Controversy over Israel penetrates global politics
Beyond polls, Israel has entered domestic politics via midterm primaries, where left-wing candidates challenge arms sales and AIPAC funding. In Europe, pariah designations have advanced further. UK participants noted that “Israel is South Africa” across cultural institutions, while French participants warned that anti-Zionism risks becoming a cultural norm.
Consequently, Jewish institutions – such as synagogues hosting aliyah sessions, camps hiring IDF veterans, Hillel groups, and BDS-targeted businesses – face intense protests, turning ordinary Jewish life into counter-cultural activity.
The authors examine how the decline in support for the two-state solution in Israel has fractured diaspora communities internally.
For decades, the two-state paradigm allowed diaspora supporters to reconcile backing Israel with democratic values by viewing the “occupation” as temporary. The abandonment of this horizon leaves defenders unequipped to counter outside critics, compounding feelings of alienation.
This alienation, particularly among young adults, intensified alongside relentless media imagery of civilian death and suffering in Gaza and the West Bank, coupled with widespread narratives accusing Israel of intentionally inflicting harm. As one working group participant warned, communities under-informed about Palestinian terror threats and saturated with reports of Israeli transgressions are becoming dangerously alienated from the moral case for Israel.
Public opinion data underscore this trend: a June 2026 AP-NORC survey reported that 24% of American Jews feel “not at all” emotionally attached to Israel, a steady rise from 20% in 2025, 14% in 2020, and 12% in 2013, with 39% of young adults aged 18 to 29 reporting no attachment. The authors’ secondary analysis of the data indicates that low emotional attachment is closely associated with secularism, skepticism regarding the justification of military actions in Gaza, and beliefs that Israel committed genocide.
Growing disagreements over Israel-Hamas war fracture communities
While Jewish organizations continue advocating for Israel, growing dissent has fractured communities, particularly in liberal regions like US blue states and coastal metros, straining central bodies and reducing their capacity to represent the community as a whole.
As the pro-Israel lobby fragments into competing right-wing, centrist, and liberal camps, and some individual synagogues divide, the rise of newly launched non-Zionist and anti-Zionist groups has caused further division and altered the public image of organized Jewish life.
The authors analyze the erosion of diaspora political influence. The absence of a viable political horizon for resolving the conflict, coupled with controversial rhetoric and policies from Israeli figures, has made pro-Israel advocacy exceedingly difficult, forcing diaspora defenders to navigate accusations that supporting Israel contradicts core democratic values.
This weakened leverage is evident internationally. In the US, anti-Israel candidates have won primary races despite heavy AIPAC spending. In Canada, the government has advanced arms embargoes and recognized Palestinian statehood while dismissing communal leaders. In the UK, authorities have pushed forward with West Bank settlement product bans over community objections.
The authors emphasize that this diminished political capacity not only harms Israel’s national security; it also inflicts a heavy toll on diaspora communities themselves. Having invested massive resources into building robust political lobbies, global Jewry now faces an erosion of its broader political power, undermining its ability to advocate effectively for its own local community interests and needs.
Diaspora Jews concerned that Israel backlash contibutes to antisemitism
The report details how the war’s management and rhetoric from senior Israeli officials have provided fuel for antisemitism and heightened anxiety, with a late 2026 Mellman Group survey showing 56% of American Jewish voters deeply concerned that Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s actions have worsened antisemitism.
This perception is matched by data; AJC polling shows 93% viewing antisemitism as serious, and ADL audits document steep surges in Israel-related incidents across the US. Left-and-right political polarization has left many American Jews experiencing political homelessness, while skyrocketing security costs force communal organizations to divert critical funds away from Jewish life.
In Canada and the UK, physical violence, including arson, stabbings, and a 2026 Yom Kippur synagogue shooting in Ontario, has accelerated, with protests targeting Jewish neighborhoods and leading some Canadian Jews to consider an “exit strategy.” Meanwhile, in parts of Europe, mounting threats have driven an ongoing process of “marranization,” where Jews feel compelled to conceal their identities to stay safe.
In their analysis, the authors address a core grievance voiced by diaspora leaders: while avoiding harm to Israel has historically been paramount, the Israeli government appears largely unconcerned with how its conflict choices impact diaspora well-being, often undermining international law through damaging ministerial rhetoric, restrictive aid policies, or unchecked settler violence.
The report stresses that the deepest long-term risk stems from the political deadlock over a permanent one-state reality without democratic rights for millions of Palestinians, which alienates Western allies and exhausts community advocacy.
Although domestic Israeli politics and public hardening post-October 7 have sidelined peace frameworks, post-election leadership must weigh broader national security needs, including democratic preservation and global Jewish ties.
While diaspora leaders have traditionally avoided criticizing Israeli policy due to a perceived lack of “skin in the game,” that premise is shattered. And yet, public critique remains intensely sensitive due to fears of aiding adversaries and internal communal divides. Ultimately, the compounding toll of these interlocking dynamics makes the diaspora’s stake in Israel’s strategic decisions undeniable, while hurting Israel’s own soft power and international standing.
INSS researchers urge Israeli officials to avoid divisive rhetoric
The report concludes with a series of concrete recommendations for Israeli policymakers to mitigate the conflict’s local fallout and help restore global advocacy capacity.
The authors urge Israeli leadership to ensure cabinet ministers avoid rhetoric that inflames human rights allegations and to publicly disavow any such statements when made. Furthermore, authorities must crack down on West Bank extremist violence and hold perpetrators accountable.
Politically, Israel must maintain a diplomatic horizon to prevent a slide into a non-democratic single-state reality while proactively communicating its commitment to a viable resolution.
The report also calls for institutional reforms. Israel must establish sustained dialogues with diaspora organizations, build collaborative strategies to improve international standing, and formally integrate systematic reviews within cabinet ministries to evaluate how domestic policy choices impact world Jewry.
The authors noted that the report’s conclusions and recommendations belong solely to the researchers and do not necessarily represent the views of every participating organization.

Syrian textbooks show pan-Arab content replaced by Islamist ideology, IMPACT-se finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
17:51:37 UTC
02:51:37 KST

An in-depth review of 130 Syrian school textbooks implemented under the administration of Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa shows that Baathist, pan-Arabist, and secular governance frameworks have been substantially replaced by Sunni-Muslim identity and political Islamism.
The findings were detailed in a report titled "The New Syria: Education Under al-Sharaa: Review of Syria’s National School Curriculum, 2025–2026," published on Monday by the Institute for Monitoring Peace and Cultural Tolerance in School Education (IMPACT-se), covering the 2025–2026 academic year.
Authored by researchers Matan Perchikov, Itam Shalev, and Yonatan Negev, PhD, the report systematically analyzed thousands of textbook pages across Grades 1-12. The researchers applied content and discourse analysis using UNESCO-derived standards for peace and tolerance, comparing current textbooks side by side with earlier editions from 2017-2018 or 2011-2012 to trace specific alterations, omissions, and updates.
The report maps out a structural transformation in how national identity is framed, substituting secular Syrian patriotism and pan-Arab nationalism with broad pan-Islamist and religious constructs. Local loyalty to the national homeland is consistently subordinated to the broader transnational Muslim community, while traditional celebrations of Arab nationalism are replaced by an emphasis on Islamic civilization.
Historical narratives have been revised to reflect this theological reorientation, with seminal events such as the Great Arab Revolt of 1916- 1918 no longer taught as a popular liberation movement against Ottoman Turkish occupation, but instead framed strictly as a rebellion aimed at breaking away from the Ottoman State.
Scientific theories heavily edited, removed as Islamization extends across subjects
This Islamization of knowledge extends deeply across subjects, targeting foundational scientific theories like evolution, the Big Bang, and biological development, which have been heavily edited or removed. It attributes natural phenomena directly to divine creation, with primary science texts replacing phrases like "nature’s giving" with "Allah’s giving."
At the same time, the curriculum normalizes armed struggle and self-sacrifice, elevating historical and regional militant figures while systematically romanticizing Palestinian armed resistance, rocket fire, and suicide bombings as acts of supreme martyrdom and justified defense.
The instructional materials also marginalize Syria’s diverse ethnic and religious minority populations. While Christianity maintains a restricted and legally subordinate presence, ethnic groups such as the Kurds, Turkmen, and Druze are nearly invisible across the curriculum, and prominent historical figures from these backgrounds are stripped of their ethnic identities. Sectarian divisions are further reinforced through the contestation of Shi’ite and Alawite symbols, including the explicit delegitimization of the Fatimid Caliphate and the sidelining of Alawite leadership figures.
The curriculum addresses Jewish communities through traditional theological grievances, repeating allegations of treachery, deceit, and broken covenants while entirely erasing centuries of local Syrian Jewish history. Jewish national identity is dismissed outright, with textbooks portraying Jews as a disjointed mix of populations rather than a legitimate nation. Israel is subjected to intense hostility, consistently referred to by derogatory designations such as the "Zionist entity" or simply the "enemy," and omitted entirely from regional maps. In historical units covering the 1948 war, military operations undertaken by the Israeli side are explicitly likened to Nazi crimes against Jews, and all past peace agreements involving Israel are condemned.
Gender roles within the new curriculum have likewise shifted sharply toward traditionalist constraints, diminishing the public visibility and rights of women. References guaranteeing gender equality under civic law have been excised, leaving women defined primarily through domestic family roles as obedient wives and mothers. Visually, textbook illustrations of women and girls have been altered to reflect stricter Islamic dress codes, frequently through the retrofitted addition of hijabs, alongside explicit curriculum content advocating for the full-body-covering burqa.
The curriculum also completely scrubbed the Baathist political legacy. Content associated with former ruler Hafez al-Assad, Bashar al-Assad, and their family has been systematically erased, dismantling the longstanding Assad personality cult and recasting the former rulers in the texts as corrupt, sectarian autocrats. Consequently, the 2011 civil war and the subsequent 2024 uprising are taught as a morally righteous restoration of authentic Islamic-Arab rule.
IMPACT-se CEO: Syria has 'rare opportunity' to revamp education system post-Assad
"The post-Assad era presents Syria with a rare opportunity to create an education system and a society based on inclusion, tolerance, and a shared civic identity, said IMPACT-se CEO Marcus Sheff. "Instead, these textbooks show a very concerning shift from one damaging ideological framework to another."
Sheff warned that the marginalization of minorities and women alongside the glorification of religiously framed violence risks shaping a generation far away from peaceful coexistence.
"This report should raise serious concerns among international leaders who hope to see Syria emerge as a partner in building a peaceful and prosperous Middle East," Sheff added.
He noted that IMPACT-se is working with policymakers in Washington and internationally to drive meaningful reforms to Syria’s school curriculum, seizing a critical opportunity for change as the new Syrian government seeks international assistance and support.

Bennett, Netanyahu helped build Western Wall's Ezrat Yisrael, but will either secure its future?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
17:51:36 UTC
02:51:36 KST

Women of the Wall is urging Israel’s political parties to commit to implementing the frozen Western Wall compromise, placing the future of egalitarian prayer at Ezrat Yisrael - and Israel’s relationship with Diaspora Jewry - before those seeking to form the next government, the organization said in a statement.
As diaspora minister, Naftali Bennett helped establish the southern prayer space in 2013. Benjamin Netanyahu’s government approved the broader agreement intended to secure its status, then froze it.
Neither leader’s record amounts to delivering the full compromise.
“In recent years, and especially since October 7, we have all come to recognize how important - even critical - our ties with Diaspora Jewry are to the existence of the Jewish people and the State of Israel,” Women of the Wall said.
“Yet Israel has repeatedly slammed the door on Diaspora Jews, sending an unmistakable message that they have no place here with us.”
For the organization, the Western Wall exemplifies that contradiction: a site meant to connect Jews to their shared heritage has become a recurring source of exclusion and political confrontation.
Bennett’s B’Yachad party approaches the issue through the language of belonging and reconciliation. Its doctrine addresses the Wall under the heading “Only Together Can We Create a Home for Every Jew.”
“The Western Wall is a sacred and unifying place, and it should be a place of Shalom Bayit [domestic harmony], not civil strife,” the document states.
Women of the Wall: Preservation is not enough
Its practical commitment is to preserve the southern prayer space while maintaining Orthodox arrangements at the main plaza.
“In this spirit, the Ezrat Yisrael solution on the southern end of the Western Wall – intended to facilitate prayer and gatherings in diverse ways – should be preserved, without disrupting Orthodox prayer arrangements at the Western Wall Plaza.”
That wording supports the continued existence of a space accommodating diverse forms of Jewish worship. It does not explicitly promise to implement the full 2016 compromise, establish its proposed management framework, or complete specified improvements within a stated timetable.
The distinction matters because Ezrat Yisrael predates the broader agreement.
In August 2013, Bennett’s Jerusalem and Diaspora Affairs Ministry announced the completion of a roughly 450-square-meter prayer platform near Robinson’s Arch. Developed in coordination with the Prime Minister’s Office and Jewish Agency chairman Natan Sharansky, it was presented as an interim solution for egalitarian and pluralistic prayer ahead of the High Holy Days.
Netanyahu’s government approved the agreement in January 2016, and it went further. It called for a recognized egalitarian prayer area, a management framework with representatives from the Reform and Conservative movements and Women of the Wall, and state funding for maintenance and services. Orthodox authorities would retain control of the main plaza. The government froze the plan in 2017 under pressure from haredi parties.
Women of the Wall described the agreement as an effort to provide a dignified, equal place for women and to represent liberal Jewish movements representing millions of Diaspora Jews. Its statement blamed haredi and hardline religious Zionist pressure for the freeze and called for the agreement’s implementation.
More recently, the dispute has extended beyond infrastructure to the authority to determine permissible prayer practices.
Last February, the Knesset advanced a private bill sponsored by far Right Noam MK Avi Maoz that would give the Chief Rabbinate authority to determine what constitutes desecration at Jewish holy sites and make it the religious representative consulted over regulations. The proposal passed its preliminary reading 56–47 and still required further readings to become law.
Netanyahu had prevented the proposal from receiving the Ministerial Committee for Legislation backing by canceling its meeting, reportedly to avoid a crisis with Diaspora Jewry. Nevertheless, it advanced by a free vote, with support from Likud Justice Minister Yariv Levin, who called for completing the legislation to end High Court intervention in the Wall’s management, a move Shas and United Torah Judaism also supported.
Women of the Wall cited Maoz’s proposal, alongside legislation submitted by Shas leader Arye Deri in 2023, as measures that it said sought to exclude liberal Jews and women and undermine the prayer rights of Diaspora Jews.
Its criticism places the issue within a broader argument about Jewish peoplehood: decisions negotiated among Israeli coalition partners also affect communities abroad whose religious practices differ from those enforced at the main plaza.
Bennett’s record raises a separate question about the distance between support for egalitarian prayer and the ability to overcome coalition opposition.
During negotiations to establish the Bennett-Lapid government in 2021, implementation of the compromise had been included in the coalition agreement at Yisrael Beytenu’s request.
This arrangement envisaged access from the main Western Wall complex and a governing board including progressive Jewish and Women of the Wall representatives.
By January 2022, however, Bennett acknowledged that his government could not implement the full plan. Speaking to The Jerusalem Post that year, he cited opposition within Yamina and New Hope, and said his government instead intended to pursue physical improvements without implementing the agreement’s other provisions.
Women of the Wall is asking parties to make that additional commitment. It urged the next government to take a broad, farsighted approach that weighs the relationship with Diaspora Jewry and the future of the Jewish people alongside political alliances with haredi parties.

The cycle of trauma and violence is failing us - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
17:51:28 UTC
02:51:28 KST

When we first arrived in the Palestinian village of Turmus Ayya, a man shouted at us with a kind of passion that stopped me in my tracks.
“You steal our olives, burn our homes.”
My heart shattered.
I found myself wondering what this man had experienced in his life. What pain, what loss, what fear had brought him to a place where a group of Jews arriving in his village could represent, to him, everything that had gone wrong?
I don't know his story. I won't pretend to. But I couldn't stop thinking about it.
The cycle of trauma and violence between Israelis and Palestinians has become so entrenched that we've started treating it as inevitable. It isn't. And it is heartbreaking, infuriating, and profoundly unhelpful to those of us who are genuinely trying to build a better future for both peoples.
Today, I witnessed just how dangerous that cycle has become.
I agreed to join a public relations trip to several Palestinian villages organized by Regavim, an organization whose values and political outlook I do not share. I made that clear when I accepted the invitation.
I'm a liberal Zionist, an educator, and an activist. My work is to help people understand Israel, its complexities, and the realities facing Israelis and Palestinians. I take that responsibility seriously. And I believe that if I'm going to speak about a place, a conflict, or a community, I have an obligation to see it for myself.
How can I educate people about something I haven't made an effort to understand firsthand? What credibility does my voice have if I'm only willing to visit places that confirm what I already believe?
Throughout my career, I've accepted invitations to visit places around the region that are complicated, uncomfortable, and sometimes dangerous. I've visited Rawabi and Kalkilya and pre-October 7 would go to speak to Gazans on the border as they cross in and out for work. I've spent time in Jewish settlements. I've spoken with people on different sides of the conflict, listened to their stories, and tried to understand the realities they live with.
That is the job. Not to agree with everyone you meet. Not to endorse every organization that invites you. And certainly not to abandon your principles at the door. It's to look, listen, ask questions, and learn enough to speak honestly about a reality that is rarely as simple as any one political camp would like it to be. But nothing about my commitment to understanding this conflict prepared me for what happened next.
Our second stop was in Area B of the West Bank. It is important to make that distinction: we were not in Area A. We were in Area B. Initially, nothing seemed particularly alarming. A couple of teenagers were riding bikes nearby. Then they pulled out their phones. They appeared to be making calls.
A few minutes later, we reached a point where a car carrying Palestinians blocked our way. The people inside began yelling at us, asking if we were Jews. Several people were on their phones, apparently telling others that Jews had arrived.
We were traveling in three cars. Fleur Hassan-Nahoum was in the first car with Cindy Seni and Jessica Cohen. I was in the middle car, and Bellamy Bellucci and Golda Daphna were behind us in the third.
The people blocking us told us we couldn't be there. We didn't argue. We didn't try to push our way through. We agreed to turn around. But more people began arriving. Cars, people on foot, teenagers on bikes. It felt as though word had spread and people were converging on us. The car blocking the road had cut off our way forward, so we turned around and started to leave.
People were shouting at us as we drove away.
Then, perhaps 30 seconds later, they began throwing what I can only describe as boulders at our cars. These weren't little rocks. They were enormous chunks of concrete.
Our guides and security personnel, who were driving us and were armed, told us to duck and cover our heads. We did exactly what they said. There was no point in stopping to get out or drawing a weapon; that would only have escalated an already dangerous situation. We needed to get out safely.
I could feel the car shaking as the concrete slammed into it. In the first car, a chunk came through the window. Cindy was injured.
It was terrifying.
We soon made it back into Israel proper and pulled over to the side of the road. We called Magen David Adom and the police. Baruch Hashem, we were all okay. But we had just experienced something I struggle to find the right words for.
It was an attempted lynching. We were targeted as Jews.
Our presence had been identified, our way forward had been blocked, and when we turned around and tried to leave without confrontation, people began hurling enormous chunks of concrete at our cars. One came through the first car's window, injuring my friend Cindy.
I don't use those words lightly. We were trying to leave peacefully. We were told to duck and cover our heads as concrete slammed into our vehicles. We were terrified, and we were fortunate to get out safely.
Whatever one believes about the politics of the organization that brought us there, none of that justifies what happened to us. No disagreement over land, no political grievance, and no history of suffering makes it acceptable to target people for being Jewish.
And yet, I keep returning to the man who shouted at us when we first arrived in Turmus Ayya.
I keep thinking about his anger, and about the possibility of the pain and fear behind it. I can acknowledge that Palestinians have experienced profound suffering without excusing an attack on Jews. I can condemn violence against Palestinians without minimizing violence against Israelis. These principles are not mutually exclusive. They have to coexist if we are ever going to move beyond this.
That is precisely why what happened today makes me so sad. The cycle of trauma and violence is not making either people safer. It is deepening the fear, anger, and mistrust that make a better future harder to imagine.
I went on this trip because I believe that seeing things firsthand matters. I still believe that. I will not allow a frightening experience to convince me that looking, listening, and learning are mistakes. Nor will I allow my disagreement with an organization to prevent me from examining the realities it wants to show me.
But bearing witness also means telling the truth about what happened, even when that truth is uncomfortable. It means refusing to look away from Palestinian suffering, and refusing to look away when Jews are attacked. It means being honest about the people and organizations we disagree with, without surrendering our own judgment.
I am a liberal Zionist because I believe Israel can and must be a country committed to democracy, human rights, and equality. I believe in Israel's future, and I believe that future requires taking the lives and dignity of Palestinians seriously, too.
That doesn't mean ignoring the threats Israelis face, excusing violence, or pretending that good intentions are enough. It means being willing to confront uncomfortable realities, including the ones that challenge our own worldview.
I went to these villages because I believe you cannot understand this conflict from a distance. What happened to us today will not make me stop asking questions or listening to people whose experiences differ from my own. But listening cannot mean looking away when people are hurt, and understanding someone's pain cannot mean excusing what they do with it.
I left Turmus Ayya thinking about the man who shouted at us. I left the West Bank thinking about the concrete that came through the window. Both experiences matter. Neither cancels out the other. And if we cannot hold both truths at once, we will keep repeating the same cycle and wondering why nothing changes.
The writer is an activist and content creator. A third-generation IDF veteran with over a decade in Israel advocacy, she has created and executed content for dozens of major organizations. She is an associate at the Tel Aviv Institute.

The European Commission released a statement condemning the violence in Albania on Sunday, saying it had "no place in a democratic society" and that the response "must remain within the law and proportionate."
Edi Rama has accused some of those taking part in anti-government protests in Albania as having crossed a "red line" as demonstrations continued across the country on Monday.
Anti-government "Flamingo" protests have been ongoing in Albania for months amid calls for Rama to resign as prime minister, but clashes ramped up early last week as a student movement calling for action over high tuition fees launched fresh demonstrations.

Violent clashes with police in recent days have seen protesters set buildings alight, hurl molotov cocktails, and shoot fireworks at officers, who have responded with rubber bullets, water cannons, and tear gas.
Hundreds of people, including police officers, have reportedly been injured in the violence.
"We will continue our movement until Rama resigns. We are not criminals, we want social peace and better living conditions in our country," Leka Sina, a 22-year-old student, told the AFP news agency.
"Violence is not a solution, but the government also needs to reflect deeply to understand this revolt," Sina added.
Rama has sought to pin the blame for the unrest on foreign influence.
The European Commission released a statement condemning the violence in Albania on Sunday, saying it had "no place in a democratic society" and that the response "must remain within the law and proportionate."
"Freedom of assembly and expression are fundamental rights and core European values, to be respected and exercised peacefully," the Commission said in its statement. "In a candidate country firmly committed to the EU accession process and making important progress on its EU path, grievances should be handled through constructive dialogue and in a peaceful manner."

====================================================================================================

Netanyahu or Eisenkot? Where their visions for Israel’s security align - and collide
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
17:51:24 UTC
02:51:24 KST

While there are many national security strategies, the next government will ultimately come down to a choice between two visions.
One is the vision of current Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who faces pressure from the Right.
The other is the vision of Yashar party leader and former IDF chief Gadi Eisenkot, who faces pressure from both his right and his left.
Netanyahu, Eisenkot differ on how to confront Iran - but not on the threat
There are few major differences between Netanyahu and Eisenkot on the Iranian threat, though there are some nuances. Both will oppose a "bad deal" if US President Donald Trump's administration opts for such a deal.
Despite Trump's endorsement of Netanyahu and statement that he probably will not help attack Iran again, the US president has few positions set in stone and is likely to act on whatever whim is convincing to him at any particular moment: Whether to cut a deal, to return to war, or to continue a marathon economic standoff of competing blockades.
In that sense, the main differences are that Netanyahu would likely be more open about opposition to a bad deal to try to influence American public opinion, even at the cost of trying to improve the deal behind the scenes.
Eisenkot, by contrast, would likely keep his opposition private in order to try to improve the deal quietly, while viewing American public opinion as something he has less control over.
Both Netanyahu and Eisenkot would be ready to attack Iran in some circumstances where the nuclear or ballistic missile threat became too close for comfort. Both of them have shown they will not jump at attacking Iran at every moment.
Most would agree that at this stage Netanyahu would be willing to take on more risk to attack Iran and might interpret the point of no return as an earlier point than Eisenkot.
Israel's political leaders have no clear plan for Gaza
Neither Netanyahu nor Eisenkot has a real plan for Gaza. Both have promised to eliminate Hamas's control of the Strip, but neither has a clear path to doing so.
Netanyahu's path is thoroughly unconvincing because he has had three years to achieve this goal. While Hamas is substantially weakened, it is still quite clearly in power.
In a recent briefing to which he invited only a small portion of the Israeli military reporters' group, leaving out The Jerusalem Post, other English-language Israeli outlets, and the vast majority of Hebrew-speaking reporters, he refused to back away from his commitment to "absolute victory" over Hamas, despite there being no evidence that he has come any closer to that goal since October 2024, when Yahya Sinwar was killed and all 24 of Hamas's battalions had already been dismantled.
Somewhere between 80% and 90% of Hamas was killed by the end of 2024.
Although the IDF took control of 60%-75% of Gaza's territory in 2025-2026, and airstrikes several times a week continue to keep Hamas on the run, the last two years have seen very little change in how close Hamas has come to losing control.
Even if the IDF undertakes another invasion of Gaza, something the Trump administration has consistently blocked, Hamas has shown that it can hide among the civilian population and outwait and outlast the IDF's ability to remain in the area in large numbers.
Netanyahu also invoked the "fortress Israel" metaphor and said he was willing to keep Gaza in ruins, with no rebuilding indefinitely, until Hamas disarms completely. This made it clear that his strategy is to try to keep Gaza miserable long enough for Hamas to simply quit.
But Hamas will not simply quit. It is a fanatical and messianic movement with perverse delusions of grandeur.
In that sense, Netanyahu has no clear plan.
He also seems ready to sacrifice all of Israel's international relations with Europe and perhaps even the US to maintain this uncompromising stance.
In contrast, Eisenkot has no clear plan of his own but is willing to move forward with Trump's cease-fire plan without resistance, including empowering Palestinian Authority-linked technocratic leaders and police, as well as international peacekeepers in Gaza.
He would likely be ready to allow partial rebuilding in exchange for partial disarmament, if for no other reason than to pause, and perhaps even push back, the diplomatic tsunami that is already threatening Israeli national security and economic stability.
This will not eliminate Hamas.
It might weaken the group politically, which could, in the very long term, lead to other groups challenging it. Alternatively, Hamas might manipulate the system, becoming a Hezbollah-style group that controls politics like a puppet master behind the scenes.
Neither of those outcomes will make Israelis feel safer now. But if Hamas is eventually weakened enough to have to share power, that would represent a fundamental shift.
Even if Hamas manages to retain its current power, as it has since October 2024 despite Israel's efforts to crush it, Israel will at least avoid a further deterioration in support from Europe, the US, and elsewhere.
These differences could have implications over the next year and beyond, but Eisenkot has made it clear that he will not move toward a Palestinian state, certainly not during a first term.
So, the differences between them are not as large as those between, say, National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir, who favors transfer, and Democrats leader Yair Golan, who would push for a two-state solution.
Netanyahu and Eisenkot are worlds apart on the West Bank
If there are strong commonalities between Netanyahu and Eisenkot on Iran and Gaza, with differences largely in the nuances, they are worlds apart on the West Bank.
The only thing they have in common is a strong commitment to fighting Palestinian terrorism as their number one priority.
But on fighting Jewish extremism and expanding Israeli settlements, their second- and third-priority issues, they are far apart.
Eisenkot would immediately reinstate administrative detention for Jewish extremists, which Defense Minister Israel Katz suspended in January 2025 and which Netanyahu has allowed to remain suspended for nearly two years, despite losing control of Jewish extremists.
In addition, Eisenkot would clean house at the police, bringing in officers who would crack down hard on Jewish extremists.
He would likely also fire Shin Bet Director David Zini and replace him with a new chief who would crack down more forcefully on Jewish extremists.
Until recently, most people were not blaming the IDF for the out-of-control situation, so the officers currently in place might be allowed to remain. However, the last few months have blemished their records as well.
It remains to be seen whether Eisenkot might also clean house among senior IDF officers. One major question is whether Maj.-Gen. Dado Bar Kalifa's appointment as the next IDF Central Command chief, scheduled to begin in January 2027, will go through.
That could depend on how strongly IDF Chief of Staff Lt.-Gen. Eyal Zamir backs "Dado" and how much the appointment is perceived as having been dictated by Katz.
Regarding the more than 100 new "farms" that Netanyahu's government established or expanded under the authority of Bezalel Smotrich within the Defense Ministry, Eisenkot would likely clear most or all of them.
He would certainly freeze new settlement construction or limit it to the "natural" expansion of existing settlements.
He would certainly block the expansion of the E1 settlement bloc near Jerusalem, which has intensified European criticism.
Collectively, these actions would help pause or even reverse the diplomatic tsunami that has begun to engulf Israel's national security and economic stability.
However, Eisenkot has no vision for resolving the standoff with the Palestinians in the West Bank, which has persisted since 1967. Once again, he opposes a two-state solution in the near and medium term.
Netanyahu is not prepared to annex the entire West Bank, as Ben-Gvir would like, but his moves to expand Israel's presence in the West Bank have, in a way, forced the final-status issues to the fore.
If he remains in power and continues taking over new parts of Area C, it is not impossible that, at some point, the Palestinians in the West Bank might become concerned enough to offer a new deal under which they receive closer to the 70% of the territory that Trump offered them in 2020.
That would be a significant reduction from the 90%-95% promised to them under the Oslo Accords, but Netanyahu's moves could shift their approach.
Netanyahu, Eisenkot largely aligned on Lebanon and Syria
There do not appear to be any major differences between Eisenkot and Netanyahu on Lebanon.
Both would maintain a security zone. Both are open to partial withdrawals in exchange for the Lebanese army partially clearing Hezbollah from the security zone, and neither trusts the Lebanese army to do its job sufficiently.
Unlike in Gaza, no one believes there is any real chance of removing Hezbollah from power.
Under light pressure from Trump, with heavier pressure likely to focus on Gaza and the West Bank, might Eisenkot agree to partial withdrawals faster than Netanyahu? Maybe.
But Eisenkot has said he would draw a line at eight kilometers to prevent Hezbollah from firing anti-tank missiles into Israel.
Eisenkot might not have destroyed as many homes belonging to southern Lebanese Shiites as Netanyahu ordered destroyed, but that has already happened, so it is unclear whether it would affect future policy.
Whoever is prime minister, there will likely be some partial withdrawals and some degree of a standoff over the security zone.
The only major difference in nuance might be that Eisenkot would try to restore France to a productive role, hoping to score diplomatic points with Paris on other fronts, whereas Netanyahu now relishes public conflicts with the French government.
There also is likely little difference between Netanyahu and Eisenkot on Syria.
Once again, both want to keep a security zone and both have dropped hints at times that they might agree to partial withdrawals, but both have strong doubts about trusting Syrian President Ahmad al-Sharaa because of his al-Qaeda past.
Once again, Eisenkot might make some partial withdrawals more easily under pressure from Trump, but Netanyahu will to if Trump presses hard enough – and the US president has made it clear that he views Sharaa as an ally, no matter what Israel thinks.
Eisenkot could repair ties with Europe and the US, but faces major challenges
Eisenkot would significantly improve relations with Europe. He might reach new understandings with Middle Eastern countries that once liked Netanyahu but now loathe him.
All of these diplomatic gains could help address various national security and economic stability issues.
Netanyahu would stick to alliances with India, the UAE, Cyprus, and Greece, insisting that if Jerusalem compromises in the way the West wants it to, Israel's national security will be gravely undermined.
But the most crucial prize is the US.
Stunningly, Netanyahu this week invoked a scenario in which Israel loses the US as an ally entirely.
That would mean Israel losing access to US-built aircraft, including the F-35, as well as various other weapons, global diplomatic support, and potentially a major source of economic stability.
This is stunning because, while such a scenario might materialize in January 2029, one would think that any Israeli prime minister would do everything possible to avoid it.
Netanyahu presented this scenario alongside the prospect of two more years of Trump in power, as if anything Israel wants to achieve must be accomplished in the next two years.
And perhaps Netanyahu might achieve things with Trump in those two years that would forever change the playing field.
But Trump's declaration of love and unconditional support for Netanyahu on Sunday was anything but unconditional.
The US president barely made the declaration and has taken numerous potshots at the prime minister over the years.
All it meant was that, given the polling a week before the election, Trump would much rather continue working with Netanyahu, whom he knows well, than have to get to know Eisenkot.
But if Eisenkot is more compliant with some of Trump's demands regarding Gaza, the West Bank, Lebanon, and Syria, the two will likely figure out how to get along.
More importantly, Eisenkot will not give up on the Democratic Party, which has turned against Israel more than at any time in decades.
He will try to hit "restart" on relations in the post-Netanyahu era.
The bad news is that he has no clear plan for doing so, and the gulf between Israeli and American expectations regarding the Middle East is substantial, even if Netanyahu exits stage left.
Whether Eisenkot could bridge that gulf would be one of the key challenges and uncertainties of his premiership.

A black bear &quot;dropped by&quot; a library in the U.S.—enjoyed snacks and ate a jar of honey

2026-10-19
20:50:50 EEST

A black bear "dropped by" a library in the U.S.—enjoyed snacks and ate a jar of honey
Kyiv • UNN
A black bear wandered into a California library and ate the staff’s supplies, including honey. The animal inspected the shelves and left on its own.
A guest worthy of the pages of a fairy-tale book visited a library in California — especially considering that this very day marked 100 years since the appearance of Winnie-the-Pooh. A black bear entered the building and, according to reports, helped itself to the staff’s food supplies and did not overlook a jar of honey, UNN reports, citing The Guardian.
Details
As library director Joseph Bopp told local outlet KMPH, at around 6:10 a.m. on Wednesday — more than four hours before the official opening at 10:00 a.m. — a black bear wandered into a branch of the Mono County Library System in the town of Mammoth Lakes.
According to the outlet, the animal got to snacks intended for employees: it ate peanut butter, canned peaches, cookies, and a jar of honey. After that, the bear walked around the library, inspected the shelves of new arrivals and the reference desk, and then went outside on its own.
On Wednesday, the Mono County Office of Education released a statement accompanied by surveillance-camera footage showing the bear walking through the library and sniffing books, a chair, and the floor.
"This morning, before the doors of the Mammoth Lakes library opened to visitors, we received a special guest," the statement said. "One might assume that this new ‘bear’ reader was looking for a copy of ‘Winnie-the-Pooh’ — the book that was published exactly 100 years ago!"
Bopp also decided to remind the unexpected guest of the rules: "Although we are always happy to welcome enthusiastic readers and understand how important this centennial anniversary is, we must remind visitors — especially our bears — that food is not part of the library collection."
It should be added
The book "Winnie-the-Pooh," written by A. A. Milne and illustrated by E. H. Shepard, tells of the adventures of the eponymous anthropomorphic bear — a great lover of honey who said of himself that he had "very little brain." Together with his friends — Piglet, Tigger, Eeyore, Rabbit, Owl, Kanga, and Roo — he lives in the Hundred Acre Wood.
The story is based on Milne’s son Christopher Robin’s teddy bear, as well as a real black bear named Winnipeg that lived at the London Zoo. This book and its three sequels remain beloved childhood works for many generations. Many people were also first introduced to Winnie-the-Pooh and his friends when The Walt Disney Company adapted Milne’s works for film and television.
To mark the 100th anniversary of the original Winnie-the-Pooh book, the Mono County public libraries invited local residents to visit any of the seven branches to borrow Milne’s classic work or other books about bears. The library network has more than 180,000 printed works and also offers additional online resources.
Although this encounter resembled a scene from a fairy tale, officials reminded residents that black bears are wild animals that must never be approached or fed.
They also urged people to use bear-resistant trash containers and to keep car doors and windows closed.

Ukraine's EU integration chief slams proposal to pick chief prosecutor in open contest
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
17:50:11 UTC
02:50:11 KST

Ukraine's EU integration chief slams proposal to pick chief prosecutor in open contest
Vsevolod Chentsov, Ukraine's deputy prime minister for European integration, spoke out in an Oct. 19 interview against the idea of an open contest for prosecutor general.
The EU has demanded a reform of Ukraine's notoriously corrupt and politicized prosecution service and called for making the procedure for picking the prosecutor general less political and more merit-based. Meanwhile, anti-corruption activists and pro-reform lawmakers have accused the Ukrainian authorities of sabotaging rule of law reforms and resisting the demand for depoliticizing the Prosecutor General's Office.
"I see experts arguing that there should be an open competition for the position of prosecutor general," Chentsov told the Ukrainian media outlet Yevropeiska Pravda. "But that is not something the EU requires, nor is it standard practice in Europe."
He argued that recommendations by Council of Europe experts "clearly emphasize the need to comply with Ukraine’s Constitution, which sets out the roles of the president and parliament in the appointment process."
"How to ensure transparency and select candidates based on their professional qualifications remains open for discussion," Chentsov said. "But personally, I see neither the need nor the possibility of holding an open competition for the position. A balance must be struck between political independence and professional competence."
According to a plan approved in December by Taras Kachka, Ukraine's former deputy prosecutor general for European integration, and EU Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos, Ukraine should "conduct a comprehensive review of the selection and dismissal procedure of the prosecutor general, with a view to aligning it with European best practice." The plan also envisages reinstating transparent contests for other top prosecutor jobs.
According to Ukraine's interim benchmarks for EU accession, Kyiv "needs to depoliticize the position of the prosecutor general, including by making the selection and dismissal procedures more objective, transparent and merit-based, taking into account European standards."
An EU official who spoke on condition of anonymity told the Kyiv Independent that the EU accession benchmarks "are not calling for it to be an elected position but the process should still change."
"For the EU, the gold standard is to have the involvement of independent, international vetters," the official said. "Separately, the EU and Ukraine launched a task force last week to implement Kachka-Kos and the EU's Rule of Law benchmarks. It serves to identify deficiencies in the current set-up, which would also include the prosecutor general's selection process."
In June, Anastasia Radina, head of parliament's anti-corruption committee from President Volodymyr Zelensky's party, submitted to parliament a bill seeking to select the prosecutor general in a transparent contest with the participation of international experts.
Radina's opponents argue that the Kachka-Kos plan does not envisage a contest involving international experts and that a contest for the prosecutor general's job contradicts Ukraine's Constitution.
Radina has denied the claim that it contradicts the Constitution.
"There may be different interpretations of the benchmark, but I'm not aware of anyone having proposed an alternative approach so far," she told the Kyiv Independent.
Ukraine's prosecutor generals are appointed by the president with parliament's approval and have been seen as closely aligned to whoever is in power. Radina's bill seeks to depoliticize the prosecutor general's appointment.
The debate on selecting the prosecutor general intensified under the previous occupant of the job, Ruslan Kravchenko.
Kravchenko faced scrutiny due to his role in the crackdown on the National Anti-Corruption Bureau (NABU) in 2025.
He was fired by parliament on Sept. 15 amid a major corruption investigation.
Within the investigation, a top prosecutor described as a “confidant” of Kravchenko was charged. Publicly revealed evidence hints at Kravchenko being implicated.
He left Ukraine on Sept. 14, under the pretext of an official trip to a conference in Paris. But the organizers told the Kyiv Independent that they had not expected him to attend, strengthening the suspicions that the trip was a fig leaf for fleeing Ukraine to avoid potential charges.
As Kravchenko left Ukraine, he simultaneously approved charges against the head of the anti-corruption agency investigating him. The charges were later dropped as unfounded.
Kravchenko later moved to Austria, the media outlet Ukrainska Pravda reported on Sept. 23.

Unknown
Unknown Publisher

17:45:52 UTC
02:45:52 KST

On the front lines, the American Starshield satellite communications system ceases to function when moving at speeds of 130–161 km/h.
This was reported by Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky.
This complicates frontline logistics and limits the use of unmanned aerial vehicles, particularly jet-powered interceptor drones.
“There was also a separate report from the Commander-in-Chief of the Armed Forces of Ukraine regarding information from units on the situation with the use of Starlink/Starshield services. Unfortunately, we have observed that in various sections of the front, the equipment ceases to function at speeds of 130–161 kilometers per hour,” Zelensky wrote.
According to the president, the situation is to be discussed again today with partners at all levels.
“Speed matters when it comes to saving lives,” he emphasized.
Meanwhile, on October 15, sources in the Ministry of Defense told Militarnyi that Starshield connectivity had been restored in Ukraine while in motion.
Starshield is a military and reconnaissance satellite system developed by SpaceX, a company founded by Elon Musk. It was created to meet the needs of the U.S. military, intelligence agencies, and government agencies.
This system can be considered a specialized version of Starlink technology, adapted for U.S. national security missions.
Both systems use related SpaceX technologies, but they are different services.
Starshield may involve the use of dedicated satellites for special missions, rather than relying solely on the Starlink infrastructure.
For Ukraine, this technology is important primarily for ensuring military communications, data transmission, and the operation of drones.

A two-day training session on international humanitarian law was held in Kyiv by the Ukrainian Red Cross Society (URCS) for representatives of the Coordination Headquarters for the Treatment of Prisoners of War and Kyiv Institute of the National Guard of Ukraine.
“The training brought together staff, lecturers and cadets from both institutions. It was delivered by specialists from the Ukrainian Red Cross International Humanitarian Law (IHL) Unit,” URCS said on Facebook Monday.

Following the training, participants discussed opportunities for further cooperation, including developing training programmes tailored to the professional needs of different audiences, delivering specialised training sessions and organising joint seminars.
The Ukrainian Red Cross noted that it continues to work with government institutions to promote understanding of international humanitarian law and encourage its practical application.

ITV’s exposé of racism and misogyny in Reform? Just a few (more) bad apples | John Crace
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
17:42:46 UTC
02:42:46 KST

It was the dog that didn’t bark in the night. After Sunday night’s ITV exposé of widespread racism and misogyny within Reform, you might have expected one of its MPs to have taken to the airwaves on Monday morning to defend the party’s honour. To try to persuade viewers that the real problem lay with the journalists who couldn’t stop themselves from investigating Reform rather than the fact that the party’s bigotry was endemic.
Instead, we got nothing. Every Reform MP was otherwise engaged. Were too busy having breakfast. Nothing from Nigel Farage. Nothing even from Robert Jenrick. Maybe he realised he had crashed and burned a few days earlier by suggesting it was just one of those things. One of life’s little mysteries. The BBC was riddled with paedophiles and Reform was awash with racists, said Honest Bob. No big deal. Every organisation had its crosses to bear.
The only MP to post on X in the morning was Richard Tice, who was feeling decidedly grumpy, having only just got married to Isabel Oakeshott. Perhaps he had a hangover. Though his main gripe was that British Airways was yet another failing British institution because it had mislaid at least one of his bags.
Dicky’s social media post had more than a touch of the “don’t you know who I am” to it. You can only imagine the baggage handler may have known exactly who Dicky was and had taken great pleasure in diverting one of the fake Louis Vuitton suitcases from Dubai to Manila. Via Buenos Aires.
The one person out and about for Reform was the one person you would have thought the party would want to keep hidden. Step forward Matt Goodwin, the party’s failed candidate for the Gorton and Denton byelection whose own views could easily pass off as borderline racist in polite circles. Matt is going through his own personal anti-growth agenda. Working hard to deconstruct himself from low-level academic to incredibly dim primate with low social skills. Almost every day, voters in Gorton and Denton thank their lucky stars for having dodged that bullet.
Matt’s defence of Reform was … unorthodox, to put it kindly. So much so that you began to wonder whether he was even conscious. Luckily for him, he was only allowed out on Times Radio. Though that was more than enough. To try to understand Matt is to make a category error. The whole point is to not understand him. That’s the way you stay sane. Because what he wanted listeners to believe was that Nige was a buffer zone against racism. That hordes of would-be racists begged to be allowed to join Reform, only to find out that Nige was a man of peace and love. The one politician who wanted nothing but good things for all immigrants.
It got better. Because Batshit Matt also wanted us to believe that the ITV documentary had just uncovered a few bad apples in the party. So in a way it had done Reform a favour. What were the chances? The ITV journalists had managed to uncover the only seven racists in the Reform ranks. Everyone else was Team Nigel. Never had a bad word for anyone. Except, there was another way of looking at this. That ITV had filmed about 10 Reform councillors and found that seven of them had views that included beheading King Charles for being a Muslim. Some statisticians might put that down as a 70% hit rate. Not so much a few wrong ’uns but a whole army of them. Poor Nige. Always the victim.
Over in the Commons, Wes Streeting was preparing for other threats during departmental defence questions. Though John Healey was not one of them. You’d have thought that Wes might have wanted to schmooze the chancellor before next week’s budget. To try to get the best funding settlement he could. Not a bit of it. Wes began by slagging off his predecessor as defence secretary for wasting money on unnecessary training exercises and then announced he was confident that Healey would reach the necessary 3% and 3.5% targets at next year’s spending review. So, no, Wes wouldn’t be resigning any time soon. Let’s hope his confidence is well placed.
Instead, Wes seemed more interested in persuading himself that there was absolutely nothing unusual in Donald Trump switching the Starlink satellite system on and off at random moments, thereby allowing Russian drones to do untold damage on Ukraine. This was just standard procedure. The only way you could tell the system was working properly was if you turned it off from time to time. Obvious when you think about. Wes was also totally chilled about Trump trying to lower US pump prices by allowing Russian imports of diesel. Fuel that the Russians had also imported from Iran and with whom, coincidentally, the US was at war.
All of this apparently made perfect sense not just to Streeting, but also to Labour and opposition backbenchers. Wes could reassure us because he had had a personal meeting with Pete Hegseth the previous week, during with the secretary for war had reiterated Trump’s claims that Nato forces had been a waste of space in Afghanistan and that the US troops had fought alone. A nice ice breaker. After that, Pete went out of his way to say Washington was totally behind Ukraine, just so long as Russia won the war.
Curiously, the shadow defence secretary, James Cartlidge, didn’t use his questions to talk up the four drones of the “Britannia shield” that the Tories were sure would protect the UK from nuclear war. So it remains a mystery. Almost as if it was a bullshit party conference announcement that was designed to be forgotten within days. Highlight of the day went to Sharron Davies, the former swimmer turned Tory peer, who demanded to know why Andy Burnham hadn’t invaded France to stop the rioting. Can you explain it to her?
