Egypt: Will Sisi really step down in 2030?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
16:49:42 UTC
01:49:42 KST

Breadcrumb
Egypt: Will Sisi really step down in 2030?
Egypt's President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi on Saturday announced plans to step down from power at the end of his third term in 2030.
Observers have long speculated about whether the president could attempt a re-run of the 2019 constitutional amendments and change the rules to allow a fourth term as the head of state.
But in a speech at the Egyptian Military Academy, Sisi vowed not to run for a fourth time and announced plans about how his potential successors would be chosen.
Here's what we know - and what we don't.
Sisi says he will step down in 2030
Speaking at a military graduation ceremony in the New Administrative Capital, Sisi said that his current term will be his last in office and pledged not to stand in the next election in 2030.
"The period leading up to 2030 will be the end of my term as president of the state, if I am still alive. This is completely settled, and there will be no discussion about it," he said.
Sisi is currently serving a six-year term after winning the December 2023 presidential election with 90% of the vote.
He also ruled out further constitutional changes to keep him in office into the next decade. Constitutional amendments in 2019 lengthened presidential terms from four to six years and enabled him to serve a third term.
There has long been speculation among political commentators and opposition figures about whether the constitution would again be amended to allow him to run for a fourth term.
"The Egyptian constitution will not be touched," he vowed.
But will he?
Sisi has a track record of reversing course on comments related to his political future. After his coup against Egypt's first democratically elected president, Mohammed Morsi, in July 2013, Sisi downplayed any ambitions to run for president, only to later enter the 2014 election race.
Three years later, he vowed to honour the constitution and not seek a third term in office. But in 2019, the constitutional amendments were passed in a landslide public vote, clearing the way for Sisi to contest the 2023 vote and remain in power for the next decade.
"I wouldn't get too secure about any assumptions about who will occupy Egypt's presidential palaces in 2031," Timothy E. Kaldas, deputy director of the Tahrir Institute for Middle East Policy, told The New Arab.
Whether or not his statements over the weekend were sincere, crises over the next four years could be used as a pretext to keep him in office, he said. Regime officials and media personalities may try to build a case that he should remain in power due to "popular demand".
"A lot could happen in the coming four years before 2030 … Whatever the real plan is today, there's no guarantee that plan will survive the coming four years of uncertainty and volatility," Kaldas added.
Military training for potential successors
Sisi announced that all potential presidential candidates will be required to undergo more than two years of training at the Egyptian Military Academy, which will teach them how to "protect the state".
Under draft legislation, the military will take charge of training potentially hundreds of people to stand in future presidential elections. Graduates of the programme could also be appointed to lead ministries and government agencies and serve as governors.
The Speaker of Parliament will lead a committee of ministers, politicians and intellectuals to draft the legislation, which will determine how candidates are selected.
"They would spend 30 months here at the academy learning what a state means, what its capabilities are, and how to protect them," Sisi said.
"We must not hand it over to just anyone. Someone who can put a few well-organised sentences together is not automatically qualified to lead the Egyptian state," he said.
The move is the latest to expand the military's power over the state during Sisi's 12-year presidency. Since coming to power, the army has significantly grown its economic footprint and acquired new influence over the government.
This includes the 2019 constitutional amendments, which broadened its role beyond protecting national security and tasked it with "protecting the constitution and democracy".
That the army will play a central role in determining future presidential candidates "reflects its continued centrality to the regime," Kaldas said.
"This is part of the growing influence of the security apparatus over civilian sectors throughout Egypt and the increased subjugation of civilian ministries and agencies to control by various security sector pillars of President Sisi's regime," he added.

Yevgeny Prigozhin’s Son Preserves Wagner’s $400M Criminal Empire in Central African Republic

- Category

Yevgeny Prigozhin’s Son Preserves Wagner’s $400M Criminal Empire in Central African Republic
Pavel Prigozhin, the son of late Wagner founder Yevgeny Prigozhin, has preserved control over parts of the mercenary group’s business empire in the Central African Republic, with annual legal and illicit turnover now estimated at more than $400 million, The Wall Street Journal reported on October 17.
According to diplomats, local officials, former Wagner members, and investigators cited by the Journal, Central African Republic President Faustin-Archange Touadéra asked Moscow not to replace Wagner fighters in the country with regular Russian forces after Yevgeny Prigozhin’s death.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Under Yevgeny Prigozhin, Wagner became one of Russia’s most notorious paramilitary forces, fighting alongside Russian troops in Ukraine and facing repeated accusations of executions, torture, and other war crimes, including during the battles for Soledar and Bakhmut. Many Wagner fighters were later redeployed to African countries including Mali and the Central African Republic, where the group has been linked to civilian killings and other abuses while building business networks tied to mining and resource extraction.
Around 500 Wagner personnel remain in the Central African Republic, where they continue providing security for Touadéra while operating alongside local police, military, and intelligence structures, The Wall Street Journal reported.
The group’s commercial operations have also expanded under Pavel Prigozhin. Investigators with the Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime estimated that Wagner’s combined legal and illicit business turnover now exceeds $400 million annually.
The Journal reported that Prigozhin inherited an empire spanning armed personnel, gold smuggling, opioid trafficking, and alcohol production after his father’s death.
Wagner had already been involved in gold mining under Yevgeny Prigozhin. Under his son, the group has taken control of additional mines and expanded production at the country’s largest gold mine to roughly $250 million a year, according to the Global Initiative.
In April, Pavel Prigozhin reportedly met Wagner leadership and Central African officials, including Mining Minister Rufin Benam Beltoungou, at Bangui’s Ledger Plaza hotel to discuss routes for exporting gold while avoiding international scrutiny.
According to local officials and analysts cited by The Wall Street Journal, shipments of gold have been sent to Belarus over the past three months.
The Journal also reported that Wagner continues trading weapons to rebel groups in Sudan and Libya while controlling production and sales of Wa Wa Wa vodka and Africa Ti L’Or beer in the Central African Republic.
Wagner has also maintained its influence operations in the country. The group finances local radio stations that support Touadéra and promote anti-Western and pro-Russian messaging, according to the report.
Pavel Prigozhin has additionally expanded into the local tramadol trade and now controls a significant share of the opioid market, The Wall Street Journal reported. Residents of Bangui provided images and videos showing Wagner fighters, accompanied by local police, detaining people accused of selling the drug outside the group’s network.
“Wagner has transformed from a powerful special-forces PMC into an unrecognized network that appears to be sliding into an organized crime group,” Lou Osborne, an investigator with Swiss nonprofit Inpact, told the Journal.
“I believe Pavel was allowed to continue his activities, meaning he either reached an agreement with the Kremlin or was made harmless,” Osborne added.
Russia’s military presence in Africa is also drawing scrutiny beyond the Central African Republic. In Mali, Russian Africa Corps personnel and local forces were accused of carrying out 47 drone strikes between April and August that killed 94 civilians, according to conflict monitoring data cited by Human Rights Watch.

Ukraine Targets Russia’s Air Defense Eyes—Radar Station in Bryansk Hit Alongside Ammo Depots
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
16:48:27 UTC
01:48:27 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Ukraine Targets Russia’s Air Defense Eyes—Radar Station in Bryansk Hit Alongside Ammo Depots
Ukrainian Defense Forces struck a Russian radar station in the Bryansk region, along with ammunition depots, artillery positions, drone operators, and troop concentrations in temporarily occupied Ukrainian territories during operations conducted on October 18 and overnight into October 19.
According to Ukraine’s military, the strikes targeted several important Russian military facilities, including a radar station near Trubchevsk in Russia’s Bryansk region.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The Ukrainian military emphasized that systematically targeting Russian radar installations creates gaps in the enemy’s radar coverage and weakens its air defense capabilities.
Such operations allow Ukrainian forces to deploy unmanned systems more effectively, from tactical missions along the frontline to strikes against military facilities deep inside Russian territory.
In Ukraine’s Kharkiv region, Ukrainian forces also struck a Russian artillery firing position and a position occupied by Russian drone crews near the settlement of Lyman Pershyi.
Additional strikes targeted Russian ammunition depots near Hrintal and Ternove in the Donetsk region, as well as a military logistics warehouse near Pelahiivka.
Ukrainian forces also reported hitting concentrations of Russian military personnel near Svobodne and Volodymyrivka in the Donetsk region, along with another troop concentration near Naberezhne in the Zaporizhzhia region.
The Ukrainian military did not provide details on the extent of the damage or the number of Russian personnel casualties resulting from the strikes.
The strikes come as Ukraine continues to develop and deploy unmanned systems for both offensive operations and air defense, including interceptors designed to counter increasingly sophisticated Russian drones.
On October 15, Oboronka reported, citing Andrii Hrytseniuk, head of the Brave1 defense technology cluster, that Ukrainian forces were already using seven types of interceptor drones to counter Russia’s jet-powered Shahed-type UAVs.
According to Hrytseniuk, Ukraine began preparing specifically to counter jet-powered Russian drones in the summer of 2025, after Ukrainian interceptor UAVs had demonstrated growing effectiveness against conventional propeller-driven Shaheds.

Putin’s Daughter Predicts Longevity Breakthrough as Russia Opens New Anti-Aging Lab
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
16:47:52 UTC
01:47:52 KST

- Category
- World
Putin’s Daughter Predicts Longevity Breakthrough as Russia Opens New Anti-Aging Lab
Russia has opened a new longevity research laboratory at its Skolkovo innovation center, as Maria Vorontsova, the daughter of Russian leader Vladimir Putin, predicts major scientific breakthroughs in extending human life within the next 10 to 20 years.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to The Insider on October 19, the laboratory’s opening comes amid growing interest in longevity research in Russia, with Vorontsova publicly expressing optimism about future advances in the field.
Vorontsova, who heads the Medical Research and Education Institute at Moscow State University, said current science has made limited progress in extending human life beyond what she described as its natural potential of 85 to 90 years.
She identified the fact that aging is not officially classified as a disease as a major obstacle to developing treatments, since clinical trials generally require a clearly defined medical diagnosis.
Vorontsova suggested that humanity’s universal fear of death could push healthcare authorities to address these regulatory barriers within the next 10 to 20 years.
The new Skolkovo laboratory will examine how longer lifespans could reshape healthcare, employment, markets, and government policy. Its researchers are expected to develop recommendations for improving older people’s quality of life.
The initiative comes amid broader Russian government efforts to develop anti-aging technologies.
In 2025, Vorontsova received a 30-million-ruble ($370,000 approximately) grant from the Russian Science Foundation to establish a laboratory studying cellular renewal and active longevity.
In May 2026, The Wall Street Journal reported that Russia was financing a $26 billion anti-aging initiative under its national healthcare technology program. The initiative reportedly includes organ bioprinting, xenotransplantation using miniature pigs, and gene therapy.
According to the report, figures close to Putin—including Vorontsova and Kurchatov Institute director Mikhail Kovalchuk—have been involved in overseeing the effort.
Kovalchuk, whose brother Yuri is a longtime Putin associate, has been described as a key intellectual architect of Russia’s longevity program, promoting the possibility of repairing and replacing human body parts to extend life.

European Commission examines EUR 70 bln financing gap for Ukraine in 2027, looks to partners’ support
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
19:47:38 EEST
01:47:38 KST

The European Commission is exploring ways to cover a EUR 70 billion financing gap for Ukraine in 2027, emphasizing the need for partners to contribute.
This was stated by Balázs Ujvari, a European Commission spokesperson for budget and economic affairs, during a briefing in Brussels on Monday. He was commenting on a directive from European Union leaders for the Commission to develop options for addressing the EUR 70 billion shortfall for Ukraine in 2027.
"We have always stressed that we cannot act alone. We cannot manage this by ourselves. Therefore, our partners, in general, need to step up. They must make commitments and follow through on them... As things stand, current pledges leave a financing gap of approximately EUR 70 billion. That is the situation today. This figure accounts for the EUR 45 billion the EU has earmarked for next year, as well as some of the commitments already made by our international partners. As the President of the European Council noted, member states want us to analyze this situation... However, it bears repeating: this must be a joint effort. Consequently, the EU and the European Commission will examine what can be done in this situation," he explained in detail.
According to the spokesperson, the European Commission will first complete the necessary preparatory work. "This means that we need to finalize what is known as a financing strategy. This document will define the amounts to be provided to Ukraine through various financial instruments, which form the basis for the EUR 90 billion loan, as well as the reforms that must be carried out as part of this process," Ujvari explained.
Commenting on the financing situation for the current year, Ujvari noted that Ukraine is set to receive an additional EUR 30 billion as part of the support loan. "For these funds to be disbursed, Ukraine must continue with the relevant reforms, including those in the defense sector. We need to conclude agreements that will serve as the foundation for the rules already established," the representative added.
Regarding Ukraine’s fulfillment of the obligations required for the next disbursement under the macro-financial assistance program, he recalled that one tranche, amounting to approximately EUR 3.9 billion, has already been provided. "The second tranche totals EUR 3.7 billion. We have observed that the Verkhovna Rada passed a number of important laws last week. We are currently analyzing them, after which we will formulate our assessment," Ujvari said.

Early voting begins in several US states ahead of Nov. 3 midterm elections
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
16:47:35 UTC
01:47:35 KST

Yasin Gungor
19 October 2026•Update: 19 October 2026
In-person early voting began Monday in several US states ahead of the Nov. 3 midterm elections, with control of Congress and numerous state offices at stake.
Early voting began in Texas, South Carolina, Arkansas, Alaska, Colorado and Connecticut, two weeks before Election Day.
Voters nationwide will elect all 435 members of the US House of Representatives and more than one-third of the 100-member Senate.
Governorships, state legislative seats and local ballot initiatives will also be decided.
 
Senate contests draw attention in southern states
In Texas, early voting runs through Oct. 30, with polling hours varying by county.
The state features a closely watched Senate contest between Republican state Attorney General Ken Paxton and Democratic state Rep. James Talarico.
South Carolina's early voting period continues through Oct. 31.
The state's Senate race features Republican incumbent Darline Graham, who was appointed following the death of her brother, Sen. Lindsey Graham, against Democratic challenger Annie Andrews.
Voters will also decide an open gubernatorial race.
Early voting is scheduled from 8.30 am to 6 pm, Monday through Saturday, with polling stations closed Sunday, Oct. 25.
Voters are required to present photo identification.
In Arkansas, early voting concludes Nov. 2 at 5 pm local time. Republican Sen. Tom Cotton faces Democratic challenger Hallie Shoffner, while Republican Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders is seeking reelection against Democrat Fredrick Love and Libertarian Colt Shelby.
State election officials require voters to present valid photo identification or qualifying official documents, including utility bills or government paychecks, before receiving a ballot.
 
Alaska Senate race, voting expands in other states
In Alaska, in-person early and absentee voting began at designated locations Monday and will continue through Election Day on Nov. 3.
The state uses a ranked-choice voting system.
The Senate contest features Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan against former Democratic Rep. Mary Peltola.
Voters will also choose a successor to term-limited Gov. Mike Dunleavy.
In Colorado, voter centers opened statewide following the earlier opening of ballot drop boxes.
Connecticut began a 14-day early voting period running through Nov. 1, with polling stations operating from 10 am to 6 pm local time.

M1A2T tanks to join southern Lien Yung drills
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
16:46:35 UTC
01:46:35 KST

US-made M1A2T Abrams tanks are to participate in a major military exercise for the second time, when the Lien Yung exercise (聯勇操演) begin next month, a military source said yesterday.
The army’s 584th Armored Brigade, which operates the US-built tanks, has already transported them to the Joint Operations Training Base in Pingtung County for the drills from late next month to December, the source said.
During the month-long joint military exercise in southern Taiwan, the tanks’ crew would test their combat coordination, said the source, who asked not to be named.
Photo: Fang Bin-chao, Taipei Times
The M1A2T Abrams tanks were included in a major Taiwanese military exercise for the first time when the nation held its annual Han Kuang exercises in August.
The nationwide Han Kuang exercises, which include live-fire drills, are Taiwan’s major military exercise, while the Lien Yung drills are the second-largest.
Held in southern Taiwan, the Lien Yung exercises serve as a major test of coordination among the three branches of the nation’s armed forces — the army, the navy and the air force — in jointly repelling an invading enemy.
Conscripts serving their mandatory one-year military service are also to participate in this year’s Lien Yung drills, the source said.
The M1A2T Abrams tanks are currently operated only by volunteer soldiers, not conscripts, said Su Tzu-yun (蘇紫雲), director of the Institute for National Defense and Security Research’s defense strategy and resources division.
However, it is important for conscripts to participate in large-scale live-fire exercises such as the Lien Yung exercise to receive more advanced training, Su added.
Under a deal approved by Washington in 2019, Taiwan has procured 108 M1A2T Abrams tanks from the US at a cost of about US$1.45 billion.
Of the 108 Abrams tanks, 38 were sent to the army’s 584th Armored Brigade in late October last year and 42 in April. The other 28 are still being tested and prepared for service.

Typhoon Champi is forecast to turn northward earlier than previously expected, sparing Taiwan a direct hit but still bringing heavy rain to the north of the country on Friday and Saturday, the Central Weather Administration (CWA) said yesterday.

However, due to the weakening of a Pacific high-pressure system the storm is now expected to turn northward earlier than initially forecast, likely around Japan’s Ishigaki Island, Cheng said.
Photo: The Central Weather Administration
As Champi brushes past northeastern Taiwan, it is expected to be a strong "moderate" typhoon or weak "intense" typhoon per the CWA’s classification system, which defines the latter as having sustained winds of more than 184kph, he said.
The CWA could issue a sea warning tomorrow night or Thursday at the earliest, and a land warning on Thursday evening or Friday, he said.
The warning would likely apply to northern and eastern Taiwan, with the north and Yilan County, in particular, facing possible heavy or extremely heavy rain on Friday and Saturday, he added.
As the typhoon approaches on Thursday, there would continue to be scattered rain showers in Yilan and northern Taiwan, Cheng said, adding that those areas could report heavy or extremely heavy rain on Friday and Saturday, while scattered showers are forecast for other regions.
As Typhoon Champi weakens and moves away from Taiwan on Sunday, cloudy to clear weather conditions would prevail in most regions, with the exception of lingering showers in the east and on the Hengchun Peninsula (恆春半島) in the south, Cheng said.

Eagles lose again as the bleeding continues
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
16:46:34 UTC
01:46:34 KST

The once-mighty Philadelphia Eagles — two seasons removed from a Super Bowl championship — have suddenly turned into an NFL punching bag.
Bryce Young threw for 281 yards and two touchdowns to Tommy Tremble, and Chuba Hubbard ran for 120 yards and a score to lead the Panthers past the injury-riddled Eagles 25-14 on Sunday.
Tremble did everything but run the Rocky steps.
Photo: Bill Streicher-Imagn Images
“Great fight in the guys,” Panthers coach Dave Canales said.
The Panthers (3-2) had little trouble in the second half picking apart the Eagles (2-4), who have lost four straight games for the first time since 2020 and were missing quarterback Jalen Hurts and running back Saquon Barkley.
Hurts is on injured reserve and would miss at least four games with a blood clot in his calf. Barkley missed his second straight game with a hamstring injury and Will Shipley and Tank Bigsby, his two backups, were sidelined by injuries.
The quarterback showdown between Young and Eagles backup Tanner McKee seemed like a mismatch entering the day. McKee, in his fourth season, made his third career start and first one without the Eagles having already clinched a playoff berth.
McKee was sacked for an 11-yard loss on the Eagles’ first play from scrimmage and he nearly had a pass intercepted on second down. McKee’s day never got much better, and he finished 26 of 45 for 215 yards and a touchdown. He hit DeVonta Smith — who missed the last two games with a hamstring injury — for a 19-yard TD that pulled the Eagles within 19-14 early in the fourth quarter.
The Eagles forced a three-and-out and then wasted their drive when McKee lost 12 yards on a fumble. It was one of several examples of miscommunication affecting the offense.
“Whether it was guys in the wrong spot, I’ve got to get them fixed or a missed call, I’ve got to get it fixed,” McKee said.
Young was happy to take advantage of the Eagles’ miscues. He sealed the win with his second TD pass to Tremble, a 19-yarder for a 25-14 lead.
Young even heard “MVP!” chants from a small group of Panthers fans there were about the only ones left inside the stadium at the end.
“All the Panthers fans being able to be out here all the way in Philly and feeling the support,” Young said. “We all show that. We all feed off of that. Whether it’s here or there, the support for all of us is huge.”
Young — who threw a 12-yard TD pass to Tremble in the second quarter — bailed out the Panthers late in the third on third-and-8 at their own 10 when he connected with Jalen Coker for a 32-yard gain. Young extended the drive with a 15-yard completion, and the Panthers converted a fourth-and-1 when Hubbard found a hole for a 19-yard run.
Hubbard finished the drive in the fourth with a 2-yard touchdown run for a 19-7 lead. Carolina’s 2-point attempt failed.
A week after the Eagles lost by a field goal on the final play against Jacksonville in London, Ryan Fitzgerald made kicks of 47 and 52 yards for the Panthers. The latter made it 13-7 and was his 11th straight successful attempt to open the season. He did miss an extra point.
The Eagles are in a world of hurt without Hurts and were forced to turn to McKee, who had lost his grip on the No. 2 spot in training camp. He regained the backup job after the Eagles cut Andy Dalton, but he looked out of place all game. Offensive coordinator Sean Mannion did him no favors by calling a series of failed screen and swing passes.
McKee threw a third-and-14 sideline pass for Smith in the third quarter that sailed out of bounds against one of the worst defenses in the NFL and was greeted by jeers.
The struggling offense is not all on McKee. The Eagles were shut out in the third quarter and have scored only six points in that quarter all season. Philadelphia had only 37 total yards in the first quarter and punted on its first five drives.
Dameon Pierce scored on a 2-yard run to cut Carolina’s lead to 10-7 at halftime.
The Panthers were penalized 13 times for 149 yards.
“A lot of times these are effort penalties, and guys are trying too hard in different situations,” Canales said.

Tulum’s ugly downfall is  a warning for Mexico
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
16:46:32 UTC
01:46:32 KST

There was a moment, in 2015 or 2016, when Tulum was the coolest town on Earth.
Every fashion magazine seemed to billboard the beach retreat on Mexico’s turquoise-water Caribbean coast as a mecca for global trendsetters. “Tulum style” came to describe a distinctive aesthetic — flowing fabrics, linen and crochet, neutral colors, bare feet, traditional craftsmanship — that blended rustic-chic, environmentalist and free-spirit ideals into the boho-luxe look of the moment.
This effervescence bubbled to a peak in July 2018, when Vogue put modeling queen Gisele Bundchen on its cover, photographed in Tulum’s tropical forest in a printed floral Ralph Lauren dress and presented as a “climate warrior.” The accompanying line was deliciously obnoxious: “Gisele: Earth Mother, Eco-Activist, Fashion Superstar.” Thus came Tulum’s “it” breakthrough.
Illustration: Yusha
Fast forward a decade, and that utopian version of the antique Mayan town, which promised ornamental indulgence, paradise views and a dose of spiritual cleansing, is long gone. These days, Tulum is grappling with overexpansion, insecurity, inadequate infrastructure, real-estate speculation and a stinking sargassum invasion. Tourists are fleeing to less pretentious destinations: Visitor numbers plunged to about 115,000 in July, almost one-third below the level of two years earlier, while hotel occupancy has averaged just 64 percent so far this year, nine percentage points below last year.
While every major tourist hotspot in Mexico, from Cancun to Puerto Vallarta, is going through difficult times due to higher airfares, the strong peso and the sargassum crisis, Tulum’s problems seem more fundamental. This is, after all, a boutique destination that could not cope with its own explosion in popularity. It still lacks basic services, including proper water and sewage systems, and struggles with degraded streets, irregular settlements and drug-trafficking activity.
It is a sad but foreseeable outcome for a place that should have resisted the model of growth at any cost. As someone who first visited Tulum in 2001, when it was little more than an off-the-grid, bucolic destination of laid-back beach camps and about 7,000 residents, I have watched its overexploitation become a bracing showpiece of what badly planned development can bring. Tulum now has more than 75,000 residents — an astonishing 61 percent increase since 2020 — while its urban footprint has expanded several times since my backpacking trip, making it one of the country’s fastest-growing urban areas. A 2023 Mexican government study estimated that by 2050, Tulum’s population together with that of the neighboring municipality of Felipe Carrillo Puerto could exceed 716,000 people.
I am no degrowth zealot, and I get that more visitors are ultimately a sign of approval. Still, nothing good can come from such anarchic expansion. Some might argue that Tulum’s travails are almost inevitable given surging demand and Mexico’s historic difficulties with urban planning. After all, less glamorous towns across the country suffer from similar shortages of basic services. At least Tulum creates jobs and economic activity.
Yet even if we grant that point, there is something deeply wrong with a town that accommodates ever more real-estate and commercial projects with scant regard for legal regulations and environmental damage. With Cancun, the region’s mass-tourism hub, just 129km north, Tulum could have followed a more constrained and sustainable expansion model.
Problems had been building for years, from land disputes and feverish property speculation to abusive prices designed to exploit naive tourists and the slow takeover of public beaches by local developers. Nightclubs and electronic music festivals followed. By 2019, a string of pharmacies had popped up along the main coastal road catering to Americans looking for over-the-counter legal medications without prescriptions. It felt like the beginning of the end; the boho-chic wonderland with eco-conscious manifestos was already turning into something much less ethereal.
Former Mexican president Andres Manuel Lopez Obrador’s controversial decision to build a dedicated international airport in the middle of the jungle — even as his administration was also developing the Maya Train line connecting Tulum with Cancun’s massive airport — boosted the strategy of chasing ever more tourists. Yet the airport, with an initial capacity of 5.5 million annual passengers, has not quite taken off — literally. Opened for commercial operations in late 2023, it is struggling to attract passengers, with traffic falling almost 34 percent this year so far, and two local airlines, Aeromexico and Volaris, recently announcing the temporary suspension of their operations. The retreat’s troubles have become so apparent that the government has launched a “Tulum Reborn” strategy to lure visitors back.
Tellingly, what was once a fashionista nirvana surrounded by beautiful cenotes and archeological sites has become the laughingstock of social media, with endless reels and videos proclaiming the death of Tulum, a deeply hypocritical place in which everything is marketed as eco-friendly, ethical and sustainable, when so little of it actually is.
That might be unfair, but the backlash reflects something real: Tulum’s betrayal of its promise of a simpler life in an unassuming and quiet paradise. Its big challenge now will be to rethink its strategy and regain what made it special in the first place.

Business groups back Taipower, CPC subsidies; scholars dissent
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
16:46:32 UTC
01:46:32 KST

Business groups yesterday backed government subsidies for state-run utility Taiwan Power Co (Taipower, 台電) and state-run oil company CPC Corp, Taiwan (CPC, 台灣中油), while some academics said that taxpayers should not bear the cost of subsidies.
Speaking at a public hearing of the Legislative Yuan’s Economics Committee, Deputy Minister of Economic Affairs Lai Chien-hsin (賴建信) said that government support is needed because both companies are required by the government to absorb surging international oil, natural gas and coal costs instead of passing them on to consumers.
Many governments have increased financial support to cushion the impact of surging international energy prices and prevent sharp increases in consumer prices, Lai said.
Photo: Wang Yi-sung, Taipei Times
Since 2020, CPC has absorbed NT$674 billion (US$20.76 billion) in oil and gas costs that it could not pass on to consumers, with accumulated losses reaching NT$91 billion as of the end of last month, more than half of its paid-in capital, company data showed.
Taipower has recorded even higher losses from absorbing higher natural gas and coal costs to avoid increasing electricity costs.
As of the end of August, its natural gas expenses had risen by more than NT$70 billion from before the US-Israel war against Iran began in February, resulting in losses of NT$20.3 billion this year and accumulated losses of NT$371.2 billion since 2020, Lai said.
Under the Administrative Act of State-Owned Enterprises (國營事業管理法), the government can compensate state-owned enterprises for policy-related losses, he said.
Lai was seeking legislative support for the NT$71.1 billion supplementary budget to subsidize Taipower approved by the Executive Yuan.
The losses were caused by war-driven increases in global energy and raw material prices rather than mismanagement and should be subsidized to avoid higher electricity rates, said Liu Shou-jen (劉守仁), secretary-general of the General Chamber of Commerce of the Republic of China.
Leu Jang-hwa (呂正華), secretary-general of the Chinese National Federation of Industries, also supported government subsidies and capital injections, but said that only losses caused by international energy price fluctuations should qualify for compensation under a transparent and accountable review mechanism.
Opposition lawmakers have rebuffed attempts by the government to subsidize the losses of the two state-run companies, and some academics agreed with that stance.
Taipower’s losses were primarily the result of Taiwan’s flawed nuclear-free energy policy, which had increased power generation costs, said Huang Yao-hui (黃耀輝), a professor at National Taipei University of Business.
Yeh Tsung-kuang (葉宗洸), dean of the College of Nuclear Science at National Tsing Hua University, also opposed the subsidies, saying that Taipower and CPC should instead improve their finances through capital injections.
The public should not bear the cost of past energy policy mistakes, Yeh said.
The different viewpoints center around the overall energy policy of the Democratic Progressive Party (DPP), which has been in power since 2016.
The DPP’s plan to phase out nuclear power also increased reliance on natural gas from 30.6 percent of the electricity mix in 2015 to 50 percent last year, and lower coal use, from 45.4 percent of the mix in 2015 to 30 percent last year.
That plan and the slower-than-expected rollout of renewable energy have resulted in surging imports of natural gas, from 17.05 million tonnes of oil equivalent (TOE) in 2015 to 26.86 million TOE last year, Energy Administration figures showed.
As imports have risen, so have prices, driven by renewed global demand after COVID-19 in 2021, Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in 2022 and the war against Iran this year.
Imported natural gas prices soared to US$575 per tonne in 2021 and US$989 in 2022 after Russia invaded Ukraine, and averaged US$716 in the first eight months of this year, Energy Administration figures showed.
Those who oppose the subsidies for Taipower argue in part that continuing the use of nuclear power would have left Taiwan less vulnerable to volatility in global fossil fuel prices.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy accused US President Donald Trump of trying to pressure Kyiv into surrendering to Russia, escalating a week-long row with Trump.
In an interview with Bloomberg in Kyiv, Zelenskiy also offered a new proposal to accede to Trump’s request to stop targeting Russian refineries, which was aimed at combating high diesel prices, in exchange for deliveries of more Patriot air-defense missiles.
“Now, we have dangerous days ahead of the elections,” Zelenskiy said on Sunday, referring to the Nov. 3 midterms in the US. “My latest model was: We don’t target Russian diesel, you give us missiles for Patriot systems to protect our facilities. But they just want us to stop attacking diesel. And if we strike that, they will disconnect us from something.”
Photo: AP
While offering an off-ramp from the escalating row, Kyiv is likely to be unsettled by a Wall Street Journal (WSJ) report that Russian President Vladimir Putin proposed a meeting with Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping (習近平) next month to discuss ending the war in Ukraine.
As relations between the US and Ukraine reached a new low, Zelenskiy laid out what he said were a series of unfriendly moves by Washington toward Kyiv.
Those include the deliberate slowing of Starlink Internet speeds, which are crucial for Ukrainian troops fighting Russia, and delaying already scarce deliveries of Patriot interceptors for ballistic missiles, which have become a nightmare for Ukrainian cities, he said.
“I believe steps have been taken to convince Ukraine to capitulate,” Zelenskiy said. “I am not saying that this is the goal our partners are pursuing. I don’t want to think that our American partners believe the war” against Russia “could be ended sooner at Ukraine’s expense. But that’s how it looks.”
Kyiv came under a Russian ballistic missile attack late on Sunday that killed at least one person, local authorities said.
Preliminary information indicated that a missile hit a medical center, they said.
Once again, the US did not share any early warning with Ukraine about the launch, said a person familiar with the matter who asked not to be identified discussing security issues. Without that warning, it was harder for Ukraine to repel the attack, as well as to alert civilians with enough time for them to proceed to shelters.
Tensions between Ukraine and the US reached a nadir after Trump struck a deal with Putin under which Washington would refrain from further tightening sanctions on Russia in exchange for Moscow supplying limited volumes of diesel to the global market to curb rising prices.
Trump sparked blowback from members of his own party when he said late on Friday he would waive part of a new Russia sanctions law named after the late US senator Lindsey Graham.
Trump said later on Sunday that he went ahead with the diesel export deal and sanctions waiver, because he did not want to drive Putin away from peace talks, while asserting that Zelenskiy wanted to prolong the war.
“He doesn’t want to end this war, and probably never did,” Trump wrote of Zelenskiy. “He could have made a better deal two years ago than he can now. His country is in shambles, a large portion of his land is lost, his oceans and seas are gone, and his male population is low, wounded, and/or dead. I WANT THIS WAR END!”
Asked about the WSJ’s report of a trilateral meeting among Putin, Xi and Trump, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said: “I think there’s been talks of a meeting,” but nothing has been finalized.
The US president is open to anything he can do to bring an end to the conflict and wants diplomatic efforts involving Russia and Ukraine to advance, he said.
“No one is winning that war,” Rubio told reporters during a visit to Uzbekistan.
When asked at a regular press briefing in Beijing about the report, Chinese Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokeswoman Mao Ning (毛寧) said she had no information to share.
“I think that the president of the United States does have a good relationship with Putin,” Zelenskiy said, speaking before the WSJ story was published. “But one thing doesn’t work here. Currently, Trump can’t force Putin to end the war.”
Zelenskiy said that relations with Washington might improve after the US midterm elections.
“Politics is very aggressive during election time,” he said. “I think it is agony now, but after elections, life will continue and I believe it will be calmer.”

Pennsylvania town spurns US$10,000 data center checks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
16:46:30 UTC
01:46:30 KST

On his terrace overlooking the forest in eastern Pennsylvania, Ed Negra lays out four letters. All are from a developer promising a US$10,000 check to each household once its data center is running.
“I call it a bribe,” the US retiree said.
The scene is picture-perfect. Autumn leaves are turning russet, and there is a stunning mountain view in this corner of Pennsylvania, a key state in the US’ upcoming midterm elections.
Photo: AFP
“We thought it was a beautiful place to retire,” said the septuagenarian, who used to manage a large building-supply store in neighboring New Jersey.
He and his wife settled in a sprawling gated community with round-the-clock security.
Eagle Rock Resort in Hazle Township has hundreds of comfortable homes scattered through the woods, two golf courses, swimming pools, an equestrian center and even a few ski slopes for the winter.
“We didn’t know until we heard all the noise” of chainsaws in late 2024, Negra said.
More than 500 hectares of land below the resort were cleared to build the future server complex.
Residents quickly mobilized. They were furious that no one had warned them, and they worried about noise and pollution.
Their fight echoes many conflicts across the US over data centers, which have become an issue in the Nov. 3 vote.
Local opposition blocked or delayed at least 75 data center projects in the first three months of this year, according to Data Center Watch, which tracks resistance to the industry.
Polls show that the hostility crosses party lines. Nonetheless, US President Donald Trump fervently backs these projects in the name of US dominance in artificial intelligence, and he chastises those who oppose them.
In Hazle Township, residents won a court-ordered halt to construction, as well as a municipal moratorium.
A few pieces of heavy equipment sit idle on the vast cleared tract. The logs have already been hauled away.
However, developer NorthPoint Development has not given up.
Its letters now flood local mailboxes, saying: “There is a lot of misinformation and fear that has circulated about data centers and our project.”
The letters also lay out a US$165 million fund for the township and its residents.
The money would pay for a new police station, lower trash fees and more.
Part of it, US$45 million, is to be paid directly to the 4,500 households once the data center’s first building goes into service.
In the former mining town, one in six residents lives below the poverty line, official data showed.
“For a young, struggling couple ... living from paycheck to paycheck, US$10,000 is a lot of money,” said Jeff Fasnacht, a retired high-school teacher who lives in the gated community.
Like Negra, he sees the offer as a bribe. He also calls it “a drop in the bucket” compared with how much value his home could lose if the project goes ahead.
“This was supposed to be pristine forest forever,” the golf enthusiast said.
Neither the developer nor township officials responded to AFP’s requests for comment.
Across the valley, residents of rural Sugarloaf Township are fighting a high-voltage power line that is likely intended to supply the data center.
They are not eligible for the possible US$10,000 check.
“There’s no amount of money that can replace or take away the beauty, the tranquility that we live in,” said Annie Vinatieri, who shares a house with her in-laws, her husband and their young son.
She has been fighting the power line for almost two years.
“This fight feels akin to a David and Goliath fight,” she said.
She takes heart in how many residents have rallied against tech interests: “The empowerment is unbelievable.”
Erika Cook, 42, lives nearby and works remotely for an insurance company.
She and her husband raise a few chickens and keep a vegetable garden. They also tap maple trees for syrup in the woods on their property.
Part of that land is now the target of an eminent domain proceeding to make room for a huge transmission tower.
Republicans dominate at the ballot box in this region. Cook said opposition to data centers has one virtue here.
“It’s bringing people together ... across party lines,” she said.

Shipments of AI servers expected to grow: TrendForce
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
16:46:28 UTC
01:46:28 KST

With strong investment by cloud service providers (CSPs), coupled with purchases from tier-two data center operators such as Tesla Inc and CoreWeave Inc, global artificial intelligence (AI) server shipments are expected to grow 32.2 percent this year to about 2.82 million units, TrendForce Corp (集邦科技) said.
Shipments are expected to remain strong next year, thanks to spending from major CSPs, neocloud providers, sovereign AI projects and new AI models and applications launched by developers of large language models, the Taipei-based market researcher said in a report on Wednesday last week.
In August, TrendForce forecast shipments of about 2.9 million units for next year.
Photo: EPA
With high average selling prices and stable shipments, AI servers are expected to generate about US$479 billion in market value this year, accounting for almost 75 percent of the overall server market’s US$639.2 billion, it said.
Next year, AI servers’ market value is forecast to rise to US$920 billion and account for 81 percent of the overall server market, TrendForce said, adding that the overall server market value is predicted to exceed US$1 trillion for the first time next year.
Separately, TrendForce said the combined capital expenditure by the world’s nine largest CSPs is forecast to exceed US$957 billion this year, up 106 percent year-on-year.
Their combined spending next year is expected to surpass US$1.5 trillion, up 60 percent year-on-year, it said.
That was 10 percentage points higher than TrendForce’s previous forecast of a 50 percent growth for next year, it said, citing higher server system prices and rising component costs caused by supply shortages.
The revision accounts for advance payments required by some component suppliers to secure supply, TrendForce said.
The nine CSPs are Alphabet Inc’s Google, Amazon.com Inc, Meta Platforms Inc, Microsoft Corp, Oracle Corp, ByteDance Ltd (字節跳動), Tencent Holdings Ltd (騰訊), Alibaba Group Holding Ltd (阿里巴巴) and Baidu Inc (百度), it said.

‘Wulongyuan’ copyright remains despite trademark dispute, IP office says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
16:46:27 UTC
01:46:27 KST

Revoking the trademark of the comic series Wulongyuan (烏龍院) would not affect copyright, the Taiwan Intellectual Property Office said yesterday, adding that it could be appealed.
The series’ creator, Au Yao-hsing (敖幼祥), said he received a trademark revocation notification from the office on Saturday, even though he has paid trademark fees over the past decade.
Someone applied to the authority to revoke his trademark, claiming that he had not used it over the past three years, he said.
Photo: Screen grab from Au’s Facebook account
The office said the revocation of the trademark numbered 02003530, “Wulongyuan and its pictures,” was filed by a third party.
The office notified both sides in written form in accordance with the Trademark Act (商標法), it said, adding that it would review evidence from both parties.
According to the act, anyone can apply for revocation of a registered trademark that, for no justifiable reason, has never been used or has been left unused for three years or more, it said.
The office confirmed that the Wulongyuan trademark remained in use in terms of hotel services, which is listed among Class 43 goods and services, the office said, adding that the trademark registration would not be revoked in this regard.
However, the registration would be revoked in accordance with the law regarding other services in Class 43, such as nursing home services, as well as tea, coffee and other beverages in Class 30, it said.
Trademark revocation would not be extended to all the rights of the trademark holder, the office said, adding that both parties can appeal.
Revoking a trademark would not affect a creator’s copyright, it said.

Economic resilience stronger than AI jitters
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
16:46:26 UTC
01:46:26 KST

The New Taiwan dollar’s weakness, led by global jitters over artificial intelligence (AI), is masking the nation’s underlying economic resilience that favors the currency’s rally into year-end, analysts say.
While the currency has come under intense pressure, Oversea-Chinese Banking Corp and ING Bank NV see it rebounding to NT$31.60 and NT$31.50 against the US dollar, respectively, implying an appreciation about 3 percent from current levels.
Underscoring those projections is Taiwan’s robust economic growth and current account surplus. Although doubts over lofty AI stock valuations continue to drive outflows and weigh on the NT dollar’s exchange rate in the short term, analysts expect fundamental trade support to prevail over the coming months.
Photo: CNA
“Record trade surpluses and AI-related exports continue to generate underlying Taiwan dollar support,” MUFG Bank Ltd head of global markets research for Asia Lin Li (林莉) said. “But foreign portfolio outflows, outward investment and the large US dollar-Taiwan dollar yield differential is creating offsetting US dollar demand at the moment.”
Lin sees the NT dollar appreciating to NT$31.8 per greenback by the end of the year before gaining to NT$30.9 by the end of June next year.
Taiwan’s current account surplus reached a record high of almost US$70 billion late last year, buoyed by unprecedented global demand for advanced chips, before narrowing moderately in the past few months. At the same time, officials raised the nation’s full-year economic growth forecast to more than 11 percent, putting the technology hub on track for its first double-digit expansion since 2010.
Still, those underlying strengths are running against a wave of foreign capital flight. Foreign investors sold NT$302.6 billion (US$9.33 billion) of Taiwanese equities on Thursday last week, the largest daily outflow on record, pushing the NT dollar to within striking distance of its year-to-date low of about NT$32.50 per US dollar.
While analysts do not view that level as a rigid line in the sand for policymakers, they are watching it closely as a comfortable zone for the monetary authority.
ING Bank NV chief Greater China economist Lynn Song (宋林) said the central bank would attempt to keep the NT dollar relatively rangebound. “I don’t think it is a firm line in the sand to defend, but it does seem that NT$31.5 to NT$32.5 range has been comfortable for them so far this year.”
The central bank is more likely to focus on easing currency volatility than target a certain level, said Jiuk Choi, Asia-Pacific macro strategist at State Street Bank & Trust Co.
“That said, we think the NT$32.4 to NT$32.5 range is an important level for US dollar-Taiwan dollar, as it marks the year-to-date high in 2026,” he added.
Beyond concerns over the tech sector, elevated crude prices are adding pressure on the NT dollar, as the nation is an energy importer. US 10-year Treasury yields sit roughly 300 basis points above similar-tenor Taiwanese sovereign bonds, offering a compelling yield pickup that continues to fuel broad US dollar strength at the expense of regional currencies.
“Near-term headwinds include foreign equity outflows and a strong US dollar amid a hawkish Federal Reserve,” LGT Private Banking foreign exchange and rates specialist Trang Le said.
“Even so, strong export momentum, robust external balances and the AI-driven semiconductor cycle leave the medium-term bias tilted toward Taiwan dollar appreciation. We expect volatility rather than sustained weakness to be the dominant theme,” she said.
Currency traders are watching earnings reports from major semiconductor manufacturers, which strategists view as the next key catalyst for cross-border equity flows and currency volatility. Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co (台積電) delivered a better-than-expected revenue outlook last week, but it failed to fully calm market worries over the broader AI buildout.
“Upcoming global tech earnings could increase Taiwan dollar volatility, particularly given the market’s heightened sensitivity to AI-related capex, profitability and Chinese competition,” Choi said.
He sees near-term room for NT dollar weakness on AI trade doubts, but expects a recovery to NT$31.80 per US dollar by year-end.
“We see Taiwan dollar one of the best hedge currencies to US dollar strength as capital and current account flows remain strong while it has one of the lowest volatilities across emerging markets,” he said.

2026 Elections: Taichung mayoral candidates propose divergent policies
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
16:46:26 UTC
01:46:26 KST

Democratic Progressive Party’s Taichung mayoral candidate Ho Hsin-chun (何欣純) proposed bus service reforms yesterday, while her Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT) rival Johnny Chiang (江啟臣) outlined an artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted public safety network.
Ho’s proposals focused on increasing passenger capacity, upgrading the city’s official bus app, reorganizing routes and improving drivers’ working conditions.
Ho, who took a Route 301 bus as part of a campaign event, said the replacement of articulated buses with smaller electric buses had reduced passenger capacity without sufficient increases in services or driver staffing.
Photo courtesy of Ho’s campaign office via CNA
Articulated buses can carry up to 141 passengers, compared with about 60 on a conventional electric bus, she said.
As a result, passengers at intermediate stops, including those serving Taichung Veterans General Hospital and Tunghai University, struggle to board crowded buses, she said.
Ho pledged to ride on public transportation periodically if elected to assess services from the perspective of commuters and address problems.
Photo: Liao Yao-tung, Taipei Times
At a separate policy presentation, Chiang proposed a “Taichung smart safety network” covering policing, social welfare and disaster resilience.
His plans include enhancing coordination through the city’s smart city development committee and establishing a sovereign AI and big data center to integrate data and analyze risks while complying with legal requirements and protecting privacy.
AI sensors could help detect unusual activity patterns among older people living alone, he said. The proposed network would integrate information on the finances, childcare needs and mental health of families considered at high risk.
Chiang pledged to give frontline social workers and nursing personnel a greater role in decisionmaking, address staffing shortages and protect their rights.
Other proposals include enhancing disaster prevention and response cooperation through a regional governance platform in central Taiwan, expanding AI-assisted water management and introducing smart noise monitoring.

Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
16:46:24 UTC
01:46:24 KST

Reigning champions Australia just about got away with a win in the first round of the Rugby League World Cup as any doubts that the Pacific island nations are a force to be seriously reckoned with were washed away on the opening weekend.
Samoa and Tonga are still technically classified as Tier 2 nations, but the former humbled France 78-4 in Sydney on Friday and the latter beat England 30-12 in a high-quality Test in Perth on Saturday.
It was Tonga’s first ever win over England in seven attempts, but an unsurprising victory, given that their squad is packed with top National Rugby League (NRL) talents like Haumole Olakau’atu, who scored two tries, and highly rated halfback Isaiya Katoa.
Photo: EPA
“We’re still quite new in terms of beating Tier One nations, and England are that,” said Tonga coach Kristian Woolf, who coaches Katoa in his day job at the Redcliffe Dolphins.
“They’re a very strong team, and we knew they were going to come out and challenge us in different ways, and they did that,” he said. “And I just thought our performance was really strong.”
Samoa, who reached the final at the last World Cup and have a squad made up almost entirely of NRL players, ran in 14 tries as they crushed a French team whose best players turn out in Europe’s Super League.
“The NRL keeps growing and keeps getting better every year,” mourned France coach Laurent Frayssinous. “The smartness, the skill the guys have under pressure, the touches, week in, week out, that’s something we need to improve in Super League, simple as that.”
England, who won three of the first six World Cups as Great Britain, now need to win their last two group matches and hope other results go their way to avoid missing out on the semi-finals for the first time.
“It’s great that Tonga is a really strong nation. It’s brilliant that Samoa’s a really strong nation,” said England coach Brian McDermott. “It’s great for the international game, but we’re not going to open the can of worms about England’s position on the international scene.
“All we can do right here, right now, is just go out and put in a ton of effort,” he added.
In the other matches over the weekend, Fiji battered the Cook Islands 40-12 in Newcastle, while Papua New Guinea made light work of Lebanon with a 42-18 win in Port Moresby.
Australia and New Zealand kicked off the tournament on Thursday night in Sydney with a blockbuster clash that the home side were a little fortunate to edge 24-22.
The visiting pack kept the Kiwis on top for much of the contest but two intercept tries, a couple of kicks to winger Jack Bostock and a brilliant individual score from fullback Reece Walsh got the Kangaroos home.

End to China group tour ban urged
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
16:46:23 UTC
01:46:23 KST

Travel industry operators on Sunday urged the government to lift its ban on group tours to China, saying the ban is unreasonable and could leave people with little recourse in the event of travel disputes.
As China continues to prohibit Chinese tour groups and independent travelers from visiting Taiwan, the Taiwanese government has maintained its own ban on group tours to China in response, but individual travel is still permitted.
Although the ban on group tours had been in place for six years, the number of Taiwanese traveling to China has continued to rise, High Quality of Travel Association chairman Ringo Lee (李奇嶽) said.
Photo: Bloomberg
Taiwanese made 2.49 million trips to China in the first eight months of this year, up 19.63 percent from a year earlier, making China the second-most popular overseas destination for Taiwanese after Japan, the latest statistics released on Saturday by the Tourism Administration showed.
The number of Taiwanese visiting China, including Hong Kong and Macau, is expected to exceed 5 million this year, Lee said.
The restrictions have prompted many travelers to join tours advertised on Facebook, Douyin, a Chinese platform similar to TikTok, and Instagram by travel agencies in China, he said.
If disputes arise, travelers often have little recourse, as Taiwanese laws and regulations cannot help them resolve the issues, leaving them to negotiate directly with Chinese operators, which poses considerable risks to their consumer rights, he added.
Travel Association of Chinese chairman Hsu Chin-ruey (許晉睿) described the ban as unreasonable, saying that policies should be guided by customer demand.
It is natural for travel agencies to provide services in response to demand from travelers, he said, urging the government to avoid imposing restrictions easily.
The current regulations prohibit travel agencies from openly recruiting customers for group tours to China, and they could be investigated by the Tourism Administration if it received reports of contraventions, said Wayne Liu (劉喜臨), a professor at National Kaohsiung University of Hospitality and Tourism.
Some agencies bypass the ban by handling individual travelers who join local tours upon arrival in China, or by helping pre-assembled private groups arrange travel itineraries, he said.
Management and insurance coverage provided through legitimate travel agencies offer safeguards for traveler safety, he said.
Those who join local tours in China must seek compensation independently if issues arise, he said, adding that the same applies to Taiwanese travelers who book day trips through local travel agencies in Japan.
Travelers choose organized tours, because they consider safety, itinerary arrangements and the assistance a travel agency can provide in an emergency, he said.
Tourism should not be entangled in politics, and normal cross-strait tourism exchanges should be restored with public safety and well-being as the top priorities, he said.
Acknowledging the government’s concerns about the Chinese market, he urged consumers to choose travel agencies carefully and ensure they have adequate protection.
Shih Chien University’s Department of Tourism Management professor Kao Ming-tu (高洺塗) said the rising number of Taiwanese traveling to China showed that there was clear market demand.
The government should avoid excessive intervention in the tourism market and allow policy to follow market mechanisms, he said.

====================================================================================================

Bill risks stability of the NHI, health minister says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
16:46:23 UTC
01:46:23 KST

The National Health Insurance (NHI) system could face collapse due to a bill passed on Friday that would exempt an estimated 83 percent of people aged 65 or older from paying premiums, Minister of Health and Welfare Shih Chung-liang (石崇良) said yesterday.
Under the amendment to the Senior Citizens Welfare Act (老人福利法), backed by opposition lawmakers, the central government would fully subsidize NHI premiums for people aged 65 or older if their income for the most recent year fell below the tax filing threshold or was taxed at an income tax rate of less than 20 percent.
Using income tax rates as the sole criteria to determine eligibility for NHI premium subsidies is too crude an approach, Shih said.
Photo: Chiu Chih-jou, Taipei Times
The government should prioritize low-income and lower-middle-income households that cannot afford the premiums, he said.
The revision only provides subsidies for premiums, while the original law allowed authorities to establish subsidies for elderly people unable to afford premiums, copayments and medical expenses not covered by the NHI, Shih said.
The core principle of the NHI system is shared responsibility, with the government providing necessary assistance, he said.
The current system does not determine people’s ability to cover medical expenses based solely on age and income tax rates, he said, warning that the “unreasonable amendment” could cause the healthcare system to collapse.
Before Article 22 of the act was amended, the subsidies primarily covered three categories of expenses: NHI premiums, NHI copayments and medical expenses not covered by the NHI, Ministry of Health and Welfare’s Social and Family Affairs Administration Director Chou Tao-chun (周道君) said.
If the revised provisions are implemented as stipulated, low and middle-income people aged 65 or older could be affected, she said.
Medical expenses not covered by the NHI include items such as subsidies for dentures, Chou said.
They might also include subsidies for out-of-pocket costs associated with some treatments, such as for intraocular lenses used in cataract surgery and cardiac stents, she said.
The actual scope of subsidies affected by the amendment would depend on the specific regulations governing each program, she said.
Asked whether the central government could cover these expenses, Chou said the subsidies for NHI copayments for low-income people in the 65-or-older age group remain authorized under the Public Assistance Act (社會救助法), enabling the central government to provide funding.
However, there is no clear legal basis under the act for subsidizing NHI copayments for middle and low-income elderly people or medical expenses not covered by the NHI for them in either income group, she said.
The provisions in Article 22 concerning subsidies for NHI copayments and medical expenses not covered by the NHI for economically disadvantaged people were removed through the amendment, Chou added.
Agencies must review laws and regulations to determine whether other legal provisions can serve as an alternative basis for continuing these subsidies, she said.

Agencies flouting China travel ban, sources say
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
16:46:23 UTC
01:46:23 KST

Some travel agencies are using labels such as “cultural visits” to advertise tours to China despite the government’s ban on organized group travel, sources from the tourism industry said on Sunday.
The number of Taiwanese traveling to China rose 19.63 percent year-on-year to 2.49 million in the first eight months of this year, making China the second-most popular overseas destination, after Japan.
Taiwan has maintained the ban since February 2024, allowing only independent trips to China. However, sources told the Chinese-language Liberty Times (the sister paper of the Taipei Times) that travel agencies are advertising China tour packages under labels such as “cultural visits” and “group independent travel.”
Photo: Reuters
Taiwan first banned travel agencies from organizing outbound tours in 2020 in response to the COVID-19 pandemic. The ban was scheduled to be lifted in 2024, but Taipei maintained the restrictions in response to Beijing’s prohibition on Chinese tour groups and independent travelers visiting Taiwan.
Statistics released by the Tourism Administration on Saturday show that Taiwanese made 14.53 million overseas trips from January through August, including 2.49 million to China, accounting for 17.4 percent of the total. Commenting on the increase, Providence University Department of Tourism associate professor Huang Cheng-tsung (黃正聰) said the increase in travel to China was consistent with the overall growth in overseas travel.
Meanwhile, sources told the Liberty Times that travel agencies were advertising itineraries to popular Chinese destinations, including Jiuzhaigou, Xinjiang, Zhangjiajie and the Yangtze River. The Web sites listed daily itineraries resembling conventional group tours, but marketed them as cultural visits or group independent travel.
However, in practice, agencies were dispatching their staff to accompany travelers, potentially violating the restrictions, they said.
When reached for comment on Sunday, Tourism Administration Deputy Director-General Huang Ho-ting (黃荷婷) said that travel agencies remain prohibited from openly soliciting members of the public to join organized tours to China. Violators face fines of up to NT$50,000 under the Regulations Governing Travel Agencies (旅行業管理規則).
An industry source who spoke on condition of anonymity said a common workaround was for associations, community groups, village and borough wardens, businesses, government agencies, or groups of friends and relatives to organize their own trips and hire travel agencies to handle the arrangements.
The source cited a bus crash involving a group of relatives and friends traveling in Gansu Province this year as an example.
Another method involves travelers departing Taiwan separately as independent travelers, then gathering in China to join an organized tour. This allows some agencies to continue recruiting participants discreetly despite the ban, the source said.
“For travel agencies, it is a strange rule that does little damage, but is deeply insulting,” the source said.
Travel Association of Chinese chairman Hsu Chin-ruey (許晉睿) said agencies might legitimately post tourism information on their Web sites for reference, provided listings do not include departure dates or indicate that trips are open for registration.
Such information might fall within the normal scope of a travel agency’s business, he said.
However, members of the public who find Web sites listing departure dates and opening registrations can report them to the Tourism Administration.
Huang said agencies may still organize visits and inspection tours, arrange trips organized by groups themselves, and book plane tickets and accommodation for travelers heading to China.
Exchange or inspection delegations invited by Chinese organizations are exempt from the suspension if they have specific purposes, designated destinations and eligibility requirements for participants, she said.
She urged agencies to comply with the rules and avoid illegally soliciting customers, which could lead to travel disputes.
If the Tourism Administration confirms that an agency has illegally solicited participants for an organized tour to China, it can order the agency to make improvements by a specified deadline or impose a fine of NT$10,000 to NT$50,000, Huang said.

EDITORIAL: The art of economic policy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
16:46:19 UTC
01:46:19 KST

Why do central bank interest-rate hikes sometimes fail to curb inflation? Why might households begin cutting back on spending even before a recession begins? These questions fit into the central theme of the research of this year’s winners of the Nobel Prize in Economics, Americans Robert E. Hall and Michael Woodford. Their research helped explain how household expectations of future income and companies’ business forecasts influence economic trends. They found that effective macroeconomic stabilization depends not only on policy implementation, but also on how central banks communicate with the public and incorporate the expectations of households and companies.
The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences on Monday last week recognized Hall, 83, a professor emeritus at Stanford University, and Woodford, 71, a professor at Columbia University, for their research establishing the “microeconomic foundations of macroeconomic stabilization,” which showed how economic models can be reconstructed to bolster stabilization policies, such as interest-rate adjustments and other measures that governments and central banks use to control inflation and maintain stable economic activity.
The idea of using stabilization policies to smooth economic cycles was popularized by British economist John Maynard Keynes during the Great Depression in the 1930s. However, that framework broke down during the oil shocks of the 1970s, when surging oil prices caused economic stagnation and further fiscal expansion led to higher inflation. As inflation and unemployment rose, developing into stagflation, governments realized that Keynesian models might not always work.
The weakness in early Keynesian models lies in the lack of a comprehensive microeconomic foundation and limited analysis of how households and businesses adjust their behaviors to economic policy changes. Another challenge facing traditional stabilization policies is the time lag between policy formulation and implementation, which causes the effectiveness of measures to fall short of expectations. Hall and Woodford aimed to address the shortcomings of traditional Keynesian models by analyzing how households decide on spending and saving, and how firms set prices.
Taiwan’s decisionmakers should incorporate the Nobel laureates’ research when formulating macroeconomic policy. For example, Hall’s research found that people do not decide how much to spend based solely on current income, but rather on their expectations of their financial situation. Other research suggests that when income rises, higher-income households tend to save a greater share of the increase, while lower-income households tend to spend a greater share. In other words, focusing support on low-income groups could have a stronger effect on overall consumption than a universal welfare approach.
Meanwhile, Woodford’s research revealed that when setting product prices, firms often consider future costs and competitors’ prices, rather than just current conditions. His work on monetary policy and inflation expectations also provided a theoretical basis for the “forward guidance” used by many central banks. That is, when central banks communicate their expectations for interest rates, households and businesses might alter their behavior even before the rates actually change. If policymakers communicate to the public what they plan to do, households and companies might adjust their expectations accordingly, and the economy could experience fewer drastic changes.
In the past few years, rising geopolitical risks, supply chain restructuring and a K-shaped growth pattern have challenged economic policymakers. Factors affecting economic development are not limited to inflation, unemployment and production, but also include people’s income expectations and corporations’ business outlook. Therefore, when drafting policies, governments cannot simply throw money around and rely solely on increased spending to stimulate the economy during downturns; instead, policymakers must consider how households and firms would react and how their responses could shape the economy. If consumers and manufacturers are optimistic about the future, they might take actions that support the economy.
The research honored by this year’s Nobel economics prize is valuable for central banks seeking to improve their forecasts and explain policy decisions to anchor market expectations during global interest-rate shifts or inflationary pressures. It also directly contradicts US Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh’s communications strategy, such as ending the Fed’s forward guidance, and shortening its post-meeting statements and news conferences. In contrast, the award appears to defend the value of transparent communication and the argument that ambiguity harms households, businesses and the economy.
Southeast Asian food delivery platform Grab Holdings Ltd in March applied to acquire Delivery Hero SE’s Foodpanda operations in Taiwan, with the Fair Trade Commission (FTC) scheduled to announce its decision on Oct. 27. On the surface, the deal is a business merger — but in substance, it involves personal data, national geospatial information and digital sovereignty. It cannot be assessed solely in terms of market share and price competition. Grab has extensive and long-standing connections to Chinese capital. In 2015, Chinese ride-hailing firm Didi Chuxing and China Investment Corp, a sovereign wealth fund, invested in Grab. Grab invested in Chinese autonomous-driving
