How to make a great film adaptation,  from ‘The Shining’ to ‘Trainspotting’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
16:46:18 UTC
01:46:18 KST

It is always fun to join in a craze, like a Victorian going mad for penny farthings. Which is probably why, against my better judgment, I went to see Christopher Nolan’s blockbuster The Odyssey this summer, buying my ticket into the popular conversation along with everyone else. This year’s other divisive adaptation, Emerald Fennell’s Wuthering Heights, had the world and his wife arguing about it before they had even watched the film. No doubt the makers of the recent Sense and Sensibility movie were also hoping for lots of people to go and see it to discover whether they hated it.
After all, very few of us leave the cinema saying: “That’s exactly how I pictured it in my head.” Or even less likely: “That was better than the book.” We’re more likely to shake our fists at how they ruined the ending, dumbed it down, unforgivably cast somebody with the wrong hair, or betrayed a beloved character, as with last year’s Thursday Murder Club debacle.
But what makes a good adaptation? Like Odysseus himself, and as every Nancy Meyers fan knows: it’s complicated. I have just written a book about the towering heights and profane depths of adaptation, The Book Was Better, for which I subjected myself to some of the worst viewing experiences possible, including the soft rock opera musical Heathcliff; 1996’s freakishly bad The Island of Dr Moreauv; and a horrible three-part version of Ayn Rand’s Atlas Shrugged. But I also saw plenty of masterpieces that equaled or sometimes surpassed the originals. Here’s what I learned.
Photo: AP
GREAT BOOKS, GREAT FILMS
The first thing to say is that the quality of the source is irrelevant. I went into my research with some pretty fixed ideas: for instance, that “the brilliant adaptations are nearly always of fiction of the second or third class,” as Anthony Burgess wrote; that some works are “unfilmable;” that classics have more “room to breathe” on TV. Soon I realized none of these were true. Yes, sometimes workmanlike novels, such as the late 60s and early 70s triumvirate Jaws, The Godfather and The Exorcist, can be tuned to a level of genius on screen. But great books can make great films, too: Trainspotting, The Go-Between, The Leopard and Burgess’s own A Clockwork Orange are just a few examples. And sometimes, in the case of The Da Vinci Code and Fifty Shades of Grey, a deeply silly book becomes a deeply silly film.
It is true that certain books lend themselves to the screen more readily. Jane Austen’s immaculate plots of love impeded are templates that can be dressed up in the clothes of any age, like the computer template Cher Horowitz uses to plan her outfits at the start of Clueless — the ne plus ultra of free-handed adaptations. Austen’s novels contain the DNA of all romcoms, just as Robinson Crusoe is found in The Martian, the gothic novel in horror films, or A Christmas Carol in every single Christmas movie. Short stories, with their twisty shocks and rush towards the end point, seem made for cinema; my favorite film, Don’t Look Now, is based on a Daphne du Maurier novella. The murky origins and elasticity of myths and their close cousins, folk and fairytales, make them ceaselessly adaptable, because they leave gaps for a film-maker to fill with their own imaginations.
Being unfaithful is usually helpful. Some of the best adaptations flirt with the source material, taking frightful liberties and then abandoning it like a tabloid love rat.
“Steal the parts that you need, and then run as fast as you can,” advised Paul Thomas Anderson; Hitchcock claimed he read The Birds once before making his version, and never thought about it again. (One screenwriter I spoke to told me he was once asked not to read the novel he was adapting as the production company thought it would be a hindrance). Books and films are entirely different beasts, “apples and giraffes,” as author-screenwriter Dennis Lehane once said. Adaptation is an act of translation from the verbal to the visual. A film-maker needs to find their own language.
One of my most beloved unfaithful adaptations is Alfonso Cuaron’s 2006 Children of Men, and not just because it stars Clive Owen at the peak of his physical perfection. It manages to transform a cerebral, theological novel by the Conservative peer PD James into a dystopian thriller about populism, terror and how we treat immigrants, one which — although now two decades old — feels fresher each year. (James was delighted with it.) Cuaron used the novel as a jumping-off point, then left it behind to follow his own adventure. What remained was the central conceit: what if we lived in a world without children? The “what if” high concepts of science fiction and speculative fiction are perfect for playing fast and loose with: a vessel into which a film-maker’s own preoccupations, and the anxieties of their age, can be poured.
‘THE BOOK NEVER EXISTED’
When writer-director Sally Potter reinvented Virginia Woolf’s time-travelling fantasia Orlando, she treated it “as if the book never existed,” turning it into a lavish nose-thumb to a UK establishment that had just passed section 28. She was, she said, cruel to the novel to be kind to the film. It’s the destruction-as-creation mantra. In the hands of the right writer and director, a source can, and should, be made to submit to their will: Stanley Kubrick betrayed Stephen King’s vision of The Shining but made a tour de force. Heart of Darkness mutated into a war epic with Apocalypse Now; Red Dragon became, well, a Michael Mann film, the hypnotic Manhunter. An adaptation should never be a hollow greatest hits album. Being too reverential towards a literary source can kill it, which is why I suspect films such as The Hunger Games and The Road, lovingly and stylishly made with few changes, felt slightly bloodless on screen to me.
Can anything really be faithful anyway, and to what? No story is 100 per cent original. (As Alien screenwriter Dan O’Bannon said: “I didn’t steal from anybody. I stole from everybody!”) I don’t even think you can be “true to the spirit” of a text, because the spirit is different for everyone. We all have our own little films running in our heads when we read. Many see The Great Gatsby as a death knell for the US; adapters tend to think: “parties!”. I think Heathcliff is a psychopath who likes to hang little dogs; successive directors clearly didn’t. I loved discovering that Jodie Foster lobbied hard for the part of Clarice Starling in The Silence of the Lambs because, for her, the novel was about a woman saving the life of another woman while “all these fucking men” get in the way. An adaptation may just be a glimpse into another mind’s eye, but their pictures seldom match the ones we had imagined.
Perhaps the most obvious example of this is casting. As sure as night follows day, Hollywood casts a better-looking actor than strictly necessary, although not always reaching
“Denise Richards in hotpants as a nuclear physicist in The World is Not Enough” levels. This can be deliberate: in Robert Bloch’s novel Psycho, Norman Bates is physically repellent; Hitchcock wanted the sweet-faced Anthony Perkins for the part to wrongfoot the audience. More often it’s because, as the critic Roger Ebert observed, cinema is a machine for generating empathy, so the thinking goes that leads should be “likable” — which backfired horribly when Bruce Willis was cast as a desiccated English journalist in the notoriously disastrous adaptation of Tom Wolfe’s The Bonfire of the Vanities. But sometimes an actor who is wrong on paper can make a role their own, whether it’s Margaret Rutherford as Miss Marple, Renee Zellweger as Bridget Jones or Michael Caine as Harry Palmer in The Ipcress File (in Len Deighton’s novels he’s a northerner and doesn’t have a name). Charisma goes a long way.
Perhaps in the end, adaptation all comes down to emotions and sensations.
“You’ve drunk the drink, and the taste that’s left in your mouth is what you go with,” as Anthony Minghella described adapting The Talented Mr Ripley. Irvine Welsh said you must smell the books. Hossein Amini, who reinvented The Wings of the Dove as “noir in costume”, wanted to recapture that ecstatic moment when “nobody else in the world understood or experienced that book exactly like I did.”
Returning to The Odyssey, I wonder why, even though Nolan did the right things, subordinating it to his worldview and faithlessly reinventing it for our age by turning a wily trickster into a traumatized veteran, the film just made me feel as if I’d been in a war: long periods of boredom and waiting punctuated by violence. Perhaps, ultimately, he overthought it and should have felt it instead? Or maybe, as the late Hilary Mantel said of adaptation, you must “put down the text, and dream it.”
In pandemic preparedness work, scientists like to focus on the technical challenges: identifying pathogens, diagnosing infections, understanding their effects and developing vaccines and treatments. Each step promises progress through human innovation, investment and planning. The WHO, for example, brings experts together to identify and prioritize emerging disease threats and collect the evidence needed to prepare for them. But preparedness depends on more than scientific innovation. As the past week has shown, politics is the elephant in the room in all of this. Lula, Bolsonaro trade insults in Brazil poll debate
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
16:46:18 UTC
01:46:18 KST

Firing off personal attacks, Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva and his rival, Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, held an acrimonious first debate on Sunday, a week before a tight presidential election runoff.
A chaotic exchange between the two men, who called each other liars on multiple occasions, accusing each other of corruption and dragging up various scandals, encapsulated the tone of a bitter election campaign in the deeply polarized nation.
Bolsonaro, 45, son of the far-right former president Jair Bolsonaro, secured a shock first-round lead over Lula earlier this month and polls predict a close battle for the runoff on Sunday.
Photo: AFP
The two men sparred over the economy, public security, healthcare, corruption and Brazil’s ties to the US.
“Brazil is going to retire you,” Flavio Bolsonaro said, seeking to unnerve his adversary by pacing up and down behind him throughout the debate in view of the camera, shaking his head, smirking and scoffing while his adversary spoke.
Lula called his rival “a habitual liar, a thug,” and said he did not want to stand close to a “militiaman,” alluding to his alleged ties to Rio de Janeiro’s paramilitary groups.
Photo: Bloomberg
Flavio Bolsonaro, who made several jabs about Lula’s time jailed for corruption on charges that were later annulled, retorted that it was better he stay at a distance “because my wallet could be stolen.”
Lula, who at almost 81 is seeking a fourth term in power, battled to control his irritation at times and repeatedly asked viewers to “look it up on Google” to prove his adversary was lying.
While Flavio Bolsonaro has led in polls since the first round, his edge slightly narrowed in two polls this week, which showed him with 51 percent of voting intentions compared with 49 percent for Lula.
Flavio Bolsonaro hammered away at the primary concerns of Brazilians, such as the cost of living and insecurity, and accused Lula of “reckless spending to get re-elected” due to various social measures he has announced while campaigning.
Lula countered by asking Flavio Bolsonaro about his plans to emulate the drastic “chainsaw” cuts to public spending implemented by Argentine President Javier Milei, which led to higher unemployment and cuts to benefits.
Throughout the debate, Flavio Bolsonaro dodged the question and pivoted to different topics.
Lula questioned him about his ties to US President Donald Trump — an ally of the Bolsonaro family — and plans to “hand over” Brazil’s rare earth minerals.
“It is striking how the Bolsonaro family is subservient to American interests,” he said.
Former president Jair Bolsonaro came up several times, including when his son asked Lula why so many prisoners had supported him in the election.
Lula said he wanted all of their votes, including that of Jair Bolsonaro — who is serving a 27-year sentence under house arrest for a botched coup bid after his failed 2022 re-election bid.
“Vote for me, Bolsonaro, you know your son, you know I’m better than him,” Lula said.
Ahead of the showdown, tens of thousands of supporters of Lula and Bolsonaro gathered in cities around the country.
In Sao Paulo, a sea of people dressed in the yellow and green of the Brazilian flag rallied for Flavio Bolsonaro, who made his way down Paulista Avenue on the back of a truck.
“The country is in a state of calamity. To make ends meet or buy anything, you have to work two or three jobs just to pay the bills,” said Sara Machado, 36, wearing a T-shirt with the slogan: “Right-wing. With pride.”
The rally drew about 71,000 people, according to monitors at the University of Sao Paulo (USP).
In Rio de Janeiro, swimmers at Praia Vermelha beach synchronized in the water to spell out Lula’s name with their bodies.
Later, on Copacabana Beach, iconic octogenarian singer Caetano Veloso led a “rally for democracy” in favor of the president, which USP monitors said drew about 56,000 people.
Fabiana Leite, a 51-year-old nurse and social worker, said Lula’s social welfare programs saved her after she was wrongly incarcerated, lost custody of her daughters and had to rebuild her life after being freed.
“You might have the desire to fight and to grow, but without the means, without social programs, it’s just not possible. That is why I am here, continuing the fight,” she said.

The Philippine Department of Foreign Affairs yesterday summoned Chinese Ambassador Jing Quan (井泉) to express its “serious concern and strong objection” about remarks by the envoy that it said conveyed a threat of the use of force.
Jing told media last week that China “may easily win” in a confrontation with the Philippines, but Beijing would not use force because “we love peace.”
He was responding to a question about the Philippine Secretary of National Defense Gilberto Teodoro Jr describing China as a regional troublemaker.
Photo: Philippine Department of Foreign Affairs’ Office of Public Diplomacy via AP
Philippine Secretary of Foreign Affairs Maria Theresa Lazaro told Jing that his comments were “provocative and unacceptable,” and aggravated the sensitive atmosphere between the two countries, the department said in a statement.
Sensitive issues should be addressed through established diplomatic channels and bilateral mechanisms that reserve space for dialogue and engagement, she said.
Diplomatic disputes between China and the Philippines, a US ally, have become more frequent in the past few years, typically over standoffs and altercations between rival vessels in the South China Sea, much of which Beijing claims sovereignty over.
Manila has accused China’s coast guard of aggressive conduct in the Philippines’ exclusive economic zone, while Beijing insists it is enforcing the law against vessels that are encroaching on its territory.
Asked about the summoning and calls by some lawmakers in Manila for Jing’s expulsion, China yesterday said it firmly opposes what it called the “malicious hyping” of China-related issues by some people.
“The Philippine side should take concrete steps to restrain such irresponsible words and actions by certain politicians,” Chinese Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokesperson Mao Ning (毛寧) told a daily press conference in Beijing.
Mao also said that improving bilateral relations would benefit both countries.
The Chinese embassy in Manila last week said Jing had been selectively quoted and his remarks overinterpreted.

Japan licenses allow ‘Taiwan’ listing
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
16:46:17 UTC
01:46:17 KST

Starting this month, Taiwanese professionals working in Japan can list “Taiwan” as their place of origin following Tokyo’s easing of rules on “nationality” in official licensing documents.
The change was announced yesterday by the Japan-Taiwan Friendship Parliamentarians’ League in Tokyo. The license revision covers 322 professions, including doctors and nurses.
Previously, Taiwanese had to list “China” as their nationality on professional certifications and licenses, but the new rules updated the “nationality” to “nationality and region” or “nationality, etc,” allowing Taiwanese to use the name “Taiwan.”
Photo: Lin Tsuei-yi, Taipei Times
The league held a meeting about the revision at the House of Representatives Members’ Office Building in Tokyo yesterday, and overseas Taiwanese were invited to attend.
Japanese Representative Keiji Furuya, head of the league, said the reform represents a significant progress in Taiwan-Japan relations, but application and local administrative procedures need further refinement.
The league’s task force will continue its work until all Taiwanese can have “Taiwan” listed on their national qualification certificates, he said.
Hirofumi Takinami, a member of the Japanese House of Councillors who is also head of the task force, said the reform started in 2022, when several Taiwanese petitioned the league to allow “Taiwan” to be listed on Japanese household registries.
The league responded by establishing a task force, which pushed the Japanese Ministry of Justice to amend ministerial ordinances, he said.
“Taiwan” was officially included in the nationality column of household registries in May last year, he said.
It continued to coordinate with government agencies, including the Japanese Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare, ultimately completing the reform for national qualification certificates, he said.
Takinami said that updating medical licenses is handled by local public health centers and administrative agencies, but, based on their experience with the household registration changes, local officials might not be familiar with the new regulations.
As such, the league has asked central authorities to request that service centers be properly notified, he said.
It also asked that the no application deadline be set, so that Taiwanese who might not have heard of the changes would still be able to apply for changes later, he said.
Norifumi Nakazato, a Taiwanese doctor practicing in Japan who used a sticker to cover the word “China” on his medical license, said the reform has a deep, personal significance, because he can finally display a license that matches his real identity.
“It brings me such peace of mind, and I am truly happy,” said Nakazato, who has been involved in the task force for the past four years.
He said that when Japanese patients saw his license in the past, they would ask in confusion: “Didn’t you say you were Taiwanese? Why does your license say Chinese?” so he had to cover it with a sticker.
Nakazato estimated that there are approximately 2,000 Taiwanese healthcare professionals who have obtained national qualifications in Japan.
Seiei Hirouchi, another Taiwanese physician who has lived in Japan for 47 years, said that when he entered a Japanese national university many years ago, the certificate issued by the school listed ‘Taiwan,” but after passing the Japanese national examination, the professional license he obtained listed him as from “China,” leaving him deeply perplexed.
While Taiwan and China have different cultures and lifestyles, Taiwanese were often mistaken as Chinese in the past due to license documentation issues, which affected their sense of identity in professional settings, he said.
Hirouchi lauded the change, calling it a major step forward for Japan’s administrative system.
He thanked the Japanese lawmakers, medical organizations and the Taipei Economic and Cultural Representative Office in Japan for their long-standing support.
Representative to Japan Lee Yi-yang (李逸洋) said many Taiwanese professionals live and work in Japan, making long-term contributions to Japanese society, yet they have been unable to have their place of origin listed accurately on their national qualification certificates.
Their long-cherished wish has finally been fulfilled, marking another big step forward in protecting the rights and interests of Taiwanese in Japan, he said.
Lee also expressed his gratitude to Keiji Furuya, Hirofumi Takinami and all the individuals across various sectors in Japan who helped promote this effort.

The Ministry of Sports said in a statement on Sunday that Lee was initially issued a “sports minister” credential, but was informed by the game organizers earlier that day that his credential had been changed to a guest of a national paralympic committee.
The ministry said the last-minute change without explanation was “regrettable” and lodged a strong protest against the organizers.
Photo courtesy of fthe ministry
Chinese National Party (KMT) Legislator Lai Shyh-bao (賴士葆) said that the Ministry of Foreign Affairs should lodge its protest through diplomatic channels because the real problem lies with the Japanese government.
“National Security Council Secretary-General Joseph Wu (吳釗燮) said that Japan is Taiwan’s big brother. If so, why does it repeatedly mistreat Taiwanese officials?” Lai asked.
Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) caucus deputy whip Chen Pei-yu (陳培瑜) urged the public to unite in condemning Beijing’s political interference in Taiwan’s right to participate in international sports events.
“We support Minister Lee’s decision to defend his position based on facts, as Taiwanese athletes, coaches or even medical staff could experience the same plight,” she said.
Executive Yuan Secretary-General Chang Tun-han (張惇涵) said the public should support Lee and the Ministry of Sports regardless of their political affiliations.
The sports ministry said it has issued a formal protest to the Asian Paralympics Committee via Taiwan’s National Paralympic Committee and is also seeking to settle the dispute through diplomatic channels.
“While we respect the rules governing international sporting events and the administrative authority of the event organizers, we believe the types of credentials and access privileges should properly reflect the duties and status of those attending the events. Any adjustments should also be made on a clear legal basis following full explanation and communication with relevant stakeholders,” it said.
All parties involved in the sports event should adhere to the principles of mutual respect and fair treatment and prevent interference from non-sports-related factors, it added.
On Sept. 18, Lee attended an Asian Games flag-raising ceremony in Japan after an hour-long delay, despite an alleged attempt to exclude him.
At the time, officials at the venue said the Olympic Council of Asia (OCA) had issued an order barring Lee, but when challenged, they could not produce it, Minister Without Portfolio Wu Cheng-wen (吳誠文) said.
Japanese organizers later attributed the delay to miscommunication with the OCA, saying it was not the Taiwan delegation’s fault.
The OCA later said that Lee’s initial exclusion was a misunderstanding, Japanese media reported.

Taiwan, which has participated in every edition of the Asian Para Games since 2010, has sent 71 athletes this year.
They are to compete in 12 categories: archery, athletics, badminton, table tennis, boccia, judo, powerlifting, shooting, swimming, taekwondo, wheelchair fencing and wheelchair tennis.

The NHI waiver raises concerns
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
16:46:12 UTC
01:46:12 KST

The Legislative Yuan has passed amendments to the Senior Citizens Welfare Act (老人福利法) that would waive National Health Insurance (NHI) premiums for most people aged 65 or older. Under the bill, advanced by Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT) and Taiwan People’s Party lawmakers and passed 60-39, the government would fully subsidize the premiums for people aged 65 or older whose income falls below the tax-filing threshold or whose income tax rate is less than 20 percent. The change essentially creates a universal waiver for people aged 65 or older, because most retirees have no taxable income. Medical associations have said that the shift could worsen generational imbalance and squeeze budgets for nurses’ salaries, rare-disease care and new drug coverage.
Critics have framed the bill as fiscal sabotage, pork-barrel politics or even an attempt by opposition lawmakers to destabilize the government. However, the debate raises a deeper question: How should Taiwan ration its finite healthcare resources?
Although the NHI has received international recognition for its efficiency, accessibility and health outcomes, growing financial pressure has raised concerns about its long-term stability. In 2024, Taiwan spent about 7.34 percent of GDP on national healthcare, significantly lower than the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development average for that year of 9.3 percent and the US’ 17.2 percent.
The Commonwealth Fund reported that budgetary constraints have contributed to significant workforce shortages in Taiwan. Hospitals struggle to recruit and retain nurses; doctors leave hospitals for cosmetic clinics where income is more predictable; and the NHI faces difficulty covering new, high-cost drugs.
Taiwan’s situation makes it clear that medical resources are finite. Indeed, all universal healthcare systems must ration care. Any politician who promises to always provide all forms of care to all people without bankrupting the system is simply lying. The question is what are the principles of ethical medical rationing?
Different countries have different approaches, but there are a few shared principles, such as maximizing clinical benefits, implementing measures to protect lower-income households and providing universal access to essential care while preserving individual choice.
The British National Institute for Health and Care Excellence evaluates the clinical benefits and cost-effectiveness of new treatments to inform coverage decisions. Germany’s system uses public funds to cover health insurance premiums for eligible unemployed people. Switzerland requires people to carry basic health insurance, while allowing them to purchase supplementary insurance for additional coverage.
These examples illustrate different ways of balancing clinical benefits, while helping lower-income people and protecting individual choice. Most systems value these principles but combine them in different ways, reflecting different priorities.
KMT lawmakers argue that elderly people are more likely to be financially vulnerable and therefore deserve help. However, age is not the same as poverty. If the goal is to protect lower-income people, why focus on age rather than directly target subsidies to those who need them? Taiwan already has income-based mechanisms; this bill bypasses them.
That leads to the issue of sustainability. The Ministry of Health and Welfare estimates that the amendment would cost NT$40 billion (US$1.23 billion) annually, which, if funded through premiums, would require people aged 20 to 64 to pay an additional NT$2,690 per person per year. If funded through taxes, each household would pay about NT$5,720 more annually. The estimated NT$40 billion would grow as Taiwan’s population ages. These numbers suggest that the new bill might be popular today, but less so as costs rise.
These estimates should inform executive responses, policy debates and broader public discussion.
The Executive Yuan should consider refusing to countersign this costly, under-deliberated bill. However, refusing to countersign risks being framed by opposition lawmakers as the central government opposing benefits for elderly people, deepening polarization.
To avoid this trap, the Executive Yuan should pair its response with an initiative to stimulate discussions between the state and civil society.
First, it should clarify the principles of medical fairness that have guided NHI policy — principles rooted in clinical need and long-term viability rather than blunt demographic categories such as age.
Second, it should propose alternative ways to support vulnerable groups and address unmet medical needs without destabilizing the system. Those could include expanding subsidies for new cancer drugs, improving coverage for rare-disease treatments or increasing support for low-income people through existing means-tested mechanisms.
Finally, the Executive Yuan should encourage broad public discussion among medical professionals, economists, patient groups and younger workers. Given the NHI’s funding shortfalls and the nation’s aging population, Taiwan needs an open debate about how to prioritize competing medical needs and secure the resources necessary to maintain the system’s fiscal integrity.
There is no need to mince words — the new bill is awful. However, the Executive Yuan should turn this into an opportunity for the public to seriously debate the fundamental issue: how society as a whole can build consensus about ethical and sustainable medical rationing.
Lo Ming-cheng is a professor of sociology at the University of California, Davis, whose research addresses civil society, political cultures and medical sociology.

2026 Elections: Academics discuss tools to fight disinformation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
16:46:10 UTC
01:46:10 KST

With the local elections approaching, academics yesterday urged the government to develop filters for artificial intelligence (AI) content and improve public media literacy, saying that Beijing increasingly uses low-cost AI tools to spread disinformation.
The Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) held a forum yesterday on Chinese election interference, inviting experts to discuss common tactics and appropriate responses.
China is interfering in Taiwan’s elections by spreading information that is “30 percent true and 70 percent false,” DPP secretary-general Hsu Kuo-yung (徐國勇) said, calling on experts to examine how China uses AI and big data to influence public perception.
Photo: Wang Yi-sung, Taipei Times
China’s short-term goal is to influence election outcomes, while its long-term goal is to deepen social division and erode trust in democracy, said professor Yeh Yao-yuan (葉耀元), chair of international studies at the University of St Thomas in Houston, Texas.
In addition to military pressure, China seeks to influence Taiwanese voters by spreading disinformation, manipulating public opinion and infiltrating social networks, pushing them to make political decisions in an environment full of unreliable information, Yeh said.
In July, the US government discovered that China had stolen 220 million US voter registration records, he said.
Given enough time to analyze it, China could identify which issues to focus on to target voters in different regions, he said, warning that Taiwan needs to enhance its safeguards.
Beijing has pivoted toward using AI to generate large volumes of text and images to interfere with elections, Shih Hsin University communications professor Liu Yu-hsi (劉玉皙) said.
For example, several Chinese immigrants registered to run for borough wardens this year, but many of their online campaign graphics contain numerous errors, Liu said.
China’s main goal is to erode the nation’s sovereignty, Asia-Pacific Elite Interchange Association secretary-general Arthur Wang (王智盛) said.
China previously relied on verbal attacks and military threats, then turned to economic inducements in 2008 before focusing on disinformation from 2016 to 2018, Wang said.
Now its tactics have shifted to targeted election interference aimed at deepening divisions and antagonism within Taiwanese society, he said.
The government should establish AI databases and filtering systems, and improve media literacy education, Wang said.
People should learn how China uses AI to infiltrate everyday life, so they can identify and verify such information, he said.
People should be suspicious of information from unknown sources or that is designed to provoke an emotional response, DPP China Affairs Director Wu Jun-zhi (吳峻鋕) said, recommending checking sources and cross-checking facts with reputable media outlets.

The UN World Food Programme (WFP) has said that funding shortages are forcing major cuts to its aid program in Gaza, leaving about 500,000 people without monthly food support in a territory where two-thirds of the population struggle to get enough to eat.
The WFP said it was reducing the number of recipients of its monthly assistance to 1.1 million people from 1.6 million.
In addition, food rations have been halved, cash assistance has been cut for 75,000 families, and the number of daily hot meals for those unable to cook has fallen to 150,000 from 250,000, with some families in hard-to-reach areas now receiving a hot meal only every other day.
Photo: AP
About 1.4 million people, or two-thirds of Gaza’s population, face crisis levels of food insecurity or worse, including roughly 200,000 people in emergency conditions, it said.
Last year’s US-brokered Gaza ceasefire calls for the eventual reconstruction of the territory, but little progress has been made toward implementing a deal to end the conflict that includes terms for Hamas to disarm and Israel to withdraw its troops.
“It’s a year into the agreement of this ceasefire. Well, life is still brutal here. There is no proper shelter... There is no basic services. There is no safety, no security,” WFP acting executive director Carl Skau said in Gaza.
“These cuts are happening just as we are facing the fourth winter. You know, I’ve been through the winters here, absolutely brutal,” he added.
The WFP said it urgently needs US$450 million over the next six months to maintain critical operations in Gaza and the Israeli-occupied West Bank.
“We tell the world now is this is not the time to look away. This is the time to step up to sustain this support, to protect the progress that has been made, but also to push for early recovery,” Skau said.

Banks’ liquidity tightening but still ample: FSC chair
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
16:46:08 UTC
01:46:08 KST

Taiwan’s banks are facing tighter liquidity conditions as economic growth and a booming stock market fuel demand for funds. but the overall supply of money remains ample, Financial Supervisory Commission (FSC) Chairman Peng Jin-lung (彭金隆) said yesterday,
Banks’ liquidity coverage ratios (LCRs) have declined from a year earlier, leaving them with less room to absorb unexpected cash outflows, Peng said during a meeting of the legislature’s Finance Committee.
Taiwan’s financial markets enjoyed abundant liquidity for years, with banks holding ample funds. However, demand for money has increased since last year alongside rapid economic growth and a rally in local stocks, putting pressure on banks’ liquidity, Peng said.
Photo: CNA
Banks’ lending decisions are shaped by their willingness to extend credit, rising personal loans and capital adequacy requirements, he said.
Peng said that Taiwan does not face an outright fund shortage, echoing the central bank’s repeated assurances that the issue lies in how money is distributed rather than in the total amount available.
The sector has deposits of almost NT$70 trillion (US$2.16 trillion), compared with about NT$50 trillion in loans, leaving a gap of almost NT$20 trillion.
However, banks cannot lend out all their deposits, as they must maintain reserves at the central bank and retain sufficient liquidity to meet deposit withdrawals and other funding needs, Peng said. The gap between deposits and loans does not represent money readily available for additional lending, he said.
The LCR measures whether a bank has enough liquid assets, such as cash and government bonds, to cover its projected cash outflows over a 30-day stress period. The statutory minimum is 100 percent.
FSC data showed that Taiwan’s domestic banks had an average LCR of 120.57 percent in late August, down 8.22 percentage points from 128.79 percent a year earlier. Although the ratio remained above the regulatory minimum, the decline indicates that banks had a smaller liquidity buffer from a year earlier.
The FSC dismissed calls to curb short selling because of stock market slides, saying the authorities should let markets reflect market information unless trading becomes irrational or market mechanisms break down.
Peng said regulators worldwide shared the same principle of respecting market forces. Markets need buyers and sellers, and investors should be given time to digest market information, he said.
The selloff reflects global developments rather than a problem unique to Taiwan, Peng said, adding that regulators should avoid intervention as long as market information remains undistorted.
He added that strong corporate revenue and earnings in the first nine months of the year should underpin Taiwan’s stock market.

Australia’s Ghost Shark sub grows some ‘teeth’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
16:46:07 UTC
01:46:07 KST

Australia is boosting its undersea warfare capability by equipping its Ghost Shark autonomous submarine with “swarms” of aerial drones and sea mines, the Department of Defence said yesterday.
US defense technology start-up Anduril jointly developed the extra large submarine drone with Australia’s defense scientists, and is building a Ghost Shark fleet for Canberra under a A$1.8 billion (US$1.3 billion) contract.
The AUKUS partners of Australia, Britain and the US pledged this year to develop interchangeable payloads for drones used in undersea warfare, in addition to their nuclear submarine cooperation.
Photo: AFP
Australian Minister for Defence Industry Pat Conroy said in Sydney that after secret trials three payloads had been approved to “do things we don’t want humans to do.”
The Ghost Shark is to carry up to 12 sea mines, equipment for special forces, and Anduril’s Altius aerial drones that can be launched at sea to form swarms to conduct reconnaissance and strike, he said.
Potential adversaries would have to consider that any shipping container at an Australian wharf could have a Ghost Shark in it, he said.
“Not only could there be Ghost Sharks in those shipping containers, but those Ghost Sharks now have teeth,” he said.
Australia, concerned at the rapid build-up of China’s navy and tensions in the South China Sea, is rapidly expanding its investment in drones.

Opposition lawmakers defend Senior Citizens Welfare bill
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
16:46:01 UTC
01:46:01 KST

Taiwan People’s Party (TPP) lawmakers yesterday defended amendments to the Senior Citizens Welfare Act (老人福利法), saying existing medical subsidies for disadvantaged seniors would remain in place.
Under the amendments to Article 22 passed on Friday, the government must cover the full National Health Insurance (NHI) premiums of people aged 65 or older whose total consolidated income in the most past year falls below the tax filing threshold or is subject to an income tax rate of less than 20 percent.
Taiwan Economic Democracy Union think tank convener Lai Chung-chiang (賴中強) said the changes inadvertently removed the legal basis for two key medical subsidies for disadvantaged people in that age group.
Photo: Lo Pi, Taipei Times
In response, the TPP caucus said Lai was misleading the public and criticized Minister of Health and Welfare Shih Chung-liang (石崇良) for fearmongering by saying that people younger than 64 would have to pay up to NT$3,000 more per year because of the bill.
TPP caucus secretary-general Hung Yu-hsiang (洪毓祥) said that medical copayments and other out-of-pocket expenses for disadvantaged people aged 65 or older were already covered under the Public Assistance Act (社會救助法), the National Health Insurance Act (全民健康保險法) and local governments’ medical subsidy regulations.
Local governments already allocate funding for these programs, and the amendments would not affect those obligations, he said.
TPP caucus director Vicky Chen (陳智菡) said the Public Assistance Act explicitly provides support for low-income and lower-middle-income households, as well as people affected by emergencies or disasters.
Local government social affairs departments administer the subsidies and allocate budgets accordingly, she said.
With separate legal provisions supporting medical assistance and local governments already budgeting for and implementing the programs, there was no basis for claiming the amendments had eliminated the subsidies, Chen said.
Expanding central government subsidies to cover NHI premiums for all people aged 65 or older could free up at least NT$20 billion (US$616.43 million) in local government funding for additional assistance to disadvantaged people, she said.
Lai was misleading the public and creating unnecessary panic, which was unacceptable, Chen added.
Responding to Shih’s warning about the potential additional costs for people younger than 64, Hung said the revised law required the central government to fully fund the subsidies through its annual social welfare budget, keeping the expense separate from the NHI fund.
The NHI fund still had about NT$200 billion and remained well above the statutory threshold that would trigger a premium increase, he said, urging Shih to stop spreading fear.
Most seniors have their NHI premiums paid by their working-age children, who are already supporting their own children and parents, he said.
Based on a monthly salary of NT$40,000, the amendments could save younger people about NT$14,000 annually, Hung added.
The Democratic Progressive Party government was spreading misinformation by portraying the policy as an additional burden on younger people, he said.
The problem with government spending was not a lack of money, but excessive and wasteful budget allocations, he said, questioning whether the government could not afford to spend a projected NT$38.8 billion annually on the policy.
"DPP mayoral candidates could advocate full NHI premium subsidies for people aged 65 and older, but opposition parties were apparently not allowed to do the same," Hung said.
Separately, KMT caucus secretary-general Hsu Yu-chen (許宇甄) said the amendments were primarily intended to transfer responsibility for subsidizing NHI premiums for eligible elderly people to the central government, expanding social protections rather than eliminating existing medical assistance.
A change to a single legal provision should not be interpreted as immediately ending all medical subsidies for disadvantaged people, Hsu said.
The National Health Insurance Act independently provides medical protections for disadvantaged people, which would remain in effect after the amendments, she said.
Article 36 of that act also provides mechanisms to help people experiencing financial hardships who cannot afford premiums or out-of-pocket expenses, including installment payments and other forms of assistance, she said.
Those protections do not depend on Article 22 of the Senior Citizens Welfare Act and would not be affected by the changes, Hsu added.
The Public Assistance Act also independently establishes the legal basis for medical subsidies for low-income and lower-middle-income households, she said.
Eligible disadvantaged people aged 65 or older could continue to apply for assistance through the social assistance system and would not lose their medical subsidies simply because the Senior Citizens Welfare Act had been amended, she added.

輕鬆華語 GO: EASY CHINESE GO

對話 Dialogue
華華：我家附近的市場開始賣菱角了，秋天真的到了！
Huáhuá: Wǒ jiā fùjìn de shìchǎng kāishǐ mài língjiǎo le, qiūtiān zhēn de dào le!
Photo: Unsplash / 照片： Unsplash
清清： 每年這個時候，我都會買一些回家吃。
Qīngqīng: Měinián zhège shíhou, wǒ dōu huì mǎi yìxiē huí jiā chī.
華華： 我很喜歡吃菱角，可是懶得剝殼。
Huáhuá: Wǒ hěn xǐhuān chī língjiǎo, kěshì lǎn de bōké.
清清： 我也是，所以我都直接買剝好的。
Qīngqīng: Wǒ yě shì, suǒyǐ wǒ dōu zhíjiē mǎi bō hǎo de.
華華： 剝好的比較貴吧？
Huáhuá: Bō hǎo de bǐjiào guì ba?
清清： 貴一點點而已，再說，吃的時候省時又省力。
Qīngqīng: Guì yìdiǎndiǎn ér yǐ, zàishuō, chī de shíhou shěngshí yòu shěnglì.
華華： 聽你這麼說，我下班也想去市場買一些。
Huáhuá: Tīng nǐ zhème shuō, wǒ xiàbān yě xiǎng qù shìchǎng mǎi yìxiē.
清清： 那你動作要快，秋天一過，就沒了！
Qīngqīng: Nà nǐ dòngzuò yào kuài, qiūtiān yí guò, jiù méi le!
翻譯 Translation
Huahua: The market near my home has started selling water caltrops. Autumn has really arrived.
Qingqing: Every year around this time, I buy some to eat at home.
Huahua: I really like water caltrops, but I’m too lazy to shell them.
Qingqing: Me too. That’s why I always buy the peeled ones.
Huahua: The peeled ones are more expensive, right?
Qingqing: They’re only a little more expensive. Besides, they save both time and effort when you eat them.
Huahua: Hearing you say that, I want to stop by the market and buy some after work.
Qingqing: Then you’d better hurry. Once autumn is over, they won’t be available for another year.
生詞 Vocabulary
1. 菱角 (língjiǎo) water caltrop
2. 懶 (lǎn) lazy; not feel like doing something
3. 剝殼 (bō ké) peel; remove the shell
4.省時省力 (shěng shí shěng lì) save time and effort
5. 直接 (zhíjiē) directly; simply
6. 剝好 (bō hǎo) already peeled; finish peeling
7. 再說 (zàishuō) besides / moreover / let’s talk about it later
8. 動作 (dòngzuò) action; movement

Starshield restrictions  disrupt Ukraine’s drone operations 烏克蘭無人機突遭「星盾」斷網　美國掌控權引發疑慮
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
16:45:59 UTC
01:45:59 KST

Sudden restrictions on Starshield — SpaceX’s military-grade version of the Starlink satellite Internet service and the backbone of Ukraine’s drone operations and communication — alarmed the country’s military and government officials last week, with commanders reporting lost drones and disrupted missions.
The episode raised fresh questions about Ukraine’s reliance on the Starshield program and who controls access to it.
The episode added to tensions between Kyiv and Washington, a relationship already strained by US President Donald Trump’s reported deal with Moscow on Russian diesel imports, which Ukraine viewed as a betrayal.
Photo: Reuters 照片：路透
What is Starshield?
Starshield is SpaceX’s satellite program for governments and the military. Built on Starlink technology, it is designed for national security missions and includes secure communications, Earth observation and satellites equipped with specialized sensors. It also incorporates additional encryption and security measures for sensitive government operations.
The Starlink system uses thousands of satellites in low Earth orbit to provide broadband connectivity to terminals on the ground, including in areas where conventional Internet infrastructure is unavailable or damaged.
Unlike Starlink, Starshield is tailored to government requirements and can include dedicated satellites and special equipment.
Starshield “is the version where you have much higher speeds, you have better connectivity and it’s not available for civilians; it’s available only for the military,” said Olena Tregub, founder and secretary-general of Ukraine’s Independent Anti-Corruption Commission.
Tregub said reliable, high-speed connectivity was essential for Ukrainian military operations involving drones and units moving rapidly on the ground and in the air. Operators need clear, real-time video feeds to identify what is happening and make decisions, she said.
Ukraine’s increasingly digital battlefield also relies on systems such as Delta, which helps manage and share battlefield data. Transmitting large volumes of information requires fast and reliable connections, Tregub said.
“It’s not just about being able to connect. We need to make sure that this speed is there, that it’s not reduced,” she said, adding that standard civilian Starlink access alone would not meet the military’s needs.
The US government is a major Starshield customer. SpaceX founder and CEO Elon Musk said last week that the US government owns and controls the system, with decisions about its use resting with the US military and, ultimately, the president. His remarks have fueled questions about who was responsible for the latest restrictions affecting Ukraine.
Photo: EPA 照片：歐新社
How are Starlink and Starshield linked?
Starlink and Starshield are different services, but they share much of the same technological foundation, including SpaceX’s satellite engineering and capabilities.
The difference lies in the customer, security needs and end purpose. Starlink provides commercial services, while Starshield is designed for government and national security missions.
The distinction is not always straightforward. Starshield can draw on the wider Starlink satellite network and related infrastructure, while also drawing on separate and dedicated satellites and systems.
Initially developed for commercial use, Starlink became a crucial communications tool after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. Its terminals have helped Ukrainian authorities, emergency services and military units stay connected despite Russian attacks on communications infrastructure.
On the front line, the service supports communications between military units and enables operations requiring a continuous connection between drones and their operators, including missions in which operators need to receive video while aircraft are in flight.
The Starlink and Starshield services are not interchangeable, even when they rely on overlapping technology.
For Ukraine, restrictions affecting particular terminals or military services do not necessarily mean the entire Starlink network has been switched off, neither does the continued operation of civilian terminals guarantee that specialized military connectivity will remain available.
The incident nevertheless reinforced the need for backup communications. Ukraine’s army was preparing alternative solutions, although they would be more expensive and less effective.(AP)
SpaceX旗下的「星盾」（Starshield）—即軍用版的「星鏈」（Starlink）衛星網路服務，是烏克蘭無人機作戰及通訊系統的重要支柱，但這項服務上週突然被限速，讓烏克蘭軍方及政府官員陣腳大亂。多名指揮官通報，部分無人機失聯，軍事任務也受到干擾。
這起事件再次引發外界對烏克蘭依賴星盾系統的疑慮，並質疑星盾的使用權限究竟是誰在掌控。
這也加劇了基輔與華府之間的緊張關係。此前，美國總統川普據報與莫斯科達成協議，開放進口俄羅斯柴油，已使美烏關係陷入緊張，烏克蘭更將這項協議視為背叛。
星盾是什麼?
星盾是SpaceX專為政府及軍方開發的衛星計畫，以星鏈技術為基礎，主要用於國家安全任務，包括安全通訊、地球觀測，以及搭載特殊感測器的衛星。星盾也採用額外的加密及安全措施，以支援涉及敏感資訊的政府行動。
星鏈系統利用數千顆部署在地球低軌道的衛星，為地面終端設備提供寬頻網路連線，涵蓋範圍包括傳統網路基礎設施無法使用或遭破壞的地區。
與星鏈不同，星盾是依照政府需求量身打造的服務，可包括專用衛星及特殊設備。
烏克蘭獨立反貪腐委員會（Independent Anti-Corruption Commission）創辦人兼秘書長歐蓮娜‧特雷古布表示：「星盾是速度更快、連線品質更好的版本，而且不對一般民眾開放，僅供軍方使用」。
特雷古布表示，對於涉及無人機，以及在地面與空中快速移動部隊的烏克蘭軍事行動而言，可靠的高速網路連線至關重要。操作人員需要清晰的即時影像，才能掌握現場情況並做出決策。
烏克蘭日益數位化的戰場，也仰賴「Delta」等戰情系統協助管理及共享戰場資料。特雷古布指出，傳輸大量資訊需要快速且可靠的網路連線。
她說：「這不只是能不能連上網路的問題。我們必須確保連線速度夠快，而且不會被降速」。她補充說，僅靠一般民用星鏈服務，無法滿足軍方需求。
美國政府是星盾的主要客戶。SpaceX創辦人兼執行長伊隆．馬斯克上週表示，美國政府擁有並控制星盾系統，其使用決策由美軍負責，最終決定權則在總統手中。馬斯克的說法也引發外界質疑，烏克蘭的星盾最近遭到限速，究竟是誰該負責。
星鏈與星盾有何關聯?
星鏈與星盾是兩種不同的服務，但兩者共享許多相同的技術基礎，包括SpaceX的衛星工程技術與相關功能。
兩者主要的差異在於服務對象、安全需求及最終用途。星鏈提供商業服務，而星盾則專為政府及國家安全任務設計。
不過，兩者的區別並不總是很明確。星盾可以利用更廣泛的星鏈衛星網路及相關基礎設施，同時也能使用獨立的專用衛星與系統。
星鏈最初是為商業用途開發，但自2022年2月俄羅斯全面入侵烏克蘭以來，已成為烏克蘭至關重要的通訊工具。儘管俄羅斯持續攻擊烏克蘭的通訊基礎設施，星鏈終端設備仍協助烏克蘭政府機關、緊急救援單位及軍事部隊維持通訊。
在前線，星鏈支援軍事部隊之間的通訊，並讓無人機與操作人員持續保持連線以執行任務，因為有些行動需要操作人員在無人機飛行時接收即時影像。
即使星鏈與星盾使用部分相同的技術，兩種服務仍無法相互取代。
對烏克蘭而言，這項區別十分重要，因為特定終端設備或軍事服務受到限制，並不一定代表整個星鏈網路都已關閉。同樣地，即使民用終端設備仍能正常運作，也不保證軍方專用的通訊服務能持續使用。
儘管如此，這起事件再次凸顯建立備援通訊系統的必要性。烏克蘭軍方正準備其他替代方案，但這些方案的成本將更高，效能也較差。
（台北時報林俐凱編譯）

Have you ever bought a product simply because everyone around you seemed to own one? Or have you ever supported an idea after seeing many classmates agree with it? If so, you have experienced the bandwagon effect, a psychological phenomenon in which people adopt certain behaviors, attitudes, or beliefs because others are doing the same. The term originates from 19th-century American politics. Campaign managers would hire a bandwagon, a decorated wagon carrying musicians, to parade through towns, attracting crowds and signaling popular support. Students need more than answers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
16:45:57 UTC
01:45:57 KST

In my English classroom at an elementary school in Taitung County, a nod does not always mean understanding. I can ask whether everyone understands, receive reassuring nods and then watch a child wait for classmates to begin before attempting the task. This happens every day.
If nodding were a reliable assessment tool, we could finish the curriculum by Wednesday — just in time for Sports Day.
That gap between appearing to understand and being able to proceed should inform how Taiwan’s schools evaluate artificial intelligence (AI). A clear explanation is valuable, but its educational worth becomes visible in what a student can do.
When I know a student needs support, I pair them with a classmate who understands the task. I become a facilitator, while the helper takes on a similar role. The helper explains, then lets their classmate try, offering guidance along the way.
The work remains the student’s own. The purpose is to help a classmate move through a difficult task, while preserving the opportunity to think through and attempt the task.
This creates two responsibilities. The student must engage with the work. The helper must make an explanation useful to someone else. Knowing an answer becomes the starting point for communication, rather than its conclusion.
My responsibility continues throughout the process. I watch who explains, who attempts the task and where guidance is needed. A correct answer matters, but so does the route by which the pair reach it. If one student supplies the answer and the other merely records it that tells me little about understanding.
There is another distinction to make. Hesitation can signal unfamiliar vocabulary, unclear instructions or uncertainty about how to begin. It does not automatically identify the problem. The teacher must investigate, and remain willing to revise an initial judgement.
These routine decisions are easily overlooked in discussions about educational technology. An explanation can be accurate and still fail to meet a learner’s immediate need. Additional information might help, but sometimes the child needs an opportunity to try with someone nearby.
This leads me to a question for Taiwanese schools considering AI: Does the assistance preserve the student’s opportunity to think, attempt and explain?
A system that supplies a finished response might make an exercise easier to complete. A system used to offer a hint, suggest another explanation or prompt a further attempt could serve a different purpose.
Schools should examine that difference when deciding how a tool should be used in a lesson, if at all. The same principle should shape teacher training. Demonstrating how to generate teaching materials is useful. Teachers also need opportunities to consider what happens after those materials reach children, how misunderstanding becomes visible, when assistance is appropriate and how to check whether a student can proceed.
Peer support is no automatic solution either. Knowing the material does not make a child an effective guide. The helper needs direction, and both students need the teacher’s attention. My classroom offers a perspective on these decisions, rather than a formula for every school.
The wider lesson is that assistance should develop a learner’s capacity to act. In elementary-school classrooms, the value of AI should be judged partly by whether it supports that work. The helper who explains and then allows a classmate to try illustrates something important: Useful knowledge must leave room for the other person’s effort.
AI might know the answer. The educator must still see the person behind the question — and help students learn to see one another.
Casper J.H. Keller teaches English and drama at an elementary school in Taitung County and has more than 25 years of international teaching and leadership experience.

Liberte, Egalite, Misery? Why France is burning
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
16:45:50 UTC
01:45:50 KST

Anyone walking along the boulevards of Paris on Sunday afternoon would have sensed the “shame and anger” described by French President Emmanuel Macron after a weekend of rioting.
Smashed-in storefronts, boarded-up windows and charred makeshift barricades hinted at the looting that hit about 1,500 stores across the country. Dozens of armored cops were still standing guard, shields raised, after a night when 500 people were taken into custody in the French capital alone. Amid the chaos, one lone bystander with a broom quietly sweeping up broken glass.
It is not only France that is feeling the heat. Anger about rising inflation, from energy prices to housing costs, has led to clashes in Italy and Portugal. It might also cost US President Donald Trump the US midterm elections given the impact of his folly in the Strait of Hormuz on oil prices, even as he gleefully tries to deflect attention by pointing fingers at Paris.
Still, France’s propensity to descend into unrest has become scarily regular, as has the inability of Macron’s administration to get a grip. Which begs the question: Why is one of the rich world’s biggest public spenders again on fire? This is after all a highly redistributive country that has racked up an extra 1 trillion euros (US$1.12 trillion) of borrowing since 2019. Yet surveys indicate that French on average lack 500 euros a month to comfortably cover their outgoings, making them vulnerable to sudden changes in their economic situation — and likelier to protest.
On one level, the sparks that lit the flames this time around included multiple short-term political failures that echo the “yellow vest” riots of 2018. The authorities clearly were not expecting more than 500,000 people to take to the streets nationwide, let alone the thousands of looters in Marseille.
The mayor of Limoges, whose town hall was broken into and gutted by fire, has called for more resources for police force he described as outgunned by far-left opportunists. The government’s inability to engage with or defuse earlier protests by high schoolers — driven by a lack of fiscal headroom to throw money at the problem as bond yields, and hence state borrowing costs, rise — fueled the fire.
However, the discontent that provided the kindling was already there. One big reason is that French public spending is allocated in a very lopsided way.
Compare the France of 2024 with that of 1974 — the last year it balanced the budget — and there has been very little change in spending on public services such as security, the courts or education as a percentage of GDP. It has risen by just 0.1-0.3 points, former government adviser Antoine Foucher said.
The biggest beneficiaries, as usual in the West, are pensioners. Spending on them has jumped by about 6.5 points, with successive governments prioritizing a generous and long retirement over the future of young people entering education and the workforce. Almost one-third of France’s education budget goes on pensions, which might explain why teachers’ wages are below the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development average.
Alongside the frustrations of underpaid public servants are signs that adding more jobs in the private sector — the focus of Macron’s labor-market reforms — increasingly does not pay. That 500 euro monthly gap in people’s monthly outgoings is hard to fill via the career ladder as lower productivity, declining education standards and an innovation lag drag wages down while ever-higher social charges eat into take-home pay. The French National Institute of Statistics and Economic Studies has estimated that an employer raising a minimum-wage worker’s salary by about 440 euros would result in a take-home gain of only 100 euros. It is perhaps no coincidence that it took a tax-free bonus of about 500 euros to quell the 2018 yellow vests’ anger. Le Monde estimates that the French median wage has risen 22.8 percent since 2017, outpaced by inflation of 23.4 percent.
That does not excuse the weekend’s violence. French purchasing power is slowing down rather than screeching into reverse. Yet the combination of grievance politics, intergenerational unfairness and an inescapable sense of decline is what makes France feel so fragile despite its size, and its still strengths — such as a nuclear-powered electricity grid and first-class engineering talent. It also makes compromise harder, with the new yellow vests bemoaning low wages and high taxes alongside the masked mobs spray-painting “ACAB,” an acronym for “all cops are bastards.”
With Macron a spent force, the question now is next year’s presidential election. The sight of towns and cities on fire would doubtless create new supporters for far-right leader Marine Le Pen. Her extreme-left opponent Jean-Luc Melenchon is being seen as the instigator of the mayhem on the streets. In a vote dominated by cost-of-living and security fears, the far right holds several cards — including the Trumpian promise of putting hundreds of euros into people’s pockets through cutting payments to the EU.
Still, six months is an age in politics. Le Pen’s plans involve billions in new spending and lack credibility, Bloomberg Economics said. Voters are slowly starting to understand that rising state debt is a problem. Meanwhile, center-left politician Raphael Glucksmann, who has ruled out an alliance with Melenchon, is enjoying a poll surge of his own.
However, what is missing in this crowded race, as elsewhere in Europe, is honesty on the reforms that are needed — from politicians and the aging electorates that are blocking inescapable change.
Lionel Laurent is a Bloomberg Opinion columnist writing about the future of money and the future of Europe. Previously, he was a reporter for Reuters and Forbes. This column reflects the personal views of the author and does not necessarily reflect the opinion of the editorial board or Bloomberg LP and its owners.

Workers rally in Taipei, demanding better wages
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
16:45:50 UTC
01:45:50 KST

Hundreds of workers yesterday rallied outside the Presidential Office Building in Taipei, demanding higher wages, increased employer pension contributions and clearer profit-sharing rules, amid a wave of strikes and strike authorization votes across Taiwan.
Participants representing dozens of labor unions from across Taiwan gathered on Ketagalan Boulevard before marching through nearby streets past the Legislative Yuan and returning to the boulevard.
Taiwan Solidarity Front Confederation of Trade Unions chairman Ho Cheng-chia (何政家) criticized what he felt was an outdated labor pension system.
Photo: CNA
Introduced in July 2005, the new labor pension system consists of retirement accounts for individual workers and requires employers to contribute at least 6 percent of an employee’s salary to the account every month.
The employee can voluntarily contribute an additional 6 percent to increase the amount saved. The total built up in the fund can be collected in a lump sum or as a monthly annuity upon retirement as long as contributions have been made for at least 15 years.
Ho said that it was time to increase the employer’s minimum 6 percent obligation, saying it was too low to ensure adequate retirement savings and that an increase would help make up for 21 years of insufficient contributions.
“We hope to raise it to 9 percent first and then gradually to 15 percent,” he said, adding that employers’ annual retirement costs per worker under the old pension system were estimated at about 12 percent of wages.
Government figures show that about 7.87 million workers had contributions made under the new system as of July, while an estimated 115,000 were exclusively under the old system as of December last year.
The new labor pension system is one of the two retirement plans that most workers in Taiwan qualify for.
The other is the “old-age benefits” under the labor insurance system. The current labor insurance premium is 11.5 percent of salaries, capped at NT$45,800 per month, with employers paying 70 percent.
Because of the relatively low salary cap, retirement benefits under the insurance system are limited to less than US$900 a month.
Both systems are run by the Ministry of Labor’s Bureau of Labor Insurance.
Ho also urged amendments to Article 29 of the Labor Standards Act (勞動基準法) to establish clearer requirements for distributing company profits to employees, saying that economic gains should benefit workers beyond the technology sector.
Chunghwa Telecom Workers’ Union chairman Teng Ke-lien (鄧克?) said its Taoyuan and Kaohsiung branches had passed strike authorization votes, with other branches set to hold votes in succession.
The union, which launched the vote to demand higher pay amid what Teng described as record company profits, has about 20,000 members across 26 branches, representing nearly all company employees.
“Striking is just a means, not our goal,” Teng said, urging management to “respond positively” to workers’ demands, adding that a walkout was unlikely before year-end.
Under Article 35 of the Labor Union Act (工會法), employers are barred from retaliating against workers for participating in union activities or labor disputes.
Responding to the protest, the ministry said it remained “open” to raising employer pension contributions, but added that changes required “careful evaluation.”
It also highlighted environmental, social and governance assessment incentives for listed companies that voluntarily increase their contribution rates.
The ministry also pointed to minimum wage reviews and collective bargaining incentives to promote pay raises and profit-sharing, urging employers to consider raising existing employees’ salaries as the monthly minimum wage increases from NT$29,500 this year to NT$30,900 next year.

Adam Hinton, the first overall pick in the TPBL draft, scored 16 points in his regular-season debut on Sunday, but his team, the Kaohsiung Aquas, squandered a 20-point lead, losing 115-114 to defending champions the Formosa Dreamers.
Playing with a protective mask due to a nasal fracture sustained during practice, Hinton added seven rebounds in the Aquas’ season opener at Taichung Intercontinental Basketball Stadium.
He scored his first professional points on two free throws less than a minute into the game, before making his first field goal on a driving layup. He finished the opening quarter with eight points and had 14 by halftime, helping the Aquas build a 63-49 lead.
Photo: CNA
The Aquas almost secured a winning start when Hinton drew a foul on a drive and sank both free throws with about 41 seconds remaining, putting the team ahead 114-113.
However, with about seven seconds left on the clock, Dreamers guard Lin Chun-chi came back with a midrange jumper. Grant Basile missed the Aquas’ final shot, sealing the home team’s comeback victory.
Hinton, a 23-year-old Cornell University graduate who was the TPBL’s first overall pick on July 16, said he regretted the loss and would review his performance, with the hope of improving before his next game.
The intensity of his debut game was as expected, he said, adding that he felt comfortable seeing several familiar faces on the opposing team.
Basile led the Aquas with a game-high 36 points and 14 rebounds. Lin and Brandon Gilbeck shared the Dreamers’ scoring lead with 23 points apiece, with Gilbeck collecting 15 rebounds.
The Dreamers won their first TPBL championship last season after overcoming a 3-1 deficit in the finals with three back to back victories, securing the franchise’s first domestic professional league title.
The TPBL is one of Taiwan’s two professional basketball leagues, alongside the P.League+.
Its seven teams each play 36 regular-season games, split evenly between home and away fixtures.
Four teams advance to the playoffs, with the top three qualifying directly, while the fourth and fifth-place finishers contest a play-in series for the remaining berth.

Group calls for penalties for e-cigarette possession
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
16:45:46 UTC
01:45:46 KST

The Alliance on Obligatory Education yesterday urged the Legislative Yuan to pass an amendment to the Tobacco Hazards Prevention Act (菸害防制法) that would provide a legal basis for issuing penalties for possessing e-cigarettes.
The act already prohibits the manufacture, importation, sale, supply, display, advertising and use of e-cigarettes.
The Health Promotion Administration (HPA) this year proposed to amend the act to add possession to that list, which was approved by the Executive Yuan and submitted to the legislature for review.
Photo: Rachel Lin, Taipei Times
“The number of disposed e-cigarette devices cannot be used to directly infer the actual circulation volume of e-cigarettes, nor does it mean the problem has been solved,” alliance president Wang Han-yang (王瀚陽) said yesterday, referring to the HPA’s e-cigarette disposal bins set up across the country.
The agency last week said it had collected about 633kg of e-cigarettes since the collection scheme began on Sept. 8.
If the HPA-proposed amendment is approved, e-cigarettes would be confiscated, but no fines would be issued within a one-month grace period, after which people found possessing them would face a fine of NT$30,000 to NT$100,000, Wang said.
An HPA survey from last year found that more than 40,000 adolescents use e-cigarettes, with 2.1 percent of junior-high school students and 5.1 percent of high-school and vocational school students saying them used them.
E-cigarettes can be used as delivery systems for illicit substances, such as etomidate, classified as a Category 1 narcotic in Taiwan, Wang said.
Tobacco use among young people is often driven by factors such as family influence, peer pressure and marketing, Taiwan Medical Alliance for the Control of Tobacco secretary-general Guo Fei-ran (郭斐然) said.
Minister of Health and Welfare Shih Chung-liang (石崇良) said the ministry hopes the legislature would pass the amendments as soon as possible.
As for opposition parties’ concern about not having enough law enforcement personnel to inspect and seize e-cigarettes, he said the ministry has discussed the issue with the Ministry of Education and local governments, and that funding would be allocated to address the shortage.

NTHU to explore research reactor development with NuCube
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
16:45:42 UTC
01:45:42 KST

National Tsing Hua University (NTHU) yesterday signed an agreement with US nuclear microreactor developer NuCube Energy to explore replacing the university’s aging Tsing Hua Open-pool Reactor (THOR).
The cooperation would assess technology, research applications and deployment feasibility to sustain nuclear education, research and medical services, NTHU said in a statement.
Potential applications include boron neutron capture therapy, a cancer treatment, and isotope production, the university said.
Photo: Lo Pei-de, Taipei Times
NTHU president W. John Kao (高為元) and NuCube CEO Cristian Rabiti signed the agreement at a news conference in Taipei, an exploratory step toward possible deployment of a NuCube microreactor to replace THOR, which began operating in 1961 and is scheduled to be decommissioned in 2040.
Speaking afterward, Yeh Tsung-kuang (葉宗洸), dean of NTHU’s College of Nuclear Science, described the partnership as mutually beneficial: The university wants to understand NuCube’s reactors, while its expertise could help expand their research and medical applications.
NuCube is planning its first deployment for the end of 2029, Rabiti told the news conference.
"Today we signed; from tomorrow the real work will start," he said. "We have a lot to do together."
NTHU hopes to install a reactor within two years after NuCube achieves commercial operation in the US, the university said.
Contact with the Nuclear Safety Commission was already under way, Yeh said.
NuCube is separately working with Idaho State University on a proposed research and test reactor intended for education and technology demonstration rather than electricity generation.
NTHU said that it would invite Taiwanese manufacturers to participate in equipment and component supply, and could share deployment experience and provide technical advice to interested companies.
The agreement follows a podcast interview released on Friday last week in which President William Lai (賴清德) said restarting existing nuclear reactors would require assurances of safety, a solution for nuclear waste and public consensus.
"We should not exclude any energy source because of ideology, nor disregard environmental sustainability for short-term benefits," Lai said.
Existing reactor restart procedures should proceed and ultimately be decided by professionals, he added.
Regarding workforce development, NTHU’s Institute of Nuclear Engineering and Science attracted 66 applicants for 11 places this year, Yeh said, describing the interest as unprecedented in the past decade.
Previously, attracting even 11 applicants had been difficult, he said, attributing the increase in interest to a changing policy climate.

Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19

01:45:41 KST

Hard lessons from a brutal tour of South Africa appear to have paid off for Dave Rennie’s All Blacks, with the team able to shrug off a litany of injuries and crush Australia in the Bledisloe Cup series.
It is going to be a depleted New Zealand squad heading north for the final Nations Championship tests against England, Scotland and Wales, with outside back Leroy Carter added on Monday to the list of players staying home after having surgery on an ankle injury.
Shannon Frizell and Samisoni Taukei’aho might be sidelined after suffering injuries in the win in Sydney on Saturday.
Photo: EPA
However, growing confidence in their squad depth a year out from the World Cup could outweigh the concerns.
Three successive defeats by world champions South Africa exposed shortcomings in Rennie’s side but they look stronger for the experience gained by fringe players and a return to form by veterans who had been written off.
The benefits were evident in their second successive demolition of the Wallabies, a 43-21 triumph following their 50-19 stroll at Eden Park.
The players unavailable for Sydney could have filled much of a starting 15, with Ardie Savea, Richie Mo’unga and Luke Jacobson among them.
They lost Jordie Barrett before kick-off and Quinn Tupaea early with concussion, but there was little sign of disruption as the All Blacks ran in six first-half tries at Stadium Australia to all but kill off the game by the interval.
“We’ve used 50-odd players this year, creating depth and competition for places. We’re missing a few influential players but other guys step up,” said Rennie.
With Savea and Jacobson missing, Peter Lakai and Wallace Sititi stood in at the back row with Tupou Vaa’i, the trio leaving the Wallabies’ back three in the shade.
The injury count has been a blessing for veterans Beauden Barrett and Damian McKenzie, with the former underlining his enduring value at fullback and the latter steering the All Blacks flawlessly at flyhalf in the absence of Ruben Love and Mo’unga.
The Wallabies had few answers for the All Blacks’ try-scoring blitzes in the second half at Eden Park and the first at Stadium Australia.
The Sydney win was another endorsement of Rennie’s up-tempo attacking game, with New Zealand rediscovering the speed, ambition and clinical finishing that were hallmarks of their back-to-back World Cup wins in 2011 and 2015.
“The Greatest Rivalry” tour of South Africa failed to live up to its billing but All Blacks fans may be glad to look back on it as a great turning point if World Cup glory awaits.

Thawing permafrost makes town’s water undrinkable
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
16:45:41 UTC
01:45:41 KST

Residents of a remote town in Norway that is in one of the fastest-warming places in the world have been told they must no longer drink tap water due to heavy metal contamination that scientists have linked to the thawing permafrost.
Longyearbyen, in the archipelago of Svalbard, gets its main drinking water supply from a 2.5km dammed lake called Isdammen, or “ice pond.” Higher temperatures as a result of the climate crisis have thawed permafrost, leading to newly exposed bedrock leaching metals into the pond.
Longyearbyen, about 1,300km from the north pole, is warming at between five and seven times the world’s average rate, with autumn temperatures rising at up to 4oC a decade.
Heavy metal contamination of the water supply is likely to be linked to two factors, researchers say: the thawing of permafrost — rock-hard ground that remains frozen all year apart from a so-called “active layer” that thaws in summer — and the geology of the former mining town.
“The combination of the thawing permafrost and the shale bedrock, which contains a mineral called pyrite, or fool’s gold, is causing contamination of its water supply,” said Marjolaine Verret, a permafrost expert and associate professor in Arctic geology at the University Centre in Svalbard.
When pyrite came into contact with water and oxygen, it oxidized and generated acidity, she said.
“The acid produced can now leach heavy metals from these rocks into the waterways. The issue we’ve been having here in Longyearbyen is manganese, but other contaminants can be leached out from the rocks,” she added.
The municipality, Longyearbyen lokalstyre, first alerted its 2,600 residents after manganese levels in the water supply were found to be 25 times higher than the 50 micrograms per liter recommended by the Norwegian Institute of Public Health, in September last year.
Longyearbyen Mayor Terje Aunevik said that while drinking water quality had never been good, due to sediment, the manganese levels had “gone ballistic.”
Prolonged exposure to high levels of manganese can cause neurological problems, particularly in children and infants.
Emergency, temporary measures were rolled out, including the installation of a central tank of free purified water, filtered by the local brewery, for residents to refill containers at the local supermarket, and an investigation was launched.
Manganese levels have since dropped, but earlier this year sulfate and nickel levels were found to exceed recommended drinking water limits. As a result, the ban remains in place.
Aunevik said that while manganese levels were “not dangerous,” government guidelines had to be followed.
The drinking water crisis had created a lot of “noise,” with some residents angry at the inconvenience, he said.
The mayor, who has commissioned an investigation into water quality, said a “completely new water mains supply” might be needed.
Potential solutions being considered were installing a filtration system to Isdammen and having a desalination plant as a backup, or the other way around.
Either way was “extremely expensive” and, due to the extreme temperatures of Svalbard, with water temperatures often below zero, would include technical challenges, Aunevik said.
“In Norway, where we have always taken for granted that we can drink the water from the tap, it is challenging to start thinking that we need to carry our water like we do now. Other small communities should be precautious and start thinking of what to do if it happens to their sources,” Aunevik said.
Verret and other scientists have warned that the contamination of water sources in Longyearbyen could be a foretaste of what is to come for Arctic communities.
“These ingredients [bedrock rich in pyrite and heavy metals] and thawing permafrost are present in other parts of the arctic so this could be a first example of how climate change can impact freshwater, for example in northern Canada and Alaska,” Verret said.
