====================================================================================================

Biohackers claim this supplement lets you drink coffee at night. No one knows if it’s safe
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
15:29:17 UTC
00:29:17 KST

Few substances are more beloved than caffeine. Every day, as many as nine in 10 Americans drink a caffeinated beverage, increasingly in a stronger form such as an energy drink. But the stimulant has a massive drawback: consume too much after a certain hour, and you can kiss your sleep schedule goodbye. To get around this, biohackers are turning to an unproven supplement to try flush caffeine out their bodies fast. It promises the best of both worlds: a quick, anytime energy boost and a good night’s sleep. But does it work?
Caffeine has a half-life of roughly five hours, meaning it takes about that time, on average, for the initial dosage to reduce by 50 percent in your bloodstream. Depending on the person, caffeine’s stimulant effects can take up to 12 hours to fully wear off. That’s why some people find themselves unable to wind down at night after a 3 P.M. coffee.
That’s where rutaecarpine comes in. Among biohacking enthusiasts and one of Silicon Valley’s most influential blogs, the substance has been touted as a way to process caffeine much faster than the body does naturally. Rutaecarpine by itself hasn’t been tested in humans, but it has been shown to help metabolize caffeine more rapidly in rats.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
More recently, rutaecarpine has been picked up by fitness influencers such as Thomas DeLauer, a YouTuber with more than four million subscribers. It’s also been promoted as a weight-loss aid that allows users to enjoy the appetite-suppressing effects of caffeine in large doses without the sleep deprivation.
We dug into what the science behind rutaecarpine is and whether the claims about its caffeine-canceling effects hold up. Here’s what you need to know.
How rutaecarpine works
Rutaecarpine is derived from the fruit of a plant called Tetradium ruticarpum; it has also been known as Evodia rutaecarpa, among other names. This fruit has been used in traditional Chinese medicine to treat ailments such as headaches, vomiting, diarrhea, abdominal pain and period pain for more than 2,000 years. Rutaecarpine hasn’t been studied, however, in clinical trials in humans.
In rats, rutaecarpine works by provoking the liver into producing more CYP1A2, an enzyme that breaks down caffeine in the body and first converts it into a compound called paraxanthine. Rats with higher-than-normal concentrations of CYP1A2 break down caffeine much faster than untreated rats.
People who promote rutaecarpine say it increases the level of CYP1A2 in your body, allowing you to enjoy the benefits of coffee without delaying sleep. Humans vary naturally in how quickly their bodies clear caffeine, which is in part because of individual differences in CYP1A2 and caffeine sensitivity, which is linked primarily to ADORA2A, the gene for the adenosine receptor that caffeine blocks.
Despite the lack of clinical evidence, rutaecarpine is readily available at mainstream online retailers such as Amazon and iHerb, both in its concentrated form and in its traditional herbal form. When sold as a supplement, it doesn’t require the same approval from the U.S. Food and Drug Administration as a medication does, meaning it is not tested for safety or effectiveness.
Is rutaecarpine safe?
A 2024 paper in Toxics that looked at mice and human cell cultures suggests that rutaecarpine could present a serious danger when it is mixed with one of the most common drugs on the planet: acetaminophen, or Tylenol. Bill Baldwin, a professor of biological sciences at Clemson University, who edited the study, says the evidence we have so far “suggests that you have to be careful with this co-treatment. You have to be very careful.”
The reason why has to do with how rutaecarpine works.
“CYP1A2, along with a couple of other enzymes, is known to take acetaminophen and produce NAPQI, which is a powerful oxidant,” Baldwin explains. “This leads to damage within the liver, and this damage would typically not happen due to acetaminophen unless you would overdose or you would take [acetaminophen] with alcohol.”
The broader research into rutaecarpine’s safety profile is more mixed, however. A 2021 mouse study, for example, found that mice that were given rutaecarpine every day for a week actually appeared protected against acetaminophen-related liver damage. Meanwhile the fruit that rutaecarpine comes from has repeatedly been linked to liver toxicity in animal studies. Again, rutaecarpine has never been through a clinical trial, so it’s hard to say what it does in humans.
Acetaminophen isn’t the only potential interaction. CYP1A2 breaks down numerous other common drugs, such as the asthma drug theophylline and the antipsychotics clozapine and olanzapine.
Pieter Cohen, an associate professor of medicine at Harvard Medical School, says that rutaecarpine “does not have safety data to support its use.” In addition, there are potential concerns around heart and liver damage raised by animal studies that should give pause, he says.
Cohen adds that he is “not aware” of any medication or substance that can “safely offset the effects of caffeine.”
If people do choose to take supplements, Cohen recommends picking substances that have only one plant extract on the label, do not make health claims and have been certified by a high-quality third-party supplement screening organization, such as the U.S. Pharmacopeia.
Are there better alternatives?
The best strategy for consuming caffeine later in the day without sacrificing sleep is to switch to beverages with a lower concentration, such as green tea. Another option is to try engaging in natural energy-boosting activities, such as taking light exercise or a quick nap. Cohen recommends not consuming more than 100 milligrams of caffeine, roughly equivalent to an eight-ounce (237-milliliter) cup of coffee, after 1 P.M.
If you must go the chemical route, safer alternatives may exist. Paraxanthine, the compound that caffeine is converted to in the body, has also been picking up steam as a supplement among biohackers. And it’s started to appear in mainstream energy drinks and supplements, including one recently co-founded by Kim Kardashian. One of the selling points of paraxanthine is that it has a shorter half-life than caffeine, meaning it reaches 50 percent of initial dosage sooner in the bloodstream.
Small-scale studies in humans indicate that paraxanthine may improve attention, reaction time and short-term memory compared with a placebo, with no known safety issues at doses of up to 200 mg. The evidence of these benefits is substantially lacking compared with that of the effects of caffeine, however, and many of the existing studies of paraxanthine were funded by supplement companies looking to sell the compound.
Considering how ever present caffeine is in our society, wanting to mitigate its unwanted side effects is understandable. T. ruticarpum may have a centuries-long history in traditional Chinese medicine, but that isn’t the same as clinical evidence.
“Any highly concentrated individual compound, regardless of whether it originated in a plant or a chemist’s laboratory, poses the same challenges,” Cohen reiterates. “We must first determine if it is safe for human consumption.”

Ethiopia’s forever wars are lesson for Iran - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
15:28:57 UTC
00:28:57 KST

Modern Ethiopia’s immense tragedy serves as a troubling example of the structural failure of the ethnic-linguistic federalism imposed upon a historical African giant, with devastating consequences for the second most populous nation in Africa.
Beyond triggering internal conflict, this model’s right to secession enabled Eritrea to secede in 1993 (and was since enshrined in Ethiopia’s constitution in 1995). As a result, Ethiopia lost access to the sea and became the world’s most populous landlocked country. This is an existential national security crisis.
Ethiopia’s experience is a warning to those advocating similar ethnic-linguistic federalism for historically cohesive states, including Iran. Modern Ethiopia’s story also illustrates the dangers of such an approach, as political fragmentation and competing ethnic interests have contributed to recurring conflict and national disintegration.
Ethiopia is historically celebrated as one of the oldest civilizations in the world, endowed with a rich and magnificent culture. The ancient Persian prophet Mani, writing in the third century CE, during the Sasanian Empire, recognized Axum (ancient Ethiopia) alongside Persia, China, and Rome as one of the four great civilizations of the world.
Yet, this millennia-old continuity was abruptly shattered in the late 1960s, hijacked not by foreign conquest, but by a toxic wave of radical Marxism. In 1969, a Marxist student activist named Wallelign Mekonnen published a highly controversial essay that marked the modern misfortune and tragedy of Ethiopia.
His fatal premise was that Ethiopia was not a cohesive, singular nation, but rather a collection of distinct “multi-nations,” where every single nation and ethnic group possessed the right to self-determination, including secession. This concept effectively turned neighbors into rivals overnight by legalizing national fracture.
Marxist military forces overthrew the centuries-old Ethiopian monarchy in 1974.
The seeds planted by Mekonnen’s ideology began to dictate state policy. The revolutionary forces that later took power ultimately institutionalized a new ethnic-linguistic federal system.
The architecture of fracture: Ethnic-linguistic federalism
Following the capture of the capital, Addis Ababa, by rebels in 1991, a system of regions based on ethnic-linguistic federalism was eventually institutionalized. The practical implementation of this system yielded disastrous consequences. People who had lived together for generations were suddenly driven out and expelled from their homes simply because they belonged to a different ethnic group.
Furthermore, each ethnic region maintained its own regional paramilitary forces.
Though the ethnic Tigrayan group constitutes about 6% of Ethiopia’s total population, the Tigray People’s Liberation Front-led forces took over the capital in 1991 and ruled the country for 27 years. During this era, the Tigrayan regional forces built the most formidable, battle-tested, and heavily armed regional militia in the country.
Eritrean independence
Driven by identity-based political changes and following a protracted war, Eritrea declared independence from Ethiopia in 1993, and Ethiopia completely lost its access to the sea.
Despite possessing a highly strategic geographic position along the Red Sea coast, Eritrea failed to prosper and devolved into a poor country, ruled by one of the most isolated, closed, and brutal dictatorships in the world.
In 1991, as Ethiopia descended into political chaos and rebel forces approached Addis Ababa, Israel launched one of the most remarkable rescue operations in the country’s history – Operation Solomon.
In less than two days, around 14,300 Ethiopian Jews were flown to Israel, escaping the rapidly deteriorating security situation. In a matter of hours, the operation changed the fate of thousands of people and became a defining chapter in the history of Ethiopian Jews. For Israel, the operation remains a source of national pride.
In 2018, Abiy Ahmed became the new prime minister of Ethiopia, promising to restore order, strengthen national unity, and dismantle or integrate regional paramilitary forces. Predictably, the Tigrayan regional forces fiercely resisted the central government’s efforts.
In 2020, operating under the banner of the TPLF, the regional forces of Tigray launched a coordinated military assault against government forces and later advanced toward the capital. They were ultimately defeated, but the human cost of this ethnic-centric conflict was staggering – between 2020 and 2022 alone, more than 500,000 people perished in the ensuing civil war. Women were among the primary victims of this tribal warfare.
Somaliland dimension
Before European colonizers arrived in the Horn of Africa, the contemporary states of Somalia (formerly an Italian colony), Somaliland (a British protectorate), and Djibouti (a French colony) did not exist.
In 1960, southern Somalia gained independence from Italy, and British Somaliland gained independence from Great Britain. Upon its independence, 35 nations, including the permanent members of the UN Security Council and Israel, recognized the State of Somaliland.
Five days later, Somaliland voluntarily entered a union with southern Somalia. However, the union proved disastrous; Somaliland suffered brutal persecution and systemic mass killings by the central government in Mogadishu. Consequently, in 1991, Somaliland dissolved the union, reasserting its independence as a distinct, sovereign nation.
This was the case of a sovereign nation that voluntarily joined a union and subsequently separated from it.
Eritrean independence stripped Ethiopia of its entire coastline, making it a landlocked nation. Consequently, Ethiopia’s vital imports have been forced to flow almost exclusively through neighboring Djibouti. Desperate for a sovereign sea outlet, Ethiopia began looking for alternatives.
Somaliland, which has over 800 km. of coastline along the Gulf of Aden, extended a historic proposition to Ethiopia: a long-term land lease to grant Ethiopia direct sea access, in exchange for official diplomatic recognition of Somaliland’s independence.
Ethiopia has not yet officially recognized Somaliland because of political considerations, although the two countries signed a Memorandum of Understanding in 2024 to lease a 20 km. stretch of coastline.
Regional alignments and hostility
This evolving geopolitical arrangement and the presence of Israel and the UAE in Somaliland have provoked a fierce counter-alignment:
1) The Turkish and Islamist alignment in Somalia:
Turkey has established a massive military presence and military bases in Somalia, a nation engulfed in a brutal civil war where a significant portion of the territory remains under the active control of the Islamist Al-Shabaab terrorist group.
Turkey’s objective of countering the UAE and Israeli presence in Somaliland will suffer a significant blow if Ethiopia officially recognizes Somaliland and establishes a close military alliance with Israel.
2) The resurgence of domestic insurgency and Eritrea:
The 2022 peace agreement in Ethiopia was suddenly shattered last month when the armed TPLF forces launched violent military offensives against Ethiopian federal government forces.
In response, Addis Ababa vehemently accused the Eritrean government of actively backing the TPLF rebels. Consequently, Ethiopia completely severed all diplomatic relations with Eritrea.
The strategic alliance with Israel
Following Israel’s official recognition of Somaliland in 2025, a critical geopolitical pathway opened for Ethiopia.
Confronted with hostile Islamist currents, Turkey’s heavy presence and Islamic terrorists in Somalia, and a Muslim Brotherhood-aligned government in Sudan, Ethiopia urgently needs serious strategic allies – above all Israel, alongside the UAE and India. This alignment centers on the development and security of Somaliland’s Port of Berbera, providing Ethiopia with a counterweight against regional adversaries and securing its maritime trade and national interests.
For Ahmed’s government, now in the midst of more civil turmoil, permanent access to the sea is more than an economic objective. Through recognition of Somaliland and a strategic alliance with Israel to access its battle-tested military technology, it has become a vital requirement for national security and state survival.
The Iranian lesson
Ethiopia’s ongoing tragedy is not an isolated African crisis. Rather, it is a live-action preview of what awaits Iran, with its multitude of ethnic groups, if it falls into the intellectual trap of ethnic-linguistic federalism.
The choice for historically cohesive nations appears obvious: either maintain a unified, citizen-based national fabric, or embrace tribal divisions and accept a future of eternal conflict, economic strangulation, and ultimate disintegration.
Tina Ghazimorad is the communications director to Prince Reza Pahlavi and an Iranian journalist who previously served as editor-in-chief of news at Manoto TV, a UK-based Persian-language television network.
Alex Winston is the news editor for The Jerusalem Post.

Inside the US defense giant: CET Sandbox helps Israeli founders find their way in America
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
15:28:57 UTC
00:28:57 KST

WASHINGTON — The US defense industrial base is a world of its own. Major contractors, military acquisition offices, government agencies, investors, and established networks of decision-makers can make it difficult for even the most promising start-up with battle-proven solutions to know where to begin.
Breaking into the US defense industrial base is not only a matter of showing up with battlefield-proven technology. It is a maze of prime contractors, acquisition offices, government agencies, and entrenched networks that can shut out even the most established Israeli start-ups. CET Sandbox arrived at AUSA determined to change that.
More than 60 Israeli founders spent the week in Washington in a program built to give them what most lack: access. Instead of wandering the vast exhibition halls hoping for chance encounters, CET Sandbox moved them directly into private receptions, curated introductions, and closed-door conversations with the people who actually shape US defense procurement.
The premise is simple. Israeli companies often bring technology validated under real operational conditions, but translating that into American contracts requires a different playbook, one built on relationships, timing, and an understanding of how the US system makes decisions. CET Sandbox is trying to give Israeli founders that playbook.
“We're extremely happy with how AUSA went,” David Yahid, co-founder and chief operating officer of CET, told Defense & Tech by The Jerusalem Post. “Seeing the founders connect with the US ecosystem was exactly what we hoped for, and the level of engagement from the US side made it clear that we're only just beginning to build this bridge with Israel.”
The week placed Israeli entrepreneurs in front of major defense contractors – Anduril, Lockheed Martin, Northrop Grumman, BAE Systems – alongside investors, government representatives, and industry specialists.
The goal was to help Israeli founders become better equipped to do business in the United States and understand who matters, how decisions are made, and what it takes to move from a promising demo to an actual program of record.
From Israeli innovation to American adoption
Avner Bendheim, co-founder and CEO of Tenna Systems, brings a particularly relevant perspective to that challenge.
Bendheim served in an elite unit operating advanced signals intelligence systems (SIGINT). He also helped establish the Israel Air Force’s space program and served as the program director, operational requirements department. He now leads Tenna, whose battlefield-tested software is designed to safeguard wireless-dependent systems across defense, aerospace, and mobility sectors, domains where connectivity has become both indispensable and dangerously vulnerable.
“The whole Israeli defense tech ecosystem is figuring out its go-to-market,” Bendheim told D&T. He explained that with all the various programs and individuals, “CET helps to understand who to engage, how to engage, and when to speak with them.”
According to him, “CET is doing a great job for the companies here and the Israeli ecosystem. It’s a whole different ballgame here in the United States than in Israel. They have been able to put all stakeholders in the same room and you get to know them all.”
“The US Department of War is a multiheaded beast, and even if the technology is operationally deployed, there is a lot of work,” he said. “The DoW is going through its own tectonic shifts in how it acquires and deploys technology.”
Israel’s defense-tech ecosystem has developed around close connections between military users, entrepreneurs, established defense companies, and investors. Meanwhile, the US market is much larger, more fragmented, and more difficult for an outsider to navigate.
Echoing Bendheim, Elad Amar, the CEO of Pyrrhus Aeronautics said that CET has helped him and his company understand the American ecosystem.
"The ecosystem here is a beast that can be hard to penetrate and maneuver within. CET helps us with a strong balance of operators, investors and venture capitalists."
Pyrrhus was conceived by Amar when he was behind enemy lines in the Gaza Strip and saw troops dropping their weapons when trying to operate drones. The technology, Laser Aiming & Drone Remote System (LADRS), can be mounted on a rifle and allow troops to operate drones without removing their hands from their gun.
While it has already been used in special Israeli army units as well as by the US Special Operations Command, in the US Army and the Marines, Amar told D&T that CET has "been extremely useful for startups like us."
The right connections can change the equation
The combination of operational experts, investors, and venture capitalists can be particularly useful for founders trying to identify the right next steps for their businesses.
Naama Zamir of Sealartec told D&T that CET understands the value of bringing together people who can help start-ups comprehend what they need to do to raise capital, reach customers, and grow.
“CET helps us make the right connections and helps us realize what questions we need to ask,” she said on the sidelines of AUSA.
Sealartec is an Israeli company founded in 2018 and based in Haifa that specializes in Autonomous Launch and Recovery Systems (ALRS) designed for both manned and unmanned surface vessels using a patented bow-capture system. The autonomous solution uses local positioning, onboard sensors, and smart algorithms to locate, identify, and physically connect with returning USVs in even challenging sea conditions.
The company has collaborated with major industry players such as BAE Systems, Elbit Systems, and Israel Aerospace Industries.
But it’s not always about connecting with the primes. Daniel Ferber of RFix highlighted to D&T the importance of connecting smaller companies with investors and local businesses that can help them establish themselves in the American market.
“CET brings inside information to the ecosystem and helps us make the right connections,” he said. The early-stage start-up already has customers, but Ferber said that events like the ones held by CET “bring in the right people to connect with the right investors, local companies, and more.”
RFix, an Israeli telecommunications and defense technology company, develops a terrain-aware RF (radio frequency) signal simulation platform. Co-founded in 2025 by Ferber and Bar Harel, the Tel Aviv-based company provides software infrastructure used by wireless engineering, aerospace, and defense teams.
For these start-ups, such relationships can provide a route into an ecosystem that might otherwise appear inaccessible. They can also help founders understand the expectations of American customers and partners before committing time and resources to expansion.
The objective is to help companies make informed decisions about how to enter the market, rather than expecting them to learn every lesson through trial and error.
Building an American presence
Omer Sharar, CEO of InfiniDome, offered a perspective on the practical work involved in establishing a foothold in the United States.
InfiniDome has been working with CET Sandbox for around two years, developing relationships and learning how to navigate the American ecosystem. But, Sharar told D&T, “we are just starting to scratch the surface of the American market.”
Sharar added that CET has built a “very unique ecosystem. Up until now, no one has had a recipe for breaking into the US defense ecosystem. CET is giving us the knowledge of how best to break down the barriers.”
For Israeli start-ups, this can be an important part of preparing for US customers and partners. But it requires founders to think beyond their technology and consider the structure, relationships, and resources needed to operate in a new market.
Relationships that outlast AUSA
The program’s significance extends beyond a week of meetings in Washington.
Yahid told D&T that “events like this, where we work with our partners to create private receptions and networking events that let the conversation go beyond the quick intros on the floor and actually start to build real relationships, showed the primes exactly what the potential is. We came away with significant demand from US primes for more and deeper engagement with the Israeli ecosystem, and a clear signal of willingness from the US side to explore what comes next.”
AUSA brings together a vast cross-section of the American defense establishment, but attending the exhibition does not automatically provide access to the people who matter most. For a start-up without established US relationships, identifying the right contacts and securing meaningful conversations can be a substantial undertaking.
CET Sandbox seeks to change that equation by preparing founders before the event and organizing opportunities to meet relevant stakeholders during and after the exhibition.
Its program included preparatory work in Israel, private receptions during AUSA week, and a closed forum with leaders from the defense industrial base. The emphasis was on giving founders a clearer strategy for entering the market, not simply maximizing the number of meetings they attend.
The real measure of success will be what happens next: whether introductions lead to investment, commercial partnerships, testing opportunities, and eventually contracts.
For Israeli start-ups, that process can determine whether a technology remains a promising capability or becomes the foundation of a scalable international business.
The American defense market is enormous, but its complexity can be daunting for companies entering it for the first time. By connecting Israeli founders with experienced people across that ecosystem, CET Sandbox is trying to make the market more accessible and help Israeli innovation find a path from the battlefield to the broader US defense industrial base.

From a seventh-grade dream to rescue flights: The story of Kazakhstan’s emergency aviation pilot Bibikhan Turusbekova
Bibikhan Turusbekova decided to dedicate her life to aviation in seventh grade. Today, she works as a co-pilot on Mi-8 and Ka-32 helicopters at Kazaviaspas JSC under Kazakhstan’s Ministry of Emergency Situations, taking part in flights to save lives and respond to emergencies, reports a Qazinform News Agency correspondent, citing the ministry.
On October 19, Kazakhstan celebrates the professional holiday of civil protection personnel, firefighters and rescuers. The Ministry of Emergency Situations shared the story of pilot Bibikhan Turusbekova, who had dreamed of working in aviation since seventh grade.
After finishing school, Bibikhan had no doubts about her future profession. She pursued a career in aviation, graduating with honors from the Civil Aviation Academy. In 2021, Bibikhan began her professional career at the ministry’s Kazaviaspas JSC. Her journey began with an interest in aviation and continues today in a demanding service dedicated to saving human lives, the ministry says.
One of the reasons behind her career choice was the opportunity to see many cities. She still remembers the impressions of her first flight. According to Bibikhan, every flight brings special emotions.
The ministry’s aviation operations focus on preventing and responding to emergencies, conducting search and rescue operations, and transporting patients by air ambulance. These tasks require a high level of professionalism, thorough preparation and strict compliance with safety requirements from flight crews.
“Every flight is a responsibility. During each flight, you are responsible not only for yourself but also for the passengers. Sometimes, weather conditions or the situation require quick decisions. But in those moments, it is knowledge and training that help, rather than emotions,” says Bibikhan Turusbekova.
Bibikhan Turusbekova continues to serve in the ministry’s aviation division. She says her main sources of motivation remain her love for the profession, her determination to achieve her goals and the support of her loved ones.
In 2021, Bibikhan Turusbekova was among ten rescue pilots who began flying independently as co-pilots.
Alongside Bibikhan, all civil protection personnel, firefighters, rescuers and specialists from the ministry’s emergency rescue services in Kazakhstan celebrate their professional holiday on October 19. The holiday commemorates the establishment of the State Committee of the Republic of Kazakhstan for Emergency Situations on October 19, 1995. It was officially designated as Rescuer’s Day in 2008.

Israel’s leaders talk about security, but what happened to peace? - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
15:28:56 UTC
00:28:56 KST

For three decades, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has spoken about peace.
The word appeared regularly in his campaign slogans, going back to 1996: “Netanyahu – Peace and Security.” Later, it became “Netanyahu. A Secure Peace.” Peace, whatever his intentions, was part of his political vocabulary.
As recently as September 2023, just two weeks before the Hamas invasion on October 7, Netanyahu stood before the United Nations and spoke extensively about peace, including peace with the Palestinians.
“As the circle of peace expands, I believe that a real path towards a genuine peace with our Palestinian neighbors can finally be achieved,” he said.
In his 2023 UN speech, Netanyahu used the word “peace” 42 times. A year later, the number dropped to 21. In 2025, it fell again, to just 13 mentions, and in his recent speech at the UN in September, he used the word only once. One time.
More significant than the numbers, though, has been the context. In 2023, many of Netanyahu’s references to peace were connected to the Palestinians. In his subsequent UN speeches, he spoke of peace in general terms or in connection with Saudi Arabia, the consequences of the war against Iran, and the possibility of agreements with Syria and Lebanon.
In other words: peace with the Palestinians – out. Peace with almost everyone else – in.
Netanyahu, though, is hardly alone.
Almost no one in the Israeli opposition – including the politicians running to replace him – talks about peace. Naftali Bennett does not speak about peace with the Palestinians. If anything, he emphasizes the opposite: that he will never allow the establishment of a Palestinian state.
Gadi Eisenkot, the former army chief and leading challenger in the polls, recently said that the idea of a two-state solution is “delusional” and a “bitter mistake.”
Even Yair Golan, leader of the Democrats – the latest incarnation of the Labor Party once led by Shimon Peres and Yitzhak Rabin – rarely talks about peace.
Think about that for a moment. The political movement whose leaders won the Nobel Peace Prize for peacemaking with the Palestinians is now led by a former IDF general who prefers discussing tactics rather than explaining how peace can be made.
How did Israel, a country that for decades took pride in saying that its hand was always extended in peace, reach the point where no politician is even willing to say the word when speaking about the Palestinians?
The obvious answer is October 7.
The Hamas assault and the war that followed did more than shatter Israel’s assumptions about Gaza. It changed the way Israelis think about security, territory, deterrence, and risk.
Before October 7, much of Israel’s defense thinking was built around the idea that territory had become less important. Israel could withdraw, rely on intelligence, advanced technology, border barriers, and overwhelming military superiority, and respond from a distance when necessary.
October 7 destroyed that confidence.
Israel views territory as essential
Today, Israel’s security doctrine has moved in the opposite direction. Territory is viewed as essential. Physical control, buffer zones, and the ability to prevent threats from developing on the other side of the border are now considered existential.
You can see that shift in Gaza, southern Lebanon, and Syria, where Israel maintains a presence to ensure that hostile forces cannot establish themselves along the border.
While buffer zones, security perimeters, and military control may be necessary responses to immediate threats, a country must have a political destination.
The disappearance of peace from our language is not merely semantic. Language defines what is politically possible. When we stop saying a word or no longer write songs about it, then we stop imagining it as part of our future. Once that future becomes unimaginable, anyone proposing it can be dismissed as naive or even a traitor.
The failures of previous peace efforts, though, do not prove that peace is impossible, but rather that the way it was pursued was wrong.
Past agreements, for example, lacked enforceable security guarantees, public legitimacy, and accountable leadership. Those failures, especially after October 7, must make Israel more cautious but not defeatist.
As the IDF has repeatedly proven over the last three years, force can destroy weapons and tunnels. But if that same military success is not converted into political outcomes, it will quickly dissipate. Hamas reemerges, Hezbollah rebuilds, and the ayatollahs remain in power.
Peace post-October 7 does not mean returning to the assumptions or hyperbolic slogans of the 1990s. Peace must include verifiable demilitarization, enforceable security arrangements, transformed Palestinian governance, and a universal, uncompromising rejection of terrorism.
It must also require Israel to answer the question its leaders have spent decades avoiding: does Israel ultimately intend to separate from the Palestinians, or permanently rule over them?
If Hamas’s objective was to derail normalization in the region, make coexistence unthinkable, and trap Israelis and Palestinians in a forever war, then removing peace from our vocabulary hands the terrorist group exactly the strategic victory it aspired to achieve.
Peace is not a prediction but a direction. If we stop saying it and abandon it as an aspiration, we risk turning every military success and victory into just another stop on the road to the next war.
Yaakov Katz is a co-founder of the MEAD policy forum, a senior fellow at the Jewish People Policy Institute, and a former editor-in-chief of The Jerusalem Post. His newest book is While Israel Slept.
Lt.-Col. (ret.) Peter Lerner is the director-general of International Relations of the Histadrut; he served for 25 years in the IDF as a spokesperson and liaison officer to international organizations.

Israeli politicians on both sides of the political spectrum reacted to the news that Blue and White party leader Benny Gantz had withdrawn from the elections on Monday, just eight days before voting.

United Torah Judaism chairman MK Yaakov Asher also responded to Gantz's withdrawal, praising him for his decades of service to Israel and describing him as a "mensch" who had contributed greatly to the country's security.
"I wish him great success and am confident that he will return to contribute his abilities and talents to the leadership of the country in the future," Asher said.
Asher also emphasized the personal relationship and mutual respect the two had maintained despite their political differences.
"Despite our differences of opinion, we have always known how to maintain a personal relationship, respectful dialogue, and mutual appreciation. Benny is living proof that friendship and gratitude do not depend on political bloc divisions."
Efrat Rayten, fourth on the left-wing Democrats party list, thanked Gantz for making what she described as the "right and responsible decision" and for his years of service to Israel.
She called for unity among parties across the political spectrum that had not been part of the current coalition, which she accused of promoting draft evasion, corruption, and Kahanism.
Rayten also expressed optimism about the upcoming elections, declaring, "Feeling the change in the air? It's really happening!" and urging Israelis to turn out in large numbers to vote.

European Jewish leaders have been working with friendly foreign ministers to block plans by European countries to impose severe sanctions on Israel ahead of the upcoming Israeli election, Ariel Muzicant, an Austrian-Israeli businessman who served as the president of the Viennese Jewish community, told The Jerusalem Post.
Muzicant said that Jewish leaders have been working quietly to stave off planned sanctions against Israel driven by EU member states such as Spain and Ireland.
“We have been working under the radar with many friendly foreign ministers in Europe to persuade them to block the sanctions until we know what the election will bring,” Muzicant said.
He noted that several European countries want to strip Israel of its preferred trade status with the European Community and cut off participation in major academic research funding programs such as Horizon 2020.
Horizon 2020 and its successor programs represent the EU’s flagship multi-billion-euro framework for funding research, development, and innovation, connecting universities and scientists across member states and associated nations.
For Israel, participation in these initiatives has historically served as a critical economic and academic lifeline, injecting hundreds of millions of euros into Israeli research institutions, facilitating student and faculty exchanges, and driving high-tech advancement.
Muzicant warned that losing access to these collaborative research networks would deliver a devastating blow to Israeli academia and research-and-development sectors.
He added that the Austrian foreign minister had spoken with European colleagues and “tried to push them to keep quiet for a few weeks until October 27.”
Continued West Bank violence puts diplomatic reprieve at risk
Muzicant cautioned that this diplomatic reprieve is fragile and comes with strict caveats regarding the composition of the next Israeli government. He told the Post that European officials have signaled that “if Ben-Gvir, Smotrich, and company are in the next government, and if the terrible activities by some extreme settlers continue, there will be dramatic sanctions.”
Muzicant noted that ongoing violence, such as recent attacks on Palestinians and international observers during the olive harvest in the West Bank, along with a lack of decisive government response, makes it extremely difficult for Israel’s defenders in Europe to defend the country.
Muzicant pointed to such incidents as the alleged violent assault on Washington Post photojournalist Heidi Levine, who reported that she was beaten by masked settlers with clubs and iron bars, and a separate attack where Bernard Baudoux, the mayor of Aulnoye-Aymeries, a town in northern France, was kicked and mobbed in the West Bank town of Taybeh as reported by Al Jazeera and The Guardian.

Threats facing Israel to impact Diaspora communities
Muzicant warned that the political pressure and economic threats facing Israel immediately will spill over onto Jewish communities across Europe.
Anti-Israel rallies and street protests in major urban hubs quickly turn into direct hostility against Jewish targets, with Muzicant pointing out that demonstrations featuring Palestinian flags in cities across France, Italy, Portugal, and Belgium have frequently devolved into physical attacks on Jewish-owned businesses, stores, and synagogues, such as incidents in Marseille and Paris.

EU’s ‘trust’ and ‘leverage’ at stake over development cuts, UN food aid boss warns
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
15:26:59 UTC
00:26:59 KST

Slashing the EU's humanitarian aid budget risks wrecking the bloc’s dominance and influence in international discussions, warned the head of the world's largest food aid organization.
As Europe's leaders clash over just how much they're prepared to fund the EU and its programs in the next seven-year budget, initial funding plans for global development have already been cut.
The latest compromise position presented by the Irish rotating presidency of the Council of the EU would carve €38 billion out of the Global Europe envelope — which funds development and external aid — shrinking it by roughly 17% to €177 billion.
Advertisement
The European Commission “has remained a predictable donor when others have cut,” Carl Skau, acting chief of the U.N. World Food Programme said. This has earned Europe “a lot of trust, a lot capital, a lot of leverage in the international system,” he added.
That influence has helped the EU shape WFP priorities, including commitments to gender equality, climate action and protecting vulnerable populations in its 2026-2029 Strategic Plan.
Now, Brussels risks throwing that advantage away, Skau warned.
World Food Programme donations are unloaded in Chichiriviche de la Costa, Venezuela on July 16, 2026. | Raul Arboleda/AFP via Getty Images
It will be “unfortunate also to do away with that muscle that Europe benefits from,” he said, urging the EU to protect the “ambitious budget.” Compared with the billions being poured into defense, he argued, humanitarian aid amounts to “peanuts.”
Talks on squeezing the EU's contribution land as other international powers have also cut their global development budgets.
The World Food Programme's global funding has plunged by 40% over the past two years, according to its official records. Its largest donor, the United States, halved its contributions in 2025 under President Donald Trump compared with the previous year. Germany, France, and the United Kingdom also tightened the purse strings.
Advertisement
Record need for aid
Funding cuts to the organization come when the need for its programs has never been higher. According to WFP projections, as many as 363 million people could face acute food insecurity this year — nearly 90% more than in 2021.
“We see the consequences of the cuts that we're now going through. They are human, because we are cutting [food programs for] women and children, who are likely to die in South Sudan, in Afghanistan, in Somalia, off our support because of these deep funding cuts we've been going through,” said Skau.
The world’s largest food aid agency is now running dangerously short of cash and has to make “impossible choices,” such as “choosing between the starving,” Skau said. Moreover, wars, extreme weather, the looming threat of El Niño and disruptions to global trade routes are deepening hunger crises worldwide.
Some officials previously warned that cuts to development aid risk fueling more migration into Europe, something Brussels has been trying to curb.
“I would not put that as my main argument, but there is a clear linkage," said Skau. “And if that's what it takes to get the resources needed to save lives in South Sudan, you know, fair enough,” he added.
Skau is serving as WFP’s interim chief following Cindy McCain’s departure. He is set to hand over to Luke Lindberg at the end of October.

Houthi attack kills 53 in biggest single loss of life since Yemen civil war reignited
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
15:25:56 UTC
00:25:56 KST

At least 53 people have been killed in a Houthi ballistic missile attack on a training camp for Yemeni government security forces, making it the largest single loss of life since the country’s civil war reignited in September.
The attack on al-Alam camp in the southern Shabwa province was said to have injured more than 200 others, mostly young recruits, and was described as a disaster by the country’s UN-recognised government. The injured were taken from the police and army training camp in the Jardan district to a hospital in the local capital, Ataq, where pleas for blood donations were made.
There will be an inquiry into how so many troops were left so exposed to a Houthi attack. In mid-September, the group began a fresh push on forces backing the UN-recognised government by pushing south along the Red Sea coast to try to take control of the Bab al-Mandab waterway.
Reliable assessments of the death toll in the fighting over the last month are hard to gather, but it is running into the many thousands. A Saudi airstrike on Sunday killed nine, including five children and two women.
Rashad al-Alimi, the president of the UN-recognised government, said those killed on Monday were new recruits, and he vowed an immediate hard response. He said the incident “affirmed that targeting the recruits reflects the Houthi militias’ approach of resorting to cowardly terrorist attacks whenever they face pressures or their Iranian-backed sabotage plots falter”.
On Monday he phoned the UN secretary general, António Guterres, to ask for the UN to classify the Houthis as a foreign terrorist organisation.
The Shabwa provincial authority said: “Targeting recruits constitutes a military escalation and a blatant assault on the province’s security.” Its governor, Awad bin al-Wazir, visited the wounded in hospitals, and called for extra air defences, saying troops were fighting across six fronts.
The killings underline the dangers of large numbers of troops gathering in one place within reach of the Houthi ballistic missile arsenal. The training camp was struck by three ballistic missiles while the recruits lined up in formation.
Houthi forces have also cut the road between government-run Shabwa and the Houthi-run Bayda governorate.
The Houthi military spokesperson said: “Our armed forces targeted the Saudi enemy’s mobilisations in al-Alam camp, which is run by Saudi officers in the eastern regions. The targeting resulted in the fall of dozens of dead and wounded from the Saudi enemy’s mobilisations, including Saudi officers.
“We warn the deceived ones against responding to the Saudi enemy’s calls to lure them with his defiled money to the pyres of death, and to exploit them instead of his soldiers who are indifferent to their lives.”
A Yemen government spokesperson said the site struck was not a military target linked to the current fighting but “a training centre where new recruits in the internal security forces of Shabwa governorate receive training and qualification programmes.”
They added: “This reveals the criminal nature of this assault, which targeted young people in the preparation and qualification phase to carry out their security duties, far from the frontlines.”
Separately the Houthis claim to have hit the anti-Houthi Giant Brigades of southern Yemen in six strikes in the areas of al-Suqya and Ras al-Ara. Southern forces are said to have been making progress in edging Houthi forces out of control of the area around the Bab al-Mandab strait, the narrowest waterway taking ships from the Red Sea to the Indian Ocean.
Fighting is also under way as Houthis try to mount a siege of Taiz, where citizens have been calling for greater air protection. In the city there seems to be a determination not to capitulate, but conditions are deteriorating as Houthis close access points.
It is not clear whether the Houthis have decided to slow the pace of attacks on Saudi airports and energy installations, or they are running low on munitions.
The Saudi Aramco headquarters was struck last weekend and some airlines have said they will not yet resume using Riyadh airport. The airport reopened at the weekend after being attacked this month.
Egypt’s parliament has postponed a vote on whether to send troops to Saudi Arabia despite extending the debate to a second day as MPs demanded more than two minutes each to speak. The vote is now likely to be held next week.
A two-thirds majority is required, and some opposition parties have signalled their intention to vote against or abstain. Disputes centre on the extent of the mission and whether it will involve sending troops into Yemen to help Saudi Arabia, and whether Egyptian troops inside Saudi Arabia would become targets for Houthi attacks.
The delay also gives the Egyptians time to see if Iran can persuade the Houthis to hold back, and for Saudi Arabia to confirm the renewal of badly needed loans to Egypt.
Egypt has resisted any ground intervention in Yemen, dating back to the 1962-67 war, when Gamal Abdel Nasser sent troops to back the republicans in North Yemen against the Saudi- and British-backed royalists. The incursion was intended to be minimal, but escalated to as many as 70,000 soldiers. Estimates of Egyptians killed range from 10,000-26,000.

MOSCOW, October 19. /TASS/. Continued monetary easing will give the Russian stock market a new boost, with real estate developers and highly indebted companies poised to benefit the most, as each percentage-point rate cut lowers debt-servicing costs and directly increases profits, Alexey Govyrin, Deputy Chairman of the State Duma Committee on Economic Policy, told TASS ahead of the central bank's upcoming rate-setting meeting.

Domestic demand is also driving growth, the lawmaker added. Consolidating the index above 2,430 points will pave the way toward 2,500; a dovish decision on rates could push the target to 2,550."
Another growth driver lies in household savings, according to Govyrin. "A rate cut will make equities more attractive to retail investors, funneling new capital into the stock market," he predicted.

====================================================================================================

From Banking to Taxis, Ukraine’s Data Center Strikes Disrupt Everyday Life in Russia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
15:23:00 UTC
00:23:00 KST

Andrei, a 39-year-old journalist from Moscow, looks at the notification on his smartphone and laughs.
“Damn! I can’t log into my Yandex Pay account, but they’re still charging me for a Yandex Music subscription that doesn’t even work,” he says.
When he tried to log in, the app displayed a message that said “Something went wrong” and asked him to try again later.
“It’s a good thing I use another bank’s card for most of my payments,” he says.
Yandex Pay is one of dozens of services whose operations have been disrupted by Ukrainian strikes on Russian data centers this month.
For many Russians, these outages have mostly meant temporary inconveniences and changes to their routines. But in a year that has already seen widespread fuel shortages, airport closures and e-commerce disruptions due to the war, they are the latest way in which the Kremlin’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine has seeped into everyday life.
The data-center strikes have disrupted everything from taxis and car-sharing services, food delivery and maps to email, banking and streaming platforms.
Problems also arose for state agencies and private firms whose products rely on Yandex infrastructure, from dating apps to access systems for residential complexes and smart homes.
‘Far more serious than we expected’
Connectivity to the Yandex Cloud platform fell to around 30% of normal levels following the Oct. 8-11 strikes, according to internet monitoring group NetBlocks. The disruptions affected 84 cloud services.
Yandex confirmed serious damage to one data center, the shutdown of another and infrastructure disruptions at a third. It has not disclosed the full extent of the damage or given a timeline for recovery.
In addition, all three of Yandex’s supercomputers were likely severely affected, which could set Russia back years in the AI race, the science news outlet T-Invariant said.
After a further strike hit a VK data center in St. Petersburg on Sunday, users also reported disruptions on social network VKontakte, including photos failing to load.
As of Monday, Yandex Pay remained only partially available. The error message had been replaced with a reassurance: “Your money is safe. Some features are unavailable. Our engineers are working to get everything up and running again.”
The Moscow Times reporter who wrote this article was still unable to access their full Yandex Taxi ride history on Monday.
A senior data analyst at Yandex told The Moscow Times that the company had been preparing for data center outages even before this month’s strikes.
“But the scale turned out to be far more serious than we initially expected,” and Yandex’s rank-and-file employees were caught off guard, said the employee, who spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss sensitive internal matters.
“We had to drop everything and focus on urgent problems with our services,” he said. “We managed to mitigate some of the effects quickly by switching applications to limited functionality, while in other cases recovery took several days.”
He said it could take much longer to fully restore services.
“I don’t think anyone expects everything to be fully restored within a few days,” the employee said.
The analyst declined to discuss how Yandex was preparing for further Ukrainian strikes, saying that disclosing those plans could create a vulnerability for the company.
From bank accounts to court hearings
While the economic damage and longer-term consequences of the strikes remain unclear, the immediate disruption has been manageable for many users.
The names of private individuals interviewed for this article have been changed for their safety.
Robert, a barista in St. Petersburg, uses Yandex Pay as his main bank account. It’s where he receives his salary and other transfers.
“I use it for payments 99% of the time,” he said. “Luckily, I had almost no money in my account when the outage happened. I’d spent everything on big purchases shortly beforehand. So I wasn’t too worried about losing it forever.”
His access to his digital wallet was restored after several days. Hee said he has no plans to stop using Yandex.
“I always keep an alternative way to pay just in case — a little cash,” he said.
The attack has nevertheless made him think about the war.
“It’s another reminder that the consequences of the war are getting closer to home — and growing in scale,” he said.
The disruptions also reached Yandex users outside Russia.
Yekaterina, a Russian woman who moved to Georgia after the invasion of Ukraine, said Yandex Go, a taxi service widely used across former Soviet countries, was temporarily unavailable in Tbilisi.
Nikolai, a Russian doctoral student in New Zealand, said he was unable to use Yandex Archives to research his dissertation.
“There weren’t many sources there, but the search was really convenient. So I sat down to write a chapter, wanted to quote something, and the archive was gone!” he said.
The data center strikes have also affected government agencies. The exiled news outlet Vyorstka reported that dozens of court hearings across Russia were disrupted due to technical problems.
Some government websites in the Kaluga region also went offline, Sarkis Darbinyan, an IT lawyer and founder of digital rights organization RKS.global, told The Moscow Times.
The outages have posed particular problems for small and medium-sized businesses whose products run on Yandex’s infrastructure, especially its cloud platform, a Russian equivalent of Google Cloud.
Tatyana, the founder of fitness app FIT&ZEN, told customers that both the app and its web version were temporarily unavailable because of “technical problems at a Yandex data center.”
“A major Yandex outage has affected many companies across the country, so unfortunately we’re not alone in this,” she wrote on the company’s Telegram channel.
A strike on Yandex Cloud hits “thousands of Russian companies at once,” Darbinyan said.
“After the Kremlin pushed Google and all its cloud competitors out of the country, Yandex played a very important role in the Russian internet, even though it did not have a dominant share of the data center market,” he said.
The greatest risks face customers that cut costs by keeping all their data in a single availability zone without backups elsewhere, he added. These include small and medium-sized businesses, regional media outlets and government agencies.
Can Ukraine knock Russia’s internet offline?
Darbinyan said the vulnerabilities exposed by the strikes are rooted partly in the structure of Russia’s internet and the rules governing where companies can store their data.
Earlier this month, the operator of Ukraine’s Parkovyi data center moved copies of customers’ data to backup sites in the European Union after it was hit by Russian strikes.
By comparison, Russian companies have little scope to do the same, Darbinyan said. Data localization laws and rules governing hosting, authentication services and critical information infrastructure require them to store data inside Russia.
Even so, Darbinyan said it would be difficult to take Russia’s internet completely offline by striking data centers.
Despite the Kremlin’s efforts to isolate it through its “sovereign internet” policy, Russia’s internet remains a vast network built along the same lines as the global internet. It encompasses more than 200 data centers, hundreds of telecom network nodes and corporate server rooms.
Its greatest vulnerability is the concentration of commercial data center capacity in Moscow and nearby regions, with much of it owned by a handful of major companies: Yandex, VK, Rostelecom and Sberbank, he said.
Serious disruptions at those companies can therefore affect services nationwide.
Nor will it be easy or quick to replace damaged infrastructure. Russia obtains almost all the necessary equipment through parallel imports, while the AI boom has driven up prices, Darbinyan said.
“If strikes become regular, the market may simply not be able to keep up with replacing what’s been lost,” he said.

MSF calls for protection of Palestinian communities after Israeli settlers injured staff member

Statement19 October 2026
On the evening of 15 October, Israeli settlers violently assaulted a Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) colleague with a hand-sized rock launched by a slingshot during a targeted attack on his village in the south of West Bank, Palestine. Our colleague required immediate medical attention. This incident is not isolated. Over the past months communities across Hebron and other areas of the West Bank have been subjected to increased violence, indiscriminate intimidation, and insecurity.
According to our colleague's account, a group of approximately 20 settlers descended from the nearby hills to attack residents, and more settlers arrived later. The settlers were armed with batons, rifles, stun grenades, and slingshots. Stun grenades and warning shots fired from rifles helped them advance further into the village and drive Palestinian residents back.
The violence experienced by our colleague, the barriers to reaching medical care, and the growing restrictions imposed on Palestinian communities are not coincidental. This is part of Israel’s strategy to undermine people's safety and curtail their freedom of movement, access to healthcare, and ability to live in dignity.
This incident took place in an area already subject to extensive closures and road restrictions due to Israeli military activity. Due to unpaved roads the ambulance could not reach the area. Eventually, our colleague was transported by a private vehicle to meet the ambulance before being transported first to a clinic, then the hospital in an effort to be treated.
We condemn all attacks against civilians and call for the protection of Palestinian communities, patients, and healthcare workers.

EU Parliament leaders set for re-election despite cracks in centrist alliance
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
15:19:44 UTC
00:19:44 KST

Manfred Weber, Iratxe García Pérez and Valérie Hayer are expected to be re-elected unopposed, even as growing tensions threaten the centrist alliance supporting Ursula von der Leyen.
The three political groups underpinning the European Parliament's centrist majority are set to re-elect their leaders on Tuesday, with little prospect of surprises despite growing tensions within their alliance.
The European People's Party (EPP), the Socialists and Democrats (S&D) and the liberal Renew Europe group will hold internal leadership elections in Strasbourg on 20 October, with the outcomes all but a foregone conclusion.
The EPP is expected to re-elect German Manfred Weber, who has led the group since 2014 and faces no challengers. “He has an iron grip on the group. No one would even think of trying to topple him,” a senior MEP told Euronews.
The main contest will be for the group's vice-presidencies, with 12 candidates vying for 10 seats. All current vice-presidents seeking re-election are expected to retain their positions, while outgoing Portuguese MEP Lídia Pereira is likely to be replaced by Hungary's Eszter Lakos.
There is little prospect of a contest among the Socialists either. Spanish MEP Iratxe García Pérez is set to be re-elected unopposed, extending her tenure and making her the longest-serving leader in the group's history.
Renew Europe chair Valérie Hayer is also the sole candidate to lead the liberal group. The French MEP, who belongs to Emmanuel Macron’s political camp, is expected to be elected by acclamation, with overwhelming support, a source within the group told Euronews.
A challenger could still enter the race at the last minute, before the vote, triggering a ballot election.
Once re-elected, Weber, García Pérez and Hayer are expected to discuss the future of the centrist alliance supporting European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen for the remainder of the parliamentary term.
The informal coalition agreement currently underpinning that alliance has come under repeated strain in the last year, as the EPP has increasingly relied on a right-wing majority, joining forces with the European Conservatives and Reformists (ECR) and far-right groups on key migration and climate files.

How has the cost of living changed in France, Italy, Spain and Portugal?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
15:19:04 UTC
00:19:04 KST

How has the cost of living changed in France, Italy, Spain and Portugal?
As protesters take to the streets across Europe over the rising cost of living, Al Jazeera looks at how prices, wages and housing costs have changed since 2000.
Student protests in France are into their second month, escalating into demonstrations across Europe.
What began in September in France with pupils protesting against overcrowded classrooms and teacher shortages has grown into wider anger at the cost of living and planned cuts to public services.
Protesters in Albania, Belgium, Greece, Italy, Portugal and Spain have also taken to the streets over the lack of affordable housing, rising costs and failing public services – with many young people saying they no longer expect to be better off than their parents.
Facing their anger are leaders such as French President Emmanuel Macron, Italy’s Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni, Spain’s PM Pedro Sanchez and Portugal’s PM Luis Montenegro. Sanchez belongs to the left, Meloni to the right and Macron and Montenegro are conservative-leaning centrists. But while their politics vary, they all face mounting unrest because of soaring costs of living.
Are they out of touch with the experiences and sentiments of youth in their countries? Al Jazeera visualises how prices, wages, housing and education have changed in France, Italy, Spain and Portugal over the past 26 years, from when Macron, Meloni, Sanchez and Montenegro were in their 20s, much like many of the protesters angry with them.
How much more expensive is it compared to 2000?
The prices paid for everyday items such as food, energy, transport and bills have risen by between 59 and 78 percent since 2000 in France, Italy, Spain and Portugal, according to Eurostat – the European Union’s statistics agency. Its harmonised index of consumer prices (HICP) is the EU’s official measure of how much everyday goods and services cost.
Spain recorded the steepest increase at 78 percent, followed by Portugal at 71 percent, 68 percent in Italy and France at 59 percent.
That means goods and services that cost 100 euros ($112) in 2000 now cost about 178 euros ($200) in Spain, 171 euros ($192) in Portugal, 168 euros ($188) in Italy and 159 euros ($178) in France.
Prices rose by about 2 percent a year on average, but jumped in 2022, when annual inflation hit 8.7 percent in Italy, 8.3 percent in Spain, 8.1 percent in Portugal and 5.9 percent in France, the highest rate in all four countries since at least 2000.
The surge was driven mainly by energy costs, which soared after Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. By October that year, eight months into the war, energy prices across the eurozone were almost 42 percent higher than a year earlier, and food prices were also rising sharply, according to Eurostat.
Between 2021 and 2023, prices increased by 12 to 15 per cent in the four countries. Wages failed to keep up, and because prices do not fall back once inflation eases, many households are still feeling the squeeze today.
How have salaries changed?
Once inflation is taken into account, the average full-time wage in Italy fell by almost 5 per cent between 2000 and 2025. Over the same period, real wages rose by 7 per cent in Spain, 11 per cent in France and 20 per cent in Portugal, according to OECD wage data adjusted with Eurostat’s price index.
In Spain most new jobs were in tourism and services, and were often seasonal and poorly paid, Jaime Velazquez, a journalist in Madrid, told Al Jazeera’s Inside Story.
Julius Fintelmann, cofounder and editor-in-chief of The European Correspondent, said ageing societies were squeezing out opportunities for younger workers, adding that the pay gap between older and younger workers has been widening across high-income economies for decades, so the promise that each generation would be better off than the last no longer holds.
How has the cost of housing changed?
Housing has become harder to afford in all four countries since 2000, according to the OECD’s price-to-income ratio. It provides a broad picture of how house prices have changed relative to incomes over time. When prices rise faster than incomes, the ratio goes up, suggesting homes are becoming less affordable on average.
However, it doesn’t show which households or regions are hit hardest, does not account for mortgage and borrowing costs, and says nothing about the quality of the homes people are paying for.
Spain has seen the biggest change. Its price-to-income ratio is 56 per cent higher than in 2000, even after falling sharply following the 2008 financial crisis.
In France, the ratio is 39 per cent higher than in 2000, though it has eased slightly since peaking in 2022.
Italy is the exception where house prices have broadly kept pace with incomes, leaving the ratio just 5 per cent higher than in 2000.
Portugal has seen the sharpest change in recent years. Its price-to-income ratio fell steadily for 15 years after 2000, meaning homes became more affordable. But since 2015 the ratio has risen by 67 per cent.
The OECD publishes the price-to-income ratio with 2015 as its reference year. To compare it with the wage and price data in this article, which started in 2000, Al Jazeera has reset the figures so that 2000 = 100.
How has state expenditure on education changed?
Education has been at the heart of the unrest in France, where protests began because of overcrowded classrooms and teacher shortages. While in Belgium and Albania, demonstrators have rallied against the rising cost of education and access to universities.
According to the latest data from Eurostat, France’s public spending on education amounts to 5.1 per cent of its gross domestic product (GDP) compared to 5.6 per cent in 2000.
Italy spent 4.4 per cent of its GDP on education compared to 4 per cent in 2024, Spain spent 4.1 per cent in 2000 and the same in 2024. Portugal spent 4.8 per cent in 2000 and 4.3 per cent in 2024.

How the Fossil Fuel Industry ‘Captured’ Australia and Maintains Its Political Dominance
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
15:19:00 UTC
00:19:00 KST

Australia is one of the world’s largest exporters of coal and gas and has among the world’s highest per capita carbon emissions. As a leading “petrostate,” it is perhaps unsurprising that the fossil fuel sector has been central in shaping the nation’s energy and climate policies.
The political capture of Australia by the fossil fuel industries has stymied any meaningful attempt to move away from fossil energy. They have historically obstructed attempts to regulate and reduce carbon emissions through lobbying, networking, and financial donations to parties in the political arena. The end game is to promote fossil energy to the public as essential to the past, present, and future of Australian society; what can be termed a form of “carbon populism.”
Unpicking this complex web of political influence is essential if meaningful decarbonization is to be achieved.
Shaping the Political Arena
The outsized political influence of the fossil fuel industries in Australia has a long history. As former political staffer Guy Pearse noted in his book “High and Dry,” the so-called “greenhouse mafia” of corporate executives and lobbyists played a key role in the years of the Howard government (1996-2007) in shaping the rejection of climate and emissions regulation. That defensive political activity continued in the campaigns against carbon pricing under the Rudd and Gillard Labor governments (2007-2013) and the following nine years of conservative rule. Indeed, under the current Albanese Labor government (2022-present) fossil fuel interests in gas and coal continue to have significant influence over energy and climate policy.
This influence has been achieved through various practices, such as lobbying, networking, and industry association representation. This has involved direct representations by corporate executives and paid lobbyists to senior government ministers and bureaucrats or more informal interactions in the halls of parliament. Here, coal and gas representatives stress their role as creators of public value through employment, revenue for public coffers and broader economic growth. Financial donations have further amplified political influence, with fossil fuel corporations donating close to AU$4 million to Australia’s major political parties during 2024-25 which included the last Federal Election.
The blurring divide between politics and the fossil fuel industry is particularly evident in the social embeddedness of industry representatives and executives within the political sphere. This involves personal and professional relationships. A common theme here has been the concept of a “revolving door” between industry and government. For example, several reports have listed the career trajectories of retiring politicians and bureaucrats as they move into senior industry and consulting roles, as well as industry representatives taking up political advisory appointments. This inter-connectedness of industry and politics has included both major political parties, highlighting a strong capital-state nexus that is committed to the continued expansion of fossil energy resources.
This close “understanding” between different levels of government and the fossil fuel sector is often explicitly highlighted in the public statements of politicians expressing their loyalty to the resources sector. Here, politicians depict the industry as the backbone of the Australian success story and deserving of a seat at the table. Examples have included: advocating for the appointment of a former resources minister to chair a peak mining industry association; the federal treasurer displaying a lump of coal in the parliament and declaring its national benefits; and a former minister for resources posting a heartfelt note of farewell to the Australian mining sector on Facebook. As one interviewee in our research acknowledged: “Yes, there is a revolving door of consultants and management personnel between ministerial offices and industry groups, and companies. There always has been!”
Winning Hearts and Minds
More broadly, the fossil fuel industry has been central to the shaping of public attitudes and understandings of economic development and national identity. For instance, as the CEO of coal giant Peabody Energy declared in promoting the continued expansion of the Australian coal industry: “Coal has transformed society over hundreds of years by fueling industrial revolutions and digital economies. It’s the pride of Australia’s past, and the pride of its future.”
In its public relations, the industry has sought to bring together a range of discourses on how coal and gas underpins the collective welfare of Australia. This has included arguments about the role of coal-fired power in providing cheap and reliable electricity, the economic contribution of export earnings and mining royalties, and employment and job creation. For instance, many of the industry’s public statements have for years stressed the way in which fossil fuel extraction is one of the nation’s highest export earners and contributes to the collective good through mining royalties and tax revenue which contribute to the provision of essential government services.
Despite being highly capital intensive, coal mining has also been presented as a major source of employment, emphasizing its role in regional development and as a key part of many communities. This focus on local communities, job creation, and regional development has been reinforced through the industry’s advertising and community programs, showcasing local conservation and sustainability programs, profiles of mine workers and their family lives, sponsorship of local sporting teams and schools and hospitals, Indigenous employment programs, and “education” programs promoting the benefits of fossil fuel energy. As critics have noted, these practices act as a form of “inoculation PR” aimed at defusing more negative perceptions of the industry and winning over the hearts and minds of local communities and the general public to the worthiness of fossil fuel extraction.
The Magical Thinking of a Fossil-fueled Future
In a context of growing public concern over worsening climate change, the fossil fuel industry has sought to highlight its current benefits and also project an image of the future in which it continues to grow. Despite the rapidly declining cost of renewable energy and growing global moves towards decarbonization, the coal and gas industries and aligned politicians have sought to promote a “fossil fuels forever” imaginary.
This has involved asserting the central role of coal and gas in the economic response to the COVID-19 pandemic as well as technological innovation and the need for energy security. Examples have included the framing of Australia’s export gas industry as a “transition fuel” in contributing to global emissions reductions, as well as the coal industry’s on-going promotion of so-called “clean coal” via phantom technologies such as carbon capture and storage. In response, state and federal politicians have continued to talk up the future of fossil energy, and new coal and gas projects continue to be green-lit.
Despite decades of political debate over climate and energy policy, Australia’s role as a major fossil energy producer remains unchanged. As current and future generations watch a world unravelling under the weight of ever worsening climate disruption, the legacy of the fossil-fuel industry’s outsized influence on the failure to decarbonize weighs heavily.

Ukraine, Russia nearing agreement on evacuation of civilians from occupied Oleshky, ombudsman says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
15:18:57 UTC
00:18:57 KST

Ukraine, Russia nearing agreement on evacuation of civilians from occupied Oleshky, ombudsman says
Ukraine and Russia are nearing an agreement on the final details of civilian evacuation from the front-line town of Oleshky and nearby settlements in the Russian-occupied part of Kherson Oblast, Ukrainian Human Rights Ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets said on Oct. 18.
Oleshky has been under Russian occupation since the early days of the full-scale invasion. Residents face severe shortages of food, water, and electricity, while mined roads, constant drone attacks, and interrogations by Russian troops at checkpoints make safe evacuation virtually impossible.
The two sides are discussing a local ceasefire to allow residents to be evacuated directly to Ukrainian-controlled territory, rather than having to travel first through Russian-occupied areas and then through Russia and Belarus, Lubinets said in an interview with Ukrainian broadcaster Espreso.
"We are making as much progress as possible. We are now moving toward agreeing on the final details to ensure a ceasefire and evacuate everyone ... directly to territory controlled by the Ukrainian government," Lubinets said.
Lubinets did not specify what direct evacuation to Ukrainian territory entails, but one possible option is to transfer civilians across the Dnipro River to the Ukrainian-controlled western bank.
He added that Kyiv has been holding daily negotiations to unblock the humanitarian evacuation and that Moscow has begun considering a proposal Kyiv put forward long ago.
"We still have some difficult issues to resolve, but I hope that in the near future we will all see concrete results from these negotiations," Lubinets said.
No final agreement has been publicly announced, and it remains unclear when an evacuation could begin.
Lubinets said on Sept. 16 that more than 6,000 people possibly remain in Oleshky and the surrounding area, including about 200 children. His office said it had verified 358 people who urgently need assistance to leave safely.
While Russian troops occupy Oleshky and the eastern bank of the Dnipro River, the Ukrainian military controls the western bank. Russian troops use towns and villages on the eastern bank to launch attacks across the river, including on the liberated city of Kherson.
Russian forces have been preventing Ukraine and international humanitarian organizations from accessing the occupied territories to provide aid.
In September, 12 people from Oleshky reached Ukrainian-controlled territory, Tetiana Hasanenko, the exiled head of the Oleshky City Military Administration, told the Kyiv Independent on Oct. 6.
In spring, evacuation volunteers still managed to help people from Oleshky leave for other occupied settlements in Kherson Oblast or Ukrainian-controlled areas in exhausting multiday trips through Russia and Belarus. Now, they said, the risk of Russian attacks and mines has made organized evacuation impossible.
In recent weeks, some residents have started walking out of Oleshky alone or in pairs to the neighboring village of Radensk on roads mined by Russian forces.

Trump defends Russia sanctions waiver, says he does not want to drive Moscow from talks
