US President Donald Trump wrote in a Truth Social post on 18 October that he did not want to “drive, foolishly, Russia away from the bargaining table.” He also wrote: “Signing that document at this time will do that, and I can sign it later, or any time that I want!”
Trump was referring to sanctions and tariffs under the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026, which he waived in an executive order on 16 October, days before the measures were due to take effect. The waiver suspends additional economic penalties intended to pressure Moscow over its war against Ukraine, while leaving earlier US sanctions in place. The decision came weeks before the 3 November midterms, in which Republicans are defending slim majorities in both chambers, and analysts said the penalties could have pushed up oil prices for Americans already paying more, largely because of the US-Israeli war with Iran, Reuters reported.
Trump says Zelenskyy could have made a better deal two years ago
A week before the waiver, Trump had announced a deal for Russia to increase diesel supplies to global markets. The Treasury also issued a license, valid until 7 April 2027, permitting certain transactions in Russian-origin diesel.
In the Truth Social post, Trump accused Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy of targeting Russian diesel refineries, saying the strikes were “seriously hurting the world diesel markets, including those in the United States.” Kyiv had paused its refinery strikes for three days at Washington’s request after Trump declared an energy ceasefire on 11 October, which Russia never confirmed, then resumed them. Since then, Russia has struck Ukraine’s energy sector 76 times, Zelenskyy said on 18 October.
Kyiv gets no warning of the first of two Russian ballistic waves, hours after Zelenskyy said US alerts were back
Trump wrote that Zelenskyy “doesn’t want to end this war, and probably never did,” and that he “could have made a better deal two years ago than he can now.”
“His country is in shambles, a large portion of his land is lost, his oceans and seas are gone, and his male population is low, wounded, and/or dead,” Trump added.
He also said Russia was “doing very little, if anything, to help” Iran and that he wanted to keep it that way.
A day earlier, Trump said he had not made a final decision
On 17 October, Trump told reporters at Mar-a-Lago that he had not announced his final decision. “A lot of you don’t know what my decision is yet, but we’ll figure it out, and you’ll figure it out,” he said, Reuters reported.
“I think the president wants to take the 60-day period of time to sort of analyze what imposing both sanctions and tariffs will mean to the global economy and even to the US economy,” US Secretary of State Marco Rubio told reporters before departing for Uzbekistan the same day.
Zelenskyy calls the waiver a pity as Republicans split
Zelenskyy called it a “pity” that Trump had waived sanctions under a law named for the late Senator Lindsey Graham, who “really believed in Ukraine.” He said he hoped Trump would change his decisions, NBC News reported.
Discussing the diesel deal on NBC’s Meet the Press, Zelenskyy said US oil prices had risen because shipping through the Strait of Hormuz was blocked, not because of Ukraine.
A month before the diesel waiver, Trump’s envoys had already pitched Kyiv on Russian gas, NYT says
On 17 October, Zelenskyy told journalists that “the decision to undo all of this, to block all of it, seems wrong to me” and that it “definitely helps only the Russians.” His remarks appeared in Ukrainian on his official Telegram channel.
“Sanctions relief will continue. I think the diesel deal and the move regarding the Lindsey Graham Act are not the end of it. Unfortunately,” Zelenskyy said.
On 19 October, Zelenskyy wrote that partners had again given no warning of Russia’s overnight ballistic attack and that blocking missiles for Ukraine’s air defense while Russia gets sanctions eased or postponed amounts to partners denying reality.
Republican Senator James Lankford defended Trump’s decision on NBC’s Meet the Press, saying the president was “choosing the American people first.”
Senator Darline Graham, Lindsey Graham’s sister, whom Trump has endorsed for a full term, said at a campaign stop on 17 October that she would “choose to keep the pressure on Russia.”
“I don’t trust Putin and I don’t trust Russia,” Darline Graham said.
She did not directly criticize Trump but said she would not have made that choice, Reuters reported.

In Germany, an amulet bearing a prayer to Jesus was found that could change perceptions of early Christianity
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
18:18:22 EEST
00:18:22 KST

In Germany, an amulet bearing a prayer to Jesus was found that could change perceptions of early Christianity
Kyiv • UNN
In Frankfurt, a 3rd-century silver amulet bearing a prayer to Jesus was deciphered. The find demonstrates the permeability of the boundaries of early Christianity.
Archaeologists have discovered an almost 1,800-year-old silver amulet bearing a prayer to Jesus during excavations of an ancient Roman cemetery in Frankfurt, Germany. The inscription on the artifact may help provide a better understanding of the spread of Christianity and the religious beliefs of people in the 3rd century AD. Popular Mechanics reports, writes UNN.
Details
In 2018, archaeologists discovered a man’s skeleton and a silver amulet at the site of an ancient Roman cemetery in Frankfurt’s Praunheim district. Inside a small capsule around the man’s neck was a rolled-up silver sheet bearing a prayer asking “Jesus Christ, Son of God” for protection from attacks and illnesses.
In 2024, researchers used computed tomography to read the fragile silver scroll without unrolling it.
The Frankfurt Archaeological Museum dates the burial to AD 230–260. The age was determined based on a clay jug and a censer buried alongside the man.
What is known about the inscription
The text consists of 18 lines. It mentions Jesus, repeats the words “holy, holy, holy,” and also uses motifs from the Apostle Paul’s Epistle to the Philippians 2:10–11, which says that every knee will bow before Jesus.
Unlike many other ancient protective texts, the inscription contains no clearly defined appeals to pagan gods alongside the Christian words.
How the discovery may change perceptions of early Christianity
Santiago Guijarro, a researcher of early Christianity at the Pontifical University of Salamanca, believes that the amulet raises questions about how closely its owner was connected to the Christian community.
According to him, the man may have entrusted his protection to Jesus while simultaneously taking part in sacrifices to the Roman gods.
Around AD 250, Emperor Decius introduced a requirement for the empire’s inhabitants to offer sacrifices to the Roman gods. The researcher notes that a person who was only loosely connected to the Christian community might not have regarded compliance with this order as a betrayal of their beliefs.
Documents preserved in papyri discovered in Egypt confirm that some Christians offered sacrifices despite their beliefs. Others obtained the relevant documents without performing the ritual.
Guijarro emphasizes that the presence of a Christian inscription confirms the spread of Christian texts in a particular place, but does not prove that the object’s owner considered himself a Christian.
In the 3rd century, the boundaries of what we call Christianity were far more permeable than later church literature suggests
In 2025, Guijarro published a study of the amulet in the journal Isidorianum. He noted that no earlier object or manuscript has preserved these verses from the Apostle Paul’s Epistle to the Philippians in Latin.
According to the researcher, the discovery is distinctive because the text was found not in a scriptorium or library, but inside a capsule worn around the neck of a man buried on the border of the Roman Empire.
Some details of the inscription remain unclear. In particular, the opening words are interpreted as a reference to Saint Titus, one of the Apostle Paul’s companions. Guijarro calls this interpretation puzzling, since known traditions of venerating Titus as a saint emerged much later.
The researcher believes that further archaeological discoveries of similar objects may help clarify how Christian prayers spread and who used such amulets.
Reconstructing this diversity does not weaken our understanding of early Christianity. It makes it more honest

Shall we have another EU referendum? Maybe – but not yet | Polly Toynbee
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
15:17:55 UTC
00:17:55 KST

When I hear that word again, a shudder runs down my spine. I want to groan, hold my head in my hands and wail. The horror! No, never again, not another referendum. But the idea is back in play as Andy Burnham looks for ways to reverse a decade of economic stagnation.
As the prime minister dared to unlock the door to a Brussels reunion, you could hear Ode to Joy burst out from all remainers. But the prospect of a re-run of the most self-destructive vote in our history is dismaying.
Remember that morning a decade ago. First came Sunderland’s 12.20am result, a 61.3% vote to leave, but there was still hope for remainers … until the BBC’s 4.40am verdict that leave had won. In that second a great rift tore across the country. Remainers, dubbed remoaners, never recovered. UK politics became a circus: we who paraded as the west’s strong and stable “mother of parliaments” ran wildly through seven prime ministers in 10 years. Both Labour and Tory parties were wrecked by the most shattering event of our political lifetime. It is a wound neither has dared to reopen.
Only now Burnham has finally broken the spell of Brexit silence, aiming to rejoin, while the Tories will stay in the wilderness until they repent the Brexit disaster they inflicted on the country.
As Burnham sets out to explore all the options, outriders scout the way back in. Making the strong case for full EU membership, IPPR, the thinktank closest to Labour, has published a weighty report this week on how it can happen and why it must: we need it for prosperity, security and democracy. It has left us dangerously alone and friendless in a world of great power blocs. Our once reliable ally, the US, is never to be fully trusted again now we know what its people are capable of voting for. And so the warmth of familiar democracies across the Channel looks welcoming (at least for now). Make this bid to rejoin about who we are, bonding with where we belong, emotionally and historically. We have discovered “sovereignty” is a mirage: every treaty and trade deal requires sharing it with allies.
Within a year, a majority of people in the UK thought Brexit was a mistake (not quite the same as regretting their own vote). Now we know that Brexit has robbed us of a walloping 8% of GDP. IPPR and Persuasion UK polling finds 52% want to rejoin, 29% to stay out. Support grows by the year, partly as older people drop off their perches and young pro-Europeans join the electoral roll. As the IPPR tested every option from Keir Starmer’s slight reset to full membership, the least popular was leaving things as they are. The current Boris Johnson/Lord Frost deal is so dysfunctional that Burnham says keeping it would be a “dereliction of duty”. As ever ignoring the public mood, last year Kemi Badenoch wrote to the EU ambassador warning that, if elected, she would repeal any change, an act of near-treason that could sabotage negotiations in Brussels that start next month. Watch Michael Gove, arch-Brexit manipulator, telling the Guardian’s Aditya Chakrabortty he regrets nothing, blaming others for failing to capitalise on those illusory Brexit benefits. Would that bleating work? I think not.
But is this shift to 52% v 29% strong enough to dare throw the dice and risk everything? No, not quite yet. The IPPR admits it is still “soft”, and there are familiar echoes of what happened last time. After years in which it felt as if we could talk about nothing else, the EU now has reassuringly low salience. But that’s just as it was until Ukip and Tory Brexiters turbocharged what had been a non-issue. As before, polling figures that encouraged David Cameron to breeze arrogantly into a referendum looked sufficient to someone who assumed he would win. This time we know better. Prepare for Dominic Cummings et al rising from their coffins with Brexit defibrillators to shock new life into the issue. Nigel Farage was at it on Sunday, claiming the EU would charge Britain £42bn a year to rejoin.
Testing arguments for both sides, this report reveals traps to avoid and what people like about rejoining. Red lights flash over joining the euro, scrapping our other trade deals, giving up fishing rights and high contributions to the EU budget. Top of the most effective reasons for rejoining is passport queues. Second comes security: Ukraine has exposed this dangerous Trump/Putin world. Third is the need to bring lost foreign investment back to Britain.
But reasoned, fact-based focus groups in a calm and rational atmosphere can’t begin to replicate the monstrous lies, fabrications and devilry of a TikTok, Instagram and X referendum campaign. Remember the £350m-a-week bus, the Turks are coming, immigration will end and, best of all, “take back control”. Of what? Everything! That’s what referendums do.
So not yet. The case for joining has to be powerfully made, the argument won overwhelmingly for allied EU forces to circle the wagons against what Peter Ricketts, ex-national security adviser, along with the head of MI5, warns are “more reckless, more dangerous” cyber-attacks on vital services, such as energy, water, transport, banking or air traffic control. The home secretary, Shabana Mahmood, meeting with the EU home affairs commissioner today to restore data cooperation on crime and migration is a reminder of how insanely self-destructive Brexit was.
In a decade, Britain has changed. Though Brexiters will threaten floods of migrants storming the border on joining the EU, IPPR polling shows freedom of movement no longer alarms voters as it once did. The cost of living is now the top national concern, not immigration. Look how poorer countries have caught up to us: per capita income in Bucharest, Romania’s capital, is far higher than Sunderland’s.
But the EU has changed too. The question is what kind of Europe we would join if Marine Le Pen and the Alternative für Deutschland became its new axis of power. Here’s the answer: that would make joining even more urgent, to be inside to influence what we can, bolstering the democrats. Staying out leaves us powerless.
This report sets to work on the campaign Burnham ignited when he proposed going “all the way”. The goal is clear and the need is growing urgent. As the EU ambassador told the Guardian’s Patrick Wintour, the ball is in our court. Brussels, he said, is “ready to engage”, once Britain decides what it wants.
Let’s decide, but proceed with extreme caution. Would you risk the next general election by putting this into Labour’s manifesto, certain to become the right’s battle-flag? Yes, when a strong pro-EU campaign makes it winnable. But there should be no referendum until public opinion is so solid that it would be a mere rubber-stamping of the overwhelming public will.
- Polly Toynbee is a Guardian columnist

U.S. firm fires cheap 3D-printed jet drones from a buggy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
15:16:07 UTC
00:16:07 KST

- Cummings Aerospace fired two Hellhound S3 drones from a vehicle-mounted launcher, with one operator controlling both autonomous missions from a single handheld system.
- The 13-pound, 3D-printed turbojet drone flies more than 60 km at up to 384 mph, and the new launcher holds up to eight.
Cummings Aerospace has fired two of its 3D-printed Hellhound S3 jet-powered drones from a launcher mounted on a utility vehicle, with a single operator using one handheld controller to send both on separate autonomous missions, the company said.
The test took place on Aug. 25, 2026, at the Pendleton UAS Range in Oregon, where an engineer from the Huntsville, Alabama-based company fired the two Hellhounds one after the other from a Polaris utility vehicle. Both carried inert payloads and flew different preplanned routes at different speeds, and Cummings Aerospace said the test met all of its objectives. The company announced the results on Oct. 12.
It was the first time the Hellhound had been fired from a vehicle after more than a dozen flight tests in its man-portable configuration, and the first use of a new launcher that can hold up to eight of the drones. It was also the first ripple-fire of the S3 and the first time one operator controlled more than one Hellhound at once.
Before launch, the operator programmed each drone’s waypoints, altitudes and flight path on the handheld fire control system. Once airborne, the Hellhounds flew those routes on their own while sending data back to the controller, so the operator could watch both flights live and change or abort either mission.
“Instead of having to manually fly a single drone or effector to a target, one Soldier using one FCS can simultaneously put multiple Hellhounds on multiple targets,” said Sheila Cummings, the company’s CEO.
The Hellhound S3 is about the size of a baseball bat and weighs about 6 kg (13 pounds). Its turbojet engine lets it fly more than 60 km (37 miles) at speeds of up to 618 km/h (384 mph), far faster than the propeller-driven quadcopters and loitering munitions common in Ukraine. Built from 3D-printed parts and commercial off-the-shelf components, it can be produced at a rate of more than 100 a month, according to the company. In its man-portable form, the drone, its launch canister and ground controller together weigh less than 11 kg (25 pounds), so one soldier can carry and launch it.
Cummings Aerospace pitches the Hellhound as a multi-mission weapon that can work as a loitering munition, a precision-guided munition, a one-way attack drone or a counter-drone interceptor. Operators can swap between four mission modules, armor-piercing, blast-fragmentation, electronic warfare and decoy, in under two minutes without tools.
“Controlling several S3s from one handheld system lets a small unit produce fires that used to take an entire battery,” said Cummings.
The new multi-pack launcher can be lifted by two people and fitted to a range of crewed or uncrewed U.S. Army vehicles. Next, the company plans to salvo-fire the Hellhound from the launcher, then fire it from the launcher mounted on an uncrewed ground vehicle and on an uncrewed surface vessel at sea.
Cummings Aerospace, a Native American woman-owned small business founded in 2009, first showed the Hellhound publicly at SOF Week in 2025, when it unveiled the turbojet strike drone and a larger S4 variant. The tube-launched S4 is 1.47 m (58 inches) long, weighs 20 kg (45 pounds) in its canister, can reach targets 130 to 140 km (81 to 87 miles) away and stay airborne for more than 1.5 hours, and the company is offering it as a low-cost cruise missile and as a gap-filling surveillance asset for the Golden Dome missile defense program.

borosilicate drinking glass creates optical illusion of liquid melting into table
originally launched in clear borosilicate glass and now available in pink and burnt yellow, the melt glass features an outward-rounded base that creates the optical illusion of liquid melting directly into the table surface.
prefer designboom on google
outward-rounded glass base creates subtle optical distortion
Designed by Federico Fontanella for Milan-based brand TRAGA, the Melt Glass reinterprets the standard drinking glass through subtle optical distortion. Its outward-rounded base alters the appearance of the liquid inside, creating the impression that the glass is slowly melting into the surface beneath it. The 300 ml vessel sits somewhere between a familiar tumbler and a small sculptural object. The shape originated from TRAGA’s own visual identity. The curvature at the base borrows from the forms found in the brand’s logo, translating a two-dimensional graphic element into a functional three-dimensional detail.
SCULPTURAL DRINKING GLASS takes on NEW COLORWAY TONALITIES
Originally released in transparent borosilicate glass, Melt now takes on two contrasting tones. Pink gives the form a softer, more playful presence, while Burnt Yellow creates a warmer and more graphic expression. The new colorways are accompanied by an editorial photography series by Agata Eliseeva, exploring the transparency, color, and sculptural qualities of the collection.
Melt Glass is made from lightweight, temperature-resistant, and recyclable borosilicate glass. Designed by Federico Fontanella for everyday use, it is suitable for water, juice, whisky, cocktails and hot drinks. Founded by Daniel Nikolovski, TRAGA approaches familiar domestic objects through small but unexpected interventions, with influences ranging from Milanese design culture to the Brutalist architecture of Nikolovski’s native Skopje.

Bulgaria will see sunny and warmer weather on Tuesday before rain, stronger winds and a drop in temperatures arrive later in the week, according to the forecast.
Temperatures today will be higher than yesterday in most parts of the country, with highs ranging from 16°C in northeastern Bulgaria to 22°C in the northwest. Sofia will reach 17°C in the afternoon, compared with Sunday’s high of 13°C. Winds will gradually weaken, while cloud cover will be more pronounced in eastern Bulgaria and along the Black Sea coast. Some areas in the northeast may receive light rain.
Isolated light showers are also possible overnight in northeastern Bulgaria. Winds will ease in many areas, and fog may reduce visibility near bodies of water and in low-lying areas by morning.
Minimum temperatures will range from 5°C to 12°C, falling to around 1°C in the valleys of western Bulgaria. Daytime highs on Tuesday will reach 18°C to 23°C, with around 19°C expected in Sofia and 17°C to 19°C along the Black Sea coast.
The day will be predominantly sunny, although clouds may increase temporarily in eastern Bulgaria, where light rain is possible in some locations before noon. Winds will be light, becoming moderate in eastern areas and blowing from the east-southeast.
Along the Black Sea coast, easterly to southeasterly winds will remain light to moderate. Morning visibility may be reduced in some places, followed by variable cloud cover during the day. Sea water temperatures are between 17°C and 19°C.
Conditions for mountain tourism will be very good on Tuesday, with sunny skies and moderate southwesterly winds. Temperatures will rise slightly at higher elevations, with maximums of 9°C at Aleko and 12°C at Borovets.
Wednesday will also bring sunshine, although fog may develop in some lowland areas during the morning. Moderate southerly winds, occasionally strong, are expected, while maximum temperatures will rise by another 1°C to 2°C.
Temperatures will remain largely unchanged on Thursday as cloud cover increases and rain reaches western Bulgaria.
Rain is forecast in many parts of the country on Friday, with substantial amounts possible in some areas. Winds will turn northwesterly and strengthen as colder air moves in, lowering daytime temperatures by 4°C to 5°C.
Cloud cover will temporarily decrease on Saturday, when temperatures are expected to edge up slightly.

Russian attacks cost Ukrainian businesses $7.7 billion in 2026, prime minister says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
15:12:29 UTC
00:12:29 KST

Russian attacks cost Ukrainian businesses $7.7 billion in 2026, prime minister says
Russian attacks have caused an estimated $7.7 billion in losses to Ukrainian businesses since the beginning of 2026, Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi said in an interview with BBC News Ukraine published on Oct. 19.
More than 1 million square meters of real estate, particularly warehouse and logistics facilities, have been destroyed or significantly damaged this year, Koretskyi said. The $7.7 billion estimate includes damage to business premises, manufacturing facilities and goods stored in warehouses.
"This is a very large figure that continues to grow," Koretskyi said.
The damage comes as Ukrainian businesses face mounting operational disruptions and weaker production as a result of Russian attacks and the ongoing invasion, now in its fifth year.
A monthly survey of 467 companies by the Kyiv-based Institute for Economic Research and Policy Consulting found that fewer businesses were operating at full capacity, while the share of companies reporting lower production volumes rose to its highest level in months.
The share of companies operating close to full capacity also fell for a second consecutive month, from 55% to 47%, according to the survey. Meanwhile, the proportion of businesses reporting lower production volumes rose from 15.6% to 22.6%.
The survey also found that 47.5% of companies said they could not forecast what their business would look like in two years, up from 40% in August.
Operational disruptions remain widespread. The survey found that 58.7% of companies lost working time because of air raid alerts, while 49.5% had to halt production during alerts.
Against this backdrop of mounting pressure on businesses, the government is considering measures to address wartime risks.
Koretskyi said in the interview that the government had proposed raising value-added tax (VAT) by one percentage point to establish a special fund to compensate businesses for insurance against war-related risks. The proposal was discussed at an online meeting with large companies several days earlier.
Discussions with businesses on other proposed policy changes have been more limited. Koretskyi said there had been no extensive consultations on changes to the rules for exempting employees from mobilization.

Canada: Alberta votes on holding independence referendum
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
15:09:00 UTC
00:09:00 KST

Canada: Alberta votes on holding independence referendum
October 19, 2026
Residents of Alberta in Canada are voting in a referendum on whether the province should begin a process that could ultimately lead to independence.
The motion does not appear likely to succeed but the vote taking place at all signifies economic and political grievances gaining some sway in the vast oil-rich region.
Separatist leaders hope that a comparatively strong showing for their cause could nevertheless pressure Prime Minister Mark Carney's government in Ottawa to pay them more heed in future.
What will happen during the vote?
Polls opened at 9 a.m. local time in the provincial capital Edmonton (1500 GMT/UTC) on Monday.
They are scheduled to close at 8 p.m. that evening (Tuesday, 0200 GMT/UTC).
Results will then be published as they come in.
At least based on opinion polls, the yes/no result is in no real doubt, but as many as 1 in 3 voters might support the proposal.
What has led to the vote?
Monday's referendum is the first on the notion of breaking away from Canada in a province other than majority French-speaking Quebec, which has a better-known separatist movement founded in language and cultural differences.
The vast oil-rich state is almost double the size of Germany in terms of land mass, but is much more sparsely populated with around 5 million residents. Almost half of them live in its two main cities, Edmonton and Calgary.
Alberta's provincial government is led by Danielle Smith of the United Conservative Party while Mark Carney's Liberal Party lead the national government.
Smith herself does not advocate independence and has urged voters to oppose the motion. But she has nevertheless authorized the vote, seemingly in a bid to assuage an increasingly vocal flank within her own ranks.
Independence advocates accuse the government of stifling Alberta's oil industry, for instance through environmental regulations, and also say they contribute disproportionately to the national public purse.
"Canada has an imbalanced system which feeds the central population and government at the expense of the outlying producing provinces such as Alberta," said Cory Morgan, founder of a pro-separation organization called Pathway to Independence.
Canadian sovereignty under pressure from within and without
Carney, who grew up in Alberta, has spent much of the past week campaigning for the "stay" campaign, appealing to national pride and urging supporters to vote to provide as resounding a result as possible — even in what might not be a close race.
The renowned economist and central banker often argued that the separatist cause might be guilty of overlooking matters more significant than dollars and drilling permits.
"Canada is not a transaction between provinces. It's not about gross and net, gives and gets," he said at an event in Red Deer on Friday.
Although polls in French-speaking Quebec suggest that enthusiasm for independence — typically a minority cause — is lower than usual during Carney's premiership, the issue is never very far from the political debate. The success of the separatist Parti Quebecois in local elections this month served as a reminder of this.
Carney is also trying to maintain national unity amid pressure from Canada's nearest neighbor and biggest trade partner.
US President Donald Trump is conducting characteristically combative trade talks with Canada that have seemed in danger of breaking down in recent months.
When at his most agitated, Trump has even called for Canada to become the "51st state" of the US. He has also tried to rename bodies of water like Lake Ontario.

The National Bank of Ukraine (NBU) has issued a written warning to NovaPay LLC, operating under the NovaPay trademark, for violations of legislation governing the payment market, the regulator said on Monday.
According to the NBU, the violations concerned the organization and proper functioning of the company's internal control and risk management systems, including controls over compliance with prudential requirements and the accuracy of information submitted to the regulator.
The NBU committee for supervision and regulation of banks and oversight of payment infrastructure adopted the decision to issue the written warning on October 16 following off-site supervision of the company's activities. NovaPay must remedy the identified violations within no more than 30 calendar days of receiving the decision.
"NovaPay will take the necessary measures to address the regulator's comments within the prescribed period. We are working to improve internal control and risk management, particularly with regard to compliance with prudential requirements and the accuracy of information we submit to the NBU," the company's press service told Interfax-Ukraine.
NovaPay added that it considered it important to maintain proper control over all processes and comply with the legislation governing the payment market.
As reported, in May 2026 the NBU imposed two fines on NovaPay for violations of payment legislation, amounting to UAH 4.88 million and UAH 3.12 million. The company told the agency at the time that it would not appeal the decisions and would pay the fines.
NovaPay was founded in 2001 as an international financial service and is part of the Nova Group, which includes Nova Poshta. It provides financial services online and at Nova Poshta branches.
In 2023, NovaPay became the first non-bank financial institution in Ukraine to receive an expanded NBU license allowing it to open accounts and issue payment cards.
In the first half of 2026, the volume of transfers through NovaPay increased by 41% year-on-year to UAH 391 billion, while the number of transfers rose by 12% to 258 million. During the period, the company paid UAH 905 million in taxes and fees, up 19% from a year earlier.

Can diplomacy stop another Ethiopia-Eritrea war?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
15:07:00 UTC
00:07:00 KST

Can diplomacy stop another Ethiopia-Eritrea war?
October 19, 2026
Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed has announced an interim government in the country's northern Tigray region, giving it six months to prepare for regional elections and restore stability.
Abiy's announcement on Friday followed a military offensive launched in September by the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF) and six other armed groups. They were ultimately forced to retreat and lost control of the region.
"To attain the peace that has long eluded them, to secure their right to self-administration, and to finally enjoy the fruits of development — which have been out of reach for many years — the people of Tigray must break free from this cycle of conflict," Abiy said in a statement posted on X.
Shishay Amare, the new mayor of the regional capital Mekelle, said they would "create the right conditions for elections by ensuring peace and stability across Tigray," as reported by French news agency Agence France-Presse.
"I am confident that this will be done within six months, according to our plan," Amare said, adding that their priorities included restoring peace, helping displaced residents return home, reopening markets and ensuring humanitarian assistance reached those in need.
Why relations with Eritrea matter
The fighting has revived concerns about a return to the devastating 2020–2022 Tigray war. Around 1 million people remain displaced from that conflict. The African Union has estimated that the war resulted in around 600,000 deaths from combat, famine and the collapse of healthcare.
The new administration faces unresolved disputes over political authority and territory, including western Tigray, which is claimed by both Tigray and neighboring Amhara state.
Ethiopia and Eritrea were once bitter enemies but signed a peace agreement in 2018. Eritrean forces later fought alongside Ethiopian federal troops during the Tigray war. But the countries' relationship has since deteriorated.
Addis Ababa has accused Asmara of supporting Tigrayan forces and violating Ethiopian territory. Eritrea has denied the accusations.
Reports of Eritrean troop movements near the border have heightened concern, although the extent of any current deployment remains disputed.
Tsedale Lemma, journalist and publisher of the prominent Addis Standard magazine, told DW earlier this month that the danger reflects years of unresolved tensions and failures to implement the November 2022 Pretoria Agreement, which ended the Tigray war.
Lemma said the international community was "absolutely underestimating" the threat of conflict. She argued that international actors had failed to ensure effective monitoring of the agreement and respond adequately as the peace process weakened.
A wider regional risk
The confrontation comes amid instability across the Horn of Africa, including Sudan's war and tensions between Ethiopia and Egypt over the Nile mega-dam project.
Ethiopia inaugurated the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam (GERD) in September 2025, a move that was not well received by neighboring Egypt and Sudan, both downstream countries.
Competition over access to the Red Sea has added another strategic dimension: Ethiopia became landlocked when Eritrea gained independence in 1993.
Journalist Martin Plaut, who specializes in the Horn of Africa, has warned that the region is at a crossroads. He has raised the possibility of Ethiopian forces entering Eritrea, but an invasion remains a scenario, not a confirmed decision by the Ethiopian government.
Any wider conflict could threaten regional trade and maritime security. The Red Sea and the Bab el-Mandeb Strait connect shipping routes between Europe and Asia, making the region strategically important well beyond Africa.
Can diplomacy avert war between Ethiopia and Eritrea?
The United States and the United Kingdom have called on Ethiopia and Eritrea to exercise restraint and return to dialogue under their 2018 peace framework.
Speaking to reporters at Joint Base Andrews in Maryland on Saturday, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio warned that the military buildup on the Ethiopia-Eritrea border could escalate into a wider conflict.
Rubio said Washington hoped lifting some sanctions would improve communication with both sides and stressed the need for a "wise and measured" response to avoid a broader regional war.
The United Kingdom has also called for renewed talks between both sides. "We urgently call for de-escalation and a return to dialogue. We reiterate our support for the African Union's role in facilitating this," said a UK government spokesperson in a statement on October 15.
For now, the recapture of towns in Tigray has changed the military balance but has not resolved tensions in the region.
Whether international pressure can prevent a wider war will depend on whether the governments involved choose dialogue over further escalation.
Negash Mohammed, Tamirat Geleta and Christine Mhundwa contributed to this report.

Add Helsinki Times as a preferred source on Google (opens Google in a new tab)
The violence followed nationwide demonstrations on Saturday against rising living costs, fuel prices and declining public services. More than 500,000 people participated, exceeding an initial police estimate of 200,000.

Paris Mayor Emmanuel Grégoire called for negotiations between the government and education organisations, arguing that the unrest required a political response.
The European Union condemned the violence while defending the right to peaceful demonstrations.
"Those who demonstrate peacefully must not be conflated with those who commit violence," EU spokesman Markus Lammert said.
The unrest also affected financial markets. France's CAC 40 stock index fell 1.3% in early trading on Monday, while the yield on French 10-year government bonds rose to 4.86%, Reuters reported.
Further demonstrations are planned for Saturday, 24 October, by organisers associated with the Yellow Vest movement. Trade unions have also called for nationwide strikes and rallies on 5 November.

Ukraine opens its first war-crime case against a ship captain for carrying off 54,000 tons of its stolen grain
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
15:06:12 UTC
00:06:12 KST

Ukraine has opened its first war-crime case against a ship captain for carrying off its stolen grain. Ukraine’s Security Service and Prosecutor General’s Office have charged the captain of the cargo ship Matros Pozynich with illegally shipping more than 54,000 tons of Ukrainian wheat that Russian forces stole from occupied territory, the Security Service said on Telegram.
Russia has looted grain across the Ukrainian land it occupies and sold it abroad as its own, a trade Ukrainian intelligence puts at more than 2 million tons in 2025 alone. The case against the Matros Pozynich captain is the first time Kyiv has classified a ship captain’s role in that trade as a war crime, prosecutors said.
The captain, a Russian citizen, twice sailed wheat from occupied Sevastopol in Crimea to the Syrian port of Latakia in 2022 and 2023, according to the Security Service. The first shipment of more than 27,000 tons left Crimea in 2022, and another 27,000-plus tons followed in January 2023.
A crime ordered from the top, investigators say
The shipments were no freelance smuggling run. The grain was removed on the decision of the Russian state’s top political leadership, the Security Service stated, in breach of the Geneva Conventions, which forbid pillaging property in occupied territory.
To hide the voyages, the captain periodically switched off the ship’s automatic identification system and transmitted false coordinates, investigators found. He was notified of suspicion in absentia under two articles of Ukraine’s Criminal Code, including the violations of the laws and customs of war. The service said it is working to identify others in the scheme.
One ship in a fleet that feeds the war
The vessel is a single thread in a much larger theft. Russia has taken roughly 15 million tons of Ukrainian grain from occupied territory between 2022 and August 2025 and earned at least $1 billion from it, money that helps fund the war.
Much of it moves through Russian-controlled ports such as Sevastopol, often relabeled as Russian produce or passed between ships at sea to hide its Ukrainian origin. Buyers have included Syria, Egypt, Turkiye, Lebanon, and others, though Egypt has since pledged to stop accepting grain tied to occupied territories.

Famine fears as aid cuts and shipment restrictions coincide in Gaza
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
15:05:16 UTC
00:05:16 KST

Famine fears as aid cuts and shipment restrictions coincide in Gaza
Displaced families in Gaza fear worsening food insecurity as planned aid cuts coincide with continued restrictions on commercial shipments entering the territory.
Deir el-Balah, Gaza Strip — Manal Abu Rabie, a displaced mother of six from Beit Lahiya in northern Gaza, received news that the World Food Programme (WFP) was cutting food assistance to the enclave with fear about what is to follow in the coming days.
Gaza has suffered from severe shortages of key staples such as eggs, flour and onions after Israel closed border crossings into the enclave on Wednesday. The prices of food and other essentials have skyrocketed, and families who can afford to do so have been bulk buying, in anticipation of a prolonged blockade.
After the WFP announced cuts to food aid, the price of a bundle of bread rose from 5 to 12 shekels (around $1.60 to $3.90).
Abu Rabie has already been struggling to provide food for her family and says she has little to fall back on if the support she needs is reduced after the announcement of aid cuts.
“We were just beginning to say, ‘Thank God,’ and now they want to cut off our food and drink,” she said. “We are going back to starvation. We are dying of hunger.”
On Monday, the WFP announced that a funding shortfall had forced it to reduce the number of people receiving monthly food assistance in Gaza from 1.6 million to 1.1 million, leaving around 500,000 people without support.
The agency is also halving food rations, meaning families receiving assistance will get one food parcel instead of two, alongside a smaller bag of wheat flour.
The number of hot meals provided daily will fall from 250,000 to 150,000, while cash assistance will be reduced for 75,000 families. The WFP said the cuts were driven by a lack of funding, despite continued humanitarian needs.
The suspension of aid shipments into Gaza for a sixth consecutive day, which is a separate development, has added to uncertainty about the availability and affordability of food, fuel and medicine.
‘I cannot afford to buy anything’
Abu Rabie, 39, who lives in al-Salam camp in Deir el-Balah, central Gaza, relies on food assistance, including parcels containing lentils, rice, flour and cooking oil.
Her family is already struggling to afford basic food items as prices rise, with a small bottle of cooking oil, which is included in WFP food parcels, now costing 10 shekels ($3.20), is beyond her means.
“It is very difficult. I cannot afford to buy anything,” she said.
She has high blood pressure, diabetes and heart disease. With no alternative, she is forced to live off the food provided in aid parcels, aggravating her digestive problems.
“If the assistance stops and the quantities become smaller, how are we supposed to get through the day? We’ll have to eat sand. That is all that will be left for us,” she said.
“I swear to God, my son asks me for things, and I cannot get them for him. My husband is injured, and I am sick.”
The approaching winter is adding to her anxiety. Abu Rabie said her family had no blankets or mattresses.
“I say, ‘God, please don’t let winter come’, because we have no blankets and no mattresses,” she said. “There is no food and no drink. God knows how we are managing.”
Warnings of worsening hunger
In a statement issued on Monday, Gaza’s Government Media Office warned that the WFP’s planned cuts could worsen the humanitarian crisis and leave hundreds of thousands of Palestinians facing greater food insecurity.
The office called on the United Nations and the international community to provide urgent funding to sustain relief programmes. It also held Israel responsible for the consequences of the restrictions on aid entering Gaza, and called for all crossings to be opened to allow humanitarian supplies to enter without interruption.
The statement urged Arab and Islamic countries, as well as international organisations, to provide financial support and help facilitate the delivery of food, medical supplies and other essential items.
The WFP, meanwhile, has attributed its planned reductions to a funding shortfall rather than a decline in humanitarian needs, appealing to donors for additional support.
Randa al-War, a displaced mother of three originally from Gaza City’s Shujayea neighbourhood, said food assistance from the WFP is a lifeline.
She now lives with her family in Sarsour camp in Deir el-Balah and said they receive no assistance from other organisations.
“We depend on the World Food Programme. We cannot live without bread, without flour. These children need to eat,” she said.
Al-War said the food parcels which her family receives every two or three months, including flour and cooking oil, last around a month.
“We get through the day if the food parcel comes. If it comes, the children eat. If it doesn’t, there is no food,” she said.
She fears that the WFP’s cuts could leave her family without the support it relies on. Buying food from the market is not a realistic alternative, she said, because neither she nor her husband can work as she is injured and he has health problems.
“I cannot work, and my husband cannot work,” she said. “We are living only on the World Food Programme and the food parcels.”
Al-War said the prospect of further cuts has left her frightened that her children will face hunger again.
“We are afraid there will be famine, because of our children. We will not be able to provide them with anything,” she said. “We are not just afraid… we are terrified that famine will return.”
Rising prices add to families’ struggles
The suspension of commercial shipments is adding to the pressure on families already struggling with reduced purchasing power and rising prices caused by the war and Israel’s siege on Gaza.
Rami al-Zayigh, a Gaza-based economic expert, said the continued closure of crossings was restricting the supply of goods in a territory already facing persistent shortages, pushing prices higher and placing further pressure on families.
“The issue goes beyond a shortage of supply,” al-Zayigh said. “Whenever the crossings close, traders and sellers raise prices, creating panic among citizens. The citizen is the biggest victim of these measures.”
Vegetables and fruit were becoming scarce in local markets, and the price of eggs had risen by about 300 percent over the past week.
Vegetables and fruit are particularly vulnerable to interruptions in supply as they risk spoiling within days, al-Zayigh said.
Citing official reports from Gaza, he said food stocks in the territory were estimated to be sufficient for only about two weeks. He warned that continued restrictions on goods entering Gaza could have further economic and health consequences, particularly for children and older people.
For families who rely on aid, the combination of reduced assistance, limited income and higher prices leaves fewer ways to secure daily meals. Al-War said families should not have to beg for the essentials they need to survive.
“We want to live like the rest of the world. We do not want to beg for these things. They should be available to us without us having to ask,” she said.
“We are human beings. We want to live, eat and drink. We want a dignified life.”

Protection against legal intimidation: why anti-SLAPP legislation matters to everyone who speaks out publicly
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
18:04:56 EEST
00:04:56 KST

Oksana Nesterenko, Executive Director of the Anti-Corruption Research and Education Centre (ACREC)
Anti-SLAPP measures protect people from lawsuits used to exert pressure on them because of their public activities. Such cases burden the courts and delay the hearing of other claims. Powerful claimants can use their financial advantage to silence journalists, activists and others who take part in public debate.
Each such case takes up the time of judges and court staff. A claimant can achieve their objective even if they lose the case: it may be enough to force a person or organisation to spend years exhausting their resources and energy on a legal defence.
Countering SLAPPs therefore serves two related purposes: protecting the courts from abuse and safeguarding freedom of expression.
On 30 September 2026, Draft Law No. 16117, “On the Protection of Persons Engaging in Public Participation from Manifestly Unfounded Claims or Abusive Court Proceedings”, was registered in the Verkhovna Rada of Ukraine. SLAPPs involve the use of court proceedings primarily to intimidate, financially exhaust or silence people because of their public participation on matters of public interest. The draft law is currently under consideration by a parliamentary committee.
The draft law aims to protect the right to a fair trial and freedom of expression. To this end, it proposes mechanisms to counter the use of litigation to exert pressure on people who raise matters of public interest.
Why is such protection necessary? Claimants do not need to win their cases. It may be enough to force someone to find a lawyer, incur substantial costs and spend years defending themselves in court. In the meantime, an investigation may be halted or a public campaign abandoned. Others, seeing the price of public criticism, may choose to remain silent. This is known as the “chilling effect”: the threat of litigation intimidates not only the defendant but also others who might otherwise raise similar concerns.
Imagine a small regional newsroom that publishes an investigation into possible misuse of public funds. In response, a powerful individual files a lawsuit alleging damage to their business reputation and seeking substantial monetary compensation.
Even if the journalists ultimately prove their case, they may spend years attending hearings, dealing with lawyers and preparing documents. This diverts resources away from journalism. Other newsrooms, seeing the consequences, may decide against conducting similar investigations. Sometimes, the prolonged proceedings alone are enough for the claimant to achieve the desired outcome.
For Ukraine, this is far from an abstract problem.
In 2020, Iryna Venediktova, then Acting Director of the State Bureau of Investigation (SBI), brought a lawsuit against the Anti-Corruption Action Center and Ukrainska Pravda over publications concerning her husband's alleged influence on staffing decisions at the SBI.
Another example is the legal dispute between Andrii Portnov, a former Deputy Head of the Presidential Administration, and journalists from the investigative programme Schemes. In September 2024, the Kyiv Court of Appeal upheld a ruling in the claimant's favour. The case prompted debate about the risks of litigation being used to pressure journalists reporting on influential public figures.
The case of environmental activist Mykhailo Berchuk is also illustrative. Berchuk documents environmental violations in Ukraine's Kirovohrad region. According to the ZMINA Human Rights Centre, a claim for UAH 5 million was brought against him. Human rights defenders regard the proceedings as an attempt to intimidate the activist and restrict his public activities.
Of course, the mere fact that a lawsuit is brought against a journalist or activist does not automatically make it a SLAPP. Whether proceedings are abusive is a matter for the court to determine. Nevertheless, these cases show why the issue deserves public attention.
In ACREC's study, “Countering SLAPP Lawsuits: Assessing the Compliance of Ukrainian Legislation with Directive (EU) 2024/1069”, we analysed existing procedural safeguards and concluded that they do not provide adequate protection against the particular risks posed by strategic lawsuits against public participation.
Draft Law No. 16117 is designed to address precisely such abuses. It neither prohibits lawsuits nor exempts journalists or activists from legal liability. Everyone retains the right of access to a court. But where litigation is used as an instrument of pressure, the court would have specific mechanisms at its disposal to respond.
Indications of abuse may include manifestly unfounded or disproportionate claims, threats, or multiple lawsuits intended to exhaust the defendant. It is for the court to assess these circumstances; the court may bring proceedings to an early end and decide on the award of costs. After all, the right of access to a court does not confer a right to use the courts to harass others. This is the essence of anti-SLAPP legislation: to protect judicial proceedings from abuse and people from pressure for participating in public debate on matters of public interest.
The introduction of the draft law has already prompted public debate. In particular, an opinion piece published by Interfax-Ukraine raised concerns that the proposed anti-SLAPP mechanisms violate the principle of legal certainty, create unjustified procedural privileges for civil society activists and conditions for their impunity, restrict other people's right of access to a court, and threaten the principle of a fair trial.
To explain why these conclusions are unfounded, let us turn to European legal standards and the findings of in-depth research conducted by respected policy and academic institutions.
Does protecting a broad range of people create legal uncertainty?
Let us begin with a simple question: should someone need a press card or membership in a civil society organisation to be able to speak out about a problem in their community without fear?
A woman living in a village might speak out against river pollution for the first time. Parents might report unsafe conditions at a school. Someone with no previous experience of public participation might investigate a questionable public procurement. The absence of professional status does not diminish the public significance of their actions.
Protection should depend on what the person actually did and on the circumstances of the dispute. Taking part in public debate does not grant permanent immunity from liability. Other people retain the right to bring a well-founded claim, including one arising from the very same public statement.
This approach is reflected in Article 4 of Directive (EU) 2024/1069. It links public participation to the exercise of freedom of expression and information, freedom of the arts and sciences, and freedom of assembly and association, in relation to matters of public interest. The definition also covers preparatory, supporting or assisting actions directly linked to such participation.
The broad range of people eligible for protection does not, in itself, make the law legally uncertain. The court must establish whether the claim is connected to the person's public participation and whether the legal grounds for special protection are met. The person's profession or membership in an organisation is not decisive.
Do evaluative legal concepts create legal uncertainty?
One criticism of Draft Law No. 16117 concerns its use of evaluative legal concepts, including the claimant's financial advantage or influence and threats made against the defendant. But does the presence of such concepts really undermine the principle of legal certainty?
Evaluative legal concepts are an integral part of Ukrainian law and judicial practice. Every day, courts determine what constitutes “good faith”, “reasonableness”, “fairness”, a “material breach of contract” or “valid reasons” for missing a procedural deadline. The law sets out legal criteria, while courts assess the specific circumstances and evidence.
This is precisely the approach taken in anti-SLAPP Draft Law No. 16117. It does not propose treating a claim as abusive solely because the claimant is financially stronger or influential. What matters is the purpose for which court proceedings are used—to prevent or penalise public participation—and the legally established indications of abuse. These include exploiting an imbalance of power, making threats, bringing disproportionate claims and engaging in procedural conduct intended to exhaust the defendant. These circumstances must be established and assessed by a court, not automatically presumed.
Moreover, Ukrainian legislation already provides for the use of evaluative concepts to identify abuses of court proceedings, and courts already apply them. In a ruling of 1 July 2026 in Case No. 910/10837/25, the Grand Chamber of the Supreme Court expressly stated that concepts such as a “knowingly groundless claim” and a “dispute of an obviously artificial nature” are evaluative and require judicial interpretation and the development of criteria for their application. The court must establish a bad-faith purpose, disproportionate use of procedural mechanisms and conduct inconsistent with the objectives of judicial proceedings. The mere presence of evaluative concepts, therefore, does not render a mechanism for countering abuses of court proceedings legally uncertain. What matters is how clearly the criteria for applying them are defined and whether judicial decisions are properly reasoned.
Legal certainty, therefore, does not require abandoning evaluative concepts. It requires clear statutory criteria that courts apply to established facts. This approach makes it possible to counter abuses of court proceedings without depriving either party of the right to a fair trial.
Does early dismissal violate the right of access to a court?
Another concern about anti-SLAPP measures is that allowing court proceedings to be brought to an early end effectively deprives claimants of the right to judicial protection. But is that really the case?
The right to a fair trial belongs to both parties. The claimant has the right to seek redress for a violation of their rights. The defendant has the right to a fair procedure that does not become a means of exhausting them. It is therefore essential to distinguish the right of access to a court from abuse of that right.
Article 6 of the European Convention on Human Rights guarantees the right to a fair trial, while Article 55 of Ukraine's Constitution guarantees the right to judicial protection. These guarantees do not, however, mean that the judicial system must remain defenceless when procedural rights are used for purposes contrary to their intended function. Moreover, Ukrainian procedural law already prohibits the abuse of procedural rights. The very idea of judicial mechanisms to counter such abuse is therefore neither new nor incompatible with the right to a fair trial.
What makes SLAPPs distinctive is that the harm may occur long before a final judgment is delivered. Imagine a small newsroom forced to choose between continuing an investigation and paying yet another round of legal fees. Even if the newsroom wins the case years later, it will not recover the time and resources lost, nor the missed opportunities to conduct other investigations. Protection that comes only after years of litigation may therefore arrive too late.
Nor is this merely a hypothetical scenario. It reflects a reality facing Ukrainian media that journalists, media lawyers, experts and members of the judiciary have been describing for years. Specific cases and the consequences of such lawsuits have been discussed, among other settings, at roundtable discussions devoted to countering SLAPPs in Ukraine.
To prevent such consequences, Article 11 of Directive (EU) 2024/1069 provides for the early dismissal of manifestly unfounded claims, while Article 13 guarantees the possibility of appealing a decision granting early dismissal. This does not mean that a case is automatically dismissed simply because the defendant is a journalist or civil society activist. The court makes its decision after examining the legal grounds, considering the parties' positions and providing adequate reasons.
At the same time, it is important to distinguish manifestly unfounded claims from abusive court proceedings against public participation. A claim can be used as an instrument of pressure even if it is not manifestly unfounded. Early dismissal and other remedies against abusive proceedings therefore have different grounds for application. Conflating these mechanisms would put the parties' procedural rights at risk.
Early dismissal of a manifestly unfounded claim does not, in itself, violate the right to a fair trial. On the contrary, it allows the legal system to protect not only the claimant's right to have a case heard, but also the defendant's right not to be subjected to exhausting litigation. The decisive issue is not whether such a mechanism exists, but how clearly its grounds and the safeguards governing its use are defined.
Who must prove abuse, and why should civil society organisations be involved in a case?
Two further criticisms of Draft Law No. 16117 concern the burden of proof and the participation of civil society organisations in court proceedings. Yet both mechanisms are intended to address the asymmetry of resources and influence between the parties that often characterises SLAPPs, rather than to create unjustified privileges for defendants.
As regards the burden of proof, special rules for allocating it have long been familiar to Ukrainian law. In particular, Part 3 of the Article 81of the Civil Procedure Code of Ukraine provides that, in cases concerning retaliation against whistleblowers, the employer must prove that its decisions were lawful and unrelated to the reporting of corruption. The purpose is to ensure equality between the parties in practice, not merely on paper. A journalist or activist acting in the public interest may find themselves facing a powerful claimant who can fund years of litigation and retain teams of expensive lawyers. Such an imbalance is expressly recognised in paragraph 4 of Part 1 of Article 2 of the draft law as one possible indication of a SLAPP.
The mechanism would work as follows. Where a claim is brought against a person on account of their public participation, the defendant may apply to the court for the proceedings to be closed if they believe the claim displays the indications of a SLAPP set out in Paragraph 4 of Part 1 of Article 2 of Draft Law No. 16117. In the application, the defendant identifies the circumstances suggesting possible abuse, but the draft law places the burden of proving the absence of those indications on the claimant. If the court finds no abuse, the case proceeds to an examination of its merits under the ordinary rules of evidence. If, however, the court finds that the claim constitutes abusive court proceedings against public participation, it closes the proceedings. In that situation, the court process is being used not to protect an infringed right but to exert pressure on public participation.
As for civil society organisations, their involvement reflects the fact that protecting public participation is about safeguarding not only an individual but also the public interest and democracy. Article 11 of the draft law, like Article 9 of Directive (EU) 2024/1069, allows organisations with relevant expertise to assist the court in assessing the nature of the dispute. Functionally, the mechanism resembles the internationally recognised concept of amicus curiae, or “friend of the court”. The purpose is not to give the defendant an advantage in numbers, but to assist the court in safeguarding the public interest. The draft law expressly provides that such organisations may join proceedings only with the defendant's consent and may not appeal court decisions.
These safeguards are therefore not a Ukrainian legal experiment. They are tools developed through years of international research on SLAPPs and expert work, and reflected in European standards. Their purpose is to ensure genuine equality of arms and a fair trial—not impunity for defendants.
Why the draft law deserves support
Draft Law No. 16117 deserves support as a step towards implementing Directive (EU) 2024/1069 and European standards for countering SLAPPs. It is intended to help in situations where the legal process itself becomes punishment for public criticism. For journalists, human rights defenders and community members, promptly stopping an abuse means being able to continue their work. For society, it means access to information about public authorities, corruption and rights violations. The story of Maltese journalist Daphne Caruana Galizia, who investigated corruption, faced numerous lawsuits and was murdered in 2017, reminds us why such protection matters for democracy.
Individual provisions of the draft law can and should be criticised. At the same time, the proposed mechanisms are grounded in international research and analysis of real cases. Ukrainian specialists worked on the draft with the participation of international experts and the support of the Council of Europe. Criticism should therefore come with proposals: what alternative tools would protect against SLAPPs, and what evidence demonstrates their effectiveness?

France on edge as curfews imposed to curb rioting and looting

France on edge as curfews imposed to curb rioting and looting
- Click here to listen to this article
-   Share via
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
- What began with peaceful protests by high school students demanding better conditions at schools has morphed into roiling protests nationwide denouncing rising living costs and inequities in French society.
- Authorities imposed curfews Monday night in an attempt to restore order. The interior minister conceded that police had ‘lost control’ of some big cities.
- Grocery stores, clothing shops, cafés, health clinics and public buildings were ransacked in Paris, Marseille, Bordeaux and other cities.
PARIS — Two large sections of central Paris were shut down in a curfew Monday night as France was reeling from a weekend of nationwide rioting and looting that left much of the country stupefied by the scarcity of police in some of the hardest-hit neighborhoods.
Grocery stores, clothing shops, cafés, health clinics and public buildings were ransacked in Paris, Marseille, Bordeaux and other cities. Overwhelmed police forces often failed to intervene as thousands of vandals, many wearing masks and caps that hid their faces, shattered storefront windows and walked off with merchandise.
Crowds of young adults set cars, electric bikes and trash cans on fire. A patchwork of blazing barricades blocked traffic on many Paris streets and shrouded nearby buildings in black smoke.
What began last week with peaceful protests by high school students demanding better conditions in schools beset by overcrowding and decrepit facilities has morphed into roiling protests nationwide denouncing rising living costs and inequities in French society.
More than 500,000 people took to the streets Saturday and although most marched peacefully, others rampaged and began looting. The violence has left many in France with a sense that their nation was unraveling with a deeply unpopular president struggling to manage a growing debt crisis amid extreme social and political divisions.
In a televised speech from the Élysée Palace as looting was resuming on Sunday evening, President Emmanuel Macron acknowledged the nation’s “anger and shame,” saying he had ordered his government to “draw every lesson” from its handling of the violence.
“I expect clear answers,” he said hours before leaving France for a three-day visit to the Middle East in what he billed as an effort to secure France’s fuel supplies amid rising costs he attributed to the U.S. war with Iran.
Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez, who conceded Monday that police had “lost control” of some big cities, offered his resignation, but Macron declined to accept it.
Macron’s 10 years as president is coming to an end next spring. The leading candidate to succeed him in the presidential election next spring is Marine Le Pen, who would be the first far-right leader of France since the Vichy regime that collaborated with Nazi Germany in World War II. She has pledged a restoration of public order, along with a crackdown on immigration and a halt to French aid to Ukraine.
On Monday, authorities imposed an 11 p.m. curfew on the République and Les Halles sections of Paris, both of them ravaged by looting over the weekend. Curfews were also declared in Lyon, Nice, Lille and other cities.
France is not the only European to experience unrest in recent days. Violent protests have broken out in Italy and Albania. Rising housing costs triggered demonstrations this year in Spain and Portugal.
In Les Halles, Assia Sanaa was unable to stop assailants from smashing windows and making off with nearly all of the sneakers and sportswear in four Shinzo shops that she owns on the Rue Étienne Marcel.
Sanaa said she called the police 20 times, to no avail.
“You know what they told me? ‘Stop calling, ma’am. You’re jamming the line.’”
She was furious at the government’s response to the unrest.
At the same time, Sanaa sympathized with the police, who were far outnumbered by vandals, many of them young men from France’s poorest suburbs, where youth unemployment is rampant.
With no police in sight, Sanaa and other shopkeepers who were targeted along the Rue Étienne Marcel watched as small groups of looters used mobile phones to tip each other off to the cops’ whereabouts, handily winning the cat-and-mouse chase.
“We were in a no-man’s land, left to fend for ourselves,” Sanaa said.
In much of Paris, graffiti spray-painted onto storefronts denounced Macron, the police and the far-right French media baron Vincent Bolloré. “Your world is burning down!” was scrawled across one shattered window near the Place de la République, where protesters tossed projectiles at police on Saturday amid clouds of tear gas.
Just down the street from the Élysée Palace, “Death to the king” was written in red spray paint on the wall of a vandalized Yves Saint Laurent boutique on the Rue Saint Honoré, one of the world’s premier luxury shopping strips.
Shaken Paris shopkeepers, who were consoled by many passersby on Monday as street cleaners swept up shattered glass, said the groups erecting barricades, setting fires and tagging buildings with political messages appeared to be distinct from both the high school demonstrators and the vandals attacking businesses.
Macron’s prime minister, Sébastien Lecornu, accused the far-left presidential contender Jean-Luc Mélenchon of trying to blame police commanders for the unrest.
Mélenchon, leader of the France Unbowed party, has denounced police tactics against high-school students — in one incident a 15-year-old student had his hand torn off by a police grenade — but has condemned protester violence.
On a grocery run in Les Halles on Monday, Jean-Pierre Frankfower, a retired actor and philosopher, blamed the government for the upheaval, saying it neglected social services and education and was too aggressive toward demonstrators.
“It doesn’t surprise me, because it had been simmering for a while,” he said.
Early Sunday morning, near the Place de la République, a part-time crossing guard named Joëlle, 71, scanned the wreckage along the Boulevard Voltaire from a bench, holding her shaggy shepherd mix, Pollux, on a leash. From her apartment window, she’d seen vandals set fires the night before.
Joëlle, who declined to give her last name because of her work for City Hall, agrees with critics of Macron who say the center-right president has favored the rich. She also lamented the chronic joblessness among young people in France.
To her, the city felt like a war zone.
“This isn’t Paris anymore,” she said.

Against the backdrop of rising nationalist violence, clashes and attacks on an American photographer and foreign diplomats by Jewish extremists over the weekend, the IDF is stepping up operations against centers of violence in the West Bank. In recent days, the military has already begun expanding enforcement efforts, with security officials seeking to send a clear message: Operations against illegal sites will continue, and additional evacuations will be carried out wherever structures built without authorization must be removed.
The decision reflects a growing recognition that arrests, vehicle seizures and financial measures against suspects must be accompanied by stronger enforcement against the physical infrastructure that enables such activity. Security officials believe responding to violent incidents after they occur is insufficient and that action must also be taken against illegal sites they assess could serve as bases for further confrontations.
Since the beginning of 2026, approximately 200 illegal sheds and structures have been cleared across the West Bank, including in Areas A and B. The figure refers to clearance operations rather than necessarily 200 separate outposts, as the same outpost may have been evacuated more than once.
At the same time, two reserve Border Police companies were deployed to reinforce the area Saturday night. The forces are intended to help manage confrontations during the olive harvest season, strengthen the security presence on the ground and expand enforcement operations. One of their assigned missions is to double the number of evacuations. Security officials have emphasized that while efforts continue to legalize settlements where permitted and support agricultural farms, illegal construction will not be allowed at sites targeted for enforcement.
One of the locations where forces have operated in recent days is the illegal Shirat Zion outpost. According to a security official, structures at the site were evacuated Sunday, and six suspects were arrested by Border Police during the operation. All six were subsequently released, with a court ordering them to stay away from the compound. The decision, however, drew criticism from law enforcement officials. They argued that the compound had already been declared a closed military zone under an order issued by the regional military commander, which remains in effect until November. In their view, barring the suspects from the site offers no effective solution because it merely prohibits them from doing something that was already forbidden.
"We need effective enforcement," security officials said, stressing that military and police operations must be accompanied by legal measures that create deterrence and prevent suspects from quickly returning to the area. Meanwhile, security forces began additional evacuations Monday morning, arresting four more suspects as part of the enforcement operations.
Security officials view enforcement against illegal outposts as one of the tools available to reduce friction and violence. Alongside arrests, vehicle seizures and financial measures against suspects, the objective is to prevent illegal outposts from remaining in place and becoming recurring flashpoints for confrontation.
The challenge for the IDF is to turn the current reinforcements and wave of evacuations into a sustained campaign rather than a one-time response to an exceptional incident. The question is whether expanded enforcement will succeed in reducing the number of violent incidents and whether cooperation between the military, police and judicial system will provide an effective response that prevents the same sites from being reestablished after their evacuation.
Amid international criticism following the violent incidents, particularly the attack on foreign diplomats, security officials are seeking to demonstrate that efforts to combat nationalist violence go beyond condemnations and arrests. For them, the real test will be on the ground: the scale of enforcement, the ability to prevent illegal outposts from being rebuilt and whether those involved in violence face meaningful consequences.
During the fall olive harvest season in the West Bank, violent incidents have been increasing, drawing international media attention this year. Last Friday, dozens of masked Jewish rioters attacked Palestinian olive harvesters in the village of Abu Falah, near Ramallah, injuring two people, including Heidi Levine, a photographer for the American newspaper The Washington Post.
A day later, Jewish extremists attacked diplomats from France, Belgium and Poland, along with Israeli activists who were visiting an olive harvest near the Palestinian village of Taybeh, considered the last remaining Christian village in the West Bank. Videos from the scene showed a group of masked men armed with sticks and stones approaching a vehicle carrying the diplomats and pursuing them on an all-terrain vehicle. Bernard Baudoux, mayor of the French town of Aulnoye-Aymeries, was later seen sitting on the ground with his back against a vehicle, wearing a French flag around his neck for identification. According to the diplomats, he was pushed during the attack.
Police announced Monday morning that they had launched an arrest operation in the West Bank under the name "Olive Leaf." Ten Jewish suspects were arrested in the early morning hours, and the operation continued into the morning. The detainees were taken for questioning by the Judea and Samaria District's central investigative unit and at police stations in the Samaria region. According to a police statement, investigators seized evidence in the suspects' possession linking them to the alleged offenses.

Voting began Monday in Canada's western Alberta province in a consequential referendum that could set it on a path toward leaving the country.
Elections Alberta said polling stations opened at 0900 AM local time (1500GMT) and will shut at 0800PM (0200GMT Tuesday). Roughly 1.3 million residents have already cast ballots through special voting or advance polling, the agency said.
The ballot contains 10 questions. The first nine address immigration and constitutional matters.
The last asks whether Alberta should stay in Canada or whether its government should start preparing a second, legally binding vote on separation. It is the first time such a question has appeared on the province’s ballot.
