China Focus: China uses digital technology to bring Long March history to life
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
22:46:15 CST
23:46:15 KST

GUIYANG, Oct. 19 (Xinhua) -- Inside the Zunyi Meeting memorial museum's exhibition hall, visitors are instantly plunged into a Long March battlefield scene after putting on lightweight virtual reality (VR) headsets, feeling as if they are surging across the Xiangjiang River under enemy fire.
Rather than observing history from a distance, they are placed inside it, with smoke filling the horizon, shells churning the water, and the voices of soldiers echoing through the simulated battlefield.
The immersive experience at the museum in Zunyi City, southwest China's Guizhou Province, is part of a broader push across China to use cutting-edge digital technology to preserve and revitalize Long March sites, as this year marks the 90th anniversary of the victory of the expedition.
The Long March, a 12,500-kilometer military odyssey from 1934 to 1936, preserved the revolutionary forces and gave the Communist Party of China a new foothold to carry the revolution to victory. Today, sites along the route serve as patriotic education centers. As younger visitors seek more interactive experiences, the museums and memorial halls are turning to digital technology to bring static exhibits to life.
The Zunyi Meeting memorial museum is one such example, featuring a VR experience system. By digitally reconstructing more than 1,000 precious artifacts and using 3D modeling and real-time rendering, it presents panoramic recreations of pivotal moments from the march, including the Battle of the Xiangjiang River.
The technology also serves a preservation purpose. Faded manuscripts and rusted weapons have been converted, through high-precision 3D scanning, into digital archives. To date, the museum has completed 3D scans of 172 artifacts, built digital records for 1,600 two-dimensional items and preserved 8,600 pages of digital artifact archives, with about 80 percent of its collection now capable of interactive digital display.
"It narrows the distance between artifacts and visitors," said Huang Chao, deputy director of the information technology department at the museum.
The impact goes beyond preservation. "Audio-visual and lighting technologies have turned one-way explanations into immersive experiences that move some visitors to tears," said Hong Min, who oversees public engagement at the museum.
Beyond physical venues, a 5G-powered cloud exhibition hall allows users to explore more than a dozen revolutionary heritage sites and thousands of artifacts through a smartphone mini-program, complete with multi-version audio guides and the ability to zoom in on artifact details.
Similar efforts are underway in other parts of the country. In southwest China's Sichuan Province, another key region along the trail, local authorities have built a database containing more than one million pages of archives, alongside a geographic information system covering the Sichuan section of the route.
At a memorial hall in Luding County, visitors wearing VR headsets can virtually step onto the iron chains of the Luding Bridge, recreating the pivotal 1935 battle in which Red Army soldiers crossed it under fire.
"We use VR, digital twin and spatial positioning technologies to engage multiple senses, bringing visitors back to those revolutionary years," said Qu Yongfan, head of the interactive display project, noting that this immersive approach complements traditional static displays and historical documents.
China has been encouraging these local efforts. The National Cultural Heritage Administration has called on 15 provincial-level regions along the Long March route to coordinate the protection, management and use of related cultural relics, with an emphasis on promoting the campaign's spirit. Across the route, museums and memorial sites are increasingly turning to immersive technologies to bring those relics and stories to life.
"We hope to break the boundaries of time and space through technology, making the Long March spirit tangible and accessible, especially for young people," said Wang Zhi'ou, chief designer of the Guizhou Long March Culture Digital Art Museum in Guiyang, the provincial capital. ■

First, upholding Africa's leadership, Mao said, citing the principles. "African people are the true masters of the continent and should therefore play a central role in regional affairs."
Second, safeguarding equity and justice. Parties should observe the purposes and principles of the UN Charter and respect the sovereignty and territorial integrity of countries concerned, she said.
Third, ceasing hostilities and building peace. "War and unilateral sanctions are never real solutions to disputes between states. Countries should respect each other, engage in extensive consultation, seek common ground despite differences, and practice mutual understanding and accommodation," Mao said.
"Fourth, addressing both symptoms and root causes. Addressing immediate security concerns should go hand in hand with long-term development planning," the spokesperson said. ■

YEREVAN, Oct. 19 (Xinhua) -- The opening plenary of the 17th meeting of the Conference of the Parties to the UN Convention on Biological Diversity (COP17) was held here on Monday.
The international community has made some progress in implementing the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework, but the pace and scale of action remains insufficient to achieve its targets, Astrid Schomaker, executive secretary of the Convention on Biological Diversity, said at the plenary.
Schomaker said the conference should advance global biodiversity governance through "accountability, alignment and acceleration." All parties should strengthen the alignment between national actions and global targets, broaden the participation of Indigenous peoples and local communities, women, youth, businesses and financial institutions, and translate international commitments into action, she said.
Armenian Environment Minister Hambardzum Matevosyan was elected COP17 president for a two-year term at the plenary.
Themed "Taking Action for Nature," COP17 runs through Oct. 30. The United Nations published a State of Biodiversity Action report on global progress in implementing the Kunming-Montreal framework in Yerevan on Thursday. ■

- Operations returned to normal after a security incident at the Leipzig/Halle airport

This blog is now closed. Below is a roundup of the stories from and about Germany on Monday, October 19, 2026.
SPD, Greens back coalition talks with the Left Party in Berlin
Berlin's Left Party, the Greens and the Social Democrats are set to move ahead on talks to form the next coalition government in the capital city.
The SPD's state leadership approved the motion with a wide majority in an online session, and the Greens voted overwhelmingly in favor of talks at a small party convention.
The Left Party has not scheduled a conference until October 31 because members of the party may be away because of school holidays.
The Left Party is hoping to have Elif Eralp lead the state government.
The coalition talks are set to open after weeks of tense negotiations and a dispute over alleged antisemitism within the ranks of the Left Party.
Merz announces partnership with Nvidia to boost AI in German industry
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz and Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang unveiled a new artificial intelligence (AI) cooperation at a glitzy investment summit in Berlin on Monday evening.
"Germany is open for business," said Merz at the Invest in Germany event, adding that the combination of German engineering and cutting-edge AI technology would help strengthen the country's economy in the long term.
"Germany is open for investment and Germany is ready to grow at a faster pace," the chancellor continued, before joking: "If I were Jensen Huang, I would put on my leather jacket, take a flight to Berlin, meet the German Chancellor, and tell him, 'I'm ready to invest.'"
The partnership with Nvidia is intended to speed up the digital transformation of German industry and secure the country's technological sovereignty.
According to the company, Nvidia invested nearly $1 billion in Germany last year and holds stakes in numerous start-ups and established companies.
But Europe's largest economy has nevertheless struggled to attract foreign investment after years of weak growth, with high energy prices and labor costs continuing to deter businesses.
German officials were hoping that Monday's summit, which was attended by more than 200 domestic and international investment executives, would showcase Germany as an attractive investment destination, highlighting its sound public finances, status as the only G7 country with a triple-A credit rating, its universities, skilled workforce and tariff-free trade within the EU single market.
Further behind-closed-door talks are set to take place on Tuesday.
READ — Bulgaria seeks suspects in Germany after Starlink sabotage
Do you remember those arrests in Germany last week, connected to an arson attempt at a Starlink control center in Poland?
The government in Warsaw called it a hybrid attack and accused Russia of recruiting organized crime elements for the alleged crime.
It's much too early to say for sure, but Bulgaria has now issued a pair of European arrest warrants against German citizens in a case that seems rather reminiscent in several regards.
The two 19-year-olds are accused of driving in from Serbia claiming to be tourists, setting fire to a series of antennae south of Sofia, and leaving the country again within a matter of hours.
Sinti Auschwitz survivor Hermann Höllenreiner dies aged 92
Hermann Höllenreiner, a Sinti German raised in Bavaria who survived the Nazis' Auschwitz concentration camp as a child, has died aged 92.
Munich's Hanser Verlag publisher and the International Auschwitz Committee said that he had passed away last Friday, October 16, in Mettenheim in Bavaria, surrounded by his family.
Höllenreiner, known as "Mano" to his large Bavarian Sinti family, spent time at the Auschwitz-Birkenau, Ravensbrück and Sachsenhausen camps as a child.
"Only later in his life did he start to tell his story and became a major witness of the era, who hauntingly reported on the horrors of Auschwitz, the perpetrators and the victims, and above all of the still-persistnent discrimination of Sinti and Roma in Europe," Christioph Heubner, executive vice president of the International Auschwitz Committee, said.
"Mano Höllenreiner's biography and tales of suffering were enough for more than one life. What he saw with his own eyes as a child in Auschwitz and what was done to him — for many decades he didn't know how to speak out about it," Heubner said, thanking Höllenreiner for his "courage and humanity" in ultimately telling his story.
Höllenriener managed to flee one of the so-called "death marches" fleeing extermination camps in as Allied armies approached.
Author Anja Tuckermann told his story in a book whose title roughly translates as: "Mano. The boy who didn't know where he was."
He was initially found on a roadside and rescued by liberated French prisoners, who took him home with them. In 1946, he was reunited with surviving relatives in Germany.
Novice driver caused fence breach at Leipzig/Halle airport: Police
Two men have admitted to breaking through a fence at Leipzig/Halle airport while one of them was practicing for a driving test, an incident that triggered a major security operation, police said on Monday.
The two, aged 20 and 32, handed themselves in to the police on Sunday evening, following the incident. The broken fence was first discovered by airport staff late on Saturday.
Police said the 20-year-old had been at the wheel despite not having a valid license.
An investigation was opened into the learner driver for fleeing the scene after breaking through the fence.
The mass-circulation Bild newspaper reported that the car involved, of which fragments were found at the site, was an Audi.
The airport was the site of a security scare in August, when an explosives-laden drone was found there near Ukrainian cargo planes.
German officials accused Russia of having planned an attack, something Moscow denied.
Rheinmetall acquires Romanian shipyard
Germany's Rheinmetall defense group on Monday announced that it had acquired Romania's Mangalia shipyard at auction in partnership with Swiss shipping giant MSC.
Rheinmetall said it had paid approximately €138 million ($154 million) for the facility.
Acquisition is expected to be finalized within a few weeks.
Rheinmetall and MSC plan to develop the Black Sea shipyard near Constanța into a dual-use site for civilian and military shipbuilding for both domestic and international markets.
Rheinmetall says its Naval Systems division will use the facility to build four vessels commissioned by the Romanian government, including two 96-meter (305 foot) offshore patrol vessels and two 43-meter diving support vessels.
The company also intends to modernize the shipyard's infrastructure and expand its capacity. 
"In doing so," said the company, "Rheinmetall is creating a scalable foundation for future projects in southeastern Europe and strengthens its position in a strategically important market."
Foreign Ministry summons Iranian ambassador over planned anti-Israel attacks
The Foreign Ministry has summoned Iran's ambassador after two men were convicted of preparing attacks on Jewish figures and pro-Israel targets in Germany at the behest of Tehran.
"We vehemently condemn Iran's activities. We will not allow Iran to threaten our liberal society," the ministry wrote on X.
"We do not tolerate attacks on Jewish life and those who defend it anywhere, and particularly not in Germany," it wrote.
A Hamburg court on Thursday sentenced a 54-year-old man and a 43-year old man respectively to 8 1/2 and 4 1/2 years in prison for having spied on the president of the Central Council of Jews in Germany, Josef Schuster, and Volker Beck, the president of the German-Israeli Society (DIG).
In the court's opinion, their actions were carried out in preparation for terrorist attacks, including the planned murders of Schuster and Beck.
The court said the 54-year-old, who was said to have also done the groundwork for an arson attack on a kosher food store in Berlin, received his orders directly from officers in the Quds Force.
The Quds Force is the branch of Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) that is in charge of extraterritorial operations.
German industry shed almost half a million jobs since 2019: Ifo Institute
German industrial businesses employed some 496,000 fewer people at the end of 2025 compared to the start of 2019, according to a survey conducted by the Ifo Institute economic think tank.
The figure represents a 7.1% decline.
Worst-hit has been the automotive industry, a key sector of the German economy, where 123,500 jobs were cut both at carmakers and suppliers, a decline of 13%.
But the metals sector also saw a marked decline in the number of jobs available, dropping 115,600 workers in the period, while the machinery sector bled 64,500 positions.
At the same time, more than 2.2 million additional jobs were created in the service sector, according to Ifo.
It said 391,000 new jobs had been established in the health sector and another 357,000 in social services, including care homes.
Joachim Ragnitz, managing director at Ifo Dresden, said the figures showed an "accelerated structural shift" in Germany.
"Ironically, the very sectors that have sustained our prosperity up to now are shrinking," he said.
"The new jobs are for the most part not being created where Germany is especially productive and innovative. That may slow down our growth potential in the future."
German woman climber dies in fall in Italy
A German woman has died in a climbing accident in the Italian Alps, mountain rescuers said on Monday.
The 32-year-old woman, who was an experienced mountaineer, fell more than 50 meters (164 feet) to her death while on the Cengia dei Camosci, a difficult route on the 2,323-meter Grande Nabois mountain near the Slovenian border.
The rescue service said the accident was caused when a climbing hold gave way under the woman, who was accompanied by an Austrian fellow climber at the time.
Her body was recovered by helicopter.
Investigations are underway to clarify the exact circumstances of her death.
Volkswagen plans to freeze pay until 2030: works council
Carmaker Volkswagen intends to freeze the salaries of some 660,000 employees worldwide until 2030 as the company, along with the entire car industry, faces a range of challenges that have impacted its profits.
Trade union IG Metall confirmed earlier media reports of the plans, citing information given to employees by the works council.
The works council described the plans as unrealistic and said there would be considerable resistance to them.
If the company does implement them, employees could lose an estimated 10% of their purchasing power by the end of the decade.
The news comes after VW decided in September to cut 50,000 jobs worldwide in the coming years in addition to the reduction of 50,000 positions that had already been agreed.
Four plants in Germany are also at risk of being closed between 2031 and 2034.
Women well behind men in leadership positions: Destatis
Less than a third of leadership positions in Germany are held by women, a lower level than the EU average, statistics released on Monday showed.
According to the Federal Statistical Office (Destatis), citing figures from the EU statistics authority Eurostat, women held just 30.3% of leadership positions in Germany, compared with 35.9% in the whole of the EU.
Only Cyprus, Italy and the Netherlands have lower rates than Germany in the bloc, while Sweden has the highest, at 44.4%, followed by Latvia, Estonia and Poland.
"The low proportion of women in leadership positions in Germany is particularly striking, as almost as many women as men are employed here," Destatis said, comparing the situation with Italy, which has almost the same level of female leadership but a much lower rate of female employment overall.
Destatis defines leadership positions as those involving the management of small companies, the management of large companies or departments within them and high administrative posts.
Merz to open investment conference
A two-day conference entitled "Invest in Germany Summit" is to begin on Monday evening in Berlin as the government seeks to shore up public-sector spending with private money.
Chancellor Friedrich Merz will deliver the opening speech at the conference, which will be attended by an expected 200 representatives from large German and international companies.
The CEO of the US chip manufacturer Nvidia, Jensen Huang, is to be one of the key guests at the conference.
The German government is looking to cooperate strongly with the company, whose products are central to the boom in artificial intelligence, in a bid to help Germany catch up in the sector.
Don't expect too much: Economic institute
The German Economic Institute (IW) has, however, warned against any too high expectations from the summit, saying that high costs for labor, energy and bureaucracy in Germany were a deterrent to investment in the country.
"It would be naive to believe that the summit will change that in the short term. Companies don't choose Germany because of a promotional event. What matters is whether they can make money here," IW director Michael Hüther told the DPA news agency.
He said it would be more effective if the government were to swiftly implement its reform agenda.
A study by Allianz Research has shown that investment in Germany fell by 6.4% between 2019 and 2025, while it grew by 6.7% in the rest of the eurozone and a whole 20.2% in the US.

Kremlin hawks savour Trump-Zelenskiy rift — if it lasts

Kremlin hawks savour Trump-Zelenskiy rift — if it lasts
MOSCOW, Oct 19 - Kremlin hawks are savouring a public rift between Donald Trump and Volodymyr Zelenskiy after a damaging week for Ukraine's president and a beneficial one for Russia, but the champagne is still on ice in Moscow.
While welcoming strains in Kyiv's relationship with its most important ally, Moscow regards the US president's behaviour as unpredictable and European leaders rallied behind Zelenskiy at a summit last week.
There has also been no end to Ukrainian drone attacks on Russia, most US sanctions remain in place on Moscow over Ukraine and Trump's actions can be seen in the light of November's midterm elections to Congress.
On the surface, there was plenty for Russian hawks to revel in after Trump repeatedly criticised the Ukrainian leader, who hit back at him, prompting the US president to say "it's time for Ukraine to get a new president".
"The ‘Man of the Year’ and the ‘new Churchill’ has been branded by his former master as a hindrance to peace and to US interests. After all, he bit the hand that fed him until it bled," former President Dmitry Medvedev, now deputy chairman of Russia's Security Council, wrote sarcastically on Telegram.
Kirill Dmitriev, President Vladimir Putin's point man for economic deals with Washington, reposted an image showing a bear symbolising Russia alongside an eagle representing the US and both creatures confronting Britain — in the form of a lion — and the European Union.
The image was captioned "Things Have Changed."
Dmitriev said he believed Zelenskiy's decision to criticise Trump had backfired, adding on X: "Zelensky overplayed his hand, and his hubris and attacks on President Trump will have significant consequences."
SCEPTICISM
Trump said on October 9 he had reached a deal with Putin to temporarily lift sanctions on Russian fuel and import Russian diesel and last week skipped new sanctions on Russia's oil buyers. In Kyiv, Ukrainian complaints about disruption to US intelligence sharing prompted talk of US betrayal.
But there appears to be a consensus in Moscow that the Trump-Zelenskiy rift has not yet delivered significant benefits.
Sergei Mironov, parliamentary leader of the pro-Kremlin Just Russia party, saw the rift as an attempt to "play to a domestic audience ahead of the Congressional elections."
"The US President needs cheap fuel prices for his voters. He also needs a scapegoat – someone onto whom he can shift the blame for price rises," he said. "But the point is that all this has little to do with Russia’s interests.”
Some Russians are also wary of what they see as frequent U-turns by Trump.
Moscow initially saw Trump's hosting of Putin in Alaska last year as a breakthrough that might lead to a peace deal in Ukraine on Russia's terms. But, like Trump's first term in office, the summit is increasingly seen as a disappointment.
The impact of the diesel deal may also be limited, as the export volumes — at least initially — are relatively small and Moscow taxes fuel production rather than exports, limiting the uplift for Russia's budget.
Trump’s decision to skip sanctions on Russian oil buyers — primarily China and India — is also not seen in Russia as a great gift, or as surprising, as such a move would increase oil prices at the very moment he wants to lower them.
A more tangible benefit to Russia may be Kyiv's complaints that it has not received recent warnings of Russian missile strikes and that there have been limits on the US Starshield system, which Ukraine uses for battlefield communications.
Writing for state media outlet RT, commentator Sergey Poletaev said Russia must be patient.
"For Russia, the task is to recognise this developing reality without mistaking it for an immediate victory," he said. "Zelenskiy has made his choice, the only question left is how long Washington will tolerate the consequences." REUTERS

Drone attack near market kills 80 in Sudan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
14:45:53 UTC
23:45:53 KST

A drone strike near a market in southern Sudan on Sunday evening killed 80 people, mostly commuters catching rides home.
Ahmed Wadi, a witness, said the attack in the town of al-Dibab in West Kordofan state left “50 bodies who I helped bury, one of them my own brother Mohamed”.
Using a satellite internet connection to circumvent a communications blackout, Wadi also said 47 other people were transported to the nearest town, al-Mujlad. A medical source, requesting anonymity for his safety, said 30 of them died from their injuries.
The medic said: “A total of 80 people were killed in the drone strike on al-Dibab, and another drone strike on al-Mujlad injured four who are currently being treated.”
Wadi said the drone struck twice, 10 minutes apart, “on a transport hub where people gather to travel back to their villages after the market day ends”.
The attack is one of the deadliest single strikes since war broke out in April 2023 when a power struggle between the Sudanese armed forces (SAF), headed by Gen Abdel Fattah al-Burhan, and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF), led by Mohamed Hamdan Dagalo, erupted into violence in the capital, Khartoum.
The RSF-declared administration, known as Tasis, accused the army of carrying out Sunday’s strike. All of West Kordofan state is under RSF control.
Sudan has witnessed an escalation in the use of drones in the war. Between January and April, drone strikes accounted for at least 880 civilian deaths, more than 80% of all conflict-related civilian deaths in Sudan.
After drone strikes on a busy livestock market in Nyala, the capital of South Darfur state, on Friday, the SAF said they had killed RSF fighters, but the RSF accused the military of killing 30 civilians.
The fighting in Sudan has killed hundreds of thousands of people and displaced many more. It has been fuelled by foreign powers with vested interests who are supporting sides in the conflict.
Last week, Rosemary DiCarlo, the undersecretary-general for political and peacebuilding affairs at the UN, warned the security council that the conflict and humanitarian crisis was deteriorating “with no breakthrough on the horizon”.
She said: “They [the warring parties] are not moving closer to dialogue. On the contrary, they seem to believe that they can make greater gains on the battlefield and that continued external support will allow them to pursue their objectives by force.”
AFP contributed to this report

UN food agency cuts Gaza assistance by one-third amid funding shortages

Unknown Publisher

23:45:27 KST

The UN World Food Program (WFP) announced Monday that funding shortages have forced it to cut food assistance in the Gaza Strip by around one-third, leaving half a million people without critical support as winter approaches, Anadolu reports.
In a statement, the agency said it is now assisting 1.1 million vulnerable people in Gaza, down from 1.6 million last month, while food rations have been halved.
Families receiving assistance will now get one food parcel instead of two, along with a smaller bag of wheat flour, it said.
The number of daily hot meals has also dropped from 250,000 to 150,000, while families in hard-to-reach areas, including near the Israeli army-controlled “yellow line,” will receive meals every other day instead of daily.
The agency has also reduced the value of cash assistance for 75,000 families.
READ: Winter rains deepen Gaza’s humanitarian crisis as displaced families face severe shelter shortages
According to WFP, an estimated 1.4 million people, or 67% of Gaza’s population, face crisis-level food insecurity or worse, including around 200,000 experiencing emergency conditions requiring immediate food assistance to prevent deaths from hunger.
Only one in five children consumes a sufficiently diverse diet, while unemployment exceeds 80%, leaving many families unable to afford nutritious food.
WFP warned that “modest” improvements in food security since the October 2025 ceasefire remain “fragile” and could quickly be reversed by further reductions in humanitarian assistance.
Funding shortages have also forced the agency to halve its assistance in the occupied West Bank, from 400,000 to 200,000 people.
The agency said it urgently needs $450 million to sustain critical operations across Gaza and the West Bank over the next six months, through March 2027.

PM estimates business losses from Russian attacks at $7.7 bln since start of year, over 1 mln sq m of property destroyed or damaged
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
17:44:51 EEST
23:44:51 KST

Losses incurred by Ukrainian businesses as a result of Russian attacks since the beginning of 2026 are estimated at $7.7 billion, with more than 1 million square meters of real estate, including warehouse and logistics facilities, destroyed or severely damaged, Ukrainian Prime Minister Serhiy Koretsky said in an interview with BBC News Ukraine published on Monday.
"As of now, losses this year are estimated at $7.7 billion. This includes the destruction of premises, businesses, production facilities and goods in warehouses. This is a very large figure, and it continues to grow," he said.
Earlier, Economy and Environment Minister Oleksandr Kravchenko estimated total business losses for the year at around $10 billion.
Koretsky expressed his deep gratitude to small, medium-sized and large businesses for their resilience, prompt problem-solving and conscientious work in the fifth year of the war.
He said the government planned to continue state support programs that had proved effective, including preferential loans under the 5-7-9% program, grants for small and medium-sized businesses, the Svitlodim program and other energy-efficiency initiatives. The prime minister said the government was completing an assessment of which programs had worked.
At the same time, the government is reviewing programs that have not met expectations and setting support priorities for next year in light of limited financial resources, Koretsky said.
"There are programs I would gladly like to continue, and there are others that we will either cancel or significantly scale back. Unfortunately, due to financial liquidity constraints, funding for these programs next year has been substantially reduced," he said.
Among other forms of state assistance, he mentioned making state-owned premises available for the relocation of warehouses and production facilities following an audit of such properties.
"We shared all intelligence and informational briefings with businesses: where strikes were taking place and what the consequences were," he added.
At the same time, he said ongoing dialogue with businesses ultimately came down to requests for compensation: "Provide additional funds," "Refinance," and so on.
"But there will not be enough money for everything. Each time, we respond to new circumstances and new realities, improve our approach, develop new programs and make new proposals," Koretsky said.

Drought and pollution threaten drinking water: Swiss conference

Drought and pollution threaten drinking water: Swiss conference
Drought and environmental pollution are posing an increasing threat to the Swiss population’s drinking water supply, according to experts.
In the search for solutions, numerous experts in wastewater and water protection are meeting in Zurich with representatives from the drinking water and wastewater sectors.
The water sector across Europe is facing major challenges. Climate change, trace substances, rising demands on quality and the financing of infrastructure have made cross-border dialogue more important than ever.
This according to the conference invitation from the Swiss Association for Water, Gas and Heat and the Swiss Association of Wastewater and Water Protection Experts to the Swiss EurEau Water Summit in Zurich.
Around 400 representatives from Switzerland and abroad are expected to attend the main event on Wednesday at the first EurEau Water Summit in Switzerland.
More
Water shortage: Switzerland’s blue gold is under pressure
EurEau is the European water sector association. It represents 38 national organisations of drinking water and wastewater service providers from 33 countries, from both the public and private sectors.
According to the press release, around 60% of drinking water – 80% of which in Switzerland comes from groundwater – can currently be supplied to the population as drinking water either without treatment or after simple treatment.
However, rising concentrations of chemical contaminants in groundwater are putting increasing pressure on local supplies. Chemical contaminants can only be removed – if at all – at great cost in terms of manpower, energy and finance. This makes the protection of groundwater all the more important.
Under these conditions, rainwater is becoming increasingly important in so-called ‘sponge landscapes’, which enhance water retention in soils, water bodies, wetlands, moors, forests and entire catchment areas.
They could help to mitigate peak flows, reduce drought stress, safeguard groundwater, minimise erosion, enhance habitats and increase the climate resilience of our landscape.
This would benefit a range of areas simultaneously: agricultural crops, forests, soil fertility, the drinking water supply, biodiversity and local recreation.

Kenyan athletes set two new records in Tokyo (VIDEOS)
Kenyan runners Agnes Ngetich and Alexander Mutiso set new course records after winning the women’s and men’s races at the Tokyo Legacy Half Marathon in Japan on Sunday.
Ngetich finished the 21.1km race in one hour, four minutes and 23 seconds (1:04:23), cutting three minutes off the previous women’s course record. Her compatriot Tabitha Njeri Kamau came second in 1:08:28, according to the results.
Mutiso won the men’s competition in 59 minutes and 51 seconds, beating the previous course record by one second. He finished five seconds ahead of fellow Kenyan Kiprono Sitonik, who took second place.
Speaking after the race, Ngetich said she that was pleased with her victory and surprised by her finishing time. She also noted that the course had been challenging, with hills and numerous sharp turns. “I didn’t think I’ll get that time. The course was not easy,” she said.
Mutiso said his victory had boosted his confidence ahead of his next marathon. He explained that he made his decisive move on a hilly section of the course between the 17km and 18.5km marks.
“I feel good. I see now I am in a good position to prepare well for [my] coming marathon,” he said.
The course began and ended at Japan’s National Stadium and followed roads used during the Tokyo 2020 Paralympic Games.
Ngetich’s victory came less than a month after she broke the women-only half marathon world record at the World Athletics Road Running Championships in Copenhagen. The 25-year-old completed that race in 1:05:15.
Kenyan distance runners have also recorded major victories in other international competitions this year. In April, Sebastian Sawe became the first athlete to complete an official competitive marathon in under two hours, winning the London Marathon in a world-record 1:59:30. Fellow Kenyan John Korir also won the Boston Marathon that month, setting a course record of 2:01:52.
The London Marathon also saw a record-breaking performance in the women’s race. Ethiopia’s Tigst Assefa set a new women’s-only marathon world record of 2:15:50.

Pakistan suspends Iran border trade, amid violence on both sides
Islamabad cites security concerns, while Tehran points to technical issues as Pakistan mediates between Iran and the US.
Islamabad, Pakistan — Pakistan has halted trade with Iran at the Taftan and Gabd-Rimdan crossings in Balochistan province, leaving freight stranded on both sides of the border.
The suspension decision emerged on Saturday, as the Quetta Chamber of Commerce and Industry (QCCI) in the provincial capital said about 2,000 trucks were stuck on both sides.
Passenger traffic at Gabd-Rimdan has continued, reported the Iranian news agency WANA.
Pakistan’s federal government has not commented publicly. Al Jazeera received no response from authorities in Balochistan, as both Islamabad and Tehran have offered different explanations for the border closure.
What each side says
Bakhtiar Ismail, deputy commissioner of Chagai district, where the Taftan crossing is located, described the move as a security measure.
“Pakistan-Iran border closure is a temporary measure to improve border management to support counterterrorism efforts. The border will be opened as soon as effective measures are in place,” he wrote on X on Saturday.
Shahid Rind, an aide to Balochistan’s chief minister on political and media affairs, wrote on X the same day that the closure was meant to address security concerns, prevent smuggling and make the border system more effective.
Iran’s Foreign Ministry spokesman, Esmaeil Baghaei, gave a different explanation.
“Due to certain technical issues and the necessity of implementing precautionary measures, cross-border movement and exchanges have been temporarily halted,” he said, according to the IRNA state news agency.
Imtiaz Baloch, a Quetta-based independent researcher who focuses on security in Balochistan, said security might be only part of the explanation.
“Although Pakistani officials have cited security concerns, the decision to close the border appears to be motivated by broader strategic considerations, with security as a possible factor amid economic sanctions on Iran,” he told Al Jazeera.
Javad Heiran-Nia, who heads the Persian Gulf Studies Group at the Center for Scientific Research and Middle East Strategic Studies in Iran, said Tehran’s wording could cover several issues.
“In my view, these expressions could refer to operational and administrative problems at border crossings, customs procedures, the verification of trade documents, financial transactions, or tighter security controls,” he told Al Jazeera.
A mediator in a war
Pakistan has mediated between Washington and Tehran since the US-Israeli war on Iran began on February 28. Islamabad brokered a ceasefire on April 8, but it collapsed within days. The US subsequently blockaded Iran’s southern ports.
With Iranian ports blocked, an April 25 Commerce Ministry order allowed third-country goods to be trucked to Iran along six routes ending at Gabd and Taftan.
In June, Pakistan and Qatar brokered the Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding, signed electronically by US President Donald Trump and Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian.
It called for the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz, lifting the blockade and 60 days of talks on a lasting settlement.
The agreement lasted about a month. In July, Iran said it was no longer bound by parts of the deal after the US resumed attacks and its naval blockade.
Washington has since widened its sanctions. On August 24, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announced a campaign called Operation Economic Outcast, extending sanctions to shipping, gold, aviation and digital assets.
Earlier this month, Pakistan’s Foreign Office spokesman Sajjad Haider Khan said Pakistan would continue to comply with all applicable sanctions regimes, without specifying which.
Official bilateral trade between Iran and Pakistan is not massive – about $2.8bn in 2023-24, including $684m in Pakistani exports, according to the Federation of Pakistan Chambers of Commerce and Industry (FPCCI). Analysts say decades of US sanctions on Iran are a major factor.
Pakistan’s own insecurity
But the US and the pressure it imposes on countries like Pakistan are not the only factors that influence Islamabad’s approach towards the border with Iran.
Balochistan, Pakistan’s largest province, covers 44 percent of the country with a population of almost 15 million in the 2023 census.
The country’s poorest province, which borders Iran, has seen several uprisings since 1948. The latest, led by Baloch nationalist rebels, has continued for two decades.
The rebels accuse the state of exploiting local natural resources while communities remain deprived.
The number of attacks has risen sharply this year. The Pakistan Institute for Conflict and Security Studies (PICSS), an Islamabad-based think tank, recorded 62 security personnel killed in Balochistan in July, up from six in June. In September, it counted 225 attacks by armed groups nationwide, the highest monthly figure in 12 years.
At least 20 police personnel were abducted from a van in Mastung district on Friday.
Two days later, an army major was killed by an improvised explosive device in Gwadar district, said the military’s media wing, Inter-Services Public Relations (ISPR).
Violence too in Chagai, the remote Balochistan district bordering Iran. Four travellers, including a customs official, were abducted from a coach there earlier this month.
Security analyst Imtiaz Baloch said Pakistani officials have long blamed the violence on porous borders.
“However, the issue goes beyond border permeability alone. Although armed groups remain active in the region, their mobilisation appears to be directed towards specific targets, and there is currently no clear indication of a broader mobilisation of armed groups on either side of the border,” he said.
Unrest across the border
Iran’s Sistan-Baluchestan province, just across the border, has also seen repeated attacks on security forces.
On October 9, Nosrat Eftekhari, a senior official in the provincial police command, was killed by a roadside bomb near Zahedan, Iranian media reported. The killing followed several other security-related incidents.
Days later, on October 14, the commander of a women’s unit of the Basij paramilitary force was shot dead outside her home in Mehrestan district, Tasnim news agency reported. Another officer was killed in a separate attack on a police vehicle in the same district.
A coalition of Baloch armed groups formed last December, with Jaish al-Adl, a Sunni Baloch armed group established in 2012, as its main member, has claimed some of those attacks in Sistan-Baluchestan province.
Tehran has long accused the group of operating from Pakistan, but Islamabad has repeatedly said it has no organised presence on Pakistani soil.
Heiran-Nia cautioned against linking the attacks directly to Pakistan.
“It is important to distinguish between the presence of armed groups in Pakistan and evidence that they crossed the border to carry out a specific attack,” he said.
Tehran-based political analyst Seyed Reza Hashemi Jebeli said Tehran wanted the Pakistani government to do more to prevent cross-border attacks.
“The key issue for Tehran is that Pakistan should meet its commitments to prevent anti-Iranian armed groups from operating in border areas,” he told Al Jazeera.
A history of suspicion
Tehran’s accusations are not new. After Jaish al-Adl claimed an attack in December 2023 that killed 11 Iranian police officers, Iran’s then foreign minister urged Pakistan to take action.
On January 16, 2024, Iran carried out missile and drone attacks in Panjgur, another border district. Pakistan said the attacks killed two children. Two days later, Pakistan struck targets in Iran’s Sistan-Baluchestan province, killing at least nine people. Intense diplomacy calmed tensions on the border and the neighbours agreed to expand security cooperation.
Heiran-Nia said a prolonged closure of the border crossings could test Pakistan’s role as mediator between the US and Iran.
“If the border dispute remains unresolved, Tehran may question whether Islamabad can simultaneously maintain productive relations with Iran and cooperate with Washington’s pressure campaign,” he told Al Jazeera.

Hundreds of thousands protested rising living costs and education funding cuts over the weekend, with demonstrations escalating into clashes with police, arson and looting.
The violence erupted Saturday as Yellow Vest demonstrations merged with student protests that began last month at a high school in Creteil, near Paris, over teacher shortages and deteriorating facilities. The movement has since broadened into protests against inequality and rising living costs, with labor unions joining in opposition to the government’s proposed 2027 budget and spending cuts.
Despite Macron’s Friday appeal for “calm and respect,” Paris endured two days of rioting. On Sunday, protesters clashed with police near Place de la Republique as vehicles and trach cans burned, shops were looted and officers deployed tear gas and water cannons.

Action and reaction
Politicians across France’s political spectrum blamed Macron and his government for the unrest, accusing the administration of undermining public services and failing to maintain order.
Marine Le Pen, who leads first-round polling for the 2027 presidential election, called Macron a president “without credibility or authority,” describing his administration as “a government on its last legs.” Jean-Luc Melenchon, leader of the left-wing France Unbowed party, blamed “ten disastrous years” of Macron weakening public services. The mayors of Paris, Marseille and Limoges accused Interior Minister Laurent Nunez and police commanders of incompetence in maintaining public order.
Nunez initially blamed “opportunistic troublemakers” for the unrest, but admitted Monday that police had suffered “a loss of control” due to poor planning. He said he offered his resignation Sunday, but Macron refused, instead ordering a new policing strategy, faster deployment and transparency over intelligence failures. Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu ordered partial curfews in several cities.
Macron condemned the rioting, insisting there was “no place for violence” and promising punishment for vandals and looters. In a televised address Sunday, he said “nothing justifies” the destruction, but pledged to address students’ complaints over school conditions. Meanwhile, he portrayed the unrest as an attempt by political opponents to disrupt the democratic process and influence voters ahead of the presidential election in six months.
Despite the unrest, Macron departed on Monday for a three-day visit to the Middle East, leaving his government to deal with the fallout at home.
The crisis comes as Macron’s approval ratings hit record lows. An October Ipsos BVA-CESI poll for La Tribune Dimanche put his approval at 15%, with 82% disapproving, the lowest since he took office in 2017. An Ifop survey recorded 17% approval and 83% dissaproval. Le Pen leads first-round polling for the April 2027 election with 32-36% support.
Protests spread beyond France
France was not alone in facing unrest over the weekend, as tens of thousands protested living costs, housing shortages and government policies across Europe. Demonstrations in several countries escalated into clashes, vandalism and arson.
In Belgium, students opposed rising education costs and reforms they say threaten access to higher education. In Italy, marches against living costs and wars turned violent in Milan and Bologna. In Portugal, tens of thousands protested low wages, rising rents and housing shortages. In Albania, student-led protests entered a fifth day, with demonstrators demanding Prime Minister Edi Rama’s resignation over corruption allegations, unemployment and poor prospects for young people.
Former Austrian Chancellor Sebastian Kurz described the unrest across Europe over the weekend as resembling “scenes from a civil war,” warning in a post on X that “we risk seeing the same scenes soon in Berlin, Vienna and Munich.”
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov described the European unrest as “bordering on chaos,” calling it a major crisis.
“It’s hard to say whether the crisis is systemic or not, but it is obvious that it is a big crisis,” he told reporters on Monday.
Some experts who spoke to RT linked the unrest to EU’s confrontation with Russia. Italian journalist Davide Carbonaro called the severing of economic ties with Moscow “economic and political suicide,” saying that young Europeans felt betrayed and deprived of a future. Serbian journalist Nebojsa Malic accused Western leaders of scapegoating Russia to hide their failures.
RT’s Chay Bowes examined how Europe’s continued support for Ukraine and sanctions against Russia are fueling economic pressures and public discontent as unrest spreads across the continent.

Pakistan providing Saudi Arabia 'whatever support needed' amid Houthi attacks: Army spokesman

Aamir Latif
19 October 2026•Update: 19 October 2026
Pakistan is providing Saudi Arabia with “whatever support is needed” to defend the kingdom amid attacks by Yemen's Houthi group, a Pakistani military spokesman said in an interview aired Sunday.
"It's non-negotiable; it's absolute as far as Pakistan is concerned," Pakistan Army spokesman Lt. Gen. Ahmed Sharif Chaudhry told Independent Arabia.
"So whatever support is needed to do that is being provided and will be provided," he said, adding that alliances do not publicly disclose the specifics or extent of military support.
His remarks came amid Houthi attacks targeting Saudi oil and financial infrastructure, including airports, in recent weeks.
Chaudhry said Saudi Arabia's sovereignty, territorial integrity and the security of the two holy mosques were "paramount" for Pakistan.
He stressed that there could be no "ifs and buts" concerning the security of the holy sites.
Pakistan and Saudi Arabia have signed two defense agreements aimed at collective deterrence – the Strategic Mutual Defense Agreement and the Mecca Joint Defense Alliance, which also includes Türkiye.
The Mecca agreement, signed Aug. 7, allows signatories to treat an attack against one member as an attack against all three.
Asked whether Pakistan's support would remain strictly defensive if Houthi attacks continued, Chaudhry said all three alliance members were "absolutely clear that this alliance has no offensive intent. It is purely defensive."
Citing Article 51 of the UN Charter, which addresses the right to individual and collective self-defense, he said the alliance was intended to deter threats to regional stability.
He said the mechanism "gives a very strong and clear message to those elements of instability, of chaos, in the region that if you directly or indirectly wage this war against any of these three countries, then the response will be collective."
"If that deterrence doesn't work, then that deterrence has to be re-established by all means that are available to the three countries," Chaudhry said.
However, he emphasized that Islamabad's interactions and discussions with the parties involved were focused on "dialing down the escalation."

Most Ukrainians reject giving Russia all of Donbas. Support for resistance on rose to 62% after new US pressure, poll finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
14:42:05 UTC
23:42:05 KST

A majority of Ukrainians reject handing all of Donbas to Russia in exchange for US and European security guarantees. Some 62% are ready to endure the war for as long as it takes, a survey by the Kyiv International Institute of Sociology shows.
Russia has spent the fall hammering Ukrainian cities, and Washington has eased sanctions on Russian diesel and cut Ukraine’s intelligence and Starlink speed, both apparently aimed at wearing Ukrainians down toward a capitulation. Instead, the majority calls the withdrawal of troops from Donbas categorically unacceptable, with 35% willing to accept it and 4% undecided, a position essentially unchanged since late summer.
The pressure campaign tracked the other way. Among those polled on 8-9 October, before the diesel deal and the pressure that followed, 57% were categorically opposed. Among those polled on 10-16 October, the figure rose to 62% afterward, KIIS reports.
In every region, at least half reject the trade. Resistance is firmest in Kyiv, which has borne a relentless campaign of ballistic and jet-drone strikes, where 66% are categorically against, the highest figure of any region. Even in the east, around Kharkiv, where the most are open to a compromise at 45%, 51% still rule it out.
Bracing for a long war, and ready for it
Few Ukrainians expect a quick end. Only 10% think the war will end by the close of 2026 and 13% in the first half of 2027, while 56% expect it to run into the second half of 2027 or beyond, the institute reports.
Who Ukrainians blame for blocking peace
The poll also measured who is seen as the obstacle. Asked to choose, 78% said Russia’s drive to subjugate Ukraine is what blocks peace, against 12% who blamed an inflexible Ukrainian government, and 92% said Russia strikes economic sites to wreck the economy and force capitulation, not in retaliation.
“The enemy, with its vile strikes by ballistic missiles and drones, is unable to break the spirit and will of Ukrainians,” KIIS executive director Anton Hrushetskyi says.
He argues that what Ukraine needs is “packages of interceptors for Patriot systems,” not an election or one-sided concessions dressed up as peace. The survey polled 1,031 adults across government-controlled Ukraine from 8-16 October.

Hindutva Goons Unleash Violence on Anti-Modi Protesters
Unknown

2026-10-19
14:42:00 UTC
23:42:00 KST

In recent weeks, New Delhi and other Indian cities have witnessed massive anti-government demonstrations and flash protests demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar, over allegations of manipulating voter rolls to benefit the ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP).
To prevent students and youth from gathering, the BJP government has used intimidation and force. In addition to arresting protesters, it has heavily barricaded roads, shut down metro stations, and deployed tens of thousands of police and paramilitary personnel, including the Delhi Police, Central Reserve Police Force (CRPF), Border Security Force, Indo-Tibetan Border Police, and Sashastra Seema Bal.
Several of these forces are normally deployed along India’s borders or in insurgency-wracked regions. For example, the CRPF companies deployed in the Delhi protests were shifted from former Maoist strongholds in Chhattisgarh and parts of militancy-hit Jammu and Kashmir. In Delhi, these paramilitary forces are being used against unarmed youth activists of the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), the All India Students’ Association, and other leftist organizations.
What makes the government’s crackdown particularly reprehensible is that un-uniformed men are being allowed to assault the protesters. These are not isolated incidents; several young women and men have come forward with horrifying accounts of the violence they faced at the hands of these thugs.
Importantly, these men are unleashing violence in full view of the police. They have the blessings of the ruling dispensation.
Photographs and videos circulating on social media show men sporting saffron scarves — saffron is the color of the Sangh Parivar, a family of Hindutva-espousing organizations, of which the BJP is a part — shouting slogans in support of the Narendra Modi government, chasing young men and women, dragging them and beating them up mercilessly with sticks. They are brazen about their violence, describing their victims as “anti-national elements” who “deserve to be thrashed.”
“Delhi Police tum lath bajao, hum tumhare saath hain” (Delhi Police, you wield the baton, we are with you), they chant, egging on the police to beat the protesters.
The police and paramilitary personnel in whose presence the vigilantes acted took no action to force them off the streets. None of them was packed into police vans the way unarmed students were dragged and pushed into buses.
A video filmed during the crackdown on October 10 in central Delhi showed goons beating up young men and women, even minors. When a woman intervened on a male victim’s behalf, the goons can be seen falling upon her, pushing her to the ground, and pulling at her clothes. All this was done in the presence of at least one policeman. The footage showed a policeman eventually intervening, but he did so not to stop the assault or restrain the assailant and detain him, but to lead him away rather gently.
The video triggered anger and outrage in India, forcing the police to eventually detain four men — Raman Saini, Vivekanand alias Vivek, Kapil Kumar, and Ravinder Singh alias Govind Hindu — of the Hindu Raksha Dal (HRD) or Hindu Protection Organization.
Admitting that the four were members of his organization, HRD chief Bhupendra Singh Tomar aka Pinky Bhaiyya described them as “warriors” who were “working for Sanatan Dharma” (literally, universal truth i.e., Hinduism). In an interview with Outlook magazine, Tomar justified the violence they unleashed at the October 10 protests. The CJP activists “tried to vitiate the atmosphere in the country” during the protests at Jantar Mantar in July. “We will deal with these people who are resorting to violence, and we will set them straight. We take pride in our actions, and we will continue to do so,” Tomar said.
Founded in 2013, the Hindu Raksha Dal is among dozens of vigilante groups that have mushroomed under Modi’s rule. They have thrived under the Sangh Parivar’s patronage. Their activists cannot be dismissed as mere street gangs. They are the Sangh Parivar’s foot soldiers and unleash violence to further its Hindutva agenda. Outfits like the HRD and the Bharatiya Gau Raksha Dal (Indian Cow Protection Organization) freely engage in violence as they enjoy state protection.
HRD activists are rarely convicted or punished. Saini, Vivek, Kumar, and Singh were caught on video and were arrested under public pressure, but they were freed on bail soon after. Delhi Police did not raise objections to their release by the courts. On their release, Tomar was there to welcome and garland the four men.
Tomar himself has over 30 cases against him for hate speech, distributing weapons, issuing death threats, damaging property, assault, extortion, and raising inflammatory slogans. The list of complaints and cases against him is long. He has been arrested in a few cases only to be let off on bail soon after. His supporters have an apt slogan to describe this: “Aaj jail, kal bail, aur phir wahi khel” (jail today, bail tomorrow and then again, the same game).
The HRD has carried out dozens of attacks on Muslims, secular Indians, and the BJP’s critics. In 2020, Tomar claimed credit for the attack on students at the Jawaharlal Nehru University (JNU) in New Delhi. “JNU is a hotbed of anti-national activities and we cannot tolerate this,” he said, taking “full responsibility” for the violence that left at least 30 people, including teachers and students, injured.
In August 2024, HRD activists burnt down houses and property of Muslims in a slum in Ghaziabad, claiming that they were Bangladeshis living illegally in India. In December 2025, Tomar and his son were arrested for distributing swords in Ghaziabad for the “self-defense” of Hindus.
Outfits like the HRD enable the Sangh Parivar and the BJP government to not only freely unleash illegitimate violence but also deny their links to the perpetrators of such violence. The membership of Sangh Parivar outfits and their fellow travelers is nebulous. Consequently, it is hard to pin such violence on the Modi government.

Migrant organizations in Germany on Monday urged the government to prepare safeguards against potential threats to migrants and asylum seekers under a possible AfD-led administration in Saxony-Anhalt.
In an open letter, the organizations called on Chancellor Friedrich Merz and state premiers to establish legal, administrative and financial protections before any government involving the right-wing Alternative for Germany (AfD) takes office in the eastern state.
"In the coming weeks, a party whose state branch has been classified as confirmed right-wing extremist by the domestic intelligence agency could join government for the first time," the organizations warned.
"It would then have a say in core areas such as police, schools and security. But there is still no concept for protecting the people who would be threatened by such a government."
The letter was signed by the Turkish Community in Germany (TGD), the Federal Conference of Migrant Organizations (BKMO), Umbrella Organization of Migrant Organizations in East Germany (DaMOst), and the Network of Migrant Organizations in Saxony-Anhalt (LAMSA).
The organizations outlined three demands aimed at protecting migrants and asylum seekers if an AfD-involved government introduces measures they consider unconstitutional.
First, they proposed a joint federal-state commission to assess risks to minorities and develop protective measures before any AfD-involved government takes office.
"The commission should determine how individuals, families, civic actors and institutions can be protected from far-right violence and from the actions of a far-right government," the letter said.
"It should also clarify in advance how the constitutional state will respond should a state-level government attempt to test the limits of the constitution."
Second, the groups called for an exemption from residence restrictions that generally require asylum seekers to remain in their assigned federal state for a specified period.
They argued that asylum seekers facing threats of racist violence should be permitted to relocate, including from states such as Saxony-Anhalt.
Third, the organizations proposed a federal protection fund for threatened nonprofit associations, counseling centers and communities.
The fund would finance security measures, protective advice, emergency planning and temporary safeguards, with organizations able to apply directly to a federal office without state approval.
The demands followed the AfD's strong performance in Saxony-Anhalt's Sept. 6 election. The party secured 43.8% of the vote and 39 of 83 parliamentary seats -- three short of the 42 needed for an absolute majority.
During the campaign, AfD lead candidate Ulrich Siegmund advocated rapid deportations of migrants required to leave Germany, mandatory work for asylum seekers and converting reception centers into deportation detention facilities.
The AfD is holding talks on forming a government, with the smaller left-wing populist BSW signaling openness to cooperation on some issues, while other parties have ruled out a coalition.
A vote to elect the state premier is expected in December.
Nationwide, the AfD has polled at around 29% to 30% in recent surveys, ahead of Merz's conservative CDU/CSU alliance.
Germany's domestic intelligence agency has monitored the AfD and various members over suspected anti-democratic activities.
In some states, AfD regional branches are classified as a “proven right-wing extremist organization,” with agencies saying parts of the party promote a racist, ethnic understanding of national identity incompatible with the country’s democratic constitutional order.

Houthi strike on Yemen government military camp kills at least 50
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
14:39:00 UTC
23:39:00 KST

Houthi strike on Yemen government military camp kills at least 50
October 19, 2026
At least 50 Yemeni government forces were killed in a strike by Houthi rebels on a military camp in the south of the country on Monday, military officials said.
The group fired three ballistic missiles at the al-Alam camp in the province of Shabwa. Some 200 recruits were also wounded, according to the provincial government.
The Houthis confirmed that they had targeted the camp.
Deadliest attack in recent surge of violence in Yemen
Military sources had originally put the death toll at 30, but this rose to at least 50 later in the day, with the Associated Press giving a toll of 53 and citing provincial authorities.
"The death toll has risen to at least 50, with more than 100 people injured, some of them in critical condition," Fahad al-Khalifi, deputy governor of Shabwa said, according to AFP.
Al-Khalifi added that local hospitals had been overwhelmed and some of the more seriously wounded had been transferred to facilities in other provinces.
The increased death toll makes Monday's attack one of the deadliest in the recent uptick of violence in Yemen.
Yemeni government vows response to Houthi attack
Fighting in Yemen between the Iran-backed Houthis and the Saudi-backed government has been going on for years, but the US-Israeli war on Iran and other factors have sparked renewed fighting in the peninsula, with the Houthis also carrying out major attacks on Saudi Arabian soil.
Officials said that the soldiers who were killed and wounded in the attack had been recruits for a new Rapid Intervention force which is supposed to defend the local area.
The missiles reportedly struck while they were lining up in formation ahead of training.
Rashad al-Alimi, head of the ruling Presidential Leadership Council, vowed a "firm response" for the killing of the recruits and said the attack reflects the Houthis' "approach of resorting to cowardly terrorist attacks whenever they face pressures or their Iranian-backed sabotage plots falter."
Monday's strikes follow several attacks over the weekend that killed more than 30 people in Houthi-held areas. The Houthis have blamed Saudi-led forces for the attacks.

Ukraine's National Guard explains military training requirements for foreign volunteers
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
17:39:00 EEST
23:39:00 KST

Ukraine's National Guard explains military training requirements for foreign volunteers
Ukraine's National Guard has stated that foreign nationals serving in the National Guard must undergo 51 days of basic military training. A shortened 14-day course is only available to those with verified military service experience who pass an initial assessment.
Source: National Guard spokesman Ruslan Muzychuk in a comment to Ukrainska Pravda
Quote: "The shortened basic military training course for foreign nationals and stateless persons is available only to those who have experience of military service."
Details: Muzychuk explained that the training of foreign nationals and stateless persons joining Ukraine's National Guard is conducted in accordance with Cabinet of Ministers Resolution No. 768 dated 12 June 2026 and an order issued by the National Guard commander approving the basic military training programme for this category of service personnel.
Under the programme, the duration of basic military training is 51 days.
The shortened basic military training course, an intensive programme, may only be offered to candidates who have previously served in the armed forces or law enforcement agencies of other countries. They must have expressed a wish to take the intensive course and have provided documentation confirming their service.
Before being accepted for the intensive course, candidates must undergo an initial assessment to evaluate their existing knowledge and practical skills.
Only those who pass the assessment may take the 14-day intensive basic military training course.
After completing basic military training, all service personnel undergo an adaptation course lasting up to 14 days, following a programme designed to prepare and further train them for combat operations.
The duration and content of the training are determined by the established requirements and the service personnel's level of preparedness. This is essential to ensure they are ready to carry out combat missions, Muzychuk said.
Background: The Ukrainian government has supported the establishment of the Centre for Recruiting Foreign Nationals and Stateless Persons within the National Guard of Ukraine.

Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
14:38:46 UTC
23:38:46 KST

Ukraine has brought home 23 more children from Russian-occupied territory over the past week, the presidential initiative Bring Kids Back UA announced on Oct. 19.
The rescued children are now receiving psychological support and assistance in restoring their Ukrainian documents, Bring Kids Back UA said.
Among the children returned to Ukrainian-controlled territory is 9-year-old Stefan, who was forced to undergo military training at a school under Russian occupation, including instruction in handling grenades and firearms, the statement said.
Another child returned to Ukraine was 13-year-old Polina, who survived a Russian combat drone strike near her home and was later afraid to go outside, the statement said.
Russian troops also raided her home and destroyed communication devices to limit access to information, according to Bring Kids Back UA.
As of September 2026, Ukraine's Justice Ministry has officially confirmed 20,610 cases of deportation and forced transfer of Ukrainian children to Russia.
Ukrainian human rights groups estimate that hundreds of thousands of Ukrainian children are under Russian control, including those who have been deported or forcibly transferred and those who remain in occupied territories and are at risk of deportation.
Ukrainian officials estimate the real figure of abducted children could be far higher. Ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets puts the number at up to 150,000, while Presidential Commissioner for Children's Rights Daria Herasymchuk has given a range of 200,000–300,000.
In 2023, the International Criminal Court issued arrest warrants for Russian President Vladimir Putin and Russia's Commissioner for Children's Rights Maria Lvova-Belova for their role in state-sanctioned child abductions.

Israeli doctor who joined ISIS sentenced to 27 months in prison
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
14:36:32 UTC
23:36:32 KST

A doctor who worked at Soroka Medical Center in southern Israel was sentenced Monday to 27 months in prison after being convicted of membership in the Islamic State terrorist organization (ISIS). The Be'er Sheva Magistrate's Court found that Dr. Mohammed Azzam had undergone a prolonged process of ideological radicalization, pledged allegiance to the group's leader after the October 7 massacre and possessed instructions for manufacturing explosives and poisons.
The court also imposed a 12-month suspended prison sentence and a fine of 15,000 shekels. According to the ruling by Judge Shosh Shitrit, Azzam systematically consumed ISIS propaganda from 2014 until his arrest in July 2024. Over the years, his identification with the terrorist organization deepened, and after the Hamas-led October 7 attack and the outbreak of the Gaza war, he decided to formally join ISIS by pledging allegiance to its leader. The court found that his radicalization intensified further after taking the oath.
Shitrit rejected the notion that Azzam's activities were driven merely by curiosity, finding that they reflected a sustained process of ideological radicalization and the development of operational knowledge and capabilities. Investigators discovered extensive extremist material on his electronic devices, including ISIS propaganda, videos of combat and executions, and manuals detailing how to manufacture explosives and poisonous substances. The court determined that possession of the materials created a serious potential threat to national security and public safety.
Prosecutors from the Southern District Attorney's Office, who sought a lengthy prison sentence, argued that the circumstances were particularly severe given the duration of Azzam's radicalization, the volume of terrorist material he accumulated and his decision to join ISIS during wartime. The court also emphasized the potential danger arising from his position as a physician at a public hospital, where civilians and wounded soldiers received treatment, and the need for deterrent sentences in cases involving membership in terrorist organizations.
"This is a serious case in which an Israeli citizen chose to join the ISIS terrorist organization and pledged allegiance to it after October 7," prosecutor Hofit Kantarovitz said following the sentencing. She noted that Azzam had spent years systematically consuming terrorist propaganda, watching combat and execution videos and downloading instructions for preparing explosives and poisons.
"The court attached particular gravity to the fact that the defendant served as a doctor at a public hospital where civilians and wounded soldiers were treated," Kantarovitz said. She described a stark contradiction between the medical profession, which is founded on compassion, saving lives and treating patients regardless of their identity, and Azzam's decision to become a member of a murderous terrorist organization.
The prosecution said the sentence reflected the seriousness of his actions and the need to deter others from joining terrorist groups. In light of the circumstances, authorities have forwarded Azzam's details to the Health Ministry for consideration of revoking his medical license.

Ukraine has liberated more territory than Russia has captured since the beginning of fall—a trend that has persisted throughout 2026, Zelenskyy says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
14:36:11 UTC
23:36:11 KST

Ukrainian forces have liberated more territory since the beginning of the fall than Russian troops have captured during the same period. This trend has persisted throughout 2026, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said in his 18 October address. He also reported that Dobropillia, Kostiantynivka, and five other settlements remain under Ukrainian control.
Russia systematically exaggerates its battlefield gains. A recent briefing by Valery Gerasimov, chief of the General Staff of the Russian Armed Forces, in which he claimed that Russian forces had captured 92 settlements since the beginning of September, as well as Kostiantynivka and Dobropillia, and advanced to within 5 kilometers of Zaporizhzhia, was based on “outright lies, manipulation, and exaggerations,” Ukrainian General Staff spokesperson Andrii Kovaliov said.
Ukraine also continues to defend areas near Kramatorsk, Zelenskyy said. He dismissed Russian claims about Zaporizhzhia.
“We are destroying Russians 20 kilometers from Zaporizhzhia, not five, as someone in Russia is fantasizing to Putin,” Zelenskyy said.
Ukrainian forces continue to hold back Russian assaults and destroy groups of occupying troops attempting to infiltrate Dobropillia, the president said. The Defense Forces are also defending positions elsewhere in Donetsk Oblast and in Kharkiv and Zaporizhzhia oblasts.
Zaporizhzhia axis: Russians seek to move artillery closer to the city
Russia seeks to advance on the Zaporizhzhia axis to bring the regional capital within range of its tube artillery, hold forward positions, and protect rear areas from Ukrainian strikes, the Institute for the Study of War (ISW) said on 18 October.
Maksym Kravchuk, spokesperson for Ukraine's Southern Group of Forces, refuted Gerasimov’s claims that Russian forces had captured Malokaterynivka, located south of Zaporizhzhia, stressing that the settlement remains under Ukrainian control, the Center for Countering Disinformation said on 18 October. Ukrainian troops recorded a video directly from Malokaterynivka to confirm this.
As of 18 October, Russian forces had advanced or infiltrated to within 24 kilometers of Zaporizhzhia, ISW said.
Dobropillia remains under Ukrainian control despite Russian assaults
Dobropillia is now a fortress anchoring Ukrainian positions along the highway leading northeast toward Kramatorsk. Russia first tried to take Dobropillia in August 2025 and is now trying again.
Russia is redeploying reinforcements to the Dobropillia axis and continues to send assault infantry through the village of Nove Shakhove despite heavy losses. Russian command will likely try to encircle or at least envelop Dobropillia and cut off Ukrainian supply routes from the direction of Bilozerske, Ukrainian military analyst Kostiantyn Mashovets wrote on 9 October.
Mashovets sees the push as the southern flank of a Russian effort to envelop the whole Sloviansk–Kramatorsk urban area.
Ukraine retook Kolodiazi north of Lyman as its drones hit 200-plus Russian vehicles in Operation Vivaldi’s last phase, Ukrainian drone officer says
Dobropillia remains under Ukrainian control, Zelenskyy said. On 18 October, footage located by analysts showed a Russian soldier hoisting a flag in the town's southeast after an infiltration, yet ISW has found no sign that Russian troops have dug in there.
Russia claimed to have captured Kostiantynivka, but ISW found no evidence
Ukrainian troops in and around Kostiantynivka are stopping Russia from locking in its gains in the city or pushing on toward Druzhkivka and Kramatorsk, ISW said on 17 October.
Russian officials claimed that capturing Kostiantynivka was an important step toward establishing control over the Sloviansk–Druzhkivka–Kramatorsk urban agglomeration and the entire Donetsk Oblast, ISW said in August. The Kremlin also claimed that Russian forces had captured the city as early as 5 July, the institute added.
A Russian military blogger claimed that Russian forces had full control over Kostiantynivka, but ISW found no evidence to support this claim, the institute said in its 16 October assessment. Russian troops had only infiltrated parts of southern and central Kostiantynivka without consolidating positions, and there was no evidence of their presence in its northern part, ISW added.

2026-10-19
