What the New China-North Korea Bridge Really Means
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
13:54:00 UTC
22:54:00 KST

The New Yalu River Bridge, which links Dandong in China’s Liaoning province with Sinuiju in North Pyongan province, has finally opened, a full 12 years after construction finished in 2014. The two countries held an opening ceremony on October 15 and began running cargo trucks across the bridge, which is known as the Amnok River bridge in North Korea.
For years the bridge symbolized China-North Korea economic cooperation and also the practical limits on how far that cooperation could actually go. Now it is finally doing the job it was built for.
The two countries agreed to build the bridge in 2009, and construction began the following year. It was a major project meant to get past the logistical limits of the existing Sino-Korean Friendship Bridge. A four-lane bridge more than 3 kilometers (1.9 miles) long could greatly expand the flow of goods between Dandong and Sinuiju. China was willing to pay for construction to open a new channel for economic cooperation with the North.
Fifteen years ago, I was reporting for Daily NK in China. Back then, Dandong was full of anticipation about the bridge. People everywhere said a new crossing would bring a surge in China-North Korea trade, and that a new economic zone would grow up around Sinuiju and Dandong. Chinese businesspeople expected trade with the North to expand, and property prices near the planned development areas began to climb.
In August 2011, Daily NK reported that work on a pontoon bridge for the construction was 70 percent complete and that nearby real estate prices were rising. Some in Dandong even speculated that the bridge might lead North Korea to open its economy more widely. I still remember that mood clearly from my time on the ground.
Reality fell short of those hopes. The bridge was finished in 2014, but the North Korean side never properly built the connecting roads or customs facilities. Ups and downs in bilateral relations, international sanctions, and the COVID-19 border closure followed, and the bridge stayed shut for years. It was a long wait for the Chinese businesspeople who had hoped for new opportunities, and for everyone who had expected trade with the North to grow.
North Korea’s insularity alone doesn’t explain the delay. The two countries’ economic interests, the political climate, sanctions, and other factors all played a part. What is clear, though, is that North Korean authorities took a long and cautious approach to how much economic contact with the outside world they would allow, and how they would manage it.
In the end, the hard part was not building the bridge. It was getting past the North Korean authorities’ extremely narrow threshold. Pyongyang wanted the economic benefits, but it never let down its guard against the changes outside contact might bring. The 12 years the bridge sat effectively unused lay bare this contradiction at the heart of the North Korean economy.
More Trade Means New Opportunities and New Tests
So now that the bridge is open, will North Korea’s economy change? In the short term, we can expect more trade and more efficient transport between the two countries. Freight that used to pile onto the Sino-Korean Friendship Bridge can now be spread out, and there is finally a route that can reliably carry larger volumes of goods.
Still, it would be a mistake to assume the opening will quickly produce a jump in trade or better lives for ordinary North Koreans. How much actually moves will depend on customs procedures, transport costs, trade permits, and how goods are distributed inside North Korea. A wider bridge does not necessarily mean North Korea’s economy has opened any wider.
The bigger story may be how distribution inside North Korea changes. Markets are still central to how ordinary North Koreans make a living. Lately, however, the authorities have not simply been suppressing the general markets. They have been using state-run stores, state grain shops, and other retail outlets to expand state control over distribution and sales.
Under these conditions, if more imports flow across the bridge, state-approved trading companies and distribution agencies are likely to benefit first. In the past, private merchants brought in imported goods through various channels and supplied them to markets. That model may give way further to one where the state manages the import and allocation of goods, with markets and retail outlets operating beneath it.
Private merchants could still find new openings. More stable logistics and a larger supply of Chinese consumer goods and raw materials could mean more choice for shoppers and steadier prices for some items. If factories and enterprises can source raw materials more easily, production could benefit too.
But if the state tightens its grip on imports and distribution, the gains could concentrate in the agencies that hold trade permits and the power to allocate goods. Private merchants would become more dependent on state-designated distribution channels, and the various costs and informal payments they face could well rise.
How the bridge ties into North Korea’s “20×10” regional development policy is also worth watching. The North is racing to build local industrial factories, but putting up a building is one thing and running a factory is another. What matters is not how many factories have been built. It is how many days a month they actually run, where their raw materials come from, and what prices residents pay for what they produce. Without a steady supply of raw materials, electricity, and production equipment, these factories will struggle to operate.
Here, more Chinese raw materials and supplies could improve operating conditions at some local factories. Yet the more these factories rely on Chinese inputs, the further they drift from the self-reliant local economy the authorities keep promoting.
Development around Sinuiju also deserves attention. According to a recent Daily NK investigation, North Korea has reportedly pitched Chinese businesspeople on a plan to develop the area behind the bridge and some 40 square kilometers (15 square miles) of southern Sinuiju into an economic hub for logistics, processing, trade, and commerce. This suggests Pyongyang wants to use the bridge’s opening to make more economic use of the border region.
We should still separate development plans from actual investment and production. Current United Nations sanctions sharply restrict imports of industrial equipment, exports of North Korean processed goods, and joint ventures. Early on, the benefits will likely be limited to better customs and logistics, with any large-scale industrial cooperation moving slowly.
Above all, North Korea’s economy could become even more dependent on China. Deeper reliance on Chinese raw materials, consumer goods, capital, and logistics networks might give the economy a short-term lift. It could also leave the economy more exposed to shifts in Chinese policy and trade conditions. The gap between the self-reliance the regime preaches and its real dependence on China could grow wider.
Ultimately, the bridge’s opening is both an opportunity and a major test for North Korea’s economy. The question is what the authorities do with the extra goods and economic openings. Will they let ordinary people expand their economic activity, or will the state tighten its hold on profits and distribution channels? The answer looks set to shape the structure of North Korea’s economy in the years ahead.
The Real Measure Is How People Live
The number of trucks crossing the bridge is not the only thing to watch. Actual freight volumes, the goods being traded, customs procedures, and shipping costs all matter. But to really judge how North Korea’s economy is changing, we need to follow where those goods go, who controls the trade, and how it ultimately affects people’s daily lives.
That means tracking specific economic indicators over time. How many trucks cross the bridge each month? How much does the share of Chinese goods in markets change? How are people’s purchases split between state-run outlets and the general markets, and how is that changing?
We also need to look at how many days local factories with more Chinese inputs actually run and how much they produce, and how more imports affect consumer prices and people’s purchasing power.
With these questions in mind, the Daily NK sees a need to keep tracking changes in North Korea’s economic structure and in people’s living conditions. Comparing trends at three months, six months, and one year after the opening should give a clearer picture of how the economy is really changing.
What matters here is the direction of change, not whether a single number rises or falls. If imports go up but purchasing power doesn’t improve, we need to find out why. If state stores see more customers, we need to know whether private market trade is shrinking or whether both are growing. More goods coming in and people finding it easier to buy things are two very different matters.
In particular, comparing economic conditions in major cities such as Sinuiju (North Pyongan province), Pyongsong (South Pyongan province), and Hyesan (Ryanggang province) can show whether more border trade is reaching people inland and in the provinces. Even if imports grow at the border, distribution costs and local supply conditions mean residents in different areas may feel the change very differently.
We also need to see whether development in Sinuiju actually creates jobs and raises incomes. New facilities, roads, and housing are hard to count as a success if residents are hit with demands for money or forced labor mobilizations along the way. Beyond how the development looks, we need to see who bears the costs and who reaps the benefits.
Sanctions enforcement also remains an important issue. Expanded trade in legitimate goods for ordinary people must be clearly distinguished from transfers of sanctioned items. We need to check whether wider economic cooperation becomes a channel for evading sanctions. At the same time, we need to look closely at how much legitimate trade and economic activity, the kind needed to improve people’s lives, is actually happening.
The people I met in Dandong 15 years ago expected North Korea to change once the new bridge was built. Instead, the finished bridge stayed closed for 12 years. Things are clearly different now. North Korea needs more trade and practical economic gains, and China wants to expand its influence through economic cooperation with the North.
Even so, we shouldn’t simply repeat the hopes of that time. Expanded China-North Korea economic ties will not automatically mean freer markets or more freedom for people to make a living. North Korea has a history of chasing economic gains while tightening control over markets and ordinary people’s economic activity.
The New Yalu River Bridge is finally open. But the true test of change in North Korea’s economy won’t be the trucks crossing it. It will be what North Korean society does with the goods they carry.
We now need to look more closely at what is happening on the North Korean side of the bridge: how state control is shifting, how the markets are adapting, and whether people’s lives are getting even a little better. What matters more than the bridge opening is how far the changes it brings actually reach ordinary North Koreans. That is where our view of the New Yalu River Bridge, open after 12 years, should begin.

MEPs have accused Albania of deploying “sneaky” practices to fast-track a proposed Trump-linked luxury resort in the country amid protests that have turned increasingly violent.
As the prime minister, Edi Rama, pledged to “listen to the voices of young people” taking to the streets, there was mounting criticism of his failure to address demonstrators who had long opposed the controversial project peacefully.
In scenes not seen in decades, students now leading the unrest have fought pitched battles with riot police in Tirana as ministerial buildings, banks and businesses have been set ablaze, attacked and looted.
Speaking to the Guardian, the Dutch MEP Tineke Strik accused Rama of inflaming the situation by doggedly pursuing plans championed by the US president’s son-in-law Jared Kushner.
“If the Albanian government had taken the ‘Flamingo Revolution’ seriously we wouldn’t be here,” she said of the popular movement launched in response to the resort being built in ecologically sensitive areas of the Balkan state. “The students are voicing the frustration of people who feel that they haven’t been listened to.”
On Monday, municipal workers could be seen removing paving stones as shopkeepers secured premises with metal sheeting following a sixth consecutive day of violent clashes in the capital in which protestors also set fire to a police station. Riot police responded with rubber bullets and tear gas as they attempted to disperse the crowds. Students have vowed to continue demonstrating until the socialist leader resigns – a demand he has resolutely refused to meet.
“This terrible resort idea was the match that lit this fire,” sighed Greta, a student in Tirana, adding that the slogan chanted by young people attending demonstrations for months had been “Albania is not for sale”.
“Now there are other issues that are whipping up the flames. We actually really care about the state of our democracy, about living standards, about education.”
The controversial project foresees construction of up to 10,000 villas in coastal areas that were environmentally protected until the government passed a contentious law allowing “strategic investors” to build in parts of the Vjosa-Narta landscape surrounding the last intact delta system in the Mediterranean.
In June, the European parliament called for the legislation to be repealed by the EU candidate country, saying it posed a direct threat to environmental standards that are “non-negotiable conditions of accession”.
The parliament’s move came after construction workers broke ground in May, igniting protests that would spread nationwide after it was discovered that ancient dunes and forest had been destroyed to create access roads in the nature reserve.
Re-elected for a historic fourth term last year, Rama is on a mission to get the Balkan state – still one of Europe’s poorest after the collapse of communism more than three decades ago – into the 27-member bloc by 2030. In a live address delivered on social media on Sunday he said: “Albanians need to think very clearly: do they want this, do they want that, or do they want the EU?”
But Strik, a Greens group MEP who led a European parliament fact-finding mission to Albania in June, said it was clear the government was also rushing to “create facts on the ground” before it was bound by EU standards. A frontrunner in the enlargement process, Albania hopes to wrap up accession talks by the end of 2027.
Citing an environmental impact study whose “scientific results” Rama recently described as key to the €4bn project going ahead, she said: “The government has submitted an environmental package to the [EU] Commission but without repealing the law allowing for construction in the protected area … it is still trying to help realise the megalomaniacal luxury resort plans of Ivanka Trump and Jared Kushner. How? By conducting a fast-track impact assessment which, if [more comprehensively] done, could never lead to the conclusion that this construction is allowed.”
Rama told a tourism forum in Brussels this month that the milestone development would be a gamechanger for a nation that had been the “North Korea” of Europe before the fall of its Stalinist regime in the 1990s.
“If construction goes ahead this will be decided not in the streets but by science,” he told the forum. “The idea that nature will take care of itself, if we simply look at it, is preposterous and old. We are trying to come out with … a [high-end] destination where nature will be highlighted and where people will holiday, and where the Albanian people will get back what they deserve: a much stronger economy.”
On 8 October, Kushner described the venture as having a single goal: “To build to the highest design and environmental standards and leave this extraordinary part of Albania greener, more biodiverse and environmentally stronger”.
Private contractors, tasked with implementing the impact study, have been seen mapping, measuring and monitoring the area, prompting environmentalists, who had initially spearheaded the protests, to counter this week that “science had already spoken”.
“It spoke when experts from the faculty of science at Tirana University elected to protect this incredible landscape in 2004,” said Aleksander Trajce at the country’s oldest conservation group, the Protection and Preservation of the Natural Environment in Albania (PPNEA). “Their decision was based on very sound scientific data. There’s no way that science can tell us more. Reopening the discussion is not only disingenuous but clearly a way to justify construction that should not be happening at all.”
Insisting an environmental impact assessment would take “at least two years” to be properly conducted, he added: “You’d need several seasons, across several years, to really examine the species and biodiversity of the region.”
With the violence showing no sign of abating, Albanians feel very angry at the EU’s lacklustre stance, said Trajce. “If it had intervened earlier and told Rama to stop, the peaceful phase of the protest movement would not have escalated into what it is today.”
Saying she had been surprised by the Albanian prime minister’s enthusiasm for such a large-scale tourism complex in an area so fragile, Strik emphasised the importance of protecting such unique shorelines on a continent that had learned from past mistakes. “I accuse Rama of serving his own interests and the interests of Kushner and not the interests of the environment and the Albanian people,” she said.
“The government clearly intends to finalise the procedures before it is legally bound by EU standards. Such sneaky and disloyal practices should be strongly criticised by the EU. If Albania seriously wants to be a reliable candidate member state, it should respect EU law and not try to circumvent it.”
Asked about Strik’s claims, Rama told the Guardian: “Please tell the honourable lady that the violence in Tirana is very real. Instead of imagining environmental plots that do not exist, she could help Albania by condemning the violence she appears to appreciate, in an unfortunate echo of the Kremlin’s own lady, Madam Zakharova [Russian foreign ministry spokesperson Maria Zakharova].”

From TAPI to CASA-1000: How can Afghanistan benefit from energy corridors?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
13:52:12 UTC
22:52:12 KST

In Herat, construction on the TAPI pipeline is advancing, raising questions about when local businesses and households might receive its gas. TOLOnews, citing Afghanistan’s Ministry of Mines and Petroleum, reported that nearly 25 kilometres of pipeline had been laid, with more of the route prepared for construction.
For Afghan consumers, the practical questions concern supply: who will receive the gas, at what price, and through which distribution network? These questions deserve as much attention as construction milestones.
TAPI and CASA-1000 could give Afghanistan a stronger role in regional energy trade. The challenge is to secure domestic gains from projects whose commercial logic extends well beyond its borders.
Two corridors, different purposes
TAPI is intended to carry Turkmen gas through Afghanistan to Pakistan and India. The Asian Development Bank describes a planned capacity of up to 33 billion cubic metres annually—a target for the completed project, rather than an existing flow.
Reuters reported in February 2026 that Turkmenistan expected to complete the first section to Herat by year-end. Herat is only the first stage of a much longer route. Financing, commercial agreements and relations between participating countries will determine whether the pipeline reaches its intended markets in Pakistan and India.
CASA-1000 follows a different model, transmitting seasonal surplus hydropower from Kyrgyzstan and Tajikistan through Afghanistan to Pakistan. Its planned capacity of 1,300 megawatts refers to the transmission system, rather than electricity available to Afghan consumers. The seasonal nature of supply also limits its contribution to year-round energy security.
According to the World Bank’s January 2026 update, construction in Afghanistan resumed in December 2024 after its suspension in 2021. Facilities elsewhere were largely complete, leaving the Afghan section essential to bringing the regional system into operation.
Hydropower introduces another consideration: drought and changing water availability can affect exportable electricity. Supply planning must account for seasonal variability, supported by regional coordination over water and energy.
Turning transit into domestic value
Transit fees could provide revenue, but their contribution to development will depend on spending decisions and the connections built between these corridors and Afghanistan’s economy.
Using TAPI gas domestically requires offtake facilities, metering, pressure regulation and networks reaching consumers. Supplying Herat’s factories and households therefore involves investment beyond the main pipeline, alongside workable supply contracts, affordable prices and trained operators.
OPINION: Why Afghanistan is becoming a pressure point for Pakistan’s Middle East ambitions
Electricity presents a similar challenge. Communities along a transmission route need distribution lines, connection equipment and purchasing arrangements to receive power. These investments require their own budgets and implementation plans.
Preparations should begin during corridor construction. Waiting until commissioning to identify customers or train technicians would delay the benefits and could leave infrastructure underused.
The World Bank identifies unreliable electricity and limited access to finance as obstacles to Afghan growth and employment. For a manufacturer, an energy corridor becomes economically useful when dependable supply reaches the premises and the business can afford the equipment needed to use it.
Local trust and financial transparency
People living along these routes bear some of the immediate costs of construction. Land acquisition, disruption to livelihoods and uncertainty over compensation can generate grievances, making community relations an important part of corridor security.
Community support programmes associated with CASA-1000 in Kyrgyzstan and Tajikistan offer experience in linking regional infrastructure with local development. Afghanistan needs verifiable commitments on compensation, employment and training, with accessible grievance procedures and provision for women and vulnerable groups to benefit.
Financial arrangements also shape what the country can gain. Under the World Bank’s ring-fenced approach, construction payments and future revenues are managed offshore, outside Taliban control. This arrangement enables implementation while restricting the handling of funds. Revenue projections must therefore be assessed against the rules governing their use, rather than treated as unrestricted additions to Kabul’s budget.
Opportunities for Iran and regional cooperation
Iran has reasons to examine both the competitive effects of these corridors and the business opportunities around them. Engineering services, local gas distribution and electricity distribution upgrades are potential areas for participation, subject to commercial feasibility, regulatory compliance and separate agreements.
Any future electricity link between Iran and South Asia would require additional infrastructure, equipment and contracts. Its prospects should be assessed independently of CASA-1000, with attention to costs, available capacity and buyers’ needs.
Gulf countries could also explore solar generation, storage and technical services. Such investments could address local needs while larger projects proceed. Afghanistan’s households and businesses need improvements in supply during the construction years as well as after commissioning.
Across the region, the commercial foundations deserve sustained diplomatic attention. Payment arrangements, enforceable contracts, dispute resolution and continuity of service during political crises will influence whether buyers, suppliers and financiers remain committed.
Afghanistan’s gains should ultimately be assessed through dependable energy supplied to domestic users, the use of transit revenues and benefits delivered to communities along the routes. Publishing those results would give citizens and regional partners a basis for judging progress. The central task for Afghan energy diplomacy is to make domestic development part of the contracts, investment plans and operating arrangements from the outset.
OPINION: From underground wealth to diplomatic power: Azerbaijan’s energy strategy

The Canary news website announces closure after ‘vicious campaign against us’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
13:52:00 UTC
22:52:00 KST

The leftwing news site the Canary has announced that it is closing indefinitely. Earlier this year the media outlet was blocked from accessing funds and has faced allegations of internal turmoil.
The outlet, founded in 2015 at the height of support for the then Labour leader, Jeremy Corbyn, said in a social media post it would be closing “for the foreseeable future”.
The announcement also included allegations that the title had faced “malicious lies” by former employees. It said such claims had been part of “multiple attacks” it had faced which had made its situation “unsustainable, both financially and operationally”.
In a statement, the Canary said: “After 11 years, we take this action with deep sadness and regret. The extent of the lies, defamation, and harassment by ex-staff – coupled with the constant attacks by the state and those who’d see us destroyed – has become too much.”
The outlet, which describes itself as an anti-austerity, anti-Zionist and pro-freedom of expression platform, said it would be closed indefinitely. However, it added: “It is not over. This week, we will publish what really happened at the Canary and push back against the vicious campaign against our team and us. We may be down, but we’re not out yet.”
Its challenges have included difficulties in paying staff and contractors, which it said was the result of Lloyds Bank unexpectedly blocking access to “a substantial amount” of its money earlier this year.
However, some journalists at the Canary have said they believed the outlet’s banking issues had been used to distract from wider financial mismanagement. They claim that additional funding received over the summer – believed to be more than £2m – had been squandered on projects including a short-lived newspaper and the purchase of other websites.
Steve Topple, the outlet’s chief executive, told staff in May that he and others in the management team had serious concerns about the integrity of the Canary as an organisation “and also the level of reputational risk”.
There are understood to be about 50 full- and part-time staff at the Canary. They have formed a branch of the National Union of Journalists (NUJ).
Staff were told over the summer that the additional funding had almost all been spent and they were facing the possibility of redundancy. At that point, they were told there was about £400,000 earmarked to guide the Canary’s operations through the rest of the year. The Canary then faced problems accessing its funds.
Staff said they had been notified that late payments of pension contributions by the company had been reported by the National Employment Savings Trust (Nest), the government-backed workplace pension scheme that helps employers meet their legal duty of automatic enrolment.
Employees have also alleged that earlier this year, they were asked by management to sign “non-negotiable” non-disclosure agreements and told that if they refused they would be subject to changes to their employment contracts.
Topple said all permanent employees had been paid up to date as of today, “though we’re still clarifying some outstanding holiday payments owed”.
“All employees’ pension contributions are up to date as of 30 September,” he said. “As for freelancers, all have been paid up to date as of 30 September.”

NATO air defenses require modern capabilities — general
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
13:50:30 UTC
22:50:30 KST

BRUSSELS, October 19. /TASS/. NATO has "quietly shifted" from air policing missions in the Baltic states, Benelux, the Balkans, and Iceland to "a unified 360-degree air defense system," which, however, lacks the necessary capabilities, first and foremost the actual means of detecting and intercepting aerial targets, Deputy Commander of NATO Allied Air Command Lieutenant General Guillaume Thomas said in an interview with the Brussels-based portal Rapporteur.
According to him, since last fall, NATO has been conducting a "single mission that is able to cover a 360-degree approach." He explained that this mission has brought together the disparate "air policing" (air patrol) missions in various NATO regions and the system for countering drones and missiles, placing them under a single command.
However, according to Thomas, apart from the change in the command structure, NATO’s new air defense mission has not received additional military resources or staff capabilities to improve coordination among the various air defense components.
Therefore, Thomas acknowledged that NATO’s air defense is lacking in everything: "We need modern tools for our command and control system. We also need sensors and a high-low mix of effectors for this 360 approach, which is a big, big challenge," Thomas said.
The general emphasized that the challenge is not only technological but also industrial, and called on NATO countries to invest in, develop, and produce more air defense systems.

Economic Watch: China rolls out measures to spur consumption through tech innovation
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
21:49:59 CST
22:49:59 KST

The State Council Information Office (SCIO) holds a press conference on accelerating technology-driven commerce, in Beijing, capital of China, Oct. 19, 2026. (Xinhua/Pan Xu)
BEIJING, Oct. 19 (Xinhua) -- China has released new guidelines to promote the application of artificial intelligence (AI) and other advanced technologies in commerce, as part of efforts to expand consumer demand, upgrade traditional businesses and improve the efficiency of goods distribution.
These guidelines, jointly issued by nine government departments, including the Ministry of Commerce, outline 18 measures covering goods consumption, services consumption, commercial distribution, innovative business applications and policy support.
"The move aims to meet the immediate need to boost consumption and invigorate the consumer market, while using technology-driven innovation to upgrade traditional commerce and foster emerging business models," Yuan Xiaoming, assistant minister of commerce, told a press conference on Monday.
To upgrade consumer goods, the guidelines call for integrating AI into product development, design, manufacturing and marketing, expanding the supply of smart devices and robots, and encouraging flexible manufacturing and AI-powered customization.
New technologies, including AI, the Internet of Things and blockchain, can help drive consumption upgrades, Yuan said. Data from the ministry showed that sales of smart glasses on major platforms rose 110 percent year on year in January-September 2026.
The measures also encourage the use of AI in healthcare and smart elderly care services, as well as the digital transformation of catering businesses, to expand services consumption.
China's retail sales of consumer goods rose 1.1 percent year on year to 37 trillion yuan (about 5.5 trillion U.S. dollars) in the first three quarters of 2026, while retail sales of services increased 5 percent, outpacing the 1-percent growth in retail sales of goods, official data released on Monday showed.
To create more personalized consumer experiences, the guidelines support emerging intelligent services such as companion robots. They also promote the use of ultra-high-definition audiovisual technology and digital twins in shopping districts, tourism, education and training.
They also call for pilot applications of AI in culture and tourism, as immersive experiences and digital performances gain traction in China's cultural and tourism market.
Data from the National Bureau of Statistics showed that revenue from emerging cultural sectors grew 9.6 percent year on year in the first half of 2026, 5 percentage points faster than the overall cultural industry.
In commercial distribution, the measures promote smart warehouses, intelligent logistics equipment and unmanned delivery, alongside digital upgrades in wholesale and retail businesses.
The guidelines also call for developing commercial AI agents for shopping assistance, business operations and logistics, expanding applications of embodied intelligence, and creating virtual shopping experiences. They additionally outline support for technology standards, digital infrastructure and financing.
The new measures build on China's broader push to accelerate the commercial application of AI and other advanced technologies.
China's AI industry has expanded rapidly, with AI-powered smartphones, intelligent connected vehicles and humanoid robots among the products seeing broader application. The country's AI core industry was estimated to have exceeded 1.2 trillion yuan in 2025.
In late 2025, China launched a special initiative to integrate AI into manufacturing. AI adoption among large industrial firms has since exceeded 30 percent, said Wei Wei, an official from the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology.
China will further develop the AI industry and expand its application in manufacturing, focusing on key AI technologies and the development of intelligent devices such as brain-computer interfaces and embodied AI systems, Wei added. ■

JOHANNESBURG, Oct. 19 (Xinhua) -- South Africa's African National Congress (ANC), the country's largest party in the governing coalition, said Sunday that all 181 of its previously excluded candidates will appear on the ballot in six municipalities in the country's Nov. 4 local government elections.
The ANC said in a statement that Chief Electoral Officer Sy Mamabolo confirmed in a letter on Sunday that verification of the candidates had been completed and that the ballots to be printed would include the ANC candidates, in accordance with a Constitutional Court judgment issued on Thursday.
The candidates comprise 51 ward candidates and 130 proportional representation candidates in Ngquza Hill, Port St Johns, Walter Sisulu and Sundays River Valley in the Eastern Cape Province, uMshwathi in KwaZulu-Natal Province, and Mangaung Metropolitan Municipality in the Free State Province.
"As the names were already with the Electoral Commission of South Africa (IEC), the IEC has simply accepted them as they are in its system, without the need for the ANC to act or do anything," said ANC Secretary-General Fikile Mbalula.
The IEC had initially rejected the ANC's nominations after the party uploaded the required candidate information but failed to complete the final online submission step before the Aug. 28 deadline. The ANC challenged the decision after the Electoral Court upheld the IEC's position on Sept. 16.
On Thursday, the Constitutional Court overturned the Electoral Court ruling and directed the IEC to take the necessary steps to include the 181 candidates in the electoral process.
The ruling prompted the IEC to extend similar relief to 32 other political parties that were found to have been in circumstances comparable to those of the ANC. The commission on Friday said it would allow the affected parties to complete their candidate nominations, citing the need for equal treatment following the Constitutional Court's decision.
A total of 10,526 council seats will be contested in the Nov. 4 elections. The IEC previously certified 136,790 candidates for the polls, which will be held across eight metropolitan municipalities, 44 district municipalities and 205 local municipalities. ■

Zelensky says he wants to run for president again
Ukrainian leader Vladimir Zelensky has said he wants to run for president again if an election is held before the conflict with Russia ends. His five-year term expired two years ago, prompting Moscow to question his legitimacy, while US President Donald Trump has called for him to be replaced.
Zelensky has refused to call a new election since his term expired in May 2024, citing martial law, which was imposed after the conflict with Russia escalated in February 2022. During his 2019 election campaign, he promised to only serve one term.
Speaking to NBC News’ ‘Meet the Press’ on Sunday, Zelensky said he would seek another term if an election is held while the fighting continues.
“If it will be during the war – of course. It’s my responsibility, because I have to defend my country from the very beginning to end of this war,” he stated.
Zelensky once again demanded a ceasefire of at least 60 days to prepare for the election, claiming that the country needs time to amend its laws and put election infrastructure in place.
Moscow has rejected the demand. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov has said Kiev could use an election as a pretext to secure a 60-day ceasefire to “regroup,” recover its military losses, and resume the fighting. He added, however, that Russia is prepared to suspend strikes on election day.
Russian President Vladimir Putin has argued that Zelensky’s presidential powers should have passed to the parliament after his mandate expired, and questioned whether he can sign binding peace agreements. He called Zelensky’s refusal to hold elections a “strategic mistake.”
Zelensky’s ambitions also face opposition at home. A survey in September by the Kiev International Institute of Sociology found that 53% of respondents believe he should only serve one presidential term, up from 46% in December 2025.
Trump has stepped up pressure on Zelensky, accusing him of prolonging the conflict while receiving billions in Western assistance. Earlier this month, he called for a new president, arguing that Zelensky has repeatedly rejected opportunities to end the fighting.
“I suggest they get a new leader who can make a deal,” Trump told reporters.
He also blamed Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries for the worsening global diesel crisis and rising prices which hurt American farmers, accusing Zelensky of creating “problems for the world” despite his repeated demands to stop the attacks.
In a Truth Social post on Sunday, Trump said Zelensky “doesn’t want to end this war, and probably never did,” arguing that he could have secured a better deal with Russia two years ago. He added that Ukraine is “in shambles,” describing its male population as “low, wounded, and/or dead.”

Europe has no 'moves' left in Ukraine conflict, expert says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
13:47:46 UTC
22:47:46 KST

MOSCOW, October 19. /TASS/. Europeans should begin reflecting on the potential trajectory of the Ukraine conflict, as they currently lack any good "moves," Andrey Sushentsov, Dean of the School of International Relations at MGIMO University and a member of the Scientific Advisory Council under the Russian Security Council, told TASS.
"Europeans lack the military and technological resources, as well as the strategic thinking and awareness of their own interests comparable to those of the Americans, which would allow them to weigh causes and consequences, determine what can and cannot be achieved through military means, and define Europe's interest in this crisis," he said.
"The course toward a years-long confrontation with their largest neighbor, which was a source of many benefits that the European economy has now lost, demonstrates the narrowness of their vision. Domestic political processes in Europe show that, following the Americans' lead, it is time for Europeans to reflect on their interests, what is achievable in the Ukrainian crisis and what is not, and what the trajectory might be. For now, Europeans have no good 'moves,' " Sushentsov noted.
The expert pointed out that while Europeans still possess a substantial financial instrument, it is essentially the only tool at their disposal. "They are managing it wastefully: the domestic debt of most major European states is approaching or exceeding 100% of GDP. They cannot obtain external compensation for military costs, and there is no hope for a Ukrainian victory. If there were hope, they would count on recovering losses at the expense of Russian resources and through new deals with Russia on new terms. None of these hopes are being realized," he added.
"Moreover, due to a lack of strategic experience – lost due to American patronage and the nuclear umbrella – Europeans are beginning to deny their own geography, denying that Russia shares the continent with them. Geography is a constant, a part of the foreign policy system that cannot be changed. Governments and historical circumstances change, but geography remains immutable," Sushentsov said.

UN food agency to cut aid to 500,000 people in Gaza as funding dries up
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
13:46:51 UTC
22:46:51 KST

Families who keep their support will get smaller rations and less cash, even though two-thirds of the territory’s population still needs help to survive.
The World Food Programme will stop monthly assistance to half a million people in Gaza because of a funding shortfall, the UN agency said on Monday.
The cuts leave 1.1 million Palestinians, around half of Gaza’s population, receiving food or cash each month. Since the October 2025 ceasefire, the WFP had been reaching between 1.5 million and 1.8 million people a month.
“This has been a lifeline. But now, rather than being able to sustain and scale up that assistance, we’re actually having to reduce it,” Shaun Hughes, the WFP’s country director, told AFP in east Jerusalem.
"And that’s not because we don’t have humanitarian access to deliver food; that’s because we don’t have funding."
Smaller rations
Families receiving food will now get one parcel instead of two and a smaller bag of wheat flour. The 75,000 families who receive cash will see monthly payments fall from 1,250 to 750 shekels ($400 to $240).
Hughes said conditions had not improved enough to justify the cuts.
“People are not safe. Airstrikes continue on a daily basis. People continue to be displaced,” he said. “Almost everybody remains without a permanent home to live in. And the humanitarian conditions are brutal.”
According to the latest assessments, 1.4 million people, two-thirds of the population, remain “acutely food insecure” and need aid to survive. The WFP warns that needs could rise again with the onset of winter.
In August 2025, the UN-backed Integrated Food Security Phase Classification declared famine conditions in Gaza, a finding Israel called a lie. The classification was lifted in December, two months after the US-brokered ceasefire, though Israeli strikes have continued.
The WFP’s resources have fallen sharply, partly because US President Donald Trump drastically cut contributions to UN agencies. It needs about $450 million over the next six months for Gaza and the West Bank, but has received only around half its usual funding for the Palestinian territories this year. In September, it halved the number of people it helps in the West Bank to 200,000.
Israel has let more goods into Gaza under the ceasefire but still blocks items it considers to have potential military use, including prosthetic limbs, according to the UN. It also accuses the UN of bias.
“Now is not the time in the history of Palestine and Gaza to turn away from what is happening in Gaza,” Hughes said.

Lavrov In Tehran Amid Questions Over Whether Moscow Is Helping Iran In War With US
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
13:46:35 UTC
22:46:35 KST

Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov traveled to Iran on October 19, meeting with President Masud Pezeshkian and Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi amid questions over what support Moscow is providing Tehran to fight its war with the United States.
Lavrov traveled to the Iranian capital directly from Manama, Bahrain, where he had attended a meeting with Gulf Cooperation Council officials. Gulf states have urged Moscow to use its influence to press Tehran to halt attacks on its neighbors.
Following talks in Tehran with his Russian counterpart, Araqchi said they discussed regional and international issues, including Lebanon, Palestine, Ukraine, and Yemen, as well as expanding economic and nuclear cooperation.
"Never in our history have Iran and Russia worked as closely as now," Araqchi wrote in a post on X.
Lavrov also met with Iran's security chief, Mohsen Rezaei, the Russian Foreign Ministry said in a statement, which described the talks in broad terms and provided little detail.
The meetings were held in "a traditionally constructive spirit" and with "an emphasis on strengthening the comprehensive strategic partnership," the Russian statement said.
It said the "importance of close coordination regarding the situation in the Middle East and the Persian Gulf region, as well as in the South Caucasus and the Caspian region, was underscored, and that Lavrov "reaffirmed Russia’s readiness" to facilitate a resolution to the situation surrounding Iran" -- meaning the war.
The Russian statement made no mention of military or intelligence cooperation -- but what was not on the public agenda was the focus of much of the world.
After battling a much more powerful adversary for almost eight months, questions about how much support Iran is getting from Russia -- which has never directly entered the war -- and in what form have simmered.
They came to a boil, however, on October 18 when US President Donald Trump said in a social media post that Russia is doing “very little, if anything, to help the Islamic Republic of Iran” compared to what it could do.
That came after he wrote earlier in the week on social media that he did not believe either Moscow nor Beijing were helping Iran “at all.”
"If they are, it's at a very low level, but I don't believe they are at all. They have too much to lose, and we would know about it, and know about it very fast," Trump wrote.
Trump's October 18 comment was made as part of his justification to waive sweeping sanctions planned against Russia, saying it could drive the Kremlin away from negotiations to end the war in Ukraine.
The Trump administration recently waived sanctions on Russian diesel exports, drawing bipartisan condemnation, as well as raising the ire of Ukraine and many of its international partners.
'Russian Support Has Been There'
Hamidreza Azizi, a senior Iran analyst at the Belgium-based International Crisis Group, told RFE/RL that while it's true Moscow has withheld heavy weaponry and deals for jets such as the Su-35 fighters have stalled, Russia has still provided Iran with military intelligence enabling “precision strikes against US bases” and helped improve Iranian-made systems, including Shahed drones, through continued military-technical cooperation.
“So, it really depends on how you define support, but Russian support has been there, and it has had a tangible impact,” Azizi said.
Several analysts point to one incident they say shows how important Russia's support for Iran is.
In March, Iran attacked the Prince Sultan Air Base in Saudi Arabia that wounded 12 American troops.
Experts noted its unusual precision was likely aided by Russian intelligence. Reports then surfaced that two days before the strike, 14 Russian spy satellites passed over the base. Later, US officials concluded that information from Moscow made the precision attack possible.
A senior EU official, speaking on condition of anonymity because they weren't authorized to speak on the record, told RFE/RL that Russian assistance to Iran has always been limited because its war against Ukraine has stretched Moscow’s resources.
The official said there was “no sign at all that they are limiting it further” and described Trump's comment as "propaganda to somehow explain to the [US] public why he [is] soft on Russia and bullying Ukraine.”
Intelligence, Drones, And Missiles
Since the United States and Israel launched strikes on Iran on February 28, media reports citing US, European, and Ukrainian officials have described growing Russian support for Tehran.
Several media outlets have cited people familiar with US intelligence that Russia has been passing Iran information on the locations and movements of US troops, warships, and aircraft -- much of it satellite imagery.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said Kyiv had evidence that Russia was providing Iran with signals and electronic intelligence.
According to Andrea Kendall-Taylor, senior fellow and director of the Transatlantic Security Program at the Center for a New American Security, and Richard Fontaine, CEO of the Center for a New American Security, "Russia’s support for Tehran has been operationally meaningful but carefully bounded."
"Even as it fights its own war in Ukraine, Moscow has found ways to help Iran strike American targets and sustain the fight through diplomatic cover and material support while stopping short of actions that could draw Russia into direct conflict with the United States," they wrote in an analysis in Foreign Affairs last week.
Amir Chahaki, an analyst based in Germany, told RFE/RL's Radio Farda that Putin wants to use Iran as leverage in his dealings with Trump in return for the US applying pressure on Ukraine.
“The more Putin can persuade Tehran to move closer to Trump’s demands, the more concessions he can extract from Trump," he said.

US Supreme Court snubs bid to revive plea deal for accused 9/11 mastermind
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
13:45:58 UTC
22:45:58 KST

US Supreme Court snubs bid to revive plea deal for accused 9/11 mastermind
Oct 19 - The US Supreme Court declined on Monday to hear a bid by Khalid Sheikh Mohammed, the accused mastermind of the September 11, 2001, attacks, to revive a 2024 agreement that would have spared him the death penalty in exchange for a guilty plea — a deal scrapped by former Defense Secretary Lloyd Austin.
The justices turned away appeals by Mohammed and two co-defendants who had also signed plea agreements of a lower court's ruling that upheld Austin's decision to void the deals. The US Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit rejected an argument that Austin, who served under former President Joe Biden, had acted too late.
The Supreme Court's action marks the latest milestone in a military prosecution of the detainees held in Guantanamo Bay, Cuba, that has been beset by two decades of legal gridlock.
In August, a US Air Force judge set the trial for Mohammed and his co-defendants for June 2028.
Mohammed remains the most well-known inmate at the Guantanamo detention facility, which was set up in 2002 by then-US President George W. Bush to house foreign terrorism suspects following the 9/11 attacks, which killed nearly 3,000 people. Mohammed is accused of orchestrating the plot to fly hijacked passenger jetliners into the World Trade Center in New York City and into the Pentagon in Arlington, Virginia.
'DELIVERING JUSTICE'
Monday's Supreme Court action "clears the path for holding those responsible for the September 11 attacks accountable. This is a critical step toward delivering justice for the victims and families on one of the darkest days in American history," a US Justice Department spokesperson said in a statement.
The plea agreements for Mohammed and co-defendants Mustafa al Hawsawi and Walid bin 'Atash had been offered and accepted by the US official overseeing the Pentagon's Guantanamo war court, prompting criticism by Republican lawmakers.
Austin revoked the deals two days later.
A military judge ruled that Austin lacked authority to invalidate the plea deals in a decision that was upheld in December by the US Court of Military Commission Review. The judge then scheduled prompt plea hearings.
The DC Circuit paused those proceedings, and in July 2025, a panel of that court — in a 2-1 vote — backed the decision to scrap the plea deals, saying that Austin "indisputably had legal authority to withdraw from the agreements."
Defense attorneys for Mohammed and al Hawsawi, including lawyers from the American Civil Liberties Union, had urged the Supreme Court to hear the case. They said Austin's action violated controlling military law and "prolonged the best chance for finality in the September 11 case in a quarter century." REUTERS

Unfortunately, we are recording that on various front sections, the equipment stops functioning at speeds of 130–161 kilometers per hour,” Zelenskyy said on X Monday.
According to him, this also limits the use of various types of drones, primarily medium-range strike drones, as well as the deployment of interceptors against jet-powered Shahed drones.
Zelenskyy noted that this situation must be discussed once again with partners today, at all levels.
"Speed matters for protecting lives," the President stressed.

Armenia is hosting the UN COP17 biodiversity talks in its capital Yerevan. (AFP Photo)
Nearly 200 nations kicked off crucial U.N. biodiversity talks in Armenia on Oct. 19 as governments face pressure to salvage a landmark nature pact whose goals are slipping out of reach.
Most countries joined a historic call four years ago to halt and reverse the destruction of nature by 2030 but governments have been slow to act on these pledges.
Many goals of the so-called “Paris Agreement for Nature” are falling behind, including a centerpiece commitment to protect 30 percent of Earth’s land and oceans.
Some of the toughest objectives of the pact, such as cutting subsidies for fossil fuels and other powerful industries, have made little progress.
Armenian Environment Minister Hambardzum Matevosyan, who is presiding over the political negotiations known as COP17, said nations had “a unique chance to correct the course” in Yerevan. “Over the next two weeks our task will be to bridge the differences, build consensus and ensure that COP17 deliver results commensurate with the urgency of the challenges before us,” he said at the summit’s opening session.

Attorney: Police should not be given right to confiscate scooters without court order
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
13:43:00 UTC
22:43:00 KST

Attorney: Police should not be given right to confiscate scooters without court order
Police should not be allowed to confiscate noncompliant personal light electric vehicles without court approval, as doing so would seriously infringe on property rights, Sorainen attorney Marcus Niin told ERR.
ERR reported Monday that amendments to the Traffic Act awaiting their second reading in the Riigikogu would give police the authority to confiscate electric scooters that do not meet legal requirements without a court order. Currently, such personal light electric vehicles can only be confiscated with court approval, but so far, courts have not granted a single request.
Attorney at law Marcus Niin criticized the proposal, noting that one important principle that must be taken into account is the inviolability of private property.
"This is an important principle for us and it can only be restricted in circumstances expressly provided for by law and generally in exchange for compensation. In other words, our legal system does not allow property to simply be taken away without compensation," Niin said.
Another consideration is that confiscation constitutes a very serious infringement of property rights, he added.
"Confiscation means property is permanently taken away without any compensation. Under the current legal framework, the Penal Code provides that confiscation can be ordered by a court and that authority should remain with the courts. Otherwise, if we start giving the executive branch the power to decide at its own discretion whether to seize someone's property, it could lead to serious infringements of rights and considerable public resentment," Niin said.
"In the longer term, this could also set a dangerous precedent. If we make a concession here, where will the next situation arise in which someone decides that, for one reason or another, the authorities should be given the power to confiscate property?" he added.
Even if compensation were paid for confiscated property, the police should not be the ones making that decision. Instead, Niin argued, the decision about what to do with the property should remain with its owner, in keeping with property rights and legal principles.
According to Niin, this is a fundamental question of whether the executive branch should be given the authority to interfere significantly with an individual's property rights when that power currently rests solely with the courts.
The attorney added that if courts have so far refused to allow police to confiscate personal light electric vehicles that do not meet legal requirements, the solution cannot be to create a legal shortcut allowing police to confiscate property directly.
According to Niin, the proposal is not made any more acceptable by the fact that the bill would require police to assess the circumstances of each case and determine whether confiscation is necessary.
"It's understandable that they want to create a system that gives officers discretion, but this question should not be left to police officers in the first place. It is such a fundamental and important matter that the decision on whether to take away someone's property should remain with the courts," he said.
--

Vanuatu clarified its position during the inaugural Nakamal Committee meeting at Parliament House in Canberra on Oct. 15, according to a joint statement issued Monday by Australia’s Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade.
Vanuatu, a South Pacific island nation about 1,750 kilometers (1,087 miles) east of Australia, said its policing arrangement with China was time-limited, while the agreement with Australia was legally binding and had no expiry date.

Vanuatu has maintained policing cooperation with China since 2023, including police training, advisers and equipment donations.

The proposed arrangement covered police training, equipment, cybercrime, transnational crime and general law enforcement.
However, a signing date for the memorandum has not been independently confirmed.
China failed to secure a region-wide security agreement with Pacific island nations in May 2022 but has pursued bilateral policing arrangements, including with the Solomon Islands and Fiji.

MOSCOW, October 19. /TASS/. It would be a mistake to view foreign interference as the primary cause of mass protests in Europe, as the roots of public discontent lie in the domestic policies pursued by the continent’s leaders, political analyst Ilya Grashchenkov told TASS.
"Blaming everything solely on foreign interference would be a mistake. The social and economic problems facing European countries are real. They have been building up for years, and the current unrest may signal the beginning of a profound transformation of Europe’s political system. In my view, these domestic factors are the decisive ones today," Grashchenkov said.
Commenting on allegations of foreign interference made by Albanian Prime Minister Edi Rama, the expert noted that no evidence had been presented to substantiate such claims.
"Various external actors may be trying to exploit the situation to advance their own information agendas. However, having an interest in a political crisis in Europe does not mean being directly involved in orchestrating it," he observed.
Grashchenkov also pointed to growing divisions among Western allies.
"There are significant ideological differences between the conservative administration of US President Donald Trump and a large segment of the European political establishment. As a result, various forces may see the protests as an opportunity to influence the future direction of Europe," he concluded.
Mass protests have taken place in France, Italy and Albania in recent days. In France, demonstrations have been driven by rising fuel prices and declining purchasing power. In Italy, protesters have voiced opposition to the policies of Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni’s government, while in Albania, demonstrators have demanded the resignation of Prime Minister Edi Rama. Hundreds of people have been detained across the three countries amid the unrest.

AI squeezes entry-level job opportunities
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

13:41:29 UTC
22:41:29 KST

AI squeezes entry-level job opportunities
Young professionals face growing barriers to employment as companies use artificial intelligence to automate junior roles and reconsider recruitment, according to research by BSI, reports a Qazinform News Agency correspondent.
The study, published in October 2025, found that 39% of surveyed business leaders said their organizations had reduced or eliminated entry-level positions through AI efficiencies in research, administration and briefing tasks. Another 43% expected such reductions over the following year.
Nearly a third, 31%, said their organizations explored AI solutions before considering hiring a person. Meanwhile, 41% reported that AI was enabling workforce reductions.
A quarter believed AI could perform all or most tasks assigned to an entry-level employee, highlighting the pressure on positions traditionally used to gain professional experience.
“There is an urgent need for long-term thinking and workforce investment, alongside investment in AI tools, to ensure sustainable and productive employment,” BSI Chief Executive Susan Taylor Martin said.
The accompanying report found that productivity and efficiency were the main reasons for investing in AI, cited by 61% of respondents. Cost reductions followed at 49%, while 43% pointed to filling skills gaps.
Some 62% expected their organizations to increase AI investment over the following year, and 59% considered the technology crucial to business growth.
Analysis of corporate annual reports also revealed an imbalance in how companies discussed the technology. Automation was almost seven times more prominent than upskilling, training or education. BSI said this raised questions about whether employers were preparing their workforces adequately for technological change.
The impact differed by company size. Half of large businesses had already cut junior roles, compared with 30% of small and medium-sized enterprises. BSI suggested smaller employers could consequently play a greater role in training young workers.
The research combined polling of more than 850 business leaders in seven countries, including the United States, with analysis of annual reports from 123 multinational corporations.
Earlier, Qazinform News Agency reported that Anthropic had warned that small artificial intelligence models could be months away from replicating themselves across internet-connected consumer devices without relying on data centers.

Ramadan, Laylat al-Qadr, Eid al-Fitr: Dates confirmed for 2027
The Spiritual Administration of Muslims of Kazakhstan has announced the dates for religious holidays and key observances in 2027, Qazinform News Agency reports.
According to the Islamic calendar, the holy month of Ramadan will begin on February 8. The month-long fast will conclude with Eid al-Fitr celebrations on March 9.
One of the most sacred nights of Ramadan — Laylat al-Qadr (the Night of Power) — falls on the night of March 5–6 in 2027.
Eid al-Adha (Feast of the Sacrifice) will be celebrated over three days next year, from May 16 to 18. The preceding Day of Arafah falls on May 15.
The calendar also outlines other key dates on the Islamic calendar. Isra' and Mi'raj (the Prophet's Night Journey and Ascension) will be observed on the night of January 4–5, and Laylat al-Bara'at (Night of Forgiveness) on the night of January 22–23. The Day of Ashura will be on June 15, while Mawlid, which commemorates the birthday of the Prophet Muhammad, falls on August 14–15. Another date for Isra' and Mi'raj in 2027 is listed for December 24–25.
The Spiritual Administration of Muslims of Kazakhstan noted that the dates of religious holidays and observances may shift by one day depending on the sighting of the new moon.
In 2026, the holy month of Ramadan ran from February 19 to March 19. Eid al-Fitr was celebrated on March 20.

French protest violence: A ‘Christmas present’ for Le Pen’s far right?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
13:41:23 UTC
22:41:23 KST

French protest violence: A ‘Christmas present’ for Le Pen’s far right?
Le Pen is positioning her party as more capable than centrist or left-wing forces ahead of the presidential election in April 2027.
As massive protests swept through cities across France over the weekend, degenerating into riots in many places, far-right politician Marine Le Pen has attempted to profit from the crisis ahead of the presidential election in April 2027.
On Sunday, the leader of the National Rally party, or RN by its French initials, railed against President Emmanuel Macron’s handling of the crisis in a video statement, saying the outgoing centre-right leader no longer has any “credibility or authority” and that the country’s people were caught between his austerity “hammering” them on the one hand and “insurrectionary activists” on the left on the other.
School protests in France erupted on September 21 in a poor borough of Paris as pupils demonstrated against dilapidated infrastructure, teacher shortages and tight class schedules. The demonstrations quickly spread across the country and coincided with a nationwide public sector strike against the government’s plans to cut public spending.
Le Pen blamed the political left and “decades of immigration” to France for the looting and destruction that trailed the demonstrations, and presented her party as capable of restoring order — without offering any firm evidence to back up assertions that the rioting was led by immigrants.
The politician is already far ahead in recent polls, and some say she is likely to be the next leader. Here’s what we know:
What happened over the weekend?
Scenes of burned cars, vandalised and looted shops and defaced public buildings emerged from across France.
Some 550,000 people demonstrated on Saturday, according to the Ministry of the Interior, although protest organisers put the figure at 800,000. Protesters included students, union groups and supporters of the “yellow vests” movement, which protested against inflation back in 2018, at the start of Macron’s presidency.
Although most marched peacefully, masked groups attacked city halls in several cities on Saturday, including the 19th-century City Hall in the city of Limoges, which was badly damaged.
In Lyon, a tourist office was set ablaze.
In Marseille, hooded individuals attacked a police station. The city has since banned protests.
Looters also targeted hundreds of shops in several locations.
In Paris, storefronts were shattered and broken glass littered the Place de la Republique. The Marianne statue, an important symbol of France, was partially dismantled. Paris police said one person died of a heart attack, but did not provide more details.
Protesters and rights groups have accused police of using disproportionate force throughout the protests. Some 2,400 people were arrested by Sunday, officials said. Several police officers were injured.
In a national address, Macron condemned rioters and accused far-left groups of attacking police and public buildings. Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu said on Monday that partial curfews would be imposed in some areas.
How could the far right gain?
Peter McPhee, a professor emeritus at the University of Melbourne, described the protests as a “Christmas present” for Le Pen’s National Rally ahead of the presidential election.
Le Pen said in a video statement protesters have “legitimate social grievances” but that Macron’s government was “exhausted, disoriented and seemingly incapable” of addressing them.
She criticised the administration’s controversial budget plans and promised to free the French from “Macronist toxic policies” while failing to mention that her party has also proposed strict spending cuts to bring down rising public debt.
The politician, who is far ahead of other candidates in the polls, fuelled right-wing narratives spreading online that immigrants, not the French people, are instigating the protests, even as the grievances driving the agitation have intersected, with flag-carrying pro-Palestinian, environmental, feminist and anticolonial movements joining in.
McPhee called Le Pen’s move “profoundly worrying”.
“It is easy for Le Pen to make the link between the violent attacks on buildings and shops with African migrants because of the Palestinian and Algerian flags,” the professor said. “People in many parts of the world are attracted to simplistic, often racist, answers to economic and social problems.”
Analysts add that far-left leader Jean-Luc Melenchon of the France Unbowed party, or LFI, who has joined the protests, could also face backlash if anger grows over the destruction, further handing Le Pen a stronger platform.
How did the far right gain ground after previous protests?
Right-wing and centrist parties have historically gained after mass protests and disorder as people, fearing anarchy, vote for them.
In May 1968, similar student-led protests erupted after millions of students and striking workers rallied against poor schooling conditions, increasing economic inequalities and stagnant wages.
Left-wing communist and socialist political parties joined the protests and called for a revolution. Then-President Charles de Gaulle’s conservative government initially struggled to control the demonstrations, even escaping to a French base in West Germany for a few days as violence spiralled and the country ground to a standstill.
However, the protest soon lost momentum amid the shutdown of public services. De Gaulle dissolved parliament and called for snap elections in June 1968, blaming the left for the violence and promising to restore order. His conservative Union for the Defence of the Republic party went on to win in an astounding landslide while left-wing parties lost more than half their seats.
Again, during the 2018 “yellow vest” demonstrations, working-class protesters rallying against Macron’s government’s decision to raise taxes found support among Le Pen’s party, although the left wing also tried to ingratiate itself with the movement.
Many of the movement’s supporters ended up voting for Le Pen’s party in the 2022 legislative elections to punish the Macron government, a move that still shapes the deeply divided parliament.

Range of Up to 290 km: Poland Receives Batch of CTM-290 Ballistic Missiles for the Homar-K
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
13:41:04 UTC
22:41:04 KST

Poland has received a batch of CGR-080 guided missiles and CTM-290 ballistic missiles for its Homar-K multiple launch rocket systems.
The Polish Armaments Agency (Agencja Uzbrojenia) reported this.
The shipment included CGR-080 missiles with a range of up to 80 km, as well as CTM-290 ballistic missiles with a range of up to 290 km.
The Polish defense ministry has not disclosed the quantity of ammunition delivered.
The deliveries are part of a program to modernize Poland’s rocket artillery, which calls for procuring a total of 290 Homar-K launch modules.
In April 2024, Poland ordered an additional 72 Homar-K launch modules along with several thousand rockets of various ranges. The contract with South Korea’s Hanwha Aerospace was worth approximately $1.6 billion.
The Homar-K is a Polish modification of the South Korean K239 Chunmoo multiple launch rocket system (MLRS), which is mounted on an eight-wheeled Jelcz chassis and integrated with the Polish TOPAZ fire control system.
The launcher has two transport-launch containers. Each can hold six CGR-080 rockets or one CTM-290 ballistic missile. Thus, a single launcher can carry up to 12 guided rockets or two ballistic missiles.
In April 2024, South Korea successfully tested the CTM-290 ballistic missile for the first time. The launch took place on April 24 at the South Korean Agency for Defense Development (ADD) test site in Anhin in the presence of representatives from the Polish Ministry of Defense.
In parallel with ammunition deliveries, Poland is working to localize CGR-080 missile production on its own territory. According to the Armaments Agency, the first missiles are expected to roll off the production line at a Polish facility as early as 2028.
In April 2025, Poland’s WB Electronics and South Korea’s Hanwha Aerospace agreed to jointly produce 239-mm guided missiles.
Subsequently, in December 2025, the Armaments Agency signed a contract with the Hanwha WB Advanced System and Hanwha Aerospace consortium for the supply of Polish-made CGR-080 rockets. Deliveries under this agreement are scheduled to begin in 2030.
In July 2026, Militarnyi reported that preparatory work began on the Hanwha WB Advanced System plant in Gożów Wielkopolski.

NEW DELHI: More than 400 Indian-origin students, researchers and alumni from universities in 27 countries have issued a joint statement condemning the ongoing protests against the Election Commission of India (ECI), describing them as a “plan to sow seeds of doubt in India’s democracy”.Titled “Spare India from Anarchy”, the statement criticises the protests against the poll body."An unconscionable and devious plan of sowing seeds of doubt in Indian democracy has been hatched by weaponising sub judice matters, which is then amplified on the streets by leaning on anarchist forces, which have historically and philosophically never believed in constitutional form of governance. All in the name of saving democracy," the statement said."We remain amazed at the irony of all. But more importantly, as informed people who have stakes in the future of this country and travel the world identifying as 'Indians,' we are deeply anguished at this state of affairs," it added.The signatories highlighted the resilience of Indian democracy and the role of constitutional institutions, stating: "In the seven decades since independence, Indian democracy has proved its resilience repeatedly.

Adverse judgements have provoked unfortunate commentary on judicial independence. Even the most apolitical institution in the country -- the armed forces -- has been gratuitously and unjustly entangled in partisan discourse," the statement read.While acknowledging that dissent was essential to democracy, the signatories said they refused to remain "silent spectators to the subversion of democratic apparatus in its guise".They urged social and political forces to resolve differences through "debate, discussion, dialogue and dissent" within constitutional institutions.The signatories are based in or have studied at universities across 27 countries, including the US, the UK, Canada, Australia, Germany, France, Japan and Singapore.Their academic affiliations include the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, the universities of Oxford and Cambridge, Harvard University, Stanford University and the London School of Economics, among others.
