‘Weight of responsibility’: Promise and perils of covering Ethiopia’s war
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
13:21:37 UTC
22:21:37 KST

‘Weight of responsibility’: Promise and perils of covering Ethiopia’s war
Al Jazeera correspondent shares his experience of covering the latest fighting between government forces and Tigray rebels.
Addis Ababa, Ethiopia – On September 23, fighting erupted in Ethiopia’s northern region of Tigray, shattering the peace agreement between the Ethiopian government and Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF) signed nearly four years ago.
The latest fighting between the federal government-backed Tigray Peace Force (TPF) and TPLF started in the Erbeti area of Ethiopia’s Afar region after the 2022 peace deal unravelled over disarmament and territorial claims.
For me, the latest war is more than a story unfolding on television. It brought back painful memories of what I had experienced during my reporting in November 2021. The previous episode of fighting killed more than half a million people and displaced about 2 million others by the time the rival sides signed a deal to end the war in 2022.
After I was assigned to cover the fighting, I was once again faced with the challenge any war correspondent faces: how to stand in the midst of active fighting as a witness to the truth.
Soon, our team set off from the capital, Addis Ababa, to the Afar region and then to Mekelle, the capital of the Tigray region, covering the journey by road.
When I reached Erbeti, about 900km (560 miles) northeast of Addis Ababa, I hoped to catch my breath for a few hours and organise our coverage. Instead, events overtook us immediately.
Residents were leaving the town, which, until the previous day, had seemed safe. Small trucks and cars were piled with belongings. Men hurried to load whatever they could carry as families tried to get away before the fighting drew closer.
As we were still figuring out what to do next, loud sounds of shelling shook us. We decided to leave Erbeti only hours after arriving as staying would put the team’s lives at risk.
That had not been the plan. But war pays little attention to a correspondent’s plans.
We withdrew towards Afdera, about 100km (60 miles) to the east via unpaved roads. Afdera is a small town that serves as the administrative centre for the district of the same name in the Afar region, known for its salt mining.
We spent the night inside our car in the middle of the desert with the temperature hovering above 35 degrees Celsius (95 degrees Fahrenheit).
Intensified fighting
The next day, we started early to review information, make calls, prepare footage for reports and coordinate with the newsroom in Doha, Qatar.
Meanwhile, the heat and humidity drained our remaining energy as the mercury hit 50C (122F). As we lay in the car trying to catch some sleep, my thoughts were still in Erbeti.
Early the next morning, we headed for Afdera. After arriving there at 7am, we found that breakfast choices were limited.
The town followed a different rhythm: Many residents ate breakfast after dawn prayers, then headed to work. It was part of a correspondent’s daily reality – arriving somewhere unfamiliar and learning its routines.
We headed north towards Erbeti again, only to find the fighting intensifying in the mountains between the government-backed forces and TPLF.
I couldn’t see the clashes directly, but their sounds filled the area. The sound of artillery firing became louder as we got closer. At one point, we were barely 3km (almost 2 miles) from the front line.
We put on body armour and helmets, picked up our cameras and approached the government troops stationed on the front line.
We managed to film some footage and record brief accounts from soldiers. Then the assignment ended abruptly when the soldiers ordered us to evacuate immediately.
There was no time to argue or capture a final shot. We gathered our equipment and left with the shelling still echoing through the mountains behind us.
For days, we travelled difficult mountain routes through the regions of Afar, Amhara and Tigray. Roads we travelled on in the morning couldn’t be used by evening. Reports received before noon needed checking again before sunset.
In villages near the front lines, fear was visible in the faces we encountered as mothers packed small bags and children watched the road with anxious eyes.
I made a point of listening with sensitivity, respecting their suffering without exploiting their emotions for the camera.
Journey to Mekelle
As our coverage continued, the journey led us towards Mekelle, Tigray’s capital. We arrived the day after Ethiopian federal forces and their allies entered the city. The TPLF forces had retreated.
But Mekelle was a different city. I had expected it to be alive with unfolding events. It looked exhausted, with the usual police and security presence absent. It seemed to be trying to absorb what had happened in the hours before.
Daily life continued cautiously. Cars moved quietly through the streets, and shops had reopened in some neighbourhoods.
We saw soldiers welcomed in some streets while others remained silent, fearful of what might come next.
Many people declined to speak on camera because they didn’t know how events would unfold. There was no disorder in the conventional sense, but apprehension was everywhere. It was difficult to establish who was maintaining order or what the coming hours might bring.
We had no assurances about what might lie ahead. The possibility that our exit routes might close weighed on every decision.
Still, we had to keep working. Our audience was waiting for pictures and news. As far as we knew, we were the only media team in Mekelle.
I felt the weight of that responsibility. When you are alone in a place like this, every word matters. You must distinguish between what you have witnessed, what residents tell you and what the warring parties announce.
In a city that has only just emerged from battle, verifying information becomes harder than obtaining it.
We maintained as normal a routine as possible, filming in the morning, returning to prepare reports and following developments hour by hour.
Preserving impartiality
The challenges extended beyond security. We also faced the demanding ethical task of preserving impartiality and professional distance in a deeply polarised war.
People in the Tigray region have historic grievances against the federal government. After coming to power in 2018, President Abiy Ahmed reformed political institutions, lifted media censorship and freed thousands of political prisoners. But ethnic tensions have since erupted in this diverse nation of 139 million people.
Documenting residents welcoming incoming government-backed troops without presenting those scenes as universal or reporting fears about withdrawing TPLF fighters without drawing definitive conclusions could expose us to accusations of bias from any party that wanted us to see the battlefield exclusively through its own eyes.
That’s why I went beyond what the camera captured, talking to residents and listening to those who preferred to speak off camera. I understood that our task involved listening not only to what people said but also to what remained unspoken.
Their accounts helped us understand the situation. With each hour in the city, we tried to weigh the different narratives, recognising that our observations and residents’ accounts offered distinct perspectives.
The exhaustion of days on the road had accumulated, but my mind stayed on the day just ended and the one ahead. Which road would we take? Where would we go? Would the events of the coming hours allow us to complete our plans?
After two weeks of moving between front lines, fatigue had become a constant companion.
While we kept reporting, rumours that we were arrested or trapped inside the city kept our colleagues and family members anxious. They searched for the smallest piece of information confirming we were safe.
Only after I appeared live on TV did I understand that it carried another meaning. For many who had been trying to reach us, it was more than a live report. It was an unintended reassurance that we were still there – and still alive.
I later learned that some Mekelle residents had discovered that government forces had taken control of their city from our broadcast.
With communications disrupted and information scarce, television was bringing people news of events unfolding close to their homes.
After three days of reporting, we left Mekelle, carrying testimonies and documented facts.
On the return journey, looking through the car window at the roads we had travelled over the previous two weeks, I reflected that memories of war are not confined to battlefields.
What remained were the faces of the people I had met along the way, the anxiety in people’s eyes and the persistent sense that life seeks to continue, even in the places closest to war.

Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
13:21:05 UTC
22:21:05 KST

El Al announced plans to introduce new bedding, amenity kits, and menus from November as part of a phased upgrade to its passenger services, including partnerships with Israeli textile brand TAKEANAP and fragrance company Jo Malone London.
The airline said it would introduce the changes gradually, with availability depending on the destination. Separately, its previously announced Starlink internet service is scheduled to begin rolling out in 2027, with free access on equipped flights, subject to terms of use.
New bedding and amenity kits
Under the TAKEANAP partnership, El Al plans to replace its existing blankets and pillows in economy, premium, and business class with products developed for the airline. The range includes blankets tailored to each cabin and pillows designed to feel like down.
Business-class passengers will also receive memory-foam pillows with cooling technology, according to the airline. The airline plans a soft seat topper for North American flights, while pajamas and slippers are among the other sleep amenities listed in the announcement.
The Jo Malone London partnership covers amenity kits for premium cabins, with socks, eye masks, hygiene products, and a velvet pouch containing the brand’s skincare and fragrance products. On long-haul business-class flights, the kits will also include perfume and hand and body cream.
Revised menus under Assaf Granit
The food changes include a choice between a sandwich and a poke bowl for economy passengers on short-haul flights to Europe. In premium cabins, El Al plans to introduce new menus and serving ware under chef Assaf Granit.
The airline said it developed the menus with a dietitian and will display nutritional information alongside each dish. The offering includes protein-rich meals and a dessert cart.
Passengers on long-haul flights will also receive chocolates developed for El Al by Israeli chocolatier De Karina as part of the welcome service.
Personalized entertainment and app updates
El Al said its new entertainment system would recommend content based on passengers’ viewing preferences and allow them to resume a program where they stopped watching on a previous flight.
The seat-screen interface lets passengers log in to their frequent-flyer accounts, view personal information, and take travel-related actions. The changes also include a new children’s interface.
The airline’s app is adding a “travel mode,” available from 48 hours before departure, that brings together information for the upcoming flight. A Live Activities feature provides updates directly on the phone screen without requiring passengers to open the app.
El Al also introduced Ella, an artificial intelligence-based customer service assistant designed to answer initial inquiries, retrieve relevant booking information, and help customers complete tasks or reach the appropriate service representative.
“The expansion of the premium products we are launching today is intended to provide additional value to customers, strengthen their loyalty, and maintain the company’s standards over time,” said Nadav Hanin, El Al’s vice president of marketing and digital.

UK should seek to rejoin EU to protect prosperity, security: Think tank
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
13:20:04 UTC
22:20:04 KST

Aysu Bicer
19 October 2026•Update: 19 October 2026
The UK should make rejoining the EU a medium-term goal to protect its prosperity, national security and democratic institutions, a British think tank said Monday.
In a new report, the Institute for Public Policy Research (IPPR) argued that "Russia's aggression, uncertainty over US policy and China's growing use of economic pressure" have undermined Britain's post-Brexit strategy.
The think tank said the UK lacked the economic and strategic scale to address these challenges alone, calling for a broader reset of relations with the EU beyond individual trade and regulatory agreements.
"The world Britain built its post-Brexit strategy for no longer exists," IPPR Executive Director Harry Quilter-Pinner said in a statement.
"We are entering an age in which economic strength, security and political influence increasingly depend on scale, and Britain cannot manufacture that scale on its own," he added.
Polling commissioned by IPPR and Persuasion UK found that 52% of voters supported joining the EU, compared with 29% who preferred remaining outside.
Among respondents expressing a preference, 64% supported membership, while 36% opposed it.
A separate experiment presenting voters with different combinations of potential benefits, costs and arguments found average support for EU membership at 52%.
The research also found that maintaining the UK's current relationship with the EU was the least popular option presented to respondents.
 
- 'We can't take back control while being an outsider in Europe'
The report argued that the EU had evolved since Britain's departure, taking on a greater security, industrial and economic role through increased defense spending, industrial policies and efforts to protect strategic supply chains.
IPPR urged the government to develop a new European strategy, including cooperation on industrial policy and public procurement, alongside the creation of a European Defense Alliance.
Under the proposed alliance, Britain could contribute capabilities in areas where Europe remains heavily dependent on the US, including satellite communications, the report said.
The think tank also recommended building stronger public support before seeking a mandate for EU membership through either a new referendum or a clear election manifesto commitment.
"It's time to stop talking about Brexit and focus entirely on the future," IPPR Associate Director Laura Chappell said.
"Whether it's protecting households from swings in the cost of living, restarting industry, or keeping us secure, we lack the weight to act alone," she said.
"In today's world, we can't take back control while being an outsider in Europe."
Meanwhile, UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said in September he will “lay out to the country” different options for the UK’s long-term relationship with the EU, arguing that Brexit “has done more harm than good.”
Last week, Burnham also accused Russia of interfering in the 2016 Brexit referendum and warned that Russian “disinformation” was affecting political debates in France and Germany.
The UK left the EU in 2020, four years after a referendum in which about 52% of voters chose to leave.

Poland denies report that Sunday’s drone was launched from Lithuanian territory
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
13:20:00 UTC
22:20:00 KST

Poland’s Defence Ministry has denied a media report claiming that a drone that exploded in Lithuania on Sunday was launched from Lithuanian territory, urging the public not to spread what it called unfounded speculation.
“We categorically deny information published in the media claiming that, according to sources in the Polish Ministry of National Defence, the drone found in Lithuanian territory was launched from Lithuania,” the ministry said in a statement provided to LRT.
“We strongly urge people not to spread these unfounded speculations,” it added.
The claim was published by Polsatnews.pl, citing an anonymous source in the Polish Defence Ministry. It said the drone had taken off from Lithuanian territory about 30 kilometres from the Polish border and flown deeper into Lithuania without entering Polish airspace.
The report prompted debate in Lithuania, where initial assessments indicated that the drone had entered the country from Ukraine via Poland.
Poland’s Defence Ministry said it was analysing radar data from systems operating in the relevant part of Poland and neighbouring countries in cooperation with Lithuanian authorities. The ministry said it was awaiting the results of the requested analyses after the Polish defence minister ordered a review of the incident.
The ministry also said the drone that entered Lithuanian airspace early Sunday had been identified as Ukrainian and that Ukraine had officially apologised to Lithuania for the incident.
Lithuanian officials have likewise rejected the report that the drone was launched from Lithuania.
Deividas Matulionis, national security adviser to President Gitanas Nausėda, said Monday that Lithuania had credible evidence the drone crossed the border from Poland.
“Very unequivocally, I can say that we have credible evidence that the drone crossed the Polish border,” Matulionis told BNS.
Defence Minister Robertas Kaunas described the Polish media report as a misunderstanding, saying Lithuania had neither allowed nor would allow another country to use its territory or airspace to attack a third country.
“The sources are unofficial, so we consider this a kind of misunderstanding,” Kaunas said.

Trump endorses Netanyahu for reelection as Israeli PM
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
13:19:20 UTC
22:19:20 KST

President Donald Trump poses for a photo with Israel's Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu before he boards Air Force One at Ben Gurion International Airport, Oct. 13, 2025, near Tel Aviv, as Israel's President Isaac Herzog watches at left. (AP File Photo)
President Donald Trump on Oct. 18 endorsed embattled Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu late in his reelection campaign, a coveted boost because of Trump’s popularity but one that the American had withheld for months as the vote neared and the leaders’ strategies in the Middle East diverged.
Trump said in a post on social media that Netanyahu “has been a Great Warrior Prime Minister, and an even greater Partner for Peace in combatting the Islamic Republic of Iran.”
Israelis are set to vote Oct. 27, in the first national elections since Hamas attacked Israel on Oct. 7, 2023.
The absence of an endorsement was a setback for the Likud politician, who had billed his tight ties to the Republican president as a selling point for staying in power.
“Thank you, President Trump, for the tremendous support and work together,” Netanyahu said in a statement in Hebrew posted on X. “Together we will complete the mission!”
His Likud Party attached to the statement a 35-second video showing clips of the two leaders together and Trump praising Netanyahu.
It was not immediately clear what impact the endorsement would have on what is expected to be a tight race. Trump is still popular in Israel, but many Israelis, including leading commentators, have expressed disappointment over the inconclusive outcome of the Iran war and Trump’s ceasefire proposal, which fell short of many of the countries’ key goals when they jointly launched the war in February.
In his post, Trump again threatened to “soon finish the job” against Iran “unless they change their ways, rapidly,” but added he might not want to if Netanyahu loses the election. “If Israel has the wrong Leader, which would be anyone other than Bibi, America will have to do this work ourselves, and I am not inclined to do so,” Trump said.
He said Netanyahu had been “Strong, Brave, and Brilliant in the face of tremendous opposition, including that coming from even Israel, itself.”
Trump endorsed Netanyahu in past elections and in November he sent a letter to Israeli President Isaac Herzog asking him to pardon Netanyahu on corruption charges.
But Trump’s comments about Netanyahu in recent months had been much more subdued, and he repeatedly demurred when asking if he would back the prime minister. The president, when asked in a Time magazine interview published this month about backing the Israeli leader, said, ”I’m not involved in politics anymore,” despite his campaigning for and endorsing U.S. politicians.

====================================================================================================

The very stable genius, nine years later
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
13:19:12 UTC
22:19:12 KST

In January 2018, after a book questioned his mental fitness, the president of the United States sat down and wrote his own diagnosis.
“My two greatest assets have been mental stability and being, like, really smart,” he tweeted. “I think that would qualify as not smart, but genius. And a very stable genius at that!”
He was 71 years old.
Nearly nine years and one reelection later, the self-assessment has not moved an inch. The facts around it have.
Start with the war he promised would never happen.
Trump campaigned twice on ending American wars, not starting them. In January, the US military struck targets across Venezuela and extracted President Nicolás Maduro, who now sits in a New York jail awaiting trial on narco-terrorism charges.
The operation followed months of strikes on small boats in the Caribbean. Well over 100 people were killed on suspicion, never proof, of drug trafficking.
Months later came Iran, a war the administration still calls “Operation Epic Fury.”
Trump recently told a rally crowd that the United States had lost “18 incredible people” in that war. Reporting by The Washington Post placed the true figure at 22 or higher.
Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth called the Post’s reporting “a complete LIE.”
The two numbers have never been reconciled.
Then there is the money.
Qatar gave Trump’s government a $400 million Boeing 747 to use as Air Force One. The aircraft was painted navy and gold to suit his taste. Trump has said it will eventually go to his presidential library when he leaves office.
READ: Lavrov says Trump’s Gaza plan remains ‘ink on paper,’ calls for Palestinian statehood
At home, he gutted the East Wing of the White House to make room for a gold-leafed ballroom costing $300 million. He covered the Oval Office in gilt cherubs and molding, creating what his own press secretary called “a golden office for the golden age.”
Critics have used different words: tacky, gaudy, a monument to ego.
On the campaign trail this fall, Trump has promised every American adult a $5,000 “dividend” if Republicans retain control of Congress in November.
It echoes two earlier promises. One offered Americans $2,000 from tariff revenue. The other promised an unspecified share of “DOGE savings.” Both were announced with fanfare. Neither was paid.
Polling suggests that most Americans do not believe this dividend will be paid either. In one recent survey, only 17 percent of adults said Trump generally keeps his promises.
His relationship with the truth is not incidental to his politics. It is the engine of it.
For decades, Trump has told audiences that he graduated first in his class at the Wharton School. The university’s own records from 1968 show that he made neither the Dean’s List nor any honors roll.
He has also said repeatedly, including as recently as this March during a meeting with Germany’s chancellor, that his father was born in “a very wonderful place in Germany.”
Fred Trump was born in the Bronx. It was Trump’s grandfather who emigrated from Germany.
These are not policy disagreements or competing interpretations of history. They are verifiable facts about his own life. He has overwritten them in public, repeatedly, at no apparent cost.
The self-praise runs in a straight line from that 2018 tweet to the present.
Trump has told voters for years, in one formulation after another, that he knows more than America’s generals, more than its diplomats, more than its intelligence agencies.
In 2018, standing beside Vladimir Putin in Helsinki, Trump was asked whether he believed the conclusion of his own intelligence community that Russia had interfered in the 2016 election, or Putin’s denial.
“I don’t see any reason why it would be,” Russia, he replied.
He spent the following week trying, unconvincingly, to recast the remark as a simple misstatement.
The pattern recurs across his biography and in matters of war and peace: a confident assertion, a contradiction from the record, and no meaningful reckoning with the distance between them.
Three wars into a presidency that promised none, Trump’s instinct to trust his own judgment over everyone else’s has survived every piece of evidence that might have revised it.
That pattern is what a group of mental health professionals has spent nine years trying to name.
In 2017, Yale psychiatrist Bandy Lee assembled 27 colleagues for “The Dangerous Case of Donald Trump.” They argued that they had a “duty to warn” the public, despite professional norms against diagnosing public figures from a distance.
OPINION: Trump could lose Congress and still expand the US war on Iran
Psychologist John Gartner, one of the contributors, has been more direct. For years, he has described Trump as a “malignant narcissist,” a term coined by psychoanalyst Erich Fromm to describe leaders who are grandiose, paranoid, and remorseless.
In 2024, more than 230 mental health professionals signed a public letter repeating the warning ahead of the election.
None of this constitutes a formal diagnosis. The signatories are explicit that it cannot. Trump has never submitted to an evaluation.
Yet the consistency of the assessment, sustained across nine years and echoed by dozens of credentialed observers, is itself a kind of data point.
So is the legal record.
Trump was indicted four times in 2023 on a combined 88 felony counts. He became the first former American president ever charged with a crime.
In New York, he was convicted on all 34 counts in the hush-money case.
He did not go to prison.
Having won reelection in the meantime, Trump received an unconditional discharge: no fine, no probation, no punishment beyond the conviction itself. The judge said it was the only sentence available for a sitting president.
The two federal cases were dropped after Trump’s victory. The Georgia case was dismissed last November.
He did not defeat the charges.
He outlasted the clock.
None of it cost him the presidency.
Trump won the Electoral College in 2024 by 312 votes to 226. He also won the popular vote by 1.5 points. It was a real victory, if a modest one by historical standards, and the second-narrowest popular-vote margin since 1960.
Enough Americans, in other words, looked at all of it: the boasting, the contradicted facts, the criminal indictments, the wars he promised never to fight. Then they voted for him anyway.
That may be the harder question, more troubling than any diagnosis.
Presidential falsehoods are not new in American life. What is new is a public that increasingly treats them as beside the point.
There was once an expectation that a president’s word could be taken to the bank.
Whether that was ever entirely true, the pretense itself is now gone.

Putin, Trump and Xi Could Hold Trilateral Meeting on Ukraine War Next Month, Kremlin Says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19

22:19:11 KST

The Kremlin said Monday that President Vladimir Putin, U.S. President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping could hold a trilateral meeting focused on ending the war in Ukraine when they gather in China next month for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit.
"Given that all three heads of state may potentially take part in the summit in China, the subject of such a hypothetical meeting was indeed raised," spokesman Dmitry Peskov said in response to a Wall Street Journal report about ongoing talks to end the war.
"It was raised, but no specific proposals or agreements were discussed or put forward by anyone, either regarding the meeting itself or the possible agenda and substance of that meeting," Peskov added.
Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha criticised the idea of holding a meeting in China without Ukraine's input.
"A trilateral meeting between the leaders of Ukraine, the U.S. and Russia could help end the war sooner. A trilateral meeting between the leaders of Russia, China and the U.S. would do only the opposite: encourage Putin to continue this war," Sybiha wrote in a post on X.
Peskov, who told reporters Monday that the U.S. was continuing its efforts to broker an end to the Ukraine war, said it was obvious that Ukraine would ultimately need to be involved in a final peace deal.
"Of course, a final settlement is impossible without the participation of someone in Kyiv who is prepared to take responsibility," he said.
The last U.S.-mediated peace talks between Russia and Ukraine took place in February, just before the United States and Israel launched a war against Iran. Ukraine and Russia remain as far apart as ever when it comes to the terms of any possible peace deal.

The ghost in Taiwan’s classroom
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
13:17:39 UTC
22:17:39 KST

The history of authoritarian rule in Taiwan usually begins with secret police, arbitrary arrests and political executions. But during the White Terror period of 1949–87, one of the KMT’s most durable instruments of control required neither firearms nor detention camps. It required a classroom chalkboard.
By enforcing Mandarin as the sole public language, the KMT used education to weaken the linguistic identities of Taiwanese, Hakka, and Indigenous peoples. That history is not merely memorial.
Beijing’s recent language and “ethnic unity” laws pursue a similar goal through more modern means: national legislation, compulsory schooling and digital platforms.
The parallel is striking. Imperial Japan (1895-1945), the KMT and today’s Chinese Communist Party all treated or treat linguistic pluralism as an existential threat. Each sought or seeks to replace the languages people actually speak with a single authorized national language.
When Japan took Taiwan in 1895, few residents spoke Mandarin. Most of the nation’s roughly 3 million people were Taiwanese or Hakka. Dozens of Indigenous communities spoke Austronesian languages entirely unrelated to Chinese.
In the late 1930s, Japan’s imperialization campaign sought to make Taiwanese subjects loyal to the emperor. It restricted Chinese-language newspapers and classical Chinese education, promoted Japanese as the national language, and punished schoolchildren who spoke local languages.
Some were publicly humiliated or forced to wear demeaning signs. By 1945, sustained pressure had produced a major linguistic shift: more than 70% of Taiwan’s population understood or spoke Japanese.
Reversing the damage
The KMT inherited the method but changed the target. After 1945, it replaced Japanese with Mandarin and used four decades of martial law to make Mandarin the language of schools, government, broadcasting and public life. Taiwanese, Hakka and Indigenous languages were pushed out of classrooms and treated as obstacles to national unity.
Taiwan’s democracy has since worked to reverse the damage. The National Languages Development Act of 2018 recognized Taiwanese Hokkien, Hakka, Indigenous languages and Taiwan Sign Language as national languages.
Yet the losses remain visible. Recent surveys cited in the original draft find that only 22.8% of self-identified Hakka people aged 19 to 29 speak Hakka fluently, while fewer than 40% of Taiwanese born in the 1990s speak Hokkien fluently. Many Indigenous languages are critically endangered.
China now applies a comparable model to a far larger population. According to census data, China has 125.4 million non-Han citizens across 55 recognized ethnic minority groups. Many live in Tibet, Xinjiang and Inner Mongolia, where language remains central to cultural and historical identity.
The revised Law on the Standard Spoken and Written Chinese Language, effective Jan. 1, makes standard Mandarin the basic language of schooling and extends Mandarin requirements to online publications, streaming services, audiovisual programs and public internet platforms.
The law also removes the former statutory exception that had allowed minority languages to serve as the medium of instruction, while requiring state-compiled textbooks. It adds a dedicated legal-liability chapter and penalties for violations.
Law of languages
The Ethnic Unity and Progress Promotion Law, effective July 1, goes further. It requires schools and government bodies to use Mandarin as their primary language, promotes Mandarin from preschool, and calls on parents to guide children toward loyalty to the party-state. It also requires Chinese characters to take visual precedence over minority scripts in public settings.
Beijing says the law protects minority languages. Article 15 does state that the country “respects and safeguards” their learning and use.
But in practice, the law subordinates them to Mandarin in classrooms, public administration and the digital public sphere. Human rights monitors, including Amnesty International, have warned that the framework amounts to forced assimilation.
If Beijing absorbed Taiwan, the consequences would be immediate. Taiwan’s multilingual legal framework would be recast as a threat to national unity.
Traditional Chinese characters could be displaced by simplified Chinese in official documents, textbooks, signage and government websites. Taiwanese vocabulary, local phrasing and idioms developed through decades of separate political development could be scrubbed from public use.
Protecting minority tongues
The pressure would also arrive before annexation. Simplified characters and mainland phrasing already enter Taiwan through cross-border e-commerce and digital platforms.
Writing in the Liberty Times, legal scholar Harper Chen emphasized how the unmitigated flood of cross-border e-commerce has led to the subtle infiltration of simplified Chinese text and non-Taiwanese phrasing across local transaction platforms. Within the framework of Han supremacism, such everyday digital anomalies serve as subtle, preliminary precursors to formal linguistic hegemony.
Under a Chinese-style system, algorithmic screening could flag Taiwanese idioms, traditional script and minority-language content as separatist or subversive. Educators, publishers and grassroots advocates could face automated detection, censorship and criminal liability.
Unlike the monitors and schoolyard badges used by Japanese and KMT authorities, Beijing would enforce linguistic conformity through a digital panopticon. Taiwan’s independent streaming services, communication apps and social networks could be drawn into China’s censorship system, where keyword filters and algorithmic suppression would operate at scale.
The crucial distinction lies in intent. Democratic states may promote a shared national language while legally protecting minority tongues. Imperial Japan, the KMT and today’s Chinese Communist Party treated or treat linguistic pluralism as a danger to be removed.
A common language can build civic cohesion. A state monopoly on language does something else: it turns a child’s mother tongue into evidence of disloyalty. Taiwan’s past shows where that road leads. China’s new laws show that the road has not been abandoned.

Russia Draws on Ukraine War Experience in Sweeping Military Drills With India
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
13:17:27 UTC
22:17:27 KST

- Category
- World
Russia Draws on Ukraine War Experience in Sweeping Military Drills With India
India and Russia have launched the Indra 2026 bilateral military exercise, expanding coordination between their armed forces across multiple domains while incorporating lessons Russia says it has drawn from its war against Ukraine, according to Zona Militar on October 18.
The ground phase is taking place in Russia’s Chelyabinsk region, south of the Ural Mountains, while the naval portion is centered on Vladivostok and the Sea of Japan.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Moscow says the exercise is intended to improve interoperability between Russian and Indian forces and test how effectively commanders and units can operate together.
The land drills will continue through October 23, with Russia’s 90th Guards Tank Division from the Central Military District providing the core of the participating force.
Russia has not disclosed the total number of personnel involved. Training will include operations against what Moscow describes as “illegal armed groups,” along with joint tactical exercises designed to evaluate coordination between the two militaries.
The naval phase is scheduled for October 16-17 in the Sea of Japan and will include live-fire exercises against maritime targets, joint maneuvering, communications drills, and training for boarding and retaking a vessel seized by a simulated terrorist group.
One of the most notable elements will be training against unmanned threats. Russian and Indian sailors are expected to practice defending against both unmanned surface vessels and UAVs, with Moscow explicitly linking the training to lessons learned from Russia’s war against Ukraine, where drones have transformed operations at sea and on land.
The Russian corvette Aldar Tsydenzhapov and Indian frigate INS Sahyadri are expected to play central roles in the naval drills.
Indra has long served as one of the main formats for military cooperation between Moscow and New Delhi. This year’s exercise comes as Russia continues adapting its training programs around technologies and tactics that have become increasingly important during its war against Ukraine, particularly drones, electronic warfare, and defenses against unmanned systems.
The air component will involve Su-30SM fighters from both the Russian Aerospace Forces and the Indian Air Force, although neither side has disclosed how many aircraft will participate. The fighters are expected to train against small drones flying at low altitude, another mission area heavily shaped by lessons from the war in Ukraine.
The exercise will also include “maneuvering air combat at medium and low altitudes,” while Mi-8 helicopters will practice emergency search-and-rescue missions in remote areas.
Earlier, reports emerged that Russia has spent nearly four years urging India to increase exports of food, medicine, machinery, and other goods, but the effort has produced little change, leaving the two countries’ nearly $60 billion trade relationship overwhelmingly tilted toward Russian oil sales.

Human Rights Education Resources for Write for Rights 2026
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
13:17:26 UTC
22:17:26 KST

Every year around 10 December – Human Rights Day – Amnesty International’s Write for Rights campaign brings millions of people together to stand in solidarity with individuals and communities facing human rights violations.
Around the world, people write letters, sign petitions, create artwork, learn together, and take action to demand justice. Year after year, these collective actions have helped change lives, showing that borders are no barrier to solidarity and that words have the power to inspire hope and drive change.
Human rights education is a central part of that movement. Alongside taking action, people come together to understand the issues behind each Individual at Risk case, reflect on why human rights matter and explore how solidarity can help protect them.
About the human rights education resources
The Write for Rights 2026 Human Rights Education resources help teachers, educators and facilitators engage learners in meaningful learning about human rights and support them to take informed action.
The resources can be used in classrooms, community groups, youth groups, activist spaces, and other learning settings. They are designed to be flexible, allowing educators to adapt them to different audiences, lesson lengths, and teaching contexts.
Each resource follows a three-part modular structure, making it possible to deliver a complete 60-minute learning journey, use individual 20-minute modules as standalone activities, or combine modules to suit the time available. This flexibility makes it easier to adapt the resources to different settings while keeping learning and action connected.
As a facilitator, you are encouraged to adapt each activity to your group’s prior knowledge, age range, learning needs, available time and whether you are working in person or online.
What’s included this year?
This year’s Human Rights Education resources explore three interconnected human rights themes through real Write for Rights Individuals at Risk’s cases from around the world.
1. Freedom of Expression and Suppression of Dissent
Discover the stories of Rokiatou Doumbia (Mali), Ruth Eleonora López (El Salvador), Imaan Mazari and Hadi Ali Chattha (Pakistan), and Ayachi Hammami (Tunisia) to examine why speaking out, defending rights, and challenging injustice matter.
This theme explores how individuals are punished for speaking out, criticizing those in power, exposing information, or publicly defending human rights online or offline.
2. Freedom of Peaceful Assembly, Association and Participation in Public Affairs
Learn from the experiences of Owen Chow (Hong Kong), Daria Egereva (Russia), and Marwa Arafa (Egypt) to explore why people come together to organise, defend communities, celebrate identity, and participate in public life.
This theme explores restrictions on people’s ability to organise collectively, express their identity, defend their communities, and participate in civic and social movements.
3. Protection from Arbitrary Detention and Enforced Disappearance
Explore the story of Humphrey Polepole (Tanzania) to understand why legal safeguards, fair treatment, and justice matter when people’s liberty is at risk. This theme explores what happens when legal systems fail to protect individuals. It focuses on rights that safeguard people from arbitrary detention, torture, enforced disappearance, and other serious abuses committed by state authorities.
Learning through participation
This approach helps learners to:
- develop critical thinking, communication, and collaboration skills.
- deepen their understanding of human rights through discussion and reflection.
- connect with real stories while respecting different experiences and perspectives.
- build empathy and recognise our shared humanity; and
- take informed, meaningful action in solidarity with people whose rights are under threat.
By bringing together learning, reflection and action, the Write for Rights Human Rights Education resources help learners understand not only what human rights are, but also why protecting them matters for everyone.

Russia Hails Its T-80BVM Tank as a Stealthy “Assassin” Despite Hundreds of Battlefield Losses
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
13:16:59 UTC
22:16:59 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Russia Hails Its T-80BVM Tank as a Stealthy “Assassin” Despite Hundreds of Battlefield Losses
Russia’s state-owned defense conglomerate Rostec has described its upgraded T-80BVM main battle tank as a stealthy battlefield “assassin” capable of approaching enemy positions undetected, despite documented losses of hundreds of these vehicles during Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to Defence Blog on October 19, Rostec presented the Soviet-designed tank’s modernization as a combination of speed, firepower, camouflage, and mobility, claiming it can perform several battlefield roles ranging from breaking through defensive lines to striking targets from long distances.
“It’s also an assassin which, thanks to a quiet and powerful gas turbine engine and camouflage, can make fast and unnoticed flanking maneuvers,” Rostec said, according to a translation published by Defence Blog.
The Russian defense company also described the T-80BVM as a “steel battering ram” capable of penetrating enemy defenses while operating under the threat of FPV drones.
In another proposed role, Rostec characterized the vehicle as a long-range “sniper,” claiming it can use reconnaissance drones to identify and engage targets approximately 10 kilometers away with only a few shots.
Rostec further promoted the tank’s mobility by calling it a “flying” tank, referring to demonstrations in which T-80 vehicles have launched off ramps during Russian military exhibitions.
The T-80BVM is a modernized version of the Soviet-era T-80BV, equipped with a 1,250-horsepower GTD-1250 gas turbine engine and a 125 mm 2A46M-1 smoothbore cannon.
Its upgrades include an improved fire-control system, additional armor protection, and the ability to launch guided missiles through its main gun.
However, the gas turbine engine that Rostec presents as an advantage also has significant drawbacks. While it provides strong acceleration and reliable operation in extremely cold conditions, it consumes considerably more fuel than the diesel engines powering Russia’s T-72 and T-90 tanks.
The tank’s claimed ability to operate undetected also contrasts with its documented battlefield losses in Ukraine.
According to open-source intelligence monitoring group Oryx, at least 1,311 Russian T-80-series tanks have been visually confirmed as destroyed, damaged, abandoned, or captured since the beginning of the full-scale invasion.
Among them are 264 T-80BVM tanks, including 150 standard variants and 114 vehicles of the 2022 modernization. The figures represent only losses supported by photographic or video evidence, meaning the actual number could be higher.
Despite these losses, Russian manufacturer Uralvagonzavod, part of Rostec, continues upgrading older T-80BV tanks from storage to the T-80BVM configuration and supplying them to Russian forces.
Earlier, Russian forces were spotted deploying T-80BVM tanks fitted with extensive steel-cable armor designed to protect against Ukrainian FPV drones.
The modifications, nicknamed “steel hedgehogs,” aim to entangle incoming drones and prevent their explosive payloads from detonating, although the additional weight and bulk could reduce the tanks’ maneuverability.

Lavrov visits Iran as Russia explores role in US-Tehran talks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
13:16:55 UTC
22:16:55 KST

Breadcrumb
Lavrov urges return to pre-war conditions in Hormuz during Iran visit
Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov has called for conditions in the Strait of Hormuz and the wider region to return to what they were before the US-Israeli war on Iran, following talks with his Iranian counterpart Abbas Araghchi in Tehran on Monday.
Speaking at a joint press conference, Lavrov reaffirmed Moscow's strategic partnership with Tehran and said Russia remained committed to its comprehensive cooperation agreement with Iran.
He described the talks as "productive" and said the two countries shared similar positions on regional developments, while pledging to continue cooperation through international organisations including BRICS, the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation and the Eurasian Economic Union.
Lavrov also announced that Russian personnel would gradually return to Iran's Bushehr nuclear power plant.
The developments come as diplomatic efforts to avert another confrontation intensify, with The New Arab reporting on Monday that a breakthrough in US-Iran mediation efforts could be announced this week.
Senior sources familiar with negotiations told TNA that Qatar and Pakistan were working to narrow differences between Washington and Tehran and secure mutual concessions, while ruling out an immediate military escalation.
Lavrov's visit, his first to Iran since the US-Israeli war began on 28 February, follows Moscow's recent involvement in exchanging messages between the two countries.
It also comes ahead of a possible visit to Tehran by Pakistan's army chief, General Asim Munir, who has been involved in mediation efforts between Washington and Tehran.
Iran and Russia blame US-Israeli attacks for regional instability
Araghchi described Iran's relationship with Russia as "strategic", saying it had taken on new dimensions since the implementation of their comprehensive cooperation agreement nearly two years ago.
He said Monday's discussions had been "extremely productive", covering regional and international developments alongside practical plans to expand political, cultural and commercial cooperation.
The Iranian foreign minister said economic ties between the two countries were developing significantly and that no major obstacles stood in the way of expanding bilateral trade.
On regional security, Araghchi blamed US and Israeli military attacks for instability in the Gulf and the Strait of Hormuz, as well as recent security incidents in the Caspian Sea involving attacks on Iranian and Russian vessels and port infrastructure.
He warned that the situation posed serious consequences for regional peace, security and the environment.
Araghchi also called for an immediate end to the genocide in Palestine, Israeli expansion in Lebanon and the war in Yemen.
The two ministers discussed tensions between Afghanistan and Pakistan, including the need to reduce tensions between Kabul and Islamabad and address threats from armed groups operating in Afghanistan.
Araghchi stressed that regional disputes could not be resolved through military means and required diplomacy and political solutions.
Lavrov, meanwhile, said opposition to US unilateralism remained a shared priority for Moscow and Tehran, with both countries seeking to strengthen multilateral institutions and uphold international law.
He also reaffirmed Russia's commitment to its comprehensive cooperation agreement with Iran.
Can Russia mediate between Iran and the US?
Despite the emphasis on regional diplomacy, neither minister publicly announced a new Russian mediation initiative between Washington and Tehran following Monday's talks.
Russia's potential mediation role began taking shape earlier this month, amid growing contacts between Moscow and Washington over the war in Ukraine.
On 10 October, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov revealed that Russian President Vladimir Putin had informed his Iranian counterpart Masoud Pezeshkian of an upcoming telephone conversation with US President Donald Trump.
The exchange followed a meeting between Putin and Pezeshkian in Turkmenistan on 9 October.
The Kremlin subsequently announced that Putin had conveyed Iran's position on a possible settlement to Trump, raising expectations that Moscow could become another diplomatic channel between Washington and Tehran.
However, Iranian officials have stopped short of recognising Russia as a formal mediator.
Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmail Baghaei said last week that, "technically, in the strict sense of the word", Pakistan and Qatar remained the actual mediators between Iran and the United States.
He added that consultations between Tehran and Moscow, particularly on the nuclear issue, were nothing new.
Ahead of his arrival in Tehran, Lavrov criticised Trump's approach towards Iran as "wrong", arguing that it would not help achieve an agreement based on mutual respect and international law.
His visit followed a stop in Bahrain, prompting speculation that he could also be carrying messages from Gulf states amid heightened regional tensions.
Experts question prospects of Russian mediation
Iranian analyst Hadi Mohammadi told The New Arab that Lavrov's visit reflected growing Russian concerns about developments in the Gulf and the possibility of further escalation.
He said Moscow appeared to be intensifying its diplomatic activities in an attempt to contain tensions, noting that the US-Iran confrontation had become closely linked to the war in Ukraine amid renewed contacts between Washington and Moscow.
Mohammadi suggested that Lavrov could be carrying messages from Washington or Israel during what he described as an extremely sensitive period.
He recalled that Putin had previously conveyed messages between Tehran and Israel, including an Israeli assurance before the latest war that it did not intend to attack Iran.
However, Mohammadi expressed limited confidence in Russia's ability to secure a breakthrough.
He argued that some international actors were making a fundamental mistake by pressuring Iran alone to accept the other side's conditions, while overlooking Tehran's position that it had been attacked and had complied with the Islamabad memorandum of understanding reached in June, which Iran accuses Washington of violating.
Mohammadi said Lavrov's visit could help reduce regional tensions but was unlikely to resolve the crisis on its own.
At best, he suggested, it could mark the beginning of further diplomatic exchanges, although he did not rule out the possibility that it represented a final attempt to avert another war.
Iranian analyst Abbas Aslani similarly told The New Arab that Lavrov's visit reflected the depth of cooperation between Tehran and Moscow in confronting Western pressure.
He said shared economic, political and military challenges had strengthened the importance of bilateral and regional coordination.
Aslani considered it possible that Lavrov was carrying a response or message from Washington, although he cautioned against drawing conclusions before the talks took place.
He also suggested that Moscow could use the visit to assess the Trump administration's position ahead of the US midterm elections on 3 November.
According to Aslani, Russia was already familiar with Iran's strategic red lines, including the conditions outlined in Tehran's seven-day proposal, and was unlikely to persuade Iranian officials to make substantial changes.
He described the visit as a potential opportunity to exchange "hard truths", but argued that any genuine breakthrough would depend on Washington accepting what he described as the new balance of power and security in the Gulf.

Signal Festival program manager Daniel Burda praised Taiwan’s vibrant new media art scene, per CNA. Russian Forces and Mali’s Military Accused of Indiscriminate Drone Strikes That Killed Scores of Civilians
Unknown

Russian Forces and Mali’s Military Accused of Indiscriminate Drone Strikes That Killed Scores of Civilians
Dozens of civilians have reportedly been killed in Mali by drone strikes conducted by the country’s armed forces and Russian Africa Corps personnel supporting the military junta’s operations against insurgent groups.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to Reuters on October 19, citing a Human Rights Watch report, some of the drone attacks carried out by Malian and Russian forces were apparently indiscriminate. The number of strikes and resulting civilian casualties increased sharply between April and August compared with the same period in 2025.
The military campaign is aimed at countering attacks by Jama’at Nusrat al-Islam wal-Muslimin, an al-Qaeda-affiliated militant group, and Tuareg-led separatists. Mali’s military leadership, which came to power through coups in 2020 and 2021, has sought Russian support in its efforts to combat the insurgency.
According to conflict monitoring data, Malian troops and Russia’s Africa Corps conducted 47 drone strikes between April and August, resulting in 94 civilian deaths.
Among the reported incidents was an August 19 drone strike on a livestock market in the Bandiagara region that killed six men. Another attack on July 29 targeted a medical facility in the northern Kidal region.
The reported civilian casualties come amid growing scrutiny of Russia’s military activities in Africa, including the transportation of equipment and personnel to support its operations on the continent.
A separate joint investigation published on October 19 by the Dossier Center, Follow the Money, Süddeutsche Zeitung, Danwatch, and Delfi revealed that Russia has reportedly been using civilian cargo ships to transport military equipment and suspected covert intelligence operatives to Africa.
Investigators identified 28 individuals believed to have traveled under fabricated identities aboard seven Russian cargo vessels carrying military supplies primarily intended for Africa Corps, a Russian Defense Ministry-controlled formation that replaced the Wagner mercenary group.

Russia Rebuilds Military Stockpiles Near NATO Borders
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
13:16:31 UTC
22:16:31 KST

Russia has begun replenishing military equipment at several storage bases, including facilities near NATO members Estonia, Latvia and Finland, according to satellite imagery analyzed by OSINT researchers as reported by the independent Russian outlet iStories on Saturday, Oct. 17.
At the 22nd Central Reserve Base in Bui, Kostroma region, satellite images show new T-90M tanks, BTR-82A armored personnel carriers and BMP-3 infantry fighting vehicles arriving between fall 2025 and October 2026. The base is about 500 kilometers (310 miles) from the borders of Estonia and Latvia, according to Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty journalist Mark Krutov, who compared imagery of the site from October 2025 and October 2026.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Researchers emphasize that the equipment is being sent to storage facilities. It has not been transferred to active military units and is not ready for immediate deployment, iStories reported.
Equipment appears at multiple storage ifaciĺities
The buildup is also visible at bases farther from Russia’s western borders.
At the 349th Central Tank Storage Base in Topchikha, Altai Krai, analysts identified about 78 refurbished T-72B3 tanks and more than 100 BMP-2 infantry fighting vehicles arriving from around June 2026.
The 6018th base has also received BMP-3 and BMD-4 vehicles, iStories reported.
In Karelia, the 374th Mobilization Deployment Support Center – about 185 kilometers (115 miles) from Finland – has been receiving Malva artillery systems and Giatsint-K self-propelled guns since 2025.
Italy Reduces Visa Processing for Russians to 45 Days
The observations were made by OSINT analysts Mark Krutov, Jompy and Covert Cabal using satellite imagery. Krutov’s satellite-image comparison shows new T-90M tanks at the Bui base.
Russia adapts its use of armored vehicles
Russian forces used a large share of their stored armored vehicles during the full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
But as drones made tanks and armored vehicles increasingly vulnerable on the battlefield, Russian forces relied more on infantry assaults and small mobile groups, Krutov wrote.
Russian factories have continued producing new equipment and repairing damaged vehicles.
Some of the equipment seen in satellite images is newly manufactured, while other vehicles have been refurbished, according to the researchers.
The renewed accumulation does not by itself show that Russia is preparing to attack a NATO country.
Krutov said the vehicles could theoretically be useful in a future confrontation with NATO, whose militaries have less experience using drones at the scale seen in Ukraine.
He also noted that Russian officials deny plans to attack NATO member states.
In June, journalists from Denmark’s DR, Norway’s NRK, Sweden’s SVT and Estonia’s Delfi reported that Russia was building and modernizing military facilities near northern NATO countries.
The latest satellite imagery adds evidence that some Russian storage bases are receiving equipment, while leaving open how and when it might be used.

19 October 2026•Update: 19 October 2026
Türkiye will host the ninth Istanbul Mediation Conference on Oct. 23-24 under the theme “Partnerships and New Perspectives for Peace: Mediation in a Changing World,” the Turkish Foreign Ministry said Monday.
The conference will be held under the auspices of Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan amid rapid and profound changes in global dynamics, the ministry said in a statement.
Türkiye, which has played an active role in promoting the peaceful resolution of conflicts, launched the “Mediation for Peace” initiative at the UN in 2010.
It is also the only country to simultaneously co-chair the Groups of Friends of Mediation at the UN, the Organization for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) and the Organization of Islamic Cooperation (OIC).
Türkiye has hosted the Istanbul Mediation Conferences since 2012, establishing the event as a leading international platform for conflict resolution, preventive diplomacy and mediation.
The ninth edition is expected to bring together relevant stakeholders to promote dialogue, address current challenges in mediation and develop forward-looking perspectives and innovative approaches, the statement said.
The conference will open with two panels titled “Mediation in a Changing World: Reclaiming the Space for Diplomacy” and “Partnerships and New Perspectives for Peace: Shaping the Future of Mediation.”
The sessions will explore how the international community can create greater space for diplomacy and how mediation can play a more effective role in preventing conflicts.
Other panels, including “Shared Commitment to Peace: Experiences and Perspectives,” “Humanitarian Efforts in Times of Conflict” and “From Prevention to Sustainable Peace,” will focus on the experiences and challenges of countries engaged in mediation.
They will also examine different approaches to mediation processes and draw on the expertise of academics, specialists and think tank representatives working in the field.

Presidential Candidate Iliana Yotova: The Status Quo
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
13:16:00 UTC
22:16:00 KST

Iliana Yotova will walk into a polling station on October 25 as the only candidate who already holds the job everyone else is competing for. She became Bulgaria's head of state on January 23, 2026, after Rumen Radev gave up the presidency to found Progressive Bulgaria and run for parliament, which made her both the first woman and the first vice president to occupy the office. Nine months later she is asking voters for a five-year term of her own beginning in January 2027 and every major pollster expects her to finish first by a wide margin. She turns 62 the day before the vote.
Presidential Candidate Andrey Gyurov: The Balance
Presidential Candidate Kostadin Kostadinov: The Vengeance (October 21st)
The case for her is also the case against her. A Yotova presidency would be a continuation of the Radev era by other means, with the same instincts on Ukraine and Russia and an office far more inclined to cooperate with the cabinet than to resist it. Voters looking for change will find little of it on ballot No. 25. Voters worn out by five years of snap elections and caretaker cabinets will find something many of them value more, which is predictability, and that trade of change for stability is the real offer on the table. She has nonetheless spent the race fending off questions about a pardon she signed in 2022, about her closeness to a government she will be expected to keep in check, and about how firmly she is willing to point at Moscow while drones strike merchant ships in Bulgaria's Black Sea economic zone.
From a Television Newsroom to Dondukov 2
Yotova was born in Sofia in 1964, graduated from the capital's French-language high school and studied Bulgarian and French philology at Sofia University, finishing in 1989, the year communism collapsed. She worked in the news department of Bulgarian National Television from 1991 before moving to the press center of the Bulgarian Socialist Party (BSP) in 1997. From there her career ran through the BSP leadership and the Sofia city council to a seat in parliament in 2005, followed by ten years in the European Parliament from 2007.
In 2016 the BSP placed her on the ticket as running mate to Radev, a former air force commander with no political record. The pair won that year and again in 2021, when they took about two-thirds of the vote in the runoff. Her BSP membership is formally frozen while she holds office, but nobody in Bulgarian politics treats her as anything other than a figure of the left who spent nine years as Radev's closest institutional ally.
An "Independent" Ticket With a Governing Majority Behind It
On paper Yotova is running as an independent, nominated by an initiative committee alongside Kiril Valchev, the director general of the state news agency BTA. Valchev is a media lawyer whom parliament reappointed to BTA in December 2025 without a single vote against, a résumé clearly chosen to signal consensus. In practice the ticket is backed by Radev's Progressive Bulgaria, which won 131 of the 240 seats in parliament in April, as well as by the BSP and the small left-wing party ABV.
That support is both the core of her strength and the core of the case against her. The Forum for Democratic Action, a civic group involved in the opposition's nomination process, published an open letter accusing her of using state resources for the campaign, pointing to presidential staff who helped file her registration documents and to employees of public broadcaster BNT who sat on her initiative committee. GERB leader Boyko Borissov has called her an ideological opponent and said he founded his party precisely to defeat the BSP, although he acknowledged that some people associated with GERB joined her committee in a personal capacity. Alpha Research found that most supporters of the Movement for Rights and Freedoms (DPS) who intend to vote are backing her.
A Medieval Tsar Comes Home Three Weeks Before the Vote
If the campaign needed a moment of national ceremony, the government supplied it. On September 29 Radev announced what he called a historic agreement with Greece on the remains attributed to Tsar Samuel, who ruled from his base around Ohrid and fought Byzantium at the turn of the eleventh century. On October 3 the sarcophagus arrived in Sofia under fighter jet escort, returned in exchange for 48 church relics that Bulgarian troops had taken from Greece in 1917, and Yotova told the state ceremony that Samuel's soul had found its way home.
Whether the timing was planned or simply fortunate, Radev's government handed the incumbent a patriotic stage no rival could match, three weeks before polling day. Yotova had already launched her campaign in Veliki Preslav, the old capital of the First Bulgarian Empire, and the Samuel ceremony reinforced the image of a president standing above party quarrels. North Macedonia, where Samuel is central to national historiography, reacted angrily, and Yotova replied that Sofia was open to talks with Skopje without ultimatums.
The Pardon That Shadowed Her Campaign
The episode Yotova would most like to forget surfaced in September, when We Continue the Change (PP) chairman Asen Vassilev disclosed that in December 2022, using presidential powers delegated to the vice president, she had pardoned Ognyan Atanasov, a drug trafficker known as the "Petrich Escobar". Atanasov had been serving a 15-year sentence imposed in Greece, and the decree cited a health condition that endangered his life. He was caught again in 2025 with five kilograms of cocaine.
Vassilev called on her to withdraw from the race. Yotova has said the decision rested on medical records and on assessments by the Justice Ministry and the presidential pardons commission, telling bTV, "I trust doctors, expert assessments, hospitals, and medical reports." She has questioned why prison footage of Atanasov never reached her administration and has not ruled out tightening the rules on pardons. A Sova Harris poll found the public almost evenly split on whether the issue should have been raised at all, which suggests the affair hardened existing views more than it moved votes.
Peace Language While Drones Hit Ships Off the Coast
Yotova's foreign policy sits close to Radev's. At the UN General Assembly in September she said there was no military solution in Ukraine and that peace could not be reached without both Ukraine and Russia at the table. On the campaign trail she has argued that Bulgaria needs a coalition for peace in Ukraine in place of a coalition of the willing, and according to the German daily taz she has promised that no Bulgarian soldier will be sent to Ukraine while she is president, although no one in Sofia has proposed sending any.
That stance has drawn sharper scrutiny since early October, when drones began striking commercial ships inside Bulgaria's exclusive economic zone and sank at least one of them. Yotova convened the Consultative Council for National Security, said Bulgaria needed firm evidence before naming who was responsible, and later suggested a Black Sea security meeting that would include the warring parties. Radev went further, saying logic pointed to Russia and calling in its ambassador, and on October 15 protesters in Sofia demanded that both of them resign.
Critics abroad have been blunter. Taz described her as a pro-Russian populist, and some media regularly recall the moment in 2018 when she knelt while greeting Russian Patriarch Kirill at Sofia Airport. AFP described her as a candidate who promotes ties with Moscow as well as with the EU and NATO and that this is probably closer to how her own voters see her.
What the Numbers Say About November 1
Polls published since the campaign opened put Yotova between 41.4 percent (Market Links) and 50.2 percent (Sova Harris) among decided voters, with Alpha Research at 44.5 percent, Gallup International Balkan at 44.9 percent and Trend at 47.8 percent. Even at the top of that range she cannot win outright on October 25, because Bulgarian law requires turnout above 50 percent for a first-round victory, and pollsters expect only 36 to 40 percent of registered voters to show up. A runoff on November 1 is therefore effectively certain.
History favors her there as well, since every candidate who has led the first round of a Bulgarian presidential election since 1992 has gone on to win the runoff. Sova Harris also found that she has the highest approval rating of any politician in the country, at 45.7 percent, narrowly ahead of Radev himself.
Her real exposure lies in how closely her fortunes are tied to his. Market Links found trust in the Radev government falling from 50 percent in May to 39 percent by late September, while its sociologist Dobromir Zhivkov warned that Radev's personal rating could turn negative within months.
***
That is the status quo she represents. A Yotova victory would place the presidency in the hands of the same camp that runs the government with a comfortable parliamentary majority, a degree of alignment Bulgaria has rarely seen since direct elections began. Her opponents warn of one-party rule and a head of state who will wave through whatever the cabinet sends her, pointing to her decision to sign the 2026 budget instead of vetoing it. Her supporters answer that a country exhausted by eight parliamentary elections in five years could use a president who keeps the machinery running instead of picking fights with the Council of Ministers. Little would change in a full Yotova term and for many of her voters that is precisely the appeal. The outcome on November 1 will depend heavily on GERB voters, nearly half of whom told Alpha Research they do not plan to vote at all.

A week in Budapest dedicated to Bulgaria and Bulgarian-Hungarian friendship
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
13:15:26 UTC
22:15:26 KST

Author
Krasimir Martinov
News
A week in Budapest dedicated to Bulgaria and Bulgarian-Hungarian friendship
Monday 19 October 2026 14:10
Monday, 19 October 2026, 14:10
The Hungarian Parliament Building
PHOTO BTA
Font size
The Day of Bulgarian-Hungarian Friendship, the 21st World Meeting of Bulgarian Media, and two anniversaries of Bulgarian cultural organisations make October a month of remembrance, continuity and spiritual ties between Bulgaria and Hungary.
On October 19, when the Bulgarian Orthodox Church honours St. John of Rila, Bulgaria and Hungary celebrate Bulgarian-Hungarian Friendship Day. In 2026, the occasion carries special significance, marking ten years since the date was officially designated as a day of friendship between the two countries. The date connects contemporary relations with a shared historical heritage and the memory of the saint whose relics were taken to Esztergom in the 12th century.
The connection between St. John of Rila and Hungary is part of the historical memory underpinning the celebration. In 1183, during a military campaign through Bulgarian lands, King Béla III of Hungary had the saint’s relics transferred to Esztergom. The relics were later returned to Bulgaria, but the memory of this historical event remains a symbol of the spiritual closeness between the two peoples.
Esztergom remains one of the places where this connection is commemorated. By tradition, the feast of St. John of Rila and Bulgarian-Hungarian Friendship Day are marked at the city’s basilica, where a bilingual memorial plaque dedicated to the saint was unveiled on October 19, 2016.
The commemorative plaque dedicated to St John of Rila at Esztergom Basilica
PHOTO BTA
The 21st World Meeting of Bulgarian Media officially opens today in Budapest, the capital of Hungary. The forum is organised and hosted by the Bulgarian News Agency (BTA).
This year’s edition is mottoed “Media and Leaders”. The event, which will take place in Budapest and Esztergom, is expected to bring together participants from 25 countries, including Bulgaria, both in person and online.
The Bulgarian National Radio is represented by its Director General, Milen Mitev.
21st World Meeting of Bulgarian Media
PHOTO BTA
Today’s programme includes a visit to the Hungarian Parliament and a meeting with MP Márton Hajdu, Chair of the Foreign Policy Committee. At 11:30 a.m., an exhibition dedicated to Bulgarian-Hungarian Friendship Day will open at the Barankovics office building. Bulgaria’s Ambassador to Hungary, Maria Anguelieva, and Simeon Varga, the representative of the Bulgarian community in the Hungarian Parliament, will deliver welcome addresses, the Bulgarian News Agency (BTA) reported.
The 21st World Meeting of Bulgarian Media will begin at 2 p.m. with a wreath-laying ceremony at the memorial plaque dedicated to St. John of Rila at the Cathedral of the Assumption of the Blessed Virgin Mary and St. Adalbert, and a prayer service led by Metropolitan Anthony of Western and Central Europe and Father Csaba, the episcopal delegate for the Esztergom Basilica.
The official opening of the 21st World Meeting of Bulgarian Media will take place at 6:30 p.m. at the Bulgarian Cultural Institute in Budapest.
The building of the Bulgarian School and Kindergarten in Budapest
PHOTO Bulgarian School and Kindergarten-Budapest
Behind the official celebrations of Bulgarian-Hungarian Friendship Day, diplomatic meetings and media forums, however, is a community that has kept the Bulgarian language, traditions and cultural memory alive in Hungary for decades. Its cultural life is sustained through schools, theatre, dance ensembles, music and Bulgarian-language publications. These organizations are not isolated from one another but form an interconnected cultural environment where generations come together and pass on their knowledge, skills and sense of identity.
“Bulgarians here are a very close-knit community. We are not just a school, a theatre or a dance ensemble operating separately”, Vanya Kotorova, principal of the Bulgarian School and Kindergarten-Budapest, told Radio Bulgaria.
This is in fact one of the most distinctive features of Bulgarian cultural life in Hungary. Children who study Bulgarian often participate in dance ensembles as well. The school organizes workshops with theatre professionals, while festivals and concerts become shared events for the entire community.
Vanya Kotorova
PHOTO Personal archive of Vanya Kotorova
“We are a small community, yet our cultural life is exceptionally rich”, says Vanya Kotorova, adding that October is a particularly eventful monthfor Bulgarians in Hungary, marked by several important cultural anniversaries.
Jantra-Bulgarian Folkdance Group and The Rositsa Folk Dance Ensemble are among the most iconic representatives of Bulgarian cultural life in Budapest.
On 23 October, Jantra-Bulgarian Folkdance Group will celebrate its 30th anniversary with the music and dance performance JANTRA 30 at the Vígszínház Theatre. The show will feature both dance ensembles, the Pravo and Slavia orchestras, and performers showcasing the richness of Bulgarian folk music and dance.
The Malko Teatro theatre company is also marking 30 years of cultural activity. Founded in 1996, it has established itself over the years as a space where theatre, music, movement and contemporary forms of stage expression come together.
Meanwhile, Hemus magazine continues to showcase Bulgarian literature, art, history and public life, creating opportunities for cultural exchange between Bulgarian and Hungarian authors and readers. The magazine’s 35th anniversary will be marked on 21 October with the opening of Danube-Bridges, an exhibition by photographer Péter Gyukics.
On 23 October, Hungary marks the 70th anniversary of the beginning of the student uprising against Soviet rule. On that day in 1956, a peaceful student demonstration began in Budapest and quickly grew into a mass protest involving more than 200,000 people. The demonstrators called for the withdrawal of Soviet troops, democratic reforms and freedom of speech.

The European Commission (EC) does not plan to resume imports of Russian gas, which the US administration is reportedly urging, EC spokeswoman Paula Pinho said.

The New York Times reported, citing sources, that the new peace proposal of the U.S. president's administration for settling the conflict in Ukraine provides for Europe to resume buying Russian gas in large volumes. The US proposed that "Ukraine ... consider resuming operation of pipelines that previously carried Russian natural gas to Europe," the newspaper said, citing sources familiar with the talks.

HARARE, October 19. /TASS/. The number of confirmed Ebola deaths in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) has exceeded 4,500 since May, with move than 9,400 cases registered in total, the country’s Ministry of Public Health, Hygiene and Social Welfare said.
"Since the beginning of the epidemic in the DRC, a total of 9,455 confirmed cases and 4,561 deaths have been recorded, with the fatality rate standing at 48.2%," the ministry said in its bulletin. It noted that the epicenter "remains Ituri Province, which accounts for 73.2% of all cases and 67.5% of new cases." The epidemic has spread to 66 of the DRC’s 178 health zones across eight provinces. A total of 269 healthcare workers have contracted Ebola.
The current Ebola outbreak began on May 15 in the DRC and Uganda. Ugandan authorities announced on July 28 that the outbreak in the country had ended. The World Health Organization confirmed this on August 25. In neighboring Kenya, the first case of Ebola was confirmed on October 6. The patient was a Kenyan national who had previously lived in the DRC. He arrived in Nairobi via Uganda on October 3 and died on October 5. As of October 19, a total of eight cases had been detected in Kenya.
