====================================================================================================

Women’s attention to beauty isn’t limited to the sex they’re attracted to, eye-tracking study finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
12:00:17 UTC
21:00:17 KST

When viewing pairs of faces, men tend to linger selectively on attractive faces that match their sexual orientation, whereas women spend more time looking at attractive faces regardless of the person’s sex. A new eye-tracking study published in Evolution and Human Behavior suggests that this preference occurs during deliberate, sustained viewing rather than in the first split-second of automatic attention. The findings also indicate that being in a committed relationship does not necessarily stop people from looking longer at attractive faces.
In psychology, attentional bias refers to the tendency for our visual system to prioritize certain types of information over others in our environment. Facial attractiveness, which is the subjective judgment of how aesthetically pleasing a face is, acts as a strong magnet for human gaze. From an evolutionary perspective, physical beauty is often thought to serve as a signal of health and fertility, which may explain why human cognition is tuned to notice desirable potential mates.
How this visual pull operates depends heavily on both who is looking and who is being looked at. In a 2003 study of young adults, researchers outlined several competing possibilities for how gender and mating motives guide our eyes. One possibility is that people focus mainly on attractive members of their preferred sex to find mates, while another suggests that both men and women look longer at attractive women: men to evaluate potential partners, and women to assess potential romantic rivals. A third proposed that men in particular would show a strong pull toward attractive faces of their preferred sex, because physical attractiveness tends to weigh more heavily in men’s mate preferences.
Subsequent research has complicated this picture by examining how relationship status and different stages of mental processing shape our gaze. For instance, a 2018 eye-tracking study indicated that single people exhibit a stronger visual pull toward attractive faces than people in committed relationships, who may dial down their attention to protect their existing bond. Similarly, a study covered by PsyPost in 2023 found that when viewing faces matching their sexual preference, people’s brains initially react strongly to both very attractive and very unattractive faces before settling into sustained neural activity specifically for the attractive ones.
Psychologists separate visual attention into two distinct stages: immediate attention and volitional attention. Immediate attention is a rapid, automatic reflex that pulls our eyes toward a stimulus before we consciously think about it. Volitional attention is the slower, deliberate process of choosing where to keep looking to gather more information.
Separating these two stages matters for attractiveness research. A 2023 study of speed-daters, led by Tom S. Roth, the senior author of the new study, found that people’s personal ratings of facial attractiveness predicted where both men and women directed their deliberate gaze, while results for quicker, more automatic glances were mixed across the sexes. However, almost all prior eye-tracking studies on facial attractiveness have relied on college undergraduates, whose casual dating habits may not reflect how older adults in long-term relationships view attractive strangers.
To address this, lead author Johanna M. Bellue and her colleagues, including Roth, an assistant professor at Utrecht University, set out to test how immediate and deliberate attention to attractive faces varies by sex, sexual preference, age, and relationship status in the general public.
“Previous studies on attractiveness bias have mostly been performed with heterosexual undergraduate students as a sample,” Roth told PsyPost. “However, to understand this phenomenon it is more interesting to see whether similar effects are present in a broader sample, containing people of different ages, relationship statuses, and sexual orientations.”
The researchers recruited 105 adults attending the Betweter Festival, an annual public science festival held at a music venue in Utrecht, the Netherlands. After excluding three non-binary participants, who all reported being pansexual and so had no “non-preferred” faces to compare, the final sample included 65 women and 37 men. The participants had an average age of 38, and most (87 of the 102) were heterosexual, while the 63 participants in exclusive relationships had been with their partners for an average of about 12.6 years.
Each participant sat in a booth about 60 centimeters away from a computer monitor equipped with an infrared eye-tracker that recorded their eye movements 300 times per second. To prevent participants from consciously altering their behavior, the researchers told them only that the study examined general face perception, without mentioning attractiveness. Across 36 main trials, participants viewed pairs of same-sex portrait photos, either two men or two women, with neutral expressions.
Each pair featured one conventionally attractive face and one less attractive face, selected from established academic photo databases based on pre-existing consensus ratings. All of the faces were of white adults, mostly in their twenties and thirties. The face pairs remained on the screen for three seconds while participants looked wherever they wanted. Afterward, participants completed a paper questionnaire detailing their age, sex, sexual orientation, relationship status, relationship length, and how many alcoholic drinks they had consumed at the festival that evening.
The authors matched each participant’s stated sexual orientation with the sex of the faces shown on screen to categorize every trial as either “preferred” or “non-preferred.” For example, female faces were coded as preferred for heterosexual men and homosexual women, while all faces were coded as preferred for bisexual participants. In their statistical models, the team controlled for alcohol consumption, which photo database the images came from, and whether the attractive face appeared on the left or right side of the screen.
When looking at immediate attention, measured by which of the two faces a participant’s eyes landed on first within half a second of the images appearing, facial attractiveness had no noticeable effect. Women looked at the attractive face first about 50.0% of the time for their preferred sex and 50.7% of the time for their non-preferred sex, which is essentially a coin toss. Men looked at the attractive face first in 53.9% of preferred-sex trials and 49.9% of non-preferred-sex trials, a difference that was not statistically robust.
Instead of beauty, the first automatic glance was heavily dictated by screen position. Participants looked at the left image first in roughly 78% of the trials, regardless of how attractive the person was. This strong leftward habit is a well-known quirk of how the human brain’s hemispheres process visual space, and it may have masked any immediate pull toward attractive faces, as could the noisy festival setting. The null result also contrasts with some earlier reaction-time studies that found a rapid pull toward attractive faces, which the authors suggest may reflect differences in the type of attention each method captures.
A different pattern emerged when the researchers examined volitional attention, which was measured by the proportion of total viewing time spent looking at the attractive face over the full three seconds. Women demonstrated a general appreciation for facial beauty, spending 55.4% of their viewing time on the attractive face when looking at their preferred sex and 54.7% when looking at their non-preferred sex. Both figures were statistically above the 50% mark that would indicate equal viewing.
Men, by contrast, were more selective with their deliberate gaze. They spent 54.9% of their viewing time on the attractive face when the pair matched their sexual preference, but only 52.0% when viewing their non-preferred sex, a figure that did not reliably differ from chance. Men’s bias toward attractive faces of their preferred sex was no stronger than women’s, and a statistical test comparing the two sexes’ patterns directly fell just short of the study’s threshold, partly because women also looked slightly longer at attractive faces of their preferred sex.
The authors note that the pattern parallels earlier research suggesting that men’s visual and physical sexual responses tend to be specific to their preferred sex, whereas women’s tend to be less specific.
“We find that men and women differ in their attractiveness bias,” Roth explained. “Men are specifically interested in attractive faces that align with their sexual orientation, while women have a general bias toward attractive faces of both sexes. This is in line with previous research. We don’t find that men have a stronger bias toward attractiveness in their preferred sex, as has been suggested by some evolutionary hypotheses.”
The findings are in line with research covered by PsyPost earlier this year, which found that more attractive faces drew more direct eye movements but did not speed reactions on a task measuring attention shifts that happen without moving the eyes. Although the two studies used different tasks, both suggest that attractiveness influences where people choose to look more than it captures attention automatically.
The researchers also ran statistical simulations to predict how a newly recruited individual would behave, rather than just looking at group averages. They found that a new female participant would have about an 80% probability of looking longer at attractive faces of either sex, while a new male participant would have a 76% probability for attractive faces of his preferred sex, but only about 62% for his non-preferred sex. This wider uncertainty at the individual level suggests that while the group trend is reliable, personal viewing habits vary considerably from one person to the next.
“While humans do seem to have an attractiveness bias of some kind, we also found that there is quite some variation between participants,” Roth noted. “While the majority of individuals indeed have a bias, others do not. This shows that it is at least not a fixed trait that generalizes to everyone.”
Contrary to expectations and some prior university-based studies, relationship status did not meaningfully alter how long people looked at attractive faces of their preferred sex. Participants in exclusive relationships spent just as much time looking at attractive faces as participants who were single or in open relationships. In addition, an exploratory check of participant age showed only weak, inconclusive tendencies, with attractiveness bias slightly increasing with age in men and slightly decreasing in women.
“We were also interested in effects of relationship status, but we did not find any,” Roth said. “We had expected that people might look less at attractive faces that aligned with their preference when they were in a relationship, as they want to ‘protect’ their relationship. However, our sample mostly contained data from participants who were already in very established relationships with a long duration. Maybe our expected effect would apply more to new relationships specifically.”
The authors noted that this difference in relationship maturity may help explain why their festival sample behaved differently from student populations. In the early stages of dating, which are common among college students, people may actively avoid looking at attractive strangers to protect a fragile new bond and build trust. Once a relationship has lasted over a decade, partners may feel secure enough that they no longer need to unconsciously police where their eyes wander during a casual viewing task. It is also possible that relationship status only dampens attention when people are first primed to think about romance or their partner, a step used in several earlier studies that this experiment omitted.
There are a few things to keep in mind when interpreting these results. “One important caveat is that we measured where people looked, not whom they wanted to date or felt sexually attracted to,” Roth added. “Women looking longer at attractive faces of both sexes should therefore not be interpreted as evidence of sexual interest in both sexes.”
Because the experiment took place at a bustling public festival, the researchers had to keep the procedure brief and relied on pre-existing average ratings to define which faces were attractive. People have diverse personal tastes, meaning a participant might not have personally found the designated “attractive” face appealing, which could dilute the measured gaze patterns.
The festival setting also meant that the researchers recruited whoever volunteered rather than sampling to balance groups, resulting in noticeably more women and coupled people than men and singles. The photo databases featured only white faces, mostly of young adults in their twenties and thirties, which may have skewed how older participants responded to the images. Future studies could test larger, evenly balanced groups using faces of many different ages, while also asking participants to rate the faces themselves and answer detailed questions about their relationship satisfaction and jealousy.
“Although our science-festival sample covered a broader age range than a typical student sample, it still overrepresents highly educated people from urban settings, and most participants were heterosexual,” Roth said. “Recruiting people from a wider range of backgrounds and sexual orientations would help us establish how broadly these patterns apply. We would also like to account more directly for individual preferences: the faces that are attractive on average are not necessarily the ones that every individual finds attractive.”
The study, “Sexual preference modulates attentional bias towards attractive faces in men, but not women,” was authored by Johanna M. Bellue, David Terburg, Mirre E. Balke, Tessa W. Coster, Jorg J.M. Massen, and Tom S. Roth.

Gurdeep Loyal’s quick and easy recipe for masala chickpea-parsnip fritters with coconut sambol | Quick and easy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
12:00:03 UTC
21:00:03 KST

These warmly spiced fritters are inspired by the tikki-chaat carts found all over India, which sizzle fresh chickpea, potato or lentil patties on hot-plates until crisp, then slather them with chutneys. The coconut sambol ushers forth the flavours of south India – coconut, mustard seeds and lime; add a teaspoon of tamarind paste to increase the tartness, if you like. A good dollop of yoghurt is a must, and a fried egg or avocado on the side turns these fritters into a satisfying supper.
Masala chickpea and parsnip fritters with coconut sambol
Prep 10 min
 
Cook 30 min
 
Serves 2-3
60g red chillies (about 4 large ones)
 
5 tbsp vegetable oil, plus extra for frying
 
4 garlic cloves, peeled and crushed
 
65g desiccated coconut
  
2 tsp black mustard seeds
  
1½ tsp fine sea salt
  
2 tbsp brown sugar
 
2 tbsp tomato puree
  
Juice and grated zest of 1 large lime, plus 1 lime extra, cut into wedges, to serve
  
400g tin 
 chickpeas, drained
 
2 large parsnips, peeled and grated
 
2 tsp garam masala
  
2 tsp coriander seeds, crushed
 
100g ricotta
  
3 
 tbsp plain flour
  
1 tbsp baking powder
  
15g fresh coriander, finely chopped, plus extra to serve
 
Yoghurt, to serve
  
Fried egg or avocado
 , to serve (optional)
In a small blender, blitz the chillies, four tablespoons of vegetable oil and two crushed garlic cloves to make a smooth paste.
Toast the coconut and mustard seeds in a small frying pan over a medium heat for one to two minutes, until they take on a little colour. Pour in the chilli paste with 100ml water, then cook for four to five minutes, until much of the water has evaporated and the paste begins to darken. Add a teaspoon of fine salt, the brown sugar, tomato puree, lime juice and zest, then cook for another two minutes, until you have a thick sambol. Empty into a bowl and leave to cool.
Blitz the chickpeas and the remaining tablespoon of vegetable oil to a coarse paste in a blender or food processor. Put this in a large bowl with the grated parsnips, the remaining two crushed garlic cloves, the garam masala, crushed coriander seeds, ricotta, plain flour, baking powder, fresh coriander and a half-teaspoon of salt. Mix together using your hands until fully combined, then shape into six large patties, about 4-5cm wide and 1½cm thick.
Heat a little vegetable oil in a nonstick frying pan, then cook the fritters in batches over medium heat for seven to eight minutes, flipping occasionally, until golden brown on both sides. Serve warm with a dollop of yoghurt, a generous spoon of coconut sambol and a fried egg or avocado, if you like. Garnish with fresh coriander and a wedge of lime.

Third Ebola case in Kenya highlights US failures amid Trump cuts to key services
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
12:00:01 UTC
21:00:01 KST

An eighth person in Kenya has tested positive for the Bundibugyo strain of Ebola in the country’s first-ever cluster of cases of the virus, as the second-largest outbreak in history has killed more than 4,300 and sickened more than 9,000 people in the region.
It highlights the diminished role the US has played in the worsening Ebola outbreak by building a controversial quarantine center in Kenya, pulling back health support globally, and banning travelers from certain countries. All of this has also reduced the ability to identify and respond to the outbreak and exacerbated mistrust.
The US created a controversial quarantine center at Kenya’s Laikipia airbase, where Americans returning from the Democratic Republic of the Congo would be required to quarantine. The center, opposed by locals, has stirred distrust in the Kenyan government, leading to protests and a Kenyan court ordering a halt to the center.
“Many Kenyans were concerned about the fact that there was no information and people did not know why the quarantine place was being set up, who was actually going to use it, and what had informed that,” said Allan Maleche, executive director of the Kenya Legal & Ethical Issues Network on HIV and Aids (Kelin). The litigation will be decided in November, he said.
In the meantime, Kenyans were “very cautious around any information that is being given by the government around Ebola”, Maleche said.
Americans who questioned whether the US has the legal authority to quarantine Americans on foreign soil and prevent them from returning home are pushing back against the quarantine center as Kenya faces its first Ebola cases.
“Is this still a viable solution for the US?” asked Jennifer Nuzzo, director of the pandemic center at Brown University school of public health. “Are we posing not only an undue burden on the Kenyan government to be able to handle this, but also is this the safest place to be bringing Americans?”
The US already has “world-class” Ebola treatment units, Nuzzo pointed out.
“American taxpayers built these units for precisely this purpose, and it’s mind-boggling to me that we’re going to leave them empty,” she said. In previous outbreaks, actively ill patients have been evacuated safely to these centers, where they have recovered without further spread of the virus.
The unease follows sweeping cuts to US health support across the world, with the demolition of the US Agency for International Development (USAID) and cuts to funding and staff at health agencies like the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).
On 1 October, the CDC closed HIV prevention offices in Angola and South Sudan, with plans to close offices in Zimbabwe. The US has slashed programs across the world – including DR Congo, where the Ebola outbreak is centered, and other countries, like Kenya, bracing for cases as the outbreak widens.
“We have had a lot of concerns after the US first cut funding for HIV promptly without any direction,” Maleche said. “It led to clinics closing. It led to a lot of anxiety among people.”
The US is now negotiating bilateral agreements with each country, including Kenya – a process that has been mired in secrecy, Maleche said. “It’s not very clear what’s the plan, who’s rolling it out, and what will be involved.”
Cuts to decades-long programs mean the affected countries and the US have less insight into what’s happening, in addition to a lessened ability to prevent and stop outbreaks. “When you pull back on those, not only do you leave those countries less prepared to deal with that day-to-day threat, but it also means that they’re less prepared to deal with future emergencies,” Nuzzo said.
The US officially left the World Health Organization (WHO) in January, making it much harder to collaborate on the response to crises like these. When the US left the WHO, it also “pulled out a substantial amount of funding”, said Maleche. That means the WHO’s response had also been “weakened”, he said.
A Kenyan man fell ill in DRC before traveling by road to Uganda and then flying to Nairobi on 3 October, where he died in a hospital two days later. Since then, seven close contacts have tested positive.
Patrick Amoth, the director-general for health, confirmed on Sunday the total number of infections in the country was eight.
Kenya’s ministry of health pointed to the success of contact tracing and quarantine. About 108 people have been quarantined in Nairobi.
“The general feeling is that the contact tracing systems are working,” Maleche said. But Kenyans are also wondering why there were “many lapses” that resulted in a sick person traveling across countries. The border between DR Congo and Uganda has been closed since May. Uganda was declared Ebola-free in August after earlier reporting 20 cases and two deaths.
A French doctor who returned from DR Congo in June tested positive, and several Americans have been evacuated from DR Congo to Europe for Ebola treatment or monitoring.
In Kenya, “the biggest fear is around how will other countries react” to the outbreak, with travel bans a particular worry, Maleche said. The US put travel bans in place from DR Congo and neighboring Uganda and South Sudan once the outbreak was detected in May, but it would be “very ironic” if the US instituted travel bans, given its quarantine center in Kenya, Maleche said.
Raphael Warnock, a Democratic senator from Georgia, and Bill Cassidy, a Republican senator from Louisiana, penned a letter in June to the Senate appropriations committee opposing the Trump administration’s plans to cut back on HIV prevention and monitoring.
Dismantling of USAID, withdrawing from the WHO, and abruptly cutting foreign aid cuts was “degrading our outbreak preparedness” and had “seriously weakened our ability to keep Americans safe from infectious disease”, Warnock said in a statement.
“These cuts to global health funding have led to the erosion of international disease-monitoring infrastructure that helps us catch threats like Ebola before they reach our shores, at a time when the world needs American leadership most.” The US should be strengthening these systems, not abandoning them, he said.
Nuzzo agreed. “It’s about having an understanding of the systems and the conditions in other countries, and eyes and ears in those countries to detect when something out of the ordinary happens, and to get that information as early as possible,” she said. That benefits the US and the countries themselves, she said.
Work such as HIV prevention “can be repurposed”, she added. “You have connections with clinical care, the ability to move medicines, the ability to conduct laboratory tests, the ability to move specimens around – all of those capacities are things that you would use in other disease emergencies.”

Gaza: Funding cuts leave half a million without food assistance
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
12:00:00 UTC
21:00:00 KST

Gaza: Funding cuts leave half a million without food assistance
Funding shortages have forced the World Food Programme (WFP) to slash assistance to hungry families in the Gaza Strip by roughly one third – a move that will affect some 500,000 people as winter approaches, the UN agency announced on Monday.
WFP said that its food assistance “has provided a lifeline for up to 90 per cent of families in Gaza” over the past three years.
Since the October 2025 ceasefire agreement between Israel and Hamas fighters, teams have reached around 1.6 million people monthly with food parcels, wheat flour, bread, hot meals, nutrition support, school snacks and cash assistance.
“Improved humanitarian access and delivery of assistance since October 2025 have helped reduce food insecurity, but these gains remain fragile and could quickly be reversed if humanitarian funding continues to decline,” the agency warned.
Rations, cash and hot meals reduced
This month, WFP is supporting 1.1 million of the most vulnerable people in the war-torn enclave, down from 1.6 million in September.
Rations have been cut in half, meaning families will now receive one food parcel instead of two, and a smaller bag of wheat flour.
The value of cash assistance given to 75,000 families has also been reduced, while the number of hot mails provided daily across Gaza will drop from 250,000 to 150,000.
“Families living in hard-to-reach areas, including near the ‘yellow line’ of Israeli military control, will receive a hot meal every other day instead of daily,” the agency said.
For now, WFP is able to continue supporting bakeries that cover a third of Gaza’s bread needs, provide nutrition assistance to 300,000 women and children and deliver healthy school snacks to 200,000 students.
Crisis-level hunger
The cuts come at a critical time in Gaza, where more than 80 per cent of the population is unemployed, leaving many families unable to afford fresh produce or protein-rich foods, even when they are available.
Roughly 67 per cent of Gazans –an estimated 1.4 million people – is experiencing acute food insecurity at crisis levels or worse. Although this is down from 77 per cent at the end of 2025, “improvement remains modest and fragile”, WFP said.
Some 200,000 people remain in emergency conditions and immediate food assistance is needed to prevent them from dying from hunger.
Meanwhile, only one in five children consumes a sufficiently diverse diet, and access to healthcare and other essential services remains limited.
Critical funding needs
WFP stressed that as winter approaches, additional resources are urgently needed to sustain emergency food assistance, provide critical engineering support and prevent malnutrition among young children and pregnant and breastfeeding women.
Funding for its operations in Palestine in 2026 amount to less than half received in previous years, and the agency urgently requires $450 million to maintain critical operations in Gaza and the West Bank through March.
WFP noted that funding shortages have also affected its operations in the West Bank, where the number of people receiving assistance was cut by half – from 400,000 to 200,000 – in September.

Guterres honours Indonesian troops who paid ‘ultimate sacrifice’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19

Guterres honours Indonesian troops who paid ‘ultimate sacrifice’
UN Secretary-General António Guterres paid tribute to Indonesian peacekeepers on Monday, laying a wreath in honour of four who recently lost their lives in Lebanon and offering a robust defence of UN peacekeeping in what he called “testing times for peace”.
Speaking to troops at the Indonesia Armed Forces Peacekeeping Centre in Sentul – some of whom are deploying to the Central African Republic (CAR) – Mr. Guterres said the fallen had paid the “ultimate sacrifice” to protect others in very difficult circumstances.
“Their service and their sacrifice will never be forgotten. No one should die serving the cause of peace,” he said, extending his deepest condolences to their families.
“Attacks on peacekeepers are grave violations of international humanitarian law and may amount to war crimes. These violations demand accountability,” the UN chief stressed, pledging to keep calling on Member States to ensure the safety and security of UN personnel at all times.
‘A source of hope’
Mr. Guterres described UN ‘blue helmets’ as “a source of hope in some of the world’s most troubled places” and, for him, “a source of enormous pride”.
Far from home and in some of the world’s most dangerous settings, the UN’s 50,000 peacekeepers de-escalate tensions between hostile parties, oversee vital aid delivery, protect civilians and create space for political solutions to take hold, he said.
Indonesia is the world’s sixth-largest contributor to UN peacekeeping, with nearly 2,000 uniformed women and men serving across seven missions. Next year, it will co-host the UN Peacekeeping Ministerial with the Netherlands.
‘Success story’ to be concluded
Addressing those troops preparing to deploy to the CAR, Mr. Guterres – who has worked with the country for 20 years, first as UN High Commissioner for Refugees – called it “a success story that still needs to be completed”.
Most armed groups have “celebrated…agreements with the Government and are giving up their arms”, he said, and the troops’ mission will be decisive in helping State institutions function across the whole territory.
With their success, the UN could then progressively downsize its mission in the country, he added.
Mr. Guterres had opened his remarks on a lighter note, telling the troops he was convinced that “no bad guys in [the Central African Republic] will dare confront the Indonesians”.
‘Better multilateralism’
In Jakarta, speaking at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Mr. Guterres hailed Indonesia as “a pillar of multilateralism” and a diplomatic bridge-builder between North and South.
With conflicts multiplying, inequality deepening and trust in institutions declining, he said many people question whether international cooperation can still deliver.
“The answer to deepening frustration with multilateralism is not less multilateralism. It is better multilateralism,” he said, calling for reform of international financial institutions and the Security Council to reflect today’s world.
‘The nightmare must end’
Speaking to reporters alongside Foreign Minister Arrmanatha Nasir, Mr. Guterres said that in Gaza, “the nightmare must end.”
“The peace plan must be fully implemented – and we cannot allow the two-State solution to disappear before our eyes,” he said, paying tribute to Indonesia for always being at the forefront of support for the Palestinian people.
He also voiced concern over Myanmar’s deepening crisis, renewing his appeal for protection of those fleeing violence and persecution, including Rohingya refugees across the region.

Haiti: Elections on hold as gangs adapt to security crackdown, Security Council hears
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
12:00:00 UTC
21:00:00 KST

Haiti: Elections on hold as gangs adapt to security crackdown, Security Council hears
Armed groups in Haiti are adapting to intensified security operations, stepping up reprisals against civilians and extending their reach into rural areas, the UN warned the Security Council on Monday.
The briefing came two weeks after presidential and legislative elections planned for 13 December were postponed indefinitely, with the UN’s top official in the country cautioning against setting new dates without a realistic assessment of whether a vote can be held.
Key points
- 1,123 Haitians were killed and 440 injured in gang-related violence between July and early October
- Sexual violence remains widespread, with 689 women and girls reportedly raped by gang members in July and August
- The Security Council-authorised Gang Suppression Force is not yet fully deployed
Changing tactics
In Haiti, security forces are intensifying their operations, but the gangs are not giving up. They are adapting their tactics, increasing reprisals against civilians and spreading violence to rural areas, according to the Secretary-General’s latest report.
“What is particularly worrying is the gangs’ ability to adapt their tactics as security operations intensify,” said Carlos Ruiz Massieu, the UN’s top official in Haiti.
Armed groups are increasingly resorting to hostage-taking, intimidation and reprisals against civilians to maintain their territory and challenge state authority.
Deadly attacks
The attack carried out on 23 and 24 August in Kenscoff, a mountainous town southeast of the capital, Port-au-Prince, illustrates this strategy.
At least 47 people were killed, 22 wounded, and 52 taken hostage, 13 of whom were later freed thanks to local initiatives supported by the UN.
In the West and Artibonite departments, 241 people were killed for allegedly resisting gangs.
Other attacks – notably in Saint-Michel-de-l’Atalaye, Marigot, and Léogâne – indicate a spread of violence into rural areas. Armed groups are also targeting farmland, homes and public infrastructure.
Security force operations also contribute to the rising death toll. They account for 52 per cent of Haitians killed or wounded since the beginning of July, or 808 people, including 148 not associated with gangs.
GSF a work in progress
Faced with this violence, the Security Council-backed Gang Suppression Force, logistically supported by the UN, is continuing its deployment.
As of 12 October, it had 1,563 uniformed members, far fewer than the 5,550 authorised by the Security Council. It has notably established a base in the Artibonite region, beyond the capital.
But, armed groups retain the capacity to retaliate.
On Sunday, an armoured vehicle transporting Salvadoran soldiers from the force was attacked in Croix-des-Bouquets, in the Port-au-Prince metropolitan area. Four soldiers were still missing on Monday, according to media reports.
Power vacuum
For Mr. Ruiz Massieu, retaking territory will not be enough.
“Experience has shown that security operations alone cannot bring about lasting stabilisation,” he warned, calling for the permanent restoration of the State’s presence and the development of disarmament and reintegration programmes, particularly for children recruited by gangs.
This persistent insecurity also jeopardises the return to democracy, he said.
Presidential and legislative elections, initially scheduled for 13 December, have been postponed indefinitely. Haiti has not held national elections since 2016.
Nevertheless, preparations are ongoing. More than 35 political parties and groups, and 3,500 candidates have registered, according to Mr. Ruiz Massieu. As of 5 October, however, only 759,257 potential voters were on the lists, out of an estimated electorate of 6.5 million people. Insecurity and mass displacement are further complicating the organization of the election.
“Setting new dates for elections without a realistic assessment of their feasibility will only erode public confidence and the credibility of Haitian institutions,” he warned.
Humanitarian crisis
Adding to this political uncertainty is a humanitarian crisis.
Nearly 1.5 million people have fled their homes, including more than 740,000 children.
The economy is expected to contract for the seventh consecutive year, while the UN’s 2026 humanitarian plan is only about half funded.
The country thus remains faced with a dual emergency: restoring security essential for holding elections, without which a return to democratic institutions remains out of reach.

‘Season of fear’: Escalating Israeli attacks on West Bank olive farmers, deadly strikes on Gaza
Israeli attacks on war-torn Gaza over the weekend killed at least six Palestinians, including children, despite a year-old ceasefire agreement. Meanwhile, in the occupied West Bank, settler violence continued through the ongoing olive harvest, with UN independent experts on Monday urging Israel to protect Palestinian farmers.
Key points
- West Bank: Five Palestinians were killed and over 240 injured by Israeli forces or settlers over the past two weeks, with 200 olive harvest-related attacks documented since the start of September
- Gaza: Israeli attacks have continued to cause deaths and injuries as nearly one million Palestinians face winter flood risks
- Funding shortages have forced UN agencies to make major cuts to food programmes
Death, demolitions along so-called ‘yellow line’
In the Gaza Strip, deadly Israeli airstrikes, gunfire and shelling occurred alongside incursions, demolitions and reported shifts in the so-called “yellow line” imposed by Israel since the year-old ceasefire agreement.
The attacks raised concerns and risks of further displacement, according to the latest updates from the UN emergency aid coordination office, OCHA.
Local health authorities told OCHA 57 Palestinians were reported killed and 319 injured between 29 September and 12 October, bringing the total number of casualties since the October 2025 ceasefire agreement to 1,493 fatalities and 5,299 injuries.
Winter storms and growing hunger
Meanwhile, around 950,000 displaced people have been assessed as living in sites at medium to high risk of flooding, including over 400,000 at high risk.
Available supplies offered partial assistance to only 18 per cent of the 294,250 families requiring shelter support for the rainy season, OCHA reported.
Daily cooked-meal production has declined by 12 per cent to approximately 614,000 amid funding constraints, while shortages of fuel, engine oil and essential supplies threaten the continuity of health and water services, the UN agency said.
Settler violence must end: Independent experts
Five Palestinians were killed and over 240 injured by Israeli forces or settler attacks in the occupied West Bank over the past two weeks, OCHA reported.
During the same period, 160 olive harvest-related settler attacks resulted in casualties, property damage or both while record demolitions displaced 96 Palestinians, the agency said.
UN independent human rights experts warned on Monday that Palestinian farmers are facing renewed threats as the annual olive harvest gets underway, urging Israel to guarantee their protection and safe access to their land.
‘Maximum pressure’ needed
“The olive harvest should be a time when farmers can enjoy, in safety and dignity, the food and livelihoods their nature and land provide, not another season of fear, loss, violence and destruction,” said the Human Rights Council-appointed experts, who are not UN staff and do not receive a salary.
“Israel is under an international legal obligation to end its occupation of Palestinian land, immediately cease new settlement activities, evacuate settlers from the Occupied Palestinian Territory and provide full reparation for the damage caused by its violations, including by returning land and allowing displaced Palestinians to return to their homes,” the experts said.
“The international community, especially States with power and influence, must exercise maximum pressure to protect Palestinian civilians, halt and reverse the rapidly expanding policies and practices of annexation and ensure accountability for decades of violations of Palestinian rights under international law,” they said, warning that the situation could worsen following new Israeli orders for uprooting olive trees and restrictions on farmers in the West Bank.

UN condemns deadly wave of drone strikes in war-torn Sudan
Drone strikes killed and injured dozens across Sudan on Monday as the ongoing war continues to cause soaring displacement and hunger.
“We are alarmed by the continued deadly drone strikes across the country that are killing civilians, including children, and that are disrupting essential services,” UN Spokesperson Stéphane Dujarric told journalists in New York.
The rising use of armed drones during the war between rival militaries comes at a time when 20 million people face acute hunger, with a rising risk of famine in parts of Darfur and Greater Kordofan.
Fighting erupted in April 2023 between the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) – former allies who had jointly seized power in a 2021 coup.
This latest escalation comes on the heels of a spate of deadly drone attacks last week.
Bloody Monday
On Monday alone, drone strikes injured at least 19 people in a busy market in Abyei and targeted several locations in the capital, Khartoum, including an area near the airport.
One civilian was reportedly killed and some flights were cancelled following the attacks.
Over the weekend, drone attacks reportedly killed at least 19, including 10 children, and injured others across West Darfur, South Darfur and North Kordofan States.
“We condemn all of these attacks unequivocally,” Mr. Dujarric said.
In response to the increasing use of armed drones in Sudan, Rosemary DiCarlo, Under-Secretary-General for Political and Peacebuilding Affairs, urged external actors to stop fuelling the violence and drone usage.
She called once gain on the warring parties to return to the negotiating table, during a briefing to the Security Council last Friday.
Aid workers targeted
Another grave concern has been the targeting of aid workers, the UN Spokesperson said.
Since the conflict began, 25 Sudanese Red Crescent volunteers have reportedly been killed while on duty.
He expressed deep sadness over the killing of a Sudanese Red Crescent volunteer last week who was providing first aid at a health centre in Um Darfa in Blue Nile State following a drone attack on the facilities.
“The targeting of those who put their own lives at risk to help others in humanitarian settings is particularly heinous,” Mr. Dujarric said, reiterating that civilians and civilian infrastructure, including medical facilities and personnel, must be protected in accordance with international humanitarian law.
Crucial aid delivered
Despite these immense challenges, the UN and its humanitarian partners continue to deliver crucial assistance wherever they can, Mr. Dujarric said.
In Central Darfur state, UN partners recently rehabilitated a water facility in Zalingei, restoring access to safe water for some 2,500 people.
More than 2,000 families have received water, sanitation and hygiene support.
“Once again, we need more funding to sustain all of these lifesaving operations,” he said, emphasising that Sudan’s humanitarian response plan is just over 43 per cent funded.

Hunger is ‘an avoidable tragedy’ in a world of plenty: Türk
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Hunger is ‘an avoidable tragedy’ in a world of plenty: Türk
More than a quarter of humanity struggles to get enough food, even though the world produces enough for everyone, UN human rights chief Volker Türk said on Monday, blaming injustice and the denial of human rights for hunger in a world of plenty.
Addressing the UN-hosted Committee on World Food Security in Rome, the High Commissioner said that while the right to food has found its way into treaties and laws, “for too many people, it has yet to find its way onto their dinner plates”.
Global food supply now exceeds 3,000 calories per person per day – a historic high – yet hunger reduction has not kept pace.
“Too much of that abundance is swallowed up by injustice and the denial of human rights,” Mr. Türk said.
Waste, inequality and war
Every day, households alone throw away more than one billion meals, he said.
Just one per cent of the world’s farms operate more than 70 per cent of global farmland, while women farmers and Indigenous Peoples often lack government support and access to land.
Conflict is also driving acute hunger in 12 of the 13 current hunger hotspots, the High Commissioner said, with restrictions on humanitarian aid and attacks on aid workers “cutting off the last lifelines”.
He called for a human rights economy built on social protection, fair taxation and agricultural policies that reduce poverty, as well as equitable access to land, water and seeds, and meaningful climate action.
“We must do our utmost to ensure the rules of war are upheld and hunger is never used as a method of warfare,” he said.
Famine ‘with impunity’
Addressing the Committee for the first time as the independent expert on the right food, UN Special Rapporteur Sofía Monsalve Suárez said the issue that concerned her most was the rapid increase in famine and the use of starvation as a weapon of war.
While chronic hunger declined in 2025, acute hunger has been rising steadily since 2016, she said.
Today, 1.4 million people in six countries face catastrophic conditions – nine times more than in 2016 – and 266 million people face acute hunger every day, in countries including Sudan, South Sudan, the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Yemen, as well as in Gaza.
“The return of famine and the deliberate use of starvation as a weapon of war is an unprecedented moral challenge for our generation. These crimes continue with impunity,” she said.
Ms. Suárez called for a stronger framework for accountability and prevention, and better coordination between the Security Council, the Committee, the human rights system and food security monitors to improve early warning.

Workshop on ‘Trauma for First Responders’ held in Tehran
TEHRAN – The Iranian Red Crescent Society (IRCS), in cooperation with the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC), has held the first three-day training workshop on ‘Trauma for First Responders’ for selected IRCS personnel, with a focus on trauma and pre-hospital care.
The training aims to enhance the emergency response and pre-hospital care capacities of the IRCS personnel, particularly in mass-casualty incidents, to provide timely and effective lifesaving services and ensure the safe evacuation and transfer of injured and sick people, the ICRC website announced in a press release on September 26.
The recent escalation of hostilities has created significant operational challenges for the IRCS Relief and Rescue Organization, one of the key actors at the forefront of emergency response. Its teams are often among the first responders at the scene of mass-casualty incidents and, in high-risk environments, are responsible for evacuating casualties, stabilizing patients and carrying out emergency transfers. This has further highlighted the importance of strengthening technical preparedness through specialized training in mass-casualty management.
The training brought together eight IRCS personnel from the Training, Relief and Rescue, and Emergency Health departments from Tehran and Alborz provinces.
In the opening ceremony, IRCS Under-Secretary-General for Education, Research and Technology, Dr. Rajaei, said the course aims to improve staff knowledge and skill levels, bring education closer to global standards, and eventually form a specialized team for pre-hospital trauma.
“The planning for the course began last year after the first hostilities.” Explained Navid Dadbin, Health Program Manager at the ICRC. “It will be implemented with three 3-day training courses followed by selection of a group of participants to be trained as trainers. A road map for continuation will be drawn up in the end,” he added.
The courses include theoretical and practical sessions, group work, scenario-based exercises covering different types of incidents, and simulation exercises.
The workshop is part of a broader capacity-building cooperation between the ICRC and IRCS, aimed at strengthening the capacities of IRCS operational personnel.
TOT workshop on psychological support for specialist teams
In August, the IRCS and the ICRC organized a Training of Trainers (TOT) workshop on ‘Delivering Psychosocial Support for the Specialist Teams of the Iranian Red Crescent Society.’
The three-day workshop, held from August 24 to 26 in Tehran, aimed at strengthening mental health and psychosocial support for IRCS emergency responders.
It responded to the psychological pressures faced by Relief and Rescue personnel working in conflict, crisis and other high-pressure environments, the ICRC website announced in a press release on August 26.
Approximately 20 IRCS psychologists from across the country participated in the training. The workshop combined theoretical learning, practical exercises and facilitated discussions, covering responder wellbeing and resilience, peer support, identification of psychological distress, referral pathways, supportive interventions and self-care.
“The initiative follows four earlier workshops conducted last year, which trained approximately 160 IRCS first responder personnel”, Roman Paramanov, the deputy head of the ICRC delegation in Iran, said in the opening ceremony of the workshop.
The workshop used a two-phase cascade training model to extend psychosocial support across the IRCS Relief and Rescue Organization. In the first phase, participants from provinces received this three-day Training of Trainers (ToT), strengthening their skills in responder wellbeing, self-care, peer support, psychological distress identification and referral.
In the second phase, the trained psychologists work in 10 co-facilitation pairs, delivering mental self-care and psychosocial support workshops to Heads of Relief and Rescue Bases and operational personnel.
Through this cascade approach, the program aims to reach approximately 600 IRCS staff, while ongoing supervision, online follow-up and technical support help ensure consistent application and sustainability.

Bank of England said to be reviewing Barclays’ handling of private credit loans
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
11:59:23 UTC
20:59:23 KST

The Bank of England is reportedly looking into Barclays’ handling of loans linked to the embattled private credit sector.
The Bank’s regulatory arm, the Prudential Regulation Authority (PRA), started reviewing the matter this year after concerns were raised by a Barclays insider, according to the Financial Times.
The concerns related to the way Barclays logged the derivatives, known as total return swaps, used to finance the loans it issues to private credit firms. Those derivatives – financial contracts that track the performance of an underlying asset – are said to have been logged in the wrong portfolio, indicating they were less risky than they actually were.
That could mean the bank was not holding enough capital to cover potential losses, and could have boosted its profitability.
Barclays is said to have built up billions of dollars’ worth of exposure to private credit loans using derivatives, according to sources cited by the Financial Times.
The bank said: “Barclays’ treatment of total return swaps is consistent with accounting and regulatory capital requirements.”
It added that it followed capital rules when deciding where to log certain assets. “Those conditions were met and supported by appropriate governance internally and by external advisers,” Barclays said.
The bank said its total exposure to the private credit sector was worth about £15bn, and that the relevant derivatives accounted for £300m of that total.
The Bank of England declined to comment.
Shares in Barclays fell by 3.5% on Monday, the second-biggest faller on the FTSE 100 index, amid a wider sell-off in the banking sector. The bank is due to report its latest financial results on Thursday.
The report could prove awkward for the new PRA boss, Katharine Braddick, who spent six years as Barclays’ head of strategic policy and senior adviser to its chief executive, before becoming head of the bank regulator this spring.
The Bank of England said Braddick was recused from all matters relating to Barclays until the end of 2026.
Last year, Barclays’ chief executive, CS Venkatakrishnan, insisted it had the right controls in place to manage its exposure to the private credit industry, where critics worry lending standards have slipped.
Private credit firms – which form a core part of the shadow banking sector – use investor money to fund their loans to companies, rather than customer loans or deposits, and face less regulation as a result.
Traditional banks, worried about missing out on a booming market, started lending directly to private credit firms or their funds, and to companies that simultaneously borrowed from private credit firms. A growing number of banks have also been partnering with asset managers on private credit deals.
However, critics worry that private credit players have been too lenient in deciding who to lend to, and regulators have said any fallout could destabilise traditional banks that are now intertwined with the industry.
Growing anxieties also triggered a multibillion-pound surge in withdrawals from some private credit funds earlier this year, forcing some to cap the amount of money that clients can pull out.
The private credit industry has been trying to recover after some high-profile company failures, including two private credit-backed US automotive companies, Tricolor and First Brands, last year, both of which were hit by fraud allegations. That was followed by the mortgage lender Market Financial Solutions (MFS), which collapsed in February amid allegations of fraud.
Barclays was among the banks that suffered losses on the back of Tricolor’s collapse, alongside JP Morgan. Barclays also took a £228m hit after the MFS failure.

WFP releases September report on Iran
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
11:57:44 UTC
20:57:44 KST

WFP releases September report on Iran
TEHRAN – The World Food Program (WFP) has released a report, expounding on activities in Iran over the month of September.
In September, WFP food assistance reached 35,739 beneficiaries, including Afghan and Iraqi refugees, through a hybrid combination of in-kind food and cash-based transfers (CBT).
Refugees are assisted with a staple food basket, which includes fortified wheat flour (a ration of 9 kg per person, reduced from 12 Kg since the month of November 2025 due to funding shortfalls).
Under CBT modality, WFP continued to provide cash assistance to support the essential living costs of vulnerable refugees. The transfer is IRR 8 million (USD 4.99) for households headed by men and IRR 9 million (USD 5.6) for households headed by women.
By September, WFP Iran helped ease the financial burden associated with the gluten-free dietary needs of 60 refugee celiac patients from WFP’s beneficiaries by providing them with an extra cash amount of IRR 9.7 million (USD 6) per person as a replacement for their usual food entitlement.
WFP supported 411 refugees with disabilities across eleven settlements, each receiving an additional monthly cash support of IRR 3 million (USD 1.8), on top of their regular aid. Initially launched in two provinces, the initiative was gradually expanded to cover 11 settlements in Saveh, Semnan, Bani Najar, Sarvestan, Bezileh, Abazar, Rafsanjan, Bardsir, Jahrom, Meybod, and Torbat-e-jam.
The school feeding program and education incentives remained suspended due to summer holidays, to be resumed with the start of the new academic year.
In September, WFP supported 27 income-generating projects in 18 settlements to improve economic resilience and self-sufficiency for 299 refugees, 38 percent of whom were women, and the remainder were youth. These activities included welding, tailoring, baking, farming, and other trades, providing opportunities for women and youth to develop practical skills, strengthen social connections, and actively engage with their communities.
As part of the response to the recent escalation, WFP started to provide cash transfers affected Iranian households, with the first round completed reaching 340 households, of which 327 were male-headed households.
During September, fourteen rounds of cash transfers were completed for members of the host community affected by the conflict across five provinces: Tehran, Alborz, Sistan-Baluchestan, Bushehr, and Hormozgan.
In total, 24,175 individuals (6,166 households) received WFP assistance during the month.
Verified and eligible households received cash assistance based on household size.
 
Households with one to three members received IRR 210,000,000; households with four to five members received IRR 350,000,000; and households with six or more members received the maximum transfer amount of IRR 420,000,000.
Operational needs in Iran remain fluid and require regular adjustment and reassessment of funding requirements.
 
Despite the uncertain response scale –driven both by continued refugee movements and the evolving needs of the host community – available resources remain insufficient to meet the needs of impacted populations under any currently foreseeable scenario.
In 2025, WFP sustained food assistance to some 33,300 vulnerable refugees living in 20 settlements across 13 provinces, including 404 refugees with disabilities (40 percent women) who received monthly cash top-ups. About 183 women and 190 men received WFP livelihood support.
WFP doubled cash transfer values since January 2025, safeguarding access to food amid price volatility and protecting the most vulnerable households.
Assistance remained uninterrupted, with targeted adjustments: wheat flour entitlements reduced from 12 kg to 9 kg (Nov-Dec) and school snacks paused (Oct-Dec) to stretch limited resources.
To promote girls’ education and reduce barriers to attendance, approximately 2,629 girl students received cash incentives as part of WFP’s commitment to empowering young women. Some 9,261 boys and girls and their teachers benefitted from WFP school snacks.
For more than four decades, the Islamic Republic of Iran has hosted Afghans fleeing conflict and hardship. In 2025, WFP remained essential to protecting the food security of vulnerable refugees residing in 20 settlements, where households rely on shelter, education and primary health care by the Government and other humanitarian actors, complemented by WFP’s monthly food assistance (through cash and in-kind modalities).
The program’s focus is on maintaining a dignified minimum basic needs while prioritizing those with the highest vulnerability, including households headed by women and persons with disabilities.
Operations are implemented in close collaboration and coordination with the Center for Alien and Foreign Immigrant Affairs (CAFIA), WFP’s primary governmental counterpart, and with International Non-Governmental Organizations (INGO) and UN agencies, mainly the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR), to ensure coherent refugee support and referral pathways.
Despite a complex year, marked by economic volatility and temporary operational risks, WFP sustained core assistance to settlement refugees. To safeguard purchasing power, WFP increased cash-based transfer values by 100 percent in January 2025 following the recommendation of a settlement-specific Minimum Expenditure Basket (MEB) assessment; this was complemented by a one-time cash top-up to cushion households during market instability and reduced income after the Iran-Israel 12-day conflict.
Targeted adjustments preserved program continuity: wheat flour entitlements were reduced from 12 kg to 9 kg per person for November-December, and the school snacks program was suspended for October to December.
These measures limit service disruptions while protecting life-saving transfers for the most vulnerable. Livelihood activities were scaled down given funding shortfalls and corporate efficiency measures, with WFP continuing to explore cost-effective, resilience-building options that can be re-activated as resources allow.
By December 2025, Iran continued to be one of the world’s largest refugee-hosting countries, sheltering approximately 2.5 million Afghans, including 773,000 individuals with official refugee status. Among them, around 35,000 critically vulnerable refugees reside in 20 settlements across 13 provinces.

Russian crimes against media rapidly increasing – temporary commission chair Kravchuk
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19

20:56:15 KST

Russian Federation crimes against media workers are growing exponentially, stated Yevheniya Kravchuk (Servant of the People faction), Chair of the Verkhovna Rada Temporary Commission of Inquiry (TCI) into crimes committed by armed formations of Russia against journalists and media professionals.
"The latest meeting of our Temporary Commission of Inquiry was held in Kharkiv... The main conclusion: Russian crimes against media are growing exponentially," Kravchuk reported on Facebook on Monday.
According to her, while at the beginning of the year Russians employed the "double tap" tactic—a secondary strike at the attack site to target first responders, medics, and journalists working on scene—they now frequently launch strikes in three or even four consecutive waves. Kravchuk recalled that in frontline areas, news crews are required to include safety officers because journalists and camera operators cannot physically monitor drone detectors and work simultaneously.
The MP emphasized that Russians continue trying to sever frontline communities from news and information, which is why Ukraine continuously restores radio towers and broadcasting infrastructure in Kharkiv region.
"In addition to Russian crimes, internal issues persist. In particular, unfair competition from anonymous Telegram channels. They violate embargoes on publishing news about strikes, which not only puts registered media at a disadvantage but frequently provides the enemy with real-time targeting data for follow-up strikes," Kravchuk noted.
She stressed that current regulatory frameworks provide almost no legal basis for holding administrators of such channels accountable, especially as they often operate from abroad, unlike local journalists.
Kravchuk highlighted that war crimes specifically directed at journalists remain complex to qualify and investigate.
"Since 2022, 6 crimes against 8 journalists and 19 crimes involving damage to media-related property (newsrooms, TV towers, equipment) have been officially documented in Kharkiv region. Only 2 cases have been submitted to court. Why so few? Because war crimes tied to media work are harder to qualify and investigate, and journalists often choose not to file official reports—for instance, when becoming targets of cyberattacks or information campaigns," Kravchuk wrote.
At the same time, she drew attention to indisputably proven cases where media personnel were the primary target of enemy strikes.
"The most egregious case remains the attack on the Kharkiv Palace hotel on December 30, 2023. Russian propaganda reported 'destroyed mercenaries,' even though the enemy knew full well that foreign journalists were hosted at the hotel. Furthermore, press conferences were regularly held in the hotel's media center," the MP stated.
Kravchuk also announced that the TCI's next session is scheduled for October 28 and will focus on Ukrainian journalists held in Russian captivity.

Nearly half of world's reef-building coral species face extinction risk: Study
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
11:55:12 UTC
20:55:12 KST

Faisal Mahmud
19 October 2026•Update: 19 October 2026
Nearly 44% of the world's reef-building coral species face an elevated risk of extinction, primarily due to rising ocean temperatures linked to climate change, according to a new study.
The research, published Thursday in the scientific journal Nature, assessed 892 reef-building coral species using the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) Red List criteria.
Of the 774 species with sufficient data, 340 were classified as threatened, including 33 critically endangered, 251 endangered and 56 vulnerable.
Researchers from institutions including the Australian Institute of Marine Science and the University of Queensland examined coral population trends and projected heat stress, updating a 2008 assessment.
The study identified climate-driven heat stress as the main cause of projected population declines.
Reef-building corals are marine animals whose hard skeletons form the foundations of tropical reefs. Rising water temperatures can cause them to expel the algae living in their tissues, which provide nutrients and give corals their color.
The process, known as coral bleaching, leaves corals vulnerable to starvation, disease and death.
Researchers warned that the assessment predates the record ocean heat and global coral bleaching event of 2023-2025, meaning the proportion of threatened species could now be higher.
Coral reefs support diverse marine life and provide food, coastal protection and livelihoods in more than 100 tropical countries.
The researchers stressed that limiting further warming remains essential to preserving coral biodiversity.

Istanbul flood toll rises to 8 as rescuers find bodies
ISTANBUL – The toll from flooding in and around Istanbul last week rose to eight on Oct 19, as rescuers found more bodies after Turkey’s largest city was battered by the heaviest rainfall in more than 80 years, officials said.
Six died in Istanbul, while the bodies of two more people from a neighbouring province were washed up on the south-eastern outskirts of the megacity, Istanbul governor Davut Gul told reporters.
The Oct 14 historic rainfall – which officials said was the heaviest since records began in 1942 – caused chaos and flash flooding, with footage showing cars and people being dragged away by the fast-flowing waters.
By Oct 15, Gul said three people had died and another five were missing as huge efforts were under way to drain the floodwaters and clear up the damage and destruction caused by the torrential rainfall.
One was a 14-year-old boy who was electrocuted when he stepped in a puddle. A fourth body was found on Oct 16 and a fifth on Oct 18 in the Golden Horn estuary, state media Anadolu said. Both were men.
On Oct 19, Gul’s office said the body of another man, who had been reported missing, was found near Ayvansaray ferry pier on the Golden Horn.
“In Istanbul, a total of six people have died, and one person is missing,” Gul told reporters, adding that another two people had died outside of Istanbul in the neighbouring province of Kocaeli.
“Two people who died in Kocaeli and were swept as far away as Pendik were found dead by our search and rescue teams. Therefore, a total of eight bodies have been found,” he said, adding that search efforts were continuing for one more missing person.
So far, the authorities have received nearly 20,000 reports about property damage as a result of the torrential rainfall and resulting floods, Gul said.
“We experienced a disaster that generated around 19,300 reports, each with different types of problems. At this point, it has been determined that around 2,000 homes and about 900 businesses... have suffered serious damage,” he said.
On Oct 16, the authorities paid out 10,000 Turkish lira (S$258) to 5,200 affected residents and will pay out the same amount to another 2,500 people on Oct 19, he said. AFP

The court ordered pretrial detention for both of them, with the possibility of bail. Under Article 62 of the Constitution of Ukraine, a person is presumed innocent until their guilt is proven by a guilty verdict of a court," the post says.

Mitsubishi to Reopen Shipbuilding Yard in Tamano Amid Rising Orders
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
11:50:37 UTC
20:50:37 KST

Mitsubishi Heavy Industries plans to resume operations at its shipbuilding slipway in Tamano, Okayama Prefecture, in fiscal year 2027.
The Japanese outlet Nikkei reported this.
The company aims to expand its warship-building capacity amid rising defense spending in Japan and growing opportunities to export military equipment.
In particular, the company is considering using the slipway to build a new support vessel for the Japan Ministry of Defense.
Mitsubishi Heavy Industries also plans to increase the number of employees involved in shipbuilding.
The slipway is at Maritime Systems’ main plant in Tamano, a subsidiary of Mitsubishi Heavy Industries. The facility was previously owned by Mitsui Shipbuilding, now known as Mitsui E&S.
In 2021, Mitsubishi Heavy Industries took over the company’s shipbuilding business after it exited the sector.
Militarnyi previously reported that the Chief of the Royal New Zealand Navy had visited the Japanese Ministry of Defense and expressed interest in acquiring Japanese frigates to modernize the country’s surface fleet.
Construction of New FFM Frigates
One of Mitsubishi Heavy Industries’ main areas of activity is the construction of Mogami-class frigates. In August 2025, Australia selected an upgraded version of the vessel to modernize its navy.
On April 18, 2026, the parties signed a contract to build the first three frigates.
Japan has also started procuring next-generation frigates under the New FFM program, known as the 06FFM. The country plans to acquire a total of 12 such vessels for the Japan Maritime Self-Defense Force. The plan calls for building up to two frigates per year, which will require expanding shipbuilding capacity.
To avoid delays from occupied dry docks and slipways, the company plans to concentrate frigate construction at Japan’s main shipyards.
Meanwhile, the company plans to shift construction of other vessel types, including support ships, to secondary production facilities.

UK faces 'economic catastrophe, moral failure' over youth unemployment: Premier
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
11:49:05 UTC
20:49:05 KST

Aysu Bicer
19 October 2026•Update: 19 October 2026
The UK faces an "economic catastrophe and moral failure" as nearly 1 million young people remain outside education, employment or training, Prime Minister Andy Burnham warned Monday.
Writing in The Times newspaper, Burnham called on the government to "invest in the success of our young people" rather than "pay for failure through the benefits system."
"Benefits will become the backstop, not the starting point," he wrote in an opinion article published Monday.
Burnham also said a long-awaited review of young people and work would be published next month, pledging to take its recommendations "seriously."
According to the latest data from the Office for National Statistics, nearly 1 million people aged 16 to 24 in the UK are not in education, employment or training.
Around 39% of them are unemployed, while the remaining 61% are economically inactive, meaning they are not seeking work, the figures showed.
Burnham attributed the crisis to several factors, including two years of COVID-19 lockdowns, social media, an education system focused on university education, limited job opportunities and failures by previous governments.
He argued that social media erodes young people's "confidence and sense of belonging."
"This is an economic catastrophe and a moral failure. And it must change," he wrote.
Burnham criticized the current welfare system, arguing that it often provides financial support without offering young people a route into employment.
"Today, the welfare system provides an assessment, a payment and, after that, goodbye," he wrote.
"Too often there is no support, no offer of skills and no opportunity to get a job."
He said the government's approach should shift toward identifying young people's ambitions and providing the assistance needed to achieve them, rather than beginning with an assessment of benefit entitlement.
"The safety net will always be there for those who cannot work. But if someone can work with the right help, the government has a duty to do everything in its power to make that happen," Burnham said.

The Sudanese army said Monday it had repelled a ground attack by the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) and its ally, the Sudan People’s Liberation Movement-North (SPLM-N), in southeastern Blue Nile state, while its air defenses intercepted a drone attack east of the capital Khartoum.
In a statement, the army’s 14th Infantry Division said its forces thwarted an attack by the RSF and SPLM-N on the Al-Baraka area in the southern sector of Blue Nile state.
The division said its troops inflicted heavy casualties and equipment losses on the attacking forces, preventing them from advancing toward army positions.
It added that several military vehicles were destroyed and the attackers were forced to retreat under heavy fire.
The division said the operation demonstrated the army’s readiness to respond to any hostile movements threatening its positions or the security of civilians and their property.
There was no immediate comment from the RSF or SPLM-N on the army’s claims.
Blue Nile state has witnessed escalating military tensions in recent weeks following attacks by the RSF and SPLM-N on several areas.
 
Drone attack
In a separate development, military sources told Anadolu that army air defenses intercepted an RSF drone attack east of Khartoum on Monday, near Khartoum International Airport.
The sources said all attacking drones were shot down but did not specify their number.
Witnesses also told Anadolu that explosions were heard in the skies over eastern Khartoum on Monday morning.
Videos circulated on social media showed a drone flying over the Sudanese capital the same day.
There was no immediate comment from Sudanese authorities or the RSF on the reported drone attack.
On May 4, Sudan’s Information Ministry reported that a site within Khartoum International Airport had been targeted by a drone, without causing casualties or material damage.
Sudanese authorities and human rights organizations have accused the RSF of targeting civilian facilities. The group rarely comments on such accusations but maintains that it works to protect civilians.
Since April 2023, the Sudanese army and RSF have been engaged in a war that erupted over disagreements concerning the integration of the paramilitary group into the country’s military.
The conflict has killed tens of thousands of people and displaced around 13 million, while worsening famine and humanitarian conditions in what has become one of the world’s worst humanitarian crises.

Koretsky: government to review draft deferral rules due to sharp rise in deferred workers
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
14:46:54 EEST
20:46:54 KST

The Cabinet of Ministers of Ukraine has decided to review the rules and criteria for the deferral procedure for draft-eligible employees, as the monthly volume of military draft deferrals has reached tens of thousands of people and is growing at an unsustainable rate, Prime Minister Serhiy Koretsky reported in an interview with BBC News Ukraine.
"Statistics over the last 6–8 months show a monthly deferral rate in the tens of thousands. And it is growing at an incredible pace. If this dynamic continues, soon absolutely everyone will be deferred. Everyone says that today obtaining a deferral to secure peace of mind from mobilization has become significantly easier. Therefore, to at least stop this dynamic, which has taken on a very negative trend, and to avoid abuse and manipulation within the system, we are proposing a revision of the rules," the head of government stated.
The prime minister denied claims that the government halted the decision to change the rules due to scandal or public criticism, dismissing such assertions as manipulation. According to him, the top priority remains the country's defense capability and meeting the General Staff's mobilization needs for troop rotations, as well as replacing the wounded and fallen.
Koretsky emphasized that the key objective of the updated mechanism is to minimize abuses where companies are created under the guise of critically important enterprises for mass employee deferrals despite not being involved in executing vital tasks. Meanwhile, the two core criteria for determining an enterprise's critical status must remain defense capability and state life support.
"Criticality comes down to two main points: defense capability and state life support. Therefore, step number one is to define what is truly critical, and there are zero questions about those. Nothing to worry about. Those who should worry are those who set up a company that produces, say, two drones a year, yet deferred hundreds of people as employees," the prime minister noted.
Speaking about the possible implementation of so-called "economic deferral," the prime minister remarked that high salary levels and an absence of tax debts are not synonymous with a company's critical importance to the state during wartime, and also raise questions of fairness regarding service members on the front lines.
The head of government expressed hope that the final details of the updated deferral system will be agreed upon and refined over the course of the current week. According to him, the changes will not harm strategic sectors, particularly energy ahead of the winter period.
As reported, news of changes to the deferral procedure emerged on October 12, when MP Yaroslav Zheleznyak cited personal sources regarding the revisions. It was later revealed that the government had approved a draft resolution subject to a five-day revision of certain provisions. However, the resolution itself was not published on the Cabinet website.
Business associations subsequently reported that they did not support the draft resolution and that the government had failed to conduct consultations regarding possible changes, urging an open discussion of the document's provisions and a dialogue with the government and relevant authorities. In particular, joint appeals were issued by the Union of Ukrainian Entrepreneurs (SUP), the European Business Association (EBA), the Federation of Employers of Ukraine (FRU), the Economic Expert Platform (comprising 16 analytical organizations), the National Association of Extractive Industry of Ukraine (NAEIU), Executive Secretary of the Ukrainian Association of Critical Infrastructure Operators (UACIO) Ruslan Holub, Tech Forces of Ukraine (TSU), the Armorers Council (132 defense organizations), the National Association of Ukrainian Defense Industries (NAUDI), volunteer organizations assisting the military, and the Union of Dairy Enterprises.
According to the draft Cabinet resolution available to Interfax-Ukraine, the document provides for the establishment of a Coordination Center as a consultative and advisory body to the Cabinet, serving as an additional clearance stage before decisions are made by line ministries regarding enterprise criticality designations.
The draft also envisages lowering the deferral quota limit from 100% to 85% for employees of defense-industrial complex (DIC) enterprises, critical companies, and contractors in the fuel and energy sector that ensure the uninterrupted operation of the power system and gas transmission network, alongside reducing the normative deferral quota for certain categories of institutions from 75% to 60%. Furthermore, increasing deferral limits beyond 50% would be possible exclusively on the basis of recommendations from the Coordination Center.
In addition, the draft introduces a mandatory clearance stage through this center prior to decisions being made by line ministries on defining enterprises as critically important.
It also regulates decision-making procedures by government bodies based on the Coordination Center's recommendations within 3 business days. According to an evaluation by the Ministry of Finance, the draft resolution was approved without objections, as its implementation does not require additional expenditures from the state budget and will not impact current-period budget indicators.
