Horrible, unmanly, indispensable
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

Listen to this essay
27 minute listen
If you were asked to think of a gun owner, then Lorenzo de’ Medici – the celebrated patron of Renaissance art – would probably not be the first person to come to mind. In fact, however, Lorenzo ‘the Magnificent’ owned five portable firearms, which are listed in his 1492 postmortem inventory. Guns and gunpowder were controversial. In art and literature, they were labelled the Devil’s work, and were perceived as fundamentally unchivalrous. Yet within half a century, by the early months of 1539, Lorenzo’s descendant Duke Cosimo de’ Medici had 91 firearms in his Florentine storerooms. Somehow, in the courts of late-Renaissance Italy, the gun had become an acceptable, even valued, weapon.
Beyond the palazzi of the peninsula’s towns and cities, guns were also making inroads into more ordinary lives. There were no standing armies in the 16th-century Italian states. Their wars were fought through temporary mobilisations, and with considerable help from companies of mercenaries. Yet as the 1506 provision that established the Florentine militia made clear, ‘little hope’ could be placed ‘in foreign and hired arms’. Far better to establish a new magistracy with ‘full authority and power’ to enlist men from Florentine territory, at least 10,000 of them. One in 10 of these men were to be equipped with firearms, and 500 handguns (schioppetti) should be kept in the Palazzo della Signoria (the city hall, now known as the Palazzo Vecchio) along with ‘such money as should be necessary for the schioppetti’, presumably to purchase gunpowder and shot. Three or four companies (bandiere) entirely of schioppettieri might also be established.
This militia, most often noted for the role of Niccolò Machiavelli in its foundation, was to be organised after the fashion of the Germans, in whose cities there was a centuries-old tradition of civic defence and a duty on every male citizen to maintain suitable arms for the purpose. In fact, one of the Florentine militia’s early constables was German (a Giovanni Tedesco); another (Giliberto Spagnolo) came from Spain, a country making the running in the use of small arms on the battlefield. Giovanni Tedesco arranged target practice for his company, which from 1508 was extended more generally among the militia, with exercises taking place on a monthly basis.
Militias were not new but, by the 1490s, large-scale foreign military intervention on the Italian peninsula was giving a new impetus to their development, as was the growing importance of infantry in the military context. In Friuli, where Venetian lands bordered Ottoman territory, the militia were using handguns from the 1490s, and city guards across the Italian peninsula were soon provided with guns too. The growth of militias was the single most important factor in the proliferation of firearms in 16th-century Italy. This is too early a period for the kind of autobiographical writing that would tell us what these men made of the process, but there was certainly ample encouragement to become familiar with firearms and acquire shooting skills.
The backdrop to these developments was the decades of war in which France and Spain contended for hegemony on the Italian Peninsula. In the 1480s, while pitching his services to the duke of Milan, Leonardo da Vinci, highlighting his potential as a military engineer, wrote:
I have also plans of mortars most convenient and easy to carry with which to hurl small stones in the manner almost of a storm; and with the smoke of this cause great terror to the enemy and great loss and confusion.
By the turn of the century, Spanish arquebusiers – named for the long, wooden-stocked gun with which they were armed – were doing precisely that on the battlefields of Italy. As the conflicts of 1494-1559 rolled on, the rulers of the peninsula’s multiple states promoted shooting in the interests of civic defence and military preparedness and, as they did, their own use of firearms shifted too.
The Medici were not the only leading family of Renaissance Italy to take an interest in this new military technology. In 1538, the duke of another Italian city-state, Urbino, described a novel firearm as ‘very dear to me’. Such appreciation, however, ran counter to the dominant image of guns in the period’s literature. Leonhard Fronsperger, once a captain of the ducal armoury in Munich, wrote of gunpowder as ‘indispensable’, but also as ‘horrible’ and ‘unmanly’. Ludovico Ariosto’s epic poem Orlando Furioso (1532) described guns as a ‘foul and pestilent discovery’, weapons through which ‘no more shall gallantry, no more shall valour prove their prowess’. Only in edgier texts, like the swashbuckling memoirs of the goldsmith and sculptor Benvenuto Cellini, did anyone hint that guns were fun. ‘Frightened’ by a plague that hit Rome in the early 1520s causing thousands of deaths, Cellini ‘began to seek relief in a sport that I found very enjoyable’. In between sketching the city’s ancient ruins, he shot pigeons. He developed his own gunpowder recipe, and boasted of his ‘really good marksmanship’, claiming to be able to shoot ‘200 yards point-blank’. This is probably exaggerated, but just as relevant is Cellini’s explanation that, by getting him out into the fresh air to go hunting, and combating his ‘naturally melancholy disposition’, his gun ‘brought me more gain than loss’.
The textual enthusiasm of both Cellini and the duke of Urbino finds a material counterpart in a growing culture of luxury weapons. The aesthetics of these high-end guns helped firearms fit into a court culture that valued beauty and craftsmanship. They were decorated with classical gods, Christian figures and mottoes, and images of the hunt, while the novelty value of combination weapons such as spears with miniature guns attached appealed to the Renaissance sense of fun.
Records of gun ownership in elite households, too, tell a different story from the literary sources. It is at court that wheellock guns – a groundbreaking technology that allowed concealed carry – first leave traces. Leonardo’s sketches of their mechanisms (probably developed in Germany) can be seen in the Codex Atlanticus. Expensive, convenient and modern, wheellocks seem to have become a status symbol. The standard military firearm of this period, the matchlock, was fired by means of a lighted cord (the match) that ignited the powder when the gun was triggered. But the wheellock was a self-lighting mechanism that avoided the need for a lighted match. It was a more complex and therefore more expensive technology, and could be unreliable (probably especially if produced on the cheap). On the other hand, wheellocks had advantages in hunting, avoiding as they did the glow and smell of the burning match cord which might alert prey to a hunter’s presence.
Designs echoed court imagery: hunting scenes, battles, motifs from ancient history and myth, biblical figures
By the start of 1539, Duke Cosimo de’ Medici owned four wheellock handguns made in the German style that he (or more likely his bodyguards) took with him when he travelled. Not a decade on, a wheellock appeared in the first portrait of a European ruler with a handgun: Titian’s equestrian portrait of the victorious Emperor Charles V after the Battle of Mühlberg, in which Charles is shown ‘in the manner in which he went against the rebels’, that is, in the garb of the wheellock-toting Spanish cavalry.
The aesthetic qualities of high-end firearms helped guns blend into the wider courtly environment. Designs echoed imagery common to the court: hunting scenes, battles, motifs from ancient history and myth, or biblical figures like Judith. A wheellock pistol made in Germany and dated 1548 features a figure of the Roman heroine Lucretia along with a Christian motto and image of the Crucifixion. By this time, guns were finding new uses in Europe’s religious wars: far from the Devil’s weapon, they were a means of asserting true Christianity against the heretics.
Back at court, novelty weapons such as the match-fired combination pollaxe and gun in the Royal Armouries, or the boar-spear with two small guns attached given to Cosimo de’ Medici, engaged with a fashion for wider theatrical and festival machines aimed at provoking wonder in their audience. These firearms functioned as marketing devices, promoting their makers – and perhaps also the cities or states of their makers – as potential providers too of the thousands of weapons that might be commissioned for use in war. A striking indication of their acceptability in elite culture comes in 1553, when Mantuan officials began to make ceremonial presents of firearms to the city’s duke in place of the crossbows they had previously given. That the gun could now appear in these ritual contexts shows it had truly arrived.
In wider society, luxury decoration was out of reach, but other factors favoured an expansion of gun ownership. Florence was not the only state to establish or revive a civic militia. In the context of long-running on-off war, it made sense for rulers across Italy to mobilise citizens and equip them with up-to-date weapons. Alongside requirements for militia drill went contests to incentivise the acquisition of shooting skills. Farmers found guns useful for pest control; hunters used them too. Thus, in the 1520s and beyond, more and more Italian states formalised or expanded their militia. Giovanni Moro, a Venetian official who had previously handled military supplies, proposed in 1525 the formation of a citizen militia of 12,000 men, of whom two-thirds would use firearms; these men would receive powder and lead for practice, and a contest would be held three times a year to encourage them. This would be, said Moro, to the ‘honour and utility’ of Venice, and of ‘great benefit’ when it came to conserving Venetian territory.
Such ambitious plans didn’t always succeed, as two cases from Tuscany show. Jacopo Pessina’s detailed study of military organisation in the Republic of Siena estimates that in the last 30 years of the republic (1525-55), between 20 and 33 per cent of adult men served in the militia, with each 500-strong battalion including 150-200 arquebusiers. A report from 1543, however, suggested that the militia was not fit for purpose, lacking not only sufficient men but also the necessary firearms and helmets. The case of Florence, moreover, where the last republican government of 1527-30 fell to the Spanish-backed Medici party after a long siege, shows the limits of a city militia in the face of a foreign army. Anticipating attack, the republican government issued new ordinances for the militia, instituting training in the use of arquebuses, and shooting contests. During the siege of 1530, artisans from shoemakers to cutlers were equipped with arquebuses. They did not, however, prevail against the much better-resourced Spanish army. Still, governments across Italy continued to expand their militia, which made firearms increasingly available to men of all social ranks.
‘Every low herdsman or shepherd you meet in the countryside today has a wheellock arquebus over his shoulder’
If militia service provided one route to familiarity with firearms, so did the related rise of shooting contests. In 1506, Venice introduced a competition to encourage the development of handgun skills among the archers serving on its naval galleys. In 1518, the first prize was 16 arms-lengths of damask fabric, worth 32 ducats, along with 6 ducats in cash. In 1520, the Republic of Lucca instituted a thrice-yearly shooting contest in order to ensure that its citizens were prepared for defence, the founding decree urging them to prefer ‘death over the loss of dear liberty and the reduction of their fatherland to servitude’. Prizes included a silver cup worth almost 20 ducats, and six arms-lengths of damask worth 5 ducats. Soldiers’ pay could be less than 30 ducats a year, so these were generous rewards. Contests, however, were not only about financial incentives. They were also about establishing an acceptable social image for the firearm, just as the iconography of luxury weapons had done at court. The language of the Lucca decree, for example, offered a new and more positive discourse of the gun, as a weapon for the defence of liberty.
Hunting was another context in which guns became familiar not just for elites but more widely. In 1552, for example, a cowherd named Vincenzo obtained a licence from the Bologna authorities that allowed him to carry arms, including a gun for the purpose of hunting. It came with the standard caveat that the weapon must not be carried in churches, at festivals or in markets. These were busy environments where an accidental misfire had higher risks than out in the countryside, and where a generalised ban on arms-bearing (staff weapons such as pikes were also included) made policing more straightforward. Such wide access to guns, however, was a matter of concern. The anonymous author of a proposition for international gun control observed, probably in the late 1570s, that if the Italian princes did not take action soon, then ‘there will be no place nor state where people are safe, given that every low herdsman or shepherd you meet in the countryside today has a wheellock arquebus over his shoulder’.
As guns became more common, so did their appearance in the criminal records. By 1600, firearms had become the predominant weapon used to commit homicide in Bologna. That said, they still accounted for only a third of offences, and in interpreting the figures we should bear in mind the relative lethality of guns when compared with other weapons. In fact, across the broad range of gun crime, it was still relatively rare to come across cases where guns were directly used in planned homicide. More commonly, they were used to threaten: the ideal outcome for the highwayman who shouts: ‘Your money or your life!’ is to ride away with the money without firing a shot.
Many of the historic investigations feature possession of illegal guns and/or their use to intimidate. In a 1554 case near the northern Italian city of Brescia, Valerio Soncino and a gang of 20 men ‘armed with various weapons, including arquebuses’, scaled the walls of a property belonging to Valerio’s brother Annibale, and ‘with various threats’ forced two of his stewards to bring them carts, which they loaded up with goods, stealing in addition cattle and a horse. The robbers got only five miles, however, before they were halted by some villagers who had got wind of what was happening and sounded the alarm. In the ensuing violence, two men and a woman among the villagers were injured. Here, the primary use of the guns was to frighten people into doing as they were told, not to kill them. That is not to say, however, that the proliferation of firearms was not risky. Criminal records from Bologna describe a case in 1575 in which an elderly woman named Giovanna was killed by a man named Pierantonio Fangarezzo; Fangarezzo had been looking over an arquebus (perhaps an early variety of flintlock) to see how it worked when it accidentally went off.
In some notionally criminal cases there was also a political motivation for gun ownership
People engaged in, or considering, political violence also used firearms. The distinction between criminal and political activity was not always straightforward. The system of exile in the Italian states – in which offenders were banned from their home territory and had their property confiscated – often made banditry an attractive option (hence the overlap between the concepts in Italian, where the word bandito is also used for an exile). Civic authorities were particularly keen to police weapon ownership when it posed a risk to the regime. The early years of Medici ducal rule in Florence (formally established in 1532) saw numerous confiscations of illegal weapons: Girolamo di Filippo Bonciani and Francesco di Piero Serragli, for example, fell foul of the law after an arquebus was found under the straw of their former stable. Some of these weapons were probably planted by city officials, but opponents of the regime might reasonably have decided to arm themselves in case of an uprising (for which there were several precedents).
Dissidents in Brescia (a subject city of Venice) also obtained weapons: testimony from 1539 shows how one alleged firearm offender, Antonio Maria, was accused of saying several times that ‘he desired nothing more than that the Emperor and the King of France should make an accord against our Venetian lords, and that he hoped to come with them to sack Brescia.’ Antonio Maria was further accused of ‘continually keeping in his house exiled men of a bad sort, who go out killing on the streets’; he had in his house around 25 guns of different types. While we typically learn about these cases from regime records, by reading between the lines it becomes clear that at least in some notionally criminal cases there was also a political motivation for gun ownership.
People in northern and central Italy owned guns for several reasons: to participate in militia service, for hunting and livestock control, and for criminal activity. Some of this ownership was purely practical: a gun would more reliably than the alternatives kill the fox eating your chickens. Some of it had political motivations, whether to defend the liberty of one’s own fatherland or to oppose a tyrannical overlord. By the middle of the 16th century, a lot of people had guns. It is challenging to establish quite how many. Based on population estimates and numbers enrolled in the militia, the historians Michael Mallett and John Hale estimated that one in 15 rural households in Venetian territory would have had a firearm following the establishment of the militia in the later 1520s: ‘the government’, they observed in Military Organisation of a Renaissance State (2009), ‘was calculatedly accepting a risk to public order’. By 1540, the ruler of Modena required that one in three countryside households should have a gun. These calculations concern militia service, however, and other people may have bought guns second-hand from soldiers, or won them via gambling.
Later in the century, larger cities had shops where guns might be mended and probably also purchased. A 1559 proclamation issued in Bologna in anticipation of riots declared that ‘shopkeepers, who sell those polearms and arquebuses, must store them in their shops in such a way that they are not ready to use’. There is no reason to think that the anonymous author who complained of wheellock-toting shepherds was greatly exaggerating the extent of proliferation.
Guns had a role to play in changing ideas about gender, both in general and with reference to images of rulership
Certain moments in wartime no doubt accelerated access to firearms. Besides the 1529-30 Siege of Florence, records of the defensive provisions in Ferrara of 1552 (when the city was likewise preparing for a possible siege) show that, out of 520 households equipped with armour, pikes, arquebuses and morions, more than half (270) had a gun. Included in this list are 18 female heads of household, of whom six had guns. This raises the question of how many women were gun-owners more generally. The answer seems to be rather few. Sieges were emergency situations in which gender norms might temporarily be suspended, such as when the women of Siena took responsibility for repairs to the city walls. Outside the wartime context, Joe Tryner’s study of court records in Bologna turned up only a single example of a woman with a firearm, and nothing in my wider survey of source material has suggested that was untypical.
In contrast, guns did come to be associated with masculinity. In The Fruit of Liberty (2013), Nicholas Scott Baker argued that the siege of 1529-30 was a particular turning point for elite identity, redefining notions of masculinity from those associated with practices of civic governance to something more ‘rugged, militaristic’. This was particularly apparent in changing clothing styles, to which the bearing of new types of arms might be added. Focusing on Florence after 1537, in Masculinity, Arms and Armour (2020), Victoria Bartels identifies guns as one factor in shifting performances of masculinity, noting that they increased the danger attached to ‘routine bouts of aggression’ that had traditionally been employed to settle disputes between men. In the context of the Italian Wars (and specific local conflicts within them), guns had a role to play in changing ideas about gender, both in general and with reference to images of rulership. This is confirmed in the account of Benvenuto Cellini, whose self-aggrandising narrative of his participation in the Italian Wars includes a comment he made to a companion, Alessandro del Bene, to persuade him to stick around and shoot back at an invading army during the 1527 Sack of Rome: ‘Now you’ve brought me here, we must show that we’re men.’
Over the course of the 16th century, familiarity with firearms grew. It was increasingly expected that men would be able to use a gun: the expansion of militias was a key factor here alongside direct soldiering experience. The acquisition of skills in shooting was positively encouraged through civic contests with generous prizes. Rhetoric about the importance of guns for civic defence and for the maintenance of honour and liberty offered a counterweight to more negative images of gunpowder weapons as diabolical, unchivalrous or impious. Guns were useful for protection of livestock from predators as well as for hunting more generally. In turn, their ready availability also made them accessible for use by bandits, during vendettas and indeed for political violence. However, their lethality shifted the dynamics of violent encounters: so effective were guns as a threat that in some cases they may have prompted victims to give up without a fight. On the other hand, with increasing proliferation came an increased risk of both accidents and casual use in interpersonal violence. Yet not all gun ownership was enthusiastic. Some applicants for arms licences evidently felt constrained to carry guns in self-defence, and cultural ambivalence about these weapons remained long after they became common objects.
As firearms became more familiar, it was as much a decision not to be a gun owner as to acquire the new technology.

Bulgaria Targets 3% Deficit as 2027 Budget Debate Exposes Divisions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

Bulgaria will seek to keep its budget deficit within the 3% limit, Deputy Prime Minister Ivo Hristov said on BNT, adding that the final budget figures would depend on parliamentary discussions and subsequent revisions.
Hristov also discussed plans to raise pensions by 8%, public sector salaries by 5%, and teachers’ pay. He argued that the increases should prioritize those most affected by rising costs rather than apply the same approach across the board.
Addressing attacks on ships in the Black Sea, Hristov said it was reasonable to suspect that the drones were Russian, but stressed that Bulgaria should not announce an official position until the investigation is complete. He cautioned that premature conclusions and calls to activate NATO mechanisms could fuel further escalation.
On the proposed moratorium on hostile military operations in the Black Sea, Hristov warned that ending attacks would not resolve all the region’s problems. Naval mines, sunken ships, environmental hazards, and high insurance premiums would continue to pose serious challenges. Restoring safety in the sea, he said, would require sustained efforts and the participation of countries in the region.
Regarding the war in Ukraine, the deputy prime minister said Bulgaria should avoid being pulled into further escalation. He opposed the continuation of military operations and the supply of weapons, describing this position as necessary to limit bloodshed.
Hristov also addressed social unrest in France, saying the roots of the protests lay in problems that had built up over many years. He linked the tensions to growing estrangement between the political elite and dissatisfied citizens, as well as persistent shortcomings in social policy and insufficient dialogue.
Plans for Bulgaria’s 2027 budget were also debated on Nova TV by financial journalist and economic analyst Stefan Antonov and economist Dr. Evgeniy Kanev. Antonov supported gradually reducing the deficit through economic growth, while Kanev argued that the private sector would bear the main cost.
The discussion focused on the government’s plan to raise around €2 billion in additional revenue, alongside criticism that it had not proposed substantial spending cuts. Figures cited during the debate put public expenditure at approximately 45% of gross domestic product (GDP).
Antonov argued that a smaller deficit did not necessarily depend on severe cuts to public spending, saying continued economic growth could reduce the shortfall as a proportion of GDP.
“For the first time in 17 years, we have a government committed to curbing the budget deficit,” Antonov said.
He referred to the austerity measures introduced after 2009, warning that excessively aggressive cuts could suppress economic activity. The current budget plan, he said, includes shifting funds between spending categories, with the changes amounting to around 0.6% of GDP.
Although nominal expenditure is expected to rise, Antonov noted that the government anticipates a gradual decline in public spending as a share of the economy. He cited plans to bring wage expenditure down from almost 11% of GDP to below 8% over three years.
Kanev challenged this approach, arguing that the budget would put additional pressure on private businesses and employees as economic conditions worsen.
“The question is: who foots the bill for this situation? The government’s solution is simple—it should be the private sector,” Kanev said.
He pointed to declining exports, inflation eroding purchasing power, and weaker investor interest. In his assessment, the prospect of eurozone membership had temporarily improved perceptions of Bulgaria, but international uncertainty and tensions in the Black Sea region were now discouraging investment.
Kanev warned that the planned increase in social security contributions would weigh most heavily on workers and businesses operating in the formal economy, while controls over the informal, or gray, sector remained insufficient. He also criticized the state for raising expenditure without presenting convincing structural reforms and questioned the value of the planned 5% across-the-board increase in public sector salaries.
Antonov countered that the government was also planning measures to tackle tax evasion. These include changes to VAT rules for sales of newly built residential properties, which are expected to bring in approximately €120 million in additional revenue.
The two economists also disagreed over whether the budget adequately accounts for the risks of possible restrictions on shipping in the Black Sea. Kanev identified this as a major weakness in the proposed financial framework, warning that disruptions to maritime transport could affect Bulgarian exports and imports of raw materials, with consequences for production and state revenue.
To address the problem, Kanev proposed establishing a temporary state fund to cover part of the higher insurance risk faced by vessels. He said rising premiums were already creating difficulties for businesses and could make Bulgarian products less competitive.
“The only way to halt the rise in these insurance premiums at present is for the state to assume part of the risk,” Kanev said.
Antonov responded that budgets needed to retain reserves for unexpected crises, with the fiscal reserve available to help manage such shocks. He also warned that excessively alarmist statements from public institutions could weaken confidence and worsen economic difficulties.
The debate also covered a possible additional tax on bank profits. Antonov distinguished between advance payments of corporate income tax and a levy specifically targeting “excess profits.” He said a one-off increase in the tax burden on a highly profitable sector could be justified if it helped reduce the deficit and prevented a general tax hike.
However, he cautioned that banks might transfer some of the additional costs to customers through higher fees and interest rates. If banking services became more expensive by similar amounts at the same time, he said, this could raise suspicions of collusion.
Kanev argued that exceptional taxation was justified when companies earned unusually high profits because of a crisis or particular market conditions. He questioned why such measures were being considered for several industries but not for Lukoil, which he believes is benefiting from current energy market conditions.
He disputed claims that the refinery was operating in financially unfavorable circumstances, arguing that its performance should be examined alongside the financial arrangements between companies within the corporate group, including the prices charged for raw material supplies.
Antonov said additional taxation would be difficult to justify if information from the special administrator about the refinery’s low profit margins proved accurate. He also warned that measures aimed specifically at one company could trigger international arbitration. According to him, a warning had been issued about a potential claim by Lukoil’s owners worth approximately 3% of Bulgaria’s GDP.
Kanev rejected the idea that taxation should be linked to the government’s position toward the company’s Russian owners. He argued that the key issue was whether the state applied the same principles to all companies earning windfall profits.
The economists also discussed plans for tighter controls on spending related to decisions on disability assessments, known as TELK, from which the government expects to save €228 million.
Antonov stressed that efforts to prevent abuse must not harm people who genuinely need assistance. Kanev welcomed stricter oversight, saying that curbing misuse could help reduce public expenditure.
Kanev also connected the issue to shortcomings in e-government, estimating that digitizing administrative processes could generate substantial savings.
He further criticized how funds were managed in the healthcare and energy sectors, arguing that the state’s extensive role in distributing financial resources in these areas created significant opportunities for abuse.

Nidal Hasan: America’s killing machine wants an audience
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
09:59:23 UTC
18:59:23 KST

Breadcrumb
Nidal Hasan: America’s killing machine wants an audience
Donald Trump has cancelled the Pentagon’s plan to livestream Nidal Hasan’s execution after an outcry from Republicans and Democrats alike. Yet the former US Army psychiatrist, convicted of murdering 12 soldiers and a civilian at Fort Hood in 2009, is still scheduled to face a firing squad on 3 December. If it goes ahead, it will be the US military’s first execution since 1961.
The prospect of broadcasting the killing provoked a political backlash. The decision to kill him remains intact.
Under the current Trump administration, one might think we have seen it all, that hardly anything can shock us. Yet almost every day, the US rulers seem to raise the threshold of what the ‘civilised world’ can tolerate, commit to and advocate.
I did not see the proposed return to public executions coming. Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth wanted an audience for the military’s next killing; Trump has decided that the public will not be allowed to watch.
American killing machine
As an opponent of capital punishment, I see no crime that requires transforming an execution into entertainment potentially available to millions, including children. But the removal of a camera should not be mistaken for a retreat from state violence.
While the military is preparing to resume executions after a 65-year hiatus, we must remember that the wider American killing machine never went away in the first place.
Individual jurisdictions have abolished capital punishment or suspended its use, but the machinery remains operational. In 2024, 25 people were executed and 47 in 2025, according to the Death Penalty Information Centre.
Beyond execution chambers, the toll is far greater. According to Campaign Zero’s Mapping Police Violence project, US police killed at least 1,314 people in 2025, an average of 3.6 every day. Even that horrifying toll represented a 5% decline from 2024, the first annual decrease in six years.
Black people were still 2.6 times as likely as white people to be killed. These figures cover police killings in many different circumstances, rather than judicial executions. But they demolish any suggestion that lethal state violence had taken a holiday.
Then there are the deaths without execution warrants or guns. A 2023 study published in JAMA Internal Medicine associated poverty with approximately 183,000 US deaths in 2019. Another study, following people identified as homeless in the 2010 census, found that those under 65 faced 3.5 times the mortality risk of housed people after accounting for demographic and geographical differences. Researchers also estimated that more than two million deaths during the 2020 and 2021 pandemic years could have been avoided if US mortality rates had matched those in 21 other wealthy countries.
Poverty, inadequate housing and denial of healthcare are silent mass killers whose victims are unlikely to make headlines or front-page news. This is structural violence, with political responsibility resting on US elites, which is otherwise conveniently obscured.
America today
Political choices shape access to treatment, decent housing, safe work, and adequate food. The ruling US elites have repeatedly subordinated those needs to profit. By all accounts, today’s America is a social Darwinist experiment on steroids. The poor are poor because they deserve it. The sick die because they cannot afford treatment, so what?
The state must not intervene to provide protection because, God forbid, that would be socialism. The cruelty is routinely dressed up as individual responsibility and economic common sense.
Trump’s administration brings a more openly vindictive politics to this inheritance. Racism, misogyny, and xenophobia feed its vocabulary of hierarchy. Take, for example, Trump’s language about immigrants “poisoning the blood” of the country. Once people are represented as contamination, cruelty toward them becomes easier to sell as national renewal. Across the country, masked ICE agents are snatching foreigners, breaking up families, and shooting protesters in the name of the law.
Abroad, the same entitlement assumes imperial proportions. US forces seized Venezuela’s president, Nicolás Maduro, in January. Trump entertained taking Greenland by force before ruling out military action at Davos. The US and Israel launched another war against Iran in February. Kidnapping a foreign president, treating another people’s territory as an acquisition, and promising salvation through bombardment revive the prerogatives of nineteenth-century colonialism.
Hegseth, who proposed the latest live-streamed execution, gives this politics a crusading aesthetic. The civilian Pentagon chief bears a Jerusalem Cross and “Deus Vult” tattoos, and has promoted conservative Christianity inside the military. His church network is associated with a patriarchal Christian nationalism. Its prominent pastor, Doug Wilson, advocates postmillennialism, envisioning Christian rule before Christ’s return. This combination of religious supremacy and military power gives the execution proposal a particularly ominous setting.
Michel Foucault helps us understand the relationship between public punishment and less visible forms of coercion. In Discipline and Punish, he argues that public execution was a ritual through which the ruling authority reasserted itself. But the retreat of the scaffold did not make punishment humane.
Power changed its methods, working through prisons, institutions and everyday routines. Live-streaming Hasan’s execution would have created a power spectacle. Does the cancellation mean a return to rationality? Not necessarily. It leaves the coercive institutions and their authority in place.
Hegseth’s supporters have presented the execution as a warning to would-be killers. The argument for deterrence, however, lacks empirical support. Existing research cannot provide any conclusions on whether capital punishment increased, decreased, or had no effect on homicide.
American rulers preside over death through several different mechanisms: execution orders, armed policing, policies that leave millions vulnerable to preventable illness and poverty, and wars waged abroad. A society cannot claim to respect human life while treating so much death as acceptable, unavoidable or even exemplary.
The self-proclaimed enlightened world should be judged by the lives it protects and the power it restrains. Trump can cancel the livestream. The machinery behind it remains.
Hossam el-Hamalawy is an Egyptian scholar-activist in Germany, focusing on the military, policing, and labour.

Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi told Iran's semi-official Tasnim news agency on Sunday that Tehran is still reviewing "comments" from the U.S. on the Iranian proposal for a seven-day ceasefire that was first presented in September, but rejected by President Trump.
"If they comply with our conditions, the Strait of Hormuz will reopen on the sixth day, and negotiations will begin on the seventh day," Araghchi said, referring to the timeline proposed by Iran, which calls for the U.S. to lift its naval blockade on Iranian ports and to ease sanctions on the country, among other concessions.
"Our conditions are fair, and if the United States is willing to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, it can meet them within a few days," Araghchi said.

Around 1575, a Mughal artist painted a cheetah family on cloth during Akbar's reign; about 450 years later, the tiny work from Prince Sadruddin Aga Khan's collection sold for nearly Rs 120 crore in London
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-19
09:58:52 UTC
18:58:52 KST

Around 1575, a Mughal artist painted a cheetah family on cloth during Akbar's reign; about 450 years later, the tiny work from Prince Sadruddin Aga Khan's collection sold for nearly Rs 120 crore in London
Around 1575, a Mughal artist painted a cheetah family on cloth during Akbar's reign; about 450 years later, the tiny work from Prince Sadruddin Aga Khan's collection sold for nearly Rs 120 crore in London
A Family of Cheetahs in a Rocky Landscape, attributed to Basawan, Mughal India, circa 1575-80 (PC: ilgiornaledellarte)
Not all paintings in the world are being sold in crores. But there’s one particular painting titled A Family of Cheetahs in a Rocky Landscape that was sold for nearly Rs 120 crore in London. It created a stir in the world of painting and made headlines. This is the painting attributed to Basawan, one of the most prominent painters associated with Akbar’s court.Back in 1575–80, when Mughal emperor Akbar was building one of the most influential courts in Indian history, Basawan created an extraordinary painting of a family of cheetahs. The painting which was made nearly 450 years ago has survived and has seen several empires rise and fall. It witnessed the ever-changing artistic tastes and centuries of collecting.In October 2025, the painting made headlines when it was sold at Christie’s in London for £10.245 million (₹119 crore at the time).What’s so interesting about the painting
Different view of the same painting
If you look at the painting, it doesn’t look like a grand royal portrait. The painting’s beauty lies in its remarkably detailed study of animals in their natural surroundings.
Yet this intimate glimpse into the wildlife of Mughal India became one of the most valuable paintings of its kind ever sold at auction.According to Christie’s, the sale also set a world auction record for a Classical Indian or Islamic painting. What makes the story particularly fascinating is that the artwork’s importance extends far beyond its extraordinary price, offering a glimpse into the artistic imagination. It shows the royal interests of sixteenth-century India.The painting belongs to a flourishing period of Mughal art. Akbar was an artist who supported a flourishing royal workshop where Indian and Persian artistic traditions came together. Painters working under imperial patronage developed a distinctive style and created masterpieces worth remembering.Who was Basawan?Basawan was a leading artist from the Akbar period. His work is largely associated with innovation and expressive figures. The cheetah painting, dated to approximately 1575–80, is attributed to him rather than being definitively signed by the artist.What makes this painting unique is its subject. Rather than depicting any royal figure or a scene from a religious book, it focuses on animals in their natural habitat. The composition brings together art and observation.When art became a record
The young Akbar’s court at the age of 13 (PC:The Art Institute of Chicago)
The Mughal fascination with animals was not just decorative. Hunting, falconry and the keeping of exotic animals were part of courtly life. Akbar and other Mughal emperors maintained elaborate courts in which artists recorded people, events, landscapes, plants and animals. Under Akbar’s successor Jahangir, naturalistic painting became prominent, with artists producing remarkably detailed studies of birds and animals.Against this background, a family of cheetahs is an evocative subject. The painting does not simply use an animal as a symbol of royal power; it presents a glimpse of wildlife as a subject worthy of close artistic attention.From a royal-era painting to a private collectionThe artwork went on to become part of the personal collection of Prince Sadruddin Aga Khan and Princess Catherine Aga Khan. Prince Sadruddin Aga Khan (1933–2003) was a diplomat and philanthropist who served as the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees from 1965 to 1977. He was also a collector of unique artwork. The couple acquired much of their collection between the 1960s and the 1980s. Many of the paintings they selected were later studied and published by scholars. They were also put you display.The collection was displayed at Château de Bellerive, their home on the shores of Lake Geneva in Switzerland. The cheetah painting was among 95 works offered at Christie’s London auction on October 28, 2025.
How a painting estimated at ₹8 crore sold for nearly ₹120 croreBefore the auction, Christie’s estimated the cheetah painting at £700,000 to £1 million. Its eventual sale price of £10,245,000, including the buyer’s premium, was approximately 14 times more than its estimate.The result was also the highlight of the wider auction, which totalled £45.76 million, six times its pre-sale estimate. Every lot sold, with bidders registered across 20 countries and four continents, according to Christie’s.

An Austrian Airlines flight from Tel Aviv to Vienna made an emergency landing in Sofia after the crew reported a possible bomb threat.

“During the flight, near the border with Romania, the crew reported a sign of a bomb threat and extraordinarily decided to land in Sofia,” Bulgaria’s Ministry of Transport and Communications said.
A Bulgarian military fighter jet escorted the passenger plane to Sofia airport.
All 51 passengers and six crew members were evacuated after the landing.
Bulgarian authorities searched the aircraft and inspected the passengers and crew. The investigation found no danger, Austrian Airlines said Monday, according to Reuters.
The airline confirmed that a threat had been made against flight OS82, forcing it to divert to Bulgaria.
Passengers were to be rebooked on the fastest available alternative flight once the aircraft had been searched, the airline said.

Russian President Vladimir Putin has proposed meeting US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping next month to discuss the war in Ukraine, The Wall Street Journal reported.
Unnamed sources told the newspaper that Putin hopes to negotiate an end to the war on terms favorable to Russia.

During that call, the leaders agreed that Russia would supply millions of tons of diesel to the United States over the coming months.

“There is not yet any clear clarification regarding the meeting itself or its potential agenda,” Peskov said.

“I don’t know if it has been finally agreed, but the president has been clear. He wants the war between Ukraine and Russia to end,” Rubio said, according to Reuters.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has not been included in the proposed meeting. A summit about the war without Ukraine’s participation would be unprecedented, The Wall Street Journal reported.
Trump’s recent suspension of sanctions against Russia and criticism of Zelenskyy have caused concern in Ukraine and among European allies.

The Danish government wants employers to pay for Danish lessons for workers from countries outside the European Union before they arrive in Denmark.
Social Democratic finance spokesperson Kaare Dybvad Bek announced the proposal Monday during the Folketing’s debate on the government’s 2027 budget bill.
“It provides a saving of 100 million DKK, but first and foremost it sends a clear signal that people who come to the country to work must speak Danish,” he said.
Dybvad Bek said the issue concerned Denmark’s understanding of itself as a society.
More foreign workers have entered the restaurant and service industries in recent years, particularly in Copenhagen. This has led to more customers being served in English rather than Danish, he said.
During the debate, Dybvad Bek also argued that Danes risk losing practical skills when they rely on food delivery services such as Wolt and artificial intelligence for manageable tasks.
He also referred to planned restrictions affecting what he called “underpaid African agricultural workers.”
Dybvad Bek further criticized Nepalese and Iranian nationals who, he said, use Denmark’s education system to enter the labor market while avoiding other requirements.
Danish home sales fall 12 percent as higher rates slow market
Denmark’s housing market is showing signs of slowing after a strong start to 2026, according to transaction figures from property portal Boligsiden.
A total of 7,709 homes were sold in September, 12 percent fewer than in the same month last year.
Housing transactions during the first nine months of 2026 were three percent below the corresponding period in 2025.
Apartment sales have fallen most sharply. Eight percent fewer apartments have been sold nationwide this year, while Copenhagen has recorded a decline of 23 percent.
Brian Friis Helmer, personal finance economist at AL Sydbank, said rising mortgage rates could partly explain the slowdown.
Fixed-rate mortgages have recently fluctuated between four and five percent, compared with 3.5 percent at the beginning of the year.
Higher prices for gasoline, natural gas and electricity are also reducing the money households have available, he said.
However, strong employment and rising inflation-adjusted incomes continue to support the housing market.
Sales of houses and terraced homes are also below last year’s level. Holiday home sales, by contrast, have increased by 4.5 percent.
Boligsiden communications director Birgit Daetz said the increase indicates that many households remain financially secure because holiday homes are traditionally purchased during periods of economic strength.
Rising property values and the possibility of rental income may also make such purchases more affordable, she said.
Copenhagen mayor disputes Frederiksen’s claims about meat in nursing homes
Copenhagen Lord Mayor Sisse Marie Welling of the Socialist People’s Party has accused Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen of presenting an inaccurate picture of food policies in the city’s nursing homes.
Frederiksen wrote on Instagram that a Copenhagen proposal could prevent nursing home residents from receiving the meat they want.
“It is a lack of respect for the elderly person’s right to make decisions for themselves,” Frederiksen wrote. “Those people in nursing homes who have toiled and slaved for our country must of course be allowed to eat meat.”
Welling rejected the claim.
“The elderly must naturally have the food they know and like. For many of them, that involves meat,” she wrote.
Welling said individual nursing homes can decide how to plan menus and how much meat to serve. She said residents’ nutritional needs should take priority over climate concerns.
The dispute follows debate over Copenhagen’s food and meal strategy, which aims to make municipal meals more sustainable and reduce purchases of beef.
A consultancy analysis reported that some nursing homes had rejected residents’ birthday requests for beef because of carbon reduction targets.
The study surveyed 200 nursing home residents and 607 people receiving meals at home.
Between 58 and 60 percent were satisfied with the food, while 8 to 13 percent reported little or no satisfaction.
Several nursing home residents criticized meat quality and said beef rarely appeared on menus. The analysis also found that residents wanted greater influence over their meals.
More than half of surveyed Danish teachers feel stressed every week
More than half of teachers in a new union survey said they experience stress daily or weekly, with most attributing it to their working conditions.
The survey by Danmarks Lærerforening, the Danish Union of Teachers, included responses from 1,901 public school teachers and kindergarten class leaders.
Sixteen percent said they felt stressed at work every day, while 36 percent experienced stress weekly and 23 percent monthly.
Nine in 10 of those experiencing stress said workplace conditions were responsible.
“We are facing a working environment problem in the public schools, while at the same time many teachers choose to leave,” union chair Gordon Ørskov Madsen said.
More than one in three respondents said they had taken sick leave from teaching because of stress.
Teachers identified classroom disruption, insufficient preparation time, heavy workloads and difficulty obtaining help for pupils with special needs as major pressures.
Some also reported that parents expected them to resolve conflicts between pupils that occurred outside school.
Nana Vaaben, an associate professor at University College Copenhagen, said teachers can experience moral stress when they know pupils need help but lack the authority to provide it.
Respondents identified fewer teaching hours, more preparation time and better support for pupils with special needs as the measures most likely to reduce stress.
The union plans to raise those proposals in upcoming negotiations with the government and other labor market parties.

Denmark and Vietnam will establish a strategic partnership during Vietnamese President Tô Lâm’s state visit to Denmark this week.
Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen of the Social Democrats and Lâm are expected to formally enter into the agreement Tuesday, the Prime Minister’s Office said.

Independent authority to investigate police strikes against photographers
The Independent Police Complaints Authority will investigate reports that police officers struck two press photographers with batons during demonstrations in Copenhagen on Saturday.
The photographers worked for Danish newspapers Politiken and Ekstra Bladet and were involved in separate incidents during demonstrations for and against remigration.
Copenhagen Police referred the cases to the independent authority, known as DUP, following criticism from both newspapers.
“The Copenhagen Police in no way wish to place obstacles in the way of the press carrying out their work,” police said.
Politiken reported that its photographer was struck several times, had his camera smashed and received treatment at an emergency room.
Ekstra Bladet’s photographer said he was struck on the arm with a baton despite carrying cameras and visible press credentials.

Ekstra Bladet editor-in-chief Knud Brix also called the reported incident “completely unacceptable.”
The Danish Union of Press Photographers and the Danish Union of Journalists have requested a meeting with the national police commissioner.
They want police leadership to explain how similar incidents will be prevented and how journalists will be protected while covering demonstrations.
Delayed UN climate reports could weaken action before COP33, Danish expert warns
Global climate efforts could face serious setbacks if the UN climate panel does not publish its next assessment reports before the COP33 summit in 2028, a Danish climate expert has warned.
“Without the reports, countries will stand on a basis that is less comprehensive. They will lack crucial knowledge,” said Adrian Lema, head of the National Centre for Climate Research at the Danish Meteorological Institute.
He said countries could spend time debating scientific facts instead of agreeing on action.
“The consequence may be that we set climate action back years, and that uncertainty is created about some of the progress we have achieved,” Lema said.
COP33 will include the next major review of countries’ progress under the 2015 Paris Agreement.
A weeklong meeting of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, known as the IPCC, ended Friday without agreement on a budget or timetable for the reports.
Lema attended as Denmark’s lead negotiator and wanted the reports published well before COP33.
Saudi Arabia, Russia, Iran, India and China argued that publication before the summit was unnecessary, he said.
IPCC decisions require consensus rather than majority votes.
Lema said an agreement remained possible but had become more difficult.
“If we can get enough countries to say it loud and clear, then the few who disagree will be under a different pressure,” he said.
Copenhagen begins separate collection of used diapers for recycling
The City of Copenhagen began installing separate waste bins for used diapers in residential courtyards and municipal day-care centers Monday.
Diapers previously had to be placed with residual waste and were incinerated. They will now be processed at Denmark’s first diaper treatment facility.
“There is a major climate benefit in recycling the diapers instead of incinerating them,” Climate, Environment and Technology Mayor Line Barfod of the Red-Green Alliance said.
The city estimates that between 85 and 94 percent of diaper waste, including liquids and feces, can be converted into new materials.
Cellulose and the contents of the diapers will become biofiber used to produce biogas, electricity and district heating.
Plastic components can be recycled into products such as car interiors. Superabsorbent polymers can become binding material for the construction industry.
Collection will expand to municipal nursing homes, senior housing and other city institutions in February 2027.
Residents of detached houses and members of allotment garden associations will also be able to join the program next year. The scheme is expected to be fully implemented in 2029.
The bins will accept diapers for children and adults, incontinence pads, paper-based cloths and wet wipes without plastic or bamboo. Menstrual hygiene products are excluded.
Diaper waste must be placed in an ordinary plastic trash bag sealed with a tight knot.
Study finds misogynistic TikTok content can appear within minutes
Young male TikTok users can encounter misogynistic content within minutes, even when they do not actively search for it, according to a Danish study.
Researchers from the Center for Digital Pedagogy and Analyse & Tal created eight fictional profiles representing men ages 16 to 19 interested in fitness, dating, investing and gaming.
After the profiles interacted with videos about those subjects, researchers allowed them to scroll automatically for one hour.
Content associated with the “manosphere” appeared after an average of three minutes. In one case, it appeared after 21 seconds.
The manosphere refers to online communities and content that degrade women or support restricting their rights and opportunities.
Researchers also examined one year of viewing data provided by 29 men ages 15 to 22. They identified an average of five to six manosphere videos in each participant’s weekly feed.
The researchers said this was a minimum estimate but emphasized that the 29 participants were not representative of all young men.
Employment and Equality Minister Ane Halsboe-Jørgensen of the Social Democrats called for stronger social media regulation and more discussion in schools and homes.
TikTok said it takes the findings seriously.
“We proactively remove 98.1 percent of the videos that violate our rules on hate and hateful behavior,” Nordic communications director Lukasz Lindell said.
TikTok said it was also working to diversify recommendations and interrupt repetitive content patterns.

Regional trains suspended between Odense and Fredericia after cable damage
Regional train services between Odense and Fredericia have been suspended until at least 2 p.m. Monday because of a severed cable.
DSB, Denmark’s national rail operator, has ordered rail replacement buses and updated its journey planner.
InterCity and express trains continue to operate on the route, although passengers may experience longer travel times.
“In Odense and Fredericia, there are staff in orange vests who can assist with guidance,” DSB said.
Banedanmark, the state agency responsible for Denmark’s railway infrastructure, is working to repair the damaged cable.
Train services on the route were expected to return to full capacity Monday after several days of disruptions. The cable damage means that this is no longer possible.
Passengers have experienced longer journeys and fewer trains between the two cities since a fire damaged a relay hut near Aarup in western Funen on October 9.
The hut contained electronic equipment used by the railway’s signaling system. The fire caused signal failures between Middelfart and Odense, disrupting services on Funen and across Denmark.
Even after more trains return, services will continue at reduced speeds near Aarup Station, where trains will temporarily be unable to stop.
Sunny Monday to give way to rainy and windy week in Denmark
Denmark can expect sunshine Monday before rain and stronger winds arrive during the rest of the week.
“On Monday, we have a beautiful autumn day in store,” Danish Meteorological Institute meteorologist Marie Timm said. “There will be some high-altitude clouds in the sky, but otherwise it is a beautiful day where there will be sun for everyone.”
After overnight temperatures fell close to freezing in some areas, daytime temperatures will rise to between 9 and 13 degrees Celsius.
Winds will generally be light to moderate, although coastal areas could experience fresher conditions.
Tuesday will begin dry with some sunshine before clouds and rain move across Denmark from the southeast.
The islands will receive rain during the morning and early afternoon, while northern Jutland will be affected later.
Timm said the amount of rain and strength of the wind remained uncertain because forecasts continued to change.
Another weather front will bring rain from the west Wednesday, with only brief dry periods expected.
Widespread rain is also forecast Thursday, followed by stronger southerly winds and further rain Friday.
Daytime temperatures from Tuesday through Friday will range from 8 to 13 degrees, while nighttime temperatures will remain between 5 and 10 degrees.
Timm advised people to bring rainwear rather than umbrellas because of the expected wind.
One in three Danish teachers reports verbal abuse from pupils
One in three Danish public school teachers experienced rude or abusive language from pupils during the previous week, according to a new survey.
Four in 10 teachers said such incidents occurred daily or several times a week, education trade publication Folkeskolen reported.
The survey was completed by 1,901 teachers and kindergarten class leaders between August 26 and September 14, 2026.
Teachers reported comments including “You fucking bad teacher,” “You are a damn idiot” and “You don’t boss me around.”
Lars Peter Sønderbo Andersen, a senior researcher in occupational and environmental medicine at Regional Hospital Gødstrup, said the language damages teachers’ working environment and undermines their authority in classrooms.
He said the problem has worsened in recent years.
In a similar survey conducted almost 10 years ago, one in four teachers reported being called derogatory terms such as “bitch,” “idiot” or “whore” at least once a month.
Danmarks Lærerforening, the Danish Union of Teachers, described the new findings as concerning.
“Some of these statements are quite severe, and we can hear from the inquiries we receive that it affects the teachers when they are spoken to like that,” union representative Thomas Andreasen said.
He called for schools to establish clear, shared rules for acceptable language. He also said having more permanent teachers in classrooms could help.
Denmark contacts more than 25 countries seeking prison spaces
Denmark has contacted more than 25 European countries about potentially renting prison spaces as its correctional system faces record overcrowding.
“The Danish Prison and Probation Service is in a serious situation,” Justice Minister Nicolai Wammen of the Social Democrats said. “We must do everything we can to resolve the capacity challenges in Danish prisons.”
Denmark already has an agreement to rent 300 prison spaces in Kosovo for foreign nationals sentenced to deportation. However, delays mean the renovated prison is not expected to begin accepting inmates until late 2027 or early 2028.
The original plan expected inmates to begin serving sentences there in early 2023.
Wammen called the Kosovo agreement important but said additional measures were needed to relieve Denmark’s prisons.
The Justice Ministry declined to identify the countries it contacted or disclose the correspondence. It said publication could risk damaging Denmark’s foreign policy interests.
Estonia’s Justice Ministry confirmed that Denmark had not entered discussions with it. Estonia is concentrating on an existing agreement under which it began receiving inmates from Sweden in 2026.
At the end of September, Denmark had about 4,650 inmates but only 4,300 prison spaces, according to the Prison Officers’ Union.
The union calculated the average occupancy rate at 105.4 percent, the highest recorded level. It stood at 102.7 percent in 2025.

Eight people were arrested Saturday in connection with a demonstration organized by the movement Det Danske Folk in central Copenhagen.

Electricity’s share of Danish energy use rises to 23.4 percent
Electricity accounted for 23.4 percent of Denmark’s total energy consumption in 2025, an increase of 1.5 percentage points from the previous year.
Green Power Denmark, an industry organization representing the Danish energy sector, said the increase was driven mainly by electric vehicles and the district heating sector’s use of electric boilers and heat pumps.
The organization said growing electrification is gradually reducing Denmark’s reliance on oil and natural gas.
“We are freeing ourselves from what is happening in the Middle East and American politics,” Green Power Denmark chief executive Kristian Jensen said.
He said Danish energy prices remain affected by developments abroad because the country still relies on prices set by global markets.
Denmark’s electrification rate rose by only 3.8 percentage points in total from 2016 through 2024, making the 1.5-point increase in 2025 significant.
Green Power Denmark wants electricity to account for 60 percent of total energy consumption by 2035.
Jensen said achieving that target would require industrial companies to replace natural gas with electricity and heat pumps.
He pointed to iron foundries and food producers, including dairy group Arla, as examples of industries already using heat pumps.
Such changes could reduce companies’ carbon dioxide emissions and energy costs while improving their competitiveness, Jensen said.
Figures for Denmark’s electrification rate in 2026 are not yet available.
The 21-year-old singer has gone from posting piano videos on TikTok to becoming one of Denmark’s biggest pop stars. On Friday, she received the top prize at DR’s annual P3 Guld music awards.
Danish singer Annika has won P3 Prisen, the main award at one of Denmark’s most prominent annual music events, P3 Guld.
The 21-year-old received the award Friday evening at DR Koncerthuset in Copenhagen, a year after being nominated for the same prize but losing out to Danish band Aphaca.
P3 Guld is the annual music awards show organised by P3, the youth-oriented music and entertainment radio station run by Danish public broadcaster DR.
The event celebrates artists who have made a significant impact on Danish music over the past year, with P3 Prisen regarded as its main award.
Annika, whose full name is Annika Wedderkopp, was selected by a P3 jury ahead of fellow nominees Zar Paulo and producer Anton Westerlin, who is also her boyfriend.
“With an authentic foundation in her own life, Annika creates massive hits about breakups and infatuations, about doubt and a steely belief that everything will naturally work out,” the jury said.
From TikTok to the Danish charts
Annika’s rise has been rapid.
She began by posting videos of herself singing at the piano on TikTok before breaking through with “Knuser hjerter” in 2024.
She followed it with several successful releases, including “Så længe jeg er sexy”, and won P3 Talentet, the event’s talent award, that same year.
Last year, she released her debut album “AW”, which includes “Stolt”, a collaboration with Danish rapper Lamin. She also opened Roskilde Festival’s Orange Stage, the festival’s largest and most prestigious stage.
Previous recipients of P3 Prisen include some of Denmark’s best-known contemporary artists, including The Minds of 99, Tobias Rahim, Artigeardit, Lamin, Tina Dickow and Jada.
Other winners
Several other awards were presented at Friday’s ceremony.
Guldimund and Saveus won P3 Lytterhittet – the listeners’ choice award – for their song “Vil du noget?”.
Zar Paulo received P3 Live, an award recognising an artist who has distinguished themselves on Denmark’s live music scene. The award returned this year after previously being presented in 2001 and 2009.
Danish-Faroese artist Friða Saiya won P3’s Næste, a new award that has replaced P3 Talentet and highlights emerging artists.
Criticism over lack of women
This year’s P3 Guld also faced criticism before the ceremony over the gender balance among its performers.
Twelve men and two women were scheduled to perform during the evening.
Ditte Christiane Jensen, head of editorial at DR Ung, defended the lineup in a written response to Ritzau.
“Talent, creativity and artistic quality are not about gender,” she said.

Trump: Greenland deal biggest real estate deal ever
The US president says he “got it for nothing” after signing a new defence agreement with Denmark and Greenland that expands the American military presence on the island.
US President Donald Trump has described a new defence and security agreement with Denmark and Greenland as potentially “the biggest real estate deal that has ever been made”.
Speaking at a Republican campaign rally in Dalton, Georgia, Trump portrayed the agreement as a major achievement for the United States.
“What do you think of the deal I made on Greenland? Got it for nothing,” Trump told supporters.
“It is probably the biggest real estate deal that has ever been made.”
Trump was campaigning ahead of the US midterm elections on November 3.
His comments come after months of tension over Greenland, an autonomous territory within the Kingdom of Denmark. Trump has repeatedly said that the United States wants control and ownership of Greenland, arguing that the island is crucial to American national security.
Two new US military bases
The United States, Denmark and Greenland signed a new security and defence agreement on Greenland at the end of September following lengthy negotiations.
The agreement was signed at the United Nations in New York shortly after Trump addressed the UN General Assembly.
It allows the United States to establish two additional military bases in Greenland.
The US currently operates Pituffik Space Base in northwestern Greenland, which plays an important role in missile warning, space surveillance and Arctic security.
The new agreement also opens the possibility of deploying parts of the planned US Golden Dome missile defence system in Greenland. The system is intended to protect the United States against threats including missiles and drones.
Despite Trump’s description of the agreement as a “real estate deal”, it does not transfer ownership of Greenland to the United States.
Trump’s comments came as Republicans campaign to retain control of Congress in the November midterm elections. Democrats are currently polling more strongly in the race for the House of Representatives, while control of the Senate remains more uncertain.
Republicans currently hold majorities in both chambers.

Denmark’s shift from fossil fuels to electricity is accelerating
Electric cars, heat pumps and electric boilers are driving a sharp increase in the share of Denmark’s energy consumption covered by electricity.
Denmark is becoming increasingly electrified as electric cars, heat pumps and electric boilers replace fossil fuels.
Electricity accounted for 23.4 percent of Denmark’s total energy consumption in 2025, according to figures highlighted by industry organisation Green Power Denmark.
That was an increase of 1.5 percentage points in just one year.
The increase is significant. Between 2016 and 2024, the share of electricity in Denmark’s total energy consumption rose by only 3.8 percentage points.
The acceleration is being driven particularly by the growing number of electric cars and by district heating companies investing in electric boilers and heat pumps.
Kristian Jensen, CEO of Green Power Denmark, says the development will gradually make Denmark less dependent on imported oil and natural gas – and therefore less exposed to international energy prices and geopolitical developments.
“We are freeing ourselves from what is going on in the Middle East and American politics,” Jensen told Ritzau.
“When Danes experience that gasoline, diesel and electricity have become more expensive than they were a year ago, it is because we are still dependent on the price set in the rest of the world.”
Target: 60 percent by 2035
Green Power Denmark wants electricity to account for 60 percent of Denmark’s total energy consumption by 2035.
Reaching that level will require a much faster transition in Danish industry, according to Jensen.
He points to heat pumps as one of the technologies that can help companies replace natural gas with electricity. Iron foundries and food producers, including dairy group Arla, have already demonstrated that large heat pumps can be used in industrial production.
Jensen argues that other companies should follow their example.
“It will not only reduce the companies’ CO2 emissions, it will also reduce energy expenses and thereby improve their competitiveness,” he said.
Figures for Denmark’s electrification rate in 2026 are not yet available, but Green Power Denmark expects the shift towards electricity to continue.

Denmark’s oldest-ever person was a member of the Danish Nazi party
Records show that 112-year-old Kirsten Schwalbe joined Denmark’s Nazi party during the German occupation. She says she did so at her husband’s request and did not sympathise with Nazism.
Kirsten Schwalbe, who this week became the longest-living Dane in recorded history, was a member of Denmark’s Nazi party during the German occupation.
The 112-year-old joined the National Socialist Workers’ Party of Denmark (DNSAP) in August 1941, according to Kristeligt Dagblad.
Her name appears in the Bovrup registry, a record of people who were members of DNSAP. Two historians have independently confirmed to the newspaper that the entry matches Schwalbe’s date of birth and address, although her surname is misspelled as “Schalbe”.
Schwalbe has confirmed that both she and her former husband were members of the party, but says she only joined because her husband urged her to do so.
She rejected the suggestion that she had sided with Nazi Germany.
“Not at all. I barely knew what it was, because I have never taken an interest in politics,” she told TV Midtvest when asked whether she had sympathised with the Nazis.
Schwalbe said she found it unfair that she should have to “pay for it” more than 70 years later, adding that “back then, wives didn’t look into such things”.
Membership does not show level of involvement
DNSAP was founded in 1930 and was strongly inspired by Adolf Hitler’s German Nazi Party, the NSDAP.
But Charlie Krautwald, a historian at the University of Copenhagen, cautioned against drawing conclusions about Schwalbe’s level of involvement from the registry alone.
The record shows that a person joined the party, he told Kristeligt Dagblad, but not why they joined, how long they remained a member or whether they paid membership fees.
A person could therefore appear in the registry without having been active in the party.
TV Midtvest has followed Schwalbe for several years and manages an Instagram account about her life. Two of the broadcaster’s employees have also recently published a book about her.
Her membership of DNSAP had not previously been mentioned. TV Midtvest editor-in-chief Marc Killigren Akselsen told Kristeligt Dagblad that the broadcaster had not known about it.
Schwalbe, who lives in Struer in western Jutland, became the longest-living Dane on record on Wednesday, when she reached the age of 112 years and 218 days.
